drills.q: Walk through the attention formula term by term.
drills.a: softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V: Q,K are linear projections of the input; QK^T scores query-key similarity; dividing by sqrt(d_k) controls variance so softmax doesn't saturate; softmax turns each row into a probability distribution over positions; multiplying by V produces a weighted average of value vectors.

drills.q: Derive why the scaling factor is sqrt(d_k) and not d_k.
drills.a: Dot product of d_k iid mean-0 unit-variance components has variance d_k (sum of d_k independent unit-variance products), so std dev grows as sqrt(d_k). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance regardless of d_k. Dividing by d_k over-shrinks variance below 1, pushing softmax toward uniform and destroying its ability to sharply prefer one key.

drills.q: What is the time and memory cost of naive self-attention, and which one actually limits you in practice?
drills.a: O(n^2*d_k) time, O(n^2) memory per head since QK^T is n x n. Memory is the practical limiter -- at n=8192 fp16 one head's score matrix alone is ~128MB, making naive attention infeasible at long context regardless of available compute.

drills.q: Compute the KV-cache reduction factor for Llama-family 70B (64 query heads, 8 KV heads via GQA) versus a hypothetical full-MHA config, and explain why pure MQA is rarely the right default.
drills.a: 8x reduction (h/g = 64/8). Pure MQA (1 shared KV head) would give a further 8x beyond that (64x vs MHA total) but measurably degrades summarization and long-context retrieval quality, since collapsing to one shared KV head removes representational diversity; GQA with a small group count recovers most of MHA's quality at most of the memory saving.

drills.q: Do the KV-cache arithmetic for a 70B model, 80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16, at 128k context, and explain the serving implication.
drills.a: 2*80*8*128*2 = 327,680 bytes/token = 0.32MB/token; at 128,000 tokens that's ~42GB for a SINGLE sequence -- larger than many GPUs' total VRAM. This means long-context serving is fundamentally a batching/admission-control problem, not just a bigger-GPU problem.

drills.q: Explain mechanically how MLA differs from GQA, and why the K up-projection can be folded into the query projection with no extra decode cost.
drills.a: MLA compresses K and V into a shared low-rank latent via a learned down-projection, caching only the latent and reconstructing per-head K/V via up-projection at attention time. Because both projections are linear, the K up-projection composes algebraically with the query projection, so it can be pre-merged into the query weights -- decode-time compute doesn't pay extra for reconstructing full-size K.

drills.q: A colleague claims FlashAttention is an approximation because it uses tiling. Correct them and explain why it's actually faster.
drills.a: Tiling changes memory access order, not the math -- FlashAttention computes the identical softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V via block processing and a running (online) softmax that rescales incrementally, which is algebraically exact. It's faster because the real bottleneck was HBM bandwidth (writing/reading the full n x n matrix), not FLOPs; keeping tiles in on-chip SRAM and only writing the final output cuts memory traffic dramatically even though FLOP count is essentially unchanged.

drills.q: Why does FlashAttention-3's speedup depend specifically on H100/Hopper hardware rather than being a pure algorithmic improvement portable to A100?
drills.a: FA3 exploits warp-specialized producer/consumer pipelining that overlaps Tensor Core matmuls with the asynchronous TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator), plus FP8 support with incoherent processing -- both are Hopper-generation hardware features absent on Ampere (A100). On A100 you'd fall back toward FA2-level gains, which come mainly from the shared tiling/IO-awareness idea rather than Hopper-specific async tricks.

drills.q: You're pretraining a new 30B model targeting 128k context on a fixed GPU memory budget. How do you approach the KV-head/latent design decision?
drills.a: Work backward from the KV-cache budget: decide max concurrent long-context sequences needed, compute bytes/token available after weights+activations, then choose n_kv_heads (GQA group count) or MLA latent rank to hit that number. Validate against long-context retrieval evals during architecture search, since an overly aggressive compression choice can't be cheaply fixed after pretraining -- it requires another training run, not a config change.

drills.q: A user reports the model "forgets" information from early in a very long conversation. Is this necessarily an attention-mechanism problem?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- full attention still computes exact scores over the whole context. More likely causes: the conversation exceeded the context window and got truncated, positional encoding degrading beyond trained lengths (a RoPE/ALiBi extrapolation issue), or serving-layer KV-cache eviction/quantization dropping those tokens' state. Diagnose by checking whether tokens are still in-window and whether the serving stack does any cache eviction before blaming attention itself.

drills.q: Why are prefill and decode described as having opposite bottlenecks?
drills.a: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in one parallel pass, reusing each weight load across many positions -- high arithmetic intensity, compute-bound. Decode processes one token per step but reads the same weight matrices plus the whole accumulated KV cache for just that one position -- arithmetic intensity falls ~5x, making it memory-bandwidth-bound.

drills.q: Derive the KV-cache bytes/token formula and compute it for a 70B model (80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16).
drills.a: 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_element = 2*80*8*128*2 = 327,680 bytes/token ~ 0.32MB/token.

drills.q: What problem does PagedAttention solve and what's the mechanism?
drills.a: Fragmentation from contiguous per-request KV-cache allocations sized for worst-case length (60-80% waste). PagedAttention partitions the cache into fixed-size blocks with a per-sequence block table (logical->physical mapping), allocating on demand and freeing immediately on completion -- waste drops under 4%.

drills.q: Explain continuous batching and why static batching underperforms, and why continuous batching depends on PagedAttention-style memory management.
drills.a: Static batching idles finished slots until the whole batch's longest sequence completes. Continuous batching evicts/admits sequences every decode iteration, keeping utilization high. It depends on block-based (paged) allocation because adding/removing a sequence's blocks independently of every other sequence's layout would require expensive memory shuffling under naive contiguous allocation.

drills.q: What is chunked prefill, what problem does it fix, and what's the cost of making the chunk size very small?
drills.a: Splits a long prompt's prefill into fixed chunks (vLLM default 2,048 tokens) interleaved with other sequences' decode steps, fixing head-of-line blocking where one long prefill would otherwise stall everyone else's TPOT. Making chunks very small raises the long-prompt request's own TTFT (more scheduling iterations to fully ingest) and adds per-chunk scheduling overhead -- it's a tradeoff, not a free fix.

drills.q: Compare vLLM's prefix caching to SGLang's RadixAttention, and explain when vLLM's simpler approach is actually preferable.
drills.a: vLLM hashes fixed-size blocks by content and reuses exact hash matches. RadixAttention organizes the whole KV-cache pool as a radix tree, automatically discovering shared prefixes across any requests. vLLM's simpler approach is preferable on workloads with little cross-request prefix structure, where radix-tree bookkeeping overhead buys nothing.

drills.q: Define TTFT and TPOT, and explain how increasing batch size affects each plus throughput -- is there a batch size that minimizes all three?
drills.a: TTFT: queueing + prefill time, scales with prompt length/load. TPOT: memory-bandwidth-bound decode step time, scales with total KV cache read per step. Bigger batch raises throughput (better weight-load amortization) but raises TPOT (more cache read per step, more contention) and can raise TTFT for new arrivals. No single batch size minimizes all three -- it's a genuine three-way tradeoff surface; you pick the point matching your SLO.

drills.q: Your KV-cache pool fills up under load. What are your options and what does each cost?
drills.a: Reject/queue new requests (safest, adds latency for that request), preempt a running low-priority sequence (wastes compute, spikes its latency), offload cold blocks to CPU/object storage (costs fetch latency if reused), or reduce max batch/context admitted (costs throughput/capability). Real systems combine admission control with offloading rather than relying on one mechanism; naive LRU-by-recency eviction can starve high-priority requests behind a burst of low-priority ones.

drills.q: Do the cost-model arithmetic: $2.50/hr GPU, 5,000 tokens/sec aggregate throughput -- compute $/million tokens, and explain whether a bigger batch always lowers this.
drills.a: 2.50 / (5,000*3,600) * 1,000,000 ~= $0.14 per million tokens. Not always -- only up to the memory-bandwidth or KV-cache-capacity ceiling; past that, added concurrency causes preemption/queueing that can raise effective cost via wasted recomputation, and it always raises TPOT, so the cost-minimizing batch size and the latency-SLO-respecting batch size are frequently different numbers.

drills.q: Design the serving strategy for a RAG chat product: short-to-medium prompts, heavily shared system prompt/retrieved-context boilerplate, tight latency SLO.
drills.a: Prioritize prefix caching or a radix-tree-native engine (heavy prefix reuse from shared system prompt/retrieval wrapper). Use continuous batching with a moderate batch size chosen from the TPOT SLO, not maximized for throughput. Enable chunked prefill with a modest chunk size to protect TPOT when a long-context request arrives. Size the KV-cache pool from measured p99 concurrent-sequence count times typical context length, with admission control (reject/queue, not silent preemption), and monitor TTFT/TPOT/queue depth separately rather than end-to-end latency alone.

drills.q: Why chunk documents at all instead of embedding whole documents?
drills.a: Embedding models compress a fixed-size input into a fixed-size vector; a whole long document averaged into one vector loses specific detail, so localized queries score poorly against it. Chunking keeps vectors focused enough for similarity search to localize the right passage.

drills.q: What does overlap between chunks cost you, in storage terms?
drills.a: Storage/embedding compute scales with chunk_size / (chunk_size - overlap); 20% overlap means roughly 25% more chunks than no overlap for the same document.

drills.q: Explain contextual retrieval and why it's affordable at scale.
drills.a: Prepend a short LLM-generated context sentence to each chunk before embedding/BM25 indexing, restoring the anchor lost when a chunk is decontextualized. Affordable because prompt caching lets the whole document be cached once and referenced, not re-sent, per chunk -- about $1.02/million document tokens.

drills.q: How does late chunking differ mechanically from contextual retrieval, and what does it require?
drills.a: Late chunking embeds the whole document first with a long-context model, then mean-pools token embeddings per chunk span -- no LLM call. It requires an embedding model with a long enough context window to see the whole document (e.g. ~8k tokens), unlike contextual retrieval which works with any embedding model but needs an LLM call per chunk.

drills.q: A recall@20 eval looks great but production users complain retrieval misses obvious answers. What's the likely cause and fix?
drills.a: Likely a distribution mismatch -- the eval set was built from documents shorter or differently structured than production documents, so a fixed chunk_size tuned to the eval didn't generalize. Rebuild the eval from real production documents/queries; prefer structural (heading/section) chunking over a fixed length.

drills.q: How does chunk size interact with reranker cost?
drills.a: Rerankers score every candidate chunk, so cost/latency scale roughly linearly with the number of chunks reranked, not their size. Smaller chunk sizes mean more chunks per document at a given retrieval depth, directly increasing reranker load.

drills.q: Design a chunking strategy for legal contracts with embedded financial tables and heavy cross-references ("as defined in Section 4.2").
drills.a: Parse with a layout-aware tool (Unstructured/LlamaParse) so tables extract as structured Markdown. Chunk by section/clause boundary, not fixed length. Apply contextual retrieval to resolve cross-references (this is exactly the decontextualization failure it fixes). Keep small tables whole with repeated headers if spanning chunks. Validate against a recall@k eval built from real contract questions; expect ~800-1000 token chunks given legal prose density.

drills.q: A candidate claims "I always use the smallest possible chunk size for maximum precision." What's wrong with this?
drills.a: Below a certain size, chunks lose surrounding context needed to be independently interpretable (decontextualization), multiply index storage and reranker load, and increase near-duplicate competition for top-k slots from overlapping tiny chunks. There is no universal "maximum precision" size -- it's a corpus-dependent tradeoff surface requiring an eval-driven process.

drills.q: Explain BM25's k1 and b parameters and why the defaults are what they are.
drills.a: k1 (default 1.2) caps how much repeated query-term occurrences inflate the score (saturation). b (default 0.75) penalizes term matches in longer documents relative to shorter ones (length normalization). Both defaults, from Lucene/Elasticsearch, work well across most corpora without tuning.

drills.q: Why does dense retrieval fail on exact-match queries, mechanically?
drills.a: Embedding models compress text into a fixed-size vector optimized for broad semantic similarity; rare, low-frequency tokens (error codes, IDs) get weakly differentiated representations since the model saw few training examples anchoring their exact meaning, so the specific literal string gets blurred into the surrounding semantic neighborhood.

drills.q: Derive Reciprocal Rank Fusion and explain why k=60 is used.
drills.a: RRF_score(d) = sum over retrievers of 1/(k+rank). k=60 isn't theoretically derived -- it's the empirical constant Cormack et al. found worked well on TREC data in 2009, and k in [40,80] performs comparably across benchmarks, which is why most systems just default to 60.

drills.q: Why does rank fusion beat naive score fusion?
drills.a: BM25 and dense retriever scores live on incompatible, uncalibrated scales (unbounded corpus-dependent BM25 vs bounded cosine similarity). Averaging raw scores lets whichever retriever has larger magnitude dominate regardless of actual relevance. RRF discards scores entirely and uses only rank position, which is comparable by construction.

drills.q: What is ColBERT's storage cost for 1 million documents and why?
drills.a: Roughly 102 GB uncompressed (200 tokens/doc x 128 dims x 4 bytes), about 34x a 768-dim bi-encoder's ~3 GB, because storage scales with total token count, not document count. ColBERTv2's residual/2-bit compression brings it to ~6 GB.

drills.q: A production hybrid search system performs worse than BM25 alone after adding a dense leg. Diagnose it.
drills.a: Likely the embedding model is a poor domain fit (generic model on jargon-heavy corpus), producing noisy dense rankings that drag down fusion in both RRF and weighted fusion. Verify by running the dense leg alone against eval; fine-tune/replace the embedding model or reduce its fusion weight rather than removing it entirely.

drills.q: Design the retrieval stage for a technical support search product mixing natural-language questions and exact error-code queries.
drills.a: Hybrid retrieval is close to mandatory: BM25 handles exact error codes (rare tokens, strong IDF, zero ambiguity), dense handles paraphrase-heavy natural language. Fuse with RRF given incompatible score scales and a corpus updated often enough to invalidate a tuned weighted-fusion alpha. Add a lightweight cross-encoder rerank over the fused top-20. Validate against separate eval slices for the two query types since a blended metric can hide a regression in one type.

drills.q: Does adding a reranker mean you no longer need hybrid retrieval? Why is this a trap question?
drills.a: No -- a reranker only reorders candidates stage-1 retrieval already surfaced. If the relevant document never made it into that candidate set (exactly what hybrid retrieval exists to prevent), no reranker can recover it. Retrieval fixes recall, reranking fixes precision; neither substitutes for the other.

drills.q: Given a 2-second end-to-end latency target, build a budget across embedding, ANN search, reranking, and generation.
drills.a: A defensible split: ~75ms embedding, ~100ms ANN retrieval, ~250ms rerank (over ~top-100), ~75ms buffer, leaving ~1500ms (~75%) for generation, which dominates because it's the least compressible stage without changing the model or output length.

drills.q: Why does generation dominate the latency budget, and what levers actually exist to control it?
drills.a: Driven by output token count and model size, mostly outside retrieval's control. Levers: smaller/faster model where quality allows, capping/guiding output length, and streaming the first token to hide total latency from perceived UX (though total time-to-completion is unchanged).

drills.q: Explain the cascade retrieval pattern and why it's structured cheap-wide then expensive-narrow.
drills.a: Stage 1 (hybrid ANN, top 50-150) optimizes recall cheaply since ANN cost is roughly flat regardless of top-k. Stage 2 (cross-encoder rerank, top 3-20) optimizes precision but its cost scales linearly with candidate count, so it can only be run over the already-shrunk stage-1 output, not the whole corpus.

drills.q: Where does an extra point of recall stop being worth buying?
drills.a: Once the correct answer is already reliably inside the narrower set the reranker/generator will use -- additional recall past that point costs reranker latency and generation context tokens without changing the outcome, and can even hurt via lost-in-the-middle effects. Find the point by sweeping top-k against a recall@k eval and watching where the curve flattens.

drills.q: Why don't retrieval-quality techniques (hybrid, contextual retrieval, reranking, reformulation) stack additively?
drills.a: They partially overlap in which failures they fix -- rerank-over-hybrid often matches rerank-over-dense-only, meaning the reranker's gain subsumes much of the hybrid leg's contribution once both are in the pipeline. Precision returns flatten while each added stage's latency cost keeps accumulating linearly.

drills.q: A PM asks for "the highest possible retrieval accuracy" with no latency or cost budget. How do you respond?
drills.a: Push back constructively: every accuracy gain trades against latency/cost, so "highest possible" isn't an engineering target. Propose naming a concrete ceiling, build the budget against it, and show what accuracy that ceiling buys -- and note that even unlimited spend has a quality ceiling via lost-in-the-middle effects from excessive context.

drills.q: Retrieval meets its 2-second latency target and passes offline eval, but online task-completion hasn't improved after three successive retrieval-quality changes. What do you do?
drills.a: Stop shipping further retrieval-side changes on faith and instrument where the pipeline actually fails -- sample failed interactions and check whether the bottleneck is upstream (retrieval missing content), midstream (bad reranking), or downstream (generation failing to use good context, e.g. lost-in-the-middle). The likely hypothesis given three non-moving retrieval changes is that the bottleneck moved downstream of retrieval.

drills.q: A teammate says "just retrieve more chunks and pass them all to the LLM -- more context can only help." What's wrong with this, and how would you convince them otherwise?
drills.a: More chunks cost reranker latency/dilution, more input tokens, and past a threshold measurably hurt quality via lost-in-the-middle effects -- attention degrades on information buried in a long context. Convince with data: run the eval at increasing top-k/context sizes and show where the accuracy curve flattens or reverses, rather than just restating the mechanism.

drills.q: Why can't you just do exact k-NN at scale?
drills.a: Exact k-NN is O(N*dim) per query -- every query touches every vector. Past a few hundred thousand vectors this blows interactive latency budgets and gets strictly worse as the corpus grows.

drills.q: What's the difference between efConstruction and efSearch, and which one requires a rebuild to change?
drills.a: efConstruction is the candidate list size at build time (affects recall baked into the graph, no query-time cost). efSearch is the query-time beam width (affects recall and latency per query). efConstruction requires a rebuild to change; efSearch is a runtime knob.

drills.q: Walk through the memory math for a 10M-vector HNSW index at 768 dimensions with M=16.
Explain IVF-PQ's nlist and nprobe, and product quantization's accuracy cost.
drills.a: nlist = number of k-means centroids partitioning the space (rule of thumb sqrt(N)); nprobe = cells searched per query, trading recall for latency directly. PQ quantizes each subspace against a small codebook, storing only the index -- this bakes in a quantization error at index time that no amount of nprobe tuning can fix.

drills.q: Why is filtered vector search harder than adding a WHERE clause to a normal query?
drills.a: ANN indexes (HNSW graph, IVF lists) are built assuming any indexed vector is a valid target. A filter restricts valid targets after the fact; pre-filtering can fall back to brute force over the filtered subset, and naive post-filtering can under-return on selective filters since the search never routed toward filter-valid graph regions.

drills.q: How does DiskANN achieve billion-scale search with limited RAM?
drills.a: Builds a single-layer Vamana graph via randomized init + two-pass robust pruning; keeps only PQ-compressed vectors in RAM for approximate first-pass distance estimates, while full vectors and graph adjacency live together on SSD so one disk read per hop returns both. Reports 5000+ QPS, <3ms mean latency, 95%+ recall@1 on SIFT1B with 16 cores/64GB RAM.

drills.q: A team wants 99%+ recall from an IVF-PQ index and can't get there no matter how they tune nprobe. What's going on and what do you tell them?
drills.a: The ceiling is quantization error, not search breadth -- nprobe controls how much of an already-lossy index you search, not the precision of what's stored. Fix: reduce PQ's compression (more subspaces/bits, trading back memory savings), or abandon PQ for flat/HNSW if recall is truly non-negotiable and the memory budget allows.

drills.q: Design a vector index strategy for a multi-tenant SaaS product sharing a 50M-vector corpus where tenant sizes range from 100 to 5 million vectors.
drills.a: Filter selectivity varies by four orders of magnitude, making a filter-aware index (ACORN-style or filterable HNSW) close to mandatory since neither pure pre- nor post-filter serves both extremes well. For the smallest tenants, per-tenant physical partitioning (brute force over a few hundred vectors) may beat a shared filtered index. For the largest tenants, per-tenant HNSW indexes sidestep the filtered-search problem at the cost of more indexes to operate. Name both the filtered-search cost and the ops cost of physical partitioning explicitly.

drills.q: Name the four memory types in one breath.
drills.a: Working, episodic, semantic, procedural.

drills.q: Which LangChain memory class is deprecated and what replaced it?
drills.a: ConversationBufferMemory, deprecated since v0.3.1. Replacement: LangGraph checkpointers for within-thread state and a BaseStore (optionally + LangMem) for cross-thread long-term memory.

drills.q: A rolling summary is dropping order IDs. Fix it without changing the summariser.
drills.a: Add a pinned, machine-generated <state> block containing IDs, entitlements, deadlines, and open obligations. It is regenerated structurally each turn and the summariser never sees it, so it cannot lose it.

drills.q: The agent retrieved a 'user wants to cancel' memory even though the user retracted it. Two root causes and two fixes.
drills.a: Causes: pure cosine ranking has no notion of negation or currency; the retraction never superseded the original fact. Fixes: composite score with exponential recency decay, and contradiction resolution that closes valid_to on the superseded fact.

drills.q: Write the write-path pipeline for semantic memory, in four stages.
drills.a: 1) Candidate extraction (cheap model, structured output, atomic claims with a source quote). 2) Gate (would this change a future unrelated answer? conf >= 0.7? not system-of-record?). 3) Dedupe/resolve against existing (subject, predicate) -> ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP. 4) Commit with provenance, validity window, and confidence.

drills.q: Give class TTLs you would defend in a design review.
drills.a: identity: none (supersedable, never expiring). stable_pref: 365d. entitlement: 30d (better: don't store it, read the API). project_state: 14d. task_local: 0, never persisted. Half-lives for ranking decay: 3650 / 180 / 14 / 7 / 1 days.

drills.q: Quality dropped after you enabled memory. Diagnose.
drills.a: The write policy is too loose, so noise is injected on unrelated turns. Check injected-memory precision (should be > 0.7). Fixes: relevance floor so zero memories is a valid result, per-predicate diversity, drop facts under 0.7 confidence, tighten the extraction gate. Verify with a memory-off baseline A/B, which you need to have had before shipping.

drills.q: Extraction added 600ms to p50. Fix it and name what breaks.
drills.a: Move extraction and embedding off the request path: post-response background task, session-end batch, or an idle-turn consolidation pass (Letta's sleep-time compute). Breaks: memory becomes eventually consistent, so a fact stated at turn 5 may not be retrievable at turn 6. Mitigated because current-session facts are already in the recent-turns window. Add a write-rate floor alert so a silently failing job is detectable.

drills.q: A user chats anonymously, then logs in. What do you do with the anonymous memories?
drills.a: Merge only on an explicit authentication event, never on a device/fingerprint heuristic (shared kiosks would import a stranger's facts). Record the merge in provenance so it is reversible, and re-run the conflict resolver over the merged set rather than blind-appending.

drills.q: Design memory for a multi-session support agent. Four tiers, one sentence each.
drills.a: In-session: checkpointer + hybrid summary/last-8-verbatim + pinned state block (ticket id, entitlement, open items). Semantic: (tenant_id, user_id, predicate) table with value/confidence/valid_from/valid_to/source_quote + pgvector, written by a NOOP-by-default extractor. Episodic: past resolutions keyed by task signature with outcomes, returned as one exemplar plus one anti-example. Procedural: escalation and refund rules in the repo, reviewed. Entitlement and ticket status are API reads, not memory.

drills.q: Build the adversarial retrieval test that proves your ranking beats cosine.
drills.a: 5,000 synthetic facts including one retracted intent that is the nearest cosine neighbour to the query. Assert pure cosine retrieves the retracted fact and the composite score with recency decay plus supersession does not. Report precision@8 both ways. Being able to name this experiment is the difference between a belief and a measurement.

drills.q: Would you use a knowledge graph for memory? Give the decision rule and the hidden cost.
drills.a: Only when query traces show genuine multi-hop entity/relation questions or temporal reconstruction over long histories. Default: typed columns for known predicates, a flat bi-temporal facts table with pgvector for the open-vocabulary residue. Hidden cost: write amplification and non-determinism at write time. Cost scales with conversation volume rather than query volume, and a bad extraction corrupts structure rather than adding one bad row.

drills.q: An agent gave a wrong answer due to a stored memory. What three artefacts must be in the trace to debug it?
drills.a: The exact injected memory block for that request; each fact's source_quote, valid_from, and confidence; and the store id. Without those the incident is unfalsifiable. Then classify: wrong at write time (extraction bug -> fix the gate, replay over a sample) vs right-then-wrong-now (invalidation bug -> TTL too long or supersession failed) vs should never have been memory (system of record exists).

drills.q: Your VP wants 'memory like ChatGPT'. Ship it in a week without building a vector store.
drills.a: Ask which of three things they mean. If it is 'stop re-asking my name and preferences': a typed profile table with ~20 predicates plus an extraction step, days of work, no vector store. If it is 'recall specifics from three months ago': a real semantic store with ranking and invalidation, weeks, plus an ongoing eval burden. If it is 'get better at my codebase': procedural memory and progress files. Ship the first, get the memory-off baseline, then gate the second on injected-memory precision.

drills.q: State the difference between a citation that exists and a citation that supports the claim, with one number.
drills.a: Existence is plausibility (resolves, right domain, on topic); support is faithfulness (the cited span entails the sentence). The 2026 deep-research audit measured link-works at 94-100% and topical relevance at 80-96% while fact-check accuracy ran 24-77%.

drills.q: Write out ALCE citation recall and precision.
drills.a: Recall(s) = 1 if the concatenation of s's cited docs entails s. Precision(d) = 1 if d alone entails s, or if removing d from the cited set breaks entailment. Report mean recall over sentences, mean precision over citations, and unsupported-sentence rate = 1 − mean recall.

drills.q: Why does a dense retriever hand you the chunk that states the opposite?
drills.a: Because it scores semantic similarity, not entailment, and negation barely moves an embedding. The chunk most similar to a claim is often the one discussing the same topic while asserting the contrary. This is the core reason relevance is not support.

drills.q: Name the architectural property that makes post-hoc citation unfixable by prompting.
drills.a: There is no reachable output meaning 'nothing supports this'. The answer precedes the search, so retrieval is confirmatory, and the instruction makes a citation mandatory. Abstention has to be a live branch in the pipeline, not a phrase you hope the model chooses.

drills.q: Your NLI verifier flags 40% of sentences as unsupported and the answers look fine. Debug in order.
drills.a: 1) Decontextualisation — flagged sentences starting with pronouns give neutral verdicts. 2) Premise length — 1,200-token premises drift to neutral; split into 3-sentence windows and max-pool. 3) Threshold — 0.5 is not universal; label ~200 pairs from your corpus and fit tau. 4) Granularity — a two-claim sentence with one supported claim correctly fails; decompose. 5) Only then, it may really be 40%.

drills.q: Attribute-first versus generate-then-verify: pick one and justify the sequence.
drills.a: Generate-then-verify first, because it is a bolt-on that immediately gives you the measurement (unsupported rate, recall, precision) and you cannot manage what you cannot measure. Then attribute-first, because verification only detects and does not raise the ceiling. Costs are opposite: verification adds latency and can only reject; attribute-first adds a pass, lowers fluency, lowers coverage.

drills.q: Why does deep-research citation accuracy fall as search depth rises? Give the numbers.
drills.a: Attention dilution during synthesis. GPT-5.4 fact-check accuracy fell 79% at 2 tool calls to 17% at 150, while link validity and relevance stayed above 92%. The models producing the most citations had the lowest fact-check accuracy, so selective citation beats exhaustive citation.

drills.q: A citation entails the claim and the answer is still wrong. Give two mechanisms and their fixes.
drills.a: Supersession — v1.4 entails it but v2.1 overrides; fix with effective_from / superseded_by metadata filtered at retrieval and retire old docs from the index. Cherry-picking — the cited span is the exception clause; fix with a contradiction sweep across the other retrieved chunks and surface the conflict instead of picking a side.

drills.q: Design the verification stage for a 20-sentence answer over 8 retrieved chunks. Give the cost.
drills.a: Decontextualise per response (1 small call), split each chunk into overlapping 3-sentence windows, build all (window, sentence) pairs and score in ONE batched forward pass with MiniCheck or HHEM-2.1-open, max-pool per sentence per doc. Roughly 20-60 pairs plus union and leave-one-out pairs for precision. Batched on GPU: tens of milliseconds. Unbatched over HTTP: hundreds. Batching is not optional.

drills.q: Does RAG solve hallucination? One sentence with the study.
drills.a: No — Stanford RegLab measured commercial legal RAG products at 17-33% hallucination versus 43% for GPT-4, a real reduction and nowhere near the '100% hallucination-free' being marketed.

drills.q: Why is a verbatim quote check the first thing you build, despite being trivial?
drills.a: It is free, deterministic, and it catches paraphrased-quote fabrication which NLI passes because the paraphrase captures the gist. A fabricated quote fails a human's eyes immediately and passes entailment, so a cheap exact check covers a gap the expensive probabilistic check leaves open.

drills.q: Verify citations for a browsing agent. What are the three non-obvious requirements?
drills.a: 1) Snapshot at fetch time with a content hash and verify against the snapshot, so verification is reproducible and a page edit cannot silently invalidate the audit. 2) Cite snapshot id + URL + timestamp, because 'the page said this on date X' is the only supportable claim. 3) Verify per section during synthesis, not once at the end, since accuracy degrades with search depth.

drills.q: When is showing citations the wrong choice?
drills.a: Single-source assistants (highlight the span instead), creative or synthesis-heavy output (section-level provenance plus on-demand sources), claims drawn from general knowledge with no source being asserted (mark unsourced), and anywhere you cannot verify, since an unverified citation is a false trust signal.

drills.q: Rank attribution interventions by effect per unit of effort.
drills.a: 1) Verbatim quote check. 2) Citation-constrained decoding over in-context ids. 3) Sentence-level entailment gate with abstention. 4) Span-level locators for one-click checking. 5) Corpus supersession metadata. 6) Attribute-first generation. 7) Claim-level atomic decomposition for the high-stakes surface. Dead last: prompting the model to cite more carefully.

drills.q: Why is your internal citation-precision of 0.94 not a comparable number?
drills.a: Automatic attribution metrics have been shown not to transfer across datasets and constructs (arXiv:2606.23915), so the figure tracks your own regressions only. Anchor it with a human audit of ~100 sentences per release before quoting it to anyone.

drills.q: Context engineering vs prompt engineering in one sentence each.
drills.a: Prompt engineering: authoring a fixed set of instructions once. Context engineering: deciding on every turn of a loop which tokens occupy a finite attention budget, most of which were generated (tool results, prior assistant turns) rather than authored.

drills.q: Why is cost quadratic in turns?
drills.a: The model is stateless, so the whole prefix re-sends every turn while it also grows. cumulative_input = turns*base + growth*turns*(turns-1)/2.

drills.q: Name the five context zones and which lever touches which.
drills.a: Zone 1 stable prefix (cache it, never reorder). Zone 2 protected: task, constraints, open items, IDs, last correction (never compacted). Zone 3 retrieved/recap (rebuilt each turn; compaction writes here). Zone 4 working set: last N turns and recent tool output (compaction and context editing operate here). Zone 5 headroom for max_tokens. Subagents and progress files move work out of zones 3 and 4 entirely.

drills.q: Turn 40, the agent used the wrong order id. Root cause and two fixes.
drills.a: The summariser dropped the identifier, because summaries lose numbers and IDs first. Fixes: a Verbatim values section in the recap schema, plus mechanical ID verification that regexes identifiers out of the compacted region and refuses the compaction if any are missing. Structural fix: put the ID in the protected block so the summariser never sees it.

drills.q: You get a 400: tool_result without a matching tool_use. What did your compactor do wrong?
drills.a: It cut the boundary between a tool_use block and its tool_result, orphaning one half. Fixes: snap the split boundary forward past any message starting with a tool_result, and refuse to compact while a tool call is pending.

drills.q: Give a context-editing config where enabling it makes things WORSE.
drills.a: A 150k stable prefix with a small trigger and no clear_at_least, clearing ~2k every couple of turns. You reclaim almost nothing and pay a full cache write repeatedly, so cost rises with no quality change.

drills.q: Anthropic reported 29% and 39%. Which is which, and what is the interesting reading?
drills.a: Context editing alone: +29% on an internal agentic-search eval. Memory tool plus context editing: +39%. The interesting reading is that 29 of the 39 points came from REMOVING stale tool results rather than adding recall, which is the strongest published evidence that subtraction beats addition on long tool-heavy runs. Separately, a 100-turn web search eval saw 84% fewer tokens.

drills.q: Cost is 4x the estimate. Six fixes in priority order.
drills.a: 1) Get the per-zone token ledger; do not guess. 2) Truncate tool results at the tool boundary. 3) Verify the stable prefix is byte-stable and cached (~0.1x on reads). 4) Enable tool-result clearing with a sensible clear_at_least. 5) Compact at 60% and route the summary call to a cheaper model. 6) Only then consider subagents or a smaller main model. The first four also improve QUALITY, because they remove distractors.

drills.q: The agent keeps retrying an approach that already failed after a compaction. Fix.
drills.a: The recap schema had no 'Failed approaches' section. Add it, and make it explicit that omitting failures causes the next turn to retry them. It is the highest-value section after Open items.

drills.q: Write the compaction survival test you would put in CI.
drills.a: A scripted-model golden run: a hard constraint at turn 1, an identifier at turn 3, an open item created at turn 10. Force three compactions. Assert at turn 90 that the constraint, the open item, and the identifier are all present and exact. Deterministic, cheap, and it catches the entire class of compaction-loss bugs.

drills.q: Design the context strategy for a 3-hour codebase migration agent.
drills.a: Zone 1: cached system prompt plus a deliberately small tool set (glob, grep, read, edit, run_tests). Zone 2: protected block regenerated each turn from progress.md - task, success criteria, the do-not-touch constraint, open items, verbatim values. Zone 3: <progress_so_far> from the last compaction. Zone 4: last ~6 turns, every tool truncating at the boundary (grep returns file:line, tests return failures only). Just-in-time retrieval over pre-loading. Tool-result clearing with keep 5 and exclude_tools protecting the plan. Compaction at 60% with the six-section schema plus ID verification. Read-only subagents for exploration returning 1.5k with pointers. Never let a subagent write.

drills.q: Three hours means many compactions. How do you stop quality collapsing?
drills.a: Make the append-only progress FILE the source of truth, not the recap chain, so each compaction seeds from the file rather than from the previous summary - otherwise you get summaries of summaries and brevity-bias collapse. Cap compactions per run and alert past ~4, because more than that means per-turn growth is the real bug and the fix is upstream at the tool.

drills.q: Defend 'more tokens makes agents worse' to a skeptical staff engineer.
drills.a: Three mechanisms: n^2 pairwise attention dilutes per-relationship mass; training distributions are short-sequence dominated so there are fewer parameters for context-wide dependencies; position-encoding interpolation trades positional precision for length. One measurement: 20-50% accuracy loss from 10k to 100k+ across 18 frontier models, with distractors and needle-question dissimilarity driving more damage than raw length. Corollary: 'just in case' retrieval is negative-value, and subtraction is the highest-leverage operation available.

drills.q: One week to improve context handling. What do you do each day?
drills.a: Day 1: instrument the per-zone token ledger; everything after is guessing without it. Days 2-3: fix the two tools returning the most tokens per call to return summaries plus pointers (free, improves cost AND quality). Day 4: enable tool-result clearing with clear_at_least sized from the cache break-even. Day 5: the protected block, a progress file, and the compaction survival test in CI. Explicitly NOT: building a subagent architecture or tuning a summariser prompt - lower leverage, higher risk.

drills.q: Define interpretability and explainability without using either word in the definition.
drills.a: Interpretability: how far a human can understand the model's internal mechanism (global, intrinsic to the model). Explainability: an account of why this particular input produced this particular output (local, usually produced after the fact).

drills.q: Your PM wants to show the model's reasoning block to users as the explanation. Give the 20-second refusal.
drills.a: CoT is not a description of the computation. Anthropic measured hint-verbalisation faithfulness at 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1, dropping to 20% and 29% on harmful prompts; Turpin et al. showed fluent rationales for biased answers with up to 36% accuracy loss on 13 BBH tasks. Ship instead: verified citations with locators, tool calls with arguments, and an explicit statement when a claim has no supporting source — all derived from the trace, so faithful by construction.

drills.q: Give the number that rules KernelSHAP out for a 50k-token prompt.
drills.a: ~2|F| + 2048 samples per explained output, so about 3k forward passes at just 512 features, before you even reach 50k tokens. Plus off-manifold masks on correlated tokens and a scalar-only output type.

drills.q: You must produce chunk-level attribution for a RAG answer with k=8. What do you run and what does it cost?
drills.a: Leave-one-out occlusion: regenerate with each chunk removed and score semantic agreement against the original answer. Cost k+1 = 9 generation calls. For interpretable results add sufficiency (each chunk alone) and a closed-book baseline: 2k+2 = 18 calls. Audit path only, not per request.

drills.q: Name the field in a trace whose absence makes every explanation unreplayable.
drills.a: Versions — model@version, prompt@version, tool schema version, and index snapshot id. Unpinned aliases like '-latest' mean two identical requests can produce different explanations and you cannot reconstruct either.

drills.q: A regulator asks why the model denied a claim. List the artefacts you produce.
drills.a: The decision record (inputs, retrieved policy sections with quoted spans, tool results, the rule or threshold that produced the outcome, all versions), the human-oversight record if gated (who reviewed, what they saw, how long they took, what they changed), the system card with eval results and documented limitations, and aggregate outcome monitoring disaggregated by group. Do not generate a post-hoc rationale by asking the model why.

drills.q: Occlusion says a chunk had zero influence. State both possible worlds.
drills.a: The chunk was irrelevant, OR the same fact was redundantly available elsewhere (another chunk or the model's parameters). Occlusion measures necessity only; with correlated evidence necessity goes to zero.

drills.q: Are attention weights an explanation? Cite the papers.
drills.a: No. Jain & Wallace, 'Attention is not Explanation' (NAACL 2019) found adversarial attention distributions with the same prediction; Wiegreffe & Pinter, 'Attention is not not Explanation' (EMNLP 2019) softened the claim without restoring attention as faithful attribution.

drills.q: You shipped explanations and users now accept wrong answers MORE often. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Plausibility rose without faithfulness — textbook automation bias. Fix: render only trace-derived verified evidence, mark unverified claims explicitly, and run an error-injection study on reviewers (corrupt a claim in a random half, compare detection with and without the explanation). If detection does not improve, the explanation is decoration and should be replaced, not tuned.

drills.q: Two claims about CoT that people conflate. Separate them.
drills.a: 1) CoT is causally load-bearing — often true; remove it and accuracy drops. 2) CoT is a faithful description of the computation — measured at 25-39% on the standard hint test. The first is why CoT works; the second is why it is not an explanation.

drills.q: Your explanation endpoint is being used to reverse-engineer a fraud model. Design the fix.
drills.a: Two-tier explanations. Internal reviewer: full trace with features, scores, thresholds. Subject: a reason code from a fixed audited vocabulary plus an appeal route — no scores, no feature ordering, no distance-to-threshold. Rate-limit the endpoint and alert on near-duplicate submissions with systematic single-field variation, which is the observable extraction signature.

drills.q: Under a latency budget you must cut one explanation component. Which, and how?
drills.a: Per-sentence NLI verification — and cut it by making it asynchronous, not by disabling it: serve the answer with citations marked 'verifying', then flag or downgrade sentences that fail. Nothing free (provenance, versions, tool args) is ever cut. State the cost: a UI that can retract is worse UX than the latency you saved.

drills.q: When do you deliberately ship no rationale at all?
drills.a: Low stake and high volume (autocomplete, search ranking, tag suggestions); adversarial decisions where the subject is the adversary (reason code + appeal instead); when the only available explanation is plausible-but-unverifiable, since that manufactures unearned confidence; and when the requirement is really a guarantee, where you build constrained generation plus verification instead. Provenance and abstention remain mandatory in all cases.

drills.q: One sentence on where mechanistic interpretability belongs in 2026.
drills.a: Post-incident forensics on open-weights models you control, plus safety research — circuit-tracer was open-sourced May 2025 — and not in a production request path, because you need a per-model transcoder and graph construction costs orders of magnitude more than the generation it explains.

drills.q: Rank explanation techniques by cost per explanation and say where each lives.
drills.a: Provenance ~0, request path, always on. NLI entailment per sentence ~10-40ms, request path for high stakes. Chunk occlusion k+1 generations, audit path. Self-consistency 5-20 generations, offline. SHAP on tabular components, hundreds-to-thousands of evals, batch job. Attribution graphs, research-grade, forensics only.

drills.q: Give a testable taxonomy of hallucination in two axes.
drills.a: Faithfulness (vs the provided source and instruction) against factuality (vs the world); crossed with intrinsic (contradicts the source) against extrinsic (source is silent). Faithfulness is testable now with NLI; factuality needs an external knowledge source.

drills.q: Why is hallucination structural? Give three reasons, one of them a theorem.
drills.a: No null token — decoding must emit something. Lossy fact storage returns plausible neighbours, which is why hallucinations are never absurd. And Kalai & Vempala (STOC 2024): a calibrated model must hallucinate arbitrary facts at a rate bounded below by the monofact rate minus miscalibration, independent of architecture and data quality.

drills.q: Why do accuracy-based evaluations increase hallucination?
drills.a: A guess has positive expected value p(correct) and abstaining scores zero, so any selection process that optimises binary accuracy selects for guessing. One hallucination benchmark cannot outvote hundreds of accuracy benchmarks. Fix the scoreboard: reward correct, penalise wrong more heavily, treat refusal as neutral.

drills.q: Someone quotes '1% hallucination' at you. Respond.
drills.a: That is the Vectara HHEM summarisation leaderboard — short source in context, summarise, check against the source, the easiest possible grounding task. On the harder FACTS Benchmark Suite no model breaks 70% (leader 68.8%); on AA-Omniscience most frontier models score below zero; commercial legal RAG measured 17-33%; clinical vignettes with one wrong detail reached 50-82%. Rate is a function of model, task, source availability, and adversariality.

drills.q: Rank hallucination mitigations, top four with a number for the first.
drills.a: 1) Grounding in retrieval — legal RAG 17-33% versus 43% closed-book GPT-4 — with a relevance filter, since irrelevant chunks make it worse. 2) Constrained decoding and structured output, which eliminate classes structurally at near-zero cost. 3) Verification passes with a small NLI checker, where Bedrock contextual grounding filters over 75%. 4) Abstention, which needs a calibrated signal and a fallback better than a guess.

drills.q: Why does temperature 0 not help? Give the measurement.
drills.a: 66.5% at zero temperature versus 65.9% default in the clinical adversarial study — statistically indistinguishable. The failure is not sampling noise; the model's mode is often the plausible falsehood. Greedy decoding buys reproducibility for debugging and evals, not truth.

drills.q: Your model upgrade improves every benchmark and hallucination rises. Cite the precedent and give the plan.
drills.a: Precedent: OpenAI's o3/o4-mini system card, PersonQA 16% for o1, 33% for o3, 48% for o4-mini. Plan: gate the upgrade on your own hallucination suite, pin model versions so an alias bump cannot do this silently, re-fit every calibrated threshold, re-check abstention specifically, and if the fabrication concentrates in one query class, route that class to the old model while compensating in the harness.

drills.q: Which detector would you put in the request path, and what does it miss?
drills.a: A small NLI grounding check — decontextualised sentences against 3-sentence context windows with max-pooling, batched into one forward pass, tens of milliseconds — plus 2-3 cheap features into a calibrated classifier. It misses anything about the world the provided context does not cover, because it only tests faithfulness. Self-consistency and semantic entropy stay out of the hot path at 5-20x tokens.

drills.q: Semantic entropy is in Nature. Why isn't it your default detector?
drills.a: Wrong cost profile and a fatal blind spot for the default case: n generations of cost, and structurally silent when all samples agree on the same falsehood, which is the confidently-wrong case that hurts most. It is the best unsupervised signal when there is no source to check against; when there is a source, grounding is cheaper and catches the class entropy cannot.

drills.q: Give the observable symptom for intrinsic hallucination, extrinsic hallucination, and RAG distraction.
drills.a: Intrinsic: NLI contradiction above threshold against a chunk that was in context — the cited chunk literally says the opposite; aggregate signature is rising contradiction count in one corpus area, usually two document versions coexisting. Extrinsic: no window entails the sentence at any threshold, scores clustered near neutral, high numeric density in the flagged sentence. RAG distraction: accuracy at k=10 worse than k=3 in an eval sweep, long low-relevance tail in context.

drills.q: Explain gate versus router in one exchange, and how you prove the router wins.
drills.a: A gate suppresses below threshold and silently discards correct answers; a router chooses among answer / flag / deeper verification / clarify / escalate so a weak signal costs compute rather than coverage. Prove it with risk-coverage curves for both policies: higher coverage at equal risk, lower risk at equal coverage, and then add the cost axis, since the router spends more on the uncertain band.

drills.q: Where in an agent loop do you put hallucination checks, and why not on the final answer?
drills.a: On the observation path before a tool result enters context, and again before any side-effecting call. Checking only the final answer is too late because the fabrication has already been acted on. Prefer cheap deterministic checks where possible — an id existence lookup beats an NLI call on a tool result.

drills.q: Internal eval scores keep improving while complaints rise. Diagnose.
drills.a: Most likely the eval rewards guessing: binary accuracy gives abstention zero. Also check whether the golden set is happy-path only, with no false premises, underspecified questions, or unanswerable cases; and whether scoring is response-level, so nine right claims plus one fabrication passes. Fix: abstention-aware scoring, adversarial cases, claim-level metrics, and a golden set built from real production failures.

drills.q: Name four risks of over-mitigating.
drills.a: Over-refusal, which users respond to by routing around the product and which is harder to detect than errors; coverage collapse from too tight a grounding threshold; latency and cost from verifying trivial-stake actions; and flag fatigue where labelling everything becomes wallpaper. Plus the subtle one: applying grounding gates to surfaces where generating novel plausible content is the product.

drills.q: Answer in one sentence: will hallucination be fixed?
drills.a: No — bounded, not fixed: there is a proven statistical floor for facts recalled from weights, so the deliverable is a measured error budget plus a human gate on irreversible actions that stays regardless of the model.

drills.q: Complete the equation and the analogy: Agent = ___ + ___. Model is the ___, context window is the ___, harness is the ___.
drills.a: Agent = Model + Harness. Model = CPU, context window = RAM, harness = operating system, agent = the application running on it.

drills.q: Name the four necessary and sufficient conditions (T1-T4) for a harness.
drills.a: T1 runtime reason/act/observe loop. T2 tool interface that can alter an external environment. T3 active, content-aware context management. T4 at least one control mechanism independent of the model's cooperation.

drills.q: Recite the 15 components in order.
drills.a: Instruction manager, context builder, model adapter, tool registry, permission engine, execution engine, state store, memory and retrieval, compactor, planner/goal controller, skill registry, MCP/connector manager, approval manager, trace and eval system, sandbox/execution boundary.

drills.q: True or false: the model calls the tool.
drills.a: False. The model returns a structured tool-call request. The harness resolves, validates the schema, checks permissions, executes inside a boundary and injects the result back. The model proposes, the harness disposes.

drills.q: Your wrapper cuts the oldest messages when the context overflows. Does it satisfy T3?
drills.a: No. T3 requires the include/exclude decision to depend on the content of the task or current observation, not merely on buffer size. A mechanical cut by size fails; task-aware selection passes.

drills.q: Why must schema validation happen before permission resolution?
drills.a: You cannot make an authorization decision about arguments you have not parsed. An unparsed path field cannot be checked against a path policy, and coercing it first is a route to policy bypass. Order is load-bearing.

drills.q: A tool returns 2.3 MB. What does a production harness do, and why not truncate?
drills.a: Persist the full output to disk and keep a ~2 KB preview plus the path in a persisted-output envelope (Claude Code's threshold is 50,000 characters). Truncation is permanent loss; if the bug is at line 500 the model can still read the file from disk, and the preview is enough to decide whether that is necessary.

drills.q: An agent ran a destructive shell command. The deny-list contained the pattern. What is the root cause and the fix?
drills.a: The deny-list is a UX pre-filter, not a security boundary; shell syntax has too many equivalent encodings for pattern matching to hold against intent. Fix: capability-based sandbox confining the working directory, filesystem, network and credentials, plus a permission engine as code that does not consult the model. Keep the pattern list only for accidents.

drills.q: Give the authority hierarchy from highest to lowest, and the one-line rule.
drills.a: Provider/system policy, org policy, product/developer policy, workspace/project policy, domain/directory policy, user task, runtime reminders, tool observations, untrusted retrieved content. Rule: retrieved instructions are data, not policy.

drills.q: Which one thing actually stops a prompt injection in a retrieved document: authority labelling or the permission engine?
drills.a: The permission engine, because it does not consult the model. Labelling lowers the probability; a model-independent control bounds the damage. Labelling alone is Level-1 instruction, not enforcement.

drills.q: Is a guardrail a harness? State the test.
drills.a: No, it is a part of one. Test: is this limiting the agent or helping it execute? Limiting means guardrail (a kind of T4 control). Guardrails are inside the harness; the harness is not inside the guardrails.

drills.q: Name three harness-only results that beat model choice, with numbers.
drills.a: Rank 30 to top 5 on Terminal Bench 2.0 with no model swap (LangChain). 2/10 to 10/10 on a SWE-bench subset by shrinking the per-phase tool space (statewright). Intent Met 45% to 75% on novel incidents by swapping 100+ bespoke tools for filesystem plus grep (Azure SRE Agent). Bonus: 5+ percentage points of benchmark swing from harness config alone.

drills.q: Argue against building a thick harness. Cite evidence.
drills.a: Every component encodes an assumption the model cannot do something, and assumptions expire. Manus refactored their harness five times in six months. Vercel deleted 80% of their agent's tools and got fewer steps, fewer tokens, faster responses. LangChain warns models can overfit to a specific harness, so elaborate custom scaffolding can be worse on the next model. Interpreter-persistence mismatch produces either ~80% missing-variable errors or 3.5x token overhead. Build to delete.

drills.q: Give the ten-item MVP harness.
drills.a: One model adapter, one deterministic context builder, narrow tool registry, strict schema validation, runtime permission checks, structured tool results with remediation, step and cost budgets, trace logging, compaction only when needed, a small eval set.

drills.q: Why is the build sequence (loop, tools, perms, obs, budgets, tracing, ...) not arbitrary?
drills.a: Each later component is undebuggable without the earlier ones. You cannot tell whether compaction hurt you without traces, and you cannot tell whether a permission rule is too tight without structured observations showing the denial. Adding components speculatively builds the thing you have to delete.

drills.q: Which maturity level is this: 'can execute low-risk actions autonomously within strict scopes, budgets and audit controls'? What does the next level up require?
drills.a: Level 4, policy-bounded autonomous actor. Level 5, long-running goal worker, additionally requires durable state, compaction, budget enforcement, checkpoints and evaluation, so it can continue across sessions toward a measurable objective.

drills.q: State two things a harness does NOT require, and why the definition stays lean.
drills.a: Multi-agent architecture and a specific model (also: fine-tuning, and a UI). Pulling them into the definition would make it too narrow and exclude systems that are legitimately harnesses, for example a faceless single-agent library that edits files and verifies the result.

drills.q: Cost is 8x your estimate and cache_read_input_tokens is near zero. Which component is broken and what is the fix?
drills.a: The context builder. Something mutates the stable prefix each turn (a timestamp, unstable dict/tool ordering, a rewritten system prompt), so the prompt cache never hits. Fix: freeze the static prefix at a sentinel boundary, place cache_control breakpoints, and snapshot-test that the assembled prefix is byte-stable across turns.

drills.q: Which component would you add first and justify it with arithmetic?
drills.a: The state store. At 85% per-step reliability a ten-step run completes ~20% of the time (95% gives ~60%), so most multi-step runs fail somewhere and every failure without checkpoints is a full restart paying the whole bill again. Checkpointing converts restart into resume.

drills.q: Why store typed events rather than a message array?
drills.a: The prompt is not a database. Typed events (tool_call, tool_result, approval_request/result, plan_update, goal_update, context_compaction, error, final_answer, and so on) give replay, audit, compaction, evals and debugging from one substrate. A message array loses the plan, the todo list, approval records, artifact paths, loaded instruction scopes and connector scopes, and cannot support a human approval that takes a day.

drills.q: Each tool is individually safe. Why can the set be unsafe, and what does the permission engine need?
drills.a: The lethal trifecta: private data access + exposure to untrusted content + external communication. Per-tool analysis misses risk that emerges from combinations. The permission engine needs a session-level property: if the session has read private data and ingested untrusted content, egress tools require approval regardless of individual annotations.

drills.q: Your agent's quality regressed. How do you determine whether it was the model or the harness?
drills.a: Harness config in git, one change per PR, a golden eval set gating CI, and traces recording model version, reasoning-effort, cache configuration, prompt hash and tool-registry hash. Then bisect. Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem: three simultaneous harness changes (reasoning-effort default, a caching bug dropping thinking history, a verbosity-limiting prompt) with zero model change.

drills.q: Give one property test on a harness that catches a whole family of production bugs.
drills.a: Snapshot the fully assembled request for a fixed conversation and assert the static prefix is byte-stable across turns. It catches silent prompt drift, cache-destroying mutations, and non-deterministic assembly (dict ordering, injected timestamps, tool-list ordering), which otherwise appear only as an unexplained 5-10x cost increase.

drills.q: Twenty tools and the agent keeps picking the wrong one. Do you split into five subagents?
drills.a: Not for that reason. Fix tool descriptions, grouping and phase-scoped visibility first; statewright's 2/10 to 10/10 came from shrinking the callable set per phase inside a single agent. Reach for a subagent when you need context isolation (subagents process ~67% fewer tokens than skills in multi-domain scenarios), real parallelism, or different permission scopes, and be able to say which.

drills.q: The agent says 'I fixed the bug.' What mechanism decides whether that is true?
drills.a: A verifier, and it must be computational: re-run the test suite in the sandbox and gate on the exit code, diff the change against the stated plan, run the linter and type checker, require a test that failed before and passes after. None of these consult the model. The failure class without one is fail-plausible: polluted or absent evidence produces confident fabrication rather than silence.

drills.q: Distinguish computational from inferential controls, and give the ordering rule.
drills.a: Computational: linters, type checkers, tests, schema validators, re-running the suite. Deterministic and cheap. Inferential: LLM-as-judge, convention matching. Probabilistic. Exhaust computational first; use inferential only where no computational check exists, and never rely on it alone for T4 since its effectiveness partly depends on the same class of system that produced the output.

drills.q: Framework, SDK, or harness? (a) routes messages between personas, no environment actions (b) exposes tool-calling primitives, you write the loop (c) single agent that edits files and runs tests
drills.a: (a) framework, fails T2. (b) SDK, fails T1 until someone writes the loop. (c) harness, satisfies T1-T4. A framework operates above a harness and can put one under each agent it coordinates; a harness needs no framework.

drills.q: Name three cases where you should not build a harness at all.
drills.a: Single-turn tasks (no loop needed; you pay latency, cost, nondeterminism for nothing). Deterministic workflows (write the pipeline; an if-statement is cheaper, testable and does not hallucinate). Long-running multi-party work needing retries across hours, day-long approvals and exactly-once side effects (use Temporal or Step Functions with LLM calls as activities, because a hand-rolled state store plus approval manager is a worse Temporal).

drills.q: What three action properties determine gate placement?
drills.a: Irreversibility, blast radius, and externality — with rate risk handled separately as a cap. Not the tool's name, and never the model's stated intent.

drills.q: An action is reversible in the database but sends an email. Which tier and why?
drills.a: Irreversible. Externality dominates reversibility: anything a third party observes is irreversible in practice regardless of what your data model can roll back. You cannot un-send.

drills.q: Give the gate ladder in five rungs.
drills.a: reversible+small → auto+log; reversible+bounded → notify-and-proceed with an undo window; irreversible or external-visible or financial → synchronous approval with a diff; irreversible with multi-record or high value → dual approval; unbounded destructive → prohibited, not in the toolset. Deletes stay gated at every autonomy level.

drills.q: Your gates are being rubber-stamped. How do you know from telemetry?
drills.a: Approval p50 latency under about 5 seconds on a decision designed to take 45-90 seconds; override rate near zero; gated volume above computed review capacity; and any bulk-approve usage on an irreversible class. Then confirm with error injection and measure the catch rate.

drills.q: Fix a rubber-stamped queue. Four changes, and one thing you do NOT do.
drills.a: Reduce the number of gates so attention concentrates; replace intent with a computed diff plus inline evidence; remove any bulk-approve affordance on irreversible classes; make rejection one click with a reason code and ensure it is respected rather than instantly re-proposed. Do NOT retrain the reviewers — this is a design failure, and the catch-rate decay is the design signal.

drills.q: Design oversight for an agent processing refunds up to $500.
drills.a: Register issue_refund as financial, compensating reversibility, external-visible, rate-risky. Under $50 with an entailed policy citation and matching invoice: auto-execute, notify, 10-minute cancel window. $50-500: synchronous single approval showing the balance diff plus the invoice span and policy section. Above $500: out of scope, escalate. Independently: a rate cap per hour and a per-day currency total. Plus SoD in the broker, 15-minute expiry failing closed, preconditions re-validated at execution, and an audit record with params, diff, policy version, evidence digest, reviewer, reason code, latency.

drills.q: The approval service is down. What happens, per tier?
drills.a: Irreversible, financial, and destructive fail CLOSED — the run suspends or abandons and notifies. Reversible bounded actions may fail open only if blocking is itself a harm, and the outcome is logged distinctly as auto-approved-by-timeout, never silently as an approval. Runs must be checkpointed so suspension is resumable, and timeout outcomes are a monitored metric.

drills.q: An agent must update 50,000 records. Design the oversight.
drills.a: Not primarily with an approval — a human cannot review 50,000 of anything. Dry run producing a diff summary (counts by change type, value distribution, the exact WHERE clause, 20 sampled before/after rows including edge cases); automated invariants (affected count in band, no rows outside the tenant, no field crossing a threshold, target matching an approved pattern); staged batch execution with abort on anomaly; one human approval of the PLAN, the invariants, and the tested undo path; plus a rate cap and idempotency keys so a resumed run cannot double-apply.

drills.q: In that bulk-update design, what is the human actually approving?
drills.a: The plan, the invariants, and the existence of a tested rollback. Their real job is confirming the intent matches the diff summary and that an undo exists — a judgment humans are good at and assertion engines are not. Approving 50,000 individual rows looks like oversight and is not.

drills.q: How do you keep prompt injection from defeating a gate?
drills.a: Gate selection is a pure function of registered action properties and computed parameters, evaluated in the harness at the tool boundary, so no text in context can change the tier. Per-agent scoped short-lived credentials make unpermitted actions fail at the API. The broker rejects any agent principal as an approver. And the reviewer sees the computed diff, never the agent's summary, which is attacker-controlled text.

drills.q: List the audit fields, then name the two most-forgotten.
drills.a: Agent@version, prompt@version, model@version; principal and credential scope; requested action with full params and the computed diff; policy id@version; reviewer, decision, reason code, decision latency; overrides; result and rollback. Most forgotten: the evidence bundle the reviewer was shown (or its hash), and the decision latency.

drills.q: State the gates-versus-value arithmetic and the case where rubber-stamping is certain.
drills.a: net = S − g·R − wait_cost, break-even g = S/R. At S=10, R=1.5 you keep 85% at full gating. At S=2, R=1.5 you keep 25% and the reviewer is the bottleneck, so the economics force speed and rubber-stamping is certain. wait_cost is the forgotten term: a synchronous gate blocks the run, which is why durable checkpointing is a prerequisite.

drills.q: How do you raise an auto-approve threshold responsibly?
drills.a: Evidence ratchet, not a meeting. Require a defined volume of the class passing approval with no reviewer override and no downstream dispute, then shadow-run the proposed policy: keep gating while recording what it WOULD have auto-approved, and compare against reviewer decisions. Promote only below a stated disagreement threshold, wire automatic demotion on incident, and never let deletes or unbounded actions participate.

drills.q: Compliance insists on a human in the loop for every action. How do you respond?
drills.a: With arithmetic and catch-rate data, not principle: review capacity, queue volume, decision p50 latency, and error-injection catch rate at the current gate count versus a narrower set. Compliance usually wants demonstrable control, and a documented deterministic control with a measured catch rate plus a sampled human audit is often a stronger artefact than an unmeasured universal gate. If they still require it, it is their risk decision, implemented with the queue staffed to capacity and stated in writing.

drills.q: Rank oversight investments by protection per unit of cost, and name the last.
drills.a: Remove the action; scoped short-lived per-agent credentials; deterministic invariants and dry-run diffs; reversibility; rate caps; narrow approval gates on the irreversible set; immutable audit with evidence digest and latency; error-injection measurement. Last: adding more gates — past the review-capacity limit, each extra gate reduces attention per gate and total protection can fall.

drills.q: A reviewer approved a bad action in three seconds. Whose failure?
drills.a: The oversight design's. A 3-second p50 on a minute-long decision means the queue was over capacity, the UI showed intent instead of a diff, or a bulk-approve affordance existed that should not. Blaming the reviewer is how organisations avoid fixing the system and how they lose the reviewer. The accountable party is the owner of the oversight design.

drills.q: Name the three things you define to build a LangGraph graph, plus the fourth step.
drills.a: State (schema + a reducer per key), nodes (functions returning partial state updates), edges (static, conditional, or Command/Send). Then compile. Nodes do the work; edges decide what runs next.

drills.q: A node returns `{"findings": ["x"]}`. What happens to the existing value of `findings`?
drills.a: Whatever the reducer for that channel says. With no reducer it is overwritten (last write wins). With `Annotated[list, operator.add]` the lists are concatenated. The node returns a partial UPDATE, not a state; merge semantics are the channel's business, not the node's.

drills.q: Quote the error you get when two parallel nodes write the same unannotated state key.
drills.a: `langgraph.errors.InvalidUpdateError: At key '<k>': Can receive only one value per step. Use an Annotated key to handle multiple values.`

drills.q: How many checkpoints does `START -> A -> B -> END` produce, and what are they?
drills.a: Four. Step -1: the input write, `next=('__start__',)`. Step 0: input applied, `next=('A',)`. Step 1: A's output, `next=('B',)`. Step 2: B's output, `next=()` meaning complete.

drills.q: Write the state schema for a Send-based map-reduce over subqueries. Which line is load-bearing and why?
drills.a:
```python
class S(TypedDict):
    subqueries: list[str]
    findings: Annotated[list[dict], operator.add]
```
The `Annotated[..., operator.add]` on `findings` is load-bearing: N parallel Send workers all write that channel in one super-step, which without a reducer is `InvalidUpdateError` N times over.

drills.q: You wrote `graph.invoke(inp, config={"configurable": {"recursion_limit": 25}})` and the limit has no effect. Why, and what is the default?
drills.a: `recursion_limit` is a TOP-LEVEL config key, not a `configurable` entry, so nesting it is silently ignored. The default is 1000 super-steps as of langgraph 1.0.6 (it was 25 for the first two years), so the framework will not stop a runaway agent for you. Set it explicitly and carry your own step/cost budget in state.

drills.q: Your graph ran both the node `Command(goto=...)` targeted AND an unexpected second node. Why?
drills.a: The node also has a static `add_edge` from it. `Command(goto=...)` ADDS a dynamic edge; it does not replace static edges, so both destinations execute. Use either static edges or dynamic routing from a given node, never both.

drills.q: Implement graceful degradation when a loop is approaching the recursion limit, without raising.
drills.a: Add `remaining_steps: RemainingSteps` (from `langgraph.managed`) to the state; the runtime populates it. Route on it: `def route(s): return "wrap_up" if s["remaining_steps"] <= 2 else "model"`. Proactive beats reactive: the graph completes normally, the partial answer is checkpointed, and the user gets a best-effort result instead of a `GraphRecursionError`.

drills.q: Your graph passed CI and raises `InvalidUpdateError` in production. How do you prevent the CLASS of bug, not the instance?
drills.a: A startup assertion or CI test that walks the state schema and fails on any list/dict-typed key with no `Annotated` reducer, plus a test exercising every conditional edge's multi-destination return. Prod hit a path CI never took: a conditional edge returning two destinations, a node acquiring a second static out-edge (which fans out in parallel), or a Send producing more than one item.

drills.q: A model calls the same per-thread subagent twice in parallel and you get checkpoint conflicts. Explain and fix.
drills.a: A subgraph compiled with `checkpointer=True` has one checkpoint namespace per thread, so two concurrent calls write the same namespace and conflict. Fixes: prevent parallel calls (disable parallel tool calling, or a tool-call limit middleware), switch to per-invocation persistence (`checkpointer=None`) if it doesn't need memory, or wrap each subagent in its own `StateGraph` with a unique node name so each gets a stable distinct namespace.

drills.q: Design the streaming for a chat UI over a LangGraph agent. Which modes, and what breaks on Python 3.10?
drills.a: `stream_mode=["messages","updates","custom"]` with `version="v2"`; filter `messages` by `metadata["langgraph_node"]` so only the user-facing node streams, tag internal structured-output models `nostream`, use `get_stream_writer()` for tool progress, and `subgraphs=True` + `chunk["ns"]` to attribute nested output. On Python <3.11 async: `get_stream_writer()` does not work (take a `writer: StreamWriter` param instead) and you must pass `RunnableConfig` explicitly into `await model.ainvoke(msgs, config)` or callbacks don't propagate and token streaming silently emits nothing.

drills.q: An interviewer asks you to justify adopting LangGraph for a five-node linear pipeline. What do you say?
drills.a: Don't. A linear pipeline with no branching, no cycles, and no resume requirement is a function; the graph adds a state schema, a serialisation step, a framework in the stack trace, and migration cost for nothing. LangGraph earns its keep when there is branching you need to audit, fan-out you need to merge correctly, or a durable-resume requirement. Saying this is a stronger signal than enthusiasm.

drills.q: Where do a Postgres connection, a tenant id, a 400KB document, and a user's food preference each belong?
drills.a: Connection: runtime context (`context_schema` + `Runtime[Ctx]`) — not serialisable, and not checkpointed. Tenant id: runtime context too, so it isn't duplicated into every checkpoint. 400KB document: object storage or the `Store`, with only the key in state, because full channel values are re-serialised every super-step. Food preference: the `Store`, namespaced `(user_id, "memories")`, because it must persist ACROSS threads.

drills.q: What is the minimum config needed to run a checkpointed graph, and what happens without it?
