Cost incidents before gateway enforcement versus after (two versus zero, with the cap firing 40-60 times a month as a normal operating event rather than a page). Then be honest about which components you defend on judgement rather than data: usually memory and the agent topology.

drills.q: Requirements change to a 3-day human review and exactly-once billing writes. Does LangGraph still win?
drills.a: No, and saying so beats defending the earlier choice. Three days of durable wait, timer-driven escalation, and exactly-once side effects across heterogeneous systems is what Temporal or Step Functions are for; a hand-rolled state store plus approval manager on a graph checkpointer is a worse Temporal. Migration path: keep the graph as the reasoning unit and make it an activity rather than rewriting the agent.

drills.q: Give a concrete example where outcome-only eval passes but the agent run is actually broken.
drills.a: An agent asked to 'pause my subscription' calls cancel_subscription instead of pause_subscription, then summarizes 'your subscription has been paused.' The final text reads correct; only a tool-call-accuracy or state check catches the wrong tool call.

drills.q: List the four eval layers for agents in order, one line each.
drills.a: Tool-call accuracy (binary, per call). Trajectory eval (golden fuzzy-match or 6-dimension judge). Task completion vs actual state (never agent's own text). Cost/steps per task (first-class, tracked as p50/p95).

drills.q: Your sandbox eval environment is fully mocked with no real side effects. How do you still check task completion correctly?
drills.a: Make the mock stateful and inspectable - a real in-memory or test database the tool calls actually mutate (as tau-bench does) - so 'state after the run' is a queryable artifact, rather than trusting the agent's or the mock's return value at face value.

drills.q: Your agent's pass@1 is 78% but pass^8 is 25%. Is the agent broken? What do you do?
drills.a: Not necessarily broken, but unreliable enough not to promise consistent behavior at that task. Investigate whether variance concentrates in one high-variance sub-step (e.g. one flaky argument-extraction case) rather than being uniform - targeted fixes to that step move pass^k more than generic prompt tuning.

drills.q: How do you build a golden trajectory, and what's the single biggest mistake teams make?
drills.a: Record a real/expert-solved run, have a domain expert edit it into canonical form, annotate required/forbidden/optional calls. Biggest mistake: building the set entirely from happy-path traces, so error recovery and policy-edge-case regressions go completely undetected.

drills.q: A tool's argument schema just changed and every golden trajectory referencing it now fails. Is that a real regression?
drills.a: No - that's golden-set staleness, not an agent regression. Version goldens alongside tool schemas; treat mass failure right after a schema change as a signal to update the goldens, not evidence the agent broke.

drills.q: Why must cost and steps-per-task be tracked as p50 AND p95, not just mean?
drills.a: A mean cost of $0.08/task can hide a p95 of $1.20/task from a small number of runs spiraling into long tool-call chains - that tail is usually where real production incidents and budget blowouts live, invisible in a single mean number.

drills.q: Design a CI gate for an agent eval suite that won't get disabled by the team within a month.
drills.a: Never gate on a single run - N>=3-5 repeats, aggregate/pass^k with a pre-registered threshold. Separate deterministic hard-gates (tool-call accuracy, state) from statistical judge-based gates (drop across a run-set). Pin agent and judge model versions. Quarantine known-flaky tasks rather than letting them block unrelated PRs.

drills.q: An agent's tool-call accuracy is perfect but users still report bad experiences. Where do you look?
drills.a: Tool-call accuracy doesn't capture trajectory quality (wasteful-but-technically-correct paths, poor error recovery, excessive step count/latency) or whether the full sequence actually solved the user's goal. Check the six-dimension trajectory judge breakdown and latency/step-count distributions specifically.

drills.q: How do the biases from LLM-as-judge apply when using a judge to score full agent trajectories, and what's the additional risk?
drills.a: Verbosity, self-preference, and position bias (when comparing trajectories pairwise) all carry over directly. Additional risk: trajectory traces are long, so the judge's own long-context degradation is a failure mode a short single-turn judge call doesn't face - calibrate with more human review time per trace.

drills.q: How would you evaluate a multi-agent system where a supervisor delegates to sub-agents?
drills.a: Evaluate each sub-agent's trajectory and tool-call accuracy independently (attributable regressions), plus the supervisor's routing/delegation decisions as their own trajectory-scored layer, plus handoff-fidelity checks - does the sub-agent's uncertainty/caveats survive being summarized back to the supervisor without being silently dropped.

drills.q: Your full eval suite takes 6 hours with N=5 repeats. How do you make this practical for CI?
drills.a: Tier it: a fast, small, high-signal subset (highest-risk/frequency tasks, full rigor) gates every PR in minutes; the full suite runs on a slower cadence (nightly/pre-release) and gates the actual release. Periodically validate the fast subset actually correlates with the full suite's failure modes.

drills.q: Why should tool-call argument correctness usually be a deterministic check rather than an LLM judge call?
drills.a: Deterministic verification (exact match, regex, range/verifier function) is cheaper, faster, and carries no judge bias for arguments that can be checked mechanically. Reserve an LLM judge only for genuinely open-ended fields (free-text search query) with no deterministic 'close enough' notion.

drills.q: Name the reference benchmark shape worth imitating for building your own domain-specific agent eval, and its key metric.
drills.a: tau-bench/tau2-bench: realistic multi-turn tool-and-simulated-user tasks against a real mutable backend, checked against actual state plus a policy document. Key metric: pass^k, which forces confronting nondeterminism instead of reporting an optimistic pass@1.

drills.q: Name the three LLM-as-judge modes and give the strongest use case for each.
drills.a: Pointwise: absolute scoring for trend lines/quality gates. Pairwise: most reliable for ranking two systems (A/B tests, model selection). Reference-based: best when a gold answer exists (factual QA, RAG faithfulness).

drills.q: Give the measured magnitude of position bias and how you neutralize it in a pairwise eval.
drills.a: 10-15 points of win-rate swing on order swap alone (Zheng et al., 2023). Run both orderings (A-then-B and B-then-A); only count a decisive winner if both orderings agree, otherwise score it a tie.

drills.q: Your two candidate answers differ mainly in length. What bias do you need to control for, and how?
drills.a: Verbosity bias - judges prefer longer answers by 15-30 points regardless of quality. Add an explicit rubric instruction against preferring length, and run length-bucketed analysis to check the preference doesn't persist when lengths are close.

drills.q: You're comparing two fine-tunes of the same base model using that same base model as judge. What's the risk and the fix?
drills.a: Self-preference bias (+10-25% for the judge's own family) can extend to close relatives sharing lineage/training data, not just identical models. Use a judge from a genuinely different lab/family for any comparison that drives a real decision.

drills.q: Walk through calibrating a judge against human labels, step by step, with the pass/fail thresholds.
drills.a: Sample 100-300 real traces, 2-3 humans label on the exact rubric, compute inter-annotator kappa/alpha. Score same traces with the judge, compute judge-vs-human kappa. <0.4 rubric ambiguous, 0.4-0.6 weak, >0.6 ship, >0.8 strong. Re-calibrate after any rubric or judge-model change.

drills.q: Cohen's kappa vs Krippendorff's alpha - when is each the right tool?
drills.a: Cohen's kappa: exactly two raters. Krippendorff's alpha: three or more raters, handles ordinal/interval scales and missing labels. Both correct for chance agreement, which raw percent agreement does not.

drills.q: Your judge-vs-human kappa comes back at 0.95. Do you ship it immediately?
drills.a: No - audit first. Suspiciously high agreement can mean judge and humans are both tracking a superficial correlate (e.g. length) rather than true quality. Test on an adversarial subset built to break that correlate (short-but-excellent, long-but-wrong) before trusting the number.

drills.q: When is a cheap judge (small/fine-tuned model) sufficient, and when do you need a frontier model?
drills.a: Cheap judges suffice for near-checklist criteria a human could apply in seconds without re-reading source material (valid JSON, cites a source). Frontier judges are needed when the criterion requires genuine judgment (nuanced correctness, subtle harm). Production pattern: cheap judge on 100% of traffic/CI, frontier judge for calibration and hard-case routing.

drills.q: Explain G-Eval's chain-of-thought-then-score approach and why it beats naive scoring.
drills.a: The judge first generates its own evaluation steps from the criterion, fills them in as a form, then takes a probability-weighted score across top logprobs rather than a single sampled token. Externalizing reasoning before committing to a score reduces anchoring; probability-weighting smooths sampling noise.

drills.q: What is the shared-blind-spot failure, and what's the only real fix?
drills.a: If judge and generator share a training-time blind spot, the judge certifies a fabrication as correct because it matches its own equally-wrong prior - the judge has no ground truth outside what it shares with the candidate. Fix: ground the judge in something external to both models (retrieved source, verified gold answer), not just its own recall.

drills.q: Design a rubric for RAG faithfulness. What's the naive mistake?
drills.a: Naive rubric conflates faithfulness (matches provided context) with factuality (matches the world) into one score, hiding whether retrieval or generation broke. Correct: scope the rubric to faithfulness only, give the judge the retrieved chunks as sole source of truth, ask it to flag specific unsupported sentences rather than one aggregate number.

drills.q: A model upgrade improves every internal LLM-judge score. Ship it?
drills.a: Not on judge score alone - if the new model shares a family with the judge, self-preference bias could be inflating the number. Cross-check with a judge from a different family, and validate against the human-calibrated set specifically before shipping.

drills.q: Build a CI gate on an LLM judge that won't flake. What are the four key design choices?
drills.a: Pin the judge model version explicitly. Run both orderings for pairwise checks, treat a flip as a tie. Gate on the judge's calibrated agreement threshold, not an arbitrary score cutoff. Monitor judge-vs-human kappa itself as a metric so drift is visible before it silently degrades the gate.

drills.q: A frontier judge model exceeds 50% error rate on an adversarial bias benchmark despite strong aggregate scores elsewhere. What does that tell you?
drills.a: A judge can look reliable on average while failing hard on the specific bias dimension a targeted eval is testing - aggregate correlation with human judgment does not guarantee robustness on every failure mode. Always run the documented bias stress-tests (position, verbosity, self-preference) as part of calibration, not just an aggregate correlation check.

drills.q: Recite the 8 phases of a 45-minute design round with their minute budgets.
drills.a: 0-2 restate + scope contract; 2-7 requirements (3-5 FRs capped, NFR table, out-of-scope declared); 7-12 numbers you will actually use; 12-17 API signatures; 17-24 data model + partition keys; 24-32 architecture; 32-38 scale; 38-43 failure modes; 43-45 wrap. Architecture must be on the board by minute 32.

drills.q: Convert 'it should be fast' into a designable requirement, then check it against physics.
drills.a: Fast for which endpoint, at which percentile, under what load: p99 of GET /feed under 200 ms at 15k peak QPS measured server-side at the gateway. Physics check: 200 ms accommodates one intra-region round trip (~0.5 ms) plus a cache hit, but not three sequential cross-region calls at 75-230 ms each. If the requirement and topology conflict, that is a design-invalidating finding, not a tuning problem.

drills.q: Give three high-value clarifying questions for 'design Twitter' and say what each decides.
drills.a: Read:write ratio (100:1 justifies precomputing timelines; 2:1 makes read-time merge cheaper). Fanout distribution / do we have 50M-follower accounts (decides fanout-on-write vs hybrid). Chronological or ranked (ranked destroys precomputation because the ordering depends on the reader). Each names two alternatives leading to different designs.

drills.q: Write the feed read and post write endpoints, and name the five points each design detail banks.
drills.a: POST /v1/posts with Authorization + Idempotency-Key, body {text, client_ts}, 201 {post_id, created_at}, errors 400/401/409/429. GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=<opaque> returning items + next_cursor. Points: /v1/ versioning; idempotency key with stored key-to-response and TTL beyond the retry window; cursor not offset because offset skips and duplicates rows on an insert-heavy list; 429 in the contract means a rate limiter belongs in the diagram; 202 elsewhere encodes async fanout before any queue is drawn.

drills.q: For a Twitter-style feed, name every table, its partition key, and whether its main query is single-partition.
drills.a: users(user_id) point read. posts(post_id hash) point read; author-scoped listing is a separate access pattern to defer. follows partitioned by follower_id serves 'who do I follow' single-partition, but fanout needs 'who follows X', which is the reverse, so an inverted table or secondary index on followee_id is required. timeline((user_id, created_at DESC, post_id)) partitioned by user_id, so the feed read is a single-partition ordered range scan of ~20 narrow (~40 B) rows.

drills.q: You are asked to design a notification service for 10M users across email/SMS/push. What is the number that reshapes the whole design, and how do you get it?
drills.a: Cost. 10M users x 5 notifications/day = 5x10^7/day; if 10% go over SMS at ~$0.007/message that is 5x10^6 x $0.007 = $35k/day, about $1M/month. So the expensive failure is a double-send, not downtime, which makes the dedup store the most important component in the diagram and makes Idempotency-Key a required header rather than optional.

drills.q: You drew a cache. Pre-empt the five questions an interviewer will ask about it.
drills.a: Key (timeline:{user_id}); value and size (sorted set capped at 800 entries x ~40 B payload, but budget ~100 B/member because a zset past 128 members becomes a skiplist); TTL and eviction (7-day TTL for inactive users, allkeys-lru under a memory cap); invalidation (write-through on fanout, delete on unfollow); and the assumed hit rate (95%, and the design must survive 0% on cold restart via single-flight coalescing and a jittered warm-up).

drills.q: Your design has six components. Rank the bottlenecks at 10x traffic and justify the ordering.
drills.a: Memory-bound state first (Redis timelines at 50M x 800 x 40 B is ~1.6 TB payload and scales with users, not traffic), single-writer state second (Postgres at 500 to 5,000 write QPS is survivable on one primary with faster storage), stateless tiers last because they only cost more. Then fix Redis without adding hardware: cut the cap 800 to 200 (4x), stop precomputing for the 60-70% inactive users, and pack the member to 8 bytes.

drills.q: Mid-answer, the interviewer says the top account has 200M followers, not the 500 average you assumed. Recover.
drills.a: Name the statistical error: the mean is wrong for a power-law distribution, so 250k inserts/s is right for the body and meaningless for the tail. One post is 200M inserts, ~8 GB of writes, and >13 minutes of fanout that head-of-line blocks the partition. This changes exactly one decision: hybrid fanout, write-fanout below a threshold (~10k) and read-merge above it. It does not change the API, schema, or read path. And the real key is followers x post_rate, not followers alone.

drills.q: Design a recommendation feed with an LLM-generated summary. Give the cost math and then cut it 100x.
drills.a: 10M DAU x 1 summary/day at 2,000 input + 200 output tokens on a Sonnet-class model ($2/$10 per M) = 10M x (2000x$2 + 200x$10)/10^6 = 10M x $0.006 = $60k/day. Unaffordable, so: generate only on first open (removes the 40-70% who never scroll), cache per (user, feed-version) with an hour TTL so re-opens are free, route non-premium users to a Flash-class model at ~20x lower unit price, and truncate context from 2k to 500 tokens by summarising titles only. Those compose to roughly 100x. The LLM is a budgeted resource with a per-user cap enforced in code, and the summary is async with a deterministic extractive fallback.

drills.q: Give the monthly cost of a 50M-DAU feed system, name the dominant line items, and say which estimate you trust least.
drills.a: Redis 1.6 TB ~ $20-25k; Cassandra cold timelines ~100 TB at 3x replication ~ $10-15k; stateless compute for 15k QPS at ~2k rps/node is 15-20 nodes, low thousands; egress 15k QPS x 6 KB = 90 MB/s = ~230 TB/month at $0.05-0.09/GB = $12-20k. Total order $60-80k/month, dominated by Redis and egress. Least confident: egress, because it depends on payload size and CDN offload ratio, both guessed, and it is the line most likely wrong by 3x.

drills.q: When should you deliberately abandon this procedure, and what invariant survives?
drills.a: When the interviewer names the area they want (follow them, compress the rest to stated assumptions); when the round has no scale dimension (front-end design, developer experience, migration strategy) so capacity arithmetic is noise; when you are handed an existing architecture to critique, which is the scale and failure phases only; and when the prompt is ML-shaped, where numbers become token/latency/cost budgets and the data model becomes feature store and index design. The surviving invariant: no box before a requirement or number that produced it.

drills.q: Name the four C4 levels, the box count for each, and which you draw in a 45-minute round.
drills.a: L1 Context: your system plus users and external systems, 5-8 boxes, no internals, worth 60 seconds only if scope is genuinely contested. L2 Container: separately deployable/runnable things with technology and edge labels, 8-15 boxes, THE interview diagram. L3 Component: modules inside one container, 5-8 boxes, deep dive only and in fresh space. L4 Code: classes, effectively dead, never draw it.

drills.q: Label this edge properly: a browser calling an API gateway on a feed read.
drills.a: HTTPS/JSON, sync, 6 KB, 15k rps peak. Grammar is protocol/format, sync-or-async (both mandatory), payload size, rate or latency. Solid line for sync, dashed for async, consistent within the diagram. Arrow direction means initiates, not data flow, and say which convention you are using because both are common.

drills.q: What is the first thing you do on a blank whiteboard, and why does it matter more than any box?
drills.a: Divide the board: ~20% left for requirements, NFRs, and computed numbers (never erased), ~55% middle for the container diagram, ~25% right kept empty until roughly minute 30 for deep dives. Then place two anchors, client far left and primary datastore far right. This prevents the two classic failures: running out of room on the right, and erasing the requirements you need to point at when justifying a decision at minute 35.

drills.q: State your drawing order and justify why the read path goes first.
drills.a: Anchors, then happy-path read end to end unbroken, then write path below it from the same entry point, then async path below a visible horizontal line, then annotate numbers in a second pass, then deep dives in the right column. Read first because it is usually the latency-critical path and because a complete narrow path is more convincing than a broad incomplete one. The horizontal async line is itself a claim: nothing below it blocks the user. For an ingestion system the order inverts, since the rule generalises to 'draw the path the hard requirement lives on first'.

drills.q: Your diagram has 30 boxes. Fix it in three moves.
drills.a: 1) Delete infrastructure that touches everything and name it in a text line instead: auth, logging/tracing, CI/CD, DNS, per-hop load balancers, mesh sidecars. 2) Collapse replicas into multipliers, so 12 boxes become one box plus 'x12 (3 AZ)'. 3) Group survivors into 3-5 labelled regions (edge, read path, write path, async, storage) so the reader chunks rather than scans. Target 12-15 boxes, since working memory is ~7 plus or minus 2. Then write a 'not drawn:' line so omissions read as scoping decisions.

drills.q: Do the scale-annotation pass on a finished container diagram. Six steps, in order.
drills.a: 1) Rate on the hot edges only (15k rps, 250k inserts/s). 2) Size on stateful boxes (1.6 TB, 100M vectors at 132 GB). 3) Replica count as a multiplier with spread (x12, 3 AZ). 4) Bottleneck double-boxed with the constraint that binds (Redis timelines, 1.6 TB, memory-bound, breaks first at 10x). 5) Partition key on every sharded store. 6) A 'not drawn' line. Second pass only; annotating while drawing means you never finish the path. If you can keep one annotation, keep the bottleneck marker.

drills.q: The interviewer asks where the latency goes in a RAG query. Which diagram, and what must it show?
drills.a: A sequence diagram, because a container diagram cannot express order or time. Show per-hop latency on every arrow: JWT verify 0.2 ms, answer-cache lookup 0.4 ms, query embed 8 ms, ANN top-50 12 ms, cross-encoder rerank 35 ms, LLM first token 420 ms, so TTFT p99 is ~476 ms and the LLM is 88% of it, which means cutting the reranker to 10 ms saves about 5% of perceived time. Also show the async escape as a dashed line to Kafka, the cache-hit path at ~0.6 ms total, and if there is time a failure variant (vector DB times out at 50 ms, breaker opens, fall back to Postgres full-text keyword search with a degraded flag).

drills.q: Draw the ingestion pipeline for a document Q&A service as a dataflow diagram. What five things must appear?
drills.a: Stages left to right: crawler (incremental by mtime, 50k docs/day) to parse (PDF/DOCX/HTML to text, ~30 GB/day, ~0.5% failure) to chunker (512 tokens, 64 overlap, 2.5M chunks/day) to embed (BGE-large 1024-dim, batch 256, ~29 chunks/s, the narrow stage) to idempotent upsert into the vector store plus Postgres metadata. Must appear: volume on every edge; the narrow stage marked with the burst policy (a 500k-doc dump is 25M chunks, about 10 days, so bulk onboarding needs a separate spot-GPU burst path); the DLQ with its failure rate and alert threshold; the idempotency key (doc_id, chunk_index, content_hash) so re-crawl is free; and the freshness SLO with the owning stage (p99 15 min, dominated by the crawler interval).

drills.q: You drew AZ boundaries on a deployment diagram. Prove the multi-AZ claim is real, then say whether losing an AZ is fine.
drills.a: The claim lives in replica placement, not the boundary lines. Stateless: 12 replicas spread by topology constraints across 3 AZs. Stateful is where it fails: a StatefulSet of 4 shards x 2 replicas is 8 pods across 3 AZs, so without pod anti-affinity guaranteeing a shard's two replicas land in different AZs, one AZ loss can take a whole shard. For quorum systems state the arithmetic per AZ, since 3 replicas across 2 AZs cannot survive losing the AZ holding two. Losing an AZ is only fine if provisioned for: 12 replicas sized at 60% utilisation become 8 at 90%, which is past the knee, so p99 roughly triples during the incident. Provision 1.5x so N-1 capacity still sits at target.

drills.q: For a multi-tenant document Q&A system, what is the single highest-value annotation on the dataflow diagram, and why?
drills.a: That the vector-store ACL filter is an optimisation, not the security boundary. A SharePoint permission change flows through an acl.changed event to a sync worker that updates acl_hash on affected chunks with no re-embedding needed, target p99 propagation 60 s. Until it propagates a user could match a stale-allowed chunk, so the FINAL authorisation check happens at read time against Postgres. Marking that distinction is what separates a multi-tenant design from a single-tenant one with a tenant column, and interviewers probe it hard.

drills.q: Two candidates draw identical boxes; one scores, one does not. Explain the difference and why it is not just cosmetic.
drills.a: The scoring diagram has a bracketed technology in every box, protocol plus sync/async on every edge, rates on hot edges, size and partition key on stateful boxes, replica counts as multipliers, a marked bottleneck, and a 'not drawn' line, so the interviewer can point at an edge and ask about p99 and failure behaviour. The other forces them to spend questions on comprehension. It is not cosmetic because labelling is a forcing function: you cannot write 'sync, p99 12 ms' without deciding that hop's latency and consistency properties, or a partition key without deciding the access pattern, so labellers find their own gaps at minute 25 rather than having the interviewer find them at minute 40.

drills.q: When is each of the four diagram types the WRONG choice?
drills.a: C4 context: wrong when scope is obvious (a URL shortener has no interesting external systems), so 90 seconds there is 90 seconds not spent on key generation. Sequence: wrong unprompted in a 45-minute round, since it costs 4-5 minutes to answer a question that may never be asked; narrate it verbally over the container diagram instead. Dataflow: wrong for a request-response service where order matters more than transformation. Deployment: wrong for a logic question about consistency or data modelling, where drawing AZs and instance types is displacement activity. And C4 level 4 is always wrong; if they want that depth, write code.

drills.q: 100M DAU, 20 requests per user per day. Average and peak QPS, and what would you size with each?
drills.a: 1e8 x 2e1 = 2e9/day / 1e5 s = 2e4 = 20,000 QPS average; peak at 2-3x for a global consumer product is 40-60k QPS. Peak sustained sizes the fleet and database; peak burst sizes the queue, connection pool, and rate limiter; peak concurrent (throughput x latency) sizes memory and file descriptors. Sanity: 20k QPS of JSON is 20-40 stateless nodes, unremarkable.

drills.q: Recite the latency ladder from L1 to cross-Pacific, then state the three ratios.
drills.a: L1 1 ns, L2 4 ns, L3 ~12 ns, DDR5 RAM 50-80 ns, 1 KB compress 1-3 us, NVMe random read 20-100 us, SATA SSD 100-200 us, same-DC RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-AZ 1-2 ms, HDD seek 5-10 ms, US east-west 60-70 ms, US-Europe 75-90 ms, US-APAC 170-230 ms, LLM first token 300-800 ms. Ratios: RAM ~1000x SSD; same-DC RTT ~1000x RAM; cross-continent ~100-300x same-DC.

drills.q: Convert 99.99% into a design constraint, then compute the SLO of five serial services each at 99.99%.
drills.a: 99.99% is 53 minutes/year, 4.3 minutes/month, which means no human in the recovery path: automatic health-checked failover, and the deploy pipeline becomes a primary risk since a bad deploy plus manual rollback exceeds the monthly budget. Five serial services at 99.99% give 0.9999^5 = ~99.95%, about 4.4 hours/year, and independence is false anyway (shared network, control plane, deploy pipeline), so the real number is worse. Fix by removing hops from the critical path, not by making five hops more reliable.

drills.q: Storage for 1M records/day at 1 KB with 5-year retention. Give the full chain and then tier it.
drills.a: 1e6 x 1e3 B = 1 GB/day; x 365 x 5 = 1.8 TB logical; x3 replication = 5.5 TB; +30% index = ~7 TB; plus WAL and backups, so 10-14 TB provisioned. Formula: records x bytes x retention x replication x (1 + index). Tier it because ~90% of reads hit recent data: hot months on NVMe, older partitions on cheap storage, beyond the query horizon in S3/Parquet via an external table. Name the boundary as a number.

drills.q: 50M DAU social feed: reads, writes, peak, payload bandwidth, and the number that actually breaks.
drills.a: Reads 5e7 x 10 = 5e8/day / 1e5 = 5,000 QPS avg; writes 5e7 x 1 = 500 QPS avg; peak x3 gives 15,000 and 1,500. Payload 20 items x 300 B = 6 KB, so 15,000 x 6 KB = 90 MB/s = 720 Mbps egress. The number that breaks: amplified writes = 500 posts/s x 500 followers = 250,000 timeline inserts/s. 1,500 write QPS is one Postgres primary; 250k inserts/s is why fanout is async.

drills.q: 15,000 peak QPS, 20 ms service time, 5 ms CPU per request. How many servers, computed two ways?
drills.a: Little's Law: concurrency = 1.5e4 x 2e-2 = 300 in flight, trivial for async, ~2-3 instances for thread-per-request. CPU: 1 core at 100% = 200 rps, at a 60% target 120 rps/core, so 1.5e4/1.2e2 = 125 cores = 16 x 8-core; x1.5 to survive losing one of three AZs = ~24 instances. The methods disagree 10x and CPU wins, because Little's Law bounds concurrency, not throughput. If service time becomes 2 s (an LLM call), concurrency is 30,000 in flight, thread-per-request is impossible, and file descriptors and provider rate limits bind instead of CPU.

drills.q: How much Redis for 50M users' timelines at 800 entries of 40 bytes? Then reduce it.
drills.a: Naive payload: 5e7 x 8e2 x 4e1 = 1.6e12 B = 1.6 TB, and that is ~3x low. Redis adds 50-100 B per key and a zset past 128 members becomes a skiplist at ~80-120 B/member, so realistically ~4.4 TB. Reduce: cache only 7-day-active users (~40%) to ~1.8 TB; cut the cap 800 to 200 entries (ten pages covers >95% of sessions) to ~450 GB; pack the member into 8 bytes to ~250 GB. That is 6-12 shards, ~$3-6k/month, not $60k. Verify with MEMORY USAGE and OBJECT ENCODING.

drills.q: Egress bill for a photo service: 500M DAU, 50 views/day, 200 KB each. Then drop the CDN hit rate from 95% to 90%.
drills.a: 5e8 x 5e1 = 2.5e10 views/day x 2e5 B = 5 PB/day, ~150 PB/month; bandwidth 50 GB/s = 400 Gbps avg, ~1.2 Tbps peak. At list $0.05/GB that is $7.5M/month; negotiated at $0.005-0.01/GB it is $0.75-1.5M, a 5-10x contract lever. Compute is negligible (~375 cores for transform-on-miss), so egress is 10-100x the compute bill. Dropping the hit rate 95% to 90% DOUBLES origin load, because origin traffic scales with (1 - hit_rate). The usual cause is cache fragmentation from arbitrary on-demand image widths, which is the real reason to restrict transforms to fixed sizes.

drills.q: Size storage for a messaging system at 100B messages/day, and name the one requirement that changes the answer by four orders of magnitude.
drills.a: 1e11/day / 1e5 = 1M messages/s avg, 3M/s peak; amplified deliveries at ~3 recipients = 3M/s avg, ~10M/s peak. If server-side history is required: ~300 B/message x 1e11 = 30 TB/day, x3 replication = 90 TB/day, ~33 PB/year. If the client is the source of truth and messages are deleted on delivery, only the undelivered backlog persists: ~1% over a one-day offline window = 1e9 x 300 B = 300 GB, which fits in memory. That is ~30,000x, driven by one product question. WhatsApp took the second branch; Slack and Teams take the first because they want server-side search. Also: 2B users at 20% concurrency is 4e8 persistent connections, ~8,000 nodes at 50k conns each, which is the actually hard part rather than the byte volume.

drills.q: Cost a RAG support assistant at 1M conversations/day, 6 turns, 4k input + 300 output tokens, then make it viable and order the levers by risk.
drills.a: Input 2.4e10 = 24,000 M tokens/day x $2/M = $48k/day; output 1.8e9 = 1,800 M x $10/M = $18k/day; ~$66k/day = ~$2M/month, unviable. Embeddings are 3e8 tokens/day at ~$0.02/M = $6/day, so retrieval is free relative to generation and must not be optimised first. Levers: prompt caching (~80% of input is a stable prefix, cache reads ~10% of input price) ~3.6x; context diet from 4k to 1.5k via top-3 reranking ~2.7x; model routing of the easy 70% to a Flash-class model at ~20x cheaper ~2.5x; Batch API -50% for non-interactive. Composed ~24x to ~$80k/month. Ship caching and context reduction first (no quality coupling) and routing last, since a wrong route on a billing question is a support escalation.

drills.q: Size a vector index for 100M chunks at 1024 dimensions, and say which is more expensive, building or serving.
drills.a: float32: 1e8 x 1024 x 4 B = 410 GB; HNSW M=32 stores up to 64 layer-0 neighbour ids at 4 B plus upper layers, ~300 B/node = 30 GB; ~440 GB total and it must be RAM-resident, so ~600 GB with headroom = 3-4 shards of 256 GB. int8 quantisation gives 4x (~132 GB, one node) at 1-2 recall points, recoverable by over-fetching top-50 and reranking against float32. Binary gives 32x (~13 GB) with an NVMe float32 rerank of the top-100. Cost ~$5,000/month to ~$700/month, a 7x lever. Serving beats building by ~40x: embedding 100M chunks at ~400 tokens = 4e10 tokens at ~$0.02/M is ~$800 one-time versus $700-5,000/month forever. So the sizing question is a MEMORY question, and re-embedding the corpus with a better model is cheap.

drills.q: Name a number you would refuse to estimate, and say how you make a decision without it.
drills.a: p99.9 latency, or anything driven by variance rather than volume: queueing under bursty arrival, GC pauses, lock contention, noisy neighbours, retry amplification. Also anything within 2-3x of a hard cliff (a memory boundary, a provider rate limit, an SLO edge), because there a 3x error changes the architecture. Instead of predicting the tail, design so the tail cannot hurt you: a timeout well inside the budget, a bulkhead so one slow dependency cannot consume the fleet, a queue so bursts become latency instead of errors, and an explicit load-shedding rule.

drills.q: First thing you do when told 'design RAG over 10 million documents'.
drills.a: Convert the number. ~6 pages and ~10 chunks of 400 tokens per doc is ~100M chunks and ~40B tokens. Only then can you choose an index, because a 10M-vector and a 100M-vector system are different architectures.

drills.q: Bytes per vector at 1024 dimensions for fp16, int8 and binary quantization.
drills.a: fp16 2 KB, int8 1 KB, binary (1 bit/dim) 128 bytes. So 100M vectors is 200 GB / 100 GB / 12.8 GB before graph overhead, which is why you search binary and rescore full precision.

drills.q: At what vector count does a dedicated vector database start earning its operational cost?
drills.a: Roughly 5-10 million. Below that, pgvector on the Postgres you already run is the right answer and adding a stateful system is cost with no measurable benefit.

drills.q: Honest production hit rate for a semantic cache, and the starting threshold.
drills.a: 20-45% for most workloads, 30-70% on FAQ-shaped traffic. Threshold is embedding-model specific (~0.83 MPNet, ~0.78 Albert); GPTCache's suggested 0.7 is too loose. Start near 0.92, watch false positives for 48 hours, tune down in 0.01 steps.

drills.q: Users with restrictive permissions report 'no results found' far more often than everyone else. Diagnose.
drills.a: ACLs are being applied AFTER retrieval, so top-k is computed over documents the user cannot see and then emptied. Trace signature: results_before_filter=10, results_after_filter=0. Fix: push tenant and ACL predicates into the ANN filter, and accept that filtered ANN is slower and filter cardinality now affects p99.

drills.q: Recall@10 dropped 30 points overnight with no change to the retriever code. What happened?
drills.a: The embedding model changed (or a library default did) without a reindex, so queries embedded with model B are being searched against an index built with model A. Fix: make the embedding model id part of the index name and refuse to query on mismatch.

drills.q: Judge scores are high and users keep reporting that the numbers in answers are wrong. Most likely cause.
drills.a: A chunk boundary split a table from its header, so the value is right and the label is wrong. Fluent, well-cited, and incorrect, which is exactly what a judge rewards. Fix: layout-aware chunking with tables atomic up to a hard cap, header propagation, and a table-specific eval slice.

drills.q: Why two-tier rate limiting in a gateway rather than just a Redis check?
drills.a: A pure Redis check adds a round trip to every request and makes Redis a hard dependency; local-only permits N-fold overshoot with N replicas. Admit locally against a leased share of the global budget, refresh the lease every ~200 ms, and state the bounded overshoot per lease window as a number rather than hiding it.

drills.q: Your gateway ledger under-reports 12% against the provider invoice. Where is the leak?
drills.a: Streaming. Tokens are accounted on normal stream close but not on client disconnect, and the provider still bills the partial generation. Fix: account on both paths, reconcile nightly against the provider usage export, and alert at 3% drift.

drills.q: One tenant's 3 AM batch job triples everyone else's p99. Two mitigations.
drills.a: Per-tenant RPM/TPM buckets so no tenant can consume shared capacity, plus a global reserve pool that no single tenant can exceed. Secondary: separate priority queues so interactive traffic is not behind batch, and a per-tenant concurrency cap on the runner pool if agents are involved.

drills.q: Uniform VLM parsing of 4M pages/day versus adaptive routing. Show the arithmetic.
drills.a: Uniform VLM: 4M x $0.006 = $24k/day = $720k/month. Routed at 60% text-layer ($0.0002) / 30% OCR ($0.0015) / 10% VLM ($0.006): $480 + $1,800 + $2,400 = ~$4.7k/day = ~$140k/month. A 5x saving, which is why the router is the first design decision and not an optimisation.

drills.q: A guardrail service adds 3 detectors at 25 ms each. How do you keep it off the critical path?
drills.a: Run the detectors in PARALLEL (not chained, so ~25 ms not 75 ms) and run the whole input rail CONCURRENTLY with retrieval, which makes it nearly free on the wall clock at the cost of retrieval work you may discard. Batch on GPU for throughput. The real cost is not compute, it is the false-positive rate.

drills.q: Your guardrail block rate dropped to zero overnight and nobody noticed. What is the bug and the general lesson?
drills.a: A detector timed out or errored and the rail failed open. Lesson: set fail-open versus fail-closed explicitly per rail (PII egress fails closed, a topic classifier fails open) and alert on a ZERO block rate, because the absence of a signal is a signal and monitoring only for spikes misses this entire class.

drills.q: Semantic cache hit rate rose from 30% to 70% after a threshold change. Ship it?
drills.a: Not without a hit-quality audit, because that is the exact shape of a false-positive increase. Shadow-sample 2-5% of hits through the miss path and compare with the judge for a continuous false-positive estimate. Track hit rate and hit QUALITY as two metrics; a hit-rate improvement with no quality audit is not an improvement.

drills.q: Agent A calls agent B across team boundaries. Whose permissions and whose budget?
drills.a: Permissions: the originating principal's, INTERSECTED with the callee's scopes, never unioned, or you have built privilege escalation by composition (a confused deputy, and the enterprise MCP identity-propagation gap in a different costume). Budget: hierarchical, with the child's spend counting against the parent's ceiling, or a nested call is an unbounded budget hole.

drills.q: GDPR erasure request against an agent memory service. Why is this not a DELETE?
drills.a: Deletion must reach fact rows, embeddings, graph edges, extraction job logs, trace payloads, downstream caches, and eval fixtures if real user data leaked into them. That is a data-lineage requirement: a per-user partition key propagated everywhere plus a documented, tested erasure job with a completion report. Answering 'delete from the memory table' shows you have never shipped this under a privacy review.

drills.q: Eval scores are up and production quality is down. Diagnose and prevent.
drills.a: Overfitting to the golden set, or the set no longer represents traffic. Prevention: a 20% holdout never used for iteration, continuous human-reviewed live sampling into the set, and a MEASURED correlation between eval-score delta and production-metric delta over the last N releases. If that correlation is weak your gate is decorative. Being able to state the correlation is a level marker; 'we have 400 evals' is not.

drills.q: How fast can a 5% prompt canary detect a 3 percentage-point quality regression, and what is the only way to go faster?
drills.a: Roughly 400 scored sessions are needed to detect a 3 pp judge delta, so at 5% of 8,000 sessions/day that is ~400/day: a one-day detection floor regardless of tooling. The only way faster is a larger canary share, which trades exposure for detection speed. State that as the tradeoff rather than promising faster detection.

drills.q: Deflection is 55% and the business is unhappy. Explain.
drills.a: Deflection alone is uninterpretable. Either the intent mix shifted toward easy categories (resets deflect >70%, nuanced complaints rarely break 25%, so the headline moves with mix not quality), or the agent stopped escalating things it should, which raises deflection while re-contact rate and CSAT fall. Diagnose by slicing by intent and pairing with re-contact; the fix is sometimes to lower deflection deliberately.

drills.q: You routed 58% of traffic to a cheap model, the bill is down 45%, and aggregate judge scores are flat. Why is that not sufficient evidence?
drills.a: Because a flat aggregate hides per-slice erosion: one intent can be down 12 points while the mean moves 0.1. Score quality PER ROUTE, sliced by intent and tenant, and alert on route-level regression, never on the aggregate. Also verify per completed TASK rather than per token, because a weaker model that malforms tool calls and loops extra times costs more and is slower.

drills.q: A table spans three pages of a PDF. What does a naive pipeline do and what is the fix?
drills.a: Page-by-page processing loses it: three fragments, none with the full header context, all individually fluent and jointly wrong. Fix: detect continuation by repeated headers and column-signature match, merge before chunking, and keep the merged table as one chunk even if it breaks the size target.

drills.q: Code assistant: why can inline completion not use the repo index?
drills.a: The latency contract. p95 200 ms leaves no room for a network round trip plus ANN plus rerank, and acceptance rate falls as p95 crosses ~300 ms. Inline uses local buffer context, imports and recent edits with a small cached model; chat (p95 ~2 s) uses graph-plus-vector retrieval; agentic edit uses tools iteratively over minutes. Three tiers, three context strategies, and conflating them is the most common error in this design.

drills.q: Design a multimodal video search system. Do not use any design from the module.
drills.a: Same six slots. Clarify: hours of video, sampling rate, is audio in scope, latency, tenancy. Write path: decode, sample keyframes, caption/embed frames, transcribe audio, align on timecode, index both modalities. Read path: two-stage, ANN over frame and transcript embeddings then a VLM rerank on top candidates, returning timecoded segments. Decisions: sampling rate against recall, per-frame versus per-shot embedding, unified versus per-modality index. Cost: frames-per-hour times embedding cost on write, VLM rerank on read. Failure: sampling misses a short event, observable as recall collapsing on brief-action queries.

drills.q: Name four GenAI designs you would refuse to build, with the threshold.
drills.a: RAG when the corpus is under ~50-100k tokens of stable content (use a cached prefix and delete five failure modes). A dedicated vector DB under ~5-10M vectors (use pgvector). A gateway below ~$10-20k/month of spend or a handful of consumers. An orchestration platform below 5-10 agents. Also: cross-session memory in v1, a semantic cache on low-repetition or auth-dependent answers, a guardrail service presented as the security boundary, self-hosting below ~40-50% sustained utilisation, and a router before the bill has been attributed.

drills.q: List the nine sections of the design-doc template in order.
drills.a: Context and constraints; requirements including NON-GOALS; architecture plus decomposition criterion; key decisions (chose X over Y because Z, accepted cost C); data model; scale numbers; failure modes symptom-first; what I would change now; hardest questions with answers.

drills.q: How many boxes in an interview diagram, and how long to narrate it?
drills.a: At most nine boxes, 90 seconds, left-to-right data flow, drill-down target in the middle. More than nine and you have drawn deployment topology instead of architecture.

drills.q: Compute the vector payload for 1.2M rows at 512 dimensions, float32, and say what it implies.
drills.a: 1.2M x 512 x 4 bytes = ~2.5 GB. It fits in memory on a single node, so a distributed vector store buys capacity you do not need, which is the first argument for indexing in place.

drills.q: 'Why not a real vector database?' Give the three reasons in priority order.
drills.a: 1) Every query is filtered by tenant and locale; colocating vectors with relational columns makes the filter a native predicate with granule pruning rather than a metadata filter on an ANN index. 2) ~2.5 GB fits in memory on one node. 3) One fewer system to keep consistent, backfill and page on. Plus a documented migration trigger: ~10x rows, a second consumer, or a hard hybrid-search requirement.

drills.q: Retrieval latency grows superlinearly as tenants are added. Diagnose it.
drills.a: tenant_id is not a prefix of the ClickHouse ordering key, so the tenant filter cannot prune granules and the query degrades to post-filtering, over-fetching by the inverse of the selectivity. It is a table-definition problem, not an ANN tuning problem.

drills.q: A tenant has only 50 skill items. Is the shared HNSW index the right retrieval path?
drills.a: No. Below a few thousand vectors an exact scan is both faster and exact, and HNSW graph connectivity degrades at small cardinality. The retrieval path should choose by tenant cardinality. A shared index with a tenant filter is still better for small tenants than a per-tenant index would be, but exact search is better still.

drills.q: Derive peak rps and the uncached downstream call rate for the recommendation platform.
drills.a: 2M users, 10% DAU = 200K; 5 views each = 1M requests/day; /86,400 = ~12 rps average; 5-10x peak = 60-120 rps. At 100+ content IDs hydrated per request, uncached that is 6,000-12,000 downstream calls/sec, which is why the cache is load-bearing rather than an optimisation.

drills.q: 'Why eight services? Convince me it wasn't resume-driven architecture.'
drills.a: Criterion: independent scaling and independent failure, not tidy entities. Three profiles diverge: latency-bound serving, throughput-bound ingestion, batch profile processing. Colocating means provisioning for the worst and letting a batch run take down serving. Then concede: eight is more than the criterion justifies, at least two would be merged today because they always changed and deployed together, and the cost was continuous (eight pipelines, eight dashboard sets, distributed tracing for one user question).

drills.q: A hot cache key expires and every replica stampedes the external API. Fix it.
drills.a: Jittered TTLs so keys do not expire in lockstep; single-flight or a short per-key lock so one fetch populates all waiters; stale-while-revalidate so waiters get the old value while one refreshes. Jitter alone is partial: the herd is a concurrency problem, not just a scheduling one.

drills.q: State precisely what MCP gives you that a shared library does not, and the cost.
drills.a: Versioned contracts and consumer independence: a library couples every consumer to your release cycle, language and runtime, so a breaking change is a coordinated upgrade across every importer. Cost: a network hop and serialisation per tool call, plus operating the servers. Wrong choice for a latency-critical inner loop; right for a pipeline measured in seconds per item.

drills.q: 'Most multi-agent systems are one agent with extra latency.' Respond, then name a merge candidate.
drills.a: State the test: separate agents only when failure modes, scaling profiles or deploy cadences genuinely differ. Transcript processing fails on malformed input, chunking fails by producing bad boundaries (a quality failure, not an error), gap detection fails by producing unaccepted findings; three different on-call responses and rollback decisions. Merge candidate: transcript processing and contextual chunking, which always run in sequence on the same input. Keep gap detection separate: different trigger and cadence.

drills.q: Three sequential agent steps at 95% each. End-to-end success? At ten steps and 85%?
drills.a: 0.95^3 = ~86%, so roughly one in seven runs fails somewhere. 0.85^10 = ~20%. This is the argument for checkpointing rather than retry tuning: checkpointing removes the multiplication by making the failed step the only work redone.

drills.q: What limits concurrency on a vLLM endpoint? Derive it for an 8B fp16 model on a 24 GB GPU.
drills.a: KV cache, not FLOPs. ~16 GB of weights leaves ~6-7 GB after framework overhead. KV per token is roughly 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x 2 bytes, order 100-200 KB/token for an 8B-class config, so ~30,000-60,000 tokens of aggregate context, i.e. roughly 15-30 concurrent sequences at 2,000 tokens. Present it as an order-of-magnitude derivation with assumptions named.

drills.q: GPU utilisation is 40% and inference is slow. What is wrong and what is the wrong move?
drills.a: KV cache exhaustion: the GPU is idle because it cannot admit more sequences, so requests wait for cache blocks. Fixes: reduce max sequence length, reduce max concurrent sequences, or add GPU memory. The wrong move is reading 40% as spare capacity and adding traffic.

drills.q: Why Bedrock batch offline and self-hosted vLLM online? Defend running two providers.
drills.a: Different workload shapes: online is latency-bound with concurrent short requests and wants owned capacity plus continuous batching; offline is throughput-bound with nothing waiting and wants the cheapest per-token option with NO capacity coupling to serving. Pushing a 1M-row job through the real-time endpoint is how a scheduled job becomes a latency incident. Two providers is only worth it when offline volume is large enough to move online p99; below that, one path with a priority queue is simpler.

drills.q: Your PySpark job calls an LLM from 20 executors. How do you avoid rate limiting, and what is the classic trap?
drills.a: Bound in-flight concurrency rather than relying on retry, because a rate limit is a throughput ceiling and retrying into it amplifies load. Trap: a per-executor budget multiplies by executor count, so 20 executors at 10 in flight is 200. A global budget requires a shared counter (a distributed rate limiter) with its own choice between failing closed (stalls the job) and failing open (recreates the problem). Reducing executor count is the wrong fix: it throttles the whole job for one stage.

drills.q: A batch inference job reports success but downstream data is incomplete. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Batch inference fails PARTIALLY: rows fail on content filtering, malformed input or length limits, and the job completes with fewer output rows. Missing rows look like absent data rather than failed processing, so it is silent. Fix: row-count reconciliation between input and output, a failure manifest, and a downstream contract that refuses partial input. Keep row_count and rows_failed in your own job table, not only in provider logs.

drills.q: 'How would you scale this 10x?' Give the four-step shape and apply it to the skill resolution engine.
drills.a: 1) Ask what is scaling: users, data, or requests per user. 2) Name what breaks first and why: the cross-encoder reranker, since it cannot be precomputed and its cost is linear in candidates times QPS. 3) Name the SYMPTOM: p99 growing while error rate stays flat, queue time growing faster than compute. 4) Fix and then what breaks next: cut top-k, batch across requests, consider a distilled cross-encoder; next constraint is index memory, sharded by tenant since tenant is already the query scope.

drills.q: Name the weakest part of each of the five flagship systems.
drills.a: Skills platform: no hybrid lexical stage, so exact matches pay for an embedding model. Recommendation platform: no off-policy evaluation, so every policy change was a live experiment. Agent pipeline: chunk quality is unmeasured and upstream of everything. LLM serving: no dollar cost model / break-even. Query Crafter: correctness was never measured, only adoption.

drills.q: 'You have described a lot of AI systems. Convince me you can do plain backend engineering.'
drills.a: Reach for the non-AI material: atomic concurrent updates on MongoDB, async client lifecycle under multi-worker servers, distributed cache design including thundering-herd handling, multi-tenant object-level authorization, a Java-to-Python migration with a verifiable cutover, an Airflow migration off Jenkins, and a pipeline rebuild from 4.5 hours to 30 minutes. None of that is AI work and all of it is why the AI systems stayed up. Reaching for another AI story after being asked for a non-AI one is the failure.

drills.q: What is a Bar Raiser, and what power do they hold?
drills.a: A trained interviewer from a different team than the hiring one, whose job is keeping the bar consistent by probing past your rehearsed layer, and who holds VETO power over the decision.

drills.q: How many LP questions should you expect in an Amazon loop, and how are they distributed?
drills.a: Roughly 12-15. Four to five back-to-back interviews, each interviewer assigned two to three specific LPs so the panel collectively covers all sixteen. Every round also has a technical component. Prepare two stories per heavily weighted LP, not one great story overall.

drills.q: Name the four LPs that cluster heaviest in engineering loops, and your lead story for each.
drills.a: Dive Deep (the OOM on 1.2M rows), Deliver Results (4.5h to 30min, ~89%), Invent and Simplify (3,447 Java lines removed for an 812-line Python service), Bias for Action (automating market risk pipelines from a Business Analyst seat).

drills.q: What does Amazon's Principal Engineering tenets material say about Deliver Results, and what replaces it as the bar?
drills.a: Deliver Results is a LOW BAR for a Principal Engineer. The bar is lasting impact that echoes through technology, product and company; clarity from complexity with problems framed in customer and business context; hands-on leading by example; educating the organisation about trends and approaches.

drills.q: Which two Amazon LPs have no story in this resume, and what is the fix?
drills.a: Hire and Develop the Best, and Strive to be Earth's Best Employer. Fix: write one real, small story each. Onboarding someone onto the platform, raising the code review bar, the 200+ tests as an enabling artifact for others, a runbook that stopped a recurring page, or running interviews. Small and true beats large and invented.

drills.q: Why does vagueness fail at Google specifically?
drills.a: Because the decision is made by a hiring committee who never interviewed you and reads only the written evidence packet. Anything that does not survive transcription (rapport, energy, the interviewer's general sense of competence) evaporates. Speak in complete sentences with the odd specific numbers: 54,486, 3,447, 307, 178,000.

drills.q: Name Google's four attributes and say what GCA is actually scoring.
drills.a: Role-Related Knowledge, General Cognitive Ability, Leadership, Googleyness. GCA scores whether your reasoning is structured and adaptive, not whether the answer was right, which is why announcing your reasoning structure aloud is itself evidence.

drills.q: Give a Googleyness story that would actually score, and one that would not.
drills.a: Scores: going back to your own service-decomposition criterion and testing each boundary against it rather than defending the design, with deploy coupling as the evidence. Does not score: saying you value intellectual humility, or a trivial regret with no cost. Googleyness must come through described behaviour, not stated values.

drills.q: Describe the Meta E6 onsite and the pre-onsite round.
drills.a: Onsite: one standard coding, one AI-assisted coding, one architecture, one design, one behavioural. Before the onsite, a Leadership Assessment interview replaces the standard phone screen at E6 and is roughly half behavioural and half coding. E7+ adds deeper design, deeper behavioural, and a cross-functional round graded on judgment under ambiguity.

drills.q: 'How do you work with AI coding tools, and when did you override one?' Give the shape of a passing answer.
drills.a: Where you use them (boilerplate, test scaffolding, unfamiliar API surfaces); where you do not (anything with a concurrency or authorization invariant); how you verify (tests you wrote yourself, reading the diff not the summary, a category rule about what you will not accept unread); then one concrete override with the reason. The authorization and concurrency work are exactly the categories where generated code is most dangerous.

drills.q: What is the Meta E6 scope bar, and which of your stories clear it?
drills.a: A disagreement must involve two or more TEAMS on a large project; impact must be on the ORG, not the team. Candidates that clear it: the credential mechanism across a service fleet, Query Crafter serving non-technical stakeholders in other functions, the Credit Suisse automation from a non-engineering seat, and Skillmaster integrated into another team's provisioning platform. Do not inflate the single-team stories; use a different one.

drills.q: What is Microsoft's As Appropriate round, how do you read it, and what should you do between rounds?
drills.a: The final round, usually a Principal Engineering Manager or Partner-level leader, tailored to your earlier performance with interviewers syncing notes first. Relaxed and pitching the team = sell mode. Aggressively probing gaps = borderline. Between rounds, write down your weakest answer and prepare the second pass; almost nobody does this and it is nearly free.

drills.q: Which four stories lead at Microsoft, and why is it the best fit on the list?
drills.a: 22-locale hardening (global readiness), cross-tenant authorization (multi-tenant security), Java-to-Python migration (legacy modernisation with a safe cutover), skill resolution engine (domain depth). Best fit because Microsoft's actual world is enterprise multi-tenancy, compliance, backward compatibility and migration of installed customers, which is where most of this resume sits.

drills.q: What must you rehearse for Netflix that no other loop demands?
drills.a: Verbal architecture with no whiteboard: number the components, state direction explicitly since there are no arrows, name them once and reuse the names. Multiple candidates report completing the Netflix system design round with no diagramming tool at all.

drills.q: How does the Netflix framing change your story delivery relative to Amazon?
drills.a: Candour is scored positively, so leading with 'eight services was too many, here's what I'd do instead' lands well. Do not over-structure: rigid STAR reads as corporate. Expect fewer prompts and keep talking through silence. Be willing to disagree with the interviewer once, well. At Amazon the same candour needs a completion: what you'd do instead and the trigger for the change.

drills.q: Describe the OpenAI loop and say where your prep effort should go.
drills.a: Resume screen, recruiter call, role-specific skills assessment, gate-format technical screen (one problem escalating across ~4 stages, usually need to clear at least two), a PAID 48-hour work trial graded on shipping speed, code quality, design choices and tests, then a loop of four to six. Prep goes to the work trial: practise implement-to-spec then refactor as constraints are added, with tests. Polishing behavioural answers for this loop is misallocated.

drills.q: 'Why did you self-host instead of using an API?' Answer for an AI lab, including the gap.
drills.a: Volume growth against linear per-token pricing, plus tenant data-handling expectations. Critically: not self-host everything, but split by workload shape (self-hosted vLLM online, Bedrock batch offline, hosted frontier for tasks that need it). The gap, stated directly: no dollar break-even model was built; you optimised for throughput and control. Then offer the derivation live rather than inventing a percentage, because an interviewer who runs GPU capacity knows the numbers.

drills.q: 'What's your view on multi-agent systems?' Take a defensible position and survive the follow-up.
drills.a: Position: most multi-agent systems are one agent with extra latency and an ambiguous failure mode; the test is whether failure modes, scaling profiles or deploy cadences genuinely differ. Then your own system as evidence, including the accepted cost (network boundaries, distributed failure model, tracing to debug one run). Follow-up 'are you defending your own?': name the merge candidate (transcript processing and chunking, same input, always sequential) and what stays separate (gap detection, different trigger and cadence).

drills.q: Which metric set do you use in which room?
drills.a: Product set (2M+ users, ~25% engagement, 50% report turnaround) for Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. Systems set (throughput, cost per million tokens, p99, 1.2M rows, ~2.5 GB index, KV-cache-bound concurrency) for AI labs and infrastructure roles. Know which set applies within the first thirty seconds of a round.

drills.q: When should you NOT apply company-specific tailoring?
drills.a: Do not name a Leadership Principle while telling the story: exhibit the behaviour, do not narrate the rubric. Do not memorise mission statements; know the loop and the rubric instead. Do not apply structured STAR at a twelve-person startup. Do not lead with product metrics for an infrastructure role. And never let tailoring override truth: if Meta wants multi-team scope and your story is single-team, use a different story rather than inflating, because inflated scope collapses on 'which teams, and what did they want?'

drills.q: State the five phases of a 45-minute design round with their minute markers.
drills.a: 0-2 restate + declare plan; 2-5 requirements (scale, 2-3 features, dominant NFR, non-goals); 5-8 estimation; 8-22 high-level breadth end to end; 22-40 deep dives; 40-45 close. Checkpoint deliberately at 22.

drills.q: Give your opening 25 seconds for 'design a multi-tenant vector search service'.
drills.a: Restate the problem in one sentence, declare the plan (four minutes on requirements, quick estimation, sketch end to end, then deep dive wherever is most useful), and end with a question asking if that works. Do not name a single technology in the first thirty seconds.

drills.q: What is the highest-value clarifying question in the round, and why?
drills.a: 'Which of these matters most: latency, consistency, availability, or cost?' It decides most of your tradeoffs and you can refer back to their answer every time you make one.

drills.q: Fix this: 'What are the requirements?'
drills.a: 'I'll assume the core is A, B and C. Anything critical I'm missing?' Propose then let them correct. Asking them to enumerate requirements asks the interviewer to do your job.

drills.q: Do an estimation for a 2M-user recommendation product and end it correctly.
drills.a: 2M users, 10% DAU = 200K; 5 views each = 1M requests/day; /86,400 = ~12 rps average; 5-10x peak = ~100 rps, which is small. Then the required ending: each request hydrates ~100 content items, so uncached that is 10,000 downstream calls/sec, which tells me the caching layer is where the design lives.

drills.q: Give the seven-step deep-dive structure and say which step is the staff signal.
drills.a: Name the problem; state the constraint; two or three real options; choose with the reason; state the cost accepted; go one level below the choice; volunteer the failure mode. The last one, unprompted, is the staff signal.

drills.q: Use the tradeoff template on: one vector index with a tenant filter, or an index per tenant.
drills.a: 'One index with a filter, because per-tenant indices multiply operational surface and small tenants would each have too few vectors for a well-connected HNSW graph. What I'm giving up is that I now have to make sure the filter prunes rather than post-filters, which is a table-definition problem.'

drills.q: The interviewer asks 'how would you scale this?' Give the four steps and do step 3 properly.
drills.a: Ask what is scaling; name the component that breaks first and why; name the SYMPTOM (p99 growing while error rate stays flat, queue time growing faster than compute time, not an error just slow); then the fix and the next constraint. Step 3 is the one that proves you have operated the system.

drills.q: Why is 'and at 100x?' a different question from 'and at 10x?'
drills.a: At 10x you tune and shard; at 100x specific architectural assumptions break and you must name which. Giving the same list of techniques at both scales is a junior tell.

drills.q: You realise your rate-limiting design is wrong. Recover out loud in six steps.
drills.a: Stop mid-sentence. 'Let me back up, I don't think that works.' Say why: a per-executor budget multiplies by executor count, so twenty executors at ten in flight is two hundred. Give the fix: the budget has to be global, which means a shared counter, i.e. a distributed rate limiter. Name the new cost: if the counter is unavailable I choose between failing closed and failing open. Move on without over-apologising.

drills.q: The interviewer says 'are you sure?' twice about a decision you believe is correct. What do you do each time?
drills.a: First push, if it is pressure without new information: restate the reasoning once and name what would change your mind. Second push: take it seriously regardless and ask directly what you are missing. Continuing to defend past the second push is disqualifying at any level.

drills.q: Rewrite each as a senior sentence: 'we'd just add a cache', 'obviously shard by user ID', 'MongoDB because it's scalable'.
drills.a: 'A cache helps here; the hard part is invalidation, so ___.' / 'I'd shard on user id, accepting that a very large tenant creates a hot partition, which I'd handle with a composite key.' / 'A document model fits because the access pattern is one read per user profile with no cross-entity joins.'

drills.q: Why is 'we need CP by CAP' a red flag, and what is the correct framing?
drills.a: CAP describes behaviour only DURING a partition, and 'pick two of three' is the classic wrong answer. The correct framing is PACELC: partition-free, this is a latency-versus-consistency choice; during a partition, here is what I would do.

drills.q: Describe a four-component system verbally with no whiteboard.
drills.a: Number them, state direction explicitly, name them once: 'Four components. One, an edge service resolving tenant and user. Two, context holding user features. Three, retrieval over a vector index. Four, scoring. Edge fans out in parallel to two and three; both feed four. Separately and asynchronously, an event processor writes into the store two reads from, so ingestion and serving are decoupled.' Then check in.

drills.q: Close a round at minute 40. Name the four elements.
drills.a: What you built; why the key decision was made; what you know is unfinished; what you would do next. Naming your own gaps at the close is the cheapest remaining calibration signal and interviewers write it down.

drills.q: Feedback says 'strong technically, concerns about communication.' Diagnose and give two fixes.
drills.a: Jargon density plus components described without tradeoffs. Fixes: the no-orphan-nouns rule (every technology followed by a 'because [this problem]' in the same sentence), and one explicit tradeoff per deep dive with the counter-argument stated ('the argument for the other side is ___, and it wins if ___').

drills.q: 'Which part of your design are you least confident about?' Answer without collapsing.
drills.a: Name a specific assumption plus the measurement that resolves it: 'the tenant-size distribution. My design assumes tenants are large enough that ANN is the right algorithm; if most have a few hundred items, exact search is both faster and exact, which changes the retrieval path.' If pressed with 'so your design is wrong', the answer is no: it is conditional on a named assumption you would verify.

drills.q: When does the framework in this module NOT apply?
drills.a: When the interviewer explicitly redirects (their signals always override the script, and following the script through a redirect is the most avoidable failure there is); in a resume deep-dive round, where there is no requirements phase; in a 30-minute round, where you compress but never cut the deep dive; at an early-stage startup, where five minutes of requirements for a 400-user system reads as heavyweight; and when you do not know the domain, where reasoning from first principles with acknowledged ignorance is a legitimate answer.

drills.q: Give the time split for a STAR answer, in percentages and seconds.
drills.a: S 10% ~15s, T 10% ~15s, A 50% ~90s, R 15% ~25s, rejected alternative 10% ~20s, redo 5% ~10s. Candidates invert it by spending most of the answer on Situation.

drills.q: How many sentences is the 60-second version, and what happens next?
drills.a: Nine: 1 Situation, 1 Task, 3 Action, 1 Result, 1 rejected alternative. Then stop and offer a direction. The 3-minute version is never given unprompted.

drills.q: The interviewer says 'tell me about the hardest bug you've debugged.' Which story, and what is the opening sentence?
drills.a: The OOM on 1.2M multilingual rows. Open on the symptom: the process was killed with no Python traceback, which is the kernel OOM killer rather than an application exception.

drills.q: Why not just raise the memory limit on the embedding job?
drills.a: Peak memory scaled with corpus size rather than batch size, because the whole ClickHouse result set was materialised into Python objects. Raising the limit relocates the failure to the next growth step, and the corpus grows by design.

drills.q: Is gc.collect() at page boundaries a good fix? Defend or concede.
drills.a: Concede: it compensates for CPython allocator and cycle-collector behaviour rather than removing the cause. The structural fix is streaming with generators and bounded batches. Placement still mattered: inside the hot loop it would destroy throughput; at page boundaries the pause amortises over thousands of rows.

drills.q: Defend the ~25% engagement uplift. What must your answer contain, in order?
drills.a: Metric definition first, comparison design second (holdout vs staged rollout vs pre/post), confounders you could not remove third. Volunteer the method before being asked. If it was pre/post, say so and name why a holdout was unavailable. Never claim a controlled experiment you did not run.

drills.q: 'Why eight services and not one?' Answer in three moves.
drills.a: 1) Name the criterion: independent scaling and independent failure, not data entities; three profiles diverge (latency-bound serving, throughput-bound ingestion, batch processing). 2) State the real cost before they do: eight pipelines, eight dashboard sets, distributed tracing needed to answer one user question. 3) Volunteer the merge: at least two would be merged today, because services that always change and deploy together are one service plus a network hop.

drills.q: Why was patching only the endpoints you found the wrong fix for the cross-tenant authz bypass, and why is middleware insufficient?
drills.a: The class of bug is authorization decided per endpoint; fixing instances leaves the class. Middleware sees the route and the token but generally cannot see which object IDs the handler is about to load, so enforcement belongs on the object-fetch path keyed on the authenticated tenant. The design fix behind the code fix: make tenant identity a required non-defaultable parameter rather than a convention.

drills.q: Someone assumes you dropped functionality going from 3,447 Java lines to 812 Python lines. Respond.
drills.a: Most of the Java was Spring Batch scaffolding: item readers, writers, processors, job and step configuration. The transformation rules were a small fraction of it. The new service also added explicit multi-tenant isolation the old one lacked.

drills.q: Why a contextual bandit rather than a gradient-boosted ranker, and what was missing from your evaluation?
drills.a: A ranker trained on logged clicks learns the previous policy's preferences, so unseen content is never shown and never generates the data that would justify showing it; offline replay cannot detect this because it scores against the logged policy. Missing: off-policy evaluation via inverse propensity scoring, which meant policy changes were effectively live experiments.

drills.q: 'Tell me about a time you failed.' Give the story and the one thing your answer must contain.
drills.a: The over-decomposition of the platform (or the knowledge-graph attribution gap: shipped alongside content embeddings, contribution never isolated). It must contain a COST: extra deploy overhead, a component you cannot justify, time spent. A failure with no cost is not a failure.

drills.q: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed.' What is the follow-up you must be able to survive?
drills.a: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed and were WRONG.' Without it, every disagreement story reads as 'I was right and they came around'. Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit is two clauses and most candidates evidence only the first.

drills.q: How do the MongoDB race and the async event loop error differ in cause, and what were the wrong fixes?
drills.a: Race: read-modify-write across a network round trip is not atomic; wrong fix is app-level locking (serialises the hot path), right fix is an atomic update operator with a filter condition. Loop error: a client created on one event loop used from another, or a module-level client outliving its loop; wrong fix is broad try/except (converts a correctness bug to a silent one), right fix is loop-scoped client lifecycle tied to startup and shutdown. Both are invisible at parallelism one, which is what most test suites use.

drills.q: Name the six stories you cannot enter a senior loop without.
drills.a: Disagreed and was wrong. A real failure with a real cost. Said no and lost. Influenced without authority. Reframed a wrong requirement. Prevented an expensive mistake.

drills.q: The write-up says 'insufficient evidence of impact beyond own team.' Which stories fix this, and what makes them work?
drills.a: The credential mechanism adopted across a service fleet, Query Crafter unblocking non-technical stakeholders in other functions, the Credit Suisse automation done from a Business Analyst seat, and the Skillmaster integration into another team's provisioning platform. What makes them work is naming which teams and what the coordination actually was, rather than inflating single-team work.

drills.q: Why must golden-baseline assertions be aggregate rather than exact-match?
drills.a: A semantic system that must return byte-identical output cannot be improved. Separate 'must never change' (locale precedence, tenant scoping, pagination: exact) from 'may drift within tolerance' (resolutions, rankings: aggregate with tolerance bands). A new embedding model changes every vector but should be a no-op at the assertion level if resolution decisions are preserved.

drills.q: Define grain and explain the asymmetry that makes it the most consequential dimensional modeling decision.
drills.a: Grain is the precise definition of what one fact-table row represents, stated as a business-process sentence. The asymmetry: you can always aggregate a fine grain up to a coarser one in a query, but you can never disaggregate a coarse grain back down once the detail wasn't captured - a wrong grain choice requires rebuilding history, not migrating it.

drills.q: Star vs snowflake schema: what's the actual tradeoff, and when would you choose snowflake over the star default?
drills.a: Star flattens each dimension into one denormalized table (fewer joins, faster typical BI queries); snowflake normalizes dimension hierarchies into sub-tables (smaller storage, easier single-point updates, more joins). Star is the default because storage is cheap and join count dominates latency; choose snowflake when a hierarchy attribute changes independently and frequently enough that updating one normalized row beats rewriting a denormalized column across a huge dimension table.

drills.q: Explain additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures, and describe the classic error each miscategorization causes.
drills.a: Additive (revenue, units) sums safely across any dimension. Semi-additive (account balance, inventory) sums safely across some dimensions (accounts, at a point in time) but not others (time) - summing across time gives a meaningless number. Non-additive (ratios, unit price) should never be summed directly; naive averaging ignores differing row weights, so the correct computation recomputes from underlying additive components (sum(revenue)/sum(qty), not avg(price)). Getting this wrong produces a plausible but silently incorrect dashboard number with no error.

drills.q: Walk through SCD Type 2 mechanics precisely and explain why it structurally requires a surrogate key.
drills.a: On a tracked attribute change, the current row is closed (valid_to set, is_current flipped false) and a new row is inserted with a new surrogate key, the new value, and an open valid_to. The natural key stays constant across versions, but a natural key alone can't represent one entity having multiple valid attribute versions without breaking key uniqueness - the surrogate key gives each version distinct identity so fact rows unambiguously reference the version correct at the time the fact occurred.

drills.q: Compare SCD Types 1, 2, 3, and 6, giving a scenario where each is the right choice.
drills.a: Type 1 (overwrite, no history): fixing a typo where history has no value. Type 2 (versioned rows): address or sales-rep changes needing point-in-time-correct historical reports. Type 3 (previous-value column): a 'current vs immediately prior' comparison report needing no deeper history. Type 6 (hybrid 1+2+3): when reports need both a point-in-time-correct join and an always-current value in the same row without a second join.

drills.q: What is a conformed dimension, and why do drill-across queries depend on it?
