drills.a: A dimension built once with consistent surrogate keys, attribute definitions, and grain, reused identically across every fact table referencing that entity type. Comparing metrics across fact tables (e.g. sales volume vs support-ticket volume by customer segment) requires both facts to agree on what the segment means and how customers map to it - without conforming, two independently-built dimension variants make cross-fact comparisons meaningless even though the query runs and returns a number.

drills.q: A fact table mixes order-level summary rows (one shipping-fee row per order) with order-line-level rows (one per product). Diagnose the problem and the fix.
drills.a: This is a mixed-grain fact table, a correctness bug: any naive SUM(amount) double-counts or miscounts unless every query remembers to filter by row type. Fix by splitting into separate fact tables at consistent grains (order-level and line-item-level), or allocating the shipping fee proportionally into the line-item grain if a single table is required - structurally removing the failure mode rather than relying on query-author discipline with a row_type discriminator.

drills.q: What is the one-big-table (OBT) debate in dimensional modeling, and where does OBT genuinely make sense versus star schema?
drills.a: Modern columnar engines' compression and vectorised execution let a fully denormalized wide table match or beat star-schema join performance, but it sacrifices conformed-dimension reuse and update locality (a changed shared attribute must be rewritten everywhere it's embedded). OBT makes sense for narrower, single-purpose marts serving a few closely related reports; star schemas remain more maintainable for warehouses serving many fact tables that need to share dimension definitions consistently.

drills.q: Design a dimensional model for a subscription business needing both 'MRR as of any historical month' and 'current subscription tier per customer', explaining the fact table type and SCD choice.
drills.a: A periodic snapshot fact table (one row per subscription per month) captures MRR and status at each month-end - semi-additive, summable across subscriptions at a point in time but not across months. dim_plan/dim_customer use SCD Type 2 so each snapshot joins the tier active in that month, correctly attributing historical MRR. Type 6 on dim_plan (current-tier column plus Type 2 versioned columns) supports 'current tier' queries without an extra join to find the latest version.

drills.q: Why is 'you can always aggregate up but never disaggregate down' the central argument for grain, and when does that argument not fully apply?
drills.a: A fine-grained fact table can always produce a coarser total via SUM(), but a coarse-grained table can never recover finer detail it never captured. The argument weakens when the source system itself never records finer-grained detail at all (you can't extract line-item detail from a source that only ever stored order totals), in which case achievable grain is bounded by the source, not a free modeling choice.

drills.q: How does a semantic layer (dbt MetricFlow, Cube, LookML) change how measure additivity is handled versus raw analyst SQL, and what does it NOT replace?
drills.a: It lets teams declare a measure's correct aggregation rule once (e.g. balance resolves to latest-value, never summed across time), enforced automatically across every downstream query or dashboard built against it, rather than depending on every analyst remembering the rule. It doesn't replace the analytical judgment of correctly classifying a measure as additive/semi-additive/non-additive in the first place - it only prevents inconsistent application of that classification once made.

drills.q: What is Kimball's bus matrix and what problem does it prevent?
drills.a: A grid of business processes/fact tables against shared candidate dimensions, built and agreed on before teams independently build fact tables. It prevents the scenario where two teams build incompatible versions of what should be the same conformed dimension (e.g. two different dim_customer definitions), catching the conflict during planning rather than discovering it after both fact tables are already in production.

drills.q: Explain why composite index column order matters, using the 'usable prefix' rule.
drills.a: A composite B-Tree index is sorted lexicographically by its key columns. Only a left-anchored prefix, ending at (and including) the first range/inequality predicate, can be used to narrow the scan; columns after that point can only filter rows already found. Equality columns should go first, the one range column last.

drills.q: What is an index-only scan, what does it require, and how do you confirm it's actually happening in EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
drills.a: A scan answered entirely from the index's leaf pages with zero heap fetches, requiring every needed column present in the index and the visibility map confirming no MVCC check against the heap is needed for the relevant pages. Confirm via 'Index Only Scan' plus 'Heap Fetches: 0' in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output; a nonzero heap-fetch count means the visibility map is stale and VACUUM is needed.

drills.q: When is a partial index the right choice over a full index, and what must be true for the planner to use it?
drills.a: When queries consistently filter on a predicate matching a minority subset of rows, giving a much smaller index with write cost only on matching rows. The planner must be able to prove the query's WHERE clause implies the partial index's condition, which is reliable for exact or closely-matching predicates but not a general theorem prover.

drills.q: Compare GIN and GiST for indexing JSONB/full-text data, including the fastupdate tradeoff.
drills.a: GIN lookups are ~3x faster than GiST but ~3x slower to build with high write overhead since a row can fan out into many inverted entries; best for read-heavy static data. GiST is lossy (executor rechecks candidates) but cheaper to update, better for write-heavy dynamic data. fastupdate on GIN buffers writes into a pending list, trading read-latency variance for cheaper writes.

drills.q: What does BRIN store and what single condition makes it completely useless?
drills.a: BRIN stores a min/max-style summary per physical block range rather than per row, giving a tiny index. It's useless if the underlying data isn't physically correlated with the indexed column (check pg_stats.correlation) - if row order on disk doesn't track logical column order, the summary covers the whole value range per block and provides no pruning.

drills.q: An UPDATE on a table with 6 indexes is slower than expected even though it changes only one indexed column. Explain why.
drills.a: Updating any indexed column disables Postgres's HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) optimization for that row's update, forcing a new entry in every index on the table, not just the one on the changed column - so a single-column update pays the write cost of maintaining all 6 indexes.

drills.q: How do you decide whether an existing production index is safe to drop?
drills.a: Check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan over a representative window long enough to capture periodic jobs (a week, not an hour) - zero scans across that window is a strong candidate. Also check redundancy: an index on (a) is often superseded by one on (a,b) via prefix usability. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY with monitoring rather than an irreversible drop.

drills.q: Why does the planner ignore a B-tree index on a low-selectivity column (e.g. a boolean or 3-value status on a 10M-row table)?
drills.a: Once estimated selectivity crosses roughly single-digit percent of the table, random-access index-then-heap-fetch reads for that many matching rows cost more than one sequential scan pass, so the planner correctly prefers a sequential scan - leaving the index as pure write overhead with zero read benefit.

drills.q: Design the indexing strategy for a multi-tenant SaaS table where over 99% of queries filter by tenant_id plus one other varying column, and discuss the noisy-neighbor tenant case.
drills.a: Put tenant_id as the leading column on several composite indexes, one per common (tenant_id, X) access pattern, rather than one giant index. If one tenant is orders of magnitude larger than others, a shared tenant_id-leading index still works correctness-wise but that tenant dominates cache residency and I/O - partitioning by tenant_id turns the skew into physically isolated data structures, which indexing alone can't solve.

drills.q: What is the single biggest performance lever on a query that already uses an index efficiently, and what's the cost of chasing it too far?
drills.a: Making it an index-only scan via a covering index, eliminating the per-row heap fetch (often the dominant cost as random I/O) - can be 5-10x+ faster when the heap doesn't fit in cache. Cost: every INCLUDEd column still needs write maintenance on every insert/update, so a covering index with a wide INCLUDE list can approach the write cost of a second copy of the table; only include what the specific hot query actually needs.

drills.q: A table has an index on (customer_id, status, created_at). A common query is WHERE created_at > X ORDER BY created_at with no customer_id or status filter. Does the index help, and what should you do instead?
drills.a: Barely, if at all - customer_id is unconstrained so the composite ordering doesn't group rows usefully for this query; scanning the whole index is generally worse than a sequential scan. A separate index on (created_at) alone would actually serve this query.

drills.q: How do you build a new index on a busy production table without blocking writes, and what's the risk?
drills.a: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids the exclusive lock a plain CREATE INDEX takes for the whole build, at the cost of requiring two full table scans instead of one and the risk of leaving behind an INVALID, unusable index if the build is interrupted - which must then be manually dropped and retried.

drills.q: Explain the read-then-write race condition in MongoDB precisely, and why findOneAndUpdate fixes it structurally rather than just 'being atomic.'
drills.a: A find() followed by a separate update() leaves an unprotected window between the read and write where a concurrent request can perform the identical read (seeing the same pre-update state) and act on the same stale decision. findOneAndUpdate evaluates the filter condition and applies the mutation as one atomic server-side operation, so there's no separate application-level check step for a concurrent caller to race against - if the condition no longer holds by execution time, it simply matches nothing.

drills.q: What is the trap that catches engineers who already know findOneAndUpdate exists, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Performing a separate prior find() to decide whether to call findOneAndUpdate at all, then basing business logic on that separate read rather than on findOneAndUpdate's own return value - this reintroduces the identical race with an extra read in front of it. The condition must be evaluated inside the atomic operation's own filter, never in application code beforehand.

drills.q: Rank the five approaches to fixing a check-then-write race in MongoDB and explain when you'd reach for something beyond the cheapest option.
drills.a: 1) Atomic update operator with the condition embedded in the filter - cheapest, for simple comparisons. 2) findOneAndUpdate with a conditional filter - when you need the document back in the same round trip. 3) Optimistic concurrency via a version field - when the condition is too complex for a simple filter comparison. 4) Unique/partial index - when the invariant is uniqueness itself. 5) Multi-document transactions - only for genuinely cross-document invariants no single atomic operation can express.

drills.q: Explain WiredTiger's document-level concurrency model and how it improved on MongoDB's original MMAPv1 engine.
drills.a: WiredTiger uses MVCC (readers get point-in-time snapshots, never blocked by writers) plus fine-grained intent locking down to the document level via optimistic concurrency control - only writers targeting the SAME document actually serialize; different documents in the same collection proceed with zero contention. MMAPv1 locked at the collection level, meaning any write could block unrelated concurrent writes to the same collection - a much coarser model WiredTiger's adoption as default (MongoDB 3.2) fixed.

drills.q: What is the unbounded array anti-pattern, why does it degrade performance well before the 16MB document limit, and what's the fix?
drills.a: An array embedded in a document that grows indefinitely (e.g. an activity log) eventually forces the document to exceed its allocated disk space on append, causing WiredTiger to relocate the entire document - turning an incremental append into a full-document rewrite with progressively worsening write latency, long before the 16MB hard limit is hit. Fix: the bucket pattern (bounded sub-documents per time window/count) or moving the growing data into its own referenced collection.

drills.q: Explain w:1 vs w:majority write concern and precisely what can happen to a w:1 write during a primary failover.
drills.a: w:1 is acknowledged once only the primary applies the write, before it necessarily replicates anywhere. If the primary fails before replicating it and a different secondary (without that write) is elected primary, the write is rolled back despite being acknowledged as successful. w:majority requires majority acknowledgment before success, and because any future primary must have replicated at least as far as any majority-acknowledged write, it survives any failover.

drills.q: What does a causally consistent session guarantee beyond plain readConcern:majority, and how is it different from linearizability?
drills.a: Plain majority reads only guarantee non-rollback-able data, but successive reads in the same session routed to secondaries with different replication lag can still appear to go backward in time. A causally consistent session tracks a logical clock across the session's operations, guaranteeing read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, and writes-follow-reads - a strictly weaker and cheaper guarantee than linearizability, which orders operations across ALL clients globally, not just within one causal session.

drills.q: Why does a monotonically increasing shard key create a worsening hot-shard problem, and what does hashed sharding trade away to fix it?
drills.a: Range-based sharding on a monotonic key means every new document's value exceeds all previous ones, so every write lands in the chunk owning the highest range on one shard - the problem gets worse as write volume grows, not better with more shards. Hashed sharding spreads monotonic values pseudo-randomly across shards, fixing the hot-shard problem, but destroys the ability to route a range query on that field to a contiguous subset of shards - range queries then scatter-gather across all shards.

drills.q: Why is $lookup typically much more expensive than a relational join, and what's the senior guidance on using it?
drills.a: $lookup performs close to a nested-loop-with-index when the foreign collection has an index on the compared field, but degrades toward a full collection scan per input document without one - a worse cost curve than a relational hash/merge join over the same data, with cross-shard $lookup adding network overhead on top. Guidance: use it sparingly, always index the foreign field when used, and treat a constant $lookup pattern on a hot path as a signal to embed the data instead.

drills.q: When should you reach for multi-document transactions in MongoDB, and why is 'we use transactions for most of our writes' considered a schema smell?
drills.a: Use them for operations genuinely spanning multiple documents/collections that no reasonable embedding could avoid, like a funds transfer between two account documents. Needing transactions across most hot-path writes suggests the schema wasn't designed around MongoDB's core strength (atomic single-document operations on well-embedded documents), and is a signal to revisit the schema rather than to keep relying on transaction overhead (held resources, execution time limits, added latency) as the default correctness mechanism.

drills.q: A sharded MongoDB cluster has one shard at 90% disk/CPU while others sit at 30%. Diagnose the likely causes and explain what MongoDB 8.0's improved resharding tools do and don't fix here.
drills.a: Likely a shard key problem: low cardinality (too few distinct values to split chunks), a monotonically increasing key concentrating writes on one shard, or skew (one dominant value, e.g. a large tenant). Diagnose via the key's value/chunk distribution (sh.status()). MongoDB 8.0's sh.shardAndDistributeCollection() makes the operational process of fixing a bad key faster once identified, but doesn't retroactively fix the underlying data/access-pattern skew itself - genuine tenant skew needs an architectural response like isolation, not just faster rebalancing.

drills.q: Design a job-claiming mechanism for a shared MongoDB job queue that guarantees no job is claimed by two workers, and explain the schema pitfall to avoid.
drills.a: Each job is its own document (status: pending/claimed/done). A worker claims via findOneAndUpdate({status:'pending'}, {$set:{status:'claimed', claimed_by, claimed_at}}, {sort:{priority:-1}}) - the atomic filter-plus-update ensures only one worker's call can transition a given job, since a concurrent worker's identical query won't match it once claimed. Add a staleness check and periodic reclaim for crashed workers. Avoid storing jobs as array elements on one 'queue' document (unbounded-array anti-pattern) - each job must be its own document in its own collection.

drills.q: Explain Postgres's xmin/xmax visibility rule precisely.
drills.a: A tuple version is visible to a snapshot if xmin's transaction committed before the snapshot was taken, and either xmax is unset (still live) or xmax's transaction has not committed as of the snapshot. Checked per-tuple during a scan.

drills.q: Why does MVCC let readers never block writers, unlike 2PL?
drills.a: A reader simply reads an older, already-committed row version instead of waiting for the newest write to finish - it never needs a lock on the current version. Writers still conflict with other writers on the same row, but reader-writer blocking is eliminated entirely.

drills.q: Name all six concurrency anomalies with a one-line definition each.
drills.a: Dirty read (uncommitted write visible), dirty write (overwrite an uncommitted write), read skew (same row, two reads in one txn, different answers), phantom read (predicate result set changes mid-txn), lost update (same-row read-modify-write, one write clobbers another), write skew (disjoint rows, writes jointly violate an invariant neither alone violated).

drills.q: Walk through the doctors-on-call write skew example in full, two transactions.
drills.a: Invariant: >=1 doctor on call. Alice's txn reads count=2 from its snapshot, decides safe to go off-call, updates Alice's row, commits. Bob's txn concurrently reads count=2 from its own snapshot, decides safe, updates Bob's row, commits. Final count=0. No write-write conflict was ever detected because the two updates touched different rows.

drills.q: Why does snapshot isolation stop read skew but not write skew, mechanically?
drills.a: Read skew is prevented directly because a fixed snapshot gives internally consistent repeated reads. Write skew is a violated cross-transaction invariant caused by disjoint writes - SI's conflict detection only checks for same-row write-write conflicts, which never occurs in write skew since the rows written are different.

drills.q: Give the real default isolation level for Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
drills.a: Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server: Read Committed. MySQL/InnoDB: Repeatable Read (with gap locks suppressing most phantoms beyond the ANSI minimum).

drills.q: Is Oracle's SERIALIZABLE actually serializable? What's the practical consequence?
drills.a: No - Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation under a different name; it implements neither SSI nor 2PL-style predicate locking. Write skew remains possible on Oracle SERIALIZABLE, so you must add explicit row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) to actually protect a cross-row invariant.

drills.q: Explain how Postgres's SSI detects write skew without blocking any reader.
drills.a: SERIALIZABLE transactions take non-blocking SIREAD locks on data they read. A later write to SIREAD-covered data creates an rw-antidependency edge. A cycle of two such edges through a pivot transaction (a dangerous structure) triggers a serialization failure, aborting one transaction for retry - all without ever blocking a read.

drills.q: An account balance goes negative despite a CHECK(balance >= 0) constraint and every individual UPDATE looking correct. Diagnose.
drills.a: Lost update or write skew between two concurrent balance-modifying transactions under Read Committed or Snapshot Isolation. A single-row CHECK constraint can't catch a cross-row/cross-transaction invariant violation. Fix: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new value, or run at SERIALIZABLE and handle retries.

drills.q: Design the fix for a flight-booking system where two transactions might both book the last seat.
drills.a: Best: atomic conditional UPDATE flights SET seats_available = seats_available - 1 WHERE id=? AND seats_available > 0, checking the affected-row count - folds check-then-write into one atomic statement, no separate stale read. Alternatives: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before deciding, or SERIALIZABLE with retry handling.

drills.q: Why do predicate locks matter, and what happens under pure 2PL without them?
drills.a: Row locks alone only guard rows that existed when the lock was taken - a newly inserted row matching the same query condition slips through unnoticed (a phantom). Predicate locks lock the range/condition itself, catching new matching rows too.

drills.q: What operational risk comes from XID wraparound, and what prevents it?
drills.a: 32-bit XIDs wrap every ~4 billion transactions; ambiguity in xmin comparisons could cause data corruption. Autovacuum's freeze rewrites old tuples' xmin to a frozen sentinel. An under-vacuumed high-write table risks Postgres forcing read-only mode as the counter approaches the limit.

drills.q: When would you choose SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over running the whole transaction at SERIALIZABLE?
drills.a: When you know exactly which rows back the invariant and want to pay locking cost only there, rather than SIREAD bookkeeping and a higher retry rate across the whole transaction. Risk: missing one of the dangerous reads silently reintroduces the anomaly with no warning - SERIALIZABLE doesn't require hand-enumerating them.

drills.q: Why does MySQL choose a stronger default isolation level (Repeatable Read) than Postgres/Oracle/SQL Server (Read Committed)?
drills.a: Historically tied to statement-based replication needing more deterministic read behavior to replay correctly across replicas - Repeatable Read's stronger per-transaction snapshot consistency reduced a class of replication correctness bugs that Read Committed's per-statement snapshot would have made harder to reason about.

drills.q: Define a functional dependency and explain how every normal form is derived from it.
drills.a: X -> Y means every row sharing the same X must have the same Y - X determines Y. 2NF forbids partial dependencies on part of a composite key, 3NF forbids transitive dependencies through non-key attributes, BCNF forbids any determinant of a non-trivial FD that isn't itself a candidate key - all defined purely in terms of which FDs are permitted relative to the candidate keys.

drills.q: Walk through 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF using an order-line table with composite key (order_id, product_id) that also stores customer_id and customer_city.
drills.a: 1NF: no comma-separated/multi-valued columns - one row per (order, product) line item already satisfies this. 2NF: customer_id depends only on order_id, not the full composite key - a partial dependency, fixed by extracting orders(order_id, customer_id). 3NF: customer_city depends on customer_id, not directly on order_id - transitive, fixed by extracting customers(customer_id, customer_city).

drills.q: What loophole does BCNF close that 3NF leaves open, and give a concrete example.
drills.a: 3NF only forbids non-key attributes transitively depending on the key; it permits a determinant that's part of a candidate key but not a full candidate key itself, in a table with overlapping candidate keys. Example: course_enrollment(student_id, course_id, instructor), key (student_id, course_id), with course_id -> instructor - this is 3NF but violates BCNF since course_id doesn't determine student_id and thus isn't a candidate key, yet is a determinant.

drills.q: Why isn't BCNF decomposition always dependency-preserving, and why does that matter operationally?
drills.a: Decomposing to BCNF can split a functional dependency across two tables such that verifying it requires rejoining them, losing a single-table constraint check that 3NF decomposition guarantees to preserve. It matters because enforcing a business rule via a cross-table join or trigger is more operationally fragile than a simple single-table constraint.

drills.q: Define a multi-valued dependency and give a 4NF violation example, distinguishing it from a plain many-to-many relationship.
drills.a: X ->> Y means the set of Y values for a given X is independent of any other attribute in the table. A 4NF violation combines two INDEPENDENT multi-valued facts into one table, e.g. product_tags_warehouses(product_id, tag, warehouse_id) forcing a cross product (3 tags x 2 warehouses = 6 rows instead of 5). A single many-to-many relationship (tags alone) needs only one join table and is already fine at 3NF/BCNF - 4NF specifically concerns combining two independent multi-valued relationships into one table.

drills.q: Name the three classic anomalies and explain why a single 2NF/3NF violation usually causes all three simultaneously.
drills.a: Update anomaly (duplicated fact inconsistently updated), insert anomaly (can't record one fact without an unrelated one), delete anomaly (deleting one fact accidentally erases another). A single misplaced/duplicated functional dependency typically causes all three at once because the same duplicated data creates update risk, blocks independent insertion, and risks accidental deletion - fixing the underlying FD via decomposition resolves all three together.

drills.q: When is denormalization a sound engineering decision rather than a shortcut, and what's the difference between denormalization and caching?
drills.a: Sound when a read-heavy access pattern pays a real cost for joins/aggregation, the duplicated data changes rarely enough for the anomaly risk to be low, AND you can name the specific anomaly reintroduced plus a consistency mechanism (trigger, write-through, CDC sync, accepted staleness). Unlike a cache (a derived, disposable copy safely rebuilt from source of truth), a denormalized column in the transactional schema is itself a claimed source of truth, raising the consistency bar.

drills.q: A customers table stores both city and state, with a business rule that every city belongs to exactly one state. Is this technically a normalization violation, and does it matter in practice?
drills.a: Technically yes - city -> state with city not a candidate key makes state transitively reachable, a 3NF violation in the strict sense. In practice it's often accepted because city/state combinations rarely change and duplication is small; it becomes worth fixing if cities need frequent corrections or state needs its own attributes (population, tax rate) requiring a join anyway.

drills.q: How do you empirically verify whether a candidate functional dependency holds in real data, and what's the limit of that verification?
drills.a: Group rows by the candidate determinant and check whether every group has one consistent dependent value - a group with multiple distinct values proves the FD is violated in the sample. Finding zero violations only strongly suggests the FD holds; it doesn't logically prove it for all future data, since a business rule can be true by convention but not yet violated in the sampled data.

drills.q: Design the schema for a projects feature with multiple collaborators (with roles) and multiple tags per project, and explain which normal form issue you're avoiding.
drills.a: projects(project_id PK, name), project_collaborators(project_id, user_id, role, PK(project_id,user_id)), project_tags(project_id, tag, PK(project_id,tag)) - two separate join tables rather than one combined table, avoiding a 4NF violation since collaborators and tags are independent multi-valued facts; combining them would force a cross product (3 collaborators x 4 tags = 12 rows instead of 7).

drills.q: Why do star schemas and OLAP dimensional models count as the clearest legitimate default case for denormalization?
drills.a: Their read pattern (few large scans, infrequent updates to dimension data) makes the anomaly risk low and the join-avoidance benefit high - denormalization there is a first-class design tool by default, not an exception requiring special justification, unlike frequently-updated OLTP data where normalization is close to a hard requirement.

drills.q: What is the practical default normal form target for OLTP schemas, and when should you go further?
drills.a: 3NF (or BCNF where they diverge) as the default - it eliminates essentially all common update/insert/delete anomalies with a manageable table count. Push to 4NF/5NF only when a genuine, identified multi-valued-dependency problem exists, not reflexively, since higher normal forms trade off against join complexity.

drills.q: Explain why row storage suits OLTP and columnar storage suits OLAP, in terms of physical layout.
drills.a: OLTP touches a few full rows (fetch/update one entity) - row storage keeps a row's fields physically adjacent so one I/O retrieves everything needed. OLAP touches a few columns across millions of rows (aggregates) - columnar storage keeps each column's values adjacent so the engine reads/skips exactly the needed columns, and each column compresses better since it's a single data type.

drills.q: Where does most of a columnar engine's 10-100x speedup over row-at-a-time execution actually come from?
drills.a: Both I/O savings (reading only needed columns, plus 5-20x compression from within-column redundancy) and vectorised execution (batch processing 1000s of values per operator call, SIMD-friendly and cache-friendly) rather than row-at-a-time interpretation. The CPU-efficiency piece from vectorisation is a large, often underestimated fraction of the total speedup.

drills.q: Explain dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, and delta encoding, and why they work better on columns than rows.
drills.a: Dictionary encoding replaces repeated values with small integer codes referencing a shared dictionary (good for low-cardinality columns). Run-length encoding stores (value, count) pairs for consecutive repeats. Delta encoding stores the difference from the previous value for monotonic columns like timestamps or IDs. All three exploit redundancy within one column's homogeneous values, which a heterogeneous row (mixing an ID, name, age, salary) doesn't have.

drills.q: State the honest limitation of HTAP systems and explain how TiDB and Snowflake Unistore each manage (not eliminate) it.
drills.a: The same CPU, memory, and I/O bandwidth ultimately serve both workloads - a zero-sum resource contention problem architecture can bound but not remove. TiDB runs two separate replicated engines (TiKV row store, TiFlash columnar), which can be placed on separate nodes - architecturally closer to CDC replication inside one product. Snowflake Unistore uses one unified engine, avoiding replication lag but paying for it with a hard throughput ceiling (~1,000 ops/sec at ~500GB active data), far below a dedicated OLTP engine.

drills.q: What is chunk skipping / predicate pushdown in a columnar engine, and what commonly breaks it even on a partitioned table?
drills.a: Columnar files are split into row-group chunks with stored min/max statistics; a predicate is checked against chunk stats before reading any actual data, letting the engine skip non-matching chunks entirely. It breaks when the filter is on a column that isn't the physical partition/cluster key, or when the filtered column is wrapped in a function (e.g. DATE(created_at)=X), preventing the engine from evaluating it against stored statistics - directly analogous to the expression-index sargability problem.

drills.q: A nightly analytics report is degrading checkout latency. What do you diagnose first, and why might a columnar engine not be the right immediate fix?
drills.a: First determine if the problem is resource contention (the report consuming I/O/cache the transactional workload needs) versus the report being inherently slow. If it's contention, routing to a dedicated read replica is simpler and faster than adopting a columnar engine, and directly solves the isolation problem - conflating an isolation problem with a genuine analytical-performance problem leads to over-engineering.

drills.q: Derive roughly how much less data a columnar query reads compared to a row-store query for a 50-column table where only 2 columns are needed, and explain when this advantage shrinks.
drills.a: Ignoring compression, roughly 25x less data (2/50 columns), and with typical 5-20x compression on top, total reduction can be 100x+. The advantage shrinks toward parity (and can reverse) as the fraction of columns needed per query approaches the whole row, since columnar storage then pays overhead reassembling many separate column files into a row with no compensating I/O savings.

drills.q: Why can't isolating compute resources alone (separate hardware for OLTP and OLAP) fully solve the OLTP-vs-OLAP problem without also choosing the right storage layout?
drills.a: Even on fully separate hardware, a row store answering an OLAP-shaped query still reads unnecessary columns and gets none of the compression/vectorisation benefit a columnar layout provides. Compute isolation and storage-layout choice are two separate, both-necessary levers, not substitutes for each other.

drills.q: Design the data architecture for a fraud-detection system needing both live transactional writes and near-real-time aggregate risk scores per user, and note where a stricter sub-second requirement changes the design.
drills.a: OLTP engine (Postgres/MySQL) handles transactional writes with full ACID guarantees. CDC off the WAL streams changes into a columnar/streaming layer (ClickHouse or a stream processor) computing per-user risk features with seconds-level freshness; the scoring service reads live transaction context from OLTP and aggregate features from the CDC-fed layer. If one specific feature genuinely needs zero staleness, compute that feature in-line in the OLTP path itself rather than making the whole pipeline real-time.

drills.q: Why did ETL-into-a-separate-warehouse emerge as the classic architecture, and what specific pain did it solve?
drills.a: Running heavy analytical queries directly against the row store serving live transactions caused multi-minute scans to hold locks and consume buffer pool/cache the transactional workload needed, degrading OLTP latency unpredictably. Physically separating the workloads onto separate hardware via nightly batch ETL eliminated that contention, at the cost of data being hours-to-a-day stale.

drills.q: When is CDC-into-a-columnar-store preferable to adopting a true HTAP database?
drills.a: When you want workload isolation without adopting a more operationally complex database product - CDC keeps the two engines fully separate (preserving the isolation that solves OLTP-starves-under-reporting) and typically achieves seconds-to-tens-of-seconds freshness, satisfying most 'near real-time' requirements without HTAP's added complexity. True HTAP earns its complexity only when sub-second consistency between transactional and analytical views is a validated, real requirement.

drills.q: State the single diagnostic question that resolves most OLTP-vs-OLAP storage placement decisions, and give the follow-up questions for the remaining cases.
drills.a: Does a single request touch one entity or millions of rows? One entity -> OLTP shape; millions -> OLAP shape (resolves ~80% of cases). For the rest: what staleness is acceptable for the analytical side (sub-second vs seconds-minutes vs hours), what's the write pattern (frequent small ACID writes vs bulk/streaming append), and is the actual pain reporting slowness or reporting degrading the transactional system (which a read replica alone may fix)?

drills.q: Why does every Postgres UPDATE leave a dead tuple behind, and does plain VACUUM shrink the table file?
drills.a: Postgres never updates in place - it marks the old tuple's xmax and inserts a new version, leaving the old one as a dead tuple until VACUUM reclaims it. Plain VACUUM only reclaims space for reuse within the existing file; it does not shrink the file on disk. Only VACUUM FULL (exclusive lock, full rewrite) or pg_repack (online) actually shrink it.

drills.q: Explain transaction ID wraparound and why Postgres responds with a hard stop rather than gradual degradation.
drills.a: 32-bit XIDs wrap every ~4 billion transactions with an unambiguous comparison window of about 2 billion in either direction; an unfrozen old xmin risks appearing invisible or ambiguous once the counter wraps, which is a correctness/data-loss risk, not just a performance issue. Postgres defends by refusing to assign new transaction IDs once the oldest unfrozen XID nears the danger zone, forcing the database read-only rather than risk silent corruption - alert on age(datfrozenxid) well before the ~2 billion hard limit to avoid ever hitting it.

drills.q: What is a HOT update, what disqualifies a row from it, and why does fillfactor matter?
drills.a: A HOT update writes the new tuple on the same page with a forwarding pointer, touching zero indexes - possible only if no indexed column changed and the new tuple fits on the same page. Breaking either condition forces a full update that writes a new entry in every index on the table. Setting fillfactor below 100% reserves free space on frequently-updated tables specifically to keep rows HOT-eligible for longer.

drills.q: Why is autovacuum's default scale_factor (0.2) dangerous specifically on very large tables, and what's the fix?
drills.a: The trigger is dead_tuples > threshold + scale_factor * total_rows; on a 500-million-row table, 20% means 100 million dead tuples accumulate before autovacuum even runs, which is far too much bloat on a high-churn table. Fix with a per-table override (ALTER TABLE ... SET autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor lower, e.g. 0.01) rather than changing the global default, which would waste I/O vacuuming small tables that don't need it.

drills.q: Explain the FIFO lock queue trap where a simple ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN causes a full outage.
drills.a: A long-running SELECT holds ACCESS SHARE; a queued ALTER TABLE needing ACCESS EXCLUSIVE waits behind it; every subsequent SELECT that arrives after the ALTER TABLE also queues, even though SELECT-SELECT would normally be compatible, because Postgres's lock queue is FIFO and the pending exclusive request blocks everything behind it. Mitigate by checking pg_stat_activity for long-running transactions and setting lock_timeout before running DDL.

drills.q: What is TOAST, and why can SELECT * on a wide table with a large JSONB column be slower than expected even for few rows?
drills.a: TOAST transparently compresses and/or moves column values over roughly 2KB out of the main 8KB page into a chunked side table, leaving only a pointer in the row. Detoast cost is paid per row for every TOASTed column actually accessed in the query - SELECT * pays this for the large JSONB column even if the application only needs a couple of small fields, whereas selecting only needed columns (or using a covering index) avoids it.

drills.q: Why doesn't raising max_connections alone fix connection exhaustion, and what does PgBouncer's transaction pooling mode trade away?
drills.a: Each Postgres connection is a full OS process with several MB of memory and real setup cost, so raising max_connections without pooling trades connection refusal for memory exhaustion and context-switch overhead. PgBouncer's transaction pooling multiplexes many clients onto fewer backend connections but breaks session-level state that doesn't persist across a shared physical connection: prepared statements, session-level SET variables, and advisory locks held outside an explicit transaction.

drills.q: Why does a random UUIDv4 primary key cause worse index bloat and cache locality than a sequential integer, and what does uuidv7() trade off to fix it?
drills.a: A B-Tree benefits from insert locality - sequential keys append near the index's 'end,' keeping recent entries clustered and cache-resident. Random UUIDv4 scatters inserts uniformly across the whole key range, causing more page splits and cache misses. uuidv7() embeds a timestamp for monotonic ordering while retaining UUID uniqueness, but this means the ID leaks approximate creation time if exposed externally (e.g. in a URL) - a real tradeoff, not a strict improvement.

drills.q: Compare pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat, and state when a dedicated vector database is still the better choice.
drills.a: IVFFlat requires a training/clustering step, is faster to build, but generally has a worse recall/latency tradeoff. HNSW needs no training and is the current default recommendation for most workloads at moderate scale. A dedicated vector database is still preferable at hundreds of millions of vectors with strict recall/latency SLAs, where purpose-built engines' specialized memory layout and query execution outperform pgvector; pgvector wins when vectors need to live alongside relational metadata at moderate scale.

drills.q: A team disables autovacuum on a huge table because it interrupts their nightly batch load window. What's wrong with this and what should they do instead?
drills.a: Disabling autovacuum risks both bloat and, more dangerously, that table's tuples aging past the freeze threshold, contributing to database-wide XID wraparound risk (age(datfrozenxid) is database-level, driven by the oldest unfrozen tuple anywhere). Better fixes: schedule autovacuum around the batch window via cost-delay tuning, or run a manual targeted VACUUM immediately after the load completes, rather than disabling the safety mechanism entirely.

drills.q: Why is sorting pg_stat_statements by total_exec_time usually more actionable than sorting by mean_exec_time, and when would you use mean/max instead?
drills.a: A query called 100,000 times at 5ms average costs far more aggregate database time (500 seconds) than a single 2-second outlier query - total_exec_time identifies where the database spends the most cumulative time, usually the more impactful optimization target. Use mean/max_exec_time instead when hunting a specific user-facing latency-SLO violation (a query occasionally spiking to 3 seconds), which is a tail-latency problem distinct from aggregate load reduction.

drills.q: Design a monitoring and alerting strategy for a production Postgres fleet covering the major internals failure modes, and say which one you'd implement first with limited time.
drills.a: Alert on age(datfrozenxid) per database well before the hard limit; alert on dead-tuple ratio per table cross-referenced with last_autovacuum timestamp; alert on logical replication slot lag/retained WAL directly; track pg_stat_statements total_exec_time trends over time; monitor pg_locks/pg_stat_activity for long-running transactions. Implement XID age monitoring first - it's the cheapest (one query, one threshold) and protects against the single most catastrophic, entirely preventable failure mode (a hard-stop outage), while the others are gradual-degradation problems with more runway to catch.

drills.q: Walk through the full pipeline a SQL query goes through before it executes.
drills.a: Parse (syntax to AST) -> rewrite (expand views, flatten subqueries) -> plan enumeration (candidate access methods/join algorithms/join orders) -> cost estimation (using pre-collected statistics, not live data) -> execution of the chosen lowest-estimated-cost plan.

drills.q: Give the three join algorithms with their complexities and best-case conditions.
drills.a: Nested loop: O(N*M), or O(N log M) with an index on the inner side - wins when one side is small/indexed. Hash join: O(N+M) - wins on large unsorted equality joins. Merge join: O(N+M) if both sides pre-sorted on the join key (else pay a sort first) - wins when both come from index scans already in order.

drills.q: What is the single most important signal in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and why?
drills.a: Estimated vs actual row count at each node. A large divergence (commonly 10x+) means the plan decisions built ABOVE that node were made on a false premise - it's usually a more direct explanation for slowness than any individual cost number, since it indicates the plan shape itself is likely wrong.

drills.q: Your WHERE clause filters on two correlated columns (city and state) and the row estimate is way too low. Why, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Classic cost models multiply each predicate's individual selectivity assuming independence; correlated columns violate that, making the combined estimate far too low. Fix with CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) ON (city, state) FROM table - the planner does not detect this correlation automatically.

drills.q: A query's plan uses nested loop join and is extremely slow on a large table. Diagnose it step by step.
drills.a: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), check estimated vs actual rows on the outer side of the nested loop. If actual is far higher, the planner wrongly believed the outer side was small. Fix: ANALYZE the table, check for correlated-column misestimation, verify autovacuum is keeping pace. Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the plan shape actually changes.

drills.q: Why does Postgres default random_page_cost to 4.0, and when should you change it?
drills.a: It models random disk access as 4x more expensive than sequential - appropriate for spinning-disk seek-time assumptions. On all-SSD storage, lower it (commonly 1.1-2.0) so the planner is more willing to choose index scans over sequential scans where appropriate - but verify improvement with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, don't assume from hardware alone.

drills.q: What is GEQO, and does it always mean a worse plan for wide joins?
drills.a: Genetic query optimization - past geqo_threshold (default 12 tables), Postgres switches from exhaustive dynamic-programming enumeration to a genetic algorithm since combinatorial join-order enumeration becomes too slow. Not always worse in absolute terms, but no longer guaranteed optimal - worth raising the threshold or restructuring the query for a frequently-run wide-join query where plan quality matters more than planning latency.

drills.q: Explain hash join's build/probe sides and what Batches>1 means in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output.
drills.a: The build side (smaller estimated input) is loaded into an in-memory hash table; the probe side streams through looking up matches. If the build side's actual size exceeds work_mem, it splits into multiple batches and spills to disk (Batches>1) - a real I/O cost the original cost estimate may not have predicted if the cardinality was underestimated.

drills.q: How do you decide whether a slow query needs a new index, updated statistics, or a rewritten query?
drills.a: Start with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Estimated/actual diverge sharply -> fix statistics first (ANALYZE, extended stats, higher target) before adding an index. Statistics accurate but no efficient access path exists -> add the index, then re-verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Both fine but still slow -> examine query shape (function-wrapped predicate, correlated subquery, SELECT *).

drills.q: You add the 'obviously correct' index and the planner doesn't use it. Why might that be correct behavior?
drills.a: If the cost estimate (correctly or not) shows the filter matching a large fraction of rows, a sequential scan can genuinely cost less than an index scan's random I/O regardless of index availability - low-selectivity predicates rarely benefit from an index. Verify the estimate justifies the index before assuming the planner is being obtuse.

drills.q: What's the operational hazard of running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DML statement, and how do you avoid it?
drills.a: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query, so an UPDATE/DELETE really happens with real side effects. Wrap it in a transaction and roll back (BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;), or test against a non-production copy.

drills.q: Why does WHERE lower(email) = 'x' defeat normal column statistics even if the email column itself has good stats?
drills.a: Statistics (MCV list, histogram) are collected on the raw column values, not on the result of a function applied to them, so the planner can't use them to estimate the wrapped expression's selectivity accurately. Fix with an expression index and/or extended statistics on the exact expression.

drills.q: Why does adaptive query execution exist in Spark SQL / cloud warehouses but not in traditional single-node OLTP planners?
drills.a: OLTP queries are short and latency-sensitive at the millisecond level, so runtime re-planning overhead is proportionally far more expensive relative to total cost than in a long analytical query over terabytes - the cost/benefit strongly favors adaptive execution for long analytical workloads, not short transactional ones.

drills.q: State Postgres's four default planner cost constants and what each represents.
drills.a: seq_page_cost=1.0 (sequential disk page fetch), random_page_cost=4.0 (non-sequential fetch, 4x sequential - spinning-disk assumption), cpu_tuple_cost=0.01 (processing one row), cpu_operator_cost=0.0025 (evaluating one operator/function per row).

drills.q: What's the fundamental structural difference between a B+Tree and an LSM-Tree?
drills.a: B+Tree updates in place, staying sorted on disk always, paying reorganization cost (splits) per write. LSM-Tree never updates in place — writes buffer in a memtable, flush as immutable SSTables, and background compaction merges them, deferring reorganization off the write path.

drills.q: Derive B-Tree height for 100M rows with fanout 680.
drills.a: height = log_680(100,000,000) ≈ 3. With top levels cache-resident, a warm lookup is typically 1-2 real disk I/Os despite the log N framing.

drills.q: Define write, read, and space amplification with typical numbers for each engine family.
drills.a: WA = physical/logical bytes written, RA = disk reads per logical read, SA = physical/logical live bytes on disk. B-Tree: WA ~3-4x, RA ~1-2x, SA ~1.1-1.5x. LSM leveled: WA ~20-30x+, RA ~1-2x tuned / 5-10x+ untuned, SA ~1.1-1.3x tuned, spikes to 2x+ mid-compaction.

drills.q: Size-tiered vs leveled compaction: what's the actual tradeoff, and which minimizes what?
drills.a: Size-tiered: lower write amplification (~10-15x), but overlapping key ranges across files raise read amplification and space can spike toward 2x mid-merge. Leveled: higher write amplification (~20-30x+, data rewritten roughly once per level), but non-overlapping key ranges per level give lower read amplification and tighter space usage.

drills.q: Mechanically, what causes B-Tree write amplification vs LSM write amplification?
drills.a: B-Tree: one row update dirties a whole page (8-16KB), and the whole page flushes even though only a fraction logically changed; splits double this. LSM: a key gets physically rewritten roughly once per compaction pass, and the number of passes it survives grows with the number of levels the dataset has grown into.

drills.q: An LSM-backed store's read latency has been climbing for two weeks. What do you check first, and why not add an index?
drills.a: Check compaction metrics first: L0 file count and pending-compaction-bytes. Compaction has almost certainly fallen behind write throughput, so more files must be checked per read. Adding an index is a red flag here — the read path already uses the LSM's sorted structure and bloom filters; this is an operational compaction-debt problem on the write/background side.

drills.q: What does a bloom filter buy an LSM-Tree, with real numbers, and what happens under memory pressure?
drills.a: It gives a fast 'definitely not present / maybe present' check per SSTable; RocksDB's default ~10 bits/key yields ~1% false-positive rate, skipping disk reads on ~99% of files that don't contain the key. Under memory pressure, bloom filters can get evicted from cache, forcing a real disk read just to check membership — a common cause of latency regressions after a memory-limit change.

drills.q: State the RUM conjecture and explain why you can't minimize write, read, and space amplification simultaneously.
drills.a: Read, Update, Memory(space) amplification form a proven tradeoff triangle: optimizing any two makes the third worse. B-Trees optimize read and space at the cost of update cost; LSM-Trees optimize update cost at the cost of read and space — neither is a strict improvement, they occupy different points on the curve.

drills.q: Design the compaction strategy for a metrics/time-series system with 30-day uniform TTL retention.
drills.a: Time-Window Compaction Strategy: bucket SSTables by write-time window, compact only within a window, never merge across windows. When a window's TTL fully expires, drop the entire file(s) rather than rewriting to remove a few expired keys — turns expiry into a cheap file delete instead of a rewrite.

drills.q: Why does an LSM sometimes need close to 2x the dataset's logical size in disk space mid-operation?
drills.a: During a compaction (especially full/major compaction), the input SSTables and the newly-written merged output file coexist on disk until the merge finishes and inputs are deleted, temporarily requiring close to double the steady-state footprint. This must be planned for in disk provisioning, not just steady-state size.

drills.q: When would you choose Cassandra/RocksDB over Postgres, and what's the mistake version of that choice?
drills.a: Choose LSM-backed storage when sustained write throughput is the primary constraint and reads are less latency-sensitive or served through a separate cache/index. It's a mistake when the workload needs multi-row ACID transactions, complex joins, or is read-dominated with unpredictable access patterns — Postgres's B-Tree plus mature planner and transactions wins there.

drills.q: Why does B-Tree lookup cost stay roughly constant as data grows, while LSM write amplification grows with data size?
drills.a: B-Tree height (log_fanout(N)) grows extremely slowly with N at typical fanouts (~680), so per-write page touches stay roughly constant. LSM levels grow (each ~10x the last) as data volume grows, and a surviving key is rewritten roughly once per level it passes through, so total write amplification for long-lived keys scales with the number of levels.

drills.q: State the write-ahead logging protocol and explain why the ordering matters.
drills.a: A change's log record must be durable before its data page reaches disk, and a commit's log record must be durable before the client is told it committed. If the page reached disk first and the system crashed before logging, recovery would have nothing to explain or undo that on-disk change from.

drills.q: Walk through ARIES's three phases end to end.
drills.a: Analysis scans forward from the last checkpoint to build the Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table, finding the minimum recLSN to start redo from. Redo replays every logged change forward (committed and uncommitted alike), skipping any change already reflected in a page (LSN <= pageLSN). Undo then rolls back never-committed transactions in reverse order using Compensation Log Records, which make undo itself crash-safe.

drills.q: Why must redo be idempotent, and how does the pageLSN mechanism achieve that?
drills.a: Recovery itself can crash and need to restart against a database that already has some changes applied from a prior interrupted attempt. Each page stores the LSN of the last change it reflects (pageLSN); redo skips any log record with LSN <= that page's pageLSN, so re-running redo produces the same result as running it once.

drills.q: What is a checkpoint actually for, and why do production systems use 'fuzzy' checkpoints rather than stop-the-world ones?
drills.a: Solely to bound recovery time by giving analysis a recent starting point instead of the whole log history. Fuzzy checkpoints avoid a full consistent stop-the-world snapshot (which would hurt latency) and are safe because redo's idempotent, LSN-driven replay tolerates an inconsistent snapshot at checkpoint time.

drills.q: Production Postgres WAL directory is growing unboundedly toward disk-full. What's the most common cause and how do you catch it early?
drills.a: A disconnected or stuck replication slot (physical or logical) retaining WAL segments because nothing is consuming them, which blocks log truncation. Catch it by alerting on replication slot lag / retained WAL bytes directly, rather than waiting for total disk usage to trip an alert.

drills.q: Describe a real fsync failure mode that causes silent data loss, and how databases now defend against the kernel-level version of it.
drills.a: A volatile write-back disk cache without battery backing can ack a write before it's physically durable, losing it on power failure despite fsync returning success. Separately, a 2018-documented Linux kernel behavior cleared the dirty-page error flag after a failed fsync, so a later fsync on the same file could falsely report success. Databases now PANIC/crash on any fsync failure instead of retrying, since retrying risks reporting false success.

drills.q: What is group commit, why does it exist, and what's its cost?
drills.a: It batches multiple transactions' WAL records into one fsync call instead of fsyncing per commit, amortizing the fixed per-fsync latency across many transactions for an often order-of-magnitude throughput gain under concurrency. Cost: a small added latency for a transaction that would otherwise commit immediately alone, since it waits briefly for the batch window.

drills.q: Explain the difference between Postgres synchronous_commit=on and off, and when off is a legitimate production choice.
drills.a: on fsyncs the WAL before acking the client (full durability, higher latency). off acks before the fsync completes, risking loss of the last fraction-of-a-second of acked commits on an OS/machine crash (not a graceful shutdown). Legitimate for workloads like analytics ingestion or non-financial event logging where that bounded risk window is acceptable for higher throughput; wrong for anything resembling a financial ledger.

drills.q: What does full_page_writes protect against in Postgres, and why does WAL volume spike right after a checkpoint?
drills.a: It protects against torn pages - a crash interrupting a page write mid-flight, leaving it partly old and partly new bytes, which normal incremental WAL replay can't repair. Postgres logs the entire page content the first time it's modified after a checkpoint so recovery can restore a known-good full page, which is why WAL volume spikes right after each checkpoint.

drills.q: A production database takes 45 minutes to recover after a crash against a 5-minute SLA. Diagnose and fix, including the tradeoff of the fix.
drills.a: The checkpoint interval is almost certainly too long relative to write volume, so redo must replay a large amount of log from the last checkpoint. Tighten checkpoint_timeout/max_wal_size (or InnoDB equivalents) to force more frequent checkpoints. Tradeoff: more frequent checkpoints cost more steady-state I/O, which should be mitigated by spreading checkpoint I/O over the interval (checkpoint_completion_target) and provisioning dedicated I/O bandwidth, not just picking a smaller interval blindly.

drills.q: Why is kill -9 an invalid test of a database's durability guarantee, and what is a valid test?
drills.a: kill -9 doesn't interrupt in-flight disk writes or drop OS page cache the way a real power loss does, so it never exercises the actual failure mode durability is supposed to survive. A valid test pulls power (or uses fault injection) on the real storage medium mid-write and verifies that exactly what was acknowledged as committed survived, nothing more and nothing less.

drills.q: Compare shadow paging to WAL as crash recovery strategies and explain why WAL became the dominant architecture.
drills.a: Shadow paging never modifies a page in place - writes go to a fresh copy, and an atomic root-pointer swap commits the transaction, giving crash safety without redo replay. But it destroys physical locality over time and complicates fine-grained concurrent transactions, since the modified path effectively needs copy-on-write. WAL keeps data pages in place and relies on a separate sequential log for recovery, preserving locality and allowing independent, finer-grained concurrency control (row/page locking or MVCC).

drills.q: A GET request is slow. Show the curl command you'd run and how you'd read the output to find out why.
drills.a: curl -w "@curl-format.txt" -o /dev/null -s <url>, reading the deltas: time_connect - time_namelookup = DNS, time_appconnect - time_connect = TLS, time_starttransfer - time_appconnect = server processing (usual culprit), time_total - time_starttransfer = body transfer.

drills.q: Walk through reading curl -v output line by line.
drills.a: * lines are connection/TLS metadata (DNS, TCP connect, negotiated TLS version/cipher, ALPN, cert chain) from curl itself. > lines are the literal bytes curl sent -- verify your intended headers actually went out. < lines are the literal response headers from the server -- ground truth that can catch a proxy silently rewriting something in between.

drills.q: The DNS lookup phase in your -w timing breakdown is slow. What do you check next?
drills.a: Try --resolve to bypass DNS and hit the known IP directly, confirming the rest of the timing is normal -- isolates resolver latency from a genuinely slow/misconfigured upstream DNS server, and check whether the client is caching resolutions at all.

drills.q: Why doesn't your POST body survive a redirect, and how do you force it to?
drills.a: curl converts POST to GET and drops the body by default on 301/302, matching browser convention; only 307/308 explicitly preserve method and body. Force with explicit -X POST, but be deliberate -- this overrides the server's semantic hint and can break a flow that intentionally wanted GET-after-redirect.

drills.q: Your JSON POST fails with a parse error server-side even though the JSON is valid. Diagnose, and explain -d vs --data-raw.
drills.a: -d/--data defaults Content-Type to application/x-www-form-urlencoded; the server's JSON deserializer is choking on a form-encoded parse. Fix: explicit -H "Content-Type: application/json". -d interprets a leading @ as 'read from file'; --data-raw sends the literal string even if it starts with @.

drills.q: How do you debug a TLS handshake failure with curl, and does -k fix it?
drills.a: curl -v and read the certificate block: 'unable to get local issuer certificate' = missing intermediate/untrusted private CA (fix with --cacert); 'certificate has expired' is literal; hostname mismatch shows subject/SAN not matching the requested host. -k doesn't fix anything -- it just stops checking, confirming the app layer works past the handshake but leaving the trust-chain problem in place for every real client that validates properly.

drills.q: --connect-timeout 3 -m 10 is set but a request still hangs 30s. What's wrong?
drills.a: Either the timeout wasn't actually applied (common when curl is wrapped by another tool/library with its own timeout config overriding or ignoring the CLI flag), or DNS resolution hung before either timer started in some resolver/curl combinations. Verify --connect-timeout is guarding the connect phase and -m is guarding the whole request; check the wrapping layer's own timeout handling.

drills.q: How do you hit one specific backend behind a load balancer without SSH access to it, and what's the difference between the two flags that do this?
drills.a: --resolve api.example.com:443:<ip> or --connect-to api.example.com:443:<ip>:443. --resolve fully overrides DNS resolution for that host. --connect-to only redirects the TCP connection target while keeping Host header, SNI, and cert validation against the original hostname -- useful when you want cert checks to still validate against the real name.

drills.q: A -k flag snuck into a shipped production health-check script. What's wrong with it, and how do you catch this in CI?
drills.a: -k disables cert verification entirely, so the health check reports 'healthy' even with an expired cert, wrong hostname, or active MITM -- exactly the failures TLS exists to catch. Catch it by grepping/linting CI for -k or --insecure in any committed shell script and failing the build on a match.

drills.q: Should you add --retry to a script calling a payment API? Justify.
drills.a: Not without checking idempotency first. --retry only retries transient transport failures and select response codes -- it has no concept of your endpoint's idempotency semantics. Retrying a non-idempotent POST risks a duplicate side effect (double charge); the decision to retry belongs with the caller's understanding of the operation, not the flag.

drills.q: A -F multipart upload works for a 1KB file but chokes on a 2GB file. Where's the likely bottleneck?
drills.a: Likely the server's max body size / multipart buffer limit, or a client library's in-memory buffering of the multipart body rather than streaming. curl itself streams from disk with @filename, so check server/proxy limits first, not curl's own behavior.

drills.q: Design a curl-based synthetic check for a critical external dependency, and name its blind spot.
drills.a: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n" --connect-timeout 3 -m 10 <url>, on a schedule, piping write-out fields into metrics, alerting on non-2xx or time_starttransfer exceeding an SLO. Blind spot: it only observes network conditions from one vantage point/region; a regional DNS or network issue elsewhere won't show up -- needs multi-region checks or explicit acknowledgment it's a coarse first-line signal, not a replacement for real APM.

drills.q: Walk through a cold DNS lookup with round-trip counts, and name where clients cache separately from the recursive resolver.
drills.a: Stub->recursive resolver; if uncached, root (usually cached days via seed hints), then TLD (usually cached ~1-2 days), then authoritative -- up to 3-4 RTT cold, commonly 1 RTT in practice. Clients also cache at the OS resolver level and often the browser level, independent of whatever the recursive resolver honors.

drills.q: Why is DNS-based failover often slower in practice than its TTL suggests, and what's the fast alternative?
drills.a: TTL is advisory -- resolvers and client stacks routinely cache longer than instructed or override it. Anycast at the IP layer with BGP withdrawal on failure converges in seconds and isn't subject to arbitrary client-side DNS caching.

drills.q: Why can't you put a CNAME at your zone apex, and how do people work around it?
drills.a: The apex needs NS (and SOA) records for delegation, and DNS disallows any other record coexisting at a name with a CNAME. Workaround: ALIAS/ANAME, a provider-specific record that resolves like a CNAME but is flattened to an A record at the provider's edge, so it can coexist with NS/SOA.

drills.q: What's the actual difference between L4 and L7 load balancing, with a concrete provider example of each?
drills.a: L4 (AWS NLB) routes on IP/TCP header only, no HTTP parsing, near-zero added latency, can't route on path/host. L7 (AWS ALB) terminates TLS and parses HTTP, enabling path/host/header/cookie routing at the cost of real per-request CPU for crypto and parsing.

drills.q: Why does consistent hashing matter for a distributed cache specifically, and why use virtual nodes?
drills.a: hash(key)%n remaps nearly every key when n changes, wiping the cache; consistent hashing bounds remap to ~1/n of keys on a node join/leave. Virtual nodes (~100-200/physical node) smooth uneven arc sizes that a single ring position per node produces by chance.

drills.q: Your health check interval is 1s with a 1-failure threshold. What can go wrong, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: A brief correlated blip (GC pause, shared dependency hiccup) across many backends at once can eject a large fraction of the fleet simultaneously, dumping traffic on survivors and cascading. Fix: require N consecutive failures, stagger check timing, cap max-ejection percentage (Envoy's outlier detection supports this).

drills.q: What does sticky-session affinity cost architecturally, and what's the alternative?
drills.a: Couples requests to a specific instance, fighting horizontal scaling (can't freely add/remove instances) and complicating deploys (must drain sticky connections). IP-hash specifically hot-spots behind shared NAT. Alternative: externalize session state (Redis) so any backend serves any request -- more upfront work, pays off at scale.

drills.q: Explain anycast and correct the claim 'anycast routes to the nearest server.' Does this matter for data residency?
drills.a: Same IP announced from multiple sites via BGP; routing follows best BGP path cost (AS-path length, policy), not physical distance -- a client can be routed farther away with better peering. Yes it matters: anycast alone gives no guarantee of which region serves a client, so data residency/compliance needs explicit regional pinning on top.

drills.q: A CDN's hit rate on a personalized page matches its miss rate at scale. Diagnose the two possible causes and their relative severity.
drills.a: Either the cache key includes something per-user (session cookie, full Authorization header), fragmenting into one entry per user (a hit-rate problem), OR -- more dangerous -- the response is cached at a shared layer WITHOUT Cache-Control: private, meaning another user could be served the first user's personalized data (a security incident). Distinguish by checking whether cached entries are reused across different sessions (leak) vs never reused (hit-rate only).

drills.q: Design DNS + load balancing for a service that must fail over across regions within 10 seconds of a region going down.
drills.a: DNS TTL alone can't guarantee 10s given uncontrolled client caching. Anchor failover on anycast: announce the IP from multiple regions via BGP, withdraw on health-check failure (BGP convergence ~seconds). Use short-TTL health-checked DNS only as a secondary mechanism for clients outside the anycast network, not the primary path.

drills.q: What is origin shielding, what specific failure does it prevent, and does it add latency on the common case?
drills.a: One CDN PoP is the sole one allowed to fetch from origin on a miss; others fetch from the shield. Prevents thundering herd when a popular object's TTL expires and many edge PoPs simultaneously miss and hit origin at once. Adds small latency only on the rare miss path via the shield hop -- no added latency on the common cache-hit case.

drills.q: Why do large systems layer anycast/GeoDNS, then L4, then L7 instead of a single L7 tier for everything?
drills.a: Each layer solves a cheaper-at-its-scope problem: anycast/GeoDNS picks a region at BGP-level cost, L4 absorbs raw connection volume at near-zero per-connection cost, L7 does the expensive HTTP-aware routing only where actually needed. Collapsing to one L7 tier means paying HTTP-parsing cost for traffic that never needed content-based routing.

drills.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2 and can't run on HTTP/1.1?
drills.a: gRPC needs trailing headers to carry the final grpc-status after the body (outcome unknown until the handler finishes), and needs true multiplexed independent streams for concurrent RPCs plus native bidirectional streaming -- both are HTTP/2-native (trailers frame, independent stream IDs) and neither is reliably available on HTTP/1.1.

drills.q: Walk through the protobuf wire format for a single int32 field, encoding field 1 = 150.
drills.a: Tag byte = (field_number<<3)|wire_type; field 1, wire type 0 (varint) = 0x08. Value 150 varint-encoded: 7 bits payload/byte, MSB=continuation flag, little-endian groups -- 150 needs 2 bytes: 0x96 0x01. Full encoding: 08 96 01, 3 bytes total.

drills.q: Give one safe .proto change and one that silently corrupts data.
drills.a: Safe: adding a new field with a new field number (old clients ignore it, new clients get a default if talking to an old server). Corrupting: reusing a field number for a different field after removal -- an old message deserialized with the new meaning applied to old bytes produces wrong data with no error thrown, since the parser never validates a number's historical meaning.

drills.q: Why does length-delimited (wire type 2) encoding matter for schema evolution?
drills.a: It lets a parser skip over an unrecognized field number by reading its length prefix and jumping past the bytes without understanding their meaning -- exactly what lets an old client safely ignore new fields a newer server added, which is the mechanism underlying forward compatibility.

drills.q: What's the difference between a gRPC deadline and a plain per-call timeout?
drills.a: A deadline is an absolute point in time set once by the originating client and auto-propagated as metadata through every downstream call derived from that request's context. A per-call timeout is independently set at each hop with no shared knowledge, so a chain of slow-but-under-timeout hops can collectively blow past what the original caller actually wanted.

drills.q: Explain cancellation propagation and name a concrete failure to watch for.
drills.a: Cancelling the parent context cancels every derived child call, so downstream services stop doing work nobody's waiting on. Failure to watch for: a downstream call made with a fresh/unrelated context instead of a derived one keeps running after the parent is gone -- wasting resources and, for a write, potentially completing a side effect the caller thinks never happened. Detect via tracing: a downstream span outliving the parent's cancellation timestamp is a propagation bug.

drills.q: Name the 4 gRPC RPC types and a real use case for each.
drills.a: Unary: fetch-a-record calls. Server-streaming: subscribing to live updates or consuming a large result incrementally (log tail, price feed). Client-streaming: uploading chunks with one final ack (chunked upload, batched telemetry). Bidirectional streaming: interactive, independently-paced exchange (chat-like protocols, live audio-to-text, multi-turn tool-call coordination).

drills.q: Why is UNAVAILABLE different from INTERNAL, and why does that distinction matter for retry policy?
drills.a: UNAVAILABLE signals the server/dependency was transiently unreachable -- safe to retry with backoff. INTERNAL signals an unexpected internal error/invariant violation -- retrying blindly rarely helps and may just repeat whatever triggered the bug. A retry policy treating every non-OK code the same either wastes resources retrying bugs or fails to retry things that safely could succeed.

drills.q: What does google.rpc.Status give you beyond a bare gRPC status code, and why not just use a detailed message string?
drills.a: Structured, typed error details (e.g. BadRequest listing which fields failed validation, RetryInfo suggesting a backoff) so a client can programmatically branch on rich error content. A message string is brittle across text/localization changes; typed details are a stable, versioned contract like the rest of the schema.

drills.q: When would you choose REST over gRPC for a new service, and would you unify on one API style for maintenance simplicity?
drills.a: When consumers are browsers or third-party developers needing to curl the endpoint, read human-readable JSON, and benefit from standard HTTP caching -- none of which gRPC gives without extra proxying (gRPC-Web). No, don't unify for maintenance convenience alone: maintaining two styles (gRPC internal, REST at the public edge) is a real ongoing cost that buys a materially better external developer experience -- collapsing to one style trades that away for engineering convenience, which is a product decision, not just an engineering one.

drills.q: A rolling deploy causes a burst of UNAVAILABLE errors, and separately one backend pod gets flooded with traffic afterward. Diagnose both.
drills.a: UNAVAILABLE burst: server likely closed connections during pod termination without draining in-flight RPCs or rejecting new ones gracefully, and/or the client's connection pool hadn't detected the backend was gone. Fix: graceful shutdown plus client-side retry with backoff on UNAVAILABLE. Flooded pod: gRPC's long-lived HTTP/2 connections mean a plain L4 load balancer only balances new connections, not individual requests -- clients reconnecting in a burst can pick unevenly. Fix: client-side or L7-aware (stream-level) load balancing.

drills.q: A field needs to change type from int32 to string. What do you do, and how do you version the API generally without breaking existing clients?
drills.a: You cannot change the existing field's type in place -- wire-incompatible, silently corrupts old data. Add a brand-new field with a new number and the new type, deprecate the old one, migrate readers/writers, then remove and reserve the old number. Generally prefer additive changes (new fields/numbers) within the same message over new service versions; reserve versioning at the package/service level (package myapi.v2) for genuinely breaking semantic changes, running both concurrently until clients migrate.

drills.q: Define safe and idempotent precisely, and explain why safety implies idempotency but not the reverse.
drills.a: Safe: no intended server-side side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). Idempotent: N identical requests leave the server in the same state as 1 (adds PUT, DELETE). Safety implies idempotency because nothing changes, so repeating changes nothing; idempotency doesn't imply safety because PUT/DELETE both change state, just to the same end state regardless of repeat count.

drills.q: Is a repeat DELETE on an already-deleted resource still idempotent if it returns 404 instead of the original 200?
drills.a: Yes -- idempotency is a property of server STATE, not of the HTTP response. 'The resource doesn't exist' is the same state whether it's the first delete (200/204) or a repeat (404); the response is allowed to differ.

drills.q: Why is PUT idempotent but POST is not, reasoning from the actual definitions rather than a memorized table?
