drills.a: No -- Manhattan distance overestimates because diagonal moves cover two axes in one step. Use Chebyshev distance (max(|dx|,|dy|)) instead, which correctly lower-bounds the number of 8-directional steps needed.

drills.q: Explain the difference between an admissible and a consistent heuristic in A*, and why consistency matters for implementation correctness.
drills.a: Admissible: h(n) never overestimates true remaining cost. Consistent: h(n) <= cost(n,n') + h(n') for every edge, a stronger triangle-inequality condition. Consistency guarantees a popped node's g-value is already optimal, so nodes never need to be reopened; an admissible-but-inconsistent heuristic can still find the optimal path but may require reopening already-visited nodes, which naive implementations often forget to allow.

drills.q: Design a greedy algorithm for maximum non-overlapping intervals and state its complexity.
drills.a: Sort intervals by finish time, O(n log n); greedily take any interval that doesn't overlap the last taken one, O(n) scan.

drills.q: Prove the interval-scheduling greedy choice is optimal using an exchange argument.
drills.a: If OPT's first interval finishes later than greedy's earliest-finishing pick, swap it in. Feasibility holds since greedy's pick finishes no later, so it can't conflict with anything the swapped-out interval didn't already conflict with; count is unchanged. Induct on the remainder to show greedy matches an optimal solution everywhere.

drills.q: Construct a concrete counterexample showing greedy-by-value/weight-ratio fails on 0/1 knapsack.
drills.a: Capacity 10; items (w=6,v=12, ratio 2.0), (w=5,v=9, ratio 1.8), (w=5,v=9, ratio 1.8). Greedy takes the first item only (value 12, can't fit the rest). Optimal takes both weight-5 items (value 18).

drills.q: Given coin denominations {1,3,4} and amount 6, show greedy largest-first fails and give the DP complexity to solve it correctly in general.
drills.a: Greedy: 4+1+1 = 3 coins. Optimal: 3+3 = 2 coins. General correct algorithm is DP: O(amount * len(coins)) time, O(amount) space -- no greedy rule is safe without first proving the coin system is canonical.

drills.q: Prove no single per-item scoring function (value, weight, ratio, or combination) can make greedy correct for 0/1 knapsack in general.
drills.a: Construct two problem instances where the same fixed scoring-based ordering produces a correct answer on one and a wrong answer on the other -- because capacity constraints create combinatorial interactions between which subset of items fits, which no single per-item score can capture; this is exactly the exhaustive combination-checking that DP performs and greedy cannot.

drills.q: Explain why the 'minimum meeting rooms' problem cannot be solved with the same exchange argument used for 'maximum non-overlapping intervals,' even though both involve intervals.
drills.a: Maximum non-overlapping intervals is a selection-maximization problem (some intervals are rejected). Minimum rooms is a concurrent-overlap-counting problem (every interval must be scheduled, just possibly in different rooms) -- it requires a sweep over start/end events or a min-heap of active end times, not a sequential accept/reject greedy choice with a one-line exchange proof.

drills.q: Implement strStr(): find the first occurrence of pattern P in text T in O(n+m), deterministically.
drills.a: KMP: build the failure function (lps array) on P in O(m), then scan T once in O(n), falling back to lps[j-1] on mismatch instead of restarting the pattern pointer.

drills.q: Why does resetting the KMP pattern pointer to 0 on every mismatch (instead of using lps) silently break the algorithm's complexity guarantee?
drills.a: It degrades KMP into the naive O(nm) algorithm -- it still produces correct matches, but loses the whole point: never re-reading text characters. The bug doesn't crash, it just erases the asymptotic benefit.

drills.q: Given a string, determine if it can be constructed by repeating a substring (Repeated Substring Pattern, LC 459), using KMP.
drills.a: Compute lps on the string itself; if n % (n - lps[n-1]) == 0, the string has period (n - lps[n-1]) and is fully periodic.

drills.q: You're building a content-deduplication service using Rabin-Karp rolling hash over user-uploaded text, with a small fixed modulus. What's the security risk and the fix?
drills.a: An attacker can construct many strings that collide under that specific known modulus, forcing O(m) verification on every window and degrading the service to O(nm) -- a denial-of-service vector. Fix: use a large randomly-seeded modulus at process start, or double hashing with independent random parameters.

drills.q: Find the longest common substring between two strings using hashing instead of the classic O(nm) DP. What's the technique and complexity?
drills.a: Binary search on candidate length L; for each L, compute rolling hashes of all length-L substrings of both strings and check for a common hash (with verification). O(n log n) total, using monotonicity: if a common substring of length L exists, one of length L-1 also exists.

drills.q: Given k patterns and one text, find all occurrences of any pattern efficiently. Why doesn't running KMP k times scale, and what's the right tool?
drills.a: Running KMP k times costs O(k*n + sum(pattern lengths)), worse than a single combined scan when k and n are large. The right tool is Aho-Corasick: a trie of all patterns with failure links (generalizing KMP's failure function to many patterns), giving a single O(n + sum(pattern lengths) + matches) scan.

drills.q: Design a structure supporting point update and range sum query in O(log n) each, with minimal memory overhead.
drills.a: Fenwick tree (BIT): O(n) space, O(log n) update and prefix-sum query using i & -i to walk ancestor/descendant chains.

drills.q: Why does the Fenwick tree trick fail for range-minimum queries even though the update/query loop structure looks identical?
drills.a: The O(log n) range-query trick relies on being able to subtract one prefix result from another (prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)); min has no inverse operation, so this decomposition is meaningless for min/max.

drills.q: Implement range-add, range-sum query support. What technique do you need beyond a basic segment tree, and why?
drills.a: Lazy propagation -- store a pending delta at the highest fully-covered node instead of pushing it to every leaf immediately; push down only when a future operation must descend past that node. Without it, range updates cost O(n) each.

drills.q: Given a static array and 10 million range-min queries with zero updates, what structure is asymptotically optimal and why not a segment tree?
drills.a: A sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) per query by precomputing min over every power-of-two window and combining two overlapping windows (min is idempotent so overlap is safe). A segment tree would cost O(log n) per query -- strictly worse when there are no updates to justify its flexibility.

drills.q: Derive why the Fenwick tree update and query loops are each bounded by O(log n) steps.
drills.a: Update: i += i & -i strictly increases the trailing-zero-bit count of i each step, bounded by the bit-width of n. Query: i -= i & -i strictly clears the lowest set bit each step, also bounded by bit-width. Both are O(log n).

drills.q: You need k-th smallest element in an arbitrary range [l,r] of a static array, with far more queries than n. What structure, and what's its space complexity?
drills.a: A persistent segment tree (merge sort tree): build a versioned root after inserting each element, and answer k-th-smallest-in-range as a difference between two versions' trees. Each update only touches O(log n) new nodes, so n versions cost O(n log n) total space, not O(n) per version.

drills.q: Given V=100,000 nodes and E=150,000 edges, which representation should you use and why?
drills.a: Adjacency list -- the graph is sparse (E close to V). An adjacency matrix would need V^2 = 10^10 cells, infeasible in memory.

drills.q: Implement cycle detection for an undirected graph. What's the critical detail that's easy to forget?
drills.a: DFS tracking the parent node; a visited neighbor is only a real cycle if it's NOT the parent you just came from -- forgetting parent exclusion makes every single edge look like a cycle.

drills.q: Course Schedule: given prerequisite pairs, determine if all courses can be completed. Why can't you use the same visited-check as undirected cycle detection?
drills.a: Directed graphs need three-color state (white/gray/black): an edge to a fully-processed (black) node can be a valid DAG convergence, not a cycle. Only an edge to a GRAY (currently active ancestor) node is a real cycle -- binary visited/unvisited can't distinguish these two cases.

drills.q: Design a bipartite check for 'Possible Bipartition' (split people into two groups given dislike pairs) and state the exact mathematical condition being tested.
drills.a: BFS/DFS 2-coloring: assign opposite colors to adjacent nodes; a conflict means not bipartite. The exact condition: a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd-length cycle -- the coloring attempt is a complete decision procedure for this.

drills.q: Design a multi-source BFS for 'rotten oranges spread to fresh neighbors each minute.' Why is this faster than running BFS once per source?
drills.a: Initialize the queue with all rotten-orange sources simultaneously at distance 0, then run standard BFS once -- O(V+E) total, versus O(k*(V+E)) if you ran BFS separately from each of k sources and took the minimum.

drills.q: Design a system that incrementally rejects any new dependency edge that would create a directed cycle in a build/dependency graph, added one edge at a time. Why doesn't plain Union-Find solve this?
drills.a: Union-Find only tracks undirected connectivity -- two nodes being in the same component doesn't tell you if a directed path exists in a specific direction, which is what matters for a circular dependency (A depends on B depends on A). You need an incrementally-maintained topological order (e.g., online topological sort) or a bounded local DFS from the new edge's target checking reachability to its source.

drills.q: Min Cost to Connect All Points (LC 1584): connect all points with minimum total Manhattan distance. Which MST algorithm and why?
drills.a: Prim's dense O(V^2) variant -- the graph is complete (E=V^2), making Kruskal's O(E log E) = O(V^2 log V) strictly worse.

drills.q: Implement max-flow between source and sink with given capacities using Edmonds-Karp. What data structure finds the augmenting path, and what must you update besides forward capacity?
drills.a: BFS finds the shortest augmenting path each iteration. Besides decreasing forward residual capacity along the path, you must increase the reverse residual capacity on each edge, allowing the algorithm to undo earlier flow assignments if needed.

drills.q: Construct a graph where naive DFS-based Ford-Fulkerson takes far more iterations than Edmonds-Karp.
drills.a: Two source-to-sink paths sharing one edge of capacity 1, with the two outer edges each having capacity N. An unlucky DFS alternates pushing 1 unit at a time through the shared edge (using reverse residual to cancel), taking up to 2N iterations, versus 2 iterations if BFS finds the two large-capacity paths directly.

drills.q: Reduce 'assign N workers to M jobs, each worker qualified for a subset of jobs, maximize total assignments' to a flow problem, and name a faster matching-specific algorithm.
drills.a: Source -> each worker (capacity 1), worker -> qualified jobs (capacity 1), each job -> sink (capacity 1); max-flow = max matching. Kuhn's algorithm gives O(V*E); Hopcroft-Karp improves this to O(E*sqrt(V)) using vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths per phase.

drills.q: After running max-flow to find the minimum number of edges to remove to disconnect source from sink, how do you find the actual set of edges in the minimum cut, not just the count?
drills.a: Do one more BFS/DFS from the source over the FINAL residual graph after max-flow terminates. The min-cut edges are exactly the original edges going from a reachable vertex to an unreachable vertex in that traversal.

drills.q: Your ride-hailing platform needs driver-rider matching in real time as both pools change continuously. Why isn't a straight Hopcroft-Karp/max-flow reduction the right production architecture?
drills.a: Hopcroft-Karp and generic max-flow assume a static bipartite graph solved once. Real-time matching needs online/incremental assignment as drivers and riders arrive and leave continuously -- production systems use online matching heuristics with competitive-ratio guarantees, or periodic batch re-optimization over short windows, trading exact optimality for responsiveness.

drills.q: Find all bridges in an undirected network (Critical Connections in a Network, LC 1192). State the exact bridge condition.
drills.a: Single DFS with discovery time and low-link; tree edge (u,v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u] (strict inequality), excluding the parent edge when checking back edges.

drills.q: Find all articulation points in an undirected network, including the root's special-case rule.
drills.a: Non-root u is an articulation point if some child v has low[v] >= disc[u]. The DFS root is a special case: articulation point iff it has more than one DFS-tree child.

drills.q: Implement Tarjan's SCC algorithm. What is the exact condition for a vertex being an SCC root, and why does the on_stack check matter (not just visited)?
drills.a: low[v] == disc[v] means the vertex is an SCC root. A vertex can be visited (disc != -1) but already popped into a previously-finished SCC (not on_stack) -- treating it as still 'in progress' if you only check visited would incorrectly merge separate SCCs.

drills.q: Given boolean clauses each with exactly two literals, determine satisfiability using 2-SAT. Build the implication graph for clause (a OR b) and state the unsatisfiability check.
drills.a: Add edges NOT a -> b and NOT b -> a. Compute SCCs of the implication graph; the formula is unsatisfiable iff some variable x and NOT x are in the same SCC (mutual implication is a direct contradiction).

drills.q: Prove why the condensation graph formed by collapsing each SCC to a single node is always a DAG.
drills.a: If distinct SCCs formed a cycle in the condensation, every vertex in every SCC on that cycle could reach every other vertex in every other SCC by chaining through the cycle -- meaning they were all mutually reachable and should have been one single SCC, contradicting the maximality of the SCC decomposition.

drills.q: Design a build system that detects groups of mutually-dependent modules that must compile together, then produces a valid build order for the resulting groups.
drills.a: Model modules and dependencies as a directed graph, compute SCCs (each is a maximal group of mutually-dependent modules), condense into a DAG (collapsing each SCC to one node, keeping inter-SCC edges), then topologically sort the condensation for a valid build order.

drills.q: You need all-pairs shortest paths on a sparse graph (V=10,000, E=30,000) that may contain negative edges but no negative cycles. Which algorithm and why?
drills.a: Johnson's algorithm, O(VE + V^2 log V) ~ 1.3*10^9 operations, vs Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) ~ 10^12 -- three orders of magnitude faster on this sparse graph.

drills.q: Derive why w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v) is always non-negative after Bellman-Ford computes h from a virtual source (assuming no negative cycle).
drills.a: Bellman-Ford's convergence guarantees h(v) <= h(u) + w(u,v) for every edge (otherwise it would still be relaxable). Rearranging: w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v) >= 0.

drills.q: After running Dijkstra on Johnson's reweighted graph, how do you recover the real shortest distance between u and v, and why does this work?
drills.a: dist(u,v) = dist'(u,v) - h(u) + h(v). It works because the reweighted cost of any path telescopes to the real cost plus the constant h(u)-h(v), which is the same shift for every path between the same two endpoints, so it doesn't change which path is shortest.

drills.q: You want to know if ANY arbitrage cycle exists across all currency pairs (not starting from one specific currency). Why does a virtual source matter here instead of picking one arbitrary starting currency?
drills.a: An arbitrary real currency node might not reach every other node (one-way convertibility or disconnected subgraphs), silently missing an arbitrage cycle unreachable from it. A virtual source connects to every currency directly, guaranteeing full reachability so Bellman-Ford's negative-cycle check covers the whole graph.

drills.q: Compare the total cost of Johnson's algorithm to running Bellman-Ford from every vertex directly (no reweighting). What does the reweighting step actually buy you?
drills.a: Bellman-Ford from every vertex: O(V * VE) = O(V^2 E). Johnson's: O(VE + V^2 log V). The reweighting substitutes V cheap Dijkstra runs for V expensive Bellman-Ford runs, paying the Bellman-Ford cost only once (for potentials) instead of V times.

drills.q: Your all-pairs shortest path system on a 500,000-node sparse graph needs repeated point-to-point queries, and even Johnson's O(V^2) output storage is too much memory. What's the production escalation beyond Johnson's algorithm?
drills.a: Contraction hierarchies or hub labeling: heavier one-time preprocessing that answers individual point-to-point queries in near-constant to logarithmic time without ever materializing the full O(V^2) distance matrix.

drills.q: What must you sort intervals by before merging, and why is that step non-negotiable?
drills.a: Sort by start value. Without sorting, overlap can't be checked in a single forward pass because a later-appearing interval in the input might need to merge with an earlier one that's already been closed out.

drills.q: You're merging [1,10] with the next sorted interval [2,3]. What does the merged block become, and what mistake produces [2,3] as the wrong answer instead?
drills.a: It stays [1,10]. The mistake is overwriting merged.end with the next interval's end instead of taking max(merged.end, next.end); [2,3] is fully nested inside [1,10] so a naive overwrite shrinks the block incorrectly.

drills.q: Prove that once intervals are sorted by start, a single forward sweep is sufficient -- you never need to reopen a merged block that was already closed.
drills.a: If interval k (sorted by start) does not overlap the current merged block, that means start[k] > merged.end. Every subsequent interval k+1, k+2, ... has start >= start[k] (sorted order), so their starts also exceed merged.end -- none of them can overlap the already-closed block either. The block is safe to close permanently.

drills.q: Why does Non-Overlapping Intervals (LC435) require sorting by END time instead of start, and what goes wrong if you sort by start?
drills.a: The greedy 'always keep the earliest-ending compatible interval' is provably optimal via an exchange argument only when processing intervals in end-time order -- keeping the interval that frees up the timeline soonest maximizes room for future intervals. Sorting by start can select a long early-starting interval first, which may block several short intervals that would otherwise all have fit, producing a smaller (wrong) kept-set.

drills.q: Design the min-heap solution for Meeting Rooms II and explain exactly when you pop versus push.
drills.a: Sort meetings by start time. Maintain a min-heap of end times for currently 'active' (room-occupying) meetings. For each meeting in start order: first pop-while the heap's minimum end time is <= the current meeting's start (that room has freed up by the time this meeting begins), then push the current meeting's end time onto the heap. The heap's maximum size reached across the whole sweep is the minimum number of rooms needed.

drills.q: A candidate solves Insert Interval by appending the new interval to the array and rerunning their O(n log n) Merge Intervals solution. Is this correct, and what's the better approach?
drills.a: It's correct but wasteful: it throws away the fact that the array was already sorted and merged, paying O(n log n) for a re-sort that isn't needed. The O(n) approach does a single linear scan in three phases: copy every interval that ends strictly before the new interval starts, absorb every interval that overlaps the new interval by expanding the new interval's own start/end bounds, then copy the remaining intervals unchanged.

drills.q: Why is Interval List Intersections (LC986) solved with two pointers across two separate lists rather than a single merge pass, and what's the rule for advancing pointers?
drills.a: The two input lists are already individually sorted and non-overlapping within themselves, but they represent two different sets that need pairwise intersection, not a union-merge. At each step compute [max(a.start,b.start), min(a.end,b.end)] and emit it if valid (start <= end); then advance whichever of the two current intervals has the smaller end value, since that interval is now fully exhausted against everything remaining in the other list (both lists proceed in increasing start order).

drills.q: A production calendar system re-sorts and re-merges its entire interval set on every single new booking insertion. At what scale does this become a real problem, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Re-sorting and re-merging from scratch costs O(n log n) per insertion; across n insertions total this is O(n^2 log n), which becomes noticeably slow once n reaches roughly the low thousands of bookings processed interactively (e.g. tens of milliseconds becoming full seconds). The fix is a balanced-BST-backed structure (Java TreeMap, Python SortedList, or a custom self-balancing tree) holding the current disjoint merged intervals, where each new booking only needs to check and merge with its immediate left/right neighbors -- an operation close to O(log n) for the lookup plus O(k) for any local coalescing, not a full re-scan.

drills.q: What range must an array's values fall into for cyclic sort to be applicable at all?
drills.a: A known, contiguous range tied to the array's own length, e.g. [1,n], [0,n-1], or [0,n]. Without that constraint the technique simply doesn't apply.

drills.q: For an array with values in [1,n], what index is the 'home' for value v, and what mistake results from off-by-one confusion here?
drills.a: Home index is v - 1. Using v directly (as if 0-indexed range) causes an off-by-one shift in every placement, or an out-of-bounds access when v equals n.

drills.q: Prove that cyclic sort's nested while loop is actually O(n) total work, not O(n^2).
drills.a: Every executed swap places exactly one value into its permanent, correct home index, and once a value is at its home it is never touched again (the loop only advances past an index once the value there is confirmed correct). Since there are only n values total, the number of swaps across the algorithm's entire execution -- summed over every outer iteration -- cannot exceed n. Combined with the O(n) outer advances, total work is O(n).

drills.q: A candidate's cyclic sort implementation infinite-loops on input [1, 1, 3]. What's the likely bug?
drills.a: Missing the swap guard nums[i] != nums[correctIndex]. With duplicate value 1 present, once index 0 holds a 1 and index 0 IS the home for value 1, the code should advance i -- but if it swaps unconditionally whenever nums[i] != i+1 without checking whether the target slot already holds the same value, it can swap the same pair back and forth indefinitely.

drills.q: Design the negative-marking approach for Find All Duplicates in an Array (LC442), and state precisely when you record a value as a duplicate.
drills.a: For each value v in the array (in original left-to-right order), compute idx = abs(v) - 1. If nums[idx] is already negative, then abs(v) has been seen before -- record it as a duplicate before (re-)negating nums[idx]. If nums[idx] is positive, negate it to mark abs(v) as seen for the first time. Using abs(v) rather than v is required because v itself may have already been negated by an earlier iteration.

drills.q: Explain why First Missing Positive (LC41) must ignore any nums[i] that is <= 0 or > n during the placement pass, rather than trying to place it somewhere.
drills.a: The array has length n, so there are only n valid home slots (for values 1..n). A value outside [1,n] has no valid home index in this array and can never itself be the answer, since the first missing positive for any length-n array is guaranteed (by pigeonhole) to lie in [1, n+1]. Attempting to compute a home index for an out-of-range value produces a negative or out-of-bounds index, which either crashes or, if silently wrapped/clamped, corrupts an unrelated slot's data.

drills.q: A problem states the input array for Find the Duplicate Number cannot be modified. Can you still use cyclic sort? If not, what do you use instead and why does it not need mutation?
drills.a: No -- cyclic sort requires swapping elements in place, which mutates the array, violating the constraint. Instead, treat nums[i] as a pointer to the next index (an implicit linked list, since values are constrained to [1,n] and the array has n+1 elements, guaranteeing a cycle by pigeonhole) and run Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection, which only ever reads array values and moves pointer variables -- it never writes to the array. Alternatively, binary search over the value range [1,n], counting how many array elements are <= mid at each step, also avoids mutation at the cost of O(n log n) instead of O(n).

drills.q: Solve Set Mismatch (LC645) using pure arithmetic (no array mutation, no extra space beyond a few scalars), and state the two equations you need.
drills.a: Let d = the duplicate value, m = the missing value. From sum(nums) - sum(1..n) = d - m (the duplicate contributes twice, the missing contributes zero, everything else cancels), and sum(nums^2) - sum((1..n)^2) = d^2 - m^2 = (d-m)(d+m). Divide the second equation by the first (d - m) to get (d+m), then combine with (d-m) to solve for both d and m via simple addition/subtraction. Watch for integer overflow on the squared sums when n is large in fixed-width-integer languages.

drills.q: What three pointer variables does the iterative linked-list reversal technique use, and what is each one's job?
drills.a: prev (the new list built so far, starts null), curr (the node currently being rewired), and next_temp (a saved reference to curr's original next node, captured before curr.next is overwritten).

drills.q: What line must always execute before curr.next = prev, and what breaks if it doesn't?
drills.a: next_temp = curr.next must execute first. If curr.next is overwritten before saving it, you lose the only reference to the rest of the original list -- the traversal can no longer advance past the current node correctly.

drills.q: Derive why iterative reversal is O(1) space while recursive reversal of the same list is O(n) space, given both perform the identical set of pointer rewrites.
drills.a: Both approaches touch each node's next pointer exactly once, so both are O(n) time doing the same work. The difference is where intermediate state lives: iterative reversal uses three fixed scalar variables regardless of list length (O(1) space), while recursive reversal pushes one stack frame per node before any rewiring happens (since you recurse all the way to the tail before starting to fix pointers on the way back up), and those frames aren't released until the full unwind completes -- O(n) stack frames outstanding at the deepest point.

drills.q: Why is a dummy node placed before the head standard practice for Reverse Linked List II (reverse between positions left and right)?
drills.a: The splice-back step needs a pointer to the node immediately before position left, so it can be reconnected to the new head of the reversed segment. If left == 1, there is no real node before the range -- without a dummy node you'd need a special case for 'range starts at head'; the dummy node guarantees a predecessor always exists, eliminating that special case.

drills.q: In Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LC25), design the check that decides whether a group should be reversed, and explain why it must happen before reversing, not after.
drills.a: Before reversing a group, walk ahead k nodes from the group's start to confirm all k nodes exist (i.e., you don't run off the end of the list). If fewer than k nodes remain, stop and leave that final partial group in its original order, per LC25's spec. This check must happen before reversing because reversing first and then discovering a short group would require un-reversing it -- extra, avoidable work and a common source of bugs.

drills.q: A candidate implements Rotate List (LC61) by reversing the whole list, reversing the first k nodes, reversing the rest, and reversing the whole thing again (the array-rotation triple-reversal trick). Is this the right tool for a linked list, and why or why not?
drills.a: It's unnecessary complexity. Triple reversal is a trick specifically for in-place ARRAY rotation, where you can't easily jump to an arbitrary position without shifting elements. A linked list lets you directly relink three pointers once you know the new head/tail boundary: compute k mod length, walk to the new tail (at position length-k-1) and new head (right after it), connect the old tail to the old head to form a temporary cycle, then break that cycle at the new boundary -- no reversal of any kind is needed.

drills.q: Explain why reversing a doubly linked list is structurally simpler than reversing a singly linked list, and what the algorithm looks like.
drills.a: A singly linked node only knows its next, so overwriting next without saving it first loses the path forward -- hence the three-pointer technique. A doubly linked node also knows its prev, so even after next is rewritten, the node retains a way back via what was its prev pointer. The algorithm is: for every node, swap its next and prev references; after the full pass, swap the list's head and tail pointers. No prev/curr/next_temp walk is required because nothing is ever lost.

drills.q: A production service uses recursive reversal on a linked list representing a user's action history, and starts throwing stack overflow errors for power users with very long histories. Diagnose the failure and propose the fix without changing the algorithm's correctness.
drills.a: Recursive reversal allocates one stack frame per node before any rewiring begins (it recurses to the tail first), so a history list with tens of thousands of entries can exceed the runtime's default recursion depth (e.g. Python's default limit of 1000 frames, or a JVM/Go goroutine's stack size limit under sufficiently deep recursion). The fix is to replace the recursive implementation with the iterative three-pointer version, which performs the exact same pointer rewrites and produces an identical result, but uses O(1) stack space regardless of list length -- no algorithmic change, only a change in how the same logic is expressed.

drills.q: At what point in the algorithm should a node be marked visited in BFS, and why does the timing matter?
drills.a: At enqueue time, not dequeue time. If you wait until dequeue to mark visited, the same node can be added to the queue multiple times through different paths before it's ever processed, wasting work and potentially degrading complexity badly on dense graphs.

drills.q: What single line of bookkeeping is required to correctly group BFS output into levels?
drills.a: level_size = len(queue), captured immediately before the inner loop that drains exactly that many nodes for the current level. Without this snapshot, level boundaries can't be distinguished in a single FIFO queue.

drills.q: Prove that BFS's first discovery of any node in an unweighted graph is via a shortest path.
drills.a: BFS processes the queue in strict FIFO order and expands one full layer (all nodes at distance d) before starting on layer d+1. By induction: layer 0 (the start node) is trivially at its shortest distance (0). Assuming every node placed into the queue at layer d got there via a shortest path of length d, any new node discovered while processing layer d must be reachable via a path of length d+1 (one edge from a layer-d node) and cannot have a shorter path, because any shorter path would have caused it to be discovered in an earlier layer already, contradicting FIFO order. So every node's first-discovery distance is its true shortest distance.

drills.q: A candidate solves Rotting Oranges by running a separate single-source BFS from each initially rotten orange and taking the minimum time per fresh orange across all runs. Is this correct? What's the complexity cost versus the standard approach?
drills.a: It's correct but wasteful. Running k separate single-source BFS passes (one per initially rotten orange) costs O(k * rows * cols) in the worst case, versus O(rows * cols) for a single multi-source BFS that seeds all rotten oranges into the queue simultaneously at minute 0. The multi-source approach also naturally produces the correct 'time each cell first rotted' in one pass without needing to combine results across runs.

drills.q: Design a 0-1 BFS for a graph where some edges cost 0 and others cost 1, and explain why a plain FIFO queue would give wrong answers.
drills.a: Use a deque. When relaering (relaxing) an edge of weight 0 from the current node to a neighbor, push that neighbor onto the FRONT of the deque; when relaxing an edge of weight 1, push it onto the BACK. Pop from the front to get the next node to process. This preserves a non-decreasing-distance processing order identical to what Dijkstra guarantees, in O(V+E). A plain FIFO queue can't do this because it always appends to the back regardless of edge weight, so a node reached via a 0-weight edge (which should be processed sooner, at the same effective distance as its predecessor) gets stuck behind previously-queued 1-weight-edge neighbors, producing an incorrect processing order and wrong shortest distances.

drills.q: Why is bidirectional BFS asymptotically better than single-source BFS for Word Ladder at scale, and under what condition does it not apply?
drills.a: Single-source BFS to a known target explores roughly O(b^d) nodes for branching factor b and target depth d. Bidirectional BFS grows two frontiers simultaneously, one from the start word and one from the target word, stopping when they intersect; each frontier only needs to reach depth d/2, giving roughly O(2*b^(d/2)) nodes explored -- a large practical difference once d is sizable. It doesn't apply (or loses its advantage) when the target isn't known in advance, since you can't grow a frontier from something you don't have.

drills.q: A candidate is asked to find the minimum number of transformations in Word Ladder II (not just the count, but all shortest sequences) and reuses the length-only version's visited set, marking each word visited the instant it's dequeued for expansion. What's the correctness bug this introduces?
drills.a: In Word Ladder II you need every valid shortest path, and multiple words at the same BFS layer can each transform into the same word at the next layer -- all of them are valid parents for reconstructing shortest paths. If you mark a word visited (and refuse to consider it as a neighbor of anything else) the instant any single predecessor discovers it mid-layer, you silently drop the other valid parent relationships from the same layer, causing some genuinely shortest transformation sequences to be missing from the final output. The fix is to only mark a word as fully visited once its ENTIRE layer has finished processing, while still recording all same-layer parents that reached it.

drills.q: A grid-based routing service uses plain BFS to compute shortest paths, but a recent change introduced express lanes that cost 0 hops to traverse while normal lanes still cost 1 hop. After the change, some computed 'shortest' routes are longer than the true optimum. Diagnose the bug and fix it without introducing a full priority-queue-based Dijkstra.
drills.a: Plain BFS's FIFO queue treats every edge as costing exactly one step regardless of the actual weight, so it can't correctly account for 0-cost express-lane edges mixed with 1-cost normal edges -- a path using more hops but more express lanes can actually be shorter in true cost, and plain BFS will process it too late relative to a longer-true-cost path that happened to be enqueued first. The fix is 0-1 BFS: replace the plain queue with a deque, pushing a neighbor reached via a 0-cost edge to the front and a neighbor reached via a 1-cost edge to the back, which recovers correct non-decreasing-distance processing order in O(V+E) without needing a full priority queue.

drills.q: What does DFS's recursion depth actually correspond to -- total nodes, or something else?
drills.a: The height of the tree, or more generally the longest path DFS descends before backtracking -- not the total node count. A balanced tree of a million nodes recurses only about 20 levels deep; a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree of the same size recurses a million levels deep.

drills.q: In iterative preorder DFS with an explicit stack, why must the right child be pushed before the left child?
drills.a: A stack is LIFO, so whatever is pushed last is popped first. Pushing right first means left ends up on top of the stack and gets popped and visited before right, matching the expected left-before-right preorder sequence.

drills.q: Explain precisely what changes and what does NOT change when you convert a recursive DFS to an iterative one with an explicit stack.
drills.a: What does NOT change: the asymptotic auxiliary space complexity, which remains O(H) in both forms (H being the maximum depth/height reached). What DOES change: which physical memory resource holds that O(H) footprint -- recursive DFS consumes call-stack memory, a small and fixed-size resource per thread (commonly a low single-digit number of megabytes, translating to roughly a thousand to a few tens of thousands of frames before overflow, and specifically about 1000 frames by default in Python regardless of available RAM); iterative DFS consumes heap memory, which is typically far larger and can grow until the process exhausts available RAM. The conversion trades a small hard ceiling for a much larger, more elastic one -- it is not a Big-O improvement.

drills.q: A candidate implements Course Schedule (cycle detection in a directed graph) using a single boolean 'visited' array: if a DFS call reaches an already-visited node, it reports a cycle. Show a valid, cycle-free dependency graph where this produces a false positive, and explain the fix.
drills.a: Consider A -> B -> D and A -> C -> D (a diamond: D depends on both B and C, which both depend on A). DFS from A visits B, then D (marking D visited), returns, then visits C, which tries to visit D again -- D is already marked visited, so the single-visited-set check incorrectly reports a cycle, even though this graph has no cycle at all. The fix is three states per node: unvisited, in-progress (currently an ancestor on the active DFS call stack), and done (fully explored). A cycle is only real if DFS encounters a node that is currently in-progress (an ancestor calling back to itself); encountering a done node via a second path is normal and expected in a DAG.

drills.q: Design the iterative postorder traversal trick using a preorder-style single stack, and explain why the reversal step produces correct postorder output.
drills.a: Run an iterative traversal that visits root, then pushes LEFT child before RIGHT child (the opposite push order from standard preorder), producing the sequence 'root, right, left' as output. Then reverse that entire output list. Reversing the sequence 'root, right, left' for every subtree recursively yields exactly 'left, right, root', which is the definition of postorder -- the reversal of a root-right-left traversal is mathematically identical to a left-right-root traversal.

drills.q: A candidate's Path Sum II solution appends the current node's value to a shared 'current_path' list on the way down, and at each leaf that matches the target sum, appends 'current_path' (the list object itself, not a copy) directly to the results list. Explain what goes wrong and why.
drills.a: The 'current_path' list continues being mutated (values appended and popped) as the DFS traversal proceeds to explore sibling branches after this leaf's match is recorded. Because all recorded results point to the SAME underlying list object, every one of them ends up reflecting whatever 'current_path' looks like at the very end of the entire traversal (likely empty, since backtracking pops every entry back off by the time DFS fully completes), rather than the specific path that existed at the moment each individual match was found. The fix is to append a shallow copy of current_path (e.g. current_path[:] in Python, or a new list constructed from it) at each match, not the live reference.

drills.q: A JSON-parsing service uses straightforward recursive descent to validate incoming payloads and starts crashing with stack overflow errors after a change allows arbitrarily nested user-submitted objects. Diagnose the failure mode and describe the fix, being precise about what does and doesn't improve.
drills.a: This is the classic deep-nesting-exhausts-the-call-stack failure: a maliciously or accidentally deeply nested JSON payload (a chain of thousands of nested objects/arrays) forces recursion depth proportional to nesting depth, which can exceed the runtime's call-stack limit (a real, exploitable denial-of-service pattern against recursive parsers on untrusted input). The fix is to convert the recursive descent into an iterative traversal using an explicit, heap-allocated stack of pending work items, which moves the O(depth) memory footprint from the small, fixed call stack to the much larger heap. This does not reduce the Big-O space complexity (still O(depth) either way) -- it only replaces a small hard ceiling with a much larger, more forgiving one. A complementary, often necessary fix is also imposing and enforcing an explicit maximum nesting depth and rejecting payloads that exceed it, regardless of which traversal style is used.

drills.q: Compare DFS-postorder-based topological sort with Kahn's BFS-based algorithm: what does each naturally give you 'for free', and how does each detect a cycle?
drills.a: DFS-postorder topological sort: run DFS to completion, recording each node in a postorder list as it finishes, then reverse that list to get a valid topological order; it detects a cycle via the same three-state (unvisited/in-progress/done) mechanism used for directed cycle detection -- encountering an in-progress node during the DFS means a cycle exists. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with zero remaining in-degree, decrementing the in-degree of their neighbors, appending removed nodes to the output in removal order; it detects a cycle implicitly, simply by the fact that if a cycle exists, some nodes will never reach zero in-degree and therefore never get removed, so the final output list will be shorter than the total node count. Both are O(V+E); DFS-postorder builds naturally on existing DFS infrastructure and cycle-state tracking, while Kahn's is often considered easier to trace by hand and gives a very direct 'stuck nodes = cycle' signal.

drills.q: What is the size-balance invariant that two heaps must maintain, and why does it matter?
drills.a: The two heap sizes must never differ by more than 1. This is what guarantees the median is always exactly at one or both heap tops, giving O(1) median access instead of requiring a deeper traversal.

drills.q: When the two heaps are equal in size, how do you compute the median? When one has exactly one more element, how do you compute it?
drills.a: Equal sizes: average the max-heap's top and the min-heap's top. One extra element (always in the max-heap/small half, by the invariant): the median is simply that heap's top alone, no averaging.

drills.q: Derive why two-heap insertion is O(log n) while inserting into a maintained-sorted array is O(n), even though both use a comparison that could be found via binary search in O(log n).
drills.a: Binary search locates the correct position in O(log n) in both cases. The difference is what happens AFTER locating the position: a heap only needs to sift the new element up or down through at most log2(n) levels to restore the heap property, touching O(log n) elements total. A sorted array must physically shift every element after the insertion point over by one slot to make room, which touches up to O(n) elements in the worst case (inserting near the front). The heap's relaxed ordering (only parent-child order, not full sequential order) is what avoids the shifting cost.

drills.q: A candidate implements the running-median insert by comparing the new value only against the current median and pushing directly into what seems like the 'obviously correct' heap, skipping the cross-heap push-and-pop step. Construct a sequence of insertions where this produces a wrong median, and explain the fix.
drills.a: Consider inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 in that order with a naive 'compare to current median, push directly' approach that never cross-validates: after 1, 2 median-ish comparisons can leave both heaps technically valid-looking but with an element in the 'wrong' heap relative to its true rank once more elements arrive (e.g., 3 pushed to the large heap based on being greater than a stale median, when it should end up as the new boundary element). The robust algorithm avoids ambiguity entirely by always pushing every new value into ONE designated heap first (say, small), then unconditionally popping that heap's current top and pushing it into the other heap, then checking sizes and moving one element back if needed. This three-step discipline guarantees the ordering invariant holds regardless of where the new value 'should' end up, because the cross-push step re-sorts across both heaps using their own top comparisons rather than trusting the caller's guess.

drills.q: Design the lazy-deletion mechanism needed for Sliding Window Median, and explain exactly when a pending removal is actually applied.
drills.a: Maintain a hash map from value to a count of how many pending removals are outstanding for that value. When the sliding window moves and an element falls out, increment its pending-removal count instead of touching the heap immediately. Whenever you're about to trust a heap's top as the current true extreme (during a median query, or during a rebalance/cross-push step), first check whether that top value has a positive pending-removal count; if so, pop it, decrement its count, and repeat the check on the new top, before using it. This defers the O(n)-scan cost of true removal until the stale value would have surfaced anyway, turning it into an O(log n) pop at that point.

drills.q: A monitoring team wants to track p99 latency incrementally across a single process using the two-heap technique, then later merge results from 200 separate processes into one fleet-wide p99. What works for the single-process case, and what breaks for the fleet-wide merge?
drills.a: For a single process, the generalized two-heap technique works well: keep the heap-size ratio at roughly 99:1 instead of 50:50, and the boundary value between the two heaps is the running p99 latency, updated in O(log n) per new data point. For the fleet-wide merge across 200 processes, this breaks down: two independent two-heap structures (each built from a different process's local stream) don't have a simple, correct way to be combined into one structure representing the true combined p99 -- you can't just merge heaps arbitrarily and expect the balance invariant and ordering guarantee to still hold relative to the full combined dataset. This is precisely the gap that approximate, explicitly mergeable sketches like t-digest or DDSketch are designed to fill: they support a defined merge operation across independently-built sketches while preserving bounded error on the resulting combined percentile estimate.

drills.q: Explain why Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LC4) is not solved with two heaps, and what the efficient approach is instead.
drills.a: Both input arrays are already fully sorted and are static (not a stream with ongoing insertions), so there's no incremental-update problem to justify building and maintaining a heap-based structure at all -- doing so would cost O(m+n) to construct the heaps for a single one-shot computation. The efficient approach is a binary search over the partition point of the shorter array (checking m+n total elements split into a 'left half' and 'right half' such that every left-half element is <= every right-half element across both arrays), achieving O(log(min(m,n))), which beats even reading through both arrays once.

drills.q: Distinguish the data structure and complexity used for 'Kth Largest Element in a Stream' from the two-heap running-median structure, and explain why conflating them is a common mistake.
drills.a: Kth Largest Element in a Stream uses a single min-heap capped at size k: if a new value is greater than the heap's current minimum once the heap is full, pop the minimum and push the new value; the heap's top is always the k-th largest value seen so far. This is O(log k) per insertion and O(k) space. The running-median structure instead uses TWO heaps holding ALL elements seen so far (not just the top k), split into balanced halves, to expose the middle value. The conflation is common because both involve heaps and streaming data, but they answer structurally different questions: 'what are the top k' (bounded retention, discard everything else) versus 'what's the value in the middle of everything' (must retain every element, split into two balanced groups).

drills.q: What are the three steps of the backtracking template used to generate subsets, permutations, and combinations, and in what order do they always occur?
drills.a: Choose (add the element to the path or mark it used), explore (recurse one level deeper), un-choose (remove it from the path or unmark it used) -- un-choose always happens after the recursive call returns, before trying the next sibling.

drills.q: Why is the total time complexity of subset generation O(2^n * n) and not just O(2^n)?
drills.a: There are 2^n leaves in the recursion tree (one per subset), but each subset must actually be copied/built as an output, and a subset can have up to n elements, so building each one costs up to O(n). The extra factor of n accounts for constructing each result, not just reaching it.

drills.q: A candidate's subset-generation code appends path (the live list object) directly to the results list at every recursion node, instead of a copy. Walk through what the final results list looks like after the full traversal completes, and explain why.
drills.a: Since every entry in the results list is a reference to the SAME underlying path list object, and that object continues to be mutated (elements appended and popped) throughout the remainder of the traversal after each entry is 'recorded', every entry in the final results list will show whatever path looks like at the very end of the entire traversal -- typically empty, since backtracking pops every element back off by the time the whole recursion completes. The fix is to store a snapshot copy (e.g. path[:] in Python) at the moment each result is recorded, not the live reference.

drills.q: For Subsets II with input [1, 2, 2], sorted, walk through why skipping index i when nums[i] == nums[i-1] AND i > start correctly avoids duplicate subsets, and explain what would go wrong if you instead skipped whenever nums[i] == nums[i-1] regardless of the i > start condition.
drills.a: With i > start required: at the branching point where start=1 (after choosing the first '1'), the loop considers indices 1 and 2, both holding value 2; skipping index 2 (since nums[2]==nums[1] and 2 > start=1) prevents choosing the second '2' as an alternative sibling to the first '2' at this same branching point, avoiding a duplicate subset like [1,2] appearing twice. If instead you skipped ANY index where nums[i]==nums[i-1] with no start comparison, you would incorrectly skip legitimate uses of a repeated value across DIFFERENT recursion levels -- for example, you'd wrongly prevent including both 2's together in the same subset ([1,2,2]) at all, since the second 2 would always be skipped relative to the first regardless of whether they're actually siblings at the same branching point or sequential picks within one path.

drills.q: Derive the correct duplicate-skip condition for Permutations II and explain, with a concrete 3-element example, why simply checking nums[i]==nums[i-1] (without the used[i-1] check) produces wrong results.
drills.a: The correct condition: skip choosing nums[i] if nums[i]==nums[i-1] AND used[i-1] is False. Consider sorted input [1,1,2]. Without the used[i-1] check, as soon as the algorithm tries to place the second '1' (index 1) anywhere immediately after having just placed the first '1' (index 0) in the SAME active path (used[0]=True at that moment), the naive check nums[1]==nums[0] would still trigger and incorrectly skip using the second '1' even though it's legitimately needed to complete a valid permutation like [1,1,2] -- causing valid permutations to be silently dropped. The used[i-1]==False condition specifically restricts the skip to the case where the previous identical value was already tried AND fully backtracked out of (unused) at this same level in an earlier sibling branch -- that's the one specific situation duplication would otherwise occur, and only that situation.

drills.q: Combination Sum allows reusing the same array element multiple times; Combination Sum II does not. What is the single-line difference in the backtracking code between the two, and why does swapping it break each problem?
drills.a: Combination Sum recurses with start=i after choosing nums[i] (the same index remains eligible to be chosen again); Combination Sum II recurses with start=i+1 (only strictly-later, unused positions remain eligible). Using start=i+1 in Combination Sum would make it impossible to ever choose the same element twice, silently making valid combinations (that legitimately reuse a value) unreachable. Using start=i in Combination Sum II would allow the same array position to be chosen multiple times, producing invalid combinations that violate the 'each element used at most once' constraint.

drills.q: A candidate is asked to count how many subsets of a large array sum to exactly a target value, and reaches for backtracking with a running counter (no need to store or print the subsets). Is this a reasonable approach, and what's the better alternative?
drills.a: It's correct but exponential: the backtracking-with-counter approach still visits every one of the up to 2^n subset branches to check whether each one's sum matches the target, even though nothing is being printed or stored. The better alternative is a knapsack-style counting DP: dp[s] = number of ways to reach partial sum s using elements processed so far, updated for each new element by iterating s from target down to that element's value and adding dp[s - element] into dp[s]. This runs in O(n * target) time (pseudo-polynomial), because it reuses shared sub-computation across many different subsets that happen to reach the same intermediate sum, rather than tracking each subset individually.

drills.q: Explain how Permutation Sequence (finding the k-th permutation directly) avoids ever generating the first k-1 permutations, and state its complexity.
drills.a: It uses the factorial number system: at the first position, there are (n-1)! permutations for each choice of the first digit (since the remaining n-1 elements can be arranged in any order after it). Dividing the target index k by (n-1)! tells you exactly which remaining digit goes first; the remainder (k modulo (n-1)!) becomes the new target index for the second position, where there are now (n-2)! permutations per remaining choice, and so on. This process directly computes each digit of the answer using arithmetic on factorials and a shrinking pool of remaining digits, without ever constructing any permutation other than the target one. Complexity is O(n^2) (or O(n log n) with a Fenwick-tree-backed 'remove the k-th remaining element' structure), versus O(n!) to generate and index into the full list.

drills.q: Given weights, values, and capacity W, write the recurrence for max value using each item at most once.
drills.a: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]]+val[i]) when wt[i]<=w, else dp[i-1][w].

drills.q: Collapse the 2D 0/1 knapsack table to 1D. Which direction do you iterate capacity and why?
drills.a: Backward, from W down to wt[i]. Forward iteration would read a value already updated by this item in the same pass, letting it be counted twice.

drills.q: Determine whether an array can be partitioned into two subsets of equal sum.
drills.a: If total is odd, impossible. Otherwise run boolean subset-sum DP for target=total/2 with backward capacity iteration; dp[0]=True.

drills.q: Count the number of ways to assign +/- signs to an array to reach a target sum.
drills.a: Reduce to subset sum: P=(total+target)/2 must be a non-negative integer <= total; count subsets summing to P via dp[w] += dp[w-n].

drills.q: Extend 0/1 knapsack to two independent budgets (e.g. at most m zeros and n ones). What changes?
drills.a: Add a second capacity axis: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i-cost0][j-cost1]+1); both axes must be iterated backward per item, same once-only argument per axis.

drills.q: An item has a bounded count c (not 1, not infinite). How do you solve bounded knapsack without an O(n*W*c) blowup?
drills.a: Decompose each item into O(log c) meta-items via binary/power-of-two split (sizes 1,2,4,...,remainder), then run standard 0/1 knapsack on the expanded item list in O(n*W*log c).

drills.q: Given coins with unlimited supply, find the minimum number of coins summing to an amount, or -1 if impossible.
drills.a: dp[w]=min(dp[w], dp[w-coin]+1) forward over capacity for each coin; dp[0]=0, others start at infinity; return -1 if dp[amount] is still infinity.

drills.q: Why must the capacity loop go forward here instead of backward like 0/1 knapsack?
drills.a: Forward iteration lets dp[w-coin] already reflect this coin's use earlier in the pass, which is exactly the unlimited-reuse behavior wanted; backward would prevent reuse.

drills.q: Count the number of distinct combinations (order doesn't matter) of coins that sum to an amount.
drills.a: dp[w] += dp[w-coin] with coins as the outer loop and capacity inner; dp[0]=1. Outer-coins prevents counting different orderings of the same multiset separately.

drills.q: Count the number of ordered sequences (order matters) of numbers that sum to a target, unlimited reuse.
drills.a: dp[w] += dp[w-n] with capacity as the outer loop and numbers inner; dp[0]=1. This deliberately counts 1+3 and 3+1 as distinct sequences.

drills.q: Prove greedy fails to minimize coin count for coins {1,3,4} and target 6.
drills.a: Greedy picks 4 first, then must use 1+1, totaling 3 coins (4+1+1); the optimal is 3+3, totaling 2 coins. Greedy is only safe for canonical coin systems.

drills.q: Items now have a cap of k uses each instead of unlimited. How do you adapt the unbounded template?
drills.a: Do not use the plain forward-iteration unbounded template as-is; decompose each item into O(log k) power-of-two meta-items and solve as 0/1 knapsack with backward iteration on the expanded item list.

drills.q: Given prerequisite pairs, determine whether all courses can be completed.
drills.a: Build a directed graph (prereq -> dependent), run Kahn's algorithm; if the processed count equals the total number of courses, yes; otherwise a cycle blocks some subset.

drills.q: Return a valid course completion order, or an empty list if impossible.
drills.a: Kahn's algorithm: queue all in-degree-0 nodes, pop and record each, decrement neighbor in-degrees, enqueue new zeros; return the recorded order if its length equals n, else empty.

drills.q: Implement topological sort using DFS, including cycle detection.
drills.a: Three-color DFS (white/gray/black); mark a node gray on entry, black on exit and push it onto a stack; a gray-to-gray edge is a cycle. Reverse the finished stack for the valid order.

drills.q: Given a sorted list of words in an unknown alien alphabet, reconstruct a valid character order.
drills.a: For each pair of adjacent words, find the first differing character and add a directed edge from the earlier character to the later one, then topologically sort the character graph; also detect the invalid case where a longer word's full prefix appears after it as a shorter word.

drills.q: Find the minimum number of semesters to complete all courses if any number of unblocked courses can be taken simultaneously.
drills.a: Run Kahn's algorithm processing one entire in-degree-zero frontier per round (layered BFS); the number of rounds until the queue empties is the answer; return -1 if a cycle prevents completion.

drills.q: Return the lexicographically smallest valid topological order of a DAG.
drills.a: Replace Kahn's plain queue with a min-heap keyed on node value, always popping the smallest currently-eligible (in-degree-0) node; runs in O((V+E) log V).

drills.q: Implement a trie with insert, search (exact match), and startsWith (prefix match).
drills.a: Each node has children plus an is_end flag; insert walks/creates nodes per character and sets is_end at the last one; search requires the path to exist AND is_end set; startsWith requires only the path to exist.

drills.q: Why is search('ca') different from startsWith('ca') even if only 'car' has been inserted?
drills.a: search must also check is_end at the final node reached; the path to 'ca' exists but is_end is false there, so search returns false while startsWith returns true.

drills.q: Find all dictionary words present in a character grid (Word Search II).
drills.a: Build a trie from the dictionary, then run one DFS from every grid cell following the trie in parallel with the grid path, pruning the moment the current path isn't any word's prefix (trie-child miss).

drills.q: Support search queries with a '.' wildcard matching any single character, backed by a trie.
drills.a: At a normal character follow the matching child; at '.', recursively try every existing child and succeed if any branch matches. Worst case O(26^k * L) for k wildcards.

drills.q: Given a dictionary of roots and a sentence, replace each word with its shortest matching root if one exists.
drills.a: Build a trie from the roots; for each sentence word, walk the trie and stop at the FIRST is_end node encountered (not the longest path) — that's the shortest valid root.

drills.q: Design an autocomplete system that ranks suggestions by query frequency rather than lexicographic order, without recomputing top-k on every keystroke.
drills.a: Maintain a cached top-k list at (or reachable from) each trie node representing a complete query, updated incrementally on writes, rather than DFS-ing the whole subtree per keystroke — full-subtree DFS on a popular short prefix is effectively O(n).

drills.q: Implement Union-Find with path compression and union by rank.
drills.a: find recursively repoints every visited node to the root; union finds both roots, attaches the shorter-rank tree under the taller, and increments rank only when ranks are equal.

drills.q: Count the number of connected components (provinces) given an adjacency matrix.
drills.a: Union every pair with a matrix entry of 1; maintain a running count initialized to n, decremented on every successful (non-redundant) union.

drills.q: Given a list of edges forming a graph that was originally a tree plus one extra edge, find the redundant edge.
drills.a: Process edges in order, calling union on each; the first edge whose union call returns false (both endpoints already share a root) is the redundant edge.

drills.q: Given == and != equality constraints between variables, determine if they can all be satisfied simultaneously.
drills.a: Union all == pairs first. Then check every != pair does not share a root; if any != pair ends up connected, the constraints are unsatisfiable.

drills.q: Explain precisely what amortized complexity union-find achieves with both optimizations, and what happens with only one.
drills.a: Both together: O(alpha(n)) amortized (Tarjan 1975). Union by rank alone: O(log n) worst case per find. Path compression alone (arbitrary union order): O(log n) amortized. Neither: adversarial order can force O(n) per find.

drills.q: Extend union-find to answer ratio queries between variables given equations like a/b=2.0 (Evaluate Division).
drills.a: Store a weight alongside each parent pointer representing the ratio to that parent; during find, accumulate (multiply) weights along the compressed path so each node holds a direct ratio to the root; union combines two components using the equation linking them.

drills.q: For each element in an array, find the first element to its right that's strictly greater, or -1 if none exists.
drills.a: Maintain a decreasing stack of indices scanning left to right; whenever the current value exceeds the stack's top, pop it and record the current value as its next-greater element.

drills.q: Given daily temperatures, return for each day how many days until a warmer temperature.
drills.a: Same decreasing-stack template as next-greater-element, but store the index gap i-j into the answer array instead of the popped element's replacement value.

drills.q: Find the largest rectangular area in a histogram of bar heights.
drills.a: Maintain an increasing stack of indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop the top and compute area as height times width between the new stack top and current index (exclusive); append a sentinel 0 to flush remaining bars.

drills.q: Explain why a monotonic stack pass over n elements is O(n) total, not O(n^2), despite a while loop inside a for loop.
drills.a: Every index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run; total pushes and pops are each bounded by n, so total work sums to O(n).

drills.q: Find the maximum in every sliding window of size k across an array, in O(n) total.
drills.a: Maintain a decreasing monotonic deque of indices; pop smaller elements off the back before pushing, and pop the front if it's fallen outside the window's left boundary. Front of the deque is always the current max.

drills.q: Sum the minimum of every contiguous subarray of an array, without enumerating all subarrays.
drills.a: For each element, find distances to the previous strictly-smaller and next smaller-or-equal element via monotonic stack passes; that element is the minimum for (left distance * right distance) subarrays, contributing value*left*right to the total sum.

drills.q: Generate all subsets of a set of distinct integers.
drills.a: Record every partial path as a valid subset (append a copy); loop from a start index, choose (append), explore (recurse with i+1), unchoose (pop) after the call returns.

drills.q: Generate all permutations of a set of distinct integers.
drills.a: Track a used[] boolean array instead of a start index; choose by marking used and appending, explore recursively when the path reaches full length, unchoose by unmarking and popping.

drills.q: Place N queens on an N x N board so none attack each other; return all valid placements.
drills.a: Track occupied columns and both diagonals (row-col, row+col) in sets; at each row, only recurse into columns with no conflict, checked before the recursive call, then unchoose after it returns.

drills.q: Find all combinations of candidates (each reusable unlimited times) summing to a target.
drills.a: Sort candidates; recurse with the same start index i (not i+1) to allow reuse; prune by breaking the loop once candidates[i] exceeds the remaining target.

drills.q: Partition a string into substrings that are all palindromes; return all such partitions, and describe how to avoid recomputing palindrome checks.
drills.a: Only recurse into a substring if it's already verified to be a palindrome, checked before recursing; precompute a 2D isPalindrome[i][j] table via DP in O(n^2) so each check is O(1) instead of O(n).

drills.q: Determine if an array can be partitioned into k subsets of equal sum, and explain why filling one bucket at a time prunes better than assigning each element to a bucket independently.
drills.a: Compute target=total/k (fail if not divisible), then backtrack filling one subset up to the target sum before moving to the next, abandoning a subset the moment its running sum exceeds target -- this collapses many equivalent element-orderings that element-to-bucket assignment (k^n raw possibilities) would otherwise explore separately.

drills.q: Name the three required elements of a disciplined chaos experiment and what specifically goes wrong if each is skipped.
drills.a: A falsifiable, specific hypothesis (skip it: no way to tell if you learned anything). A bounded blast radius (skip it: the experiment can become an actual uncontrolled outage). A pre-defined, measurable abort condition with a real person watching (skip it: nobody has the authority or trigger to stop things before they cascade).

drills.q: Explain what Toxiproxy does mechanically and why fault injection through it doesn't require touching application code.
drills.a: Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy placed between the service and a real dependency; the service connects to the proxy instead of the dependency directly, and faults ('toxics': latency, bandwidth limits, timeouts, connection resets) are toggled on/off externally via Toxiproxy's HTTP API. Because injection happens at the network/proxy layer rather than inside the application, no test-mode branches are needed in the code, which keeps the experiment realistic (it exercises the real production code path) and trivially reversible.

drills.q: A team's pod-kill chaos experiments (via Litmus/Chaos Mesh) pass cleanly every time, but the service still fails badly when a real downstream dependency becomes fully unreachable. Diagnose.
drills.a: Pod-kill chaos tests the orchestration/infrastructure layer -- whether Kubernetes correctly detects and replaces a killed pod -- which is a different failure layer from application-level handling of a slow or unreachable dependency connection (retries, circuit breakers, fallback logic). Passing pod-kill tests says nothing about that second layer; the team needs network/connection-layer fault injection (Toxiproxy-style latency, timeout, or blackhole faults) specifically to exercise and validate the application's own resilience code.

drills.q: Why did Netflix build Chaos Monkey, and what specific organizational pain was it addressing?
drills.a: After Netflix moved to AWS, instance failure became a frequent, expected event rather than a rare one, and engineers needed services that were genuinely fault-tolerant, not just services whose fallback code looked correct in review but had never actually been exercised (and could have silently bit-rotted). Chaos Monkey randomly terminated production instances during business hours specifically to force continuous, real validation of fault tolerance, with engineers present to observe and respond immediately rather than discovering gaps from unattended logs later.

drills.q: Walk through the full structure of a game day from planning through retrospective, naming the step most commonly skipped and why that skip matters.
drills.a: Pick one specific, plausible failure scenario; write and get sign-off on a falsifiable hypothesis and measurable abort condition beforehand; assign explicit roles (fault injector, dashboard watcher monitoring the abort condition, note-taker, incident commander with real abort authority); run the injection against a bounded scope; hold a retrospective. The most commonly skipped step is converting retrospective findings into a tracked, owned fix with a deadline -- without it, a discovered resilience gap just quietly persists until the next game day (or production) rediscovers it.

drills.q: Why do the Principles of Chaos Engineering call for running experiments in production or production-like environments, rather than staging, and what makes this safe?
drills.a: Staging environments systematically fail to reproduce real production's actual traffic patterns, data shapes, and scale, so a staging-only chaos program risks validating the wrong thing entirely -- confidence that doesn't transfer to real conditions. Safety in production comes from the discipline itself (bounded blast radius, a pre-tested abort mechanism, mature observability to detect the abort condition quickly), not from avoiding production altogether.

drills.q: A staff engineer proposes moving from quarterly human-run game days to continuous, automated chaos experiments in production, Netflix-style. What has to be true first, and what's the honest risk of skipping the prerequisites?
drills.a: Continuous automated chaos requires the hypothesis/blast-radius/abort-condition discipline to work without a human curating each run: automated, reliable steady-state measurement; an automated, tested abort/rollback mechanism that doesn't depend on a human noticing in time; and observability mature enough to attribute a specific degradation to the specific injected fault rather than unrelated noise. Skipping these while only automating the scheduling of fault injection reproduces the 'experiment becomes a real incident' failure mode, just on an unattended, higher-frequency, harder-to-catch cadence -- automating the cadence is the easy part; automating trustworthy detection and abort is the harder prerequisite most orgs underestimate.

drills.q: Your team's chaos game days have confirmed the same hypotheses cleanly every quarter with no surprises. Should the program be scaled back, and how do you decide?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- repeatedly confirming a hypothesis is genuine evidence a resilience property still holds as dependencies, code, and traffic patterns evolve, so 'still true' is real, non-wasted information. Scaling back is warranted only if the hypotheses themselves have stopped being meaningfully risky or informative; the correct response then is escalating blast radius or targeting newer, previously-untested failure modes (a recently added dependency, a recently changed critical path) rather than stopping the program, prioritized by tracking which parts of the dependency graph haven't yet been exercised.

drills.q: How do you decide the appropriate blast radius when running an entirely new type of chaos experiment for the first time, and what does it mean if even the smallest reasonable scope feels too risky to run?
drills.a: Start at the smallest scope that can still produce a meaningful signal -- one instance, one canary, single-digit percent of traffic -- and only escalate after that smaller step runs cleanly (hypothesis confirmed, abort condition never triggered) at least once; never start a new, untested experiment type at wide blast radius regardless of confidence. If even the smallest version feels too risky to run at all, that itself is useful information: the system likely isn't ready for chaos testing of that specific failure mode yet, and the actual next step is improving observability/rollback capability first, not skipping the experiment and hoping it would have gone fine.

drills.q: A circuit-breaker fallback path passed code review but failed the first time it was actually triggered in production. What's the root cause pattern, and what chaos-engineering practice prevents recurrence?
drills.a: Root cause: the fallback path was never empirically exercised since it was written, so it silently bit-rotted -- a config value drifted, a downstream API shape changed, or a latent bug went unnoticed because the path never actually ran. Prevention: run the specific fault that triggers this path (via Toxiproxy or equivalent) as a recurring, automated CI or scheduled check rather than a one-time manual verification, so the fallback is continuously proven to still work as the surrounding system changes.

drills.q: Define contract testing and explain how it differs from integration testing.
drills.a: Contract testing verifies a consumer and provider agree on the shape of an interaction by replaying the consumer's actual recorded requests against the provider's real implementation. Integration testing verifies your code against a copy of the dependency (stub/Testcontainers) that you control, which can drift from what's really deployed. Contract testing catches drift between deployed services; integration testing catches bugs in how your own code talks to a realistic dependency.

drills.q: What is the Pact Broker and what does `can-i-deploy` do?
drills.a: The Pact Broker is a registry storing pact files and verification results, keyed by consumer/provider versions. `can-i-deploy` queries it to check whether the exact provider version being deployed has a recorded successful verification against the exact consumer version currently in the target environment (and vice versa); a non-zero result blocks the deploy pipeline.

drills.q: A provider verification build is green every time, but a real consumer's integration broke in production last week. Diagnose two possible causes.
drills.a: Either the consumer never wrote a pact covering the interaction that broke (so nothing protected it), or the pact used an exact-value matcher that happened to still technically match despite a semantic change. Fix: audit pact coverage against real production traffic to find missing interactions, and replace brittle exact matchers with shape/type matchers where the exact value doesn't carry contractual meaning.

drills.q: Why do exact-value matchers in pacts tend to get muted or deleted over time, and what should replace them?
drills.a: They freeze the contract to one moment's data; any legitimate data change (new valid enum value, changed but still-valid quantity) fails the pact repeatedly, and after enough false positives the team stops trusting or deletes the assertion. Replace with shape/type matchers (like(), eachLike(), regex) by default, reserving exact-value assertions for fields with real contractual meaning like a fixed status enum or error code.

drills.q: When should a team use OpenAPI-based schema diffing instead of consumer-driven contract testing (Pact)?
drills.a: When consumers are numerous, unknown, or uncooperative -- e.g. a public API -- CDC requires every consumer to write and publish a pact, which doesn't scale to unenumerable consumers. OpenAPI diffing plus semantic versioning and deprecation windows handles structural compatibility at scale without requiring consumer participation, though it can't express semantic contracts CDC captures (e.g. 'field X is always present when status is Y').

drills.q: How is contract compatibility enforced for asynchronous Kafka events, and how does BACKWARD compatibility mode help a topic with slow-to-redeploy consumers?
drills.a: Via a schema registry (Confluent, AWS Glue) enforcing a compatibility mode on schema registration.
