BACKWARD compatibility means a new producer schema can still be read by code written against the old schema, so producers can deploy schema changes without requiring consumers to redeploy immediately -- decoupling producer and consumer release cadence.

drills.q: Your org has both Pact-based CDC and OpenAPI-based schema diffing running, and for one change Pact says compatible while the OpenAPI diff flags it as breaking. How do you reason about the disagreement, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Both can be simultaneously correct: the OpenAPI diff caught a structural change (e.g. a field removed from the documented spec) that no actual consumer pact exercises -- a real break relative to the documented contract but not relative to any real consumer in production. This exposes a documentation/reality gap. Favor CDC as authoritative for internal service pairs where consumers are enumerable and it reflects real usage; favor the schema diff when consumers are unknown, since 'nobody's using it yet' isn't a safe assumption. The durable fix is to either write a pact for the real dependency or remove the unused field from the spec, not to silently prefer whichever gate is convenient.

drills.q: How would you roll out contract testing across a 40-microservice org with no prior practice, and what's the most common way this rollout fails?
drills.a: Start with the single highest-incident-cost consumer/provider boundary, wire it fully through the broker with can-i-deploy as a genuine CD gate, and prove concrete incident prevention before expanding by boundary criticality rather than mandating full coverage day one. The most common failure is adopting Pact without making can-i-deploy a hard gate -- contract tests that don't block a deploy decay into unread documentation, and pacts go stale within months because nobody is forced to keep them current.

drills.q: A provider team refuses to write verification tests against a consumer's published pact. What's the actual risk, and how do you frame it to leadership?
drills.a: CDC requires both sides to participate -- a consumer's pact with no provider verification provides zero actual protection, because nothing is proving the real provider implementation satisfies it. This isn't a technical gap, it's an organizational dependency risk: frame it as an unverified cross-team contract with a known, specific incident class (silent breaking changes shipped without detection) rather than treating the unverified pact as partial coverage.

drills.q: Your provider verification suite takes 25 minutes and sits on the critical path of every deploy. What are two likely causes and their fixes?
drills.a: Likely verifying against every pact version ever published rather than only versions relevant to active environments -- fix with broker retention/pruning and tag-based verification (verify only pacts tagged prod/main). Also check whether provider-state setup (seeding real DB state per interaction) rather than the HTTP replay itself is the actual bottleneck, and optimize or parallelize that setup. Do not fix this by running verification less frequently on the deploy path -- that reopens the exact race condition CDC exists to close.

drills.q: What specific class of bug does E2E testing catch that integration testing structurally cannot, and why?
drills.a: Seam bugs in the actual deployed wiring between components -- e.g. a frontend build pointing at the wrong API version, a broken post-login redirect, or a race condition that only shows up under real network latency between genuinely deployed services. Integration tests prove each side works against a realistic copy of its dependency; only E2E proves the real, currently-deployed wiring is correct.

drills.q: Why did Selenium-era E2E suites earn a reputation for flakiness, mechanically?
drills.a: Selenium had no built-in auto-waiting -- every async UI interaction needed a hand-written explicit wait (e.g. WebDriverWait until element clickable), and missing or mistuning one either raced the page (intermittent failure) or slowed the suite unnecessarily. Combined with manual driver-binary version management and no native parallelism, this produced widespread ad hoc, inconsistent flakiness across large suites.

drills.q: An E2E suite is flaky specifically in CI but passes reliably locally. Walk through the diagnosis and fix.
drills.a: Most likely cause: shared or polluted test data under parallel CI execution, since CI runs specs concurrently against shared staging state in a way a local single-threaded run never stresses; CI resource constraints (CPU throttling, network jitter) can also expose real timing races invisible on a warm local machine. Fix: provision isolated data per test or per parallel worker via direct API calls (not through the UI), and confirm auto-waiting is genuinely in use rather than a hidden manual sleep race before assuming 'CI is just different.'

drills.q: Explain the tradeoff between CSS/XPath locators and role/label-based locators (get_by_role, get_by_label) in terms of maintenance cost.
drills.a: CSS/XPath selectors couple a test to markup structure, so an unrelated visual or structural refactor breaks the test with zero behavioral change -- the largest source of untraceable 'why did this break' maintenance tickets in real E2E suites. Role/label-based locators couple the test to the semantic contract a real user relies on, which is far more stable across refactors and incidentally improves accessibility coverage.

drills.q: What does Playwright's storageState solve, and why is it more than a performance optimization?
drills.a: It captures authenticated session state (cookies, local storage) once and lets subsequent tests start already logged in, instead of driving the full login UI flow per test. Beyond saving time, it removes login -- itself a multi-step async flow -- as a shared source of flakiness across every test that isn't specifically testing the login/auth flow itself.

drills.q: A staff engineer asks you to justify cutting an 80-spec E2E suite down to 15. Give the argument, and the honest counter-risk you should acknowledge.
drills.a: Identify the 15 as the genuinely revenue-critical, cross-system journeys, and show the remaining 65 either duplicate what integration tests already prove or cover low-business-impact paths relative to their measured flakiness and CI runtime cost -- back this with real flake-rate and time data, not a general principle. Counter-risk to acknowledge: one of the cut 65 might catch a real regression later; the honest position is that this trade is usually worth it (a permanently slow, low-trust suite people route around costs more), unless that specific journey's business risk (compliance, revenue exposure) genuinely justifies the ongoing maintenance cost.

drills.q: Explain the E2E 'rot loop' end to end -- what starts it, and where in the loop does the real fix need to be applied?
drills.a: It starts with unisolated shared test data: one test's side effect corrupts another test's assumed state, causing a flaky failure. The team responds by rerunning until green or merging on red, which erodes trust in red E2E builds generally. The suite then grows with more journeys added 'just in case' since testing discipline has already broken down, increasing the flakiness surface and compounding the cycle. The real fix is at the start of the loop -- per-test/per-worker data isolation -- not at the symptom (adding retry logic or telling engineers to stop merging on red).

drills.q: Why should visual regression testing (Percy/Chromatic-style pixel diffing) and functional E2E testing be treated as separate signals even if they share the same browser-automation infrastructure?
drills.a: They catch different bug classes: a checkout flow can visually shift (color, layout) while still functionally completing correctly, or render pixel-identical while being functionally broken. Conflating the two in one report muddies what a red result actually means and routes failures to the wrong owner -- a visual diff typically needs design/product review, a functional failure needs engineering -- slowing triage in both directions.

drills.q: Your company is adopting AI-assisted E2E test generation that can produce dozens of new specs per sprint. What's the risk, and what governance would you apply?
drills.a: Faster spec authoring doesn't change the underlying economics that cause E2E suites to rot -- data isolation, environment strategy, and criticality triage are unaffected by how fast specs are written, so ungoverned AI-generated specs will produce the same large/slow/flaky/ignored suite, just faster. Apply the same criticality rubric (revenue-critical, genuinely cross-system, isolated test data) to AI-generated specs before merge as to human-authored ones, and treat growing auto-generated coverage as a metric to scrutinize rather than celebrate by itself.

drills.q: How do ephemeral per-PR environments change the E2E test-data-isolation problem, and what do they NOT solve?
drills.a: They eliminate cross-PR contention entirely by giving each PR its own full-stack environment and dataset, removing the shared-staging-pollution failure mode that causes many CI-only flaky failures. They do NOT solve intra-PR parallelism -- multiple E2E specs running concurrently within the same PR's environment still need per-test/per-worker data isolation (unique tenants/users), since the ephemeral environment is shared across those parallel specs.

drills.q: Explain the open-model vs closed-model distinction in load testing, and give an example of when each is the correct choice.
drills.a: Open model: requests arrive at a rate independent of system response time (Poisson process, exponential inter-arrival) -- correct for public, unauthenticated, arrival-driven traffic like a public API or marketing site, since a slow system there experiences real, unbounded queue buildup as new users keep arriving. Closed model: a fixed number of virtual users loop request-wait-response-repeat, so a slowing system causes each user's effective request rate to drop, making throughput look artificially stable -- correct for genuinely bounded populations, like an internal tool used by exactly 500 named employees who cannot exceed that concurrency.

drills.q: A load test script sends the next request the instant the previous response arrives, with no delay. What's wrong with this, mechanically?
drills.a: It eliminates think time, which massively overstates each simulated user's real request rate. A real user issuing roughly one request every several seconds gets modeled as issuing requests as fast as the network allows -- requiring far fewer virtual users to reach a target aggregate throughput than reality would need, and consequently testing a fundamentally different connection/concurrency scenario (unrealistic per-connection request rate) rather than realistic user behavior.

drills.q: Why is a fixed, uniform sleep() between requests still an inadequate model of think time, even though it's better than no delay at all?
drills.a: Real user pauses follow a right-skewed (log-normal) distribution -- most users pause a typical amount, but a real tail of users pauses much longer. A uniform fixed delay smooths out this variance, eliminating the burst/lull pattern real traffic has, which understates the tail behavior that often drives real system stress (e.g., a burst of near-simultaneous requests after a batch of users all finish a similar-length pause).

drills.q: A load test 'passes' cleanly at high sustained throughput on a single endpoint, but production falls over at a fraction of that load under real usage. Diagnose the likely test-design flaw.
drills.a: The test was almost certainly closed-model with zero think time against one endpoint in isolation, which measures the load generator/endpoint's raw throughput ceiling rather than realistic concurrent-user behavior across a real traffic mix. Fix: rebuild as an open-model (arrival-rate) test with realistic think time and a weighted multi-endpoint mix derived from actual production traffic logs, so shared resources (connection pools, caches, downstream services) are stressed the way they would be in reality.

drills.q: Why should JMeter's actual load-generation runs always be executed via CLI (non-GUI) mode, and what goes wrong if you don't?
drills.a: JMeter's GUI is a heavyweight Java Swing application that does live rendering and listener updates during the test; this competes with the load generator itself for CPU and memory, producing both lower achievable throughput and less trustworthy latency numbers than the same plan run headless. Build the test plan visually in the GUI, but execute real load runs with `jmeter -n -t plan.jmx -l results.jtl`.

drills.q: In k6's ramping-arrival-rate executor, what's the difference between preAllocatedVUs and maxVUs, and what does it mean operationally if a test run hits maxVUs?
drills.a: preAllocatedVUs is the pool of virtual users k6 starts with to sustain the target arrival rate; maxVUs is a hard ceiling k6 can grow into if responses slow down and more concurrent VUs are needed to keep the arrival rate constant. Hitting maxVUs during a run is itself a finding: it means the system under test cannot sustain that arrival rate without unbounded concurrency/queue growth -- the correct response is to investigate why, not simply raise the ceiling and rerun.

drills.q: A load test shows near-100% cache hit rate and low latency at a given throughput; production shows 60% hit rate and much higher latency at the same throughput. What's the likely test flaw and the fix?
drills.a: The test almost certainly reused a small, fixed set of request parameters (the same handful of product IDs or search queries) repeatedly, giving the cache an artificially easy workload. Real traffic has a much wider access distribution, often Zipfian-skewed (a few popular items, a long tail of rarely-requested ones); sampling request parameters from a distribution matching real access patterns -- not a fixed small set, and not necessarily uniform random either -- reproduces realistic cache-miss behavior.

drills.q: Explain why testing only a gradual ramp, or only a step-function spike, each miss a distinct real failure mode, and give a production scenario each would catch that the other wouldn't.
drills.a: A step-function ramp (instant jump to target load) stresses simultaneous connection setup, TLS handshakes, and cold caches -- it catches burst-driven failures like a flash-sale traffic spike or a viral link overwhelming connection pools all at once. A gradual ramp stresses organic growth -- it catches degradation that only appears under sustained load, like a memory leak that manifests after tens of minutes, or an autoscaling policy that reacts too slowly. Running only one misses the failure mode specific to the other.

drills.q: When would choosing Gatling over k6 for a new load-testing initiative be a mistake despite Gatling's superior per-machine throughput and reporting?
drills.a: When the team maintaining the tests has no Scala/JVM background and a tight deadline -- Gatling's Scala DSL has a real learning curve, and a load-testing practice only one Scala-literate engineer can read or extend becomes a bus-factor risk and a black box to the rest of the team. In that context, k6 (JavaScript) or Locust (Python), written and maintained by the whole team, is the more durable choice even at somewhat lower per-agent efficiency.

drills.q: Your team runs a 2-minute k6 load test on every PR and it has never failed a threshold, yet production has had three load-related incidents this year. Diagnose and propose a plan.
drills.a: A 2-minute test cannot surface the failure modes actually responsible for those incidents -- connection pool exhaustion under sustained load, memory growth that only appears after tens of minutes (soak-test territory), or a genuine capacity breakpoint well above the load a short smoke-style test reaches. The team is likely treating a fast PR-gate regression check as their entire performance-testing practice. Plan: keep the fast per-PR test for catching obvious immediate regressions, and add a separate, less frequent (nightly/pre-release) test program covering soak, spike, and breakpoint scenarios against realistic traffic models -- don't try to make the PR-gate test longer, since that destroys development velocity for a benefit better achieved with a properly scoped separate cadence.

drills.q: Name the four distinct ML test layers and, in one phrase, what each validates that the others don't.
drills.a: Data tests: is the training/serving input itself trustworthy (schema, nulls, label balance) before any model is trained. Model tests: does the model meet a performance bar per SLICE, not just in aggregate. Behavioral tests (CheckList-style): does the model have a specific capability, independent of whether aggregate accuracy happened to cover it. Metamorphic tests: does a defined input-output relation hold, without needing ground-truth labels for the perturbed case -- plus ongoing production drift monitoring as a fifth, continuous layer.

drills.q: Explain CheckList's three test types (MFT, INV, DIR) with an example of a bug each is specifically designed to catch.
drills.a: MFT (Minimum Functionality Test): a simple, targeted example checking a basic capability exists, e.g. 'I don't like this' correctly predicted negative -- catches outright capability gaps. INV (Invariance): a label-preserving perturbation like swapping a name shouldn't change the prediction -- catches spurious correlations/shortcut learning (e.g. the model secretly keys off names correlated with sentiment in training data). DIR (Directional Expectation): adding a clear negative clause to a positive review should lower the positive score -- catches a model that's sensitive to input but not sensitive in the correct direction, a subtler failure than the other two.

drills.q: A model posts 0.90 aggregate AUC and ships, then is found post-launch to discriminate badly against an 8%-of-traffic minority slice sitting at 0.65 AUC. Diagnose the testing gap and the fix.
drills.a: The evaluation only checked aggregate AUC and never sliced results by the relevant demographic/segment dimension -- the aggregate metric mathematically dilutes a minority slice's poor performance into near-invisibility when that slice is a small fraction of the overall test set. Fix: add per-slice model tests as a required promotion gate, with slices chosen deliberately (known sensitive attributes, known underrepresented segments) rather than whatever the evaluation script happens to compute by default.

drills.q: Why is metamorphic testing particularly valuable for fairness testing specifically, compared to a standard labeled model test?
drills.a: Metamorphic testing asserts a RELATION between an input perturbation and the expected output change (e.g., swapping the gender field on a credit application shouldn't increase predicted default risk) without requiring a ground-truth label for the perturbed, counterfactual input. Standard labeled model tests can't be constructed for these cases because a real, labeled 'correct' outcome for a hypothetical counterfactual applicant usually doesn't exist -- metamorphic relations sidestep that requirement entirely.

drills.q: Distinguish data drift from concept drift, and explain why concept drift is the more dangerous of the two to monitor for.
drills.a: Data drift is a shift in the input feature distribution (e.g. average customer age rising over time); concept drift is a shift in the actual relationship between inputs and the correct output (the same input now genuinely warrants a different prediction due to a real-world change). Concept drift is more dangerous because it can occur with NO detectable shift in the input distribution -- distributional monitoring (PSI, KS test) alone would completely miss it, which is why downstream performance/business-metric monitoring must be paired with distributional monitoring rather than substituted for it.

drills.q: What do PSI thresholds conventionally mean, where does the convention come from, and why is PSI generally preferred over a raw KS-test p-value for production monitoring?
drills.a: PSI < 0.1 conventionally means no significant drift, 0.1-0.25 means moderate drift warranting investigation, and > 0.25 means significant drift warranting action -- a convention originating in credit-risk scorecard monitoring in financial services, now applied broadly. PSI is generally preferred over a raw KS-test p-value in production because KS-test significance becomes oversensitive at the large sample sizes typical of production traffic, flagging even trivially small, practically irrelevant distribution shifts as 'statistically significant,' whereas PSI's binned, magnitude-based score gives a more actionable, practically interpretable signal.

drills.q: A PSI-based drift alert fires on a feature that turns out to be a benign seasonal pattern (e.g. holiday shopping). What monitoring design flaw caused this, and how do you fix it without losing the ability to catch real drift?
drills.a: The reference distribution was likely a single static training-time snapshot that didn't account for known cyclical/seasonal variation, so a normal seasonal shift got flagged identically to genuine concerning drift. Fix by comparing against a reference window that accounts for known seasonality (e.g. this December vs. last December) or tracking PSI trend across comparable periods, rather than one static forever-baseline -- while still tracking a shorter-window trend in parallel so a large deviation from both signals is treated as the stronger, more trustworthy alert.

drills.q: Why can't a CheckList-style behavioral test suite be produced by mechanically running a generic template, and what specifically made CheckList's own published results (2x tests, 3x bugs found) strong?
drills.a: The value came from practitioners applying real, task-specific domain judgment to decide which linguistic/behavioral capabilities and perturbations actually matter for their particular model's use case -- a generic template run without that judgment produces shallow coverage, because deciding 'what capability matters here' and 'what perturbation would a real edge case or adversary produce' are domain questions no generic tool can answer on its own. CheckList provides the matrix/vocabulary and tooling, but the demonstrated bug-finding yield required practitioners to fill it in with real task understanding.

drills.q: A stakeholder says 'you told me the model passed testing' after a specific behavioral capability (e.g., sarcasm handling) that the business cares about is found to fail badly, despite passing data and per-slice model tests. How do you explain this without implying testing is unreliable in general?
drills.a: Explain that 'passed testing' was never one binary claim -- data and model tests validate that training data was clean and the model meets a statistical performance bar on held-out data, which is necessary but says nothing about specific behavioral capabilities that may be underrepresented in that held-out data's distribution. Behavioral testing is a distinct, additional, cumulative layer specifically because a model can be statistically strong in aggregate while having a systematic capability gap the other layers structurally can't see. If behavioral tests genuinely weren't run before this point, own that as a real process/coverage gap directly, rather than implying it was an unavoidable limitation of ML testing as a discipline.

drills.q: Leadership wants to reduce ML testing investment because aggregate metrics have been stable for two years. What's the strongest response, grounded in the specific blind spots stable aggregate metrics have?
drills.a: Two years of stable aggregate metrics is weak evidence of true system health for two specific, named reasons: aggregate metrics structurally can't reveal slice-level degradation (a slice could silently worsen while other slices compensate to keep the aggregate flat), and stable input distributions don't rule out concept drift (the input-output relationship can shift with no detectable change in input distribution). The response should name the cost asymmetry rather than argue 'test more' on principle: continuous per-slice and drift monitoring are comparatively cheap and ongoing, while an undetected fairness incident or a silent concept-drift-driven business decline is expensive and typically discovered late -- propose keeping the cheap continuous monitoring layers while being open to scaling back the more expensive behavioral-suite-authoring effort only if the task's capability surface has genuinely stopped changing.

drills.q: Name the four standard performance test types and, in one phrase each, the specific question each answers.
drills.a: Baseline: what does normal look like (reference point for comparison). Soak/endurance: does it degrade over hours-to-days of sustained load (leaks, resource exhaustion). Spike: does it survive a sudden burst and recover cleanly afterward. Breakpoint: where's the real capacity ceiling, and how does it fail (graceful shed vs. cascading collapse).

drills.q: With a concrete numeric example, show why average latency can badly mislead even when most requests are fast.
drills.a: If 990 of 1000 requests take 40ms and 10 (1%) take 4000ms, mean = (990*40 + 10*4000)/1000 = 79.6ms -- looking like 'somewhat slower than typical.' p50 = 40ms correctly shows typical latency is fine; p99 >= 4000ms correctly reveals the broken 1% tail. At 10,000 req/s that tail is 100 requests/sec experiencing a 4-second response continuously -- completely invisible in the single averaged number.

drills.q: A service 'passed load testing' before launch (a single 15-minute test) but OOM'd in production after 30+ hours. Diagnose the methodology gap.
drills.a: No soak test was run. A short load test cannot surface accumulation effects (memory leaks, connection pool exhaustion, disk/log growth) that only manifest after hours to days of sustained load -- a leak growing 2MB/hour is noise in 30 minutes (60MB) and fatal over 48 hours (~100GB). The fix is adding a soak test at expected load for a duration exceeding the realistic accumulation window to the pre-release checklist for any service with long-lived connections, caches, or in-memory state.

drills.q: A spike test shows the system survives a sudden 5x load burst without errors, but support tickets report the service stayed slow for an hour after the spike passed. What went wrong with the test design, and what's the real failure mechanism?
drills.a: The test only measured survival during the spike, not recovery afterward. The real failure mechanism is likely a connection pool or cache that got exhausted or poisoned during the burst and doesn't self-heal, keeping latency/error rate elevated well after load returned to baseline -- sometimes requiring a manual restart. Fix: extend the spike test to hold a post-spike measurement window long enough to confirm p99/error-rate actually returns to the pre-spike baseline, not just trends downward.

drills.q: Explain the difference between a benchmark and a load test, and give an example where each can show a result the other misses entirely.
drills.a: A benchmark measures a fixed, isolated unit of work (e.g., a serialization function) under controlled, repeatable conditions to compare implementations or catch a regression between commits -- scope comparable to a unit test. A load test measures whole-system emergent behavior under realistic concurrent traffic. Example one direction: a microbenchmark can show an 8% regression in a hot function that's 0.01% of end-to-end latency, invisible at the system level. Example the other direction: a load test can show a system-level p99 regression (new lock contention, worse cache eviction under real concurrency) with zero change in any individual function's benchmark, because the regression is purely an interaction/concurrency effect.

drills.q: During a breakpoint test, what does it mean mechanically when total throughput starts decreasing as offered load continues to increase, and why is this a more reliable signal of the true ceiling than watching latency alone?
drills.a: It means the system has passed its actual capacity and entered resource-contention collapse -- added load now consumes resources (CPU on retries, connection churn, lock contention) faster than it produces completed work, so completed throughput falls even as more requests arrive. It's more reliable than latency alone because latency can degrade gradually well before this point, while a throughput inflection is an unambiguous signal the system is now actively losing capacity to contention rather than just slowing down.

drills.q: Why does the FAILURE SHAPE at a breakpoint (graceful degradation vs. cascading collapse) matter more in a production risk assessment than the raw capacity number itself?
drills.a: A system that sheds load gracefully past its ceiling (rejecting new requests with 503s while continuing to serve existing capacity) is fundamentally safer in production than one that cascades -- where a slow dependency causes upstream thread-pool or connection exhaustion that takes down otherwise-healthy capacity, the classic 'one slow dependency takes down the whole fleet' incident pattern. The raw ceiling number (e.g., '2,400 req/s') tells you when trouble starts, but the failure shape tells you the blast radius and recoverability once it does.

drills.q: A microbenchmark shows a hot function got 8% slower after a refactor; the system-level load test shows no measurable p99 change. Do you block the release, and how do you reason about it?
drills.a: Both results can be simultaneously correct and non-contradictory -- an 8% slowdown in a function that's a tiny fraction of total request time is real but practically invisible at the system level today. Don't block on the microbenchmark alone, but do track the regression rather than discard it, since 'doesn't matter today' isn't the same as 'will never matter' -- many small untracked microbenchmark regressions compounding over time is its own real failure mode ('death by a thousand small regressions'). Gate user-facing release decisions on the system-level load-test number; use the microbenchmark for early, cheap detection with a separately calibrated, looser threshold.

drills.q: When is running a multi-day soak test the wrong investment for a given service, and what's the correct duration criterion instead of a blanket 'always soak for days' rule?
drills.a: If the service's real instances are recycled well before any realistic leak could accumulate to matter -- e.g., an autoscaled stateless service where instances live only 30 minutes by design -- a multi-day soak test exercises a scenario the architecture already prevents, making it a disproportionate investment. The correct criterion is that soak duration should be at least as long as the realistic instance lifetime or accumulation window for that specific service, which can itself be short; it does not mean skipping soak testing entirely just because a service is stateless, since accumulation effects can still matter within a short lifetime.

drills.q: Leadership questions why the team needs a separate soak/breakpoint testing cadence when a load test already runs in CI on every PR. Make the case, and state the strongest reasonable counter-argument.
drills.a: The per-PR CI test answers a narrow, valuable, fast question -- did this specific change introduce an obvious immediate regression -- at a duration (minutes) that structurally cannot answer the soak question (hours-to-days accumulation) or safely run the breakpoint question (deliberately pushing past failure, unsafe to do on shared infrastructure every PR). Make the case using the real cost of the gap: name concrete incident patterns this causes (multi-hour OOMs, cascading collapse at an unknown capacity ceiling) and show a dedicated, less-frequent test cadence answers a genuinely different question on a genuinely different timescale, not a redundant one. Strongest counter-argument to acknowledge: for a smaller org, you don't necessarily need wholly separate infrastructure -- scheduling the same test designs on a different cadence (nightly/pre-release) against existing infra can be a reasonable middle ground; the substantive requirement is that these test types run somewhere on an appropriate cadence, not that they require dedicated hardware.

drills.q: What does a passing snapshot/golden-master test prove, and what's the concrete failure mode when that assumption is wrong?
drills.a: It proves the current output is unchanged from a previously captured baseline, nothing about whether that baseline is correct. If the baseline was captured from buggy behavior, the test actively certifies the bug going forward -- it will keep passing while the bug ships in every future run.

drills.q: Given Google's reported stat that ~84% of pass-to-fail transitions are flaky rather than real regressions, what CI policy problem does this create if unaddressed?
drills.a: A naive 'red build blocks merge' policy trains engineers to distrust red builds in general, since the overwhelming majority of failures aren't real bugs -- eroding the signal value of the entire suite and making engineers more likely to ignore or bypass a genuine regression when it does appear.

drills.q: Describe the four-stage flake-management pipeline used in production CI systems, with the deadline that makes it actually work.
drills.a: 1) Rerun-on-failure to distinguish flake from hard failure. 2) Historical pass-rate tracking per test over a trailing window. 3) Auto-quarantine: remove from the blocking gate once a test crosses a flakiness threshold, but keep running/tracking it. 4) A hard fix-or-delete SLA (Microsoft uses two weeks) -- without this deadline the quarantine list grows indefinitely and becomes a second, ignored suite.

drills.q: How do you mechanically distinguish a flaky test from a test that's correctly detecting a real intermittent bug in the system under test?
drills.a: Rerun the exact same commit/build artifact multiple times. If the result varies with nothing else changing, that's test/infrastructure flakiness (unmocked time, race in test setup, shared state). If results are stable per-commit but the underlying system genuinely behaves nondeterministically in production, the test is correctly catching a real bug -- don't quarantine that one, since retry-based suppression would hide a genuine concurrency issue.

drills.q: A team habitually runs the snapshot-update command whenever CI fails on a mismatch, to unblock merges quickly. What's wrong with this as a default, and what should replace it?
drills.a: It converts every mismatch into an automatic, unreviewed re-baseline; if the mismatch stems from a real bug, the bug becomes the new golden master and the suite certifies it forever. Replace it with a rule that a human reads the diff and confirms the new output is actually correct before running the update, and that reasoning must appear in the PR review -- treat update-snapshot as a deliberate action, not a CI-unblocking reflex.

drills.q: A regression suite for a retrained ML pipeline breaks on every retrain even when the new model is expected to be better. What's the fix, and what's the risk if it's tuned wrong?
drills.a: Replace exact-output golden-file diffing with tolerance-banded assertions on the metrics that matter (e.g., accuracy within X%, latency within Y ms) instead of literal prediction-by-prediction comparison, separating expected retrain drift (deliberately updated baseline) from unexpected regression (metric moves outside tolerance without an intentional retrain). Risk: if the tolerance band is too loose, a real regression can slip through silently -- the band should be set from historically reviewed-acceptable variance and revisited whenever a slipped regression is later found in production.

drills.q: List three concrete, named root causes of test flakiness and the specific fix for each.
drills.a: 1) Unmocked wall-clock time/timezone-dependent assertions -- fix by injecting/freezing a controllable clock. 2) Fixed sleep() instead of wait-for-condition on async operations -- fix with explicit polling or wait-for-assertion utilities. 3) Shared mutable state (a DB row, global counter, fixed temp path) racing across parallel test workers -- fix with per-worker isolation such as unique DB schema/prefix or tmp_path-style fixtures.

drills.q: Leadership wants CI time cut and won't invest in root-causing flaky tests right now. How do you make the case that flake management still helps immediately, and what's the risk of the alternative leadership might propose (deleting all flaky tests outright)?
drills.a: Quarantining the worst flaky offenders off the blocking gate reduces CI time and rerun overhead immediately, without requiring the larger fix-everything investment leadership is resisting -- a cheap first move justified by numbers (rerun cost, developer-hours lost to false failures) rather than a request for headcount. Immediate deletion without triage is riskier: some 'flaky' tests may actually be surfacing a real intermittent bug in the system under test (per the flaky-vs-real-bug distinction), so deleting undifferentiated risks losing detection of a genuine concurrency issue along with the noise -- quarantine-with-a-deadline is reversible and visible; deletion isn't.

drills.q: Is 'regression testing' a fourth layer alongside unit/integration/E2E, or something orthogonal? Explain with an example at each layer.
drills.a: Orthogonal -- regression/golden-baseline testing is about WHEN a test matters (protecting a specific prior behavior against silent drift), and can exist at any layer: a unit-level snapshot of a pure function's output, an integration-level golden file for a generated report, or an E2E-level baseline for a critical page render. The decision to add a regression baseline is separate from which layer (unit/integration/E2E) already covers that behavior's correctness.

drills.q: Your org's flaky-test rate sits at 40% by pass-rate tracking, but you have no budget to fix them all at once. What's the prioritized, numbers-driven approach to bringing this down?
drills.a: Don't attempt to fix all 40% at once -- rank flaky tests by trailing pass rate and by how often they sit on the critical/blocking path, quarantine the worst offenders immediately (cheap, reduces reruns and CI time right away), and apply the fix-or-delete SLA uniformly so the quarantine list can't grow into a permanent graveyard. Track the aggregate flakiness percentage over time (as Microsoft did, reporting an 18% reduction in six months from enforcing the deadline alone) to make the ongoing investment case with a real trend line instead of anecdotes.

drills.q: What does 'autoregressive' mean for a language model, precisely?
drills.a: The model factorizes joint sequence probability as a product of conditionals, each token conditioned only on prior tokens: p(x_1..x_n) = prod p(x_t|x_<t). Trained to maximize this likelihood; at inference samples left-to-right, each new token conditioned on everything generated so far.

drills.q: Why is teacher forcing used instead of feeding the model's own predictions during training?
drills.a: Teacher forcing conditions position t's prediction on the TRUE prefix from the dataset, so every position's loss can be computed independently within one parallel forward pass -- no position waits on another's output. This is what makes trillion-token pretraining computationally tractable, at the cost of a train/inference distribution mismatch (exposure bias).

drills.q: Define exposure bias and its observable production symptom.
drills.a: Mismatch between training (true-prefix conditioning) and inference (self-generated-prefix conditioning). Symptom: compounding degradation over long free-running generations -- quality holds early, one error shifts context out-of-distribution, everything after is affected -- while teacher-forced held-out perplexity can look completely normal.

drills.q: Why can't a causal Transformer's inference forward pass work the same way as its training forward pass?
drills.a: At training time the whole sequence is already known, so one masked pass computes all positions. At inference, future tokens don't exist yet -- they ARE what's being generated -- so generation must proceed sequentially: generate token t, append it, then compute token t+1. Training is parallel; generation is inherently sequential.

drills.q: A model writes a great first paragraph then drifts into repetitive, off-topic text by paragraph four. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: Check if it's length-dependent (shorter targets avoid it -- consistent with exposure bias); check positional-encoding extrapolation (is total length near/past trained context length); check decoding config (greedy/low-temperature is more prone to repetition loops once context is slightly off) before concluding it's exposure bias specifically.

drills.q: Derive the autoregressive training loss and explain what 'the loss decomposes over positions' buys operationally.
drills.a: L(theta) = -sum_t log p_theta(x_t | x_<t). Each term depends only on the TRUE prefix, so all n terms compute from one forward pass through a causally-masked network -- one GPU pass yields n supervised signals per sequence, not one.

drills.q: What is multi-token prediction and how does it relate to teacher forcing and exposure bias?
drills.a: DeepSeek-V3/Meta 2024 technique: auxiliary heads predict several future tokens per position, still fully teacher-forced (all targets are true tokens). Gives denser pretraining signal and implicit lookahead pressure, but does NOT eliminate exposure bias -- generation is still one token at a time at inference.

drills.q: Explain scheduled sampling and why it's rarely used at LLM pretraining scale today.
drills.a: Bengio 2015: feed the model's own sampled prediction instead of ground truth during training, annealed up over time, directly targeting exposure bias. But it reintroduces a sequential dependency (input at t may need position t-1's sampled output), breaking the parallel-pass property that makes trillion-token teacher-forced pretraining affordable -- RLHF/DPO/GRPO achieve a similar effect as a smaller post-training stage instead.

drills.q: Why does RL-based post-training (GRPO/RLVR) matter specifically for reasoning models in the context of exposure bias?
drills.a: Chain-of-thought traces are long; one wrong intermediate step compounds into a wrong final answer -- the exposure-bias failure shape. GRPO/RLVR trains on full autoregressive rollouts scored against verifiable outcomes, so gradient signal reflects the model's own compounding behavior, unlike teacher-forced pretraining which never sees self-generated chains.

drills.q: Design an evaluation protocol to catch an exposure-bias regression before shipping a model fine-tuned for long-form report generation.
drills.a: Don't rely solely on teacher-forced perplexity. Add: free-running generation at production-representative lengths scored for late-generation quality; a length-stratified eval tracking quality vs. position within generation (watch for a cliff); self-consistency checks across repeated generations from the same prompt. Set a concrete threshold, e.g. quality at the last quartile must not drop more than X% versus the first quartile.

drills.q: Explain BPE end to end: how is the vocabulary built, and how is a new word encoded?
drills.a: Start with a base alphabet (bytes/chars); repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair into a new symbol, recording the rule in order, until vocab hits target size. To encode new text, replay the learned merges in training order against the new text's base-symbol sequence until none apply -- no frequency counting at encode time.

drills.q: Why is byte-level BPE the standard for production LLM tokenizers rather than character-level?
drills.a: Base alphabet is the 256 byte values -- every Unicode character in any script decomposes to 1-4 UTF-8 bytes, so any input is representable with no <UNK> fallback. Character-level BPE must cover 140,000+ Unicode code points and rare characters may never earn merges.

drills.q: What's actually different between BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece?
drills.a: BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pair; WordPiece merges by max corpus likelihood under a unigram LM (small practical difference). SentencePiece isn't a competing algorithm -- it's a library implementing BPE or Unigram over the raw byte/Unicode stream, treating whitespace as an ordinary symbol, which is why it's the multilingual default.

drills.q: Why do tokens not correspond to words, and what determines whether a word is one token or several?
drills.a: A token is whatever chunk accumulated enough BPE merges during training -- purely frequency-driven, no linguistic notion of 'word'. Common words in the dominant training language merge fully into one token; rare words or words in underrepresented languages fragment into multiple subword tokens.

drills.q: A user reports identical requests in English and Hindi are priced very differently. Diagnose it.
drills.a: Likely tokenizer fragmentation: if the tokenizer's training corpus was English-dominated, Hindi words never earned full BPE merges and decompose into many more subword/byte tokens for the same content, inflating token-based cost. Confirm by measuring tokens-per-sentence for matched content in both languages against the exact tokenizer in use.

drills.q: What happens when a tokenizer encounters a completely novel string or random bytes -- does it ever fail?
drills.a: Never fails outright with byte-level BPE: the string decomposes to its base byte sequence and learned merges apply wherever they match; unmatched bytes remain individual byte-tokens. No <UNK> fallback needed since the byte alphabet is complete by construction -- but novel text uses more tokens per character, the same mechanism behind the multilingual cost problem.

drills.q: Explain why vocabulary size is a real tradeoff, not 'bigger is strictly better'.
drills.a: Larger vocab reduces tokens-per-word (cheaper inference, more effective context) but the embedding table and output projection scale with vocab_size * d_model, directly growing parameter count and per-step softmax compute. GPT-2's 50k vs GPT-4o's ~200k (o200k_base) trades shorter sequences against real parameter/compute cost.

drills.q: How do special tokens like <eos>/<bos>/chat-template markers interact with BPE merging, and what breaks if templating gets whitespace wrong?
drills.a: Special tokens are matched as literal atomic strings before BPE merging runs and never fragment. But tokens adjacent to them can tokenize differently depending on surrounding whitespace (since leading space is often part of the following word's leading symbol in byte-level BPE), producing a token sequence the model never saw in training -- looks like a model regression but is a templating bug.

drills.q: Fine-tuning a base model on a new low-resource language or heavily code-mixed domain gives poor results despite plenty of data. What tokenizer-level cause would you check first?
drills.a: Check tokens-per-sentence for the new domain against the base tokenizer -- heavy fragmentation means the model spends context budget reconstructing fragmented subwords instead of modeling the domain, which more fine-tuning data alone can't fix. Requires vocabulary extension (add tokens, resize embeddings, continue pretraining) or a domain-adapted tokenizer.

drills.q: Design a tokenizer strategy for a product shipping across 22 locales with a strict per-request cost/latency SLA.
drills.a: Measure actual tokens-per-equivalent-sentence for each locale against the exact tokenizer in use, rather than assuming a uniform ratio. Set per-locale cost/context-length budgets from that measured data. If certain locales are severely underserved, factor tokenizer/vocab balance into model/vendor selection -- this can't be patched at the serving layer once a model is chosen.

drills.q: Why can't you compare a cosine similarity score between vectors from two different embedding models?
drills.a: Each model learns its own vector space during training with no guaranteed alignment; the score would be a number but a meaningless one.

drills.q: What is Matryoshka Representation Learning and why does it matter operationally?
drills.a: It trains a contrastive loss at multiple nested prefix lengths of the same vector so any prefix is a usable embedding, turning dimensionality into a runtime truncation knob instead of a model-selection decision.

drills.q: Walk through the cost of embedding a 10M-chunk, 250-tokens-average corpus with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, and its full-precision storage footprint.
drills.a: 2.5B tokens * $0.13/1M = $325 one-time. Storage at 3072d fp32: 10M*3072*4 bytes ~= 123 GB before index overhead; truncating to 512d drops it to ~20.5 GB.

drills.q: A model card says to prefix queries with 'query: ' and passages with 'passage: '. What happens if you skip this, and how would you catch the bug?
drills.a: Retrieval quality silently degrades because query/passage vectors no longer sit in the geometric relationship the contrastive training established. Catch it with a recall@k regression test in CI, not manual inspection.

drills.q: Your team wants to switch from OpenAI text-embedding-3-small to Cohere embed-v4 for better multilingual coverage. What does this actually require?
drills.a: A full reindex: re-embed every chunk (incompatible vector spaces), rebuild the ANN index, shadow-evaluate recall@k and answer quality before cutover. Budget it as a migration project, not a config change.

drills.q: Why might quantization hurt recall more unpredictably than Matryoshka truncation, and would you ever combine both?
drills.a: Quantization is applied post-hoc with no trained guarantee of even tolerance across dimensions/models, unlike MRL's trained-in graceful degradation. You can combine both for extreme storage savings, but each stacked step needs its own recall@k validation -- losses aren't simply additive.

drills.q: Design the embedding strategy for a RAG system serving English and low-resource-language queries against a shared corpus under a strict latency budget.
drills.a: Check per-language coverage (not aggregate MTEB/MIRACL) against actual target languages since coverage is uneven; self-host a Matryoshka-truncated model for the query-embedding hop (on the critical path) rather than an API round trip; validate low-resource recall with its own eval set; consider translation-to-pivot-language as a fallback and say so explicitly.

drills.q: How would you decide the dimension to actually deploy for a given corpus, without guessing from a blog post?
drills.a: Build a labeled (or synthetic) eval set, embed the corpus at several candidate truncation dimensions, measure recall@k and nDCG at each, and deploy the smallest dimension where the metric plateaus.

drills.q: Why can't a cross-encoder search a 10M-document corpus directly?
drills.a: Its score is a function of the query-document pair jointly, so nothing can be precomputed; scoring the whole corpus per query would require 10M forward passes, infeasible at interactive latency.

drills.q: Give real numbers for Cohere rerank-3.5's cost and latency, and BGE-reranker-v2-m3's latency.
drills.a: Cohere rerank-3.5: $2/1K searches, +80-150ms p50 (real e2e ~600ms w/ network). BGE-reranker-v2-m3: GPU 50-100ms, CPU ~130ms per 16-pair batch, open weights.

drills.q: A reranker was added and offline eval improved, but production p99 blew the SLA. What happened and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Likely reranking too many candidates (k1 too large) synchronously in the request path. Fix: reduce k1 to the recall-plateau point, batch reranker calls, reconsider whether all candidates truly need reranking.

drills.q: A reranker fails to improve answer quality even though it's working correctly. How do you diagnose this?
drills.a: Measure recall@k1 of the first stage alone against a labeled eval set; if the gold chunk isn't in the candidate set, the reranker is blameless -- the fix is in retrieval, not reranking.

drills.q: Explain ColBERT-style late interaction as an alternative to full cross-encoder reranking, including its cost.
drills.a: Keeps token-level embeddings for query and doc, aggregates via MaxSim (each query token attends to its best-matching doc token); doc token embeddings are precomputable, giving much of cross-encoder precision at lower query-time compute -- but costs far more index storage (one vector per token vs one per doc).

drills.q: Design a three-stage retrieval cascade for a high-value use case like legal document search.
drills.a: Stage 1: hybrid search (BM25+bi-encoder+RRF) for high recall, ~150-300 candidates. Stage 2: cross-encoder rerank down to top 10-20. Stage 3 (gated to high-value queries only, given cost): LLM-as-judge pass over the final handful for precision.

drills.q: Design the reranking strategy for a multi-tenant SaaS product with tenant corpora from a few hundred to millions of documents, under a shared latency SLA.
drills.a: Small tenants may need no reranking stage at all (little ranking error to fix); large tenants get the standard cascade with k1 tuned per-tenant against their own recall@k1 curve. Model cost as queries/sec * k1 * cost_per_candidate per tenant rather than a flat line item.

drills.q: What silent truncation bug affects cross-encoder reranking of long documents, and how do you catch it?
drills.a: The concatenated query+document pair silently truncates at the model's max sequence length (often 512 tokens), hurting accuracy on chunks needing the most context. Catch it by monitoring truncation rate as an explicit metric, since it won't surface as an obvious error.

drills.q: Name three GRASP patterns and what question each answers.
drills.a: Information Expert (who owns behavior given the data it needs), Creator (who instantiates X), Controller (what receives a system-boundary event and delegates), among others like Low/High Cohesion, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations.

drills.q: Two validation functions are byte-identical today. A teammate says 'DRY this up.' What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether they represent the same underlying knowledge/policy or are coincidentally identical because they solve unrelated problems the same way right now — merging coincidental duplication creates false coupling that surfaces as boolean flags and branches when they diverge.

drills.q: What's wrong with using KISS to justify removing a bounds check on a discount percentage input?
drills.a: KISS argues against unnecessary structural complexity, not against correctness guarantees. A missing bounds check is a latent bug (e.g. pct=1.5 makes total negative), not simplicity.

drills.q: Explain how YAGNI can be correct at the team level and still produce an org-level failure.
drills.a: Every team correctly skips building shared cross-cutting infrastructure (e.g. an event schema registry) because their own immediate need doesn't justify it. In aggregate, nobody builds it until multiple teams need it simultaneously during an incident, costing more than early investment would have — a coordination failure, not a flaw in YAGNI's per-team logic.

drills.q: Fix this Law of Demeter violation: order.customer.billing_address.country.tax_treaty_exempt
drills.a: Delegate one hop at a time: order.is_tax_treaty_exempt(), where Order asks Customer, which asks Address. Each object reaches only one level deep so a refactor of Address only touches Customer.

drills.q: When is strictly enforcing the Law of Demeter the wrong call?
drills.a: Inside a single cohesive aggregate that changes as a unit — forcing delegation methods for every internal traversal produces wrapper explosion with no real encapsulation benefit since the whole aggregate changes together anyway.

drills.q: A Penguin subclass of Bird overrides fly() to throw NotImplementedError. Diagnose and fix using composition.
drills.a: This models 'is-a' for taxonomy when callers depend on behavior (an LSP violation). Fix: extract flight as a FlightBehavior strategy injected into Bird; Penguin composes a CannotFly behavior instead of inheriting and overriding to fail.

drills.q: What is Pure Fabrication and how does it differ from the anemic-domain-model mistake?
drills.a: Pure Fabrication invents a non-domain class (e.g. PricingEngine) purely for cohesion/coupling reasons — appropriate for cross-cutting orchestration/infrastructure logic. It differs from the anemic-domain mistake, which extracts an entity's own invariant-protecting logic externally; that should stay on the entity.

drills.q: A teammate proposes a shared BaseEntity class with common CRUD methods inherited by every domain entity. Critique it.
drills.a: If it's truly shared mechanical data (id, created_at, equality) a shared base is fine. If 'CRUD methods' means persistence behavior, prefer composition (inject a repository per entity) since persistence constraints diverge per entity and a shared base will accumulate overridden methods that throw or no-op — the same LSP smell as Penguin/Bird.

drills.q: Rank DRY, KISS, YAGNI by how often each is invoked incorrectly in real code review, and explain why.
drills.a: DRY is misapplied most often because similarity is visible immediately while knowledge-vs-coincidence requires business context; KISS second, usually to skip a guard rather than an abstraction; YAGNI least often at the individual level since its failure mode is structural/org-level rather than a per-PR reflex.

drills.q: Define SRP using the actor-based definition, not 'one method per class'.
drills.a: A class should have one reason to change, meaning one actor/stakeholder whose requirements drive changes to it — a class can have many methods and still satisfy SRP if they all serve one actor.

drills.q: You see a class OrderProcessor with validation, pricing, persistence, and email notification all inline. Name the actors and the SRP violation.
drills.a: Four actors: product/business rules, finance, DBA, marketing. Each drives changes to the same file for unrelated reasons, causing PR collisions and untestable pricing logic without a live DB/email client.

drills.q: What is the honest counter-argument to SRP, and name the anti-pattern it produces when overapplied.
drills.a: Overapplying SRP to domain entities produces the anemic domain model — logic stripped from entities into external services, breaking encapsulation of invariants.

drills.q: When would you deliberately NOT introduce a strategy pattern despite an if/elif chain technically violating OCP?
drills.a: When there are only 2-3 known variants with no evidence of more coming — the abstraction costs more reading time than the conditional, and introducing it is speculative generality (YAGNI violation).

drills.q: A ReadOnlyCache implements a mutable Cache interface by raising NotImplementedError on set(). What's wrong and how do you fix it?
drills.a: LSP violation — callers relying polymorphically on Cache.set() get a runtime surprise. Fix: split into Readable/Writable protocols so ReadOnlyCache only implements Readable, making the illegal call a type error instead of a runtime exception.

drills.q: Name the real anti-pattern caused by overapplying ISP, and describe its symptom.
drills.a: Interface bloat — one interface per method (IReadable, IWritable, IDeletable, IListable), forcing callers to compose many narrow types and making generic code hard to write; documented as a named anti-pattern from enterprise Java.

drills.q: Distinguish Dependency Inversion Principle from dependency injection as a mechanism.
drills.a: DIP: high-level and low-level modules should both depend on an abstraction the high-level module owns conceptually. DI: a runtime mechanism (constructor/setter/framework) for supplying a concrete implementation of that abstraction. You can follow DIP with manual constructor injection and no framework at all.

drills.q: Your team lead insists on 'always follow SOLID, it's best practice.' Give a staff-level pushback that isn't dismissive.
drills.a: Agree on the goal (cheap, safe change), then ask which axis of change is actually live in this code and apply only the principle(s) addressing it — citing e.g. an interface-per-implementation pattern in the repo's own git history that has never had a second implementation land, as evidence the ceremony isn't earning its cost.

drills.q: Design the tool-interface boundary for an agent's tool registry. Which SOLID principle is load-bearing and which is most likely to be misapplied?
drills.a: OCP is load-bearing — new tools register rather than edit a dispatcher. ISP is most likely misapplied if every tool is forced to implement cancel()/estimate_cost()/supports_streaming() even when irrelevant; query capability via isinstance/protocol checks instead of a monolithic Tool interface.

drills.q: What two conditions justify skipping DIP (injecting an abstraction) entirely for a dependency?
drills.a: Exactly one implementation with no plan for a second, and no test-isolation need a manual fake couldn't satisfy without the extra interface/container indirection.

drills.q: Your app depends_on db and connects immediately at startup. It works locally every time but fails intermittently in CI. Diagnose.
drills.a: depends_on without condition: service_healthy only waits for the container to start, not for the app inside to be ready. CI machines are often slower/more loaded, widening the window between container start and actual readiness (e.g. Postgres data dir init/WAL replay). Fix: add a healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy.

drills.q: A service's healthcheck flaps healthy/unhealthy only during its first 15 seconds after cold start, then is rock solid. What's the fix and why not adjust retries/interval instead?
drills.a: Increase start_period to comfortably exceed the measured cold-start time. Adjusting retries/interval would also affect steady-state flap detection and could mask a genuine post-startup problem that appears later.

drills.q: How would you actually force a genuine port replacement (not addition) across override files if the Compose Specification supports it?
drills.a: Use the Compose Specification's merge directives (!reset/!override in newer spec versions) to explicitly replace rather than merge that key; absent that, avoid duplicating the value across files -- only set it in whichever file should own it.

drills.q: A teammate commits their docker-compose.override.yml with local debug ports exposed to everyone. What's the actual process fix, not just telling them not to commit it?
drills.a: Add docker-compose.override.yml to .gitignore from project start, and provide a checked-in docker-compose.override.yml.example template for developers to copy locally -- the mechanism meant to stay local can't leak by accident.

drills.q: A service with profiles: [debug] is also depended on unconditionally by an always-on service. What happens when you run plain docker compose up?
drills.a: Compose still starts the dependency to satisfy depends_on, effectively activating the profiled service implicitly even without its profile being requested -- profile gating isn't airtight against an unconditional depends_on.

drills.q: docker compose config shows the environment variable you expect, but the running container's printenv shows something different. What else could be overriding it?
drills.a: The image's own baked-in ENV instructions from build time, or the application's own config-loading logic (e.g. a .env file loaded by an app library inside the container) further overriding what Compose passed in -- docker compose config shows what Compose passes in, not necessarily what the process ultimately uses.

drills.q: How would you prove, after the fact from logs, that a sleep-based race actually caused a failure rather than some other cause?
drills.a: Correlate the app's connection-failure timestamp against the dependency container's own 'ready to accept connections' log line timestamp. If the app's first attempt is earlier than the dependency's actual ready line, that's direct proof of the race.

drills.q: A service has no healthcheck defined. What does docker compose up --wait do for it?
drills.a: Nothing extra -- a service without a healthcheck is considered healthy the instant it starts since Compose has nothing to poll. --wait gives zero additional readiness guarantee; the actual fix is adding a real healthcheck.

drills.q: A one-shot migration container exits with code 0 but the migration actually failed silently. What does Compose's condition: service_completed_successfully do, and how do you prevent this class of bug?
drills.a: Compose considers the dependency satisfied since it only checks exit code 0 -- it has no visibility into internal logic failures. Prevention is at the app level: ensure migration scripts propagate real failures as non-zero exit codes instead of swallowing exceptions.

drills.q: Compare Compose's restart policies and explain why the default (no) is wrong for a long-running local dev service.
drills.a: no/always/on-failure[:N]/unless-stopped. The default (no) means a service that crashes once just silently stays down, which is a worse local-dev debugging experience than a service that restarts and re-surfaces the same error on a loop, useful as recurring signal -- though restart: always during active debugging of a crash loop floods logs and should be temporarily disabled.

drills.q: docker inspect shows ExitCode 137 and OOMKilled: false. What are your next two hypotheses and how do you distinguish them?
drills.a: A manual/orchestrator-issued docker kill or force-termination (check orchestrator events/deploy logs for a stop command around that timestamp), or a host-wide OOM event that killed the process without tripping this specific container's cgroup flag (check dmesg/journalctl -k on the host for an OOM invocation at the same timestamp).

drills.q: You see exit code 143 on every deploy, consistently. Is that necessarily a bug?
drills.a: Not automatically -- 143 (SIGTERM) is the expected outcome of a graceful shutdown that completes and then exits. The real question is whether the app's SIGTERM handler completed its cleanup work within the grace period, not whether 143 appeared.

drills.q: Walk through two valid ways to debug a running distroless container with no shell.
drills.a: 1) nsenter --target <pid> --mount --net --pid -- <command> from the host (root/CAP_SYS_PTRACE required), running a host-originated static binary inside the target's namespaces. 2) An ephemeral debug sidecar sharing namespaces: docker run --pid=container:X --network=container:X busybox sh, or kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container>.

drills.q: After fixing a Dockerfile to properly multi-stage, dive's waste score drops to near zero but the image is still 500MB. What does that tell you and what do you check next?
drills.a: The remaining size isn't avoidable layering waste -- it's the genuine footprint of what's shipped. Check docker history sorted by layer size to find the specific dependency/asset dominating size, not further layer restructuring.

drills.q: A Kubernetes pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Relate this precisely to plain Docker's exit-code/OOM diagnosis.
drills.a: Identical underlying diagnosis (same exit code, same OOM-or-not distinction) -- the kubelet is just the one restarting it, applying exponential backoff (~10s doubling to a cap around 5min) between attempts instead of restarting immediately, to avoid hammering a genuinely broken workload.

drills.q: Your orchestrator stops routing traffic to a container because its healthcheck is flapping, but the container never actually crashed. What's the production consequence and the actual fix?
drills.a: You can induce a self-inflicted outage on a container that was actually fine. Fix: loosen the healthcheck's timeout/retries to match real observed latency under load, not restart or de-route a healthy process because its healthcheck was miscalibrated.

drills.q: You confirm an app logs to a file inside the container, not stdout. What are two options to see those logs with standard Docker tooling, without changing the app's config, and what's the durable fix?
drills.a: docker exec in (if a shell exists) and tail -f the file directly, or docker cp the log file out for inspection. Durable fix: reconfigure the app to log to stdout/stderr so docker logs and any log aggregation actually captures it.

drills.q: You switch a working image's base from Debian to Alpine and immediately get exit code 127 on a command that worked before. Why?
drills.a: Alpine's minimal base uses BusyBox's ash/sh, not bash, and lacks many binaries a Debian-based image had available implicitly. The entrypoint likely assumed bash-specific syntax or a binary that isn't part of Alpine's default package set.

drills.q: Walk through diagnosing 'the image is 600MB and I don't know why' using docker history and dive.
drills.a: docker history <image> first for a quick per-instruction size breakdown -- often reveals an obviously oversized RUN/COPY layer immediately. If not obvious (spread across layers or hidden by added-then-removed files), dive <image> for the layer-by-layer diff and wasted-space analysis, which catches what docker history's per-layer view can't.

drills.q: dive shows 0% wasted space but the image is still 600MB and the team wants it smaller. What's the actual remaining lever, and what's NOT the lever?
drills.a: The remaining size is genuine dependency/application footprint, not layering waste. Lever: reduce actual dependencies (prune unused packages, lighter libraries, move to distroless if not already there). Not the lever: further Dockerfile restructuring, since dive already confirmed no structural waste remains.

drills.q: Define image vs container precisely enough to survive a follow-up question.
drills.a: Image: read-only, content-addressed layers plus config JSON (entrypoint, env, ports). Container: that image plus one writable layer, plus namespaces (pid/net/mnt/uts/ipc/user) and cgroups enforcing resource limits.

drills.q: You reorder a Dockerfile so requirements.txt is copied and installed before COPY . ., but builds are still slow on every commit. What do you check next?
drills.a: Whether the build context itself is large and slow to hash/send due to a missing .dockerignore (pulling in .git, node_modules, a venv), or whether something upstream of the dependency install layer (like the base image tag) is actually changing on each build.

drills.q: A container exits immediately with exit code 0 but you expected a long-running server. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check docker logs for what actually ran, then the entrypoint/CMD itself -- a common bug is a script that backgrounds the server (server &) and then exits, taking PID 1 and the whole container down even though the backgrounded process was technically still alive from the shell's view.

drills.q: docker stats shows healthy memory usage right up until the container dies with exit 137. What's likely happening and how do you confirm the real cause?
drills.a: Page cache/buffer memory and short-lived allocation spikes (e.g. a GC pause building up garbage before collecting) can exceed the cgroup memory limit between docker stats polling intervals. Confirm via dmesg/kernel OOM logs for the actual kill event rather than trusting the last stats sample.

drills.q: You bind-mount your whole project directory, including node_modules built on macOS, into a Linux container. What breaks and why?
drills.a: Native binary dependencies (compiled node modules, some Python C extensions) built for the host OS/arch get shadowed into the container and won't run if the container's OS/arch differs. Fix: exclude node_modules/venv from the bind mount, install fresh inside the container.

drills.q: Two plain `docker run` containers can't resolve each other by name, but the same setup works under docker-compose up. Explain and fix without Compose.
drills.a: Embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) only works on user-defined bridge networks; the default bridge doesn't have it. Fix: docker network create mynet, run both containers with --network mynet.

drills.q: docker system df shows 40GB reclaimable in images but docker image prune -a only frees 5GB. Why the gap?
drills.a: prune -a still respects images referenced by any container (running or stopped) or tagged with something other than <none>. Check docker ps -a for stopped containers holding references that count as 'in use' even though nothing is actively running.

drills.q: Your app needs 25 seconds to drain in-flight requests on shutdown, but production shows connections cut off abruptly. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The default docker stop grace period (10s) is shorter than the app's drain time, so SIGKILL lands mid-drain. Fix: docker stop -t 30 (or the orchestrator equivalent, e.g. terminationGracePeriodSeconds in Kubernetes); confirm via exit code 137/forced-termination correlated with truncated connections at the deploy timestamp.

drills.q: docker build fails in CI with 'no space left on device' but works locally every time. Root cause and the durable fix, not just the quick one.
drills.a: CI runners reuse the same disk across builds without a developer's implicit periodic cleanup, so /var/lib/docker fills with unpruned layers. Quick fix is docker system prune -af; the durable fix is CI-native layer caching (BuildKit --cache-from/--cache-to against a registry) with an explicit size/TTL policy instead of relying on manual pruning.

drills.q: Explain why PID 1 inside a container needs special signal handling, and how a shell-wrapped CMD breaks it.
drills.a: PID 1 in a namespace gets no default signal handlers and must reap zombie children; without an explicit handler, SIGTERM is ignored until the grace period expires and SIGKILL lands. `CMD ["sh","-c","python app.py"]` makes the shell PID 1, so the signal never reaches the actual app process -- use exec form or `exec` inside the script.

drills.q: Your multi-stage build's final image is still large. What are the two most likely culprits?
drills.a: 1) COPY --from=builder is copying more than the compiled artifact (whole /build dir including source/object files instead of just the installed package/binary). 2) The final base image itself isn't minimal (not -slim/distroless), still carrying unnecessary OS weight.

drills.q: A teammate removes a leaked secret with RUN rm /tmp/secret.txt in a later Dockerfile layer and calls it fixed. Are they right?
drills.a: No -- the earlier layer containing the secret is still part of the image's immutable layer history and can be extracted directly from the image tarball or via docker history --no-trunc, regardless of later instructions.

drills.q: You add a BuildKit cache mount for pip but CI build times don't improve. Why might that be?
drills.a: Many CI providers run each build in an ephemeral environment where BuildKit's local cache mount storage doesn't persist across runs unless configured with a persistent volume or the CI system's own layer-cache feature -- a cache mount only helps across builds sharing the same builder/cache storage.

drills.q: A debug sidecar sharing --pid=container:X can see the target's processes but can't read files under /proc/<pid>/fd. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Sharing the PID namespace doesn't grant filesystem/mount namespace access. Fix: also share the mount and net namespaces, or use nsenter --target <pid> --mount --net --pid from a privileged debug container to enter all relevant namespaces at once.

drills.q: Give a concrete production symptom of the Alpine musl libc vs Debian glibc incompatibility risk.
drills.a: Intermittent or environment-specific DNS resolution failures for hostnames that resolve fine outside the container (musl's resolver handles certain nsswitch/multi-A-record scenarios differently), or a native extension segfaulting only on the Alpine-based image despite identical source and dependency versions on Debian.

drills.q: You've correctly ordered manifest-copy before source-copy, but the build context upload itself takes 20 seconds every build. What's missing?
drills.a: A .dockerignore file. Without one, the entire build context (.git history, venvs, node_modules, build artifacts) gets tarred and sent to the daemon before any cache lookup happens, regardless of cache hits later in the Dockerfile.

drills.q: Does docker history on your final shipped image reveal a secret used only in a discarded intermediate builder stage?
drills.a: No -- docker history on the tagged final image only shows that image's own layer chain. The risk is in the build cache, CI logs, and any --cache-to registry target that might retain the builder stage's layers separately, not in the final image's own history.

drills.q: Your Dockerfile has three stages and BuildKit's parallel execution isn't speeding anything up. Why?
drills.a: Check whether the stages are genuinely independent in the dependency graph, or whether each FROM <previous-stage>/COPY --from=<previous-stage> creates a strictly linear chain -- parallelism requires sibling stages, not a chain relabeled as multiple FROM lines.

drills.q: Explain the mechanical reason ordering matters: why does copying requirements.txt separately from source code speed up builds?
drills.a: COPY layers are cache-keyed on the content of exactly the files copied. Copying only the manifest first keeps that layer (and the potentially multi-minute install layer after it) cached when only source changes; copying everything together invalidates the install layer on any file change anywhere in the context.

drills.q: Your app needs to bind port 80 but you want to avoid running as root. Two valid approaches?
drills.a: Grant the specific Linux capability (--cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE with --cap-drop=ALL, non-root USER), or avoid the problem entirely by binding a high port (8080) inside the container and mapping it to 80 at the host/load-balancer layer.

drills.q: What does a git blob object store?
drills.a: Only raw file content -- no filename, path, or permission bits. Those live in the tree object that references the blob.

drills.q: Physically, what is a git branch?
drills.a: A file holding a 40/64-hex commit SHA under .git/refs/heads/<name>. Moving a branch overwrites that file.

drills.q: Your teammate ran `git reset --hard` and lost three commits of unpushed work. What's your first command?
drills.a: git reflog -- find the SHA the branch pointed to before the reset, then git branch <name> <sha> to recreate a pointer to it.

drills.q: Why does rebase produce different commit hashes even when the resulting code is identical?
drills.a: A commit hash covers tree sha, parent sha(s), author/committer, and message. Rebase changes the parent field, changing the hash regardless of tree content.

drills.q: What specific race does `--force-with-lease` prevent that plain `--force` doesn't?
drills.a: It refuses to push if origin/<branch> as your local git last saw it doesn't match what's actually on the remote right now -- i.e. someone force- or regular-pushed since your last fetch. Plain --force overwrites blindly.

drills.q: A `git bisect run` script needs to report a commit that simply doesn't build. What exit code, and why not just call it bad?
