drills.a: Exit 125 (skip). Calling an untestable commit 'bad' would corrupt the binary search by treating a build failure as evidence of the actual regression.

drills.q: Can the same branch be checked out in two different git worktrees at once? Why or why not?
drills.a: No -- all worktrees share one object database and one set of refs; two worktrees both holding that branch could each move the single ref independently with no reconciliation mechanism, so git refuses.

drills.q: You need to recover a commit, but git reflog on your machine shows nothing for it and it was never pushed anywhere. Is it recoverable?
drills.a: No -- the reflog is local-only and the object was never transmitted to any remote or other clone. This is the actual boundary of git's recoverability.

drills.q: A CI-automated git bisect converges on a commit inside a branch that was merged and fully reverted months ago. What's actually happening, mechanically?
drills.a: A revert commit undoes content but leaves the original commits fully present as ancestors in the DAG; bisect only evaluates the checked-out state at each commit and has no concept of 'later undone' -- it can land inside the reverted range if intermediate states reproduce the symptom differently.

drills.q: What is the default gc.auto threshold of loose objects before git repacks them into a .pack file?
drills.a: Roughly 6700 loose objects.

drills.q: Walk me through a forward pass of a GPT block, tensor shapes included.
drills.a: x:(B,T,C) -> LN -> QKV proj to (B,T,3C) -> split/reshape to (B,nh,T,hd) -> SDPA -> reshape back to (B,T,C) -> proj -> add residual -> LN -> MLP (C->4C->GELU->C) -> add residual.

drills.q: Why is weight tying between embedding and LM head not just a parameter-saving trick?
drills.a: Saves ~31% of GPT-2(124M) params, and empirically also slightly improves quality by forcing input/output token representations into a compatible space (Press & Wolf 2017).

drills.q: Derive why gradients vanish/explode more in deep post-norm transformers than pre-norm.
drills.a: Post-norm: x_{l+1}=LN(x_l+f(x_l)), gradient passes through L LayerNorm Jacobians compounding over depth. Pre-norm: x_{l+1}=x_l+f(LN(x_l)), residual path is unmodified by normalization end to end.

drills.q: Compute the compute budget for training GPT-2(124M) on 10B tokens using 6ND, and estimate wall-clock time on 8xA100.
drills.a: 6*1.24e8*1e10 ~= 7.4e18 FLOPs. At ~1.4e15 FLOP/s achievable on 8xA100, ~5300s ~= 90 minutes.

drills.q: Your loss goes to NaN at step 340. Debug it live.
drills.a: Check precision first (fp16 overflow vs bf16), then verify gradient clipping is actually applied, then inspect the batch at that step for a pathological input (very long repeated sequence).

drills.q: What does torch.compile actually buy you and what's the catch?
drills.a: ~2x throughput via kernel fusion and reduced Python dispatch overhead; first call compiles (slow), and variable input shapes trigger repeated recompilation that can silently kill throughput.

drills.q: Explain depth-scaled initialization (1/sqrt(2*n_layer)) and what breaks without it.
drills.a: Without it, residual stream variance grows roughly linearly with depth as each block adds unit-variance output; scaling each block's output projection keeps cumulative variance ~constant. Skipping it shows up as slower convergence and worse asymptotic loss, not necessarily NaN.

drills.q: A colleague says 'just double model size and tokens, it'll be strictly better.' True under fixed compute?
drills.a: No -- 6ND means doubling both roughly quadruples compute; within a fixed budget there's a loss-optimal ratio (Chinchilla-style), not simply 'more of everything'.

drills.q: Validation loss looks great but generated samples are repetitive and low quality. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check if this is a decoding artifact (greedy decoding on an undertrained model loops) vs a training problem -- compare measured perplexity against expected scaling-law value for the model's size/token budget before concluding training failed.

drills.q: Design a from-scratch nanoGPT build for someone with one consumer GPU and two evenings.
drills.a: Tier 1: char-level Shakespeare (minutes) to validate pipeline correctness (masking, target shift, loss, sampling). Tier 2: small subword model on a few hundred million tokens overnight, with compile/bf16/clipping/schedule present from the start.

drills.q: State the Chinchilla scaling result and the compute-budget arithmetic behind it.
drills.a: N and D both scale as C^0.5 for fixed compute C; optimal ratio ~20 tokens/param. FLOPs ~= 6ND connects budget to N and D.

drills.q: Why did LLaMA train deliberately past the Chinchilla-optimal ratio?
drills.a: A smaller model cheaper to serve at inference beats a training-FLOP-optimal larger model once serving cost (paid indefinitely) is accounted for.

drills.q: Explain MinHash+LSH deduplication mechanically and why it avoids O(n^2) comparison.
drills.a: Documents represented as n-gram shingle sets; MinHash signature approximates Jaccard similarity; signature split into bands, documents matching within any band go into a candidate bucket -- only bucket-mates get directly compared.

drills.q: Why does FineWeb deduplicate per-snapshot instead of globally?
drills.a: Global dedup was found to systematically favor whichever snapshot was processed first/last, discarding valuable older content due to processing order rather than quality.

drills.q: What did Muennighoff et al. find about repeating pretraining data across epochs?
drills.a: Up to ~4 epochs: negligible degradation. Up to ~16 epochs: diminishing but real gains. By ~40 epochs: benefit essentially gone; marginal value of k-th repeat decays geometrically.

drills.q: Derive the compute-time estimate for training a 7B model at Chinchilla ratio on an 8-GPU node.
drills.a: D~1.4e11 tokens, FLOPs=6ND~5.9e21. At ~1.5e15 FLOP/s achievable on 8xA100, time ~3.9e6s ~= 45 days.

drills.q: What is 'curriculum' in modern LLM pretraining and how does it differ from classic curriculum learning?
drills.a: Staged domain mixture (web-heavy then curated/synthetic mid-training stage), not per-example easy-to-hard ordering as in classic curriculum learning.

drills.q: A staged (curriculum) training run underperforms a uniform-mixture baseline at the same token budget. First hypothesis?
drills.a: The LR schedule -- curriculum training needs a more moderate decay than uniform training; reusing the uniform schedule wastes the late high-quality stage's value.

drills.q: What's the difference between heuristic filtering and classifier-based quality filtering in data curation?
drills.a: Heuristic filtering uses fixed rules (length, alphabetic ratio, boilerplate); classifier-based filtering scores documents against a reference-quality target and is reported as the largest per-token quality lever in most pipelines.

drills.q: Design the data pipeline and scaling-law approach for a $2M budget with 500B unique tokens.
drills.a: Dedup+quality-filter first to get the real usable token count; fit IsoFLOP scaling laws on the actual filtered pipeline at small scale; decide model size vs repetition tradeoff using Muennighoff's discount curve; bias smaller/more-overtrained if serving at real production traffic.

drills.q: Walk through what temperature does mathematically, including both limits.
drills.a: p_i = exp(z_i/T)/sum(exp(z_j/T)). T->0 collapses to one-hot argmax (greedy). T->inf flattens toward uniform. T=1 is the raw trained distribution.

drills.q: Explain top-p's specific failure mode that motivated min-p.
drills.a: Cumulative probability threshold can still admit a long tail of near-irrelevant tokens at confident steps since it only checks cumulative mass, not individual token relevance.

drills.q: Derive the min-p threshold and explain why it adapts to model confidence automatically.
drills.a: threshold = min_p * P(top-1 token). Confident steps raise the threshold (shrinking eligible set); uncertain steps lower it (widening eligible set) -- moves with model confidence unlike fixed top-k/top-p.

drills.q: Why is beam search the wrong default for chat/open-ended generation?
drills.a: Human text lives in the 'typical set' not the probability-maximizing mode (Holtzman 2019); beam search's success at maximizing joint probability is exactly why it produces bland, repetitive text.

drills.q: Explain speculative decoding's correctness guarantee -- why is it exact, not approximate?
drills.a: Accept draft token with prob min(1,p_target/p_draft); on rejection resample from residual (p_target-p_draft) normalized, not from p_target directly. This construction makes the output distribution provably identical to sampling the target model alone.

drills.q: What happens if someone resamples from p_target directly on speculative-decoding rejection instead of the residual?
drills.a: It silently biases the output distribution away from the target model's true distribution by double-counting probability mass the draft already had a chance to place -- breaks the exactness guarantee.

drills.q: What acceptance rate does EAGLE-3 achieve and what architectural choice gets it there?
drills.a: 0.80-0.88 on coding/instruction-following, achieved by training the draft head on the target model's fused multi-layer internal features rather than raw token embeddings.

drills.q: How does constrained decoding guarantee valid JSON, and what does it NOT guarantee?
drills.a: Compiles schema into an FSM/PDA; masks invalid tokens to -inf logit each step, guaranteeing syntactic validity. Does not guarantee semantic correctness -- model can emit valid-but-wrong structures.

drills.q: A colleague sets temperature=0 for a support bot 'to make it more reliable.' Evaluate this.
drills.a: Greedy decoding is deterministic but not necessarily correct -- most likely token can still be confidently wrong, and it's the mode most vulnerable to repetition loops. Low nonzero temperature plus mild repetition penalty, or constrained decoding for structured needs, is usually better.

drills.q: Design the decoding stack for a coding assistant needing low latency and valid code blocks.
drills.a: EAGLE-3-style speculative decoding for latency (high acceptance on code tasks), constrained/grammar decoding for structured output validity, moderate temperature+top-p/min-p for prose explanations, no beam search anywhere.

drills.q: Why did RAG exist before context windows got large?
drills.a: Early context windows (2K-16K tokens) couldn't fit a knowledge base at all, so retrieval was the only mechanism for exposing external knowledge to a model, not a design choice.

drills.q: What did 'Lost in the Middle' actually measure?
drills.a: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval with the relevant document/fact placed at different positions in context, showing a U-shaped accuracy curve -- best at start/end, worst (20+ pp degradation in some configs) in the middle.

drills.q: A PM wants to remove the vector database because the new model has a 2M-token window. What do you ask first?
drills.a: What fraction of the corpus a typical query needs, query volume, how often the corpus updates, whether citations are needed, and the task shape (lookup vs multi-hop/aggregation) -- if most queries need a small slice, volume is high, and citations matter, keep RAG regardless of window size.

drills.q: Why doesn't NIAH benchmark performance generalize to real production accuracy?
drills.a: NIAH tests the easiest case: one unambiguous fact, simple factoid question, no cross-fact reasoning. Production questions are often multi-hop or require aggregation, where benchmarks like RULER show effective context length is shorter than advertised even for models that saturate NIAH.

drills.q: When does context caching fail to save money even though it's set up correctly?
drills.a: If query-specific content is inserted before the cacheable prefix, or the static portion gets reordered/personalized, the exact-prefix-match requirement breaks and every call becomes a full-price cache miss.

drills.q: How do you tell apart a RAG retrieval-recall failure from a long-context utilization failure?
drills.a: Check whether the correct information was actually present in the retrieved context/prompt at all. If yes and the model still got it wrong, that's a utilization (positional-attention) failure. If it was never surfaced, that's a retrieval recall failure -- different fixes follow.

drills.q: Design the retrieval strategy for a legal-document Q&A system where some queries need one clause and others need to reason across the whole contract.
drills.a: Route by query shape: single-clause lookups go through standard RAG (fast, cheap, precise); whole-contract risk-reasoning queries load the full contract into a long-context call, ideally cached if a session asks multiple follow-ups. Use a query classifier or cheap first-pass check to decide the route.

drills.q: Your team says removing RAG for long context improved eval accuracy. Do you trust it?
drills.a: Check whether the eval set is dominated by single-fact lookup (long context's saturated strength) versus multi-hop/aggregation, and whether the eval corpus size matches production scale. Without a task-shape-diverse, production-scale eval (ideally RULER-style, not just NIAH), the result doesn't generalize.

drills.q: Why is post-retrieval ACL filtering in application code a security problem, not just a recall problem?
drills.a: It under-returns when the allowed subset is small (recall issue), and any code path that skips the discard step leaks another tenant's data outright -- a breach, not a quality bug.

drills.q: Compare Pinecone namespaces vs Weaviate per-tenant shards for multi-tenancy.
drills.a: Pinecone namespaces are a cheap logical partition scaling to 100K+ tenants but not cryptographic isolation. Weaviate gives each tenant a physically separate HNSW shard for stronger isolation, at the cost of per-shard overhead for tiny tenants (mitigated by cold storage).

drills.q: Why can't you fix a PII leak by filtering the model's output after generation?
drills.a: The PII was already retrieved and placed in context before generation -- output filtering can't undo its influence on the response, and paraphrased PII can slip past pattern-matching filters even when ingestion-time redaction would have caught the original text.

drills.q: Walk through a zero-downtime migration for switching embedding models.
drills.a: Build the new index fully in parallel; dual-write new/changed docs to both during the build window; validate against a golden query set; atomically swap an alias with instant rollback available; retain the old index for a bounded window (~24h) before decommissioning.

drills.q: What's the risk of a nightly batch ACL sync between a source permission system and a RAG index?
drills.a: A staleness window up to the sync interval exists between a permission revocation and it taking effect in retrieval, during which a revoked user can still see documents they should no longer access. Fix with webhook-driven near-real-time sync.

drills.q: Break down where cost actually goes in a production RAG query and where you'd optimize first.
drills.a: Embedding and vector search are cheap; reranking is moderate; generation (context+question+answer tokens) dominates. Optimize generation model choice and retrieval precision (smaller, better-targeted context) before touching vector search infrastructure.

drills.q: Design the multi-tenant retrieval architecture for a SaaS product where tenants range from a handful of documents to millions.
drills.a: No single strategy fits both ends: small tenants can share a logically-partitioned index cheaply (low query volume, low noisy-neighbor risk); large tenants benefit from physical shard isolation to avoid noisy neighbors and filtered-search recall problems. An adaptive strategy by tenant size/volume threshold is the honest answer, with the added complexity of a migration path when a tenant crosses it.

drills.q: A corpus changes continuously at thousands of updates/hour with a 5-minute searchability SLA. Design the incremental indexing strategy.
drills.a: Batch reindexing can't meet the SLA; use streaming ingestion directly into the live index (HNSW supports native incremental insert). Deletes/updates get tombstoned, not cleanly removed, so schedule periodic compaction/rebuild based on monitored tombstone ratio and query-quality metrics rather than a fixed interval.

drills.q: Name the 11 GoF behavioral patterns and classify each as 'fully absorbed by the language', 'still commonly built explicitly', or 'real but rare.'
drills.a: Absorbed: Strategy (function param), Iterator (generator), Template Method (overriding). Still built explicitly: State, Observer, Command, Chain of Responsibility. Mechanics absorbed but still earns its keep in stable-type/growing-ops domains: Visitor. Real but rare: Mediator, Memento, Interpreter.

drills.q: Distinguish Strategy from State with a concrete example of each.
drills.a: Strategy: the caller supplies the algorithm per call with no persistent identity, e.g. sorted(data, key=lambda x: -x). State: the object itself owns which behavior applies and it changes as a side effect of lifecycle events, e.g. an Order object whose valid next transitions depend on whether it's PENDING, PAID, or SHIPPED.

drills.q: An event bus subscriber throws mid-notification and every subscriber registered after it stops receiving events. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The publish loop is propagating the exception instead of isolating it per-handler, so one bad subscriber aborts the whole fan-out. Fix: wrap each handler call in its own try/except, log the failure, and continue to the next handler -- the publisher's job is fan-out, not all-or-nothing execution.

drills.q: Explain when Visitor still earns its keep over match/switch pattern matching, and when pattern matching wins instead.
drills.a: Visitor wins when the type set is fixed/stable and the set of operations grows over time (e.g. a compiler's AST with many passes) -- each new operation is a self-contained visitor class touching zero existing node classes. Pattern matching wins when operations are fixed/few but types grow, since adding a new type only needs new cases added to the (few) match sites, not a new class satisfying every existing visitor interface.

drills.q: Why doesn't Command collapse into a plain function the way Strategy does, even though both wrap behavior?
drills.a: A function call can't be queued, serialized, logged with actor/timestamp, retried, or undone without extra machinery bolted on. Making the action a first-class object with execute()/undo() gives all of that for free -- the object-ness is only worth its cost when at least one of those needs (queueing, logging, undo) is real; otherwise Command degenerates to a function call same as Strategy.

drills.q: Why were java.util.Observer/Observable deprecated in Java 9, and what does that history suggest about pub/sub API design generally?
drills.a: Observable is a concrete class (forcing single inheritance so you can't extend anything else), not thread-safe, and uses raw Object arguments from a pre-generics era. The general lesson: baking pub/sub into a base class you must extend (rather than composing it as a standalone EventBus/publisher object) is a design mistake independent of language -- it constrains your class hierarchy for a cross-cutting concern that should be composable.

drills.q: Design a state machine for an order lifecycle and explain precisely what the State pattern buys you over scattered if-statements.
drills.a: Model states as an enum (PENDING, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED) with an explicit transition table (dict/map of current state to allowed next states) checked on every transition attempt. This buys a single, auditable source of truth for legality -- a jump like PENDING to DELIVERED is a loud, caught error -- versus scattered if-checks where a missing branch silently allows an illegal transition. Full per-state subclasses with polymorphic handle() are only needed when each state has meaningfully different processing behavior, not just different allowed transitions.

drills.q: Map the saga pattern's orchestration-vs-choreography distinction onto GoF behavioral pattern names, and explain the risk of the orchestration side.
drills.a: Orchestration maps to Mediator: a central coordinator sequences and routes calls between services that never reference each other directly. Choreography maps to Observer/pub-sub: each service reacts to events with no central coordinator. The risk on the Mediator/orchestration side: the central coordinator can absorb all business logic over time and become a God Object, so it must be kept to pure routing/sequencing rather than embedding domain rules.

drills.q: Why doesn't naive Memento (deep-copying full object state per command) scale, and what do production undo systems and durable execution frameworks (Temporal, LangGraph) do instead?
drills.a: Deep-copying an entire large document/graph on every single command is a real memory and latency cost when state is large and commands are frequent (e.g. per keystroke). Production systems instead store the inverse command (undo by reversing the last Command) or incremental diffs, falling back to full snapshots only at coarser checkpoints -- exactly what LangGraph/Temporal checkpointers do when persisting enough state to resume a run after a crash without serializing everything on every step.

drills.q: Name the 5 GoF creational patterns and which language feature each was mostly a workaround for.
drills.a: Singleton (no first-class module state), Factory Method (no first-class functions), Abstract Factory (no interfaces for coherent product families), Builder (no keyword arguments), Prototype (no generic copy protocol). All are C++/Smalltalk-era workarounds per Norvig's 1996 analysis.

drills.q: Why is a class-based Singleton considered an anti-pattern today, and what's the fix?
drills.a: It hides global mutable state behind a private constructor, breaking test isolation and risking races, and structurally prevents 2 coexisting instances. Fix: a DI container's singleton scope or a cached provider function (@lru_cache, sync.Once) — the single-instance decision lives in the wiring layer, not the class.

drills.q: Distinguish Factory Method from Abstract Factory with a concrete example of when you'd upgrade one to the other.
drills.a: Factory Method dispatches to produce ONE product type. Abstract Factory bundles multiple factory methods to produce a coherent FAMILY. Upgrade example: you start with create_document(kind), then add create_exporter(kind) that must match the document's format — bundling both under one factory interface prevents mismatching a PDF document with an HTML exporter.

drills.q: Explain why Java needs a fluent Builder class but Python and Go typically don't, and name each language's actual idiom.
drills.a: Java lacks keyword arguments, so optional-heavy constructors become unreadable telescoping calls, hence a staged .builder().build() class. Python has keyword args + defaults, so a validating dataclass/Pydantic model does the job. Go has neither keyword args nor classic inheritance, so it uses functional options: variadic ...Option function parameters that mutate the struct being built.

drills.q: A team has an AbstractDatabaseFactory with a single PostgresFactory implementation and a comment 'add MySQL later.' Diagnose and recommend.
drills.a: Speculative generality / YAGNI violation: the abstraction cost (extra indirection, an interface to maintain) is being paid before a second implementation exists to justify it. Recommend collapsing to a plain PostgresConnection constructor now, reintroducing Abstract Factory only when a second real backend is scheduled work — unless the interface exists purely for test-fake substitution, which is a separate, valid justification.

drills.q: What's broken about Java's Cloneable interface, and what do production Java codebases use instead?
drills.a: Object.clone() is protected, performs only a shallow copy by default, can throw a checked CloneNotSupportedException even when cloning is always supported, and doesn't compose with generics or final fields. Production code typically uses a copy constructor or a static factory method like Config.copyOf(other) with explicit deep-copy logic.

drills.q: State Peter Norvig's 1996 argument about GoF patterns and evaluate whether it fully applies to all 23 patterns.
drills.a: Norvig argued ~16/23 GoF patterns vanish or become trivial in a language with first-class functions, closures, and multiple dispatch, since most patterns compensate for C++/Smalltalk's missing features. It's substantially right for creational patterns (Factory Method, Builder, Prototype collapse easily) but less complete for patterns whose value is structural coordination rather than missing syntax, e.g. Abstract Factory's family-coherence guarantee, or Observer/Iterator in the other GoF categories.

drills.q: Design the object-construction strategy for a multi-tenant SaaS backend needing a different storage backend (S3, Azure Blob, local disk) per tenant, chosen at request time. Explain where a naive Singleton would break this.
drills.a: Use Abstract Factory keyed by tenant config (StorageFactory interface with S3Factory/AzureFactory/LocalFactory), resolved per request or cached per tenant — not a process-wide Singleton, since Singleton allows only one instance per process and the requirement is multiple coexisting instances. Construction params (bucket, creds, region) flow through a validating config object (dataclass/Pydantic, the Builder's job) so malformed tenant config fails fast at construction. A naive StorageClient.getInstance() Singleton would immediately break this because it can only ever bind to one backend for the whole process.

drills.q: Why is Prototype risky for objects that hold live connections or other side-effecting resources?
drills.a: Cloning (deepcopy or a clone constructor) copies the reference/handle to the resource rather than establishing a fresh one, so two logical objects end up sharing one underlying socket or connection — violating the assumption that a clone is an independent, safely-mutable copy. Prototype is safe for pure-data templates, not for objects wrapping I/O handles.

drills.q: Name the 7 GoF structural patterns and group them into 'common in real backends' vs 'rare/situational.'
drills.a: Common: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy. Situational/rare: Composite (needs genuinely recursive domain data), Bridge (needs 2 independently-varying hierarchies), Flyweight (needs measured extreme object-count memory pressure).

drills.q: Distinguish Adapter, Facade, Decorator, and Proxy along two axes: does the interface change, and is new behavior added?
drills.a: Adapter: interface changes, no new behavior (compatibility). Facade: many interfaces simplify to one, no new behavior (simplicity). Decorator: interface stays the same, adds stackable behavior (extension). Proxy: interface stays the same, controls access, sometimes adds behavior like caching (control).

drills.q: A vendor payment SDK is called directly from 200 call sites and the vendor just deprecated a method. What should have been in place, and what's the fix now?
drills.a: An Adapter layer (a PaymentGateway interface with one vendor-specific implementation) should have confined vendor-specific code to one file. The fix now is a wide, mechanical, risky refactor to introduce that adapter retroactively -- exactly the cost the pattern exists to avoid paying later.

drills.q: Explain why decorator stacking order is not commutative, with a concrete logging+caching example.
drills.a: @logged over @cached (logged outermost) logs every call including cache hits, since logged wraps the whole cached call. @cached over @logged (cached outermost) means cache hits short-circuit before ever reaching the logger, so hits go unlogged. Outermost decorator always sees the call first and the return value last.

drills.q: Diagnose: an ORM-backed endpoint iterating 1000 orders and reading order.customer on each is making 1000 extra queries. What pattern is responsible and what's the fix?
drills.a: This is the classic N+1 failure mode of a lazy-loading Proxy: accessing the relation transparently triggers a fresh query per access instead of one batched query. Fix with explicit eager loading (joinedload/selectinload in SQLAlchemy, Preload in GORM, JOIN FETCH in JPQL) on the hot path.

drills.q: A Facade class has grown to 40 public methods, imports from 15 modules, and contains its own conditionals and state. What's wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: It has drifted from a thin delegation layer into a God Object wearing a Facade's name -- the tell is business logic living inside the facade instead of in the components it should delegate to. Fix: split along real subsystem boundaries (e.g. OrderFacade, RefundFacade, ReportingFacade) so each stays a pure composition of calls.

drills.q: When is Bridge actually justified versus being over-engineering, and how does it differ from Strategy?
drills.a: Bridge is justified only when there are 2 independent hierarchies (e.g. N shape types x M rendering backends) that would otherwise multiply into an NxM subclass explosion. If only one implementation exists on one side, plain DI with a single interface is enough. Structurally Bridge and Strategy are nearly identical (interface + swappable implementation); they differ only in intent -- Bridge prevents a hierarchy explosion, Strategy swaps one algorithm.

drills.q: Design the integration layer for a service supporting 3 LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, local vLLM) behind one internal call, and explain the limit of the pattern when providers have different capabilities.
drills.a: Define an LLMClient interface (generate(prompt, **kwargs) -> Response) with one Adapter per provider translating each SDK's distinct auth/streaming/usage-field shape into the common interface, confining provider-specific breaking changes to one file each. The limit: Adapter can't paper over genuine capability gaps (e.g. only one provider supports function calling) -- that needs an explicit capability-detection/registry layer rather than silently no-op'ing unsupported features inside the adapter.

drills.q: Why is Flyweight rarely hand-built in Python or the JVM, and when would you still build one?
drills.a: Both runtimes already deduplicate the common cases (Python's small-integer cache and string interning, the JVM's string pool and boxed-Integer cache), so a custom Flyweight adds redundant complexity for primitive-sized data. Build one only when profiling shows real, measured memory pressure from millions of larger near-duplicate domain objects (e.g. font glyphs, tokenizer vocab entries, game tile types) that the runtime isn't already sharing.

drills.q: Name the five universal debugger primitives that every language's debugger implements in some form.
drills.a: Breakpoint, step-over, step-into, inspect locals, evaluate expression.

drills.q: Which flag/setting pauses execution until a debugger connects, for Node and for Java respectively?
drills.a: Node: --inspect-brk. Java: suspend=y in the -agentlib:jdwp= connection string.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why delve can attach to an already-running Go binary with zero prior instrumentation, while Node's inspector protocol cannot attach to an already-running unmodified Node process.
drills.a: Delve's attach uses ptrace directly at the OS level against the live process -- no cooperation or prior setup from the target process is needed. Node's inspector is an application-level WebSocket protocol the process itself has to open a listening port for, which requires the --inspect flag to be present at process start; there's no way to retrofit that listening capability onto a process already running without it.

drills.q: You need to catch a bug in Python code that runs at module import time, deep in a dependency chain, not in the top-level script itself. How do you do it with pdb?
drills.a: Run python -m pdb script.py, which pauses before the script begins executing at all. At the pdb prompt, before your first continue, set an explicit breakpoint on the suspect module and line (b module_path.py:line), since python -m pdb doesn't automatically stop at every nested import -- you need at least a rough hypothesis about which module to break in first.

drills.q: A watchpoint set on a struct field in rust-gdb never triggers even though you're certain the value changes. Give two mechanistic reasons this can happen.
drills.a: 1) The value is being mutated through a different memory location than the one watched -- an alias, a raw pointer, or a copy of the struct being changed instead of the original the watchpoint tracks. 2) Hardware watchpoint limits (often only 4 per architecture) have been exceeded, and the debugger either silently fell back to a slower software watchpoint or failed to set it, without erroring loudly on some debugger/OS/architecture combinations.

drills.q: dlv attach <pid> fails with a permissions error inside a Kubernetes pod. Diagnose the cause and give two valid fixes, with a preference stated between them.
drills.a: Cause: delve's ptrace-based attach requires CAP_SYS_PTRACE, which most container security policies strip by default as a hardening measure. Fix 1: add securityContext.capabilities.add: [SYS_PTRACE] to the specific container, temporarily, for the debugging session. Fix 2 (preferred): use an ephemeral debug container (kubectl debug --target=<container>) sharing the target's PID namespace, since this scopes the elevated capability to a short-lived sidecar rather than granting it to the long-running production container itself.

drills.q: During an active production incident, is print-statement-and-redeploy or attaching a debugger the better move, and why, specifically compared to using a debugger routinely during normal development?
drills.a: Attach a debugger (preferring a non-invasive dump/snapshot mechanism like py-spy dump or jstack over interactive stepping) rather than redeploy-with-logging, specifically because redeploying mid-incident adds deployment risk and delay on top of an already-degraded system, whereas a read-mostly attach/dump gets you state faster without another deploy cycle. This is the opposite tradeoff from routine development debugging, where a quick log-and-redeploy loop is often cheaper than standing up remote debugging infrastructure.

drills.q: Why is setting suspend=y as a standing default on a production JVM "just in case someone needs to debug something" a serious operational mistake?
drills.a: Every restart of that JVM -- a deploy, a crash-restart, an autoscale event -- would hang indefinitely waiting for a debugger connection that usually isn't coming, which looks exactly like a hung, unresponsive deployment to any monitoring or orchestration system watching startup. suspend=y should be a deliberate, temporary choice scoped to an active debugging session, never a standing production configuration.

drills.q: State Zeller's scientific debugging loop in order.
drills.a: Observe the failure, invent a hypothesis consistent with observations, use it to make a prediction, test the prediction by experiment, repeat/refine until the hypothesis fully explains the failure.

drills.q: Why is "something's wrong with the network" not a usable debugging hypothesis?
drills.a: It isn't falsifiable as stated -- there's no specific experiment whose result would let you say definitively it's disproven. It needs a stated mechanism (e.g. "the load balancer drops idle connections after 60s, causing this timeout") that a concrete test could confirm or kill.

drills.q: A bug reproduces 7 out of 10 tries. Is that a usable reproduction? What's the first move?
drills.a: Usable but noisy -- roughly 3 in 10 experiments will give a false negative reading. Before hypothesizing about cause, try to correlate the 3 misses against load, input variant, or timing to see if the 70/30 split resolves into a cleaner deterministic condition, which is usually cheaper than compensating statistically by over-running a noisy experiment.

drills.q: Walk through delta-debugging a 3000-line config file that crashes a parser: what's the halving procedure and roughly how many steps to a minimal repro?
drills.a: Check if the first half (1500 lines) alone still crashes it; if yes, discard the other half and repeat; if no, the bug needs content from both halves, so try a different split or isolate which removed section mattered. Converges in roughly log2(3000) ~= 12 steps versus up to 3000 one-line removals, assuming a deterministic crash/no-crash check each step.

drills.q: A commit range contains two unrelated bugs -- one introduced early and fixed later, another introduced near the end. What happens if you run git bisect across the whole range, and what should you check first to avoid this?
drills.a: Monotonicity is violated (good -> bad -> good -> bad instead of one clean transition), so bisect's reported "first bad commit" will be unreliable or wrong depending on where midpoints land. Before trusting an automated bisect, confirm the SAME specific failure (not just "some failure") is present at the bad end and absent at the good end.

drills.q: A bug is present across every recent commit but only manifests on large inputs. Why would bisecting on commit history waste time here, and how would you detect this before running a full bisect?
drills.a: The bug wasn't introduced recently -- it's old and was simply never triggered by the inputs used in earlier testing -- so every commit in a reasonable range is "bad" and bisect converges on nothing useful; commit history isn't the axis the failure actually varies along. Detect it cheaply first: check whether the failure reproduces at the oldest commit under consideration using the exact same triggering input as the newest; if it reproduces at both ends, the axis doesn't discriminate and bisecting it further is guaranteed to waste time.

drills.q: Your falsifying experiment just contradicted your hypothesis, but your manager already told the team 'we found it, it's the cache.' What do you do, and why?
drills.a: Discard the hypothesis and keep searching based on the actual evidence, and flag the correction to the team rather than quietly continuing to search while the wrong explanation stands publicly uncorrected. The social cost of being wrong is real but irrelevant to whether the hypothesis is true -- patching the hypothesis to survive contrary evidence because it was already announced is the same sunk-cost error the discipline exists to prevent.

drills.q: You've correlated an intermittent production bug against every available dimension (deploy timing, traffic shape, tenant, time of day, concurrent load) and found no pattern. Is the bug now truly unreproducible, and what's the practical next move?
drills.a: It's reasonable to call it genuinely unreproducible on-demand at that point, since the correlation effort was actually exhaustive rather than superficial. The practical shift is from reproduction-driven falsification to inference-from-evidence: instrument more aggressively before the next occurrence (structured logging, always-on lightweight tracing, crash core dumps) so the next occurrence -- even if still not reproducible on demand -- leaves enough evidence to support or falsify a hypothesis after the fact.

drills.q: State the five-layer PR review order from memory.
drills.a: Correctness, security, design, tests, style.

drills.q: What three commands would you run in the first two minutes of triaging a 2000-line PR?
drills.a: git diff --stat to find highest-churn files; a check for which changed files have no corresponding test touched; a targeted grep for sink patterns (subprocess, os.system, eval, string-built SQL) across the diff.

drills.q: Why does a correctness bug get reviewed before a security bug, given security is arguably higher severity?
drills.a: The ordering is about what invalidates downstream review, not severity ranking -- a correctness bug usually means substantial rewrite is coming, making security commentary on the current shape wasted effort. Both still get full attention; the order matters most for triage under time pressure.

drills.q: A PR shows 100% line coverage on a new module. Argue concretely why this doesn't guarantee good tests.
drills.a: Line coverage only measures whether a line executed during the test run, not whether any assertion would fail given a wrong implementation. A test can execute every line and assert against a mock or assert nothing meaningful about output, hitting 100% coverage while catching zero regressions. Mutation testing (deliberately break a line, see if any test goes red) is the concrete way to expose this gap.

drills.q: An endpoint's GET handler checks resource ownership but the newly added PATCH handler in the same PR does not. How would you have found this, mechanically, and what pattern does it represent?
drills.a: By reading every handler for the resource, not just the one the PR description highlights, and specifically diffing the authorization check present in the sibling GET handler against the new PATCH handler. This is a copy-paste-and-forget-the-check pattern, a specific and common IDOR variant.

drills.q: An author dismisses your blocking security comment as "an edge case that won't happen in practice." What's the most effective next move, and why does the abstract argument usually fail?
drills.a: Produce a concrete repro (a crafted request, a curl command, a script) demonstrating the exploit, rather than continuing to argue in the abstract. "This could be an IDOR" is arguable; "here is the exact request that returns another user's private data" is not -- concrete evidence ends the dispute where assertion does not.

drills.q: You must review a PR modifying a shared utility used in 12 call sites, in a language you're not deeply expert in. Design your review strategy.
drills.a: Weight review toward what transfers regardless of language expertise: edge-input handling (empty/null/boundary/concurrent), untrusted input reaching a sink unsafely, and whether tests assert real behavior. Grep every call site for the utility and check whether the changed behavior (not just signature) is compatible with each caller's assumptions -- don't rely solely on each caller's existing tests passing, since weak coverage at a site can mask a real behavior change. For language-specific idioms you're unsure of, say so explicitly and loop in someone who is expert rather than approving on faith.

drills.q: The author says your proposed better design costs two extra days, and this needs to ship today. How do you decide whether to hold the block, and what determines the answer?
drills.a: Evaluate whether the identified cost of the current approach is bounded (a one-time cleanup later, cheap to pay once) or compounding (every future feature in this area has to work around the wrong abstraction). If bounded, approve now and file a tracked follow-up. If compounding, the two-day cost now is cheaper than paying a smaller cost repeatedly forever -- state the tradeoff in those explicit terms rather than a flat refusal or a rubber-stamp approval.

drills.q: List the ten LLM-code failure modes in the order this module checks them.
drills.a: Fabricated API/import, deprecated/removed API, silently swallowed errors, missing edge cases, over-abstraction, tests asserting implementation not behavior, plausible-but-wrong concurrency, confidently wrong comments, idiom mismatch, unjustified complexity for scale.

drills.q: Why can't you use "the code reads confidently" as a signal of correctness for AI-generated code?
drills.a: LLM fluency is a token-probability property generated identically for real and hallucinated APIs -- there's no internal signal distinguishing certainty from plausible invention, unlike a human author whose confidence tracks actual certainty.

drills.q: A generated module has 100% test coverage. Explain concretely why this doesn't guarantee the tests catch regressions, and how you'd prove it either way.
drills.a: Coverage measures line execution, not assertion quality -- a test can execute every line while asserting only that a mock was called, which can't fail even against a broken implementation making the same call. Run a mutation-testing tool (mutmut/Stryker/PIT) to deliberately break the implementation and confirm at least one test goes red for each mutation; surviving mutations expose exactly which "covered" lines have no real assertion behind them.

drills.q: Explain the check-then-act concurrency bug: why does a lock in the code not guarantee safety, and why do unit tests typically miss it?
drills.a: A lock acquired around only the check, or only the act, but not both atomically, leaves the combined check-then-act sequence exposed -- two concurrent callers can each pass the check before either performs the act. Unit tests run sequentially by default and essentially never inject real thread interleaving at exactly the check-act boundary, so the bug doesn't manifest until real contention under production load hits that exact timing window.

drills.q: What is slopsquatting and why does it make a hallucinated import a security issue, not just a build failure?
drills.a: Slopsquatting is attackers registering package names LLMs are observed to hallucinate frequently. A build failure only occurs if the fabricated name doesn't exist; once an attacker registers that exact name, the install succeeds and pulls in malicious code -- CI passing on install is not evidence the dependency is legitimate.

drills.q: Rank and justify review priority for a single PR containing: a hallucinated import, an over-engineered factory, a swallowed exception in a payment path, a stale comment, and a mock-only test covering the payment path.
drills.a: 1) Swallowed exception in the payment path -- highest severity, silent money/data corruption. 2) Hallucinated import -- blocks build or resolves to a malicious package. 3) Mock-only test on the payment path -- compounds with #1 since the fix wouldn't actually be verified. 4) Over-abstraction and 5) stale comment -- real but lower severity, non-blocking or same-PR-but-not-urgent.

drills.q: A teammate says increased general attention when reading AI-generated code makes a fixed checklist unnecessary. What's the gap in that argument?
drills.a: General careful reading catches what careful human review has always caught -- typos, obvious logic errors, style issues -- but fabricated-but-plausible API calls, mock-only tests, and check-then-act races don't look wrong on a careful read; they look like ordinary correct code. A checklist forces the specific mechanical checks (import resolution, exception handling, test-assertion quality, concurrency trace) that fluency makes easy to skip, freeing remaining attention for genuine judgment calls like design fit.

drills.q: Why is a comment mismatch in AI-generated code categorically different from typical human comment drift, and what review implication follows?
drills.a: Human comment drift usually starts accurate and goes stale after a later code change, often carrying residual signal (it was true once) and sometimes reading slightly inconsistent as a tell. A generated comment can be wrong from the moment of creation with no prior accurate state, generated with full fluency regardless of match to the code -- so "this comment looks stale" is not a reliable tell here; every behavior-describing comment must be verified against the code directly, not triaged by how old or confident it reads.

drills.q: What single fact in a VPC determines whether a subnet is public or private?
drills.a: The subnet's route table -- specifically whether its default route (0.0.0.0/0) points at an Internet Gateway (public) or a NAT Gateway / nothing (private). The subnet itself has no inherent public/private property.

drills.q: A private subnet's app reads heavily from S3 and the NAT gateway bill has tripled. What's the fix and why is it free?
drills.a: Add a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3, associated with the private subnet's route table. It's implemented as a route-table entry (no ENI, no hourly or per-GB charge), and it keeps the traffic on the AWS backbone instead of through the NAT gateway at $0.045/GB.

drills.q: Explain, mechanically, why a NACL that only allows inbound port 443 breaks a working connection even though the security group is correctly configured.
drills.a: NACLs are stateless -- allowing inbound 443 says nothing about the response. The response leaves the server on an ephemeral source port; unless the NACL has a matching outbound allow rule for the ephemeral port range (roughly 1024-65535), that outbound packet is dropped. The SG is irrelevant here because SGs are stateful and would have allowed the return traffic automatically -- the NACL is evaluated independently and blocks it anyway.

drills.q: A partner requires a static IP allowlist entry for your HTTP API, which currently runs behind an ALB with path-based routing to three microservices. Design the fix.
drills.a: Put an NLB in front of the ALB using the 'ALB' target type, and allocate Elastic IPs to the NLB (one per AZ). The static IP satisfies the partner's allowlist requirement while the ALB behind it continues doing the path-based routing across the three services. A plain NLB alone can't do path routing; a plain ALB alone can't guarantee a static IP.

drills.q: You have 12 VPCs across 4 teams, all needing transitive connectivity to each other plus hybrid VPN access to on-prem. Peering or Transit Gateway, and why?
drills.a: Transit Gateway. Peering is non-transitive and would require up to 66 pairwise connections (12*11/2) with independently maintained route tables. Transit Gateway gives every VPC one attachment to a hub with transitive routing to all others, centralized per-attachment route control (so prod/staging can still be segmented), and a single place to fan out the VPN/Direct Connect hybrid connection to all 12 VPCs.

drills.q: Why does PrivateLink support overlapping CIDR ranges between provider and consumer VPCs when Peering and Transit Gateway do not?
drills.a: PrivateLink is a proxy, not a routing merge -- the consumer's interface endpoint is just an ENI in the consumer's own VPC that forwards to the provider's service over AWS's internal PrivateLink infrastructure. Neither side ever needs to route packets directly into the other's CIDR space, so there's no CIDR conflict possible. Peering and Transit Gateway both work by merging route tables across VPCs, which fails immediately if the CIDRs overlap.

drills.q: Diagnose: an ALB's health checks are passing, but 30% of requests to one target return connection refused, and it correlates with a recent NACL change locking down the private subnet.
drills.a: Check whether the NACL's outbound rules still allow the ephemeral port range back to the ALB subnet -- a partial/asymmetric NACL lockdown can drop return traffic for some but not all connections depending on load balancer node placement across AZs. Also verify the NACL wasn't accidentally scoped to block traffic between AZs within the same VPC if the ALB nodes and targets aren't co-located.

drills.q: Why is 'anycast beats DNS for fast failover' true even when your Route53 TTL is set to 5 seconds?
drills.a: TTL is a request to caching resolvers and clients, not an enforced contract. OS-level resolvers, corporate/ISP resolvers, and some client stacks cache longer than instructed or apply their own minimums, so a 5s TTL doesn't guarantee 5s propagation across your actual client population. Anycast (e.g. Global Accelerator) sidesteps this because failover happens by withdrawing/rerouting at the network layer, which every client observes without any cache to expire.

drills.q: Design network isolation for a shared internal recommendation API consumed by 20 independent product teams' VPCs, some of which use the same CIDR range (10.0.0.0/16) by historical accident.
drills.a: PrivateLink. Put the API behind an NLB, create a VPC endpoint service, and have each of the 20 consumer VPCs create an interface endpoint into it. Since PrivateLink doesn't merge routing tables, the overlapping 10.0.0.0/16 CIDRs across consumer VPCs are a non-issue -- Peering or Transit Gateway would both fail outright or require re-IP'ing several teams' VPCs first.

drills.q: A gRPC service behind an ALB shows p99 8ms higher than an identical NLB-fronted deployment. Should you switch, and what's the actual decision criterion?
drills.a: Not automatically -- the criterion is whether you're using ALB's L7 features (host/path routing across services, ACM-managed TLS termination, WAF). If yes, an 8ms overhead against inference calls that take hundreds of milliseconds is very unlikely to be the real bottleneck, and the operational simplicity of ALB usually wins. If the service is genuinely latency-critical (sub-millisecond budget matters, e.g. a bidding system) and doesn't need L7 routing, switch to NLB.

drills.q: Given a route table with 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT Gateway in AZ-a, and a private subnet in AZ-b routing through that same NAT gateway, what two costs does this incur beyond normal NAT charges, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Cross-AZ data transfer charges (roughly $0.01/GB each direction) on top of the NAT's own per-GB processing charge, plus a single point of failure -- if the AZ-a NAT gateway or its AZ has an outage, AZ-b's private subnet loses outbound connectivity too. Fix: deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and route each private subnet to its own-AZ NAT gateway.

drills.q: Trace this: a = [1,2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a). What prints, and why?
drills.a: [1, 2, 3]. b = a never copies — b is a second name bound to the same list object as a, so mutating via b is visible through a too.

drills.q: When, if ever, is `is` the correct operator to use instead of `==`?
drills.a: Only for singleton/identity checks: x is None, x is True, x is False, or comparisons against a sentinel object created specifically for that purpose. Never for general value comparison of ints, strings, or custom objects.

drills.q: Explain precisely why `grid = [[0]*3]*3` produces a grid where mutating grid[0][0] changes grid[1][0] and grid[2][0] as well.
drills.a: [0]*3 evaluates once, producing a single inner list object. The outer *3 builds a new outer list containing three references to that same inner object, not three independently constructed rows. So all three 'rows' are literally the same object, and mutating it through any one index is visible through all three.

drills.q: Write the correct way to construct a 3x3 grid of independent rows and explain why it avoids the aliasing bug.
drills.a: [[0]*3 for _ in range(3)] — a list comprehension re-evaluates its expression [0]*3 fresh on every one of its 3 iterations, so three distinct inner list objects are created instead of one shared object referenced three times.

drills.q: You do `shallow = copy.copy(original)` where original is a list of lists. Appending to shallow doesn't affect original, but appending to shallow[0] does. Explain both halves of this behavior.
drills.a: copy.copy creates a new OUTER list, so appending to shallow itself only changes the new outer container, leaving original's outer list untouched. But the elements inside shallow are the same object references as in original (only one level was copied), so shallow[0] and original[0] point to the identical inner list, and mutating it through either name is visible through both.

drills.q: How does copy.deepcopy correctly handle a self-referential list like `a = []; a.append(a)` without infinite-looping?
drills.a: deepcopy keeps a memo dict keyed by id() of objects currently being copied. It registers the newly created (still partially built) copy in the memo BEFORE recursing into the object's contents. When it encounters the same object id again mid-recursion, it returns the already-registered copy instead of recursing again, terminating the cycle correctly while preserving the self-reference in the result.

drills.q: Give two concrete situations where using copy.deepcopy is the wrong engineering choice, and what you'd do instead in each.
drills.a: 1) Only top-level isolation is actually needed (you'll only add/remove elements, never mutate nested elements) — use copy.copy instead, which is O(top-level size) versus deepcopy's O(entire reachable graph). 2) The object holds a live external resource (file handle, socket, DB connection, lock) — implement __deepcopy__ to keep that attribute shared or reconnect explicitly, since naively deep-copying a resource handle either raises or produces a broken duplicate.

drills.q: Implement __deepcopy__ for a TreeNode class with value, children, and parent attributes such that deep-copying a subtree does not walk upward through parent and copy the whole tree.
drills.a: def __deepcopy__(self, memo): new = TreeNode.__new__(TreeNode); memo[id(self)] = new; new.value = copy.deepcopy(self.value, memo); new.children = copy.deepcopy(self.children, memo); new.parent = self.parent  # deliberately shared, not deep-copied; return new. Registering in memo before recursing also keeps this safe if a node is reachable via multiple paths.

drills.q: Why does relying on `is` for integer comparison sometimes pass in unit tests and then fail in production with real data?
drills.a: CPython caches small integers in [-5, 256] as singletons, so is happens to agree with == for small literals used in tests. Once production values exceed 256 (a growing counter, a database-generated ID), they're typically separate objects even when equal in value, so is silently returns False where == would return True — no exception is raised, just a wrong answer.

drills.q: How does pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write default (made the only mode as of the January 2026 release) relate to the shallow-copy aliasing bugs covered in this module, and what specifically changed for chained assignment?
drills.a: Pre-3.0, pandas indexing sometimes returned a view (memory shared with the original, like a shallow copy) and sometimes an actual copy, depending on undocumented internal memory layout, so chained assignment like df[df.x>0]['y']=1 could silently mutate the original or silently do nothing. Pandas 3.0 makes every operation behave as a logically independent copy (sharing memory lazily underneath until a write forces an actual copy), and chained assignment now raises explicitly instead of behaving unpredictably.

drills.q: Rewrite `@dec\ndef f(): ...` without decorator syntax, and state precisely when the rewritten assignment happens.
drills.a: def f(): ...\nf = dec(f) — this runs once, at definition (module import) time, not on each call to f.

drills.q: You decorate a function without functools.wraps. What does `decorated_func.__name__` print, and name one framework-level consequence beyond cosmetics.
drills.a: It prints 'wrapper' (or whatever the inner function was named), not the original name. Consequence: frameworks that introspect the signature via inspect.signature (e.g. FastAPI's dependency injection) see (*args, **kwargs) instead of the real parameters and can break.

drills.q: Expand `@retry(times=3)` above `def call(): ...` into the equivalent explicit assignment, naming what each nested function layer is responsible for.
drills.a: call = retry(times=3)(call). Layer 1 (retry) takes the decorator's own arguments and returns the real decorator. Layer 2 (the returned decorator) takes the function and returns the wrapper. Layer 3 (wrapper) is what actually replaces calls to call.

drills.q: Given `@a` above `@b` above `def f(): ...`, write the equivalent assignment, then state which wrapper's code executes first when f() is called.
drills.a: f = a(b(f)). At call time execution is outside-in: a's wrapper code runs first (it's now the outermost callable), which then calls into b's wrapper, which finally calls the original f.

drills.q: A class has `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` directly on an instance method `predict(self, x)`. Explain precisely why instances of this class never get garbage collected.
drills.a: The cache is attached to the function object shared across the class, and the cache keys include self as part of the argument tuple. Every instance that has ever called predict() is therefore referenced by the cache for the process's lifetime, so its refcount never reaches zero and it can't be collected.

drills.q: What's the correct fix for the lru_cache-on-instance-method leak if you need a cached value computed once per instance?
drills.a: functools.cached_property — it stores the computed value directly in the instance's own __dict__ rather than in a class-level cache, so the cached value is collected along with the instance itself.

drills.q: Why does `@lru_cache` raise TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' when a function is called with a list argument, and why is this treated as a feature rather than worked around by hashing the list's contents?
drills.a: The cache builds its key by hashing the arguments, and list/dict/set are unhashable. It's deliberate: even if the contents were hashed, using a mutable object as a cache key is a correctness hazard, because mutating that same list object after the call wouldn't invalidate the now-stale cached result.

drills.q: You add functools.wraps to a decorator but a static type checker (mypy) still doesn't flag a caller passing wrong argument types to the decorated function. Why, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: functools.wraps only restores runtime metadata (__name__, __doc__, __wrapped__) — it does not change the wrapper function's own static type signature, which is still (*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any. Fix by typing the decorator with ParamSpec and TypeVar: def dec(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R], with wrapper typed as (*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R.

drills.q: Distinguish a class decorator from a class used as a decorator, and give a reason to prefer the latter.
drills.a: A class decorator is a function applied to a class (receives/returns a class object, e.g. a registration pattern). A class used as a decorator implements __call__ and wraps a function; prefer it when the decorator needs to hold non-trivial state or expose extra methods to callers (e.g. a call counter with a .reset() method), which is awkward to expose cleanly from a plain closure.

drills.q: A function that worked fine with multiprocessing.Pool suddenly fails to pickle after you added a decorator to it. functools.wraps is present. What are the two most likely root causes?
drills.a: (1) The wrapper function is defined as a local/nested function rather than at module scope — pickle resolves functions by reference (module + qualname), and a purely local function can't be looked up that way regardless of wraps. (2) The decorator's closure captures something unpicklable (a lock, file handle, or lambda) that gets serialized along with it. wraps fixes the __name__/__qualname__ metadata but doesn't make an inherently unpicklable closure picklable.

drills.q: Explain why `@app.route('/x')` above `@login_required` above `def handler(): ...` runs the routing framework's wrapper code before the auth check, and what would go wrong if you needed metrics wrapped around the entire request including auth.
drills.a: Build order is handler = app.route('/x')(login_required(handler)), so app.route's wrapper is outermost and runs first at call time, then calls into login_required's wrapper. A metrics decorator placed inside login_required (closer to handler) would only time the work after auth passed, missing time spent in the auth check itself — it needs to be placed outside login_required, closer to app.route, to capture the whole request.

drills.q: Define the iterator protocol precisely: what two methods, what does each return, and what signals completion?
drills.a: __iter__() returns an iterator (often self); __next__() returns the next value or raises StopIteration to signal completion.

drills.q: State precisely: is every iterator a generator? Is every generator an iterator? Give a concrete counterexample.
drills.a: Every generator is an iterator. Not every iterator is a generator — e.g. a hand-written class implementing __iter__/__next__, or a zip/file object, is an iterator with no yield anywhere.

drills.q: You write `gen = (x*x for x in range(5))` and then run `print(list(gen)); print(list(gen))`. What prints the second time, and why?
drills.a: [] the second time. The generator is exhausted after the first list() call; StopIteration fires immediately on the next next(), which list() silently interprets as zero items — no error is raised.

drills.q: Why does calling a generator function not execute any of its body immediately, even code before the first yield?
drills.a: Because any function containing yield anywhere is compiled as a generator function; calling it only constructs and returns a generator object. Execution begins only when next()/send() is first called on it.

drills.q: Explain what yield from adds beyond a plain `for x in sub: yield x` loop.
drills.a: yield from forwards send()/throw()/close() calls made on the outer generator into the sub-generator, and captures the sub-generator's return value as the result of the yield-from expression — a manual for-loop does neither.

drills.q: You call `g = my_gen(); g.send('hello')` on a freshly created generator. What happens and why?
drills.a: TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator. There is no suspended yield expression yet to receive the value; you must prime it with next(g) or g.send(None) first.

drills.q: You run itertools.groupby on data=[('a',1),('b',2),('a',3)] keyed by the first element, without sorting first. How many groups come out, and what are their keys?
drills.a: Three groups: 'a', 'b', 'a' — groupby only merges consecutive equal keys, and the second 'a' isn't adjacent to the first, so it starts a new group.

drills.q: When does itertools.tee stop being cheap, and what's the worst-case memory cost?
drills.a: When one of the resulting iterators is consumed much faster than another; tee must buffer every element the slower consumer hasn't reached yet, so in the worst case (one branch fully consumed before the other starts) the memory cost approaches that of materializing the entire sequence as a list.

drills.q: Give three concrete situations where reaching for a generator instead of a list is the wrong engineering call.
drills.a: Needing len() up front (progress reporting, preallocation); needing random access, indexing, or more than one pass over the data (retries, multi-statistic passes, multiple consumers); the dataset is small enough that materializing is essentially free and the generator only adds debugging friction.

drills.q: What does PEP 479 change about a StopIteration raised inside a generator's body, and what production bug did it fix?
drills.a: Since Python 3.7 it's enforced that an unhandled StopIteration escaping a generator's body is converted into a RuntimeError instead of propagating as-is. Before this, a stray StopIteration (e.g. from calling next() on an exhausted sub-iterator) would silently truncate whichever for-loop was consuming the outer generator, with no error at all.

drills.q: Design a memory-bounded pipeline that reads a 50GB log file and returns only the first line containing 'ERROR', without loading the file into memory. What's the peak memory profile?
drills.a: Chain a line-reading generator (iterating the file object directly, which reads one line at a time) into a filter/find function that returns on first match. Peak memory is one line at a time; if the match is near the top of the file, the rest is never read, unlike f.readlines() which loads everything up front regardless of where the match is.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why df.apply(func, axis=1) is slower than df.a + df.b, even though both are one line of code.
drills.a: apply calls a Python function once per row, and pandas has to assemble each row's values into a Series-like object per call, executing entirely in the Python interpreter. The vectorised form runs a single compiled NumPy loop over contiguous column memory with no per-row Python function-call overhead at all.

drills.q: A Series is created from [1, 2, None, 4]. What dtype does it get, and why?
drills.a: float64. NumPy's int64 has no bit pattern to represent a missing value, so pandas upcasts the entire column to float64 (which can represent NaN) the moment any value is missing — every value, including the non-missing ones, becomes a float.

drills.q: Given df.groupby('team')['score'].transform('mean'), what shape does the result have relative to the input, and how does that differ from .agg('mean')?
drills.a: transform returns a result with the SAME shape (same number of rows) as the input, broadcasting each group's mean back to every row belonging to that group. agg('mean') instead collapses each group to one row, returning one value per group, not per original row.

drills.q: You need, for each row, its deviation from its group's mean (score - group_mean). Write this using transform, and explain why agg alone can't do it in one step.
drills.a: df['score'] - df.groupby('team')['score'].transform('mean'). agg alone produces one row per group, so subtracting it from the original per-row score requires re-aligning the per-group value back onto every original row — which is exactly the broadcast transform performs internally; with agg alone you'd need a separate merge back onto the original frame on the grouping key.

drills.q: What does merge(df1, df2, on='key', validate='one_to_one') check, and what happens if the check fails?
drills.a: It verifies that 'key' is unique in BOTH df1 and df2 before performing the merge. If either side has duplicate keys, it raises MergeError immediately, before any rows are silently fanned out by the merge.

drills.q: Prior to pandas 3.0, what made SettingWithCopyWarning ambiguous rather than a clear error, and what specifically changed in pandas 3.0 (January 2026)?
drills.a: Whether df[mask] returned a view (sharing memory with the original) or an independent copy was an undocumented implementation detail depending on internal memory layout, so the same-looking chained assignment code could silently mutate the original in one case and do nothing in another. Pandas 3.0 made Copy-on-Write the only mode — every operation behaves as an independent copy by contract — removed SettingWithCopyWarning entirely, and made chained assignment raise an explicit error instead of warning.

drills.q: Design a pandas approach to expand a table of (contract_id, start_date, end_date) rows into one row per (contract_id, month) for every month the range spans. Name the specific edge case that requires a guard.
drills.a: For each row, generate pd.date_range(start_date, end_date, freq='MS').tolist() to get the list of month-start timestamps in range, store it in a column, then call df.explode() on that column to turn each row's list into separate rows, duplicating the other columns. The edge case: a row whose start and end fall within the same calendar month produces zero month-start boundaries strictly between them, giving an empty list — without a fallback (e.g. defaulting to [start_date.replace(day=1)]), that row silently disappears entirely under explode.

drills.q: Give the SQL equivalent of the date-range-to-month-rows expansion, in both a generate_series form and a calendar-table form, and state when you'd prefer each.
drills.a: generate_series form (Postgres/DuckDB): CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(date_trunc('month', start_date), date_trunc('month', end_date), interval '1 month') per contract row — terser, no auxiliary table, but engine-specific. Calendar-table form: JOIN a pre-populated date-dimension table ON cal.month BETWEEN date_trunc('month', start_date) AND date_trunc('month', end_date) — more portable across engines lacking generate_series (e.g. older SQL Server), common in data warehouses that already maintain such a table.

drills.q: Explain why rolling(window=7) can give a misleading answer on a datetime-indexed daily series that has a gap (a missing day), and how to fix it.
drills.a: By default rolling windows by a fixed number of ROWS, not by elapsed calendar time. If there's a gap in the index, 'the last 7 rows' actually spans more than 7 calendar days, silently including data further back in time than a caller expecting a 7-day window would assume. Fix: use a time-based window string, rolling('7D'), which pandas resolves against the actual datetime index rather than row count, correctly handling gaps.

drills.q: A groupby aggregation over 100 million rows is taking over 100 seconds (or exhausting memory) in pandas. Diagnose two likely contributing factors and name the tools you'd consider switching to, with the rough scale threshold that justifies each.
drills.a: Likely factors: pandas executes single-threaded with no query optimizer, and grouping/aggregating with a custom Python callable (rather than a named/vectorised function) forces a per-group Python callback instead of a compiled path. Above roughly 1-5GB or needing multi-core execution, switch to Polars (multi-threaded by default, lazy query optimization) — the same groupby often finishes in well under 30 seconds there. For SQL-shaped aggregation directly over files larger than RAM without a separate warehouse, DuckDB is the better fit.

drills.q: When does converting a string column to category dtype NOT help, and why, especially considering pandas 3.0's new default string dtype?
drills.a: It doesn't help on high-cardinality columns (mostly-unique values like UUIDs or free text) — the codes array approaches the same size as just storing the values directly, plus the overhead of maintaining the category mapping. Pandas 3.0's PyArrow-backed default string dtype is already meaningfully more memory-efficient than the old object dtype, narrowing the gap category used to close, though category still wins decisively for genuinely low-cardinality columns since it avoids storing repeated string content at all.

drills.q: State the LEGB order and identify which scope is searched first vs last.
drills.a: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in, in that order — Local is searched first, Built-in last; lookup stops at the first scope containing the name.

drills.q: A function reads a variable x on line 1 and assigns to x on line 3. Is x treated as local for line 1? Why?
drills.a: Yes. The compiler scans the entire function body for assignments before execution; any assignment anywhere makes the name local for the whole function, including lines textually before the assignment. Line 1 will raise UnboundLocalError at runtime.

drills.q: Predict the output: `funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; print([f() for f in funcs])`. Explain the mechanism, not just the answer.
drills.a: [2, 2, 2]. All three lambdas close over the same cell object for the loop variable i (not a value snapshotted at creation time); after the loop finishes, that shared cell holds 2, and every lambda reads it when called.

drills.q: Give two independent fixes for the late-binding closure trap and explain the mechanism each relies on.
drills.a: 1) lambda i=i: i — default argument values are evaluated once, at function-definition time, immediately capturing the current value instead of deferring to the shared cell. 2) A factory function def make(i): return lambda: i — each call creates a genuinely new local scope (and thus a new cell) for that i.

drills.q: When does `nonlocal x` raise a SyntaxError, and how is that different from what `global x` would do in the same situation?
drills.a: nonlocal x raises SyntaxError at compile time if no enclosing function scope already defines x — it never falls back to global. global x, by contrast, always succeeds, creating a module-level binding if one doesn't already exist.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why `def f(bucket=[]): bucket.append(x); return bucket` returns a growing list across unrelated calls.
drills.a: The default value [] is evaluated exactly once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function object. Every call that doesn't pass its own bucket argument shares that same list object, so appends from unrelated calls accumulate in it.

drills.q: A class body defines `multiplier = 3` then `doubled = [v * multiplier for v in range(5)]`. Does this raise NameError? Explain using scope rules, and contrast with a plain for loop written directly in the class body.
drills.a: Yes, NameError: name 'multiplier' is not defined. A comprehension has its own scope which does not include the enclosing class body (only the outermost for-clause's iterable is evaluated in the class body's scope first). A plain for loop written directly in the class body, by contrast, executes in the class namespace itself and can see multiplier as a bare name.

drills.q: What is func.__closure__ and func.__code__.co_freevars, and how do they explain the shared-mutation behavior of nonlocal?
drills.a: __closure__ is a tuple of cell objects, one per free variable named in co_freevars. Each cell is a mutable box referenced by both the enclosing function's frame and the nested function; nonlocal x; x += 1 mutates that shared cell's contents in place, which is why the enclosing scope sees the change immediately.

drills.q: A loop spawns threads with `threading.Thread(target=lambda: worker(i)).start()` for i in range(5). Describe the failure mode and why it's worse than the single-threaded version of the same bug.
drills.a: All five lambdas close over the same shared cell for i. Because thread scheduling means the main loop typically finishes (and i reaches its final value) before the spawned threads actually invoke their lambdas, most or all threads end up calling worker with the same final value rather than their intended distinct index. It's worse than the single-threaded version because the exact outcome is timing-dependent — it can pass in testing and fail differently under production scheduling.

drills.q: Does Python 3.12's PEP 709 comprehension inlining change whether a comprehension's loop variable leaks into the enclosing scope? What did PEP 709 actually change?
drills.a: No, scoping is unchanged by design — the loop variable still does not leak. PEP 709 is a performance change: comprehensions are inlined into the enclosing frame instead of compiled as a separate nested function call, avoiding the overhead of a full function call and frame creation per comprehension, while preserving the existing scoping semantics.

drills.q: You have 40 confirmed anomaly labels out of 2 million records. Do you train a supervised classifier on them?
drills.a: Generally no -- 40 positive examples is usually too few to train a reliable discriminative classifier, especially if the anomaly type might evolve. Better to use semi-supervised/unsupervised detection methods and use those 40 labels for threshold calibration and evaluation instead of classifier training data.

drills.q: A fraud model reports 99.8% accuracy at a 0.2% true fraud rate. Is this a good result?
drills.a: Not necessarily meaningful at all -- a model that predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction would score 99.8% accuracy while catching zero fraud. Accuracy is useless here; check PR-AUC and precision/recall at the actual operating threshold instead.

drills.q: An IsolationForest model is flagging 30% of all records as anomalies, which the team knows is far too many. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
