drills.a: The contamination parameter is set too high (or left at a default/guess that doesn't match the real anomaly rate), directly shifting the decision threshold. Set contamination from a validated estimate of the true anomaly rate and re-validate periodically.

drills.q: A OneClassSVM model trained with default parameters never flags anything as anomalous. Diagnose.
drills.a: nu is likely left at its default of 0.5, which assumes roughly 50% of training data is contamination -- an assumption wildly wrong for a real anomaly rate under 1-5%. This produces a decision boundary calibrated to the wrong assumption. Set nu near the actual expected anomaly rate.

drills.q: A fraud detection system has 1,000,000 legitimate transactions and 1,000 fraudulent ones. A model has a 1% false positive rate. Compute the absolute number of false alarms and explain why ROC-AUC won't reflect how bad this is.
drills.a: 1% of 1,000,000 = 10,000 false alarms -- 10x the actual fraud count. ROC-AUC's false positive rate is computed relative to the huge true-negative count (999,000), so a 1% FPR barely moves ROC-AUC even though the absolute false-positive volume swamps the true fraud count and makes the alert queue operationally unusable.

drills.q: An autoencoder-based anomaly detector worked well for a month after launch, then false positives suddenly spiked. What's the most likely cause and what should have been in place to prevent it?
drills.a: The underlying 'normal' distribution drifted (seasonality, product change, evolving behavior) and the reconstruction-error threshold, computed once at launch, is now miscalibrated against current normal behavior. A periodic threshold recalibration process against a recent known-clean window should have been in place.

drills.q: A team wants to use a deep autoencoder for fraud detection on a dataset with only 12 tabular features. Push back with the tradeoff.
drills.a: On 12 tabular features, Isolation Forest or LOF will very likely match the autoencoder's detection quality at a fraction of the engineering cost -- no architecture design, training stability concerns, or non-trivial reconstruction-error threshold calibration to solve. 'More complex model' doesn't imply 'more accurate model' on simple, low-dimensional tabular data.

drills.q: Design the end-to-end production pipeline for a manufacturing defect detection system, from raw sensor signal to a final human decision, including the piece most systems skip.
drills.a: Feature/signal pipeline -> scoring model -> raw anomaly score -> threshold tuned against real cost tradeoff (missed defect vs false-alarm inspection cost) -> alert routes to human inspection queue -> inspector confirms/rejects -> that label feeds periodic retraining. The piece most systems skip is the feedback loop from confirmed/rejected labels back into retraining -- without it the model can't adapt as the true defect distribution drifts.

drills.q: Your anomaly detection system has run for 8 months with no retraining and performance is degrading. Feature distributions look stable when compared against the training snapshot. What's your next hypothesis?
drills.a: The anomaly TYPE itself has evolved rather than the baseline normal distribution -- fraud patterns, intrusion techniques, and defect modes often adapt specifically because they're adversarial or upstream processes changed in ways not captured by current features. This points toward needing new features or an expanded label set from recent confirmed cases, not just threshold recalibration.

drills.q: You compare Isolation Forest and an autoencoder on a labeled evaluation set of only 30 confirmed historical anomalies, and the autoencoder shows a slightly higher PR-AUC. Should you deploy the autoencoder?
drills.a: Be cautious -- PR-AUC computed from only 30 positive examples has high variance, and a marginal difference could easily be noise. Bootstrap the comparison or report confidence intervals, and weight the decision toward the simpler, more maintainable model (Isolation Forest) unless the more complex option shows a meaningful, not marginal, improvement.

drills.q: A LOF-based fraud system is missing a fraud pattern the team knows is real: transactions that are extremely large in absolute terms but happen to sit near other large-transaction accounts. Why does LOF miss this, and what fixes it?
drills.a: LOF measures density relative to a point's LOCAL neighborhood -- if the fraudulent large transactions sit near other legitimately large-transaction accounts, they look locally normal even though they're a clear GLOBAL outlier. Combine LOF with a global method (Isolation Forest, z-score/IQR) since no single anomaly definition covers both local and global cases.

drills.q: List the five stages of an ordered EDA process.
drills.a: 1) Grain and shape 2) per-column univariate checks (dtype, missingness, skew, cardinality) 3) relationships between features (Pearson and Spearman) 4) relationship to target (binned means, class balance) 5) leakage and imbalance hunt, done last.

drills.q: A feature has mean=520, median=310 on a transaction-amount column. What does this tell you and what should you check next?
drills.a: Mean > median indicates right skew (a long tail of large transactions). Check scipy.stats.skew() to quantify it, and if |skew| > 1, avoid z-score outlier detection on this column -- use IQR or modified z-score instead.

drills.q: You compute Pearson correlation between a feature and the target and get r=0.05. Is it safe to conclude the feature has no useful relationship to the target?
drills.a: No. Pearson only measures linear relationship strength. A monotonic-but-nonlinear relationship (e.g. y=x^3) or even a strong non-monotonic (U-shaped) relationship can produce a near-zero Pearson r. Check Spearman for monotonic relationships and a binned-mean plot for any shape.

drills.q: Your z-score outlier filter (threshold=3) on a right-skewed latency column flags almost nothing, yet you know from domain knowledge that some requests take absurdly long. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The std is inflated by the distribution's own long tail, so genuinely large values no longer register as '3 std away' because the std baseline is already stretched by other tail values. Switch to IQR-based detection (Q1-1.5*IQR to Q3+1.5*IQR) or modified z-score using median/MAD, both robust to the skew.

drills.q: A feature 'discharge_disposition' includes the category 'transferred to hospice' and correlates at 0.4 with a hospital-readmission target. Is a 0.4 correlation low enough to rule out leakage?
drills.a: No. A moderate correlation doesn't rule out leakage -- a leak can be partial (encoding an intermediate variable or only some of the outcome) and still meaningfully inflate offline metrics without hitting a too-good-to-be-true threshold. The real test is whether this value could exist, in this form, at the moment the prediction needs to be made -- 'transferred to hospice' is recorded at essentially the same event that determines readmission status, which is a leakage red flag regardless of correlation magnitude.

drills.q: Design an EDA check that would catch a feature like days_since_last_payment being null only for accounts in good standing (a classic leakage pattern), beyond a simple correlation check.
drills.a: Group by the feature's missingness (df.groupby(feature.isna())[target].mean()) and check whether the target rate differs sharply between the missing and non-missing groups -- if missingness itself correlates strongly with the target, the feature's EXISTENCE pattern is leaking information, even if a raw correlation on the non-null values looks unremarkable.

drills.q: You have a 99.5%/0.5% imbalanced fraud dataset. List three specific things this changes about your EDA and evaluation plan, beyond 'don't use accuracy'.
drills.a: 1) Stratify train/test/CV splits or a fold can end up with too few positive examples, making its metric noise. 2) Reconsider what 'outlier' detection is even for -- IQR/z-score-flagged points might be the minority class's characteristic signature, not noise. 3) Prefer PR-AUC over even ROC-AUC, since ROC-AUC can also look deceptively good under extreme imbalance.

drills.q: Explain what Anscombe's Quartet demonstrates and derive the practical EDA rule that follows from it.
drills.a: Multiple datasets can share identical mean, variance, and Pearson correlation to several decimal places while looking completely different when plotted (one linear, one with an outlier driving the fit, one a clean curve, one two clusters). Rule: never trust a correlation number or summary statistic as a final verdict -- use it to triage which pairs deserve an actual scatterplot, then look at the plot before concluding anything.

drills.q: You need to EDA a 500-column, 50-million-row dataset but full profiling would take hours. Design a scaled-down approach, and name the risk you're accepting.
drills.a: Sample rows (compute cost scales with rows more than statistical precision does past a threshold), then use a cheap full-column pass (single tree model feature importances or per-column mutual information against target) to shortlist plausible predictors before running expensive O(p^2) pairwise correlation only on the shortlist. Risk accepted: a rare but genuinely important interaction living in a column outside the shortlist could be missed -- mitigate with the cheap full-pass importance step rather than relying purely on domain-knowledge shortlisting.

drills.q: A model trained and validated on a historical snapshot has excellent offline test AUC but degrades in production within weeks. Standard train/test evaluation didn't catch it. What EDA step would have?
drills.a: Comparing feature distributions between the training snapshot and current production data (e.g. via a sweetviz-style comparison report) -- a train/test split from the same historical snapshot can't detect that the world has moved on since collection. This is EDA applied to the pipeline over time, not just the static dataset.

drills.q: Name the three families of feature selection in one line each.
drills.a: Filter: score feature vs target, no model, cheap, misses interactions. Wrapper: use real model performance as the score (RFE), expensive, most accurate. Embedded: selection is a byproduct of training one model (L1, tree importance), cheap and interaction-aware but inherits model bias.

drills.q: Your colleague fits SelectKBest(k=20) on the full dataset, then does train_test_split, then reports a 0.90 CV AUC. What's wrong?
drills.a: Selection leakage -- the top-20 features were partly chosen using label information from rows now in the test set, inflating the reported score. Selection must be inside a Pipeline, refit per CV fold.

drills.q: A random forest's feature_importances_ ranks a 50,000-category zip+4 column as the #1 feature, above a domain-known strong predictor. What do you suspect, and what do you check with instead?
drills.a: Gini/MDI cardinality bias -- more candidate split thresholds on the high-cardinality column produce spuriously good-looking splits (Strobl et al. 2007). Re-check with permutation importance or SHAP on held-out data.

drills.q: You have y = X1 XOR X2 in your data, plus 50 other genuinely irrelevant features. You run a chi2 filter and keep the top 10. What happens to X1 and X2, and why?
drills.a: Both get dropped. Filter methods score each feature marginally against y; X1 and X2 are each individually uncorrelated with y by construction of XOR, so chi2 sees no signal in either, regardless of the joint relationship.

drills.q: Design a permutation-importance check that would catch the failure mode where two highly correlated features both score as 'unimportant' despite the pair mattering.
drills.a: Cluster features by correlation (hierarchical clustering on 1 - |corr|) before running permutation importance, then compare within-cluster importance sums against between-cluster importance, rather than trusting individual per-feature scores -- shuffling one of a correlated pair barely hurts the score since the model still has the redundant other one.

drills.q: You're selecting features via L1 logistic regression and one feature is measured in the thousands (revenue) while others are 0-1 flags. Selection keeps revenue and drops flags that domain knowledge says matter. Diagnose.
drills.a: L1 penalty acts on raw coefficient magnitude, and it wasn't scaled -- revenue's larger raw scale means a smaller coefficient achieves the same predictive contribution, so it's penalized less per unit of value than the properly-scaled flags. Fix: scale all features before L1, since the penalty is scale-dependent.

drills.q: You need to run RFECV on 400 features with a 500-tree gradient boosted model and 5-fold CV, but only have a 2-hour compute budget. What do you change and what do you give up?
drills.a: Increase step from 1 to something like 0.1 (drop 10% of remaining features per round) or switch to embedded selection (native gain importance, CV-validated threshold, trains once). Tradeoff: coarser stepping evaluates and drops features in batches, so a borderline feature might get cut alongside genuinely weak ones -- an explicit accuracy-for-speed tradeoff.

drills.q: Design the feature selection stage of a fraud model with 10,000 candidate features, a 3-week deadline, and a hard requirement that a regulator can audit which features drove decisions. Outline the pipeline.
drills.a: Stage it: filter (variance threshold + mutual information) cuts 10,000 to a few hundred plus manual removal of identifiers/leakage candidates; embedded selection (gradient boosted tree gain importance, CV-validated threshold) cuts to 30-60; SHAP on the final model provides both accuracy insight and audit documentation via its local-accuracy and consistency guarantees. Every step lives inside the CV loop; final feature list is pinned and versioned, not recomputed at serve time.

drills.q: Explain the curse of dimensionality with a concrete number, and state which model families are most vs least affected.
drills.a: Matching the sample density of N points in 1D requires N^d points in d dimensions -- N=100, d=10 needs 10^20 points. Distance/density-based methods (kNN, LOF, kernel SVMs) are hit hardest since they depend on meaningful distances; tree ensembles degrade more gracefully since they partition axis-by-axis.

drills.q: You add 200 new features to a fraud model. Offline AUC improves by 0.03 but the online A/B test shows zero lift. Give your top two hypotheses in order.
drills.a: 1) Training-serving skew in the new features specifically -- offline features often use info not actually available or correctly computed online (stale batch aggregate, or a feature with a downstream-event leak). 2) The 0.03 offline lift itself leaked through feature selection or tuning done on the same data used to report it. Check feature parity between training and serving before doubting the online experiment's power.

drills.q: Why might explicit feature selection provide zero accuracy benefit on a well-tuned XGBoost model with reg_alpha/reg_lambda and min_child_weight set, and could it ever hurt?
drills.a: Regularized gradient boosted trees are already fairly robust to irrelevant features, so selection mainly buys latency and interpretability rather than accuracy. It can actively hurt if it drops a feature that only carries signal in combination with another (an XOR-style interaction), since single-feature importance scores can't see that.

drills.q: A sensor randomly drops readings due to transient hardware noise unrelated to the true value. What missingness mechanism is this, and is drop/mean-impute valid?
drills.a: MCAR. Both dropping rows and mean-imputing are unbiased under MCAR, though still lossy -- you throw away information even if you don't introduce bias.

drills.q: You mean-impute a column with 30% missing values. The imputed column's correlation with the target drops sharply compared to what it was in the observed-only subset. What happened?
drills.a: Mean imputation collapsed variance -- every imputed value is identical, so those rows contribute zero variance and dilute whatever real correlation existed in the observed rows proportionally to the missingness rate.

drills.q: Income is missing far more often for self-employed respondents than salaried ones, and employment_type is fully observed. Which mechanism, and what's the valid fix?
drills.a: MAR -- missingness depends on an observed variable (employment_type), not the missing income value itself. Fix: model-based imputation (KNN or MICE) that conditions on employment_type and other observed columns, not a flat mean.

drills.q: A feature is 0% missing throughout training but starts showing 5% missing values in production three weeks after deploy. The XGBoost model's predictions on those rows look wrong. Diagnose.
drills.a: XGBoost never learned a split direction for that feature's missingness because it never saw a missing value during training, so it falls back to a fixed default direction (documented as right branch) that may be arbitrarily wrong for this feature. Fix: monitor per-feature missingness rate in production and retrain/explicitly impute once a previously-complete feature starts showing nulls.

drills.q: df.describe() on an 'age' column shows a minimum of -999 next to a 25th percentile of 24, with -999 appearing exactly 340 times. Is this an outlier or something else, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: A sentinel value, not a real outlier or missing value -- a real outlier wouldn't repeat the exact same number 340 times. Recode -999 to NaN explicitly, then run it through the normal MCAR/MAR/MNAR diagnosis rather than leaving it as a numeric value that wrecks the mean and any distance-based method.

drills.q: You're building a credit scoring pipeline with both a logistic regression and an XGBoost model. Design the missing-data handling for each.
drills.a: XGBoost: no explicit imputation, rely on native missing-value handling, but monitor per-feature missingness rate so a newly-missing feature doesn't silently hit an unlearned fallback. Logistic regression: fit MICE or KNN imputation on training data only, freeze the fitted imputer, apply identically at serving -- never refit live on serving data. For any column where missingness correlates with an observed field, add a was_missing flag to both models.

drills.q: A regulator asks why you imputed missing income instead of dropping those rows in a credit model. Justify your choice.
drills.a: Dropping is only defensible under MCAR. Income missingness in a credit context is plausibly MAR (correlated with employment type) or MNAR (high earners under-reporting) -- dropping those rows would systematically bias the training population away from exactly the applicants the model needs to score correctly, a fair-lending concern as well as a statistical one.

drills.q: Your train/test split shows an unrealistically small generalization gap. You suspect duplicate rows from a retried ingestion. Why is df.duplicated() insufficient, and what do you check instead?
drills.a: df.duplicated() only catches exact row equality and misses near-duplicates from truncation, floating-point differences, or slightly different timestamps on a re-ingested retry. Check for a true business key (transaction ID or hash of immutable fields) and look for test-set rows that are near-duplicates of training rows by that key.

drills.q: A categorical column has 3x the cardinality domain knowledge suggests it should. What are the two most likely corrupt-data causes, and how do you distinguish them?
drills.a: Encoding mojibake (wrong charset on read, garbling non-ASCII characters into extra fake categories) or silent truncation (a length limit cutting off values, creating near-duplicate prefix categories). Distinguish by checking whether extra categories are byte-garbled versions of real ones (mojibake) or clean prefixes of longer existing categories (truncation).

drills.q: Explain why MNAR data can't be fixed by any imputation method that only uses observed data.
drills.a: By definition, missingness under MNAR depends on the missing value itself (e.g. high earners refusing to report income) -- imputing from observed data alone at best recovers a conditional mean given what you CAN observe, which is a biased estimate of the true missing value precisely because the value's own magnitude drove the missingness. The honest fix is a was_missing flag plus explicit documentation that the feature is unreliable for that subpopulation, not a cleverer imputer.

drills.q: A colleague says 'the p-value was 0.02, so there's a 98% chance our hypothesis is true.' What's wrong with this statement?
drills.a: A p-value is P(data this extreme or more | H0 true), not P(H0 true | data) or P(H1 true | data). Getting from one to the other requires Bayes' theorem and a prior probability on the hypothesis, which the p-value alone doesn't supply.

drills.q: Define Type I and Type II error in one sentence each.
drills.a: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis -- a false positive, controlled by alpha. Type II: failing to reject a false null hypothesis -- a false negative, related to power via power=1-beta.

drills.q: You want to compare mean response time across 4 different server configurations. Which test do you run first, and what does a significant result tell you?
drills.a: One-way ANOVA. A significant result tells you at least one configuration's mean differs from at least one other -- it does not tell you which pair(s) differ. Follow with a post-hoc test (Tukey's HSD) to find which configurations differ.

drills.q: Your experiment report tests 20 different metrics and 2 come back significant at raw p<0.05, uncorrected. How suspicious should you be, numerically?
drills.a: Very. At k=20 independent tests each at alpha=0.05, you'd EXPECT about 20*0.05=1 false positive by chance alone even if every null were true, and the family-wise probability of at least one false positive is 1-0.95^20 ~= 64.2%. Two 'hits' out of 20 uncorrected tests is weak evidence; apply Benjamini-Hochberg or Bonferroni correction before trusting them.

drills.q: An A/B test dashboard shows significance on day 3 of a planned 3-week test, and the team ships immediately. What statistical problem does this illustrate, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Peeking -- checking a running experiment and stopping the moment it looks significant inflates the true Type I error rate far above the nominal alpha, since each check is effectively another implicit test. Fix: commit to a fixed sample size/duration decided by a power analysis beforehand, or use a sequential/always-valid testing method designed to control Type I error under continuous monitoring.

drills.q: An A/B test configured for a 50/50 split shows an actual observed split of 55/45 with a chi-square goodness-of-fit p<0.01. What do you do with the experiment's headline result?
drills.a: Treat the experiment as invalidated, not just flag it as a footnote. This is sample ratio mismatch -- it signals a broken randomization/logging/bot-filtering pipeline, and whatever caused the skewed ratio may also have skewed group composition, confounding the treatment effect estimate regardless of what its own p-value shows.

drills.q: Aggregate A/B results show variant B converting worse than A overall, but B wins within every individual traffic segment (mobile, desktop, new users, returning users). Diagnose and explain the likely cause.
drills.a: Simpson's paradox. The aggregate comparison is confounded by unequal segment allocation between arms -- e.g. treatment happened to receive a disproportionate share of a lower-converting segment -- even though each within-segment comparison is clean. Check segment balance between control and treatment before trusting the aggregate number; report segment-level breakdowns as standard practice.

drills.q: You expect a true effect size of Cohen's d=0.1 (very small) but only collected n=200 per group for your test, which came back non-significant. What should you conclude?
drills.a: Little to nothing about whether the effect exists -- detecting d=0.1 at standard alpha=0.05/power=0.80 requires roughly 1,570 per group, so a sample of 200 is drastically underpowered. 'Not significant' here means 'insufficient data to detect it,' not 'no effect' -- report power alongside the null result rather than treating it as evidence of absence.

drills.q: Design the statistical plan for a checkout-flow A/B test expecting a ~1% relative conversion lift, given the team has a history of peeking and post-hoc metric shopping.
drills.a: Pre-register one primary metric and compute required sample size via power analysis using the expected small effect size and historical variance (likely a large sample given how small the effect is). Use a sequential/always-valid testing framework so the team can monitor without inflating Type I error from peeking. Run an automatic SRM check before surfacing any result. Restrict secondary metrics to a pre-declared list with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; treat anything else discovered post-hoc as a new hypothesis for a follow-up experiment. Report segment-level breakdowns to catch Simpson's-paradox-style confounding.

drills.q: You run a chi-square test of independence on a 2x5 contingency table and several expected cell counts are below 5. What's the problem and the fix?
drills.a: Chi-square's p-value relies on a large-sample approximation to the chi-square distribution that becomes unreliable with sparse tables -- a common rule of thumb requires expected count >= 5 in at least 80% of cells. Use Fisher's exact test instead, which computes exact probabilities without relying on that asymptotic approximation.

drills.q: Derive the sigmoid derivative from sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^-x) and state its maximum value.
drills.a: sigma'(x) = sigma(x)(1-sigma(x)). This is maximized when sigma(x)=0.5, i.e. at x=0, giving 0.5*0.5=0.25. As x moves away from 0 in either direction sigma'(x) decays toward 0.

drills.q: A network has 6 stacked sigmoid hidden layers. What is the theoretical ceiling on the gradient reaching the first layer relative to the last, ignoring weight magnitudes?
drills.a: 0.25^6 ~= 2.44e-4. Each sigmoid layer contributes a factor of at most 0.25 to the backprop chain, so 6 layers compound to roughly 1/4096 of the original gradient magnitude in the best case -- real weights typically make it worse.

drills.q: Why is tanh preferred over sigmoid for RNN hidden states even though both saturate?
drills.a: Tanh is zero-centered (range -1 to 1), avoiding the zigzag gradient descent that sigmoid's always-positive outputs cause in the next layer's weight updates. It doesn't fix vanishing gradients -- it still saturates just as hard -- it only fixes the sign-constraint/zigzag issue.

drills.q: Write a forward hook or logging approach that would let you detect dying ReLU units during training, and describe what a truly dead unit looks like in that log versus a merely quiet one.
drills.a: Hook the layer's output and compute (activations <= 0).all(dim=0) across a full evaluation batch (or several batches) per unit. A dead unit shows exactly 100% zero activation indefinitely across batches; a merely quiet unit's zero-fraction fluctuates across batches instead of staying pinned at 100%.

drills.q: Your deep ReLU CNN shows 35% of units dead after a few epochs at a high learning rate. What are two concrete fixes, and which would you try first?
drills.a: Lower the learning rate (reduces the odds of a large negative weight update pushing a unit's pre-activation permanently negative) and/or switch to Leaky ReLU/PReLU (gives a small nonzero gradient for negative inputs so units can recover). Try the learning-rate fix first since it addresses the likely root cause rather than just patching the symptom with a different activation.

drills.q: Explain why SwiGLU needs roughly 50% more parameters in the FFN block than a ReLU FFN of the same hidden width, and how production implementations compensate.
drills.a: A plain ReLU FFN needs one projection matrix (d -> d_ff); SwiGLU's gating mechanism needs two (W and V, both d -> d_ff) to compute Swish(xW) elementwise-multiplied by (xV). To keep total parameter count roughly matched, implementations shrink d_ff to about 2/3 of the 4d a ReLU FFN would use.

drills.q: A multi-label image tagger uses softmax + categorical cross-entropy. What breaks, and how would you observe it in evaluation metrics?
drills.a: Softmax forces all class probabilities to sum to 1, so the model is mathematically prevented from expressing high confidence in two co-occurring labels simultaneously -- raising one necessarily lowers the others. You'd observe that predicted confidences for genuinely co-occurring label pairs never both exceed roughly 0.5, even though per-tag AUC (a ranking metric) may look fine since it doesn't see joint confidence.

drills.q: Prove that subtracting the max logit before exponentiating in softmax does not change the output.
drills.a: softmax(z)_i = e^z_i / sum_j e^z_j. Substituting z_i - c for any constant c: e^(z_i-c) / sum_j e^(z_j-c) = [e^z_i * e^-c] / [e^-c * sum_j e^z_j] = e^z_i / sum_j e^z_j, since e^-c cancels between numerator and denominator. The result is identical; only numerical stability changes.

drills.q: At what logit magnitude does float32's exp() overflow, and why does that matter for a hand-rolled softmax without max-subtraction?
drills.a: Roughly x~89, since e^89 is near float32's max representable value (~3.4e38). A hand-rolled softmax without max-subtraction will produce inf for any logit above that threshold, and then NaN when computing inf/inf in the normalization step.

drills.q: Derive the gradient of categorical cross-entropy loss with respect to the pre-softmax logits, and explain why frameworks fuse log_softmax with the loss instead of computing them separately.
drills.a: For the true class i: dL/dz_i = softmax(z)_i - 1. For any other class j: dL/dz_j = softmax(z)_j. In vector form this is softmax(z) - onehot(y). Frameworks fuse log_softmax + NLL (or expose cross_entropy on raw logits) because computing softmax then log separately can underflow softmax outputs to exactly 0, producing log(0)=-inf; the fused form computes the log directly without that intermediate.

drills.q: You inherit a 6-layer sigmoid MLP with no batch norm. Training loss decreases steadily but validation accuracy is stuck near random. Walk through your diagnosis and one confirming experiment.
drills.a: Six sigmoid layers with no normalization is a textbook vanishing-gradient setup: gradients reaching early layers are attenuated by up to 0.25^6 before weight magnitudes apply, so early layers barely update while later layers overfit to whatever near-frozen early representations they get. Confirm by logging the L2 norm of the gradient at each layer during a few training steps -- a vanishing-gradient case shows norms shrinking by orders of magnitude from output to input layers; if norms are roughly flat, the bug is elsewhere (data leakage, label noise, wrong loss).

drills.q: Why can't you retrofit SwiGLU onto an already-pretrained ReLU-FFN transformer checkpoint the way you might swap a serving-time optimization like quantization?
drills.a: SwiGLU changes the FFN's structure itself -- it needs a second projection matrix (V) that a ReLU FFN's checkpoint simply doesn't have weights for, and the gating behavior is learned jointly with the rest of the network during pretraining. This is an architecture decision baked in during training, not a drop-in inference-time transform like quantization or KV-cache tricks that operate on an unchanged computational graph.

drills.q: Compute the parameter count of a 3x3 convolution with 128 input channels and 128 output channels, and compare it to what a fully-connected layer would cost mapping a 56x56x128 feature map to another of the same shape.
drills.a: Conv: 3*3*128*128 = 147,456 params, independent of spatial size. FC equivalent: (56*56*128)^2 ~= (401,408)^2 ~= 1.6e11 params -- roughly 6 orders of magnitude more, illustrating why weight sharing makes CNNs tractable on images.

drills.q: Compute the output size of a convolution with input 112, kernel 3, stride 1, padding 1.
drills.a: out = floor((112 + 2*1 - 3)/1) + 1 = floor(111/1) + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112. Same-padding with a 3x3 kernel and stride 1 preserves spatial size exactly, which is why it's the default choice inside residual blocks.

drills.q: Explain the degradation problem in your own words and state why it is NOT the same phenomenon as vanishing gradients in a sigmoid network.
drills.a: Adding depth to a plain (non-residual) CNN made TRAINING error worse, not just validation error, indicating an optimization failure rather than overfitting. It's not vanishing gradients in the classic sense because these networks used ReLU, which doesn't saturate on the positive side -- the actual issue was that stacked nonlinear layers struggled to learn even an identity mapping, which residual connections solve directly by providing that identity path as a default.

drills.q: You're given 50,000 labeled images for a new visual classification task and told to pick a training strategy. Would you train a ViT from scratch? Justify with the ViT paper's own findings.
drills.a: No. The ViT paper shows it underperforms comparable ResNets when trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k (~1.3M images) -- 50K images is far below even that threshold. Use a CNN (ResNet/ConvNeXt) trained from scratch or fine-tuned from ImageNet pretraining, or fine-tune (not train from scratch) a ViT that was already pretrained on a much larger corpus.

drills.q: Walk through why Faster R-CNN is faster than R-CNN, and why YOLO is faster still, in terms of what each architecture changed structurally.
drills.a: R-CNN runs each of ~2000 region proposals through a full CNN forward pass separately. Faster R-CNN shares one backbone feature extraction across the whole image and learns proposals via a Region Proposal Network on top of those shared features, eliminating the redundant per-region forward passes. YOLO removes the two-stage propose-then-classify structure entirely, directly regressing boxes and classes from a single forward pass over a grid -- no separate proposal stage at all.

drills.q: Your detector achieves strong overall mAP but performs poorly on small objects specifically. List two architectural causes and their fixes.
drills.a: Cause 1: repeated downsampling (pooling/strided convs) dilutes fine spatial detail by the time features reach the detection head -- fix with a feature pyramid network for multi-scale detection or higher input resolution. Cause 2 (if using a transformer detector like DETR): global attention dilutes local detail -- fix with a deformable/sparse-attention variant that samples locally instead of attending globally.

drills.q: Explain SAM's two-stage inference design (image encoder vs prompt encoder/mask decoder) and why it's structured that way.
drills.a: The ViT-based image encoder is the expensive part and runs exactly once per image, computing embeddings. The lightweight prompt encoder and mask decoder run per-prompt in milliseconds. This split means a user can click multiple points/boxes on the same image and get near-instant mask updates without re-running the expensive encoder each time -- the design is optimized for interactive use.

drills.q: A fine-tuned model's validation accuracy drops sharply right after you unfreeze all backbone layers and continue training at the same learning rate you used for the head. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting: the learning rate that was appropriate for training just the new head is too high for the pretrained backbone layers, causing large updates that wipe out useful pretrained features within a few steps. Fix: use a much lower LR for fine-tuning the backbone (often 10-100x lower than head-only training), ideally with discriminative per-layer LRs and a warmup period.

drills.q: Design a segmentation strategy for a production pipeline processing 5 million images per day into a fixed set of 12 product categories. Would you use SAM directly? Justify.
drills.a: No, not as the primary model. SAM's value is zero-shot generality and interactive prompting, which isn't needed for a fixed, narrow, high-volume category set. A task-specific fine-tuned model (U-Net or Mask R-CNN trained on the 12 categories) will typically be faster and more accurate at that scale and specificity. SAM (or a SAM-distilled lightweight variant) is better suited to annotation tooling or genuinely open-vocabulary segmentation needs.

drills.q: Explain why batch norm's train-time and eval-time behavior differ, and derive the failure mode that appears when fine-tuning with a batch size of 2 on a memory-constrained GPU.
drills.a: At train time, batch norm computes mean/variance from the current mini-batch; at eval time it uses accumulated running statistics instead, since a single inference example has no batch to normalize against. With batch size 2, the per-batch mean/variance estimates are extremely noisy, and the running statistics take longer to stabilize, producing a mismatch between train-time normalization and eval-time behavior that shows up as validation metrics not tracking training metrics reliably. Fix: increase effective batch size via gradient accumulation, or switch to GroupNorm/LayerNorm which don't depend on batch statistics at all.

drills.q: Derive the receptive field advantage of stacking two 3x3 convolutions versus one 5x5 convolution, including the parameter comparison for 64 input/output channels.
drills.a: Two stacked 3x3 convs (stride 1) reach an effective 5x5 receptive field: the first 3x3 conv's output at a given position depends on a 3x3 input window; the second 3x3 conv applied to that output depends on a 3x3 window of those outputs, which maps back to a 5x5 window of the original input. Parameters: two 3x3x64x64 convs = 2*36,864=73,728 vs one 5x5x64x64 conv = 5*5*64*64=102,400 -- fewer parameters for the same receptive field, plus an extra nonlinearity between the two smaller convs.

drills.q: A DETR-based detector needs 3x the training epochs of a Faster R-CNN baseline to reach comparable mAP, and a stakeholder wants faster iteration. What's your recommendation and why?
drills.a: Switch to a deformable-attention DETR variant (e.g. Deformable DETR), which restricts attention to a small set of learned sampling points near each query's reference location instead of full global attention. This directly addresses DETR's known slow-convergence limitation (a documented consequence of its bipartite-matching + global-attention training dynamics) while keeping the anchor-free, NMS-free framing that made DETR attractive in the first place, and it also tends to improve small-object performance as a side benefit.

drills.q: State the RNN hidden-state update equation and explain why it forces sequential (non-parallel) computation during training.
drills.a: h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + W_xh x_t + b). Computing h_t requires h_{t-1} to already be computed, so step t cannot start until step t-1 finishes -- there is no way to compute all h_t values for a sequence in a single parallel batched operation the way attention can, because each depends on the previous one's output value, not just its existence in the computation graph.

drills.q: A vanilla RNN needs to connect information from position 1 to position 50 in a sequence. How many sequential recurrent steps does that require, and what does this imply about gradient magnitude in the worst case?
drills.a: 49 sequential steps. In the worst case, the gradient connecting those two positions is a product of 49 Jacobians dominated by W_hh and the activation derivative (max 1.0 for tanh, decaying elsewhere) -- if that per-step factor is consistently below 1, the compounded gradient after 49 multiplications can be vanishingly small, which is why vanilla RNNs struggle past roughly 10-20 step dependencies in practice.

drills.q: Derive why the LSTM cell-state update is described as an 'additive' gradient highway, contrasting it explicitly with the vanilla RNN's multiplicative update.
drills.a: Vanilla RNN: h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + ...), so dh_t/dh_{t-1} involves W_hh and tanh'(*) multiplied together at every step -- a genuinely multiplicative chain. LSTM: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * g_t, so dc_t/dc_{t-1} = f_t (plus a smaller term from i_t*g_t's dependence on c_{t-1} through the gates, typically minor). When f_t is learned to be close to 1, this derivative is close to 1 regardless of depth, unlike the RNN case where the effective per-step factor is baked into W_hh and doesn't adapt.

drills.q: Explain what each of the four LSTM components (forget, input, candidate, output) computes and why the candidate uses tanh while the gates use sigmoid.
drills.a: Forget gate f_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of c_{t-1} to keep. Input gate i_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of new info to write. Candidate g_t = tanh(...): the actual new content, needs a signed range (-1,1) so it can add to or subtract from the cell state. Output gate o_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of c_t to expose as h_t. Gates use sigmoid because they represent a 0-1 fraction (how much to let through); the candidate uses tanh because it needs to be able to push the cell state up or down, requiring a signed value.

drills.q: You're choosing between LSTM and GRU for a resource-constrained edge deployment at hidden size 128. Estimate the relative parameter savings of GRU and explain the structural reason.
drills.a: GRU has 3 gate weight sets (update, reset, candidate) versus LSTM's 4 (forget, input, candidate, output), each roughly the same size at a given hidden size, so GRU uses about 3/4 = 75% of LSTM's gate parameters, i.e. roughly 25% fewer. The structural reason: GRU merges LSTM's forget and input gates into one update gate and eliminates the separate cell-state vector, folding long-term memory into the hidden state itself.

drills.q: A transformer's attention score matrix at sequence length n=8,192 with fp16 precision is roughly how large per head, and why does this become the practical bottleneck rather than the O(n^2) FLOP count itself?
drills.a: n^2 * 2 bytes = 8192^2 * 2 ~= 134MB per head. Memory becomes the practical bottleneck before compute because materializing that full matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for every head, every layer, exceeds typical GPU memory budgets well before the FLOP count itself becomes infeasible on modern accelerators -- this is exactly what FlashAttention addresses via tiling, without changing the O(n^2) FLOP count.

drills.q: You need to deploy a keyword-spotting model on a microcontroller with 256KB RAM, processing a continuous, unbounded audio stream. Justify why neither a transformer nor a large 1D CNN is the right architecture, and what is.
drills.a: A transformer's KV cache grows linearly with how much of the stream has been processed, which is incompatible with an unbounded stream and a fixed tiny memory budget -- there's no natural point to cap context without losing detection ability. A large 1D CNN has a fixed receptive field, so while its per-step cost doesn't grow, it also can't accumulate state across the stream beyond that window, and the model itself may not fit the memory budget if using many layers/channels. A small LSTM or GRU is the right choice: its state is a small, constant-size vector updated one frame at a time, independent of how long the stream has been running.

drills.q: Explain the difference between a classical (S4-era) state-space model and Mamba's 'selective' state-space model.
drills.a: Classical SSMs have fixed transition parameters (the discretized linear dynamical system's matrices) regardless of the input content, so they process every position with the same fixed dynamics and can't dynamically decide what to remember or discard. Mamba makes the step size and transition matrices functions of the current input token, letting the model selectively prioritize or deprioritize information based on content -- conceptually similar to LSTM gating, but built on a state-space formulation with a parallel-scan algorithm that keeps training efficient despite the input-dependent recurrence.

drills.q: A colleague claims Mamba has already replaced transformers for large language models as of 2026. How would you correct this, precisely?
drills.a: Overstated. Mamba and other selective state-space models are a real, actively developed direction with strong reported results on specific benchmarks (language, genomics, sequences up to ~1M tokens on some tasks) and a genuine linear-time/constant-memory-per-step advantage over O(n^2) attention. But as of 2026, pure SSMs have not displaced transformers as the default for frontier general-purpose LLMs, and a meaningful share of current research builds hybrids interleaving attention and SSM layers rather than committing to either exclusively -- this is unresolved, not settled.

drills.q: Design the architecture selection reasoning (not just the answer) for a genomics model that needs to process sequences of up to 1 million base pairs to find long-range regulatory interactions.
drills.a: A vanilla or gated RNN would need ~1M sequential steps, making training painfully slow and gradient flow to distant positions unreliable even with LSTM gating at that scale. A standard transformer's O(n^2) attention at n=1,000,000 is computationally infeasible to materialize even with FlashAttention's memory savings, since the FLOP count itself is still quadratic. A 1D CNN has a fixed receptive field that would need enormous dilation/depth to reach 1M-length range and still wouldn't offer content-dependent, dynamic long-range weighting. This is exactly the regime where a selective state-space model (Mamba) is the strongest fit: linear-time, constant-memory-per-step scaling with input-dependent selectivity, and it has reported demonstrated benefits at sequence lengths around 1M tokens on some tasks -- while flagging that this is a less mature, less battle-tested choice than a transformer would be at more moderate lengths.

drills.q: Explain why an LSTM's constant per-step inference cost is actually a meaningfully different cost profile from a transformer's decode-time cost, even ignoring training-time parallelism entirely.
drills.a: An LSTM's per-step decode cost is O(1) regardless of how many tokens have already been generated or seen, because its state is a fixed-size vector. A transformer's per-step decode cost grows with context length: even with a KV cache avoiding recomputation, each new token's attention must still compute scores against every cached previous key, so decode cost per step grows linearly with sequence length so far (and the KV cache's memory footprint also grows linearly), unlike the RNN's genuinely flat cost.

drills.q: Explain in one sentence why BERT can't be used for autoregressive text generation.
drills.a: Bidirectional attention lets every position see the entire sequence including future tokens, so there's no valid next-token-given-only-the-past distribution to sample from.

drills.q: Name BERT's two pretraining objectives and say which one RoBERTa removed.
drills.a: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). RoBERTa removed NSP and matched or beat BERT with more data, longer training, and bigger batches.

drills.q: You have a base BERT checkpoint (not fine-tuned) and need sentence embeddings for semantic search. Which pooling strategy, and why?
drills.a: Mean pooling over all token vectors, masking padding. [CLS] pooling is unreliable here because [CLS]'s only pretraining signal was the weak NSP objective, so it was never optimized to summarize sentence meaning.

drills.q: Define bi-encoder and cross-encoder in terms of what can and cannot be precomputed.
drills.a: Bi-encoder: query and document encoded independently, document vectors precomputed offline, O(1)-ish ANN lookup at query time. Cross-encoder: query+document encoded jointly with attention across both, score depends on both together, cannot be precomputed, costs one full forward pass per candidate.

drills.q: Estimate: a cross-encoder reranker takes ~1ms/pair batched on GPU. Running it over a full 10M-document corpus per query would take roughly how long, and what do you do instead?
drills.a: Roughly 10,000 seconds (~2.8 hours) per query — infeasible. Instead run a cheap first-stage retriever (BM25 or bi-encoder ANN) to narrow to ~100-500 candidates, then cross-encode only that shortlist.

drills.q: A teammate says ColBERT is 'basically a cheap cross-encoder.' Correct them.
drills.a: It isn't — ColBERT never jointly encodes query and document. It precomputes per-token document embeddings independently (like a bi-encoder) and only combines query and document at the final MaxSim scoring step, which is what keeps it precomputable and cheap at index time.

drills.q: Your team wants to use a GPT-4-class LLM to classify support tickets into 5 fixed categories at 2M tickets/day. What do you propose instead, and why?
drills.a: A fine-tuned NER/classification encoder. Five fixed labels is bounded-output classification; at 2M/day the cost and latency gap (encoders run roughly 15-250x faster and 20-200x cheaper at equal-or-better accuracy) becomes a real infrastructure decision, not a rounding error.

drills.q: Why can't you cache a cross-encoder's per-document representation the way you cache a bi-encoder's document vector?
drills.a: Joint attention means the document's internal representations at every layer are shaped by the specific query tokens attending into them during that forward pass — there's no query-independent intermediate state to freeze and reuse across different queries.

drills.q: Retrieval accuracy after adding a cross-encoder reranker is still poor. Before assuming the reranker is broken, what do you check first?
drills.a: First-stage recall@N — whether the retriever's shortlist actually contains the relevant documents at all. A reranker can only reorder what's in the shortlist; if recall is bad upstream, perfect reranking still returns wrong results, and the fix is on the first-stage retriever, not the reranker.

drills.q: Explain why ModernBERT's changes (RoPE, Flash Attention, alternating local/global attention) don't change the fundamental encoder-vs-LLM decision, but do change something else. What?
drills.a: They keep the same bidirectional-encoder-plus-MLM recipe, so they don't change when you'd choose an encoder over an LLM in kind. What they change is the ceiling on what encoders can handle well — longer documents (8192 tokens) and higher throughput — strengthening the case for encoders on tasks that used to be borderline due to context-length limits.

drills.q: A classifier fine-tuned with a head on [CLS] performs worse after someone 'simplifies' the code to use mean pooling instead, without retraining. Why did that break it?
drills.a: The classification head's weights were trained specifically against the [CLS] vector's post-fine-tuning representation. Swapping to mean pooling feeds the head a differently-distributed vector it was never trained on, so the learned decision boundary no longer applies — pooling strategy must match how the model was actually trained, not be chosen independently at inference time.

drills.q: In one sentence, why does freezing early layers and fine-tuning only late layers usually work well for a task close to pretraining?
drills.a: Early layers encode general, broadly reusable features that transfer directly, so only the task-specific late-layer mapping needs to be relearned.

drills.q: Name the two variables that determine where on the adaptation spectrum (frozen -> full fine-tune) you should sit.
drills.a: Dataset size and domain distance from the pretraining distribution.

drills.q: A model fine-tuned to output terse structured JSON starts giving degraded, terse answers on unrelated general chat afterward. Name the failure mode and one fix.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting. Fix: lower the learning rate, freeze more of the base, add rehearsal data, or switch to PEFT so the base weights never change.

drills.q: Why is a hard label a weaker training signal than a teacher's softened probability distribution in distillation?
drills.a: A hard label treats every wrong class as equally wrong. A teacher's distribution encodes real similarity structure between classes (dark knowledge) that a one-hot label discards, and that structure is extra useful signal for the student.

drills.q: Why does the distillation loss multiply the KL term by T^2 instead of using it plain?
drills.a: Softmax with temperature T shrinks gradient magnitude roughly as 1/T^2 as T increases; multiplying by T^2 corrects for that shrinkage so the soft-target term doesn't get numerically drowned out relative to the hard-label CE term.

drills.q: You need to compress a BERT-scale model as aggressively as possible while retaining close to baseline accuracy. TinyBERT beats DistilBERT's ratio — what's the mechanistic reason?
drills.a: TinyBERT uses feature-level distillation (matching intermediate hidden states and attention matrices across a two-stage general-then-task-specific process), giving a much richer per-layer training signal than DistilBERT's response-only (final logits) distillation.

drills.q: Legal flags a plan to generate training data by scraping outputs from a competitor's hosted LLM API to fine-tune your own small model. What's the real risk, concretely?
drills.a: Most frontier providers' terms of service explicitly prohibit using their outputs to train a competing model — this is a live legal issue, not theoretical, matching the substance of OpenAI's dispute with DeepSeek over alleged ToS-violating output extraction for distillation.

drills.q: Your team has 50,000 labeled examples for a new classification task and is debating distillation vs direct fine-tuning of the small target model. Which do you recommend, and why?
drills.a: Direct fine-tuning of the small model. Distillation earns its cost when your own labeled data is too thin to teach the decision boundary well; with 50,000 labeled examples you likely have enough signal already, so skip the teacher-management and licensing overhead.

drills.q: Explain why PEFT is structurally immune to catastrophic forgetting in a way full fine-tuning is not.
drills.a: PEFT freezes the base model's weights entirely and trains only a small set of added parameters (e.g. LoRA's low-rank matrices), so the original weights — and thus the base capabilities they encode — never change. The adapter can even be removed to recover exact original behavior.

drills.q: You only have API access to a frontier teacher model (no logprobs). How does your distillation approach change, and what do you lose?
drills.a: You do sequence-level distillation: generate (input, teacher-output) text pairs and supervised-fine-tune the student directly on the generated text as the target. You lose the dark-knowledge benefit, since you never see the teacher's full probability distribution over alternative tokens, only its chosen output.

drills.q: A small internal tool serving 50 requests/day is considering distilling a large fine-tuned model into a smaller one for cost savings. Is this worth it?
drills.a: Usually not. At that volume the inference-cost savings are negligible relative to the engineering cost of building and validating a distillation pipeline — ship the large model and revisit only if traffic grows enough to change the cost-benefit calculation.

drills.q: In one sentence, what's the key difference between stemming and lemmatization?
drills.a: Stemming chops affixes by fixed rule with no dictionary and can produce non-words; lemmatization maps to a real dictionary base form using part-of-speech and is slower.

drills.q: Why does 'saw' not stem toward 'see' even though they're the same verb?
drills.a: Stemming works by chopping shared surface affix patterns; 'saw' and 'see' share no common substring for a rule to exploit. Only a lemmatizer with dictionary/POS knowledge can resolve irregular forms like this.

drills.q: A search for the phrase 'The Who' returns results about the interrogative word 'who' instead of the band. What preprocessing step likely caused this, and why?
drills.a: Stopword removal stripped 'the' from the query, changing 'The Who' into just 'Who' — an entirely different, more common query with different correct results.

drills.q: Derive why a term appearing in every document of a corpus contributes zero to a TF-IDF score.
drills.a: IDF(t) = log(N/df(t)). If the term appears in every document, df(t) = N, so IDF = log(1) = 0, and TF-IDF = TF * 0 = 0 regardless of term frequency.

drills.q: BM25 with b=0 behaves differently than with b=0.75. Explain the difference and which is likely misconfigured.
drills.a: b controls length normalization; b=0 disables it entirely, so long documents score higher purely by having more chances to contain query terms, regardless of relevance. b=0.75 is the standard default balancing saturation against over-penalizing legitimately long documents. b=0 in a general-purpose search system is usually a misconfiguration.

drills.q: A colleague proposes stemming all documents before feeding them to a BGE embedding model to 'normalize' the text. What's wrong with this plan?
drills.a: The embedding model was trained on natural, unstemmed text; feeding it stemmed non-words (e.g. 'univers' instead of 'universal') produces token sequences it never saw in training, degrading embedding quality silently since it still returns a vector, just a worse one.

drills.q: Two documents contain visually identical text but one uses NFC-normalized Unicode and the other NFD. A user's query matches one but not the other. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: NFC vs NFD represent the same visual character with different byte sequences (precomposed codepoint vs base character + combining mark), so exact-match/hashing treats them as different strings. Fix: normalize all text to NFC (or NFKC) at ingestion, applied consistently to both the query and document indexing paths.

drills.q: Your product serves 22 locales and relies on a stem-then-BM25 pipeline for lexical search. What's the specific production risk, and what's the mitigation?
drills.a: Stemmers exist as high-quality resources for only a few dozen languages; many locales have no maintained stemmer at all, so retrieval quality is silently uneven across languages until a locale-specific bug surfaces. Mitigation: push morphological normalization onto the dense embedding leg (which learns cross-lingual structure from data) and restrict BM25's job to exact-token matching rather than linguistically correct stemming in every locale.

drills.q: A SKU code like 'iOS17-PRO' gets mangled by a stemmer before indexing and users can no longer find it by exact search. What's the fix?
drills.a: Exclude exact identifiers (SKUs, version strings, error codes) from stemming entirely — stemming rules apply uniformly by surface pattern with no awareness of identifier semantics, so the lexical leg needs an identifier-detection step (or simply skip stemming for the BM25 leg) to preserve exact matches for this class of term.

drills.q: Ingested documents from a legacy CMS show up in your search index with garbled characters like 'Ã©' instead of 'é'. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: This is mojibake — text decoded with the wrong character encoding upstream. It degrades both the lexical index (garbage terms matching nothing) and embeddings (vectors for noise). Fix by enforcing UTF-8 end-to-end and correcting the decode step at ingestion; downstream patching is unreliable since the original bytes may already be unrecoverable.

drills.q: When is a full classical preprocessing pipeline (stem, stopword removal, lowercase) still the right choice in production?
drills.a: For a pure BM25/lexical-only system with no dense embedding leg — log search, code search, structured lookup — where exact-term matching dominates, a mature stemmer exists for the languages involved, and the latency/cost budget can't support an embedding model.

drills.q: In one sentence, what do few-shot examples mostly teach a model that already has task competence?
drills.a: Output format and label space, more than the underlying task capability.

drills.q: Name the caveat in Wei et al.'s original chain-of-thought finding that most casual summaries drop.
drills.a: The benefit is emergent with model scale/capability — below a certain threshold, CoT prompting shows flat or negative effects rather than universal improvement.

drills.q: You add 15 few-shot examples to a sentiment classification prompt and accuracy doesn't improve past what 5 examples gave you. What's happening?
drills.a: Returns plateau after roughly 4-5 examples for standard classification tasks; additional examples compete for context budget and can introduce noise or conflicting patterns rather than continued lift.

drills.q: A fixed few-shot prompt ends on an unusual edge-case example and the model starts producing edge-case-like outputs even for typical inputs. Diagnose.
drills.a: Recency bias — the last example in the prompt has disproportionate influence on the model's output. Fix by ensuring the most representative, highest-quality example is placed last, not an outlier.

drills.q: You append 'think step by step' to prompts sent to DeepSeek-R1 and measure a small accuracy regression versus not adding it. Explain why this is plausible.
drills.a: R1 is trained via RL to already produce extended internal reasoning before answering — that's an architectural, trained behavior. An explicit external CoT instruction can impose a reasoning structure that conflicts with the model's own trained process, which is consistent with reports of CoT prompting hurting reasoning-native models.

drills.q: Derive, at a high level, why self-consistency's majority vote improves accuracy over a single CoT pass.
drills.a: Reasoning errors tend to be idiosyncratic to a specific flawed path (uncorrelated across samples), while correct answers tend to be reachable through multiple different valid paths that converge on the same result — so majority vote across N independent samples statistically favors the correct answer as N grows, given each path is better than chance.

drills.q: Your team applies self-consistency with N=40 to every single production request. What's wrong with this, and what's the fix?
drills.a: It multiplies token cost and latency by 40x uniformly, even though gains plateau and can decline on easy problems the model already solves correctly. Fix: gate self-consistency behind a confidence signal (e.g. low agreement in a cheap initial small sample) and apply it only to genuinely hard requests.

drills.q: A prompt tweak shows a 3-point accuracy improvement on a 12-example manual spot check. Should you ship it?
drills.a: Not on that evidence alone — a 12-example check has essentially no statistical power to distinguish a real 3-point improvement from noise. Build or use an eval set sized to detect the effect you care about before concluding the change helped.

drills.q: A RAG system gives wrong answers even after extensive prompt-wording iteration. What should you check before iterating on the prompt further?
drills.a: Retrieval and context quality first — no prompt wording fixes a model reasoning correctly over irrelevant or missing retrieved context. Also verify the eval set has enough examples and validity to detect real improvement at all.

drills.q: When would least-to-most prompting outperform standard chain-of-thought?
drills.a: When the problem has genuine compositional structure (e.g. a multi-hop question decomposable into an ordered sequence of simpler subproblems) that a single continuous CoT trace tends to skip or conflate steps on. Least-to-most explicitly solves each subproblem in order and feeds answers forward.

drills.q: A teammate cites a blog post claiming that promising the model a tip improves accuracy, and wants to ship it to production. How do you respond?
drills.a: Ask for controlled evidence, and if none exists, test it against your own eval set before shipping — most such 'magic phrase' folklore does not survive measurement against a real benchmark and tends to circulate from uncontrolled single anecdotes.

drills.q: Someone says 'we deployed it on SageMaker.' What's your immediate follow-up question and why does it matter?
drills.a: Which inference product specifically — Real-Time Endpoint, Serverless, Async, or Batch Transform. Each has a completely different cost model and latency profile, so the answer changes the entire cost/latency conversation.

drills.q: A workload has bursty, unpredictable traffic averaging 50 requests/hour. Real-Time Endpoint or Serverless Inference?
drills.a: Serverless Inference — it scales to zero and bills per invocation, avoiding paying for an always-on instance serving mostly idle time; accept the 1-5s cold start tradeoff for infrequent bursts.

drills.q: Explain in one sentence why Bedrock and self-hosting have structurally different cost curves as volume grows.
drills.a: Bedrock's cost is linear in tokens processed (pay only for usage), while self-hosting's cost is a step function in provisioned instance-hours (pay for capacity whether it's used or idle), so self-hosting's effective per-token cost falls as utilization rises toward the linear Bedrock rate and below it.

drills.q: Design the serving path for a workload doing 500K requests/day with steady, predictable traffic and a loose 2-second internal SLA. Justify the choice.
drills.a: Self-hosted vLLM on EC2/EKS sized to steady-state throughput with modest autoscaling headroom — 500K req/day steady traffic is well above typical self-hosting crossover estimates, and the loose SLA is easily met, so unit economics favor self-hosting over Bedrock on-demand at this volume.

drills.q: Your team's Bedrock bill tripled with no increase in request volume. Walk through your diagnosis in order.
drills.a: 1) Check token counts per request per prompt-template version first — a context-length regression is the most common invisible cause. 2) Check for a fallback path silently routing to a pricier model tier. 3) Check for unintended Priority-tier usage. 4) Check for an unpinned model alias resolving to a different-priced model version.

drills.q: A compliance team says 'no third-party process may touch our data, even within our own cloud account.' Does Bedrock or SageMaker satisfy this?
drills.a: Neither, under that literal wording — both are AWS-operated managed services running within the customer's account boundary, but AWS's compute is still the entity processing the data. Only genuinely self-hosted infrastructure the organization directly controls end-to-end satisfies that specific requirement.

drills.q: Your team signed a 6-month Bedrock Provisioned Throughput commitment and traffic has since grown 3x, hitting the reserved capacity ceiling. What are your options?
drills.a: Purchase additional model units (a new/expanded commitment), or overflow excess traffic to on-demand as a burst valve. Provisioned throughput isn't automatically elastic, so an overflow path should be designed in from the start rather than assumed.

drills.q: A team wants to self-host for cost reasons but the task requires frontier-model reasoning quality that no open-weight model currently matches. How do you respond?
drills.a: The cost arithmetic is moot if no self-hostable model meets the quality bar — recommend staying on the hosted API and revisiting self-hosting once open-weight model quality closes the gap, rather than degrading product quality to chase infrastructure savings.

drills.q: Leadership asks for a cost comparison between Bedrock and self-hosting, but only gives you total monthly spend, not usage data. What do you ask for before running any numbers?
drills.a: Requests/day, average input/output token length distribution, and traffic steadiness (peak-to-average ratio) — the crossover point depends heavily on all three, and total spend alone can't distinguish a high-volume-cheap-token workload from a low-volume-expensive-token one.

drills.q: A team already runs EKS comfortably for other services and needs a fine-tuned open-weight model not on Bedrock. Do you recommend SageMaker or plain self-hosted EKS, and why?
drills.a: Plain self-hosted EKS — since the team already has mature Kubernetes tooling and on-call practices, SageMaker's abstraction adds AWS-specific configuration surface without adding capability they don't already have, and avoids introducing a second, SageMaker-specific operational paradigm alongside the existing stack.

drills.q: Present the case for migrating an existing Bedrock product to self-hosted, addressing both cost and risk, in a form a non-technical leader could act on.
drills.a: State the scale-relative-to-crossover finding plainly (e.g. 'we're at Nx the estimated crossover volume, self-hosting likely saves $Y/month net of ops cost'), and name the migration risk explicitly if models differ (re-validating quality against an open-weight alternative is a real evaluation project, estimated at Z weeks) rather than hedging with 'it depends' and no conclusion.

drills.q: Name the three types of distributional shift and state which one necessarily degrades accuracy.
drills.a: Covariate shift (P(X) changes), prior/label shift (P(Y) changes), concept drift (P(Y|X) changes). Only concept drift necessarily degrades accuracy.

drills.q: A feature's PSI comes out to 0.31. What's your read and next step?
drills.a: Above the 0.25 action threshold — investigate. Check whether it correlates with a known event, and check a multivariate/performance signal before deciding to retrain; PSI alone doesn't tell you whether this is concept drift or benign covariate shift.

drills.q: Why would a KS test alert on nearly every window once daily traffic exceeds a few hundred thousand samples?
drills.a: Statistical power scales with sample size; at that scale, even a trivial real difference between two samples produces a near-zero p-value under the null hypothesis of identical distributions.

drills.q: Every univariate PSI/KS check on a feature set passes, but the model is degrading. What technique would you add, and how does it work?
drills.a: A domain classifier: train a model to distinguish reference-window rows from current-window rows using all features jointly. AUC significantly above 0.5 reveals multivariate drift (a changed joint relationship) that no univariate test can see.

drills.q: Your drift monitor uses a rolling 7-day reference window and has never fired despite two years of known gradual model staleness. Explain why, and fix it.
drills.a: A rolling reference absorbs slow drift into its own baseline — each week looks only mildly different from the week before, hiding large cumulative drift. Fix: keep a frozen training-time reference for long-horizon detection alongside the rolling window.

drills.q: Design a retraining trigger policy for a system with a 45-day label lag, avoiding the failure mode of retraining on statistical noise.
drills.a: Use a scheduled floor cadence, gated by a cheap threshold check to skip unnecessary scheduled retrains during quiet periods, escalated to an out-of-cycle retrain only when drift is corroborated by a fast proxy signal (since true labels are too slow) — not on drift alone.

drills.q: Compare PSI and Wasserstein distance on a feature that shifts from bucket [0,10] to [10,20] versus one that shifts to [90,100], with equal proportion of mass moved in both cases.
drills.a: PSI (and KL/JS) report identical drift magnitude in both cases since they only track proportions per bucket. Wasserstein correctly reports the second shift as far more severe because it accounts for how far the actual values moved, not just the proportion.

drills.q: A fixed holdout set shows flat accuracy for months while PSI on three input features climbs steadily. Is this a problem, and what's the one condition that would make it one?
drills.a: Likely covariate shift without concept drift — not an emergency by itself. It becomes a real problem if the fixed holdout itself is stale and no longer represents the current input population, meaning 'flat accuracy on holdout' is measuring the wrong thing.

drills.q: Your retraining pipeline's compute cost rose 30% and leadership asks whether it's worth it. Using this module's concepts, how do you audit it?
drills.a: Check retroactively whether each historical retrain was preceded by drift alone or by drift plus a performance signal. The fraction triggered by drift alone with no subsequent accuracy improvement in the new model is a defensible estimate of wasted spend, pointing to adding a performance-corroboration gate.

drills.q: How do you distinguish gradual drift from a slow seasonal cycle when you only have three months of monitoring history?
drills.a: You often can't reliably from three months alone — you need history spanning at least a full seasonal cycle before concluding 'gradual trend' rather than 'recurring seasonal pattern'; short monitoring windows commonly misdiagnose seasonality as drift.

drills.q: Explain what CBPE-style performance estimation without labels actually computes, and name its key limitation.
drills.a: It estimates accuracy/AUC from the model's own confidence outputs plus observed drift, calibrated against the labeled training/validation distribution. Limitation: it's an estimate that itself degrades under severe or novel drift — exactly the situations where you'd most want to trust it — so it needs periodic validation against real labels once they arrive.

drills.q: Name what transformers, datasets, and accelerate each own in the HF stack.
drills.a: transformers: uniform model/tokenizer interface. datasets: Arrow-backed memory-mapped/streamable data loading. accelerate: topology-agnostic training launch and mixed precision, used internally even in single-GPU trl training.

drills.q: You download a .bin checkpoint from an unfamiliar Hub repo. What's the risk and what should you do instead?
drills.a: Pickle-based .bin can execute arbitrary code on load via __reduce__. Prefer a safetensors version of the same model if available, and never load an untrusted pickle checkpoint.

drills.q: A colleague proposes deploying a new production LLM service on TGI in 2026. What do you tell them?
drills.a: TGI entered maintenance mode in December 2025; HF itself recommends vLLM or SGLang for new production serving. Building new infrastructure on a maintenance-mode dependency accumulates avoidable migration risk.

drills.q: Compute the trainable-parameter reduction from LoRA on a 4096x4096 weight matrix with rank r=16.
drills.a: Full: 4096×4096 ≈ 16.8M params. LoRA: r(d+k) = 16×(4096+4096) = 131,072 params — roughly 128x fewer trainable parameters for that matrix.

drills.q: You need to fine-tune a 70B model on a single 80GB GPU. What combination of techniques makes this feasible, and why?
drills.a: QLoRA: load the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 quantization (with double quantization) to shrink its memory footprint roughly 4x, then train LoRA adapters in bf16 on top — full-precision fine-tuning of the whole model would require multiple 80GB GPUs.

drills.q: Your model's production behavior changes overnight with no deploy on your team's side, loaded via from_pretrained without a revision argument. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Loading from an unpinned 'main' branch means the repo owner's latest push is what gets loaded on the next cold start/cache miss. Fix: pin an explicit commit hash via revision="<hash>" in every production from_pretrained call.

drills.q: A data pipeline using datasets in streaming mode can't reproduce a proper global shuffle across epochs. Why, and what are the options?
drills.a: Streaming mode has no random access, only iteration with buffer-based approximate shuffling. Options: accept approximate shuffling with a large buffer, pre-shard and shuffle shard order per epoch, or switch to non-streaming (memory-mapped) mode if local disk can hold the data.

drills.q: A CTO wants to rewrite an existing working LangChain-based product entirely off LangChain after reading a blog post. How do you respond?
drills.a: Audit what's actually being used first — LangGraph-based durable agent state is a different, often still-justified case from simple LCEL chains that could be a few lines of plain Python. A full rewrite trades a real, bounded rewrite/regression risk for a benefit that may only apply to part of the codebase.

drills.q: Explain why nobody actually swapping vector databases in production undermines one common argument for using LangChain's retriever wrapper layer.
drills.a: The wrapper's main pitch is portability across vector stores, but since teams rarely swap vector DBs once committed, the portability benefit is rarely exercised while the abstraction still costs a layer of indirection over the native client's fuller control (custom filtering, hybrid search tuning).

drills.q: You need to post-train a model on a task with a cheap, automatically verifiable correctness check (e.g. unit tests passing). Would you reach for DPO or GRPO, and why?
drills.a: GRPO — it exploits verifiable reward signals directly via group-relative advantage estimation from sampled completions, whereas DPO requires collecting preference pairs, which is unnecessary overhead when a cheap verifier already exists.

drills.q: Training loss looks good but held-out eval is worse than the base model after a LoRA fine-tune. What are your first two hypotheses?
drills.a: 1) Catastrophic forgetting from too-aggressive a learning rate or too many epochs on a narrow dataset relative to LoRA rank. 2) The adapter isn't actually being loaded at eval time (get_peft_model wrapping omitted), silently evaluating the frozen base instead.

drills.q: Name the four layers of ML monitoring in order and what each catches.
drills.a: Infra (system falling over) → Data (input no longer matching training assumptions) → Model (model behaving differently before labels exist) → Business (the metric that actually pays, slowest to move).

drills.q: A classifier's accuracy dashboard has been flat for two weeks. Does that mean the model is healthy?
drills.a: Not necessarily — if labels lag two weeks, the accuracy dashboard hasn't seen any post-incident data yet. Check layer-3 (prediction distribution, confidence) for a real-time read instead.

drills.q: Why is average latency a worse metric to alert on than p99 latency?
drills.a: Average hides the tail; a small fraction of very slow requests (which is usually what causes user complaints and cascading failures) can be invisible in an average while dominating p99.

drills.q: Design an alert for prediction-mean drift that won't page on routine weekly seasonality. What's the key change from a static threshold?
drills.a: Compare against a seasonality-aware baseline (same hour/day-of-week last week) and alert on rate-of-change rather than an absolute value; require correlation with a second signal (e.g. a data-layer anomaly) before paging.

drills.q: Walk through the silently-truncated-feature failure mode end to end: what breaks, what stays green, and what catches it.
drills.a: An upstream pipeline truncates a feature; prediction mean steps at the deploy time; null rate stays 0% because the field is populated, just shorter; infra metrics stay flat; accuracy stays flat because labels lag. Only prediction-distribution (layer 3) monitoring, correlated with deploy timestamps, catches it before the label-lag window closes.
