drills.q: Your LLM system's monthly cost triples with flat request volume. What do you check first and why?
drills.a: Token counts per request per prompt-template version first — a context-length regression is invisible in latency and error rate but shows up immediately in token counts, and is a far more common cause than a pricing change.

drills.q: Design the logging/sampling strategy for a consumer LLM product doing 5M requests/day, being mindful of both cost and PII exposure.
drills.a: Log 100% of structured metadata (ids, latency, token counts, confidence, model/prompt version) cheaply. Sample 1-10% of full prompt/completion text, oversampling errors and low-confidence/flagged outputs. Redact PII before storage or restrict raw text to a separate, tightly access-controlled store with a short retention window.

drills.q: A fraud model's labels (chargebacks) take 60-90 days. Design real-time monitoring that doesn't rely on those labels.
drills.a: Layer 3 (prediction score distribution, confidence, feature-importance shift) carries the real-time burden. Add a faster proxy label (manual review disagreement, customer-reported disputes) to get a partial ground-truth stream well before the 60-90 day window closes.

drills.q: A model's refusal rate jumps 15% overnight with no deploy on your team's side. Diagnose and prevent recurrence.
drills.a: Check whether the model is pointed at a rolling alias on a managed provider — the provider likely updated safety tuning. Prevent recurrence by pinning an explicit model version and treating refusal rate as a first-class monitored metric with its own alert.

drills.q: How would you measure whether your team's monitoring dashboards are actually being used, and what would you do with a dashboard that scores zero?
drills.a: Track dashboard view events correlated with incident timestamps and general usage over time. A dashboard with zero views outside the week it was built is a signal to delete it or fold its key panel into an existing, actually-used dashboard rather than adding more panels to something nobody opens.

drills.q: Your team wants judge-score monitoring added to all 40 of your production prompt templates. As the reviewing engineer, do you approve it as-is?
drills.a: No — prioritize by request volume and business criticality per template first. Judge calls have real per-call cost; uniformly instrumenting a low-traffic internal tool at the same rigor as a customer-facing flow is misallocated spend.

drills.q: Name the two libraries FastAPI is built on and state one thing each contributes.
drills.a: Starlette: ASGI web layer (routing, middleware, WebSockets, BackgroundTasks). Pydantic: validation, serialization, settings management.

drills.q: A validation failure returns what HTTP status code by default in FastAPI, and what's the class raised internally?
drills.a: 422 Unprocessable Entity, raised as RequestValidationError.

drills.q: True or false: `response_model` only affects what's shown in the OpenAPI docs, not the actual response body.
drills.a: False. It actively filters the return value at runtime before serialization -- fields not on the schema are dropped from the real response, not just hidden from docs.

drills.q: An endpoint declares two dependencies that both call `Depends(get_db)`. How many times does get_db actually execute for one request, and why?
drills.a: Once. FastAPI caches a dependency's result per request, keyed by the callable, so both call sites share the same session/connection unless use_cache=False overrides it.

drills.q: For a dependency chain A -> B -> C (C depends on B depends on A), write the setup order and the teardown order, and explain why teardown is reversed.
drills.a: Setup: A, B, C. Teardown: C, B, A (LIFO, via AsyncExitStack). Reversed because B's cleanup code might still need A to be alive; tearing down in setup order would risk using an already-closed resource.

drills.q: Explain the specific mechanism (not just the word 'testable') by which FastAPI avoids needing import-path mocking in tests.
drills.a: Every external dependency is expressed as a Depends() callable rather than a module-level import. app.dependency_overrides is a dict keyed by that callable; setting it to a fake swaps the real dependency for the test's version for the override's lifetime, with TestClient exercising the real request/response cycle against the fake.

drills.q: A team complains their clients expect 400 for bad input but get 422. What's the one-line fix, and why does 422 happen in the first place?
drills.a: Register `@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)` and remap to 400 in the handler. 422 is FastAPI's default for requests that parse fine but fail Pydantic schema/semantic validation, distinct from 400's reservation for structurally malformed requests.

drills.q: Diagnose: a FastAPI service's throughput collapses as concurrency rises, but every dashboard shows CPU sitting idle. What's the most likely cause and why does CPU stay low?
drills.a: A blocking synchronous call (sync HTTP client, blocking DB driver, time.sleep) inside an async def handler. It stalls the single event loop entirely, so every other coroutine queues behind it -- CPU is idle because the process is blocked on I/O, not computing.

drills.q: Why is it wrong to use BackgroundTasks for sending a payment confirmation that triggers a refund workflow? Name the specific failure and its observable symptom.
drills.a: BackgroundTasks runs in-process with no broker or persistence; a SIGTERM during a rolling deploy or autoscale event drops the in-flight task silently. Symptom: a support ticket ('I was charged but got no confirmation') with zero trace in any log, since the process that would have logged the failure is already gone.

drills.q: Write the global exception handler pattern that avoids leaking internal exception text, and explain what the error_id buys you.
drills.a: @app.exception_handler(Exception) that logs the full exception server-side with a generated uuid and returns {"detail": "internal server error", "error_id": id} with no traceback or exc text. The error_id is a correlation key: a user can report it, and you grep structured logs for it to find the real exception without ever exposing internals to the client.

drills.q: Explain why `extra="forbid"` isn't the Pydantic/FastAPI default, and name one real cost of applying it globally across a public API.
drills.a: Default is extra="ignore" because most APIs want forward compatibility -- tolerating extra fields from newer clients without breaking. Applying "forbid" globally on a versioned public API with independently-deployed clients breaks rolling deploys where a newer client sends a field an older server never declared, since that request now 422s instead of degrading gracefully.

drills.q: A `def` (sync) endpoint's threadpool is saturated by legitimately slow synchronous work. Does this affect requests hitting unrelated `async def` endpoints on the same process? Why or why not.
drills.a: No, not directly -- the threadpool (default cap ~40 threads) is separate from the event loop that async def endpoints run on. Sync endpoints queue waiting for a free thread, but the event loop keeps serving async endpoints normally, unless something else (a blocking call inside an async def, or the sync work somehow touching a shared resource) couples the two.

drills.q: Name the query language for RDF, for Neo4j's property graph, and for TinkerPop-compliant engines.
drills.a: RDF -> SPARQL. Neo4j -> Cypher. TinkerPop (e.g. Neptune, JanusGraph) -> Gremlin.

drills.q: True or false: Amazon Neptune can be self-hosted on-premise.
drills.a: False. Neptune is fully managed only, with no self-hosted option, unlike Neo4j and ArangoDB.

drills.q: What does index-free adjacency claim, and in one sentence, why does a relational JOIN not get the same guarantee?
drills.a: A single-hop traversal is O(1) because each node stores a direct pointer to its adjacent relationships. A relational JOIN's cost scales with the size of the tables being joined and compounds with every additional hop, since each hop is a fresh index lookup, not a stored pointer.

drills.q: A team wants a graph database because 'we have relationships between entities.' What's the first question you'd ask, and why?
drills.a: What's the actual traversal depth and fan-out of the real query pattern? Most 'we need a graph' requirements are shallow and fixed-depth, which a recursive CTE on the existing relational schema handles with no new infrastructure -- the graph model only earns its cost when traversal depth is unpredictable/unbounded and is the primary access pattern.

drills.q: Explain why a 'Country: USA' node connected to every US user is a production problem for a Neo4j-style graph, using the specific mechanism.
drills.a: It's a supernode: traversing from it fans out to millions of relationships, breaking the O(1)-per-hop assumption of index-free adjacency in practice, because even a pointer-walk over millions of edges from one node has real cost. Fix by remodelling (bucket by region) rather than modelling shared attributes as edges to one universal node.

drills.q: Compare Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, and ArangoDB on one axis each: traversal depth, AWS integration, and data-model breadth.
drills.a: Neo4j: deepest traversal-specific optimization and graph-algorithm tooling (GDS). Neptune: deepest native AWS integration (S3, IAM, CloudWatch, SageMaker), fully managed only. ArangoDB: broadest data-model breadth -- document + graph + search + vector in one engine via AQL, at the cost of specialist graph depth.

drills.q: Why does entity resolution stall real knowledge-graph projects more often than entity extraction does?
drills.a: LLMs made extraction cheap, but resolution -- deciding whether 'Bob Smith', 'R. Smith', and an email address are the same entity -- has no clean automated solution and is chronically scoped as a one-time cleanup step, when it's actually an ongoing pipeline stage that reopens with every new data source added.

drills.q: What does GraphRAG add over vector-only RAG, mechanically, and roughly what does full Microsoft-style indexing cost per million tokens?
drills.a: It extracts entities/relationships into a graph, clusters them into communities (Leiden algorithm), and pre-summarizes each community with an LLM, enabling global/cross-corpus questions no single chunk answers. Roughly $20-40 per million tokens of source corpus, a one-time indexing cost.

drills.q: A corpus's query logs show 95% single-document lookups and 5% cross-document synthesis questions. Do you build full GraphRAG? Justify with the cost tradeoff.
drills.a: Generally no -- hybrid search plus reranking already serves the 95% cheaply and well; paying $20-40/million tokens to index the entire corpus to serve a 5% minority is usually the wrong sizing decision unless that 5% carries disproportionate business value, in which case a scoped/lighter (LightRAG-style, ~$0.50/M tokens) approach targeted at just that slice is worth evaluating first.

drills.q: Write the recursive CTE (in words, not full SQL syntax required) that would replace a 'find everyone within 3 hops' graph query on a `follows(follower_id, followee_id)` table, and state the depth guard.
drills.a: A WITH RECURSIVE CTE: base case selects direct followees of the starting user at depth 1; recursive case joins the follows table against the CTE's prior result to find followees-of-followees, incrementing depth; a WHERE depth < 3 guard stops the recursion at 3 hops; final SELECT DISTINCT dedupes users reached via multiple paths.

drills.q: Two ingestion pipelines create the same real-world entity as two different nodes at the same moment. What's the root cause and the fix?
drills.a: A race in upsert-by-external-key logic with no database-level constraint enforcing uniqueness on that key. Fix: a unique constraint on the external key so the second concurrent create fails or merges instead of silently duplicating, plus a periodic reconciliation job to catch near-duplicates entity resolution missed.

drills.q: Why would you explicitly choose ArangoDB over a specialist graph engine for a given workload, and name the one scenario where that choice would be wrong.
drills.a: Choose ArangoDB when the workload is genuinely mixed (documents plus moderate graph traversal), to consolidate three separate systems (document store, graph DB, search engine) into one operational surface with one consistency model. Wrong when the workload is graph-first and graph-heavy -- deep algorithmic traversal, community detection, or centrality analysis at billions of edges -- where a specialist's years of traversal-specific query-planner optimization outperforms a generalist's graph layer.

drills.q: Your query-based incremental pipeline uses `WHERE updated_at > watermark`. A row was deleted from the source yesterday. What happens on the next run, and how would you detect it?
drills.a: Nothing — the deleted row produces no result row, so it's invisible to the extractor. Detect it via periodic full reconciliation (diff source vs target counts/checksums) or by moving to log-based CDC, which emits explicit delete events from the transaction log.

drills.q: Name the default delivery guarantee for Kafka consumers, Airflow task retries, and webhook redelivery, and explain why 'exactly-once processing' is a slightly misleading term.
drills.a: All default to at-least-once. 'Exactly-once processing' really means at-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent sink/write path — exactly-once isn't a property the messaging layer gives you, it's something you engineer at the merge/upsert layer.

drills.q: A merge/upsert keys on `order_id` alone with no other guard. A redelivered, older CDC event for that order arrives after a newer event already landed. What goes wrong, and what's the one-line fix?
drills.a: The older event overwrites the newer data (regression), because keying on the natural key alone makes the merge idempotent against duplicates but not against out-of-order delivery. Fix: add a monotonic guard, e.g. `WHEN MATCHED AND src.updated_at > tgt.updated_at THEN UPDATE`.

drills.q: Finance reports a 3% revenue discrepancy at quarter close, but your nightly incremental pipeline has shown normal row counts and zero errors all quarter. What's the most likely root cause, and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: A stuck/blind incremental watermark — likely hard deletes or updates that bypassed the `updated_at` column (e.g. a raw backfill UPDATE). Confirm by reconciling source vs. warehouse counts/checksums on the affected table to find the first date the gap appears, then backfill that window.

drills.q: A DBA runs a direct `UPDATE` on 50,000 rows outside the application, bypassing the ORM trigger that maintains `updated_at`. Your extractor is query-based incremental. What is the concrete operational consequence, and what's the structural fix (not just 'catch it earlier')?
drills.a: Those 50,000 rows are permanently invisible to the extractor since nothing in queryable state signals they changed — the warehouse serves stale data indefinitely with no error. Structural fix: move that table to log-based CDC, which reads the transaction log directly and doesn't depend on any column being maintained by the write path.

drills.q: Your team wants to add Kafka + Flink streaming CDC to a table that feeds one dashboard, refreshed once a day at 8am for finance. Make the case against it.
drills.a: Nothing downstream consumes sub-minute freshness, so streaming buys nothing but adds always-on infra cost (3-10x a nightly batch job) plus an entire new correctness surface: exactly-once sink semantics, late-data/watermark handling, ordering guarantees. A 20-minute nightly batch job is cheaper, simpler, and self-healing on rerun.

drills.q: Your Kafka Connect CDC cluster has been down for 4 days. The source database's binlog retention is 2 days. What do you have to do to resume ingestion, and why can't you just restart the connector?
drills.a: You must perform a full re-snapshot of the table. Restarting the connector alone won't work because the transaction log events from before the retention window have already been purged from the binlog — there's no incremental history left to replay from, so the connector has nothing to catch up from.

drills.q: Design idempotent ingestion for a third-party webhook that can redeliver the same event up to 5 times over 24 hours, where the third party's event ID uniqueness across their own retries is not guaranteed.
drills.a: Use a dedup store (Redis with TTL > 24h, or a unique DB constraint) keyed on the vendor's event ID when present; when it isn't reliable, fall back to a content hash of the payload plus a coarse time bucket. Check via INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and affected-row count, not read-then-write, to avoid a race window on concurrent redeliveries.

drills.q: A nightly batch load crashes entirely because 1 row out of 2 million has a malformed timestamp. What's wrong with the pipeline's design, and what's the fix?
drills.a: A single bad row shouldn't be able to fail the whole batch — that's an availability bug on top of a data-quality issue. Fix: route rows that fail validation/type coercion to a dead-letter table with the payload, error, and timestamp, and continue processing the rest; alert on dead-letter volume crossing a threshold rather than failing the batch or alerting per-row.

drills.q: A source SaaS API adds a new field to its payload. At the bronze/raw ingest layer, should the pipeline fail, and why or why not?
drills.a: No — bronze/raw should be permissive and additive: accept the new field (e.g. flow it into a variant/JSON column or as an additional column) without failing the load. Failing loudly on structural changes belongs at a contracted silver/gold layer where an existing field changing type should break the build, not at ingest where a genuinely new field showing up is expected drift.

drills.q: Compare Debezium and AWS DMS for log-based CDC and state when you'd pick each.
drills.a: Both tail the transaction log for near-complete, low-latency change capture. Debezium is open source, Kafka Connect-native, gives you a raw event stream you own and can fan out to multiple independent consumers, but you operate Kafka Connect yourself. AWS DMS is managed and integrates natively with RDS/Aurora sources and S3/Redshift targets with less operational overhead, at the cost of less flexibility. Pick Debezium for multi-consumer fan-out or non-AWS stacks; pick DMS for a simple AWS-native S3/Redshift target.

drills.q: You call one .collect() at the end of a 10-transformation pipeline. How many Spark jobs run, and what decides where stage boundaries fall within that job?
drills.a: One job (one action = one job). Stage boundaries fall at every shuffle dependency (wide transformation: groupBy, join without broadcast, repartition, distinct). Chains of narrow transformations between shuffles are pipelined into a single stage.

drills.q: Explain why `df.rdd.map(lambda r: (r.k, r.v*2)).toDF()` defeats Catalyst even though the logic is trivial.
drills.a: The .rdd conversion forces UnsafeRows to be deserialized into full Python objects (crossing the JVM/Python boundary), runs the map as opaque Python bytecode Catalyst cannot inspect, then toDF() re-infers a schema and repacks into UnsafeRow. Everything Catalyst could have done to this trivial multiply (push it into codegen, fuse with neighboring operators) is lost even though the logic itself is simple.

drills.q: A DataFrame reads a 200-column Parquet table, does `.select("a","b").filter("a > 100")`, and `explain()` shows FileScan with PushedFilters:[IsNotNull(a), GreaterThan(a,100)] and a 2-column ReadSchema. What two Catalyst optimizations does this output prove happened, and at what plan phase were they decided?
drills.a: Column pruning (ReadSchema limited to a,b) and predicate pushdown (filter reached the reader). Both are decided during the Optimized Logical Plan phase (rule-based rewrites) and then realized by the physical FileScan operator.

drills.q: You have a 500GB shuffle with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions left at the default. Walk through, quantitatively, why this is likely to cause spill or OOM, and what a better static value would be (ignoring AQE for this question).
drills.a: 200 partitions over 500GB is ~2.5GB/partition. A single task's shuffle-read memory allocation (a fraction of executor memory) is very likely smaller than 2.5GB under any reasonably shared executor config, forcing spill to disk or an OOM if spill can't keep up. Target ~100-200MB/partition: 500GB / 150MB ~= 3,400 partitions.

drills.q: Why does Catalyst separate the 'Analyzed Plan' phase from the 'Optimized Logical Plan' phase instead of resolving and optimizing in one pass?
drills.a: Analysis establishes correctness (resolve column/table refs, typecheck) and can fail fast with AnalysisException. Optimization assumes correctness is already settled and applies rewrite rules to a plan already known valid. Keeping them separate means optimization rules never have to handle unresolved references, and errors surface before any optimization or execution work is wasted.

drills.q: An executor dies midway through writing shuffle output for a stage with 500 upstream tasks, 300 of which had already written and been read by downstream tasks. What does Spark do, and why is this more expensive than losing an executor during a narrow-transformation stage?
drills.a: Spark must recompute the lost partitions (the ones this executor was responsible for, both unwritten and any already-written-but-now-inaccessible shuffle files) via lineage replay against their parent stage. It's more expensive than a narrow-stage failure because shuffle output represents materialized, already-computed intermediate state that downstream tasks depend on; losing it forces re-running upstream computation, not just re-scheduling a straightforward map task.

drills.q: Two engineers argue: one says 'DataFrames are always faster than RDDs, full stop.' The other says 'it depends.' Resolve this with a concrete counterexample where the gap is small or reversed.
drills.a: 'It depends' is correct. A tight Scala RDD reduce over primitive types with a JIT-friendly function can approach DataFrame performance because it avoids PySpark's JVM<->Python serialization tax (which doesn't exist in Scala) — the biggest, most reliable DataFrame advantage (predicate pushdown, column pruning, codegen) still applies, but the margin is narrower in Scala than in PySpark, where every RDD lambda pays a cross-process round trip per row.

drills.q: You inherit a job where explain() shows a BroadcastNestedLoopJoin between two multi-hundred-GB tables and the job is timing out. Diagnose the likely cause and the first thing you'd check.
drills.a: BroadcastNestedLoopJoin appears when Spark has no equality condition to build a hash join on — usually a non-equi join predicate (a.start <= b.ts AND b.ts < a.end) or an accidental cross join (missing/wrong join condition). First check: print the actual join condition being used; a nested-loop over two huge tables (one broadcast, but still O(n*m) comparisons) explains the timeout directly. This is rarely intentional at that data size.

drills.q: Explain precisely why off-heap Tungsten memory changes the shape of your OOM errors rather than eliminating them.
drills.a: UnsafeRow moves row storage off the JVM heap into memory Spark manages directly via sun.misc.Unsafe, so you stop seeing java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space for that data. But the off-heap region is still finite (bounded by spark.memory.offHeap.size when enabled, or the executor's overall memory budget otherwise); exhausting it surfaces as a Spark-level TaskMemoryManager OutOfMemoryError, or triggers spill-to-disk first for operators that support spilling (sort, aggregate). The failure moved, it didn't disappear.

drills.q: A staff interviewer asks: 'If Catalyst's whole point is to optimize the plan before execution, why does whole-stage codegen happen at the very end, after the physical plan is already chosen?' Answer this.
drills.a: Codegen is an execution-strategy decision, not a plan-shape decision — it doesn't change what operators run or in what order (that's settled by the time you have a physical plan), it changes how each operator's logic is compiled and dispatched at runtime (fused JIT'd bytecode vs interpreted Volcano-style iterator calls). Doing it last means it operates on the final, already-optimized operator graph, so it only needs to reason about fusing adjacent operators into one function, not about query semantics or plan equivalence, which were already resolved in earlier phases.

drills.q: You're asked to justify, with numbers, why a 30GB nightly batch job should NOT be moved from a single r6i.8xlarge (256GB RAM) pandas/DuckDB job to a Spark cluster. Make the argument.
drills.a: 30GB fits comfortably in memory on a single 256GB box with headroom for intermediate copies. Spark's fixed costs — driver/executor JVM startup, task scheduling overhead (ms per task across potentially thousands of tasks), shuffle serialization and network transfer for any wide transformation, cluster provisioning time — are pure overhead when the alternative is one process doing in-memory work with zero network shuffle. The Spark version would likely have higher wall-clock latency and definitely higher infrastructure cost (a multi-node cluster vs one box) for no correctness or scalability benefit at this data size.

drills.q: Why is 16 kHz the ASR standard rather than 44.1 kHz (music) or 8 kHz (telephony)?
drills.a: By Nyquist, 16 kHz captures frequencies up to 8 kHz, which covers essentially all speech-intelligibility-critical energy. 44.1 kHz is overkill for speech (only useful for music's fuller hearing range). 8 kHz telephony (4 kHz Nyquist) loses higher-frequency consonant detail like the s/f distinction, a real accuracy cost.

drills.q: List the six MFCC pipeline steps in order.
drills.a: Framing, windowing (Hamming), FFT, mel filterbank, log, DCT.

drills.q: Define WER with its formula.
drills.a: WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / (number of words in the reference transcript), computed via minimum edit distance (Levenshtein) alignment between reference and hypothesis.

drills.q: Explain why CTC needs a blank token, using the word 'hello' as an example.
drills.a: CTC's collapse operation merges consecutive repeated characters in an alignment down to one. Without a mechanism to separate them, the two L's in 'hello' would incorrectly collapse into one L. A blank token emitted between the two L positions in the alignment prevents that incorrect merge, letting the collapse correctly preserve both L's as distinct.

drills.q: A team's Whisper-based transcription pipeline produces fluent-sounding text during long silences in the audio. Diagnose the cause and give a mitigation that doesn't require retraining.
drills.a: Hallucination: Whisper's generative decoder is trained to always produce output, so a mostly-silent 30-second chunk can still generate fabricated but fluent text. Mitigation: run voice-activity detection before transcription and skip non-speech segments, and/or post-filter output on anomaly signals (low average log-probability, high repetition) correlated with hallucination.

drills.q: A model hits your WER target in eval but a downstream intent classifier still fails frequently in production. What's the most likely explanation, and what would you add to the eval?
drills.a: WER treats every word error identically, but the model's errors may be concentrated on high-impact words (entities, negations, numbers) rather than low-impact filler words -- the aggregate score hides this. Add task-specific metrics: entity exact-match rate, intent/slot accuracy, negation-preservation checks, layered on top of WER rather than relying on it alone.

drills.q: Why did Kaldi-style classical ASR pipelines fall out of favor for new product development? Name the specific pain, not just 'deep learning is better.'
drills.a: Each of the three components (acoustic model, pronunciation lexicon, language model) needed separate, language-specific data and expertise, and none of it transferred to a new language -- building a competitive system per language took real specialized engineering-months. End-to-end neural models learn the mapping directly with no per-language lexicon or hand-built HMM topology.

drills.q: You're comparing a 2018 diarization paper's DER of 15% against pyannote 3.1's reported DER of ~13% on AMI and conclude pyannote barely improved. What check should you run first?
drills.a: Check whether both numbers score overlapping speech. Classical NIST DER historically didn't score overlap at all, giving partial credit to systems that just picked the dominant speaker -- an overlap-unaware DER looks artificially better than an honestly-scored overlap-aware one, so the comparison may be apples-to-oranges rather than showing marginal improvement.

drills.q: Explain the streaming-vs-batch ASR tradeoff precisely, and why simply running Whisper on a sliding window doesn't give you a real streaming system.
drills.a: More lookahead context improves accuracy (model sees more of the utterance before committing) but directly adds latency (must wait for that future context to arrive) -- an unavoidable single dial, not two separable knobs. Whisper's architecture does full attention over a fixed 30-second window with no native incremental output; running it on overlapping sliding windows is a workaround that still can't reach the sub-second latency a genuine streaming architecture (e.g. RNN-Transducer family) is built for, and adds hallucination-stitching complexity at the window seams.

drills.q: A client requires audio to never leave their premises. Walk through how this constrains your model AND deployment choice for a domain-specific ASR fine-tune.
drills.a: This forces self-hosting regardless of which base model (Wav2Vec2 or Whisper) you fine-tune, ruling out any managed API entirely. If labeled domain audio is scarce (minutes to a few hours), Wav2Vec2's self-supervised-pretrain-plus-CTC path fits that low-label regime directly. If you have tens of hours of labeled domain audio and want to keep Whisper's broader robustness, fine-tuning Whisper itself is reasonable. Either way, surface the on-prem constraint before building any cloud-API-based prototype that could never ship.

drills.q: Quote the concrete numbers that make Wav2Vec2's low-resource result significant, and explain what it demonstrated about the labeled-data bottleneck.
drills.a: 10 minutes of labeled data, pretrained on 53,000 hours of unlabeled audio (Libri-light), achieved 4.8/8.2 WER on clean/other. It demonstrated that the labeled-data bottleneck -- the entire reason classical per-language pipelines were expensive to build -- could be sidestepped by self-supervised pretraining on abundant unlabeled audio plus a small labeled fine-tuning set, not eliminated (some labeled data is still required).

drills.q: A realtime voice assistant uses full Whisper large-v3 as its ASR backend and users complain it feels laggy despite excellent transcription accuracy. Diagnose the architectural mismatch.
drills.a: Whisper is batch-oriented (30-second window, full attention over the whole chunk, no native partial/incremental output), which cannot deliver the sub-second turn-taking latency a responsive voice UI needs regardless of transcription quality. The fix is switching to a purpose-built streaming ASR architecture (RNN-Transducer family or similar) and explicitly accepting the accuracy-for-latency tradeoff that a pure accuracy-focused evaluation would never have surfaced as necessary.

drills.q: An Athena table costs $4,500/month. What are the first three things you check, in order?
drills.a: 1) File format -- is it Parquet/ORC (columnar) or raw CSV/JSON (row-oriented, reads everything). 2) Compression -- is Snappy or gzip applied. 3) Partitioning -- does the table have a partition column (usually date) that queries actually filter on. These three together commonly produce 90%+ reduction in bytes scanned, which is the entire Athena bill.

drills.q: What's the difference between what Firehose and Kinesis Data Streams let you do with the same event stream?
drills.a: Kinesis Data Streams is a durable, replayable stream that up to 8 independent consumers can read from within the retention window (24h default, up to 365 days). Firehose is a one-way managed delivery pipe to a single destination (S3, Redshift, OpenSearch) with automatic format conversion and batching, but it cannot be read back or replayed by a second consumer -- if you need multiple consumers or replay, Firehose alone can't do it.

drills.q: A Glue ETL job that used to run in 20 minutes for $8.80 now takes 3 hours and costs $75+ with no data volume increase. Diagnose.
drills.a: Most likely cause is partition/data skew -- one Spark executor doing disproportionately more work than the rest while others sit idle, often from a join key or groupby key with a heavily skewed value distribution, or a shuffle-heavy join lacking a broadcast hint for a small table. Check the Spark UI for stage-level task duration variance; the fix is repartitioning on a better key or adding a broadcast join hint. If this keeps recurring, it's also a signal the job may be better suited to EMR where you have more granular Spark tuning control.

drills.q: Why does 'cluster-billed vs query-billed' matter more than raw feature comparison when choosing between Redshift and Athena for a new analytics workload?
drills.a: Because it determines what your cost curve looks like against usage pattern, not just what queries you can run. A cluster-billed system (Redshift, outside Serverless) charges for provisioned time regardless of query volume -- great for steady, high-concurrency BI workloads, terrible for spiky or rare ad hoc queries where you'd pay for idle capacity. A query-billed system (Athena) charges only for bytes scanned -- zero cost when idle, but no low-latency persistent compute for high-concurrency dashboard use. Picking based on feature checklist (both can run SQL joins) misses that the economics diverge completely depending on query frequency and concurrency shape.

drills.q: Your team has an existing Kafka Streams application with custom serializers and Kafka Connect sinks. Someone proposes migrating to Kinesis Data Streams for 'AWS-native simplicity.' What's your response?
drills.a: Push back unless there's a specific unmet need Kinesis solves that MSK doesn't -- migration cost of rewriting Kafka Streams topology, custom serializers, and Kafka Connect sinks to Kinesis-native equivalents (which don't have a 1:1 mapping for most of that tooling) consistently exceeds the operational benefit of avoiding MSK's broker management, especially since AWS manages the MSK broker infrastructure already. Recommend MSK unless the actual driver is something Kinesis does that Kafka fundamentally can't (e.g. specific AWS-native IAM integration requirements).

drills.q: Design a pipeline for: a table with 3 years of daily-partitioned clickstream data, where the Glue crawler now takes 25 minutes to run and the partition count in the catalog is over 1 million.
drills.a: Migrate the table to partition projection instead of registered/crawled partitions. Since the partitions are predictable (year/month/day), configure projection.dt.type=date with a range and format, and set storage.location.template to compute the S3 path algorithmically. This removes the need to run the crawler on this table at all (partitions are computed at query time, not stored as catalog metadata), which both eliminates the 25-minute crawler cost and removes the per-query metadata-lookup overhead Athena was paying against a million-partition catalog entry.

drills.q: A Redshift cluster is 'healthy' by CPU/memory metrics but query queuing is increasing under normal load. What do you check first and why?
drills.a: Distribution key choice on the tables involved in the slow queries' joins. A DISTKEY mismatch forces a cross-node shuffle on every join referencing that table, which shows up as query latency and queuing rather than as CPU/memory pressure on any single node -- the cluster looks healthy in aggregate because the cost is network/shuffle time, not compute saturation. Check SVV_TABLE_INFO or Redshift Advisor for dist/sort key recommendations before considering a cluster resize, since resizing compute doesn't fix a shuffle-bound query pattern.

drills.q: When would you deliberately choose OpenSearch over a purpose-built vector database for a RAG system, given that a dedicated vector DB is usually less operational surface?
drills.a: When the production retrieval pattern is genuinely hybrid -- combining BM25 lexical scoring with vector similarity in a single query, which is the pattern that beats pure vector search on retrieval quality in most production RAG systems -- or when the team is already operating OpenSearch for logs/full-text search and vector search is incremental cost on infrastructure that already exists, rather than a new operational commitment.

drills.q: Explain why Redshift Spectrum querying an S3 table doesn't reduce your RA3 managed storage bill even if you stop loading new data into the cluster.
drills.a: Because Spectrum queries data in place in S3 without ever loading it into the cluster's managed storage -- it's a separate query path, not an ingestion mechanism. If your goal is to reduce managed storage costs by moving cold data to S3, you need to actually UNLOAD or delete the data from Redshift's managed storage and re-point queries at the S3 copy via Spectrum; simply adding Spectrum access to an S3 table alongside existing loaded data does nothing to the existing managed storage footprint.

drills.q: A monthly reporting workload causes huge concurrent query bursts against an otherwise near-idle warehouse. Compare provisioned Redshift, Redshift Serverless, and Athena for this shape.
drills.a: Provisioned Redshift means paying 24/7 for burst-capacity headroom that sits idle most of the month -- poor fit. Redshift Serverless bills per RPU-second consumed, giving the low-latency BI-dashboard experience only when actually queried -- strong fit as long as the burst doesn't exceed the workgroup's max RPU ceiling (if it does, provisioned Redshift with concurrency scaling is the fallback). Athena would be cost-efficient for the idle periods but loses the sub-second, connection-pooled, BI-tool-friendly query experience that Redshift's engine is built for, so it's a weaker fit if dashboard responsiveness during the burst matters.

drills.q: State the full IAM policy evaluation order from first check to last.
drills.a: Explicit deny anywhere > SCP > RCP > resource-based policy > permissions boundary > session policy > identity-based policy > default deny.

drills.q: A role's identity policy grants s3:*. It still can't touch a bucket. Name three possible ceiling-layer causes.
drills.a: An SCP not explicitly allowing s3 actions at the OU/account level; an RCP restricting the resource side; a permissions boundary attached to the role that excludes S3. Any one of these caps the identity policy regardless of how permissive it looks.

drills.q: Why doesn't a resource policy alone satisfy a cross-account access request the way it does for same-account access?
drills.a: Cross-account access requires both sides to explicitly allow: the resource policy on the owning account's side, AND the identity policy on the calling account's principal. Same-account grants can rely on the resource policy alone since the identity is already inside the trust boundary being evaluated by that resource.

drills.q: Explain the confused deputy problem and how sts:ExternalId fixes it.
drills.a: A third-party vendor with AssumeRole access into many customers' accounts could be tricked or buggy in a way that acts on the wrong customer's account, since role ARNs can look similar or be stored incorrectly. ExternalId is a per-customer secret placed in the trust policy condition that the vendor must include on every AssumeRole call for that specific customer, so a mismatched or missing ExternalId fails the assumption instead of silently succeeding against the wrong tenant.

drills.q: Why is iam:PassRole considered a privilege-escalation path rather than a benign permission?
drills.a: PassRole lets a principal attach a role to a service resource (like a Lambda function) without being granted that role's permissions directly. If the principal can also create the resource type that accepts the role (e.g., create a Lambda), they can run code under that role's full permission set, effectively escalating to whatever the passed role can do.

drills.q: Contrast aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount with a concrete scenario for each.
drills.a: aws:SourceArn: 'only my exact SNS topic ARN may invoke this Lambda' — single-resource, strongest confused-deputy defense. aws:SourceAccount: 'any S3 bucket in account X may trigger this' — trusts the whole account when the exact resource ARN isn't fixed ahead of time.

drills.q: What's the mechanical difference between IRSA and EKS Pod Identity for granting a pod AWS credentials?
drills.a: IRSA: per-cluster OIDC provider registered with IAM, role's trust policy references that OIDC issuer and a specific service-account subject, a mutating webhook injects a projected token into the pod. Pod Identity: an EKS Auth API association plus a Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet on each node fetch credentials on the pod's behalf, with the trust relationship managed by EKS itself rather than the role's own trust policy, making the role portable across clusters.

drills.q: What gap in SCP coverage did Resource Control Policies (RCPs, GA November 2024) close?
drills.a: SCPs only restrict identity policies of principals within the org, so they can't stop an in-org identity from writing a resource policy that grants access to a principal OUTSIDE the org. RCPs act as a ceiling on the resource-policy side directly, capping what any resource policy can grant regardless of which identity authored it.

drills.q: What are permissions boundaries designed to enable operationally, beyond just 'restricting a role'?
drills.a: Delegated IAM administration — letting app teams self-service create their own roles and policies (often via CI/Terraform) while a mandatory boundary caps the maximum they can ever grant themselves, so central security reviews the boundary policy once instead of every team's individual role definitions.

drills.q: You're debugging an unexpected AccessDenied. What's the first command you run and why?
drills.a: aws sts get-caller-identity, to confirm which principal is actually making the call. Using the wrong CLI profile or an unexpectedly still-assumed role is the most common self-inflicted cause of a denial that looks inexplicable given the policy you think applies.

drills.q: What does IAM Access Analyzer's 'unused access' feature actually measure, and what's its blind spot?
drills.a: It measures permissions not exercised in observed CloudTrail activity over a lookback window and flags them as removal candidates. Its blind spot: legitimate but rarely-used permissions (annual DR runbooks) get flagged as false positives, and it cannot distinguish a permission used once legitimately from one used once maliciously.

drills.q: Name the three phases of a Lambda invocation and which one runs only once per execution environment.
drills.a: Download/INIT/INVOKE. INIT (runtime bootstrap plus global-scope code) runs once per execution environment lifetime; INVOKE runs the handler on every single call, warm or cold.

drills.q: Why does SnapStart take Java from 5+ seconds to under 150ms, mechanically?
drills.a: It snapshots the execution environment's memory and disk state AFTER init has already run once (JVM booted, classes loaded), caches that snapshot, and restores from it on subsequent cold starts instead of re-running the full JVM boot and class-loading sequence from scratch.

drills.q: A SnapStart-enabled function occasionally returns the same 'random' UUID across different cold starts. What's the bug?
drills.a: The UUID was generated during init and got frozen into the snapshot, so every cold start restored from that snapshot returns the same value. Fix: generate the UUID inside an afterRestore runtime hook (or per-invocation, not at init) so it's fresh on every restore.

drills.q: Is VPC attachment still a meaningful cold-start cost in 2026? What changed and when?
drills.a: No. The 2019 Hyperplane networking change replaced per-execution-environment ENI creation (10-15 seconds) with pre-created ENIs shared per subnet+security-group. VPC attachment now adds well under 50ms. The remaining real cost of VPC attachment is a NAT Gateway bill for internet egress.

drills.q: Function X is being throttled with 429s. Is this a latency problem or a capacity problem, and what two Lambda settings address it?
drills.a: A capacity problem -- concurrent executions have exceeded the account or function-level limit. Reserved concurrency sets a guaranteed floor/ceiling isolating this function from others; provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but doesn't by itself raise the concurrency ceiling -- a quota increase may also be needed.

drills.q: An SQS-triggered Lambda has no ReportBatchItemFailures configured. One message in a batch of 10 throws an exception. What happens to the other 9?
drills.a: The entire batch of 10 becomes visible again in the queue and is retried, including the 9 that already succeeded -- their side effects can run twice unless the handler is idempotent.

drills.q: Contrast retry behavior for synchronous vs asynchronous Lambda invocation.
drills.a: Synchronous invokes are never retried by Lambda itself -- the caller (API Gateway, SDK) must implement its own retry/backoff, and a failure returns immediately. Asynchronous invokes (S3, SNS, EventBridge) are queued internally and Lambda retries automatically, by default about 2 additional attempts, invisible to whatever triggered it.

drills.q: How does memory configuration control CPU in Lambda, and what's the key number to remember?
drills.a: CPU is allocated proportionally to configured memory rather than set directly. 1,769 MB is the threshold at which a function gets one full vCPU; at the 10,240 MB max it gets roughly 6 vCPUs.

drills.q: A team doubled a function's memory to 'make it faster' and their AWS bill went up with no latency improvement. What's the likely explanation, and what should they have done instead?
drills.a: The function was I/O-bound (waiting on a downstream call), not CPU-bound, so extra CPU from the memory increase didn't reduce duration -- billing is duration x memory, so cost rose with no offsetting duration drop. They should have run AWS Lambda Power Tuning against real payloads to find the actual cost-optimal setting instead of guessing.

drills.q: Why can't you just chain Lambda self-invocations to handle a 40-minute job past the 15-minute limit?
drills.a: The 15-minute ceiling is a deliberate architectural boundary, and self-chaining produces fragile, effectively manual orchestration with no clean resumption from partial failure, no built-in state tracking between invocations, and risk of runaway recursive costs on a bug. Step Functions (bounded steps with tracked state) or Fargate/Batch (single long-running process) are the correct tools instead.

drills.q: List four scenarios where Lambda is architecturally the wrong tool even though it would technically run the workload.
drills.a: Steady high/predictable throughput (loses the cost crossover to always-on compute past a real utilization threshold); jobs needing more than 15 minutes; GPU-dependent inference (zero GPU support); and infrequently-invoked functions with large, slow-initializing dependencies where cold starts dominate perceived latency and provisioned concurrency's continuous cost isn't justified.

drills.q: A DAG file has `config = Variable.get('my_config')` at module scope, outside any task. What's wrong with this, concretely?
drills.a: The scheduler's DAG File Processor re-parses the file on every scan interval (a few seconds), so this line — and the DB hit it makes — executes on every single parse, not once at authoring time. Move it inside a task callable so it only runs at task execution time.

drills.q: A DAG is scheduled `@daily` starting 2026-01-01. For the run whose logical_date is 2026-08-01, when does it actually execute, and why?
drills.a: Shortly after midnight on 2026-08-02. The scheduler can't guarantee it has complete data for the interval [2026-08-01, 2026-08-02) until that period has fully elapsed, so it waits until the interval ends before starting the run.

drills.q: A task uses `context['ds']` to compute 'data through today' for a filter condition. What's the bug, and what should it use instead?
drills.a: `ds`/logical_date is the START of the data interval, not the end — using it as 'through today' silently shifts the filter window back by one interval. It should use `data_interval_end` for 'data through the end of this period'.

drills.q: 50 DAGs each run an S3KeySensor in default poke mode, waiting up to 6 hours for files to land, against a worker pool sized for 20 concurrent slots. Diagnose the cluster-wide symptom and fix it.
drills.a: Worker-slot starvation: each poke-mode sensor blocks a worker for its entire wait, so with 50 long waits against 20 slots, unrelated tasks across the whole cluster queue and run late with no crash anywhere. Fix: set deferrable=True on the sensors so they hand the wait to the triggerer and release the worker slot entirely.

drills.q: A task returns a full pandas DataFrame from a `@task`-decorated function and a downstream task consumes it as an argument. Why is this a design smell, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Return values are passed via XCom, whose default backend stores values in the metadata database — sized for small control values, not bulk data; it degrades DB/UI performance for the whole instance. Fix: write the DataFrame to durable storage (e.g. S3 parquet) and return just the path/URI through XCom.

drills.q: 20 independent DAGs each cap their own concurrency at max_active_tasks=5, but they all query the same downstream Postgres replica, which starts refusing connections during peak hours. Why didn't max_active_tasks prevent this, and what fixes it?
drills.a: max_active_tasks caps concurrency within a single DAG only — it has no visibility into other DAGs, so 20 DAGs at 5 each can still open 100 concurrent connections to the same resource. Fix: create a named pool sized below the replica's safe connection limit and assign every task touching that resource to it, capping concurrency across all DAGs collectively.

drills.q: Your team relies on Airflow's SLA feature to page on-call when a DAG misses its freshness target. After upgrading to Airflow 3.0, SLA-based DAGs stop working. What replaced it, and what's the actual behavioral improvement, not just the API change?
drills.a: Deadline Alerts (3.1+) replaced SLAs (removed in 3.0). The old SLA mechanism only evaluated whether a deadline was missed after the DAG run finished — late detection if the DAG ran long. Deadline Alerts evaluate at the calculated deadline itself and fire within roughly one scheduler heartbeat, materially faster for on-call paging.

drills.q: A mapped task (`.expand()`) fed by an upstream task that returns a list from an unvalidated API response explodes to 40,000 task instances overnight, and the scheduler becomes unresponsive. What guard should have prevented this, and what else besides scheduler CPU gets hurt?
drills.a: max_map_length (default 1024) should cap the expansion, plus validating/capping the upstream list size before mapping. Besides scheduler CPU, the metadata database takes damage too — every mapped instance is rows in task_instance tables, so a runaway expand() degrades DB write throughput for every other DAG sharing that database, not just the offending one.

drills.q: Explain what changed about worker-to-metadata-database access in Airflow 3.0 and name one real migration pain point it causes for teams upgrading from 2.x.
drills.a: Workers no longer connect to the metadata DB directly; all state transitions, XCom, heartbeats, and connection/variable fetching go through a new Task Execution API (REST layer), improving security and enabling non-Python runtimes. Migration pain point: custom operators that previously queried the metadata DB directly via raw SQLAlchemy (e.g., checking another DAG's state) break entirely and must be rewritten against the supported API or mechanisms like ExternalTaskSensor.

drills.q: What are Airflow Assets (formerly Datasets) and how do they reduce reliance on ExternalTaskSensor-style cross-DAG polling?
drills.a: An Asset represents a logical piece of data a task declares it produces. Downstream DAGs can be scheduled to trigger the instant an upstream task updates an Asset they depend on — push-based and data-centric — instead of a sensor polling another DAG's task state, which still occupies a worker or triggerer slot doing the polling.

drills.q: Design pools and priority for a cluster running one deadline-critical nightly warehouse rebuild alongside 40 small hourly DAGs, all hitting the same Postgres read replica.
drills.a: Put every task touching that replica (from any DAG) into one named pool sized below the replica's safe connection limit. Give the nightly rebuild's tasks a higher priority_weight so it wins scheduling contention for that pool near its deadline. Set max_active_runs=1 on the rebuild DAG to prevent an accidental overlapping run from doubling load on the same resource.

drills.q: A stage's task duration histogram shows 199 tasks at ~4 seconds and 1 task at 38 minutes. What's your first diagnostic step, and what would confirm it's skew rather than a hardware issue?
drills.a: Check that outlier task's shuffle-read size in the Spark UI. If it's a large multiple of the median shuffle-read size across sibling tasks, it's data skew (one key dominating a hash-partitioned shuffle). A hardware/slow-node issue would instead show normal data volume with abnormally slow processing per byte, and typically GC or scheduler-delay metrics standing out instead.

drills.q: Your job has AQE enabled with default settings and still shows classic skew symptoms on a sort-merge join. List the two threshold conditions AQE's skew-join feature requires, and give a scenario where both pass but skew handling still doesn't apply.
drills.a: Both spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor (default 5x the median partition size) AND spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (default 256MB) must be exceeded. Even if both thresholds are cleared, skew handling only applies to sort-merge joins — if this is actually a groupBy aggregation or a non-equi join, AQE's skew-join feature doesn't engage at all regardless of thresholds.

drills.q: Write the salting pattern for a skewed groupBy aggregation (sum by key) that AQE cannot fix, and explain why it requires two groupBy stages instead of one.
drills.a: salted = df.withColumn('salt', (F.rand()*N).cast('int')); partial = salted.groupBy('key','salt').agg(F.sum('value').alias('p')); final = partial.groupBy('key').agg(F.sum('p').alias('total')). Two stages are needed because the first groupBy spreads the hot key's rows across N salted sub-keys (each landing on a different partition, breaking the skew), producing N partial sums per original key; the second groupBy combines those N partial sums back into one true total per key — a single groupBy on the salted key alone would leave the results incorrectly split by salt value.

drills.q: A join between a 5GB fact table and what you believe is a 50MB dimension table runs as a sort-merge join, not a broadcast. Diagnose two possible causes and how you'd verify each.
drills.a: 1) Table statistics are stale or were never computed, so the optimizer's size estimate for the dimension table exceeds autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10MB default) even though the real size is 50MB over that but the estimate might be far higher; check with explain(mode='cost') and compare against ANALYZE TABLE output. 2) autoBroadcastJoinThreshold itself is still at the 10MB default and 50MB genuinely exceeds it; check the configured value and consider raising it (with fresh statistics) or adding an explicit .hint('broadcast').

drills.q: You convert a slow @udf(...) function to a @pandas_udf and get only a 1.5x speedup instead of the expected 10x+. What kind of UDF logic would explain a small gain like this?
drills.a: Logic that doesn't vectorize well — e.g. a UDF that calls an external network API per row, does row-dependent sequential computation, or branches heavily per element in a way that can't be expressed as NumPy/pandas vector operations. The pandas UDF still reduces JVM<->Python transfer overhead via Arrow batching, but if the actual per-row work itself can't be batched (each row still requires its own external call or scalar Python loop inside the pandas UDF), most of the win from vectorization is unavailable, leaving only the serialization-overhead reduction.

drills.q: An executor OOMs during a broadcast join, but Spark UI shows plenty of spill capacity was never used. Why didn't spill save it?
drills.a: The broadcast build side is materialized fully in memory by design — building and holding the broadcast variable isn't an operator that supports spilling to disk (unlike sort or shuffle-based aggregation). If the 'small' side turns out larger than the size estimate assumed, there's no fallback path; it's a hard OOM rather than a graceful disk-backed degradation.

drills.q: Explain, in terms of the Unified Memory Manager, how heavy caching on one part of a job can cause spill or slowdown on an unrelated concurrent operation in the same job.
drills.a: Cached data occupies storage memory within the Unified Memory region (bounded by memory.fraction of the heap, split by storageFraction between storage and execution as a soft boundary). Execution memory (needed for a concurrent large sort, aggregation, or hash-join build) can reclaim space from storage under pressure, but if the cache is large and actively pinned/reused, contention increases and the execution-hungry operator is more likely to be forced into disk spill than it would be without the concurrent cache pressure — the cache didn't directly cause the OOM/spill, but it shifted the effective available execution memory for everything else running at the same time.

drills.q: Design a bucketing scheme for two tables (orders, 2TB, and customers, 200GB) that are joined on customer_id in a nightly job that runs the same join pattern for the next year. Justify the bucket count and the risk if either table's write path changes.
drills.a: Bucket both tables by customer_id with the same bucket count, e.g. bucketBy(200, 'customer_id') sized so each bucket lands in a reasonable target size (roughly 2TB/200 = 10GB and 200GB/200 = 1GB per bucket, well within a single task's comfortable working set). This lets every nightly join skip the shuffle+sort entirely since both sides are pre-partitioned identically. Risk: if a future write to either table uses a different bucket count or a different write path that doesn't preserve bucketing (e.g. an ad hoc overwrite via a tool that ignores bucket metadata), the join silently falls back to a full shuffle join with no error, just a slower job — this needs to be caught by monitoring the job's plan (explain()) for the loss of the bucketed-join physical operator, not assumed to persist forever.

drills.q: A principal engineer asks you to justify, with the actual mechanism, why 'just throw more executors at it' is often the wrong first response to a slow Spark job. Give the mechanistic argument, not just 'sometimes it doesn't help.'
drills.a: Adding executors increases available parallel task slots, which only helps if the job's actual critical path is bounded by insufficient parallelism across many roughly-equal-sized tasks. If the critical path is instead one oversized skewed task (bounded by that single task's data volume on one core), a serial bottleneck (driver-side collect, one broadcast build, few output partitions), or a per-row Python UDF's CPU-bound interpreter overhead (bounded by per-core throughput, not core count), then idle additional executors simply wait alongside the existing ones for the same bottleneck to clear — the job's wall-clock time is set by its longest dependency chain, not by aggregate cluster capacity, and Amdahl's-law-style serial/skewed portions dominate exactly when scaling out stops helping.

drills.q: Contrast pandas UDFs and Arrow UDFs precisely: what conversion step does the Arrow UDF skip, and what's the measured tradeoff?
drills.a: A pandas UDF receives Arrow-batched data but Spark converts it into a pandas Series/DataFrame (and underlying NumPy arrays) before handing it to the user function, and converts the result back to Arrow after. An Arrow UDF operates directly on the Arrow columnar batch without that pandas/NumPy materialization step. Measured tradeoff: Arrow UDFs are reported roughly 10% faster and use about 40% less memory than pandas UDFs, with better native support for complex/nested types, at the cost of writing against the lower-level Arrow API instead of the more familiar pandas API.

drills.q: A colleague says 'we deployed on SageMaker, it costs $X/month.' What's your first clarifying question and why does it matter?
drills.a: Which inference mode -- real-time endpoint, Serverless Inference, Async Inference, or Batch Transform. Each has a fundamentally different billing shape (per instance-hour 24/7, per invocation with scale-to-zero, per invocation with scale-to-zero and queuing, or per offline job) so 'SageMaker costs $X' is meaningless without knowing which of the four is being billed.

drills.q: Why can't you serve a fine-tuned Bedrock model on-demand?
drills.a: Bedrock requires Provisioned Throughput for any custom fine-tuned model -- on-demand pricing is only available for the base foundation models AWS hosts at shared capacity. This changes the cost model of fine-tuning: even a lightly-used fine-tuned model commits you to a flat hourly model-unit rate, not pay-per-token.

drills.q: Your team ran the numbers and self-hosting vLLM 'saves 60% vs Bedrock' based on GPU-hour cost alone. What's missing from that analysis?
drills.a: Engineer-hours for ongoing operation -- monitoring, patching, incident response, and model updates for a production self-hosted fleet are commonly estimated at 10-20 hours/month minimum at $75-150/hour, adding $750-3,000/month that a pure GPU-hour comparison omits. Redo the comparison with a realistic labor line item before committing to the migration; the naive comparison very often erases most or all of the claimed savings at low-to-medium volume.

drills.q: Design the inference architecture for a 200-page PDF summarization pipeline with a same-business-day SLA and bursty arrival. Which SageMaker/Bedrock components and why not a real-time endpoint?
drills.a: Textract (matched to the actual document structure) for OCR into S3, then either SageMaker Async Inference (self-hosted model, large payload, no strict latency need) or Bedrock on-demand (foundation model) triggered by a queue. A real-time endpoint would bill per instance-hour 24/7 regardless of whether a document is actively being processed -- the wrong cost shape for bursty, non-latency-critical traffic where idle capacity between bursts would be pure waste.

drills.q: A team wants 'a RAG system' but hasn't decided between Kendra, OpenSearch, and Bedrock Knowledge Bases. What's the one question that resolves it fastest?
drills.a: Is the product a search experience for humans (with access control, connectors to SharePoint/Confluence/etc., a UI) or is it purely 'feed an LLM good context'? If the former, Kendra. If the latter and the team wants zero index ops, Bedrock Knowledge Bases. If the latter but retrieval quality needs custom tuning (chunking strategy, hybrid BM25+vector scoring, a specific reranker), direct OpenSearch.

drills.q: Your Textract bill is dominated by AnalyzeExpense calls but investigation shows most input documents are plain-text internal memos, not invoices. What happened and what's the fix?
drills.a: The pipeline is calling the wrong API for the document type -- AnalyzeExpense is priced for structured invoice/receipt field extraction (~$10/1,000 pages) when DetectDocumentText (~$1.50/1,000 pages) would suffice for plain text, a roughly 6-7x avoidable cost difference on this subset alone. Fix: classify document type first (even a cheap heuristic or Comprehend custom classifier) and route to the cheapest Textract API that satisfies the actual extraction need.

drills.q: A SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint shows latency spikes correlated with periods of low traffic, not with request complexity. Diagnose and give two possible fixes with their tradeoffs.
drills.a: Cold starts -- Serverless Inference scales to zero when idle and pays a provisioning penalty on the next invocation after a gap. Fix 1: switch to a real-time endpoint, eliminating cold starts entirely but paying for capacity 24/7 even during genuinely idle periods -- only worth it if traffic volume is high enough that idle cost is small relative to total cost. Fix 2: if available for the workload, use Provisioned Concurrency for Serverless Inference to keep some capacity warm without going fully real-time -- a middle ground that still has a cost for the warm capacity reserved.

drills.q: Explain why 'self-hosting is cheaper above 11B tokens/month' and 'self-hosting is cheaper above 100M tokens/month' can both appear as cited figures without either being wrong.
drills.a: They come from different underlying assumptions -- which frontier model's on-demand price is the baseline, whether GPU utilization is assumed high (e.g. >60%) or conservative, and critically whether engineer-labor cost is included in the self-hosting side. A comparison against an expensive frontier model with optimistic GPU utilization and no labor cost produces a much lower break-even than one against a cheaper model with realistic utilization and a labor line item. The lesson: never quote a break-even number without also stating its assumptions, and always re-derive it for the specific case rather than reusing someone else's snapshot.

drills.q: A team building a new agent wants to know if they should use AgentCore or their existing hand-rolled LangGraph-on-EKS deployment. What's the actual decision framework, not just 'AgentCore is newer so it's better'?
drills.a: Identify what specific undifferentiated infrastructure the current LangGraph deployment has already built (session isolation, identity/auth for tools, persistent memory, observability) versus what it's missing or fragile on. If the existing stack already solves these well and is stable, migrating purely because AgentCore exists adds risk (it's new, GA mid-2026, opinionated about its execution model) for uncertain benefit. If the team is actively fighting to build session isolation or observability themselves and it's slowing feature work, AgentCore's managed runtime is solving exactly that gap and is worth evaluating concretely against the specific pain points, not adopted wholesale on reputation.

drills.q: Why does SageMaker Feature Store matter for a team already using PySpark/EMR to compute features for training?
drills.a: Without it, training-time feature computation (batch, in Spark/EMR) and serving-time feature computation (often a separate, hand-written low-latency path) can silently diverge -- different code paths computing 'the same' feature slightly differently is a classic and hard-to-detect cause of training/serving skew that degrades a model in production without any obvious error. Feature Store gives one feature definition with both an offline store (for bulk training reads) and an online store (for low-latency serving lookups), closing that gap structurally rather than relying on two implementations staying in sync by discipline.

drills.q: Name the two independent axes in choosing AWS container compute, and give one example combination.
drills.a: Orchestrator (ECS vs EKS) and compute engine (Fargate vs EC2). Example: EKS+EC2 for a GPU-based Kubernetes-native inference workload.

drills.q: A team wants to run GPU inference on ECS Fargate. What do you tell them?
drills.a: It's not possible -- Fargate has zero GPU support on either ECS or EKS. They need EC2 launch type with a GPU-family instance (p/g series), on either ECS or EKS depending on their other requirements.

drills.q: Decode m7g.xlarge and state what kind of workload it suits.
drills.a: m = general-purpose family, 7 = 7th generation, g = Graviton (ARM) processor, xlarge = size tier. Suits general-purpose workloads where ARM64 compatibility is available, typically better price/performance than the Intel equivalent.

drills.q: Rank Spot, Compute Savings Plans, and Standard Reserved Instances by discount range and flexibility.
drills.a: Spot: up to ~90% discount, zero commitment, but reclaimable with a 2-minute notice. Compute Savings Plans: up to ~66%, most flexible (covers EC2/Fargate/Lambda, any instance family/region). Reserved Instances: up to ~72%, highest discount among committed options but locked to one instance family for the term.

drills.q: A new AWS-only project has no existing Kubernetes investment. What's the pragmatic default compute choice, and when should they deviate to EKS?
drills.a: ECS on Fargate by default -- zero control-plane fee, minimal ops. Deviate to EKS only for a concrete trigger: multi-cloud/hybrid strategy, a tool that only ships as a Kubernetes operator, or an existing platform team fluent in kubectl serving many internal tenants.

drills.q: You need to process 30,000 independent video files with no dependencies between them. Why AWS Batch array jobs over a hand-rolled SQS worker fleet?
drills.a: Batch array jobs give per-child retry handling, automatic compute-environment scaling matched to the array size, and a single job ARN for aggregate status tracking -- all of which a hand-rolled system has to build itself. Note the 10,000-child limit per array job means 30,000 files need at least 3 array job submissions or grouping files per child.

drills.q: Why does a warm pool cut ASG scale-out latency without keeping instances fully running and billed?
drills.a: Warm pool instances can be kept in a Stopped state, which only incurs EBS storage cost while idle -- when scale-out is needed, ASG starts the pre-initialized instance instead of booting cold from the AMI and running full bootstrap, cutting latency from minutes to seconds at a fraction of always-running cost.

drills.q: Distinguish the Spot 2-minute interruption notice from a rebalance recommendation.
drills.a: The interruption notice is a fixed 2-minute hard warning immediately before reclaim. The rebalance recommendation is a separate, earlier signal for elevated interruption risk with more (but not guaranteed) lead time, meant to let Capacity Rebalancing proactively launch replacement capacity before the hard notice fires -- the two aren't always both present with the same timing.

drills.q: ECS Fargate tasks are stuck in PENDING and never reach RUNNING. Name three things to check in order.
drills.a: Fargate vCPU/memory account quota for the region, subnet IP availability (each task needs an ENI/IP), and capacity provider strategy or placement constraints that might be unsatisfiable together. If those are fine, check the task execution role's permission to pull the container image.

drills.q: Why would you deliberately choose ECS over EKS even for a team that already knows Kubernetes well?
drills.a: If the workload is a small number of straightforward services with no need for the broader Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, service mesh, multi-cloud portability), the team's existing K8s fluency doesn't offset ECS's lower operational surface and zero control-plane cost -- the decision should be driven by the workload's actual requirements, not by sunk-cost familiarity with a tool.

drills.q: What's the difference between lifecycle hooks and warm pools in an ASG, and how do they combine?
drills.a: Warm pools pre-initialize instances so scale-out can pull a ready instance instead of booting cold. Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so custom automation runs before it's marked in-service or terminated. Combined, a warm pool instance still needs a lifecycle hook if final steps (like registering with a load balancer) must complete before it's considered fully in-service.

drills.q: A payment consumer occasionally double-charges customers under normal (non-error) load. What's the first thing to check?
drills.a: The SQS visibility timeout against the handler's actual p99 processing time. If the timeout is shorter than real processing time, the message reappears and a second consumer processes it concurrently with the first, causing the duplicate charge -- this is the single most common cause of this exact symptom.

drills.q: Why is SNS message filtering insufficient once you need to route events by their JSON body structure rather than by metadata attributes?
drills.a: SNS filter policies only match on message attributes (key-value metadata attached at publish time), not on the actual event payload's structure or nested values. EventBridge event patterns match the JSON body itself with richer operators (prefix, numeric range, exists checks), which is the actual capability gap that pushes teams toward EventBridge once routing logic needs to inspect content, not just tags.

drills.q: A workflow processes 8 million short (under 3 second) IoT events per day and occasionally losing one on failure is acceptable. The team built it on Step Functions Standard because 'it has better visibility.' What's wrong with that choice and what should change?
drills.a: At that volume, Standard's per-state-transition billing ($0.025/1,000 transitions) is dramatically more expensive than Express's per-request-plus-duration billing -- the cited comparison shows roughly a 40x cost difference at 10 million executions of a similarly-shaped workflow. Given the stated tolerance for occasional lost events (matching Express's at-least-once/at-most-once semantics) and the sub-5-minute duration, Express is both cheaper and semantically appropriate here; Standard's exactly-once guarantee and full visual history aren't needed for this workload and are being paid for at a steep multiple.

drills.q: Design ingestion for 6 SaaS vendors' webhooks, each with different schemas, needing per-vendor downstream processing and the ability to replay the last 24 hours if a bug is found in one consumer.
drills.a: EventBridge as the central bus: receive each vendor's webhook (via API Gateway or EventBridge's native SaaS partner sources where supported), define a per-vendor event pattern rule routing to that vendor's specific downstream target, and enable an archive on the bus with at least 24-hour retention scoped to the relevant event patterns. This uses EventBridge's schema registry, content-based routing, and native archive/replay together -- capabilities SNS+SQS would require custom-building.

drills.q: A new internal microservice API has no partner-facing tiering requirement. REST or HTTP API Gateway, and what changes the answer?
drills.a: HTTP API by default -- roughly a third of REST's per-request cost, and REST's differentiating features (usage plans, request/response transformation, native WAF, richer authorizer config) aren't needed without partner tiering. The answer changes if a specific REST-only feature becomes a hard requirement later (e.g. a partner needing a rate-limited API key with a monthly quota, which requires usage plans, REST-only) -- at that point either migrate just the partner-facing routes to REST or implement quota enforcement in application code instead of migrating the whole API surface.

drills.q: Explain why raising an SQS visibility timeout reduces but does not eliminate duplicate processing.
drills.a: SQS guarantees at-least-once delivery unconditionally, independent of visibility timeout tuning -- a consumer can crash or lose its network connection after successfully processing a message but before calling DeleteMessage, in which case the message becomes visible again and is legitimately redelivered regardless of how generous the timeout was. Visibility timeout tuning only addresses the specific case of the timeout expiring while processing is still genuinely in progress; it cannot address post-processing-pre-delete failures. This is why an idempotency key is not optional defense-in-depth but the actual correctness mechanism.

drills.q: A workflow needs a human approval step that could take from minutes to several days, followed by automated processing. Standard or Express Step Functions, and what specific feature makes this clean to implement?
drills.a: Standard -- Express's 5-minute maximum duration makes it structurally unable to represent a multi-day wait. Standard supports the waitForTaskToken callback pattern, which pauses the state machine (at effectively no cost while waiting) until an external system calls SendTaskSuccess/SendTaskFailure with the token, giving a clean way to model human-in-the-loop or other long-running external approval without polling.

drills.q: Your team argues API Gateway is 'always cheaper than running our own load balancer and containers.' Is this true, and how would you actually settle the argument for a specific service?
drills.a: Not universally true -- it depends on sustained request volume. API Gateway's pricing is linear per request with no cap; ALB+Fargate/EKS cost is roughly fixed within a given provisioned capacity. At low-to-spiky traffic, API Gateway wins because there's no idle infrastructure cost. At high, sustained volume, the linear-vs-fixed cost curves cross and ALB+compute can become cheaper, plus avoid Lambda's per-invocation cold-start variance. Settle it by modeling both cost curves against the service's actual projected sustained request volume, not by assuming either answer as a default.

drills.q: A producer changed their event schema and an EventBridge rule silently stopped matching, causing missing downstream processing for an unknown period. How do you prevent recurrence?
drills.a: Use EventBridge's schema registry to track and version the actual event shapes on the bus, treating any producer schema change as a coordination event (versioned event types or a reviewed migration) rather than a silent deploy. This doesn't eliminate the need for manual pattern updates but converts a silent failure into a visible, reviewable diff before the change reaches production -- pair it with a synthetic 'canary event' check or a rule-match monitoring alarm that fires if a previously-active rule stops matching for an unusual period.

drills.q: Design idempotent processing for an SQS consumer where legitimate duplicate content (identical event bodies representing genuinely distinct real-world events) can occur.
drills.a: Content-based deduplication (hashing the message body) is unsafe here since it can't tell apart two distinct real events with identical payloads.
