drills.a: It reads content in the PDF's internal object order, which for two columns is often interleaved line-by-line across columns, producing fluent but semantically scrambled text. It's dangerous because no exception is thrown and nothing looks obviously broken -- it can survive all the way to a confidently wrong answer.

drills.q: Compare markdown serialization, per-row records, and summary+reference for table handling. When would you pick each?
drills.a: Markdown serialization (default, small-medium tables). Per-row records when the full markdown exceeds the chunk budget -- split by row, header carried along, row index as metadata. Summary+reference for very large/wide tables where per-row chunking produces too many near-duplicate low-signal chunks.

drills.q: Why must code be split on AST boundaries instead of character or line counts, and what happens when a single function is still too large?
drills.a: Character/line splitting can cut a function mid-body or drop its enclosing class/import context, producing an unusable fragment. AST-aware splitting via tree-sitter guarantees syntactically complete chunks; for an oversized function, real implementations recurse into nested AST boundaries (blocks, statements) rather than falling back to a raw character cut.

drills.q: What is parent-child hierarchical retrieval and what specific problem does it solve that one flat chunk size can't?
drills.a: Small leaf chunks are indexed for precise similarity search, but the parent chunk is substituted at retrieval time when enough children are retrieved together (LlamaIndex AutoMergingRetriever). It solves documents whose sections vary widely in natural density -- a short definition and a dense multi-page procedure can't both be served well by one chunk size.

drills.q: Why is an image caption a lossy representation, and what's the practical consequence for retrieval?
drills.a: A caption compresses the image's full information into text, so retrieval only succeeds for queries the caption's text actually captures. A vague caption gives retrieval nothing to match a specific query against even though the answer is visible in the image -- caption quality directly bounds which queries can succeed.

drills.q: What can knowledge-graph RAG answer that flat chunk retrieval structurally cannot, and what's its real cost profile?
drills.a: Multi-hop questions connecting facts across documents and whole-corpus 'global' summary questions. Cost: ~3-5x token inflation for entity/relation extraction, early indexing runs around $33k for a large corpus, and 2-3x higher query latency from graph traversal -- though indexing cost has dropped to roughly 0.1% of that within ~18 months via better prompting/caching.

drills.q: A PDF ingestion pipeline works well on single-column test documents but silently degrades once multi-column financial statements with tables start flowing in. Diagnose.
drills.a: The test set almost certainly didn't exercise multi-column or table-heavy layouts, so the parser's reading-order and table-flattening behavior was never validated. Diagnose by comparing extracted text against the source document's visual layout on the actual failing documents -- the existing eval structurally can't surface this class of bug if it never included these document shapes.

drills.q: When is it wrong to build a parent-child hierarchy or a knowledge graph, even though both are more sophisticated than flat chunking?
drills.a: Parent-child hierarchies waste complexity on short, structurally flat documents (FAQs, tickets) with no meaningful density variation across sections. Knowledge graphs waste cost and latency on corpora/query patterns that are fundamentally single-hop lookup rather than multi-hop/relational -- profile actual query patterns before adopting either.

drills.q: Design the ingestion pipeline for a corpus mixing scanned invoices, a multi-column technical report, a codebase, and a 300-page policy manual.
drills.a: Route by detected source type before chunking: OCR fallback (triggered by text-density detection) plus per-row table serialization for invoices; a layout-aware parser validated for multi-column reading order (Docling/Marker-PDF) with tables serialized to markdown for the report; tree-sitter AST-boundary splitting for the codebase; parent-child hierarchical chunking with auto-merging for the policy manual since its sections vary widely in density. Every unit carries provenance metadata (source type, extraction method, document/page/section ID) so ingestion failures are diagnosable separately from retrieval or generation failures.

drills.q: Would you build a knowledge graph across a corpus of invoices, reports, and policies just because they're relationally connected in principle?
drills.a: Only if the actual query pattern requires multi-hop reasoning across those sources (e.g. 'which invoices reference a vendor mentioned in this policy exception'). If most real queries are single-source lookups, the graph's cost and latency tax isn't justified regardless of how relationally connected the underlying data theoretically is.

drills.q: Why does a metadata filter break both pre-filtering and post-filtering when applied to an ANN index?
drills.a: Every ANN index is built assuming any indexed vector is valid. Pre-filtering has no index over the filtered subset, degenerating toward brute force. Post-filtering discards non-matches after the unfiltered search, which can silently under-return since the greedy search never routed toward the filter-valid region.

drills.q: Walk through the mechanism of post-filter under-return with a concrete number.
drills.a: A filter matching ~10% of the corpus with ef_search=40 retrieves on average only ~4 filter-valid candidates by chance, well short of a k=10 request, even though far more valid matches exist elsewhere in the graph that the search never routed toward.

drills.q: Define cardinality and selectivity. Why is a high-cardinality filter the expensive case for both strategies?
drills.a: Cardinality is the number of distinct values a field can take; selectivity is what fraction of the corpus one value matches. A high-cardinality field like tenant_id (millions of values) produces high selectivity per value -- worst case for pre-filter (small unindexed scan) and post-filter (severe under-return).

drills.q: Why must ACL filtering be enforced in the retrieval query itself rather than as a post-retrieval check?
drills.a: If unauthorized documents are retrieved and filtered out afterward in application code, they may already be logged, cached, briefly present in a response payload, or exposed via a timing/count side-channel before the discard runs. The ineligible data must never leave the boundary, not merely be removed before a user notices.

drills.q: Compare RBAC and ABAC for retrieval filtering, and explain why production systems move toward ABAC.
drills.a: RBAC attaches permissions to roles -- simple, coarse-grained. ABAC computes permissions from user/resource/context attributes, supporting finer-grained dynamic rules (e.g. department match AND clearance level). Systems move toward ABAC as access rules grow more contextual, but often layer both rather than replacing RBAC entirely.

drills.q: Why is oversampling before post-filtering only a mitigation and not a fix?
drills.a: It increases the chance enough filter-valid results appear in a larger candidate set, but doesn't change the underlying mechanism -- the search still isn't routing toward the filter-valid region deliberately, so a selective enough filter (or too-small oversample factor) can still under-return, at proportionally higher compute cost.

drills.q: A pgvector-backed filtered query that used to return in milliseconds now takes seconds. What's your diagnostic path?
drills.a: Check whether filter selectivity changed (new tenant, data growth) pushing the query from a cheap high-selectivity case into one requiring hnsw.iterative_scan or a partial index/partition. Confirm by measuring current selectivity directly. If selectivity is unchanged, check for index bloat from tombstoned HNSW deletions or concurrent write contention.

drills.q: Design the metadata schema and multi-tenancy strategy for a SaaS RAG product with tenants ranging from 100 to 5 million documents.
drills.a: Denormalize tenant_id, ACL, and filterable fields onto chunk records. Given the four-order-of-magnitude skew, tier by size: smallest tenants use brute-force/in-memory search; mid-size tenants share a filter-aware index (ACORN-style or iterative scan); largest tenants get dedicated physical index isolation. ACL is enforced as a query-time filter in all three tiers, never post-retrieval.

drills.q: A customer reports search results including another customer's tenant data after a routine ingest pipeline update. Walk through your incident response.
drills.a: Treat it as a security incident first: determine immediately whether the ACL/tenant filter is a query-time condition or a post-retrieval check -- if post-retrieval, that's very likely root cause. Check whether the ingest change altered tenant_id/ACL denormalization (sync bug, race condition during backfill). Audit logs/caches for whether leaked data was already exposed downstream, not just currently visible. Remediate by moving enforcement to query-time filtering and adding database-level row-level security as defense-in-depth.

drills.q: Why is schema evolution usually cheap when adding a new filterable field, but risky when changing an existing field's type or semantics?
drills.a: Adding a field is typically a metadata backfill only -- the vector is unaffected, no re-embedding required. Changing type/semantics (boolean to enum) requires auditing every dependent code path and index assumption, and partial rollout can produce silently inconsistent filtering -- needs a transitional sentinel state and validated 100% backfill before cutover.

drills.q: Why does cross-lingual retrieval work with zero shared vocabulary between query and document?
drills.a: The embedding model was trained with a contrastive objective on cross-lingual pairs known/inferred to share meaning, pulling translation-equivalent text together in vector space regardless of shared tokens -- the training signal only ever optimized for shared meaning, not shared language.

drills.q: What is tokenizer fertility and give its rough cost multiplier for non-English languages.
drills.a: Tokens produced per word/character. Non-English, especially morphologically rich or non-Latin-script languages, often pay 1.5-2x+ the per-character token cost of English -- a direct compute/latency/context-budget tax.

drills.q: A 22-locale product's blended recall@k dashboard looks healthy but one locale is quietly broken. Explain the mechanism and the fix.
drills.a: A blended metric averages across all locales, so one language collapsing to near-zero is mathematically absorbed by the other 21 healthy languages. Fix: report and alert on recall@k/nDCG per locale as a hard requirement, never rely on a single blended number.

drills.q: Compare the operational cost of a shared multilingual index versus per-language indexes.
drills.a: Shared index is simplest to operate (one index, one model, one monitoring surface) but risks cross-lingual leakage hidden by blended metrics. Per-language indexes isolate quality and allow language-specific models but multiply build/monitor/reindex work by locale count -- a real cost at 22 locales, not a rounding error.

drills.q: Why does a whitespace-based lexical tokenizer break on CJK text, and what's the fix?
drills.a: CJK scripts have no whitespace between words, so a whitespace tokenizer either treats every character as its own token (destroying word-level meaning BM25 needs) or fails to segment. Fix: dedicated segmenters like Jieba (Chinese) or MeCab (Japanese) before lexical indexing.

drills.q: A user types a romanized query for a language natively written in a non-Latin script and gets zero results. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The index holds only native-script content and the romanized query shares no tokens or embedding-space proximity with it. Fix by normalizing via transliteration at index time, at query time, or choosing/fine-tuning a model with demonstrated transliteration robustness -- romanized input is common, not a rare edge case.

drills.q: How should a language detector handle a code-switched query like "what's the estado del clima today"?
drills.a: Single top-1 detection forces an artificial single-language label on inherently mixed content. Use top-k predictions; when top-2 are close in confidence, run retrieval across both candidate languages and fuse, or fall back to the shared multilingual embedding space, which doesn't need a language label at all.

drills.q: Why might a model advertised as supporting "100+ languages" still underperform for several of your active locales?
drills.a: Aggregate language-count claims say nothing about per-language training data volume. Low-resource languages sit in the weaker tail by construction. Validate per-locale against your own golden set rather than trusting the vendor's headline benchmark.

drills.q: Design the per-locale evaluation and monitoring strategy for a 22-locale RAG product going into production.
drills.a: Build a golden set stratified by language, ideally native-speaker-annotated (not machine-translated from an English set). Report recall@k/nDCG per locale as a first-class metric with independent alerting thresholds. Track tokenizer fertility/cost per locale separately. Route language detection with a confidence threshold and shared-embedding fallback for ambiguous queries. Re-run the full per-locale eval on every embedding model swap or reindex.

drills.q: When would translate-then-retrieve still be the right call in 2026 despite multilingual embeddings being the modern default?
drills.a: For a genuinely low-resource language where the multilingual embedding's alignment is weak from insufficient training data -- translating the query into a high-resource pivot language, retrieving there, and translating results back can outperform a poorly-aligned multilingual embedding, since the translation model may have stronger signal for that language pair.

drills.q: Name the three caching layers in a production LLM stack and which one carries real correctness risk.
drills.a: Exact-match and prefix/prompt caching both require byte-identical matches (full request or shared prefix) and carry zero correctness risk. Semantic caching, matching by embedding similarity above a threshold, is the only layer that generalizes across paraphrasing -- and the only one that can be wrong on a hit.

drills.q: Is prompt/prefix caching the same thing as semantic caching?
drills.a: No. Prefix caching reuses the transformer's KV cache for a byte-identical shared prefix up to a cache breakpoint -- it does nothing for paraphrased queries and carries zero similarity-threshold risk, the opposite failure profile from semantic caching.

drills.q: Give a concrete example of a semantic-cache false hit and explain the mechanism.
drills.a: "Refund policy for annual plans" vs "...for monthly plans" can embed above 0.95 cosine similarity since they differ by one word, but the answers may be opposite. It happens because embedding closeness reflects overall topical/lexical similarity, not whether the one token that changes the answer was preserved.

drills.q: Why are static similarity thresholds fragile, and what does vCache do differently?
drills.a: A single global threshold assumes one cutoff fits every query cluster, but some tolerate loose matching safely while others (embedded dates/tiers/quantities) need tight matching. vCache learns a per-entry threshold online with a formal error-rate guarantee, reporting up to 12.5x higher hit rate and 26x lower error rate than static baselines at matched error budget.

drills.q: Walk through the cost arithmetic for a semantic cache at 40% hit rate, 1M queries/day, $0.003/query LLM cost, $0.0001/hit cost.
drills.a: Without cache: 1,000,000 x $0.003 = $3,000/day. With cache: 400,000 x $0.0001 + 600,000 x $0.003 = ~$1,840/day, a ~39% reduction that tracks the hit rate closely since the hit cost is near-negligible relative to a full LLM call.

drills.q: Why is a shared semantic cache across tenants dangerous, and what's the fix?
drills.a: If tenant A's query embeds close enough to a cached response built from tenant B's data, tenant A can receive an answer derived from tenant B's private content -- a real data leak, not just a wrong-answer bug. Fix: make tenant_id a hard filter in the cache lookup query itself, never a check applied after a candidate is retrieved.

drills.q: Design an invalidation strategy for a RAG semantic cache backed by a corpus that updates daily.
drills.a: Prefer event-driven invalidation: tag cache entries with the document/chunk IDs that fed their answer, and have the ingestion pipeline emit invalidation events for exactly the entries touched by an update. If per-entry tracking is too costly, fall back to versioned cache namespaces (reindex creates a fresh namespace) rather than TTL alone, which serves stale answers for the whole window and evicts unaffected entries too early.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants "as high a cache hit rate as possible." How do you respond?
drills.a: Hit rate isn't the objective alone -- pushing it up by loosening the threshold directly increases false-hit rate. Propose a target false-positive rate the business can tolerate, then tune hit rate as high as possible subject to that bound, ideally via an adaptive per-item method rather than a single guessed threshold.

drills.q: When is semantic caching actively the wrong choice? Give three categories.
drills.a: Personalized answers (same phrasing, different correct answer per user), time-sensitive information (stock prices, live inventory) where correctness decays faster than any safe TTL, and high-stakes domains (medical/legal/financial) where any residual false-hit rate has real consequences.

drills.q: Design the caching architecture for a multi-tenant, 22-locale RAG customer-support product where support policies vary by locale and change monthly.
drills.a: Layer all three caches, all keyed on tenant_id + locale. Exact-match and prefix caching run first with zero risk. Semantic caching is namespaced by (tenant_id, locale) as a hard filter in the lookup, never post-hoc, since both tenant leakage and cross-locale answer bleed are real risks. Use event-driven invalidation tied to the policy-ingestion pipeline, scoped per locale. Set similarity thresholds per locale (ideally adaptive) since paraphrase risk differs by language, and measure hit rate/positive-hit-rate per locale, not blended.

drills.q: Why doesn't boolean retrieval count as "ranking" at all?
drills.a: Boolean retrieval evaluates a match/no-match expression (AND/OR/NOT) with no relevance scale -- documents either satisfy the expression or don't, ordered by date/ID, not relevance. There's no way to express "somewhat relevant."

drills.q: Explain vocabulary mismatch precisely with an example, and what dense retrieval trades away to fix it.
drills.a: BM25 scores purely on shared tokens; "car" scores zero against a document that only says "automobile" despite being relevant. Dense embeddings fix this by mapping both to nearby vector-space points, but trade away precision on rare/exact tokens the embedding model barely saw in training.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks why "semantic search" still fails on order-number lookups. What's the fix, and why isn't a better embedding model the answer?
drills.a: Pure dense retrieval structurally can't guarantee exact-token recall -- the embedding model has no principled way to prioritize an exact rare-string match over a topically-similar one. The fix is hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense, fused), not a better embedding model, because the failure is architectural.

drills.q: What's wrong with training an LTR model directly on raw click logs?
drills.a: It bakes in position bias -- users click higher-ranked results more regardless of true relevance, so the model learns to reinforce whatever ranking already existed. Fix with inverse propensity scoring or randomized interleaving to collect unbiased labels.

drills.q: Describe the four-stage cascade architecture (matching -> pre-ranking -> ranking -> mix-ranking) and how it relates to retrieve-then-rerank.
drills.a: Matching does cheap corpus-scale candidate generation; pre-ranking narrows millions to thousands with a lightweight model; ranking scores thousands to tens with the full LTR/neural model; mix-ranking applies business rules (diversity, ad interleave, dedup). It's the same narrow-then-spend-more-compute pattern as retrieve-then-rerank, just with more stages and business features layered on.

drills.q: When is a full learned-to-rank layer the wrong investment, and what should you use instead?
drills.a: When there isn't enough real interaction data -- small catalogs, low traffic, cold-start. A GBDT trained on sparse/synthetic labels overfits; use hand-tuned boosting (weighted BM25 + recency + popularity) instead, which is transparent and effective at that scale.

drills.q: Why can LLM-based query rewriting (HyDE, keyword expansion) hurt some queries while helping others?
drills.a: It can distort the original intent or overamplify rare terms the user never cared about for certain query types, while genuinely helping others (conversational follow-ups, typo-heavy input). It needs per-query-type evaluation, never blanket adoption.

drills.q: Design the ranking stack for a marketplace search product with natural-language queries, exact SKU lookups, and sponsored listings as a monetization objective.
drills.a: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 for SKU/brand exact lookups, dense for paraphrased queries) fused with RRF. Cross-encoder reranks the fused top-100 to a top-20-40 shortlist. An LTR model (LambdaMART baseline) reorders using relevance + CTR + conversion + price + inventory + personalization, trained with propensity-corrected labels. Sponsored listings interleave as a separate mix-ranking step, not blended into the LTR score, to preserve auditability.

drills.q: Would you train one unified end-to-end ranking model instead of a staged retrieval -> rerank -> LTR pipeline? Why or why not?
drills.a: A single end-to-end model is tempting but sacrifices debuggability and the ability to independently audit each stage (e.g. proving sponsored placement doesn't bias organic relevance). Staged systems remain the practical default specifically because of that auditability requirement at real business complexity.

drills.q: A candidate says "reranking and learned-to-rank are basically the same thing." What's the correction?
drills.a: A cross-encoder reranker optimizes text relevance alone via joint attention over the query-document pair. LTR optimizes a business objective using a broader feature set (which can include the reranker's own score as one input) plus signals like CTR, price, and personalization that no text-similarity model can see -- they answer different questions.

drills.q: Name the two mandatory nodes create_react_agent wires into a StateGraph, and what each one does.
drills.a: agent: calls the model with tools bound and appends the AIMessage. tools: a ToolNode that dispatches every tool_call on the last message and appends matched ToolMessages.

drills.q: Your agent's output ends with the exact string "Sorry, need more steps to process this request." Did the graph crash? What actually happened?
drills.a: No crash. The remaining_steps graceful-degradation check fired (remaining<2 with pending tool calls, or remaining<1 with a return_direct tool), and the graph short-circuited to a synthetic final message instead of raising GraphRecursionError.

drills.q: What's the difference between should_continue and tools_condition, and which one would you actually import into your own code?
drills.a: should_continue is create_react_agent's internal three-way router (tools/structured-response/end), never called directly. tools_condition is the public two-way utility you'd import when building your own StateGraph and want the same tool-calls routing rule.

drills.q: A pre_model_hook you wrote is supposed to summarize old turns for this call only, without changing persisted history. It returns {"messages": [summary_msg]}. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Returning "messages" writes through add_messages into permanent state — it's a real, persisted edit. For a transient, this-call-only view, return {"llm_input_messages": [...]} instead.

drills.q: You add a post_model_hook that filters out messages it considers low-value before routing. Tool dispatch starts silently skipping calls that should have executed. Diagnose.
drills.a: post_model_hook_router determines pending tool calls by diffing tool_call ids on the last AIMessage against existing ToolMessages in state. If the hook drops or reshapes messages and breaks that id relationship, the router can conclude tool calls are already satisfied when they aren't, skipping dispatch.

drills.q: Explain the behavioral difference between version="v1" and version="v2" tool dispatch, specifically around retry policies.
drills.a: v1 dispatches all tool calls from one message inside a single ToolNode invocation as one graph step, so a retry/timeout policy on the tools node applies to the whole batch. v2 turns each tool call into its own Send targeting its own ToolNode task, so retry/timeout policies apply per individual tool call.

drills.q: A tool you registered raises an uncaught exception mid-run. What does the model actually see, and why doesn't the run crash?
drills.a: ToolNode catches the exception by default and returns it as a ToolMessage containing the error text rather than propagating it — the framework's version of 'errors are observations, not exceptions,' letting the loop continue.

drills.q: You pass response_format to create_react_agent. Does this change how the model reasons and calls tools during the loop?
drills.a: No. response_format only appends a terminal generate_structured_response node reached after the loop would otherwise exit to END. It makes one additional schema-constrained model call at the very end and writes state["structured_response"]; the loop itself is unaffected.

drills.q: You want interrupt_before to gate only the delete_record tool, not every tool call. Can you do this with interrupt_before=["tools"]? What's the actual fix?
drills.a: No — interrupt_before=["tools"] pauses before ANY tool call, since there's only one tools node. For per-tool gating you need a post_model_hook that conditionally calls interrupt(), or you've outgrown the prebuilt and should hand-roll the StateGraph with per-tool routing.

drills.q: Is create_react_agent still functional in LangGraph 1.0? What replaces it, and what does the replacement add?
drills.a: Yes, still functional with no published removal date, but deprecated in favor of create_agent from the langchain package. The replacement runs on the same graph shape but adds a composable 6-hook AgentMiddleware system instead of the two fixed pre_model_hook/post_model_hook slots.

drills.q: Your team needs to add a validation phase between two rounds of tool execution — search, then a separate validation-tool pass, then answer. Should you configure this with hooks on create_react_agent?
drills.a: No. The prebuilt has exactly one tools node and no seam to add a second tool-execution phase. This is the signal to drop to a hand-rolled StateGraph with real nodes and edges for each phase.

drills.q: Why does the AgentState messages key need the add_messages reducer specifically, rather than operator.add, given create_react_agent supports checkpointer-based resume and human-in-the-loop edits?
drills.a: add_messages merges by message id, replacing an existing message when the incoming one shares an id. This is what makes an update_state correction to an in-flight tool call land as an edit instead of appending a near-duplicate — critical for HITL edit flows and resumed runs.

drills.q: State the Raft quorum formula and compute it for N=3, N=4, and N=5. Why is N=4 wasteful?
drills.a: Quorum = floor(N/2)+1. N=3 -> 2 (tolerates 1 failure). N=4 -> 3 (tolerates 1 failure -- same as N=3). N=5 -> 3 (tolerates 2 failures). N=4 costs an extra node and vote for zero additional fault tolerance over N=3, which is why production clusters use odd sizes.

drills.q: Why is Raft's election timeout randomized instead of fixed?
drills.a: A fixed timeout means every follower times out at the same instant, causing a split vote every time (no candidate gets a majority). Randomizing from a range like 150-300ms means one node almost always fires first and wins before others become candidates.

drills.q: What is a Raft "term" used for, and what happens when a node receives a message with a lower term than its own?
drills.a: Term is a logical clock over leadership epochs, incremented on every election. A node rejects any RPC carrying a lower term than its own -- this is what lets everyone safely ignore a stale, isolated leader's heartbeats once the rest of the cluster has moved to a higher term.

drills.q: Distinguish "replicated" from "committed" in a Raft log, and explain why the distinction matters for when a client gets acked.
drills.a: Replicated means appended to some follower's log, possibly a minority. Committed means replicated to a majority. A client should only be acked after commit, because only majority-replication guarantees the entry survives any future leader election (via the election restriction).

drills.q: Explain the Raft election restriction and the safety property it guarantees.
drills.a: A candidate can win a vote only if its log is at least as up-to-date (by last-entry term, then length) as the voter's own log. This guarantees any future leader's log is a superset of all previously committed entries, so committed data can never be silently lost across a leader change.

drills.q: Raft vs Paxos: did Raft win because it's more powerful? Justify with evidence.
drills.a: No -- they are proven equivalent in the conditions under which they can make progress (both require a live majority). Raft won on comprehensibility: the 2014 user study of 43 students found most scored better on Raft comprehension questions than Paxos after learning both, because Raft decomposes the problem into independently explainable subproblems (election, replication, safety).

drills.q: What is a fencing token, and why does it have to be checked at the storage layer rather than the lock service?
drills.a: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued on every lease/leadership acquisition. It has to be checked where the actual state-changing write happens because the lock service has no way to intercept a stale, paused client's write after it wakes up -- only the storage layer sees that write and can reject it if its token is lower than the last one seen.

drills.q: A Lamport timestamp of event A is less than event B's timestamp. What, precisely, can you conclude?
drills.a: Almost nothing about their causal relationship. If A causally precedes B, C(A) < C(B) is guaranteed, but the converse doesn't hold -- two fully unrelated, concurrent events can end up with any relative ordering due to arbitrary tie-breaking. Lamport clocks give a total order, not a causality guarantee.

drills.q: Why do vector clocks not scale in high-churn distributed systems, concretely?
drills.a: A vector clock carries one integer per participating node (O(n) space), and n grows with every node or client that has ever contributed to that data's history and doesn't shrink without active pruning. In high-churn systems this becomes real, growing bandwidth and storage overhead per stored version.

drills.q: Explain how a Hybrid Logical Clock computes its next value, and why it avoids the vector clock's scaling problem while still giving causal ordering.
drills.a: HLC keeps (physical_time, logical_counter). If current wall-clock time exceeds the max of last-seen HLC values (own and received), adopt it and reset the counter to 0; otherwise keep the higher physical component and increment the counter to break ties. This gives causal ordering like Lamport clocks, but at O(1) space per event since it's a single pair, not one entry per node -- no vector clock-style per-participant blowup.

drills.q: A candidate claims "we use Raft so we're split-brain proof." Where is this wrong, with a concrete example?
drills.a: Raft's split-brain prevention holds only for the log it manages -- it prevents two leaders from both committing entries in the same term. It says nothing about side effects a stale leader triggers OUTSIDE the log, e.g. a scheduler that calls an external email API on every tick: that call isn't gated by commit-index checks, only by in-memory leader state, which can be stale for as long as the partition lasts before heartbeat timeout forces a step-down.

drills.q: Design lease-based leader election for a job scheduler needing exactly one active scheduler. What is the failure mode if you skip fencing tokens, and what specifically triggers it?
drills.a: Without fencing tokens, a scheduler process that experiences a GC pause or OS preemption longer than the lease TTL keeps believing it's leader when it wakes up, because it has no way to know time passed while paused. It can then dispatch a job concurrently with the new leader (which acquired the lease after the old one's expired), producing a duplicate execution -- the fix is a monotonically increasing fencing token on every acquisition, checked by whatever system executes the scheduled jobs.

drills.q: Why does Redis being single-threaded make every command atomic?
drills.a: Only one command executes at a time with no interleaving, so no other command can observe or mutate state mid-command.

drills.q: What's wrong with running KEYS * against a production Redis instance with 10M keys?
drills.a: It walks the whole keyspace on the single command thread, blocking every other client's commands for the entire scan duration.

drills.q: You need to safely iterate all keys matching a pattern in production. What do you use instead of KEYS?
drills.a: SCAN with a cursor, doing bounded work per call so other commands can interleave; note it isn't a point-in-time-consistent snapshot.

drills.q: Your appendfsync is set to everysec and the server crashes. How much data can you lose?
drills.a: Roughly one second of writes (up to about two seconds worst case), since fsync happens on a background thread on a one-second cadence.

drills.q: A Cluster client issues MGET on two keys and gets CROSSSLOT. Why, and how do you prevent it going forward?
drills.a: The two keys hashed to different slots, which can live on different nodes, so a single-node multi-key command can't serve them. Prevent it with hash tags ({tag}:key1, {tag}:key2) so both hash to the same slot.

drills.q: Your cache-only Redis instance is throwing OOM errors on writes even though reads still work. What's misconfigured?
drills.a: maxmemory-policy is left at the default noeviction. For a pure cache, set it to allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu so old data is evicted instead of writes failing.

drills.q: A worker acquires a lock with SET k v NX EX 10, then experiences a 15-second GC pause. What can go wrong?
drills.a: The lock's TTL expires during the pause and a second worker acquires it; when the first worker resumes it may still believe it holds the lock, so both can now act concurrently on the protected resource.

drills.q: What specific gap did Kleppmann identify in Redlock, and what actually closes it?
drills.a: No fencing token, so a paused-then-resumed holder can write after a new legitimate holder has acquired the lock. Closing it requires a monotonically increasing fencing token that the protected resource itself validates and rejects if stale.

drills.q: Give the one-line honest verdict on Redis distributed locks for a system moving money.
drills.a: Treat them as a performance optimization to avoid duplicate work, not a correctness mechanism -- for money-moving mutual exclusion, use a fencing token validated at the resource or a consensus-based lock service.

drills.q: You need automatic failover for a Redis dataset that comfortably fits in one node's memory. Sentinel or Cluster?
drills.a: Sentinel -- it solves availability/failover for a single dataset that fits on one node; Cluster is for sharding a dataset too large for one node.

drills.q: A Redis Stream's memory keeps growing even though every consumer group has acked every message. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: XACK only marks a message as no longer pending, it doesn't delete it -- Streams are append-only. Fix with XTRIM (MAXLEN or MINID), either as maintenance or inline on XADD.

drills.q: You're choosing between Redis Streams and Kafka for an event pipeline expecting 2M events/sec with multiple independent consumer systems. Which fits, and why?
drills.a: Kafka -- that throughput exceeds Streams' comfortable range (~200k events/sec per stream) and independent uncoordinated consumers with durable disk retention is exactly Kafka's design point.

drills.q: What is the rough memory-per-parameter cost of full fine-tuning with Adam, and what does it total for a 7B model?
drills.a: ~16-18 bytes/param (bf16 weight+grad, fp32 master weight, fp32 momentum+variance) -> ~112-140GB for 7B, before activations.

drills.q: Write the LoRA forward pass formula and state how B and A are initialized.
drills.a: h = Wx + (alpha/r) B A x. A: small random init. B: zero init, so delta W = 0 at the start of training.

drills.q: A manager wants to fine-tune a model on internal docs so it 'knows the product.' What do you recommend instead, and why?
drills.a: Recommend RAG: knowledge injected via fine-tuning is frozen at training time, goes stale as docs change, requires a full retrain per update, and gives no provenance. Retrieval updates immediately and can cite the source chunk.

drills.q: Compute the LoRA parameter count for a 4096x4096 weight matrix at rank 16, and compare to full fine-tuning of that matrix.
drills.a: Full FT: 4096x4096 ~= 16.8M params. LoRA r=16: 4096x16 + 16x4096 = 131,072 params -- about a 128x reduction.

drills.q: Name the three QLoRA-specific tricks and what each one buys you.
drills.a: NF4 (4-bit bins at normal quantiles, fits weight distribution better than linear INT4), double quantization (quantizes the block scaling constants themselves, ~0.37 bit/param saved, ~3GB on 65B), paged optimizers (page Adam state to CPU RAM on gradient-checkpointing memory spikes instead of OOMing).

drills.q: Explain mechanically why a merged DoRA adapter adds zero inference latency despite decomposing magnitude and direction separately.
drills.a: Both the magnitude vector and the LoRA-adapted direction are linear compositions on the frozen base weight; the whole decomposition folds back into a single weight matrix before serving, identical in cost to a plain merged LoRA adapter -- no extra runtime computation.

drills.q: A team fine-tunes a support model and general coding ability regresses afterward. Diagnose and give two mitigations.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting: training pushed weights toward the narrow distribution and degraded unreinforced capability. Mitigate with LoRA/QLoRA instead of full FT, cap training epochs, mix in general instruction data, and evaluate on an out-of-domain probe set before shipping.

drills.q: Your LoRA adapter at rank 16 plateaus below full-FT quality on a code-generation task. What two changes would you try before concluding LoRA has hit a ceiling?
drills.a: Raise rank (e.g. to 32-64, since 2025 research favors intermediate ranks for complex tasks) and expand target_modules to all linear layers including MLP up/down/gate projections, not just attention Q/V, since code tasks stress MLP capacity.

drills.q: Design the fine-tuning approach for a ticket-triage model given ~5,000 historical labeled tickets. What eval-set mistake would silently hide a real production regression here?
drills.a: Fine-tune with QLoRA at r=16-32 targeting all-linear, after checking whether few-shot prompting already suffices. The eval mistake: using a random split instead of a temporally-held-out slice -- ticket types and routing categories drift over time, so a random split from the same historical window can show 95% accuracy while production routing has already shifted.

drills.q: Explain how vLLM's multi-LoRA serving avoids the cost of one full model copy per customer adapter, and what happens if you naively merge each adapter instead.
drills.a: The base model stays resident once; each adapter is applied per-request as a small batched matmul, so throughput stays near base-model speed across hundreds to thousands of adapters. Naively merging each adapter into the base produces a full-size model copy per adapter, reintroducing the storage/swap cost multi-adapter serving exists to eliminate.

drills.q: A colleague wants to fine-tune purely to shrink a long production system prompt for cost reasons. Legitimate use of fine-tuning or not, and what's the catch?
drills.a: Legitimate -- it's distilling a behavior/format pattern into weights, not injecting facts, which is exactly what fine-tuning is good at. The catch: if the few-shot examples embedded specific facts (prices, policies) rather than pure formatting/behavior, fine-tuning on them re-introduces the knowledge-injection failure mode by the back door.

drills.q: State the data-quality rule of thumb for deciding whether you have enough data to fine-tune, and the risk of ignoring it.
drills.a: 1,000 curated, diverse examples typically beat 100,000 noisy ones. Ignoring it and training on a large but low-diversity or inconsistent set causes overfitting to incidental patterns, which a held-out split from the same source won't reveal -- only an out-of-domain probe set catches it.

drills.q: Give the memory of a 70B model's weights at fp16, fp8/int8, and int4.
drills.a: fp16: 140GB. fp8/int8: 70GB. int4/nf4: 35GB.

drills.q: Is LLM decode memory-bound or compute-bound, and why?
drills.a: Memory-bandwidth-bound: at low batch size each decode step reads the full weight set from HBM and does roughly 1 FLOP of work per byte read, far below the compute/bandwidth ridge point -- the GPU's compute units sit idle waiting for weights.

drills.q: Name the two quantization methods discussed for weight-only PTQ and the core mechanism of each.
drills.a: GPTQ: layer-wise Hessian-based error correction. AWQ: protects salient weight channels identified via activation magnitude, using per-channel scaling.

drills.q: Explain why naive INT8 quantization of activations fails on LLMs specifically, when weight quantization doesn't have the same problem.
drills.a: Activations develop systematic outlier channels 20-100x larger than the rest in fixed feature dimensions across nearly every token (models >~6-7B params). A max-based INT8 scale either clips those outliers, losing important signal, or wastes nearly all its precision accommodating them. Weight distributions are uniform and don't have this outlier structure.

drills.q: Derive/state the SmoothQuant identity and explain why it's mathematically exact rather than an approximation.
drills.a: (X/s)(sW) = XW for any per-channel scale s -- dividing activation channels by s and multiplying the corresponding weight channels by s leaves the matmul output unchanged. It's exact because it's algebra applied before quantization, not a lossy transform of the computed function.

drills.q: Your team quantized weights to 4-bit with AWQ and saw a general chat eval improve almost not at all in loss, but throughput barely moved at batch size 64. What's the likely explanation?
drills.a: Batch size 64 is likely compute-bound (prefill/large-batch), not memory-bound. Weight-only quantization mainly reduces bytes moved from HBM, which helps memory-bound decode, but doesn't unlock faster matmul throughput since dequantization still happens before the matmul -- need weight+activation (W8A8/FP8) quantization to move the needle here.

drills.q: Rank general chat, long-context retrieval, multilingual, and math/code by how early they degrade under aggressive quantization, and explain why math/code is worst.
drills.a: Chat/summarization degrades least, then long-context/multilingual, then math/code degrades first and hardest -- math/code requires precise compounding multi-step reasoning where one early quantization-induced error invalidates the rest of the output, unlike open-ended chat.

drills.q: A long-running agentic coding session degrades in correctness the longer it runs, only after switching to INT4 KV cache. Diagnose.
drills.a: INT4 KV-cache quantization error compounds across every subsequent attention read of the cache -- errors accumulate over many decode steps, exactly the failure signature of long, reasoning-heavy sessions. Switch to INT8 or FP8 KV cache for this workload.

drills.q: You calibrated AWQ on 500 samples of English customer-support chat but deploy to a multilingual assistant. What breaks and why?
drills.a: The salient channels AWQ protects were tuned to English activation patterns; non-English (especially low-resource-language) inputs may activate different channels that weren't protected, causing degradation invisible in an English-only eval. Recalibrate on a sample matching the real multilingual traffic mix.

drills.q: A colleague says 'quantization always costs under 1% quality, it's basically free.' Give a concrete counterexample with a number.
drills.a: GPTQ 4-bit on HumanEval trails fp16 by roughly 10 points (46% vs 56.1%); some aggressive/naive quantization schemes have shown HumanEval pass-rate drops as severe as 92% on smaller (13B-class) models, since smaller models have less redundant capacity to absorb quantization error.

drills.q: Design a quantization strategy for a coding assistant with both a low-batch interactive path and a high-batch batch-review path.
drills.a: Interactive (memory-bound decode): AWQ 4-bit weight-only + INT8/FP8 KV cache, validated on a HumanEval-style held-out set, avoiding INT4 KV since code is a fragile task. Batch-review (compute-bound, large batch): add W8A8 (SmoothQuant-style) or FP8 activations to actually engage tensor-core throughput, calibrated on real code samples, not generic web text.

drills.q: When should you skip quantization entirely?
drills.a: When you have ample GPU memory headroom, the workload is latency-insensitive at your actual batch sizes, or reproducibility against a known fp16 baseline matters more than the memory savings -- the calibration and task-specific validation cost of doing quantization correctly is real and sometimes not worth paying.

drills.q: A colleague recommends AutoGen for a brand-new 2026 multi-agent project. What's your pushback?
drills.a: AutoGen is in maintenance mode; Microsoft redirected its roadmap to Microsoft Agent Framework (GA 1.0, 2026-04-03), which merges AutoGen's orchestration with Semantic Kernel's production features. New work should target Agent Framework, not a frozen project.

drills.q: Your ADK-based agent works fine in dev but loses all session state on every restart in production. Diagnose.
drills.a: Almost certainly still using InMemorySessionService, which is explicitly a development-only convenience. Production needs VertexAiSessionService backed by Vertex AI Agent Engine.

drills.q: A task needs durable resume across a crash and a multi-day human approval gate, but the team is building on OpenAI's Agents SDK because it's simple. What's missing, and what are the options?
drills.a: The SDK has no native cross-process checkpointing — Sessions cover in-run memory, not crash durability. Options: build durability yourself, put the agent behind a durable orchestrator like Temporal, or switch to LangGraph/ADK which have native checkpointing.

drills.q: A CrewAI-based workflow now needs 'if the ticket is high-priority, route to path A with extra validation, else path B, then converge on a shared summary step.' Can CrewAI's Process express this cleanly?
drills.a: No — CrewAI's Process is sequential or hierarchical, neither of which expresses conditional branching-then-convergence cleanly. Either bolt external dispatch logic around separate crews per path, or migrate the branching portion to a graph-based framework.

drills.q: A benchmark leaderboard shows Framework X scoring 15 points higher than Framework Y on a public agent benchmark. Should this decide your framework choice?
drills.a: Not directly. Framework choice alone has been shown to swing benchmark scores by up to 30pp on the identical model, which means the swing is dominated by graph design and tool set, not framework brand. Benchmark your own representative task before committing.

drills.q: You need real-time voice and video interaction with an agent, not request-response chat. Which framework has a genuine edge, and why?
drills.a: Google ADK — it ships native bidirectional (Bidi) multimodal streaming (text/audio/video) as a first-class production feature, ahead of the other frameworks' streaming maturity for this specific use case.

drills.q: Your team is building a 3-tool research agent, no approval gate, no multi-agent need, single model provider. Which framework, and why?
drills.a: Hand-rolled, or the thinnest SDK from your model provider. No durability, HITL, or multi-agent requirement exists, so every heavier framework on the matrix is paying for problems this task doesn't have.

drills.q: Why might a framework with a fixed multi-agent topology built two years ago be worse with a 2026 model than it was with a 2024 model?
drills.a: Per the Bitter Lesson framing, every structural component encodes an assumption the model can't do something, and those assumptions expire as models improve. A rigid decomposition built for a weaker model can actively fight a stronger model that would do better with fewer tools and a shorter loop.

drills.q: Code written against LangGraph's streaming API from 18 months ago just broke after a routine upgrade. Why, and how do you prevent it next time?
drills.a: LangGraph has been through three streaming wire formats in fifteen months (v1 tuples, v2 StreamPart, v3 typed projections). Prevent it by pinning version= explicitly rather than relying on the default, and treating the streaming surface as unstable across releases.

drills.q: Compare LangGraph's interrupt()+resume to OpenAI Agents SDK's guardrails as human-oversight mechanisms.
drills.a: interrupt() suspends the run to durable storage at an arbitrary point and Command(resume=...) continues, supporting a multi-day approval. Guardrails run input/output validation in parallel and fail fast — a real safety check, but not a durable, arbitrary-point pause; it stops a bad output rather than holding a run open for a human days later.

drills.q: You inherit a working AutoGen codebase. Leadership asks if you should rewrite it immediately. What do you say?
drills.a: No immediate rewrite needed — maintenance mode still means bug fixes and security patches flow, so a working system isn't on fire. Stop new AutoGen-specific feature development, evaluate Microsoft Agent Framework's migration path, and prioritize migration by how much the code leans on AutoGen's conversational-turn-taking patterns that don't map cleanly onto the successor.

drills.q: Both LangGraph and OpenAI's Agents SDK support multi-agent, but neither makes it the core abstraction the way ADK and CrewAI do. What's the design tradeoff?
drills.a: LangGraph (subgraphs/Send) and the OpenAI SDK (handoffs) treat multi-agent as composition on top of a single-agent primitive, so you don't pay a multi-agent abstraction tax for tasks that don't need it. ADK/CrewAI bake it in from the start, which is convenient if you know you need delegation but can bias teams toward premature decomposition when a single agent with good tools would suffice.

drills.q: Is Kafka's ordering guarantee per-topic or per-partition? What mechanism actually delivers per-key ordering?
drills.a: Per-partition only, never per-topic. Per-key ordering is a side effect of hash-based routing: messages with the same key always land on the same partition, so in-partition append order preserves per-key order. There is no cross-partition ordering guarantee.

drills.q: Define consumer lag. What does a linearly climbing lag indicate versus one partition's lag being far above the group average?
drills.a: Lag = latest_offset - committed_offset. Linearly climbing lag across the group indicates sustained under-capacity (slow processing or too few consumers for the throughput). One partition's lag far above the average indicates key skew -- a hot key concentrated on that partition -- which adding more consumers does not fix.

drills.q: What is Kafka's default log retention, and how does cleanup.policy=compact differ from the default delete policy?
drills.a: Default retention is 168 hours (7 days) under cleanup.policy=delete, which discards whole segments past that age. Compact instead retains only the latest value per key regardless of age, turning the topic into a durable snapshot of current state rather than a time-bounded event history.

drills.q: State precisely what Kafka's exactly-once semantics guarantees, and identify the boundary where it stops applying.
drills.a: The idempotent producer deduplicates retried sends (via producer-id + sequence number) and transactions make multi-partition writes plus offset commits atomic, giving effectively-once processing entirely within Kafka's own write/read path. It stops applying the instant a consumer's processing has a side effect outside Kafka (a DB write, an API call) -- that boundary is back to at-least-once and needs its own idempotency mechanism.

drills.q: Explain the difference between eager and cooperative consumer group rebalancing, and name the KIP and default assignor for the fix.
drills.a: Eager rebalancing is stop-the-world: all consumers revoke every partition and the group pauses until reassignment completes, even for unaffected consumers. Cooperative rebalancing (KIP-429, CooperativeStickyAssignor) is incremental and two-phase, revoking only the partitions actually moving while unaffected consumers keep processing.

drills.q: A tombstone was written to a compacted topic 3 days ago with delete.retention.ms at its default. A consumer does a fresh replay from the beginning today. Does it see the tombstone?
drills.a: No. The default delete.retention.ms is 24 hours; past that window the tombstone is physically removed during compaction. The key is simply absent from the replay -- there's no tombstone left to observe, so 'seeing a tombstone' only works for consumers reading continuously within the retention window.

drills.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve, and what specific mechanism does Debezium use to relay outbox events to Kafka?
drills.a: It solves the dual-write problem: an app writing to its own DB and separately publishing to a broker has no atomicity between the two operations. The outbox pattern writes an outbox row in the same DB transaction as the business data (making it atomic by construction), and Debezium reads the database's transaction log directly (binlog/WAL), not by polling the table, to relay those changes to Kafka in near real time with zero extra load on the table.

drills.q: Distinguish tumbling, hopping, and session windows, and give a case where session windows are the only correct choice.
drills.a: Tumbling: fixed-size, non-overlapping. Hopping: fixed-size, overlapping (advance step smaller than window size). Session: bounded by a gap of inactivity rather than a fixed clock. Session windows are correct when the natural grouping boundary is a behavioral gap, e.g. grouping a user's clickstream into browsing sessions defined by 30 minutes of inactivity -- a clock-based window would arbitrarily cut a continuous session at a boundary with no relationship to actual behavior.

drills.q: Why does stream processing need watermarks when batch processing has no equivalent concept?
drills.a: A batch job's input is complete and bounded by definition, so there's no ambiguity about when an aggregation is final. A streaming job's input never definitively ends and records can arrive late relative to their event time; a watermark is the explicit policy for how long to wait for stragglers before considering a window closed, an accuracy-vs-latency tradeoff that simply doesn't exist when the dataset is already complete.

drills.q: A customer reports a duplicate charge despite the producer having idempotence enabled. Where do you look, and why doesn't producer idempotence prevent this?
drills.a: Look at the consumer's side effect boundary (the payment API call). The idempotent producer only deduplicates retried sends from producer to broker via producer-id and sequence number -- it has nothing to do with what a consumer does downstream. The likely cause: the consumer called the payment API, then crashed before committing its offset, so on restart it legitimately re-read the same message (at-least-once redelivery) and called the payment API again with no idempotency key on that call.

drills.q: Design the partitioning key for an order-processing topic where one customer generates 40% of orders and per-order-id sequencing (not per-customer) is the actual ordering requirement. What key do you choose and why?
drills.a: Partition by order_id, not customer_id. Since the ordering requirement is per-order (a single order's state transitions must be sequential), keying by order_id spreads the heavy customer's orders across partitions via independent hashes, avoiding the key-skew hotspot that keying by customer_id would create, while still satisfying the actual ordering requirement.

drills.q: Compare Kafka's and Pulsar's storage architecture and state the concrete operational tradeoff Pulsar's design accepts in exchange for its benefits.
drills.a: Kafka couples compute (broker) and storage (local partition segments on the broker's disk) in one process. Pulsar separates them: stateless brokers handle routing while a separate distributed log layer (BookKeeper) holds the data, enabling independent scaling of compute vs storage and native tiered storage. The tradeoff: Pulsar requires operating two distributed systems (brokers and BookKeeper) instead of one, which is genuinely more operational complexity than Kafka for teams that don't need the independent-scaling property.

drills.q: A query filters on a column that is the leading prefix of ORDER BY. Why is it fast?
drills.a: The sparse primary index can binary-search directly to the candidate granule range for that column, so ClickHouse reads only those granules instead of the whole part.

drills.q: Is the MergeTree primary index unique per row?
drills.a: No -- it stores one entry per granule (default 8192 rows), so many rows share the same index entry.

drills.q: Your ingestion pipeline switches from batched inserts to one insert per event. What error should you expect and why?
drills.a: Too many parts -- each insert creates a new part, and per-event inserts create parts far faster than background merges can absorb, eventually hitting the protective part-count ceiling and getting rejected.

drills.q: What's the client-side fix for too-many-parts, with concrete numbers?
drills.a: Batch inserts to roughly 10K-500K rows per insert, at a cadence of about one insert every 1-2 seconds, instead of many small/per-row inserts.

drills.q: A GROUP BY over a billion rows with 200M distinct keys OOMs. What's actually driving the memory cost?
drills.a: The aggregation hash table needs roughly one entry per distinct group (200M), not per row scanned (1B) -- cardinality of the grouping key drives memory, not the rows-scanned count.

drills.q: How would you prevent that GROUP BY from crashing the whole server instead of just failing cleanly?
drills.a: Set a realistic max_memory_usage per query so ClickHouse's own limit throws a clean exception before the server-wide memory ratio is breached, and enable max_bytes_before_external_group_by so aggregation spills to disk instead of growing unbounded.

drills.q: After an OOM incident, how do you find which query actually caused it?
drills.a: Query system.query_log WHERE type = 'QueryFinish' ordered by memory_usage descending to identify the highest-memory query pattern.

drills.q: You must join a 2GB dimension table against a fact table. What goes wrong with a naive JOIN and what are two fixes?
drills.a: The default hash join loads the entire right-hand table into memory, so a 2GB dimension table can exceed max_memory_usage. Fixes: use a Dictionary engine for the dimension, or denormalize the dimension's attributes onto the fact table at ingestion time.

drills.q: A ReplacingMergeTree table returns duplicates in a query run seconds after insert. Is this a bug?
drills.a: No -- deduplication happens at merge time, not insert time, so unmerged parts still contain duplicate versions. Use FINAL for an immediate correct read at extra CPU cost.

drills.q: When would you choose a projection over a materialized view for a slow filter?
drills.a: When you need fast filtering on a column that isn't a prefix of the base table's ORDER BY and want the optimizer to transparently pick an alternate layout with no separate table to manage or route to -- provided the query doesn't need a cross-table join.

drills.q: A team wants to use ClickHouse as the primary store for an OLTP service with frequent single-row updates and point lookups gating purchase decisions. What do you tell them?
drills.a: Don't -- ClickHouse mutations are heavyweight async part rewrites, not cheap row-level updates, and it has no general ACID transaction guarantee; use a row-store OLTP database for that workload and feed ClickHouse asynchronously for the analytical side.

drills.q: Why does over-partitioning by a high-cardinality key (e.g. per-customer) make too-many-parts worse over time?
drills.a: ClickHouse never merges parts across partitions, so each high-cardinality partition value gets its own small independent pool of parts that individually may never accumulate enough volume to merge efficiently, multiplying the total unmerged part count.

drills.q: You index a document and immediately search for it and get zero hits. Is this a bug?
drills.a: No -- documents become searchable only after the next refresh (default every 1 second), so a sub-second gap between index and searchability is expected near-real-time behavior.

drills.q: What's the difference between what refresh guarantees and what flush guarantees?
drills.a: Refresh guarantees visibility to search (new segment created). Flush guarantees durability (segments fsync'd to disk and translog cleared). A refreshed-but-not-flushed document is searchable but relies on the translog for crash recovery.

drills.q: A term query against a text field for an exact multi-word value returns no results even though the data is clearly there. What's wrong?
drills.a: The text field is analyzed into separate tokens; a term query compares the raw string against those tokens and never matches a whole phrase. Use a keyword field/sub-field for exact matching instead.

drills.q: You're about to bulk-load 500M documents. What's the standard refresh_interval playbook?
drills.a: Raise refresh_interval (or set -1) before the bulk load to reduce segment churn and merge pressure, then re-enable it and optionally force a refresh once the load completes.

drills.q: What do the BM25 parameters k1 and b each control?
drills.a: k1 controls term-frequency saturation (diminishing returns for repeated term occurrences); b controls document-length normalization (discounting term frequency relative to average document length).

drills.q: Should a hard condition like tenant_id = 42 go in a query clause or a filter clause, and why?
drills.a: Filter clause -- it's a yes/no eligibility check with no relevance contribution, and filters are cacheable and cheaper than scored query clauses.

drills.q: Cluster heap usage keeps climbing and latency degrades even though data volume has been flat for months. What should you suspect?
drills.a: Oversharding -- too many small shards accumulating per-shard memory and cluster-state overhead unrelated to actual data volume.

drills.q: What's the recommended shard size range, and how do you fix an already-oversharded index?
drills.a: Roughly 10-50GB per shard. Fix by reindexing into fewer, larger shards (or using _shrink for read-only indices) -- primary shard count can't be reduced live in place.

drills.q: A dashboard needs to page through 200,000 search results sequentially. from/size or search_after?
drills.a: search_after -- from/size cost grows with page depth and hits a hard ceiling (max_result_window, default 10,000); search_after uses a cursor from the last result's sort values for depth-independent sequential paging.

drills.q: A cardinality aggregation on a high-cardinality field returns a count that's off by a couple percent. Is this a bug?
drills.a: No -- cardinality aggregations use HyperLogLog++ by default, an approximate algorithm trading exactness for bounded memory. precision_threshold can be raised for tighter accuracy at higher memory cost.

drills.q: Users report search rankings look wrong for certain queries. What's your first diagnostic step, mechanically?
drills.a: Run the query with explain:true (or the _explain API) to get the exact per-term BM25 score breakdown, rather than guessing at relevance tuning blind.

drills.q: Your team already runs Elasticsearch for log search and now wants semantic search over the same documents at moderate scale. Add a dedicated vector DB or use Elasticsearch's native vector search?
drills.a: Use Elasticsearch's native dense_vector/HNSW support with hybrid RRF fusion -- it avoids new infrastructure and lets one request blend lexical and vector scores on the same documents; a dedicated vector DB is justified mainly at very large pure-vector scale with heavy filtering/multi-tenancy needs.

drills.q: Name the three years and authors behind hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture.
drills.a: Cockburn 2005 (hexagonal), Palermo 2008 (onion), Martin 2012 (clean). Same idea, different vocabulary.

drills.q: A code reviewer sees a domain object with only getters/setters and a service class named OrderService.cancelOrder(order). What's the diagnosis?
drills.a: Anaemic domain model -- behavior that should live on the Order entity (order.cancel()) has been pushed into an orchestrating service instead, a common failure mode of layered architecture with no enforced dependency direction.

drills.q: What is the one rule that hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture all enforce, regardless of naming?
drills.a: Dependencies point inward toward the domain; the domain defines interfaces for anything it needs from the outside (a database, an API), and outer layers implement those interfaces, never the reverse.

drills.q: You inherit a codebase with folders named orders/, inventory/, billing/, but orders/ directly queries inventory's tables via SQL join. Is this a modular monolith?
drills.a: No -- shared/joined tables across modules violate the no-shared-tables requirement. It's a monolith with folder names implying boundaries that aren't enforced.

drills.q: What 2026 statistic supports 'modular monolith by default' over 'microservices by default'?
drills.a: 42% of organizations that adopted microservices have consolidated some services back into larger units, with satisfaction down 19 points vs 2024 and infra costs reported 3.75x-6x higher for equivalent functionality.

drills.q: A team split their monolith into an auth-service, a validation-service, and a database-service. Diagnose the likely outcome.
drills.a: Chattiness anti-pattern: splitting along technical layers rather than business capability means a single business operation now fans out across multiple network hops for what used to be in-process calls, with none of the independent-deployability benefit real bounded-context splits provide.

drills.q: Five engineers own fifteen microservices, and every deploy requires coordinating across most of them. What is this, and what's the fix?
drills.a: A distributed monolith -- network cost of microservices without independent deployability. Fix: consolidate services with correlated release cadence and no real scaling divergence back into a modular monolith.

drills.q: State Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver in one sentence each.
drills.a: Conway's Law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Inverse Conway Maneuver: deliberately restructure teams to match your target architecture, since moving team boundaries is cheaper than holding a service boundary against actual communication patterns.

drills.q: Describe the strangler fig pattern for extracting a microservice, and its hardest part in practice.
drills.a: Route a growing percentage of traffic to the new service via a routing layer while the old path stays live, cut over once proven, then delete the old path -- always releasable. Hardest part: keeping data consistent between old and new paths during the transition, usually requiring outbox/CDC machinery.

drills.q: Give a concrete, defensible reason to split off a microservice from day one rather than starting with a modular monolith.
drills.a: A component with an inherently different scaling/cost profile known up front, e.g. a GPU-bound transcoding pipeline next to a CPU-bound web app, where co-locating would force over- or under-provisioning one side.

drills.q: How do you enforce a modular monolith's boundaries so they don't erode under deadline pressure?
drills.a: Tooling, not convention: fitness-function tests (ArchUnit + Spring Modulith in the JVM, import-linter in Python, dependency-cruiser in JS/TS) that fail the build on a cross-module internal import or a cross-module table join.

drills.q: When is hexagonal/onion/clean architecture NOT worth adopting?
drills.a: For a CRUD app with one datastore that will never realistically be swapped and thin domain logic -- the ports/adapters/use-case indirection costs more in navigation and boilerplate than it returns in testability or swappability.

drills.q: Name the two failure interleavings in a direct dual write (DB + broker, no outbox).
drills.a: Commit succeeds, publish fails: event never sent, silent loss. Publish succeeds, commit fails/crashes: false event sent for a state change that never happened.

drills.q: Why doesn't two-phase commit fix the DB-to-broker dual write problem in practice?
drills.a: Most brokers, including Kafka, never implemented an XA resource manager, because a coordinator blocking all participants on the slowest one kills availability at scale, so nobody who runs a broker at scale wants it.

drills.q: Your outbox relay crashed between publishing an event and marking the row done. What happens on restart, and what must the consumer do about it?
drills.a: The relay republishes the row on restart (at-least-once delivery). The consumer must dedup using the inbox pattern, inserting the message id in the same transaction as applying the effect.

drills.q: Explain why a compensating transaction is not the same as a rollback.
drills.a: A rollback undoes an uncommitted transaction that nothing else ever saw. A compensation undoes a committed effect that other systems/users may have already observed or acted on -- it's a new forward-moving operation, not an erasure of history.

drills.q: A saga reserves inventory, then stalls waiting on a payment service that never responds. What's the risk, and how do you prevent it?
drills.a: Semantic-lock problem: the inventory stays reserved indefinitely because nothing but the saga's own logic is holding it, and the saga died. Prevent it with a timeout on every step that triggers compensation.

drills.q: You're designing a 5-step checkout saga. Orchestration or choreography, and why?
drills.a: Orchestration -- with more than 2-3 steps and real compensation logic, a central coordinator gives one place to query saga state and add steps, avoiding the implicit distributed state choreography produces.

drills.q: True or false: CQRS requires event sourcing. Justify.
drills.a: False. CQRS is just separate read/write models; the read model can be a plain denormalized table updated by a projector consuming ordinary domain events via an outbox. Most CQRS systems are not event-sourced.

drills.q: A user submits a form and is redirected to a page reading from a CQRS projection, which shows stale data. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The eventual-consistency window between the write committing and the projector applying the event. Fix with read-your-writes (route the immediate read to the write model) or an optimistic UI that doesn't wait on the projection.

drills.q: What makes schema evolution uniquely hard in an event-sourced system compared to a normal table?
drills.a: There's no ALTER TABLE for an immutable append-only log -- every event ever written stays forever, so every consumer must handle every historical shape, via versioned event types and upcasters.

drills.q: A team event-sourced a service 'for future flexibility' with no stated audit or temporal-query requirement. What's your assessment and recommended path?
drills.a: This is the most common event-sourcing regret -- the cost (schema evolution, GDPR crypto-shredding/forgettable-payload infra, replay-based debugging) is being paid for a benefit (CQRS-style read/write separation) that plain CQRS over normal tables gives without it. Plan a migration if the pain is real, but expect it to be multi-quarter since every event consumer needs a replacement.

drills.q: A saga step's compensation itself fails after retries. What should happen?
drills.a: There's no compensation for a failed compensation, so the saga needs a terminal failure state that pages a human rather than silently giving up -- otherwise you get a permanently double-charged customer or permanently short inventory discovered only by reconciliation.

drills.q: Design the reliability layer for a checkout flow across Orders, Inventory, and Payments services in two sentences.
drills.a: Each service publishes domain events via a transactional outbox drained by CDC; an orchestrated saga on a durable-execution engine coordinates the steps with per-step timeouts and compensations, while consumers dedup via the inbox pattern and a CQRS projection serves the order-status page without event sourcing unless there's a named audit requirement.

drills.q: Assign a blast-radius band to each: (a) list_open_tickets, (b) soft_delete_draft, (c) close_ticket, (d) issue_refund, (e) drop_table.
drills.a: (a) read_only. (b) write_reversible -- a real, cheap undo exists. (c) write_irreversible -- externally visible, no real undo. (d) financial -- moves credit/money. (e) destructive -- permanent and typically unbounded scope.

drills.q: A tool technically has a reverse-charge compensating action for a refund, but the customer already saw the transaction on their statement. What band, and which axis decided it?
drills.a: write_irreversible in practice (financial band specifically, since it's a refund), decided by externality, not by reversibility. A third party (the customer, their bank) observed it, so "you can't un-send" applies even though a compensating action exists in your own ledger.

drills.q: Explain in one paragraph why deny rules must be checked before allow rules in a permission pipeline.
drills.a: If allow were evaluated first, narrowing a broad grant would require enumerating every safe pattern instead of the handful of unsafe ones -- infeasible at scale. Deny-first lets an operator grant broadly by default (e.g. allow all Bash) and carve out exceptions (deny Bash(rm *)) that hold regardless of mode or later rule changes. This is the same guarantee AWS IAM gives across five policy types and Claude Code gives even under bypassPermissions.

drills.q: Write the resolution tuple (the minimum set of fields a permission rule must match against) and explain why tool name alone is insufficient.
drills.a: (principal, tool, argument-pattern, resource, tenant, session). Tool name alone can't express that write_file under ./src is write_reversible while the same tool under ./.github/workflows or ./secrets is destructive -- the argument pattern is what actually determines risk for many tools, not the verb.

drills.q: Diagnose: an agent's read_only search tool returned another tenant's invoices. The permission engine's rules were all correctly scoped by tool tier. What's the likely root cause and the fix?
drills.a: Tenant scoping was enforced only in the query-construction code, not bound into the credential/session context itself. A bug in that application code (missing WHERE tenant_id = ...) bypassed it entirely, and a read_only tool had no permission-layer gate because reads were assumed safe. Fix: bind tenant id into the credential so even a malformed query is mechanically confined -- belt-and-braces, not a substitute for fixing the query bug.

drills.q: Design the token scope for an agent that manages custom domains via a CLI, informed by the Railway/PocketOS incident. What specifically should the token NOT be able to do?
drills.a: Scope the token to exactly the domain-management API surface (add/remove/list custom domains for a named project), time-limited, and reject at the authorization server any request outside that surface -- including any destructive database or infrastructure operation. The Railway incident happened precisely because the token was created for one narrow purpose but carried blanket account permissions with no scope isolation; the fix is scope isolation at issuance, not detection after the fact.

drills.q: An on-call engineer needs to run one destructive query today. Design the grant using time-boxed + one-shot semantics, and state what happens if it goes unused.
drills.a: Issue a grant scoped to (principal=engineer, tool=destructive_query, tenant=X) with a short TTL (e.g. 15-30 minutes) and one_shot=True. First matching call consumes it and resolves ALLOW; consumption is logged as a separate audit event from issuance. If unused by expiry, it simply lapses -- no residual access, no manual revocation step required. The grant does not create a standing allow rule and does not override any existing deny rule for that tool/tenant.

drills.q: Explain why 'the model decided this action was safe, so we allowed it' is a permission-system defect, not a feature, referencing the confused-deputy framing.
drills.a: The entire mechanism of a prompt injection is to convince the model it is authorized. If the permission layer treats the model's own belief as evidence of authorization, then any successful injection automatically clears the gate -- the tier collapses to whatever the attacker's text says. The tier must be a static property of the tool and argument pattern, evaluated in code, independent of what instruction produced the call.

drills.q: You inherit a system where every mutating tool requires synchronous human approval, 'to be safe.' Approval p50 latency is 3 seconds and override rate is near zero. Diagnose and propose a redesign using this module's taxonomy.
drills.a: The gates are decorative -- 3-second decisions on tasks that need real judgment and a near-zero override rate both indicate rubber-stamping (T07-human-oversight).
