Redesign by band: read_only stays auto+log; write_reversible gets notify+undo window; write_irreversible gets a dry-run diff plus deterministic invariant checks (allowlists, regex, thresholds) instead of a human for the routine case; reserve synchronous human approval for financial-above-threshold and bounded destructive actions where judgment genuinely can't be automated. This concentrates human attention where a check can't substitute for it instead of diluting it everywhere.

drills.q: Rank in order of leverage: (a) prompt instructing the model to be careful with destructive tools, (b) scoped short-lived credentials, (c) deny-first ternary resolution with argument-pattern scoping, (d) audit records separating acting identity from authorizing principal. Justify the ranking against the two worked incidents in this module.
drills.a: b > c > d > a. Scoped credentials (b) remove the hazard entirely -- an agent that never holds account-wide access can't misuse it, which would have prevented Railway's incident outright. Ternary resolution with scoping (c) bounds damage when a credential is broader than ideal. Audit separation (d) doesn't prevent the incident but makes it detectable and attributable. Prompting (a) does nothing against a credential that is simply valid and broad, which both Replit and Railway demonstrate -- neither model was 'confused' in the colloquial sense, the authorization boundary itself was the defect.

drills.q: A permission engine denies a destructive_query call. The underlying platform credential would actually have allowed it if called directly. What does this mismatch tell you, and what should you do?
drills.a: The engine can only ever narrow what the platform permits, never widen it, so this specific mismatch is safe by construction -- not a security incident. But it signals the engine's model of the platform's real scope may be stale elsewhere too, possibly in the unsafe direction (believing something is denied when the platform would actually allow it, producing false confidence). Audit for divergence in both directions between the engine's decisions and the platform's actual enforced scope.

drills.q: RED or USE: which applies to a connection pool, and which applies to an HTTP endpoint?
drills.a: USE applies to the connection pool (a finite resource). RED applies to the HTTP endpoint (serves discrete requests).

drills.q: How many minutes of downtime per month does a 99.95% SLO allow?
drills.a: 21.6 minutes (0.05% of 43,200 minutes in a 30-day month).

drills.q: A histogram with 10 buckets is tracked across 50 services with no other labels. How many time series does this create in classic (non-native) Prometheus histograms?
drills.a: 500 time series, before adding any further label like region or version.

drills.q: A GPU-serving inference endpoint's request latency has doubled, but GPU utilization metrics look completely normal. What does RED/USE tell you to check next, and why?
drills.a: The disagreement between RED (endpoint latency up) and USE (GPU utilization normal) rules out the GPU itself as the bottleneck and points upstream -- check request queueing before the GPU, batching/scheduling changes, or a different saturated resource in the path (network, preprocessing) that isn't being measured. Instrument the queue itself as its own USE resource.

drills.q: Design a burn-rate alert that pages when a service is on track to exhaust 2% of its 30-day error budget in 1 hour. What burn rate and windows does this correspond to, per the Google SRE Workbook?
drills.a: 14.4x burn rate on a 5-minute short window and a 1-hour long window, both must breach simultaneously (multi-window multi-burn-rate) before paging.

drills.q: An alert fires constantly with no real incident behind it and gets muted by the team within weeks. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
drills.a: Likely a single-window threshold alert too sensitive to short blips, or a cause-based (CPU/memory) alert with no real correlation to user impact. Fix: replace with a symptom-based burn-rate alert using multi-window multi-burn-rate to require both current and sustained confirmation.

drills.q: A Grafana dashboard panel takes 20-30 seconds to load. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: An expensive PromQL aggregation is being computed live on every page load with no recording rule backing it. Fix: add a recording rule that precomputes the aggregation on ingest, and point the panel at the precomputed series.

drills.q: Your team's release velocity has ground to a halt because the error budget is exhausted almost every month within the first week. What's actually wrong, and what are the two possible fixes?
drills.a: Either the SLO target is set stricter than the system's actual reliability supports, or there's a recurring root cause never fixed between windows. Fixes: revisit whether the SLO matches real business criticality, and/or ensure the budget recovers on a rolling window rather than a punitive hard calendar reset -- and separately, root-cause and fix whatever's chronically consuming budget.

drills.q: A team 'fixes' alert fatigue by raising every alert threshold by 20% across the board. Why is this the wrong fix, even though it will reduce page volume?
drills.a: It's tuning, not fixing -- it doesn't address whether each remaining alert is actually actionable or correlated with real user impact, and it risks quietly increasing false negatives (missing real incidents) as a side effect of chasing a lower page count. The real fix is symptom-based burn-rate alerting plus deleting non-actionable alerts.

drills.q: Two teams' dashboards disagree about whether an incident happened last Tuesday. What's the likely root cause, and how does Grafana 13's dashboards-as-code help prevent this?
drills.a: Each team's dashboard likely defines 'success' for the same underlying SLI slightly differently (different latency threshold, different error-code inclusion) with no central source of truth. Git-backed, PR-reviewed dashboards make SLI/SLO definitions explicit, version-controlled, reviewable artifacts instead of tribal knowledge embedded separately in each team's panel config.

drills.q: Should a low-stakes internal admin tool used by 3 employees have a formal SLO/error-budget process with on-call paging? Justify the answer and name the trigger that would change it.
drills.a: No -- the operational cost (on-call burden, engineering time chasing a tight budget) exceeds the actual business impact of occasional downtime for a genuinely low-stakes tool. The trigger to revisit: the moment that tool's blast radius changes, e.g. it gets embedded in a customer-facing workflow -- re-evaluate then, not on a fixed schedule.

drills.q: Which of the four platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, Laminar) can you self-host without an enterprise sales conversation?
drills.a: Langfuse, Phoenix, and Laminar. LangSmith requires an Enterprise contract (reportedly $100K+ minimum) for any self-hosted deployment.

drills.q: Which platform's license is source-available but NOT OSI-approved open source?
drills.a: Arize Phoenix, under Elastic License 2.0.

drills.q: Roughly what's the cost gap between LangSmith and Langfuse at 1M trace events/month?
drills.a: LangSmith ~$2,514/mo vs Langfuse ~$101/mo -- over a 20x difference.

drills.q: A procurement policy requires OSI-approved open-source licenses only. Which of the four platforms fails this bar and why, and which two pass cleanly?
drills.a: Phoenix fails -- Elastic License 2.0 is source-available but not OSI-approved. Langfuse (MIT) and Laminar (Apache 2.0) both pass cleanly; LangSmith isn't open source at all.

drills.q: Design an instrumentation strategy today that minimizes lock-in risk regardless of which of these four platforms you pick.
drills.a: Instrument with raw OpenTelemetry using the GenAI semantic conventions rather than a platform-specific SDK/tracer, routed through an OTel Collector so the export destination is a config change. This works cleanly against Phoenix and Laminar; it reduces but doesn't eliminate migration cost off LangSmith/Langfuse since some platform features expect their own SDK shape.

drills.q: Legal flags Langfuse's ClickHouse acquisition as a risk. What's the accurate, non-alarmist answer?
drills.a: Both companies publicly committed to keeping Langfuse MIT-licensed and self-hostable, and ClickHouse has an open-source track record. But license commitments made during acquisition press cycles have a documented pattern of quietly reversing 12-18 months later (MySQL, Redis, Elastic) -- track the LICENSE file and changelog on a recurring cadence rather than treating it as permanently settled.

drills.q: Why does Laminar's ~20x trace compression matter specifically for agent workloads, and what's the catch?
drills.a: Agent runs are chatty (40-75 spans typical, mostly compressible text like prompts/tool args), so compression directly lowers data-volume-based billing for exactly this workload shape. Catch: compression trades some query/analysis latency for storage cost, and the ratio is workload-dependent -- structured/numeric-heavy traces won't compress as well.

drills.q: A team fully committed to LangGraph as their agent runtime is choosing between LangSmith and an OTel-native alternative. Make the case for LangSmith despite its cost/lock-in.
drills.a: LangSmith's node-by-node LangGraph state diffs, 'replay against a new model' regression isolation, and first-party Prompt Hub with zero assembly are genuinely deeper than a generic OTel-native platform offers for that specific stack -- the cost and lock-in is a real tradeoff against real day-one integration depth, not an oversight.

drills.q: A startup with no compliance requirements is choosing an observability platform. What do you pick, and what do you explicitly defer, and why?
drills.a: Pick Langfuse's free cloud tier or Laminar's free self-host tier -- low setup cost, full core features, no enterprise sales cycle. Defer OSI-license-purity concerns and self-hosting infrastructure investment until an actual trigger appears (a customer contract requiring data residency, or cloud pricing starting to bite at volume) -- building for a compliance requirement that doesn't exist yet is premature.

drills.q: Your team picked Phoenix for its OTel-native tracing but now needs a dashboard-and-alert-first tool for 24/7 on-call. Is Phoenix the wrong tool entirely? What's the fix?
drills.a: Not automatically wrong -- its OTel-native tracing and free self-hosting are still real strengths for deep-dive investigation. Since Phoenix is OTel-native, export the same trace data to a dashboard/alerting-first backend in parallel (see T08-classic-obs for alert design), using Phoenix for investigation and the other tool for on-call-facing alerts.

drills.q: Explain why comparing these four platforms on a feature checklist (tracing, evals, prompt management, datasets) is misleading, and what should replace that comparison method.
drills.a: All four now claim near feature parity on a checklist. The real differentiators (license terms, self-hosting cost/accessibility, cost curve shape at 10-100x pilot volume, and how much instrumentation would need rewriting to leave) only surface when you model your actual growth trajectory and constraints against each platform -- build a cost model at projected volume, confirm license/self-host terms against real requirements, and prototype the OTel-portability swap.

drills.q: What is the span naming convention for a chat completion call, and what does it look like for a call to Anthropic?
drills.a: {operation} {gen_ai.system}, so a chat call to Anthropic is named 'chat anthropic'.

drills.q: Is prompt/completion content captured by default in OTel GenAI instrumentation? What controls it?
drills.a: No, off by default. Controlled by the OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT environment variable, and content goes into span events, not attributes, when enabled.

drills.q: Name the three agent-lifecycle span types in the GenAI conventions.
drills.a: create_agent, invoke_agent, and execute_tool.

drills.q: A colleague wants to add `conversation_id` as a label on a Prometheus-style metric so they can filter dashboards by conversation. What's wrong with this, and what should they do instead?
drills.a: conversation_id is unbounded, so it creates unbounded time series (cardinality explosion), inflating cost and degrading the backend. Keep conversation_id as a span/trace attribute only; use exemplars to drill from a metric into a specific trace if the backend supports it.

drills.q: Design the span hierarchy for an agent that takes 3 turns, calling one tool on turn 2. Name each span level.
drills.a: Run span (invoke_agent) at top; 3 step spans as children, one per turn; each step span contains a model span (chat {provider}); the turn-2 step span additionally contains an execute_tool child span. Reasoning goes on each step span as an event.

drills.q: Your team is deciding between head-based and tail-based sampling for a new agent feature's traces. Make the case for tail-based.
drills.a: Head-based sampling decides upfront probabilistically, discarding rare/expensive/erroring traces at the same rate as routine ones. Tail-based decides after the trace completes, letting you keep 100% of errors, 100% of cost outliers (e.g. over $0.50), and sample only routine traffic at 5-20% -- biasing the trace store toward what an incident review actually needs.

drills.q: A trace shows an agent made 14 nearly-identical execute_tool spans before failing, but content capture was off. What can you diagnose, and what can't you, and what would fix the gap?
drills.a: You can see the tool was called 14 times and how long each took, but not whether it was retrying the same failing argument, escalating, or genuinely exploring different approaches -- that needs tool argument/result events, which weren't captured. Fix: enable content capture (redacted or feature-flagged) or add a lightweight error-reason attribute on the tool span even when full args are withheld.

drills.q: Why is hardcoding a per-token dollar price directly into your instrumentation/span-emission code a mistake, even beyond the price going stale?
drills.a: It also can't correctly represent historical cost trends -- if prices change, spans emitted after the change report the new price against old requests unless the price table is versioned with effective-date ranges and looked up per span timestamp downstream, not baked in at emission.

drills.q: Your gen_ai.usage.input_tokens numbers don't match the provider's billing dashboard. Walk through the debugging steps.
drills.a: First check whether the convention's cached+uncached combined definition is being double-counted against a separately reported cache-token line item in your cost pipeline. Reconcile against the provider's own usage/billing API directly. If still mismatched, check whether retried requests (each a full token-consuming call) are being summed across every model span in a trace, not just the last successful one.

drills.q: Your org runs OpenInference-instrumented code (Arize's convention) alongside OTel-GenAI-instrumented code, and the same underlying concept (token usage) shows up under two different attribute keys in different spans of the same trace. How do you fix this without rewriting either instrumentation library?
drills.a: Add a normalization step in the OTel Collector -- an attribute-processor rule that maps OpenInference keys to OTel GenAI keys (or vice versa) at ingestion, so downstream dashboards and queries see one consistent vocabulary regardless of which library produced the raw span.

drills.q: A single-call LLM feature (one prompt, one completion, no tools) is about to get a tool added. At what point should you refactor from a single span to the full run/step/tool hierarchy, and why not wait longer?
drills.a: Refactor as soon as there's a second decision point or a tool call that can itself fail or branch -- that's exactly when 'why did it do that' becomes a real question a flat single span can't answer. Waiting for a second or third tool means shipping blind through the first incident that needs that visibility.

drills.q: Name the two computational primitives that every RAGAS/DeepEval metric reduces to.
drills.a: Claim decomposition plus judge verdict (faithfulness, context recall), and reverse-question generation plus embedding similarity (answer relevancy).

drills.q: A faithfulness score of 1.0 comes back on an answer you suspect is wrong. What's the first thing to check?
drills.a: Whether the retrieved context itself is correct -- faithfulness only checks the answer against retrieved context, never against the world, so a faithful answer grounded in a wrong chunk scores 1.0.

drills.q: Roughly how many LLM calls does a single faithfulness computation cost, and why?
drills.a: About 4-7 calls: 1 to decompose the answer into 3-6 atomic claims, plus 1 per claim to check support against context.

drills.q: Your team wants to run RAGAS, DeepEval, and LangSmith evals in parallel on every PR 'for redundancy.' Push back on this.
drills.a: All three implement close variants of the same claim-decomposition judge primitive, so this roughly triples judge-call cost and CI time for correlated noise, not three independent signals. Pick one calibrated source of truth per metric family instead.

drills.q: Faithfulness moved from 0.82 to 0.77 after a prompt change on a 300-row eval set. Is this a real regression? What do you do before concluding either way?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- continuous judge scores have rerun noise (~14% flip rate on comparisons) and bootstrap CI half-widths of ~3-5pp. Run a paired difference test on the same examples before/after rather than comparing raw means before concluding it's real.

drills.q: Design a sample-size argument for how many paired examples you need to trust a 5-point faithfulness delta as real.
drills.a: Using n ~ 2*sigma^2*(z_alpha/2+z_beta)^2/delta^2 with sigma~0.15-0.25 and delta=0.05, you land around 100-250 paired examples at 80% power and alpha=0.05 -- below that, a 3-5pt swing is indistinguishable from noise.

drills.q: Explain what DeepEval's assert_test() is doing mechanically, and why it makes your test suite inherently flakier than a normal pytest suite.
drills.a: It's a normal pytest assertion, but the value under test is a continuous score from a noisy LLM judge call rather than a deterministic computation -- so thresholds need headroom above the metric's known noise floor, and single-run failures shouldn't be treated as proof of a regression.

drills.q: A teammate proposes using Promptfoo's llm-rubric assertion as the sole quality gate for a RAG feature. What's the specific gap?
drills.a: llm-rubric doesn't decompose retrieval from generation the way RAGAS/DeepEval's four metrics do, so you lose the attribution table that tells you whether a regression is a retrieval problem or a generation problem.

drills.q: Your nightly RAGAS suite costs $40/night with a frontier judge. Leadership wants it cut to $10 without losing the ability to catch real regressions. Design the fix.
drills.a: Route the bulk of examples to a cheap judge, escalate only borderline/near-threshold scores to the frontier judge for adjudication (cheap/frontier router pattern), and batch per-claim verdict checks into fewer calls where structured output supports it. Recalibrate against human labels specifically for the cheap judge before trusting its absolute numbers.

drills.q: After upgrading DeepEval to a new minor version, your faithfulness scores shift by 6 points overnight with no code or prompt change. Diagnose and fix the process gap.
drills.a: The framework's default metric prompt or judge model likely changed silently between versions with no changelog entry read. Treat any framework version upgrade like a judge-model swap: pin versions explicitly, and re-run human-label calibration before trusting post-upgrade scores.

drills.q: A stakeholder sees a 95% pass rate on your DeepEval suite and wants to ship, but support tickets are rising. What's missing from the suite that would explain this gap?
drills.a: The suite's canned metric rubrics were likely never calibrated against human labels for this product's actual definition of quality, and/or the golden set has gone stale relative to current production traffic -- a passing suite only means the system agrees with an uncalibrated judge's opinion of itself.

drills.q: Before naming a model architecture for any ML system design prompt, what must you establish first?
drills.a: The exact label definition, including its delay, its blind spots, and whether it's a direct observation or a proxy. Architecture, features, and metrics all follow from the label the way a conventional design's architecture follows from the API contract and schema.

drills.q: A fraud model's offline AUC is 0.97 on a problem where 0.80-0.90 is the realistic ceiling. What's your first hypothesis?
drills.a: Leakage, almost certainly from a non-point-in-time feature join or a random (rather than temporal) train/test split. An implausibly high offline metric is a red flag before it's good news.

drills.q: Why is ROC-AUC a poor primary offline metric for spam and fraud detection?
drills.a: Extreme class imbalance (positive rate often under 1%) means ROC-AUC is dominated by how well the model ranks the huge negative class, and stays high even for a model that's weak on the rare positive class that actually matters. Use PR-AUC and precision/recall at the operating threshold instead.

drills.q: A feed ranking model's offline calibration and NDCG both look great, but online engagement is flat. Name two structural reasons this can happen with zero leakage and zero bugs.
drills.a: (1) Off-policy bias: offline eval only has labels for items the CURRENT policy already showed, so it can't measure how unseen candidates would perform. (2) Feed effects (novelty, habituation) compound over days/weeks, invisible in a single-session offline slice.

drills.q: Design the cascade architecture pattern shared by fraud detection, spam/abuse detection, and content moderation. What's the shape and why?
drills.a: A fast, cheap deterministic rules layer (blocklists, velocity limits, known-bad hashes) filters obvious cases in single-digit ms, followed by a supervised model producing a calibrated risk score for everything the rules pass, with the model's uncertain-middle region routed to human review rather than auto-decided. Shape is forced by cost: running the most expensive check on 100% of high-volume traffic isn't economically viable when most of it is unambiguous.

drills.q: A churn model has excellent offline AUC and the retention campaign built on it shows a high 'success rate' among targeted users. Is that enough to prove the campaign works? Why or why not?
drills.a: No. A high success rate among flagged users just confirms the model found at-risk-looking accounts; it says nothing about whether the campaign caused them to stay. Without a held-out control group of flagged-but-untreated users, you cannot distinguish 'the campaign saved them' from 'the model found loyal users who were never going to churn anyway.' This is fundamentally an uplift-modeling problem hiding inside a classification framing.

drills.q: You have a feature store deployed. A model's online performance drops right after a migration. Walk through your first diagnostic step and why it's a feature-store-specific bug class.
drills.a: Run an online-offline value-parity check for every feature the model consumes: for a sample of entities, compare what the online store returns against what a point-in-time offline query would return for the same timestamp. A migration is exactly when transformation logic most commonly gets reimplemented in the new pipeline and silently diverges from the old one -- the feature store guarantees shared storage, not shared transformation code.

drills.q: An A/B test on a dynamic pricing change needs to avoid spillover contamination. What randomization unit do you choose and why, and name the tradeoff of your chosen method.
drills.a: Cluster-based randomization at the geographic-market level (or a switchback design alternating the whole market between treatment/control over time), because a treated rider's unfilled request changes the supply available to a control rider in the same market -- individual-level randomization is contaminated by definition. Tradeoff: switchback designs need buffer/burn-in windows between switches or carryover effects (drivers repositioned based on yesterday's price) contaminate the read.

drills.q: A spam-detection model's aggregate false-positive rate looks low and stable, but complaints from a specific user segment are rising. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
drills.a: Aggregate metrics can hide concentrated harm: a uniformly low false-positive rate is fully compatible with one segment (a language, region, or account type) experiencing a much higher rate that's diluted by a large, low-risk majority. Fix: slice every offline and online metric by relevant segments before shipping, prioritizing segments with known historical sensitivity, rather than discovering the disparity from a support-ticket spike.

drills.q: Design the retraining-cadence policy across ads CTR, spam/abuse, and churn. Should they share one cadence? Justify the driver for each.
drills.a: No single cadence fits all three. Ads CTR retrains near-continuously (hours) because inventory and campaigns turn over hourly. Spam/abuse cadence should be tied to the empirically measured half-life of an attack pattern (can be days), because the adversary actively probes and adapts to the deployed model. Churn retrains weekly to monthly because behavioral drift is slow and the label horizon (30-90+ days) is long. The generalizable rule: cadence follows how fast the label's underlying reality changes relative to how fast you can detect that it changed.

drills.q: An interviewer asks you to design an A/B testing platform. There's no trained model here -- what's the platform's equivalent of 'the label,' and what's the equivalent of a leaked feature?
drills.a: The equivalent of 'the label' is the metric definition and the statistical significance test used to decide a winner. The equivalent of a leaked feature is computing an experiment's outcome metric using data from users exposed to the surface but not actually assigned by that experiment's randomization (common when experiments overlap on the same surface), which inflates or deflates the read the same way a leaked feature inflates offline AUC -- caught by auditing that the metric's population exactly matches the randomized population.

drills.q: Aggregate GPU utilization on an ML training platform is reported at 70%, but teams still complain about long queue times for large distributed jobs. What's the likely cause and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: Fragmentation, not a capacity shortage: free capacity is scattered in small non-contiguous chunks across many nodes rather than concentrated in one allocatable block large enough for a big distributed job. Confirm by tracking allocatable-contiguous-capacity per node/rack, not just an aggregate busy/idle ratio, which hides exactly this failure mode.

drills.q: Is FAISS a vector database? What is it instead?
drills.a: No. It's a C++/Python library of ANN algorithms with no server, persistence, filtering, replication, or multi-tenancy built in.

drills.q: Give the HNSW memory formula.
drills.a: bytes_per_vector ~= 1.1 * (4*dim + 8*M)

drills.q: Compute bytes/vector and total GB for 1M vectors, 768 dimensions, M=16.
Name the three concrete forcing functions to leave pgvector for a dedicated vector database -- not 'vector count'.
drills.a: Build/rebuild time exceeding the maintenance window, filtered-query p99 missing an SLA, and needing horizontal write scaling.

drills.q: A top search result is confidently wrong but latency and infra look healthy. What's the first thing to check?
drills.a: Embedding model/version mismatch between index time and query time -- the most common real cause.

drills.q: Describe the concrete diagnostic for a suspected stale or drifted embedding pipeline.
drills.a: Re-embed a known corpus item with the current pipeline, compare cosine similarity to the stored vector for that same item -- should be ~1.0. If not, the pipeline (model version, normalization) has drifted.

drills.q: How does Weaviate's multi-tenancy architecturally differ from Qdrant's and Milvus's, and what problem does it sidestep?
drills.a: Weaviate physically isolates tenants (dedicated shard/collection per tenant), sidestepping the filtered-ANN reconciliation problem entirely. Qdrant/Milvus filter within a shared index (payload field / partition), inheriting pre/post-filter cost tradeoffs.

drills.q: Name four scenarios where vector search is the wrong retrieval tool entirely.
drills.a: Exact lookups (B-tree), pure structured filter queries (SQL), small keyword-heavy corpora (BM25 wins), and hard explainability requirements (opaque cosine score).

drills.q: Why is a high-cardinality filter like tenant_id the expensive case for both pre-filtering and post-filtering, across every HNSW-based vector database?
drills.a: Pre-filter has no index over an arbitrary small subset, degenerating to brute force. Post-filter's greedy search routes through nearest unfiltered neighbors and can strand away from filter-valid nodes. High cardinality shrinks the valid subset the most, worsening both -- structural to HNSW, not vendor-specific.

drills.q: A team running a 200K-document internal search tool wants to adopt Milvus. What's the pushback?
drills.a: At 200K documents none of Milvus's differentiators (K8s-native compute/storage separation, billion-scale headroom) are used, but the team pays full operational cost of a distributed system. Push back toward naming the actual requirement; without one this is precautionary over-engineering -- pgvector or FAISS-backed service would serve this scale cheaply.

drills.q: Design the vector storage strategy for a platform starting at 500K vectors on pgvector, expected to reach 80M vectors with multi-tenant ACL requirements in 18 months.
drills.a: Start on pgvector. Instrument the three forcing functions from day one (HNSW rebuild time trend, filtered p99 by tenant size, write throughput ceiling). Re-evaluate against measured numbers as corpus grows, since pgvector's viable ceiling keeps moving upward. If fine-grained per-tenant isolation is the dominant driver, that points to Weaviate; if raw scale is the driver, that points to Milvus -- name which axis is actually forcing the eventual migration.

drills.q: What's the corpus-level question, as opposed to the single-skill question?
drills.a: Does the whole corpus stay one coherent system as it grows -- composition, collisions, shared invariants -- not just does any one skill fire correctly.

drills.q: Roughly what does one skill's listing entry cost in tokens?
drills.a: About 100 tokens (name + description), paid every session regardless of whether it's used.

drills.q: Name the four skill composition patterns.
drills.a: Serial, parallel, conditional routing, and recursive/nested invocation.

drills.q: Which composition pattern scales best and why?
drills.a: Serial composition through a shared artifact on disk -- it doesn't require one skill to know another exists, only that both agree on the artifact's shape.

drills.q: Name the corpus-scale failure mode where two skills each pass their own trigger test individually.
drills.a: Description collision -- the same or similar prompt fires a different skill on different sessions because their vocabularies now overlap.

drills.q: How do you detect description collision across a corpus?
drills.a: Run every skill's should-trigger prompts against the WHOLE corpus and flag any prompt that fires more than one skill.

drills.q: How does composition/collision risk scale with corpus size?
drills.a: Combinatorially -- n skills yield up to n(n-1)/2 possible pairwise compositions, and the same arithmetic for pairwise collisions.

drills.q: In this repo's reference architecture, what is the fragments-not-aggregates invariant and what does it buy?
drills.a: Every content-writing skill writes its own fragment file rather than hand-editing generated aggregates; a build step merges by id, letting many independently-invoked skills run in any order with no race.

drills.q: What is the weakest link in this repo's fragments-not-aggregates invariant?
drills.a: It's enforced by README convention only, not by code -- Level 1 instruction, not Level 3 enforcement; nothing stops a new skill from hand-editing the aggregate directly.

drills.q: Why does a skill's cost model change inside a forked subagent?
drills.a: A subagent's preloaded skills inject full content at startup rather than following the regular session's progressive name+description listing -- a cheap skill in the main session can be a real cold-start cost once nested.

drills.q: Is a marketplace with hundreds of thousands of community skills a quality signal?
drills.a: No -- it's adoption evidence for the format, not a quality or safety signal for any individual skill in the pool.

drills.q: When is a skill-mediated architecture the wrong corpus-level design?
drills.a: When most capability is unconditional (belongs in a rules file) or deterministic-and-fragile (belongs in scripts/tools) -- padding a corpus with misclassified content dilutes listing budget for the skills that actually need progressive disclosure.

drills.q: Name two things agents are genuinely good at in architecture review.
drills.a: Consistency checks across a large codebase against a stated invariant, and missing-case enumeration against a contract (also: drafting and drift detection).

drills.q: Why can't an agent judge whether a tradeoff is right for a specific org?
drills.a: That judgment depends on institutional memory (past outages, political compromises, customer contracts) never written down anywhere the agent could be shown.

drills.q: Which ADR field must always require a named human, and why not agent-filled?
drills.a: The Decision field -- it's the one place the org's actual judgment must appear, attributed to someone accountable for it.

drills.q: Name the failure mode of agent-generated design docs from an existing codebase.
drills.a: Confident-description drift -- describing what the code looks like it does rather than what it actually does, with equal fluency whether right or wrong.

drills.q: Why is a model reviewing its own design output a weak check?
drills.a: It checks whether the design looks like the kind of thing generated correctly, not whether it matches reality -- the same weights rationalize the same shortcut twice.

drills.q: What three properties define an effective adversarial design review?
drills.a: A different model family, no shared reasoning context (read-only, cold), and 'enumerate every failure mode' framing instead of an approve/reject verdict.

drills.q: How do you mechanically check a design doc against real code?
drills.a: Extract every checkable claim, locate the implementing code, report match/mismatch with file+line evidence, and track unverifiable claims as a separate category from confirmed matches.

drills.q: Why must 'could not verify' never collapse into 'matches' in a drift checker?
drills.a: It reintroduces the confident-description failure the check exists to catch, one layer up -- a false confirmation is worse than an honest unverified flag.

drills.q: What's the estimated annual documentation-drift cost for a 50-person engineering team, and why does it compound under agent-assisted development?
drills.a: Upward of $200K/year; commit velocity is higher with agent assistance, so more surface area drifts, faster.

drills.q: State the accountability line for AI-assisted architecture review in one sentence.
drills.a: The agent does not own the decision, at any point in the pipeline, regardless of how good its draft was -- this is a governance requirement, not a capability gap that better models fix.

drills.q: Is a bot that auto-approves PRs conforming to accepted ADRs a complete review solution?
drills.a: No -- it's reliable for mechanical conformance but can't judge whether the underlying ADR itself still holds; that still needs periodic human review with institutional context.

drills.q: If two different models independently agree a design is sound, how much should that weigh?
drills.a: Less than it sounds -- both may share a systematic blind spot in how models reason about that problem class. It's evidence to weigh, not a decision made automatically.

drills.q: Which of Claude Code and Codex leads Terminal-Bench 2.0, and by roughly how much (as of 2026-08-01)?
drills.a: Codex leads, 77.3% vs Claude's 65.4%.

drills.q: Which tool wins blind pairwise code-cleanliness review, and roughly how often?
drills.a: Claude Code, roughly 67% of the time.

drills.q: Why can't Cursor run headless in CI?
drills.a: It's an IDE -- the interaction model assumes a human watching diffs. This is architectural, not a settings gap.

drills.q: Is Microsoft Agent Framework a fourth finished coding agent competing with Claude Code/Codex/Cursor?
drills.a: No -- it's an SDK for building a harness, one level down the stack; it competes with hand-rolling your own loop.

drills.q: What's the Agent Framework gotcha that silently kills long sessions?
drills.a: Compaction is disabled unless BOTH MaxContextWindowTokens and MaxOutputTokens are supplied, with no error on omission.

drills.q: What Claude Code permission mechanism does NOT fire in headless (-p) mode, and what replaces it?
drills.a: PermissionRequest hooks don't fire; enforcement must be re-derived via PreToolUse hooks or --allowedTools.

drills.q: Distinguish model lock-in from workflow lock-in for Cursor specifically.
drills.a: Low model lock-in (BYO API key reaches Claude/GPT/Gemini); high workflow/IDE lock-in (extensions, keybindings, muscle memory are Cursor-specific).

drills.q: What's the difference between 'configuration control' and 'implementation control' over an agent loop, and which tools offer implementation control?
drills.a: Configuration control tunes an existing loop (hooks, permission rules -- all three finished products). Implementation control means rewriting the loop itself -- only Agent Framework or hand-rolling.

drills.q: A team needs an agent's permission decisions to consult an internal compliance policy service per call. Which tool fits and why do the other three fall short?
drills.a: Agent Framework -- it needs implementation control over the permission engine, which none of the three finished products expose past fixed hooks or diff-accept UIs.

drills.q: Why should a hard requirement like headless CI disqualify a tool rather than just lower its average score?
drills.a: A tool great on 8 axes but structurally unable to meet a required 9th is disqualified, not '8/9 good' -- averaging hides an architectural gap that surfaces later as a costly switch.

drills.q: Why does this module explicitly warn that its own cited benchmark numbers will be stale?
drills.a: Four vendors ship monthly; any specific score is a snapshot. The nine evaluation axes are durable; the numbers on them are not.

drills.q: Does picking the 'best' harness substitute for code review discipline?
drills.a: No -- harness choice affects speed and cleanliness of generation, not whether architecture and review are sound. Weak review produces bad outcomes on any of the four, just at different speed.

drills.q: What is the central design decision when authoring an MCP server?
drills.a: Tool granularity -- neither too fine (ORM-shaped) nor too coarse (a god-tool with an action string).

drills.q: What is the linguistic tell of a too-fine tool set?
drills.a: Naming a tool requires 'and' -- it's doing an assembly/join step the caller's code should have done.

drills.q: What is the linguistic tell of a too-coarse tool (a god-tool)?
drills.a: Naming it requires 'or' -- a decision got hidden inside a string argument instead of the tool boundary.

drills.q: At roughly what tool count does selection accuracy start collapsing, per 2026 benchmark data?
drills.a: Around 20 tools accuracy is still ~19/20; by ~107 tools it approaches complete failure. A pooled unfiltered catalogue scored 13.62% in one stress test.

drills.q: GitHub Copilot cut its tool count from 40 to 13. What did it gain?
drills.a: A ~400ms latency reduction and a 2-5 percentage point accuracy improvement on the same tasks.

drills.q: List the three fixes for tool-selection collapse, cheapest first.
drills.a: Namespace by service prefix; curate to real workflows instead of auto-wrapping every endpoint; progressive disclosure (list_capabilities/invoke) or topic-scoped sub-servers.

drills.q: Why should a tool never accept a secret as an argument?
drills.a: The model holds the value in its own context and can echo it into a later call, a log, or its final response. Read secrets server-side at call time instead.

drills.q: Explain the difference in purpose between dry_run and an idempotency key on a mutating tool.
drills.a: dry_run previews the effect before it happens, for trust and plan verification. An idempotency key makes a retried call return the stored result instead of double-executing. They solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other.

drills.q: Derive an idempotency key for a tool call and name the common bug in doing so.
drills.a: hash(session_id, tool_name, sorted(args)). Common bug: not sorting the args, so logically identical calls with differently-ordered keys hash differently and the mechanism silently fails.

drills.q: Where should a tool's failure be surfaced in an MCP response, and what breaks if you get it wrong?
drills.a: As isError:true content in the tools/call result, never a raw JSON-RPC protocol error. Getting it wrong raises a client-side exception that kills the whole run instead of giving the model something to react to.

drills.q: What are the two separate evals needed to validate an MCP server, and what does each expose?
drills.a: Selection accuracy (right tool, valid args -- exposes granularity problems) and task success (right outcome -- exposes schema/error-message problems). A server can pass one and fail the other.

drills.q: When is building an MCP server the wrong call for an internal tool?
drills.a: When exactly one agent in one process will ever call it -- a direct function call is faster and has no schema/subprocess/network overhead, and MCP earns its cost only with a genuinely different consumer.

drills.q: Name the three multi-tenancy isolation models in order of increasing resource sharing.
drills.a: Silo (dedicated stack per tenant) -> bridge (mixed, some shared some siloed by tenant tier) -> pool (everything shared, isolated logically).

drills.q: A pool-model service enforces tenant isolation only via 'remember to add WHERE tenant_id = ? to every query.' What class of bug does this produce, and what's the durable fix?
drills.a: Cross-tenant object-level authorization bypass (OWASP API1) -- a convention gets violated the first time an endpoint is written under deadline pressure. Durable fix: enforce at a layer new code can't bypass, e.g. Postgres row-level security or a mandatory data-access wrapper requiring a tenant context to construct any query.

drills.q: State the unit-cost formula and identify what makes a cost breakdown actually actionable versus just informative.
drills.a: unit_cost = (direct allocations + shared costs / stated allocation method) / units delivered. It's actionable when it names the DOMINANT line item -- the one that scales linearly with the growth metric -- not just a total; a breakdown with 15 roughly-equal items tells you nothing about what to optimize.

drills.q: Compute: 10M requests/month, LLM inference at avg 800 tokens in + 200 out, blended $6/M tokens. What's the monthly inference cost, and why does this number matter more than the total bill?
drills.a: 10M x (800+200) tokens = 10^10 tokens = 10,000M tokens x $6/M = $60,000/mo... using the module's blended rate: 1M tokens/req total x 10M req = 10,000M tok x $6/M = $60,000/mo (module example used slightly different mix, ~$48k). It matters more than the total because it's the line item that scales LINEARLY with the metric the product wants to grow -- doubling usage without a caching/routing change doubles this cost specifically, not the whole bill uniformly.

drills.q: Distinguish what dual-write-with-reconciliation validates versus what shadow traffic validates in a migration.
drills.a: Dual-write + reconciliation validates DATA consistency: does the new store's data match the old store's data. Shadow traffic validates BEHAVIORAL correctness: does the new system's computed output/decision match the legacy system's, using duplicated (not routed) production requests, before any user-facing traffic depends on it.

drills.q: A team's reconciliation job has reported zero drift for two weeks. Is it safe to decommission the legacy system? What must be checked first?
drills.a: Not automatically. Check whether the reconciliation job would actually catch every class of drift it claims to (a checksum comparison can miss a row-level replacement that happens to produce the same checksum), and verify it against an injected known-bad record. A clean report could mean the job stopped running silently, not that the systems agree.

drills.q: Why does decommissioning the legacy system immediately after cutover looks fine but is actually a rollback failure waiting to happen?
drills.a: Rollback's cheapness depends entirely on the legacy system still being live and capable of resuming service. Removing it as soon as the new system 'looks stable' trades away the safety net before confidence in the new system was actually earned (proven via a stated observation window), not just assumed because nothing broke yet.

drills.q: Write a one-sentence test for whether an RFC's 'alternatives considered' section is real analysis versus decorative filler.
drills.a: Could a smart reader who disagreed with your recommendation use this section, in your own words, to argue for a different option -- i.e. does each rejected alternative state its actual cost AND the scenario where it would have been the correct choice, rather than being strawmanned or left cost-free.

drills.q: An RFC gets approved, then re-litigated three weeks later when a senior engineer raises an objection nobody addressed. Diagnose the PROCESS failure, not the technical decision.
drills.a: The objection was predictable but wasn't surfaced before the review -- either the draft wasn't routed past the people most likely to raise it, or the risks-and-mitigations section didn't anticipate it. Fix: route future drafts past the harshest likely skeptic before the formal review round, treating 'what would the harshest reasonable reviewer say' as a required pass, not an optional nicety.

drills.q: How should the rigor of a decision document (Slack message + ADR vs. full RFC) scale, and who decides which category a decision falls into?
drills.a: Scale rigor to how expensive the decision is to REVERSE and how many teams it constrains -- a cheap two-way door doesn't need a 5-page RFC, an org-wide one-way door does. The categorization rule itself needs to be a stated, lightweight, discoverable norm (e.g. 'touches more than one team's data model or is expensive to reverse -> RFC'), not a fresh judgment call each time, or the norm itself becomes a recurring point of disagreement.

drills.q: You inherit a multi-tenant system with no documented isolation tier per tenant, no cost attribution, and no migration history. What do you audit first and why?
drills.a: The isolation boundary first: verify tenant scoping is enforced at a layer that can't be bypassed (RLS, mandatory wrapper) rather than only by application convention. It's the highest-blast-radius unknown -- a cross-tenant data exposure is a failure you don't get a second chance to catch before it's exploited or reported, whereas cost attribution and migration documentation are recoverable if delayed a quarter.

drills.q: A migration project is being deprioritized against feature work. Reframe the 'we should modernize this' argument in the same unit-cost language the rest of this module uses.
drills.a: Name the ongoing ost in comparable terms: engineering hours/quarter spent on workarounds, incident rate or MTTR delta attributable to the legacy system, and a specific dated cliff (vendor EOL, scaling ceiling with a stated headroom number) if one exists. Separate the 'cliff' argument (time-boxed, revisable if the estimate is wrong) from the 'ongoing tax' argument (accrues regardless of the cliff date), so a revised cliff estimate doesn't kill the whole business case, only the urgency framing.

drills.q: What does a p-value actually mean, and what's the most common wrong answer?
drills.a: P(data this extreme | null hypothesis true). Wrong answer: 'probability the null hypothesis is true' -- that requires a posterior and a prior, which a p-value never computes.

drills.q: Derive the Beta-Binomial posterior update rule.
drills.a: Multiply Binomial likelihood theta^k(1-theta)^(n-k) by Beta prior kernel theta^(alpha-1)(1-theta)^(beta-1); exponents combine to theta^(alpha+k-1)(1-theta)^(beta+n-k-1), the kernel of Beta(alpha+k, beta+n-k).

drills.q: Variant A: 95/1000 conversions. Variant B: 120/1000. With a flat Beta(1,1) prior, what are the posteriors and roughly what's P(B>A)?
drills.a: Posterior A = Beta(96,906), mean ~9.6%. Posterior B = Beta(121,881), mean ~12.1%. Monte Carlo sampling both gives P(B>A) around 97%.

drills.q: Why is a credible interval not the same claim as a confidence interval?
drills.a: A credible interval says P(true parameter in range | data) = 95%, a direct probability statement. A confidence interval is a statement about the procedure over repeated experiments -- 95% of such intervals would contain the true value -- and says nothing about the probability for the one interval you computed.

drills.q: What are R-hat and ESS, and what thresholds indicate a trustworthy MCMC run?
drills.a: R-hat (Gelman-Rubin) compares between- vs within-chain variance across multiple chains; should be < 1.01. ESS corrects raw sample count for autocorrelation; should be > ~400 per parameter. Also check for near-zero divergent transitions in HMC/NUTS.

drills.q: Explain the funnel geometry problem in hierarchical models and its fix.
drills.a: When the population-level variance (tau_pop) is small, group-level parameters are forced tightly together, creating a narrowing funnel shape that breaks HMC's fixed step size and causes divergent transitions. Fix: non-centered parameterization -- sample z ~ Normal(0,1) and construct theta = mu + tau*z instead of sampling theta directly.

drills.q: Is Bayesian A/B testing immune to the peeking problem that inflates frequentist false positives?
drills.a: Not unconditionally -- true immunity requires a pre-registered, fixed stopping/decision rule. An analyst staring at a live posterior and stopping 'whenever it looks good' is still a data-dependent stopping rule and can bias results, just typically less severely than naive frequentist peeking.

drills.q: Why does HMC/NUTS need far fewer iterations than Metropolis-Hastings for the same effective sample size?
drills.a: HMC uses the gradient of the log-posterior to simulate Hamiltonian dynamics, producing long, informed, low-autocorrelation trajectories instead of a random walk. This gives 10-100x fewer iterations needed for equivalent ESS; NUTS further automates step size and trajectory length.

drills.q: Design a Bayesian hierarchical framework for evaluating a content template across 200 campaigns with traffic ranging from 200 to 500,000 impressions/month.
drills.a: Model logit(theta_i) ~ Normal(mu_pop, tau_pop), non-centered, estimated jointly across all 200 campaigns. Add a regional second level if a natural grouping exists. Run offline (MCMC doesn't need live-dashboard latency), refresh daily/weekly, flag campaigns still dominated by the prior (too little own data). This prevents small campaigns from generating false winners/losers off single-digit conversion counts.

drills.q: A colleague's informative prior, 'based on similar past campaigns,' happens to favor the launch they already wanted. How do you evaluate this without assuming bad faith?
drills.a: Ask how the prior was derived -- a pre-specified reference class of past campaigns is legitimate; a prior fit after seeing this campaign's early data is prior-hacking, equivalent to p-hacking. Run a sensitivity check: refit with a flat/uninformative prior. If the launch recommendation only holds under the informative prior, that's a load-bearing modeling choice that must be surfaced to decision-makers, not buried in a final probability slide.

drills.q: An SVP wants a yes/no launch call off a single posterior probability of 92%. How do you handle the room?
drills.a: State plainly what 92% means (given the data, ~92% chance the true effect is positive), then immediately attach the credible interval for effect size so they see whether it's a strong win or a rounding error. Give the recommendation implied by the pre-agreed decision rule (probability threshold AND expected-loss threshold), not a rule invented on the spot to satisfy the demand for certainty.

drills.q: Why is a conversion-probability model the wrong tool for deciding who to target with a promotion?
drills.a: It predicts P(convert|X), which is high for both sure things (convert regardless) and persuadables (convert because of treatment) -- it can't distinguish them, so targeting off it wastes spend on sure things.

drills.q: Define CATE.
drills.a: tau(x) = E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x] -- the expected difference between a unit's potential outcome under treatment and under control, conditional on its features.

drills.q: What's the main weakness of the two-model (T-learner) uplift approach?
drills.a: The treated and control models are fit independently and can have different bias/variance behavior; subtracting two independently-noisy models can amplify noise rather than cancel it, especially with imbalanced arm sizes.

drills.q: What assumption does difference-in-differences rely on, and why is it fundamentally untestable?
drills.a: Parallel trends -- absent treatment, the treated and control groups' outcomes would have moved together. Untestable because it's a claim about an unobserved counterfactual after treatment; you can only support it with pre-treatment trend evidence and placebo tests.

drills.q: What is propensity score matching's core assumption, and name a real critique of the method.
drills.a: Unconfoundedness/ignorability: conditional on measured covariates, treatment is as good as random (no unmeasured confounders) -- unfalsifiable. King & Nielsen (2019) showed matching on a single propensity score can increase covariate imbalance and model dependence versus full/exact matching in some regimes.

drills.q: Explain the exclusion restriction for instrumental variables with a marketing example.
drills.a: The instrument must affect the outcome ONLY through treatment. Example: an ad-server outage shifting who sees an ad, used as an instrument for exposure -- broken if the outage also correlates with a site-wide issue that independently affects purchasing, giving the instrument a second pathway to the outcome.

drills.q: How do causal forests differ from standard random forests?
drills.a: Standard forests split to reduce outcome prediction error. Causal forests split to maximize heterogeneity in the ESTIMATED TREATMENT EFFECT across leaves, using honest splitting (disjoint samples for choosing splits vs estimating effects) to give asymptotically valid confidence intervals on tau(x).

drills.q: Why can't you evaluate an uplift model with ordinary classification AUC?
drills.a: There's no single ground-truth uplift label per individual to score against (you never observe both potential outcomes for one person). Instead use the Qini curve / uplift AUC on a randomized holdout, which measures cumulative incremental conversions within top-k ranked slices by comparing treated vs control conversion rates.

drills.q: Legal has blocked withholding personalization from any user, so you can't run a clean randomized holdout to measure a new email campaign's causal lift. Design a measurement plan.
drills.a: First push to get even a small (e.g. 5%) holdout approved -- usually defensible and far superior to any observational method. If truly blocked, fall back to a geo-level staggered rollout, estimating lift via DiD or synthetic control comparing rolled-out vs not-yet-rolled-out markets, checking pre-period parallel trends. Use PSM only as a secondary sensitivity check, flagging its unconfoundedness assumption as the weak link, not the primary estimate.

drills.q: A colleague wants to target retention offers using a churn-propensity model's output directly. What's the flaw, and what's a 'sleeping dog' in this context?
drills.a: The model predicts P(churn|X), not the effect of the offer -- some high-churn-propensity users will leave regardless (wasted spend) and some low-propensity users might be exactly who the offer would save. A sleeping dog here is a user for whom the retention offer actually INCREASES churn (e.g. an email reminding an inattentive customer they have a subscription, prompting cancellation) -- only an uplift/CATE model can surface this negative-effect segment.

drills.q: Why is brand voice conditioning insufficient protection against hallucinated facts?
drills.a: Tone and factual accuracy are orthogonal properties of generated text controlled by different mechanisms -- a model can be perfectly on-brand while stating a completely fabricated fact.

drills.q: What claim types should never be openly LLM-generated in production marketing copy?
drills.a: Price, availability, policy terms, and health/safety statements -- anything a customer could reasonably rely on and later hold the company to. These need retrieval-grounding or template-filling from verified data, not free generation.

drills.q: Summarize the Air Canada chatbot case and its architectural implication.
drills.a: The airline's chatbot fabricated a bereavement-fare policy; a tribunal held Air Canada contractually bound, rejecting the defense that the chatbot was a separate entity. Implication: claims customers could rely on must be grounded in verified retrieved data, not left to open generation with a disclaimer.

drills.q: Compare few-shot/prompt-based brand voice conditioning to fine-tuning.
drills.a: Few-shot: cheap, fast to iterate, weaker under distribution shift/unusual inputs. Fine-tuning (typically LoRA/QLoRA): more robust and consistent at scale, slower/costlier to update, risks baking in any errors in the curated training corpus.

drills.q: What does a production content quality gate score and what should it do with the scores?
drills.a: Brand-voice adherence, factual-risk flags (price/date/superlative/health/financial claims), compliance flags, fluency -- via a lightweight fast classifier, not another LLM call. It should TRIAGE by risk: auto-publish/spot-check for low-risk, mandatory human review for flagged or uncertain content.

drills.q: What is the rubber-stamping failure mode in human-in-the-loop review and how do you detect it?
drills.a: When review volume outpaces capacity or the gate mostly produces false positives, reviewers stop genuinely scrutinizing content and approve by default. Detect by sampling approved content for independent secondary review -- a near-zero disagreement rate with high throughput signals rubber-stamping.

drills.q: Why does a quality gate calibrated on English content fail on other locales?
drills.a: Hallucination rates and voice-adherence baselines differ by language -- lower-resource languages typically have higher error rates due to less training representation, and tone/formality norms differ by culture. An English-tuned threshold is usually too permissive elsewhere and needs per-locale recalibration.

drills.q: Why is a source-fact-to-claim audit trail treated as a compliance requirement, not just engineering hygiene?
drills.a: Given FTC enforcement priorities on deceptive AI marketing claims, EU AI Act labeling requirements, and legal precedent (Air Canada) holding companies liable for AI-generated statements, being able to show which verified source grounded a specific published claim is the difference between a defensible and indefensible position if challenged.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants to remove human review entirely for a high-volume content category to cut costs. How do you evaluate the request?
drills.a: Assess the content category's risk tier: genuinely low-stakes, highly templated content with a strong quality-gate track record can move to spot-check or auto-publish. Anything touching price, availability, legal claims, or flagship messaging should stay behind mandatory review regardless of gate performance, because the cost asymmetry of one bad instance vastly outweighs throughput savings.

drills.q: Design the content-generation architecture for a travel company shipping property descriptions across 22 locales where amenities and pricing must never be fabricated.
drills.a: Verified structured property data feeds a RAG-constrained generation step (ideally template-filling factual fields directly, LLM-generating only surrounding prose). Brand voice via locale-specific fine-tuning/few-shot, calibrated per locale, not inherited from English. A per-locale-calibrated quality gate routes by risk, with mandatory human review for price/availability/policy language regardless of locale. Full audit trail logs source-to-claim mapping for every published description.

drills.q: Why is DCO better framed as a bandit problem than a static A/B test?
drills.a: Creative performance is non-stationary -- it fatigues over time. A bandit continuously reallocates traffic and can pull back from a decaying 'winner' in near-real time, unlike a fixed-horizon test that makes one discrete decision at the end.

drills.q: What heuristic signals commonly flag creative fatigue?
drills.a: CTR decline of roughly 10%+, CPA rise of roughly 15%+, and impression frequency exceeding roughly 3 per user in prospecting campaigns -- category-dependent heuristics, not universal constants.

drills.q: Why does full-combination DCO across many creative components hit a traffic wall?
drills.a: Each unique combination needs roughly the per-arm sample size a standalone test would, so total traffic requirement scales with combination count (L^k-style) -- e.g. 4 headlines x 5 images x 3 CTAs = 60 arms needing individual convergence.

drills.q: What do feature-level (component) DCO bandits assume, and when does that assumption break?
drills.a: They assume components combine roughly additively. It breaks when a specific pairing has a real interaction effect the additive model can't capture -- that pairing then needs to be tested as its own dedicated arm.

drills.q: Why doesn't a standard bandit automatically account for creative fatigue?
drills.a: Its reward estimate is an un-decayed average/posterior over all history, implicitly assuming stationary reward. It keeps over-allocating traffic to a fatiguing creative because the historical average lags the true declining trend.

drills.q: Name two mechanisms to make a bandit fatigue-aware, and explain why they're complementary rather than substitutes.
drills.a: Exponential decay/sliding window on the reward estimate (tracks population-level average decline over time) and explicit per-user frequency capping (hard limit guaranteeing no single user gets excessive repeat exposure, independent of the reward signal). Decay alone doesn't protect any specific user from over-exposure, so the two work together.

drills.q: What's the difference between reactive and proactive creative fatigue detection, and why does it matter for spend?
drills.a: Reactive detection fires only after an aggregate metric crosses a threshold, meaning real spend already went to a decaying creative before detection. Proactive detection predicts the decay trajectory from early engagement-curve shape, catching likely fatigue before the lagging metric visibly crosses a threshold, reducing wasted spend.

drills.q: A component-level DCO bandit predicts headline X + image Y should perform well individually but the actual combination underperforms. What's going on and how do you catch this systematically?
drills.a: A real interaction effect the additive component model can't capture -- the same tradeoff fractional-factorial designs accept explicitly. Catch it systematically by periodically spot-checking full combinations against component-model predictions and flagging large residuals as candidates for dedicated per-combination testing.

drills.q: Design a creative optimization system for a campaign with 6 headlines, 8 images, and 4 CTAs (192 combinations) on a moderate traffic budget.
drills.a: Reject full-combination testing given the traffic math. Use a component-level (or low-rank contextual) bandit learning marginal performance per element, composing top-scoring combinations for serving, while periodically spot-checking full combinations against predictions to catch interaction effects. Layer exponential-decay reward estimation and per-user frequency capping for fatigue, and route any auto-generated creative through brand-safety/quality gates before it enters the bandit's action space.

drills.q: What creative-specific bug is a common real-world cause of sample ratio mismatch in creative tests?
drills.a: A broken image asset or truncated headline that fails to render on a specific device/browser for one variant, silently dropping that variant's impressions/clicks in a non-random way across the audience -- the same SRM discipline from experiment design applies directly to creative tests.

drills.q: What is the cell count for a full factorial design with 3 factors at 2 levels each?
drills.a: 2^3 = 8 cells, each needing roughly the same per-arm sample size as a standalone A/B test.

drills.q: How is sample ratio mismatch (SRM) detected?
drills.a: A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test comparing observed vs expected traffic split between arms, commonly triggered at p < 0.001.

drills.q: Derive/compute: baseline conversion 5%, want to detect a 10% relative lift, alpha=0.05 two-sided, 80% power. Roughly how many visitors per arm?
Why does halving the MDE roughly quadruple the required sample size?
drills.a: The effect size (p2-p1) is squared in the denominator of the sample size formula, so halving it multiplies the required n by roughly 4x.

drills.q: Explain CUPED and derive why it reduces variance.
drills.a: Y_cuped = Y - theta*(X-E[X]), theta = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X), using a pre-experiment covariate X unaffected by treatment. From OLS variance algebra, Var(Y_cuped) = Var(Y)*(1-rho^2), so a covariate correlated at rho=0.7 with the outcome cuts variance ~51%.

drills.q: A triggered SRM check coincides with a treatment arm that looks significantly better. Do you trust the result?
drills.a: No. SRM invalidates the causal comparison until root-caused -- the missing/excess users are systematically, not randomly, different, so the headline result is unreliable even if it looks convincing.

drills.q: Why does a network-effect-sensitive feature (e.g. referrals) require cluster randomization rather than user-level randomization?
drills.a: Even at user-level randomization, a treated user's action (sharing/referring) can affect a control user, leaking the treatment's effect across arms. Cluster randomization (by friend-group or geo-market) contains spillover within one arm.

drills.q: Your team wants a 3-factor MVT (headline x image x CTA color) with only 15,000 visitors/week. Design the study.
drills.a: Compute cell count (e.g. 2^3=8) and per-cell sample size needed for the acceptable MDE; compare to available traffic over a reasonable duration. If it doesn't fit, propose a half-fraction fractional factorial (4 cells, aliasing the 3-way interaction with a factor judged implausible to interact), or test the two most-likely-to-interact factors as a full 2x2 and the third sequentially. Show the traffic math explicitly rather than running an underpowered design.

drills.q: Walk through the pipeline stages where SRM can originate and how you'd root-cause a triggered check.
drills.a: Assignment (bucketing bugs, ID collisions), execution (a variant's own bug, often JS, breaking tracking/redirect), logging (asymmetric join dropping rows by arm), analysis (asymmetric post-hoc filter). Root-cause stage by stage starting from raw assignment-service bucket counts before any downstream filtering, then check for elevated error rates or missing events specifically in the affected arm.

drills.q: A stakeholder says the test showed 'no significant difference' and concludes the treatment has no effect. Why is that not the same claim, and what should you report instead?
drills.a: A null result only rules out effects larger than the test's actual MDE at the collected sample size; it says nothing about smaller, still-meaningful effects. Report the achieved MDE alongside any null result and phrase the conclusion as 'we can rule out an effect larger than X%' rather than 'no effect.'

drills.q: Why does MMM need no individual-level identity data?
drills.a: It's built entirely from aggregate spend and outcome data (e.g. weekly channel spend vs weekly sales), regressed via adstock/saturation transformations -- no cookies, device IDs, or per-user tracking required.

drills.q: What is a geo holdout test?
drills.a: Withholding a marketing treatment from a subset of geographic markets and comparing outcomes against exposed geos (via difference-in-differences or synthetic control) to get a direct causal estimate of incremental lift.

drills.q: Why is multi-touch attribution 'mostly wrong' as a causal measurement even with sophisticated data-driven models?
drills.a: It can only allocate credit across observed touchpoints and credit is not the same as causation -- a touchpoint can get significant credit while contributing zero incremental conversion if the user would have converted regardless. Better math doesn't fix either limitation.

drills.q: Give the concrete reported bias of last-click attribution for SEO and branded search.
drills.a: Last-click undervalues SEO's pipeline contribution by roughly 2-3x and overvalues branded paid search's incremental contribution by roughly 40-60%, because branded search captures users already searching for the brand by name.

drills.q: Explain adstock and saturation in MMM.
drills.a: Adstock models a channel's effect as decaying carryover across subsequent periods (this period's spend still influences later outcomes at a decreasing rate). Saturation models diminishing marginal returns as spend increases, via a concave response curve.

drills.q: Why has MMM adoption roughly tripled while MTA adoption has also grown, rather than one replacing the other?
drills.a: MMM's structural immunity to identity loss (cookie deprecation, ATT) drove its resurgence for strategic decisions; MTA's growth reflects it being increasingly PAIRED with MMM for tactical in-channel optimization within its shrinking regime of strong identity resolution, not trusted alone as it once was.

drills.q: What benchmark do published geo holdout experiments report, and how should it be used?
drills.a: A 225-experiment dataset reports a median incremental ROAS of 2.31 with 88.4% reaching statistical significance. Use it as a plausibility check on your own result's order of magnitude, not as a specific target for any given channel.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants to justify next quarter's budget with a geo holdout test run 14 months ago. What's the concern and what do you recommend?
drills.a: Incrementality results are point-in-time; market conditions, competition, and creative have likely shifted meaningfully since. Recommend a fresh re-validation test, or if infeasible, explicitly flag the result's age and reduced reliability rather than presenting it as current -- move toward rolling/continuous incrementality testing.

drills.q: A company just lost most of its third-party cookie tracking and is panicking about losing marketing visibility entirely. How do you reframe and respond?
drills.a: Cookie loss specifically degrades MTA, not measurement as a whole. Pivot strategic allocation to MMM (never needed cookies), anchor with periodic geo holdouts for causal validation, and retain MTA only where first-party identity (logged-in users, CRM) still supports it. Frame as an architecture shift, not a capability loss -- and note MTA's granular numbers were already partly wrong (correlational), so the actual decision-quality loss is smaller than the reported-granularity loss.

drills.q: Why can't MMM fully replace MTA even in a fully post-identity-resolution world?
drills.a: MMM's aggregate, channel-level granularity structurally cannot answer tactical, sub-channel questions (which specific creative or audience segment to prioritize) -- MMM has a granularity ceiling that mirrors MTA's identity ceiling, so some tactical measurement gap remains regardless.

drills.q: Why does a model predicting 'O' for every token still score high token-level accuracy?
drills.a: Real NER corpora are dominated by O (outside-entity) tokens, often 80-95%+, so predicting O everywhere matches the majority class most of the time while extracting zero actual entities.

drills.q: What's the difference between the forward algorithm and Viterbi decoding in a CRF?
drills.a: The forward algorithm (with backward, for training) sums over ALL possible tag sequences to compute Z(x) and expected feature counts for the gradient. Viterbi uses max instead of sum to find the single best-scoring legal sequence for prediction. Same DP structure, different operation and purpose.

drills.q: Derive why naive computation of a CRF's partition function is exponential and how forward-backward fixes it.
drills.a: Z(x) = Σ over every possible tag sequence y', T^n of them for T tags and n tokens -- exponential. The score decomposes into a sum of local terms depending only on adjacent tag pairs, so the forward algorithm computes it via DP in O(n*T^2): the forward variable at position t aggregates all paths ending at each tag from position t-1's forward variables.

drills.q: A transformer NER model performs well on aggregate metrics but produces inconsistent boundaries specifically on multi-word brand names. What's the likely bug and how do you catch it before shipping?
drills.a: Likely a subword-to-word label alignment bug: labels applied inconsistently across a word's subword pieces (e.g. full B-TYPE label copied onto every subword instead of only the first, with remainder masked/relabeled). Catch it with a unit test using a known multi-subword entity that round-trips through tokenize -> align labels -> train step -> decode -> reassemble to word-level spans.

drills.q: Design an active learning loop for a new entity type your model performs poorly on.
drills.a: Score the unlabeled pool with the current model, rank by uncertainty (margin between top-1/top-2 Viterbi sequence scores, or aggregated token entropy for softmax models), send highest-uncertainty sentences to annotators, retrain, repeat. Combine with diversity sampling (cluster sentence embeddings) to avoid repeatedly selecting near-duplicate hard examples. Stop when marginal F1 gain per labeled batch drops below a cost-justified threshold.

drills.q: Why might a hybrid rule-plus-model approach beat a pure NER model for entities like PRICE or FLIGHT_NUMBER?
drills.a: These have highly regular surface forms (currency symbols/digit patterns, airline-code-plus-digits) that a regex handles with near-perfect precision at zero training cost. Reserve the trained model's capacity for linguistically variable entity types (hotel names, amenities) that rules genuinely can't capture.

drills.q: How do you handle nested entities like a city name inside a full airport name, given standard BIO tagging can't represent them?
drills.a: Options: redesign the schema to avoid the nesting if the inner entity isn't independently needed, run a layered extraction pass (extract outer span, then re-run a focused extractor on its text for the inner entity), or adopt a nested-NER-specific architecture (span-based/hypergraph) only if nesting is frequent and both entities are independently needed downstream.

drills.q: Compare fine-tuned transformer NER against zero-shot LLM extraction for a high-volume production content pipeline, and describe a hybrid that captures both advantages.
drills.a: Fine-tuned NER wins at high volume/low latency/cost per document (thousands of docs/sec feasible). Zero-shot LLM wins for new or rapidly-changing low-volume schemas where fine-tuning cost isn't justified. Hybrid: use LLM extraction to weakly label a large unlabeled corpus quickly, human-review a sample (active-learning-prioritized), and train a cheaper fine-tuned model on that data to serve production traffic.

drills.q: Design the end-to-end entity extraction pipeline for a hotel-listing corpus needing DESTINATION, ROOM_TYPE, PRICE, and AMENITY tags at millions-of-documents scale.
drills.a: Split by regularity: PRICE via regex (near-perfect precision, negligible cost). DESTINATION/ROOM_TYPE via a fine-tuned BiLSTM-CRF or lightweight transformer, evaluated with entity-level F1 via seqeval, cheap enough for full corpus scale. AMENITY (open-ended, growing) via active learning with periodic retraining as new phrasings appear. Bootstrap model training data via LLM weak-labeling plus human review rather than fully manual annotation. A single architecture for the whole schema is the wrong call.

drills.q: Why does global normalization in a CRF fix the label bias problem that plagues MEMMs?
drills.a: MEMMs normalize transition probabilities locally at each step, which structurally biases the model toward states with fewer outgoing transitions regardless of the actual observation. A CRF normalizes once, globally, over the whole tag sequence via the partition function Z(x), so no state is penalized purely for having a smaller local branching factor.

drills.q: What does the log scaling in TF-IDF's term-frequency component prevent?
drills.a: It prevents raw repetition count from linearly inflating a document's score -- a document saying a word 40 times isn't 40x more relevant than one saying it once; log-scaling captures diminishing returns.

drills.q: Why can lemmatization not run correctly without a POS tagger upstream?
drills.a: The correct lemma depends on part of speech -- 'meeting' lemmatizes to 'meet' as a verb but stays 'meeting' as a noun. Without POS context the lemmatizer guesses and gets ambiguous words wrong.

drills.q: Derive why BM25's k1 parameter produces term-frequency saturation while raw log-scaled TF-IDF does not.
drills.a: BM25's tf component is tf*(k1+1)/(tf+k1*(1-b+b*|d|/avgdl)), which approaches a hard ceiling of k1+1 as tf->infinity. Log-scaled TF (1+log(count)) keeps growing without bound, just more slowly -- it's a softer, unbounded version of saturation.

drills.q: A production TF-IDF classifier's accuracy drops sharply after a new content batch ships. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: Suspect vocabulary drift first: the fitted vocabulary from training doesn't cover new terms (new brand names, slang), so those tokens are silently dropped at transform time.
