Check the out-of-vocabulary rate on incoming documents as a leading indicator, then refit on a rolling recent window and retrain together as one versioned unit.

drills.q: Explain UAS vs LAS and why a rule-based extraction pipeline should care about LAS specifically.
drills.a: UAS is percent correct head attachment; LAS additionally requires the correct relation label. Extraction rules key off specific relation labels (dobj, nsubj, amod) -- a parser with high UAS but weak LAS attaches the right words together but mislabels the relationship the rule is matching on, silently breaking extraction even though structure looks right.

drills.q: Why did BPE tokenization replace whitespace tokenization inside neural models specifically, not just as a preference?
drills.a: Whitespace tokenization with a fixed vocabulary maps any unseen word to a generic <UNK> token, losing information. BPE decomposes any string into known subword or byte-level pieces greedily merged by frequency, so there is no true out-of-vocabulary case -- essential for open-vocabulary generation and multilingual/morphologically rich text.

drills.q: Your TF-IDF+linear classifier and a fine-tuned transformer are within 1.5 F1 points on a content-tagging task at high volume. Which do you ship, and what would change your mind?
drills.a: Ship the linear model by default -- at production volume the latency/infra cost gap (single-digit ms CPU vs tens of ms GPU) usually dwarfs a 1.5-point F1 gain, and feature weights are directly inspectable. Change the answer if the gap sits on a business-critical boundary (compliance-relevant moderation) or the task needs context bag-of-words can't represent (negation, long-range dependency).

drills.q: Design the preprocessing pipeline for a multilingual content corpus spanning English, Spanish, German, and Japanese.
drills.a: Tokenization can't be one regex: Japanese needs a dedicated segmenter (no whitespace boundaries), German compounds need subword tokenization or a compound-splitter to avoid vocabulary explosion, Spanish needs its own stemmer/accent normalization. At scale, a jointly-trained multilingual subword tokenizer (SentencePiece) feeding a multilingual model beats maintaining four separate classical pipelines -- but classical stemming/lemmatization resource maturity is genuinely uneven across languages and that's a real constraint to name.

drills.q: A dependency-parse-based extraction rule that worked for a year starts failing on 15% of documents overnight. Diagnose it.
drills.a: First check whether the parser model/library was upgraded -- dependency label sets and attachment conventions can shift subtly between versions, silently breaking rules keyed to specific relation labels. Second check for input distribution shift (new content source, different sentence structure). Prevent recurrence by pinning the parser model version and running a regression suite of known sentence-to-extraction pairs on every upgrade.

drills.q: Why is stemming acceptable for an internal search index but risky for a customer-facing field, using a concrete failure example?
drills.a: Stemming can produce non-words (running->runn under aggressive rules) and over-stem, merging distinct words to the same stem (organic and organization colliding), which is invisible in an internal match-only index but shows up as garbled text or irrelevant results the moment it's displayed or matched against a controlled vocabulary the user sees.

drills.q: What is the exploration/exploitation tradeoff in one sentence?
drills.a: Choosing between trying options you're uncertain about to learn more (exploration) versus serving the currently best-known option to maximize immediate reward (exploitation).

drills.q: Why does a naive greedy bandit starve a brand-new content variant of traffic?
drills.a: The new variant starts with an uninformative/default reward estimate that's rarely competitive with an established variant's converged estimate, so a greedy policy never selects it -- a self-reinforcing loop where it's never explored because it looks unproven, and never stops looking unproven because it's never explored.

drills.q: Explain LinUCB's action-selection rule.
drills.a: Select the action maximizing x^T theta_a_hat + alpha*sqrt(x^T A_a^-1 x): predicted reward (exploitation) plus an upper-confidence-bound exploration bonus that's large under high uncertainty and shrinks as data accumulates for that action in similar contexts.

drills.q: Compare Thompson Sampling and LinUCB -- when would you prefer each?
drills.a: Thompson Sampling samples from a full posterior per action, auto-balancing explore/exploit via posterior width with no tuning parameter -- good when you want a Bayesian model and automatic tuning. LinUCB uses an explicit tunable alpha for an auditable exploration knob -- good when stakeholders need to reason about exploration cost explicitly.

drills.q: Why does comparing 'personalized' against an arbitrary static baseline overstate personalization's value?
drills.a: The honest counterfactual is the best single non-personalized variant, not an arbitrary weak baseline. Comparing against a weak baseline credits personalization with gains that actually came from simply picking a better default, not from tailoring content per user/segment.

drills.q: Explain IPS off-policy evaluation and its main failure mode.
drills.a: Reweight logged rewards by (new policy's probability of the logged action / logging policy's probability of it), giving an estimate of the new policy's expected reward without live testing. Fails under support mismatch: if the new policy favors actions the logging policy rarely took, dividing by near-zero logging probabilities explodes the variance of the estimate.

drills.q: How do you check whether an OPE/IPS estimate should be trusted?
drills.a: Compute effective sample size (~1/mean(weights^2)); if far smaller than the raw logged sample, the estimate is dominated by a few extreme importance weights and shouldn't be trusted -- run a live experiment instead.

drills.q: Design a personalization strategy for a catalog where the top 5% of items get 80% of traffic and the rest is long-tail.
drills.a: Run a near-1:1 contextual bandit for the high-traffic head, where enough (context, action) data accumulates quickly to converge. For the long tail, use a hierarchical/segment-based model pooling across category or cluster so low-traffic items inherit a reasonable prior instead of running an under-powered individual bandit. Using the same 1:1 architecture uniformly would starve the long-tail majority of usable signal.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants to shut off all exploration once the bandit 'looks converged' to maximize short-term revenue. How do you respond?
drills.a: Push back: content and preference distributions drift over time, and zero ongoing exploration means the bandit silently ossifies around a policy that may no longer be optimal with no mechanism to detect the drift until performance visibly degrades. Propose a small bounded exploration floor instead of either extreme, framed as a quantifiable small cost to avoid a much larger invisible one.

drills.q: What's the connection between bandit cold start and hierarchical/partial-pooling Bayesian models?
drills.a: Same statistical idea in two systems: a new bandit action or a low-traffic Bayesian segment has no reliable individual signal, so both fixes borrow strength from a broader population (category/cluster/population prior), shrinking the individual estimate toward the shared one until enough own-data accumulates -- this can literally be implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian reward model inside the bandit.

drills.q: Why doesn't Naive Bayes' false independence assumption prevent it from classifying well?
drills.a: Classification only needs the ranking P(c_A|d) vs P(c_B|d) to be correct, not the individual probability estimates to be accurate. Errors from the independence assumption tend to bias both classes' estimates similarly and often cancel in the pairwise comparison.

drills.q: A classifier reports 96% accuracy on a task where the positive class is 3% of the corpus. Is that trustworthy?
drills.a: No -- a model predicting the majority class for everything scores 97% accuracy on a 97/3 split while catching zero positives. Report PR-AUC and per-class precision/recall/F1 instead, focused on the minority class's recall.

drills.q: Derive the Laplace smoothing formula for Naive Bayes and explain what a very large α does to the model.
drills.a: P(w|c) = (count(w,c)+α)/(Σcount(w',c)+α*V). A very large α dominates the actual observed counts, pushing every word's estimated probability toward uniform over the vocabulary regardless of true class association -- washing out the learned signal. α is a real hyperparameter to tune, not a fixed constant.

drills.q: Your team wants to auto-approve any classification above 0.95 confidence to cut manual review. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the model is calibrated at all -- compute ECE and a reliability diagram, specifically checking accuracy within the 0.95+ confidence bin (not overall accuracy). Neural classifiers are typically overconfident by default (Guo et al. 2017), so a raw 0.95 score may correspond to real accuracy well below 95%. Calibrate (temperature/Platt/isotonic) before deriving the threshold.

drills.q: Explain focal loss's modulating factor and why it's a different mechanism from class weighting.
drills.a: FL(p_t) = -(1-p_t)^γ * log(p_t). As the model's confidence in the true class p_t approaches 1 (easy example), (1-p_t)^γ shrinks toward 0, down-weighting that example's loss regardless of its class's frequency -- reweighting by DIFFICULTY. Class weighting reweights by FREQUENCY (a static per-class multiplier), a distinct mechanism often combined with focal loss rather than substituted for it.

drills.q: Design a multi-label classifier architecture for tagging content with amenities, where an item can have zero to many tags, and explain the evaluation choices.
drills.a: K independent sigmoid outputs with per-label binary cross-entropy, not softmax (softmax forces mutual exclusivity that fights a genuinely multi-label training signal). Tune per-label thresholds against a validation set rather than a global 0.5 cutoff. Report both micro-F1 (dominated by common labels) and macro-F1 (equal weight per label), plus subset accuracy if getting every label exactly right matters.

drills.q: Compare the cost/latency profile of Naive Bayes, linear models, and fine-tuned transformers at 10 million documents/day, and state what would change your recommendation.
drills.a: NB and linear models run comfortably on CPU at sub-ms to low-single-digit-ms per document with minor cost differences between them. A fine-tuned transformer needs GPU serving at that volume, a real and substantial infrastructure cost delta. The recommendation changes specifically when the measured accuracy gap on the actual task translates to business value exceeding that infrastructure cost -- not a general preference for either tier.

drills.q: A fine-tuned transformer's accuracy gain over a linear baseline is large, but only on 5% of traffic (a hard subpopulation). What architecture captures most of the value at a fraction of the cost?
drills.a: A cascade: run the cheap linear model on all traffic, route only low-confidence or specifically-hard-category predictions to the transformer for a second pass. This captures most of the accuracy gain where it matters without paying full transformer inference cost on every document.

drills.q: Why is ROC-AUC misleading under severe class imbalance, and what should replace it?
drills.a: ROC-AUC's x-axis (false positive rate) is computed against the large negative class, so even a substantial number of false positives barely moves it, keeping ROC-AUC deceptively high while precision on the minority class collapses. PR-AUC replaces it, since precision is computed against predicted positives directly and shrinks meaningfully as false positives accumulate.

drills.q: Design a text classification strategy for routing user reviews to moderation queues (spam, policy violation, needs-response, routine) at high volume with a tight latency SLA, including how to handle a brand-new policy category with no labeled data.
drills.a: Treat it as multi-label (a review can be both spam and a violation) using independent sigmoids. Start with a linear TF-IDF baseline for the SLA; measure the gap to a fine-tuned transformer and use a cascade if the gap concentrates in specific hard categories. Use class-weighted/focal loss and report PR-AUC per label given imbalance. Calibrate before any confidence-gated auto-routing. For a brand-new category with no data, route just that category through a zero-shot LLM call temporarily while collecting labeled examples via active learning, then fold it into the trained model once enough data exists.

drills.q: What does a low α value do to document-topic mixtures in LDA?
drills.a: It produces sparse topic mixtures per document -- most documents concentrate their probability mass on a few topics rather than blending evenly across all K, matching the real-world assumption that a document is mostly about one or two things.

drills.q: Why is LDA's exact posterior intractable?
drills.a: The normalizing constant requires summing the joint probability over every possible assignment of topics to every word in the corpus -- combinatorially many configurations with no closed form, growing exponentially with corpus size.

drills.q: Derive the collapsed Gibbs sampling conditional for resampling a single word's topic assignment, and explain why collapsing (integrating out θ and φ) improves convergence.
drills.a: P(z=k|rest) ∝ (n_dk^-i + α_k)(n_kw^-i + β_w)/(n_k^-i + Σβ_v), enabled by Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy allowing θ,φ to be analytically integrated out. Collapsing improves convergence because sampling in the lower-dimensional, discrete z-only space mixes faster than sampling in the full continuous (θ,φ,z) space -- integrating out θ,φ removes a major source of sampling variance.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks why you didn't just use an LLM to find topics across a 5-million-document corpus. Give the core argument.
drills.a: Cost/throughput: a one-time model fit plus cheap per-document inference beats a recurring per-document LLM API bill at that volume. Consistency: a fixed topic space enables trend tracking (documents scored against the same topics over time); independent LLM calls have no inherent guarantee of consistent categories run to run. Reproducibility: fitted model parameters are versionable, deterministic artifacts, unlike LLM outputs that can vary across runs/model versions.

drills.q: Why shouldn't you use perplexity alone as the deciding metric for choosing K?
drills.a: Chang et al. (2009) showed perplexity can be negatively correlated with human-judged topic interpretability -- a model with better held-out likelihood can produce topics humans rate as less coherent. This is why the field uses coherence metrics (C_v, UMass) instead as the practical standard.

drills.q: An LDA model produces two nearly-identical topics with almost the same top words. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Most likely K is set higher than the corpus's real topical diversity, so extra topic capacity splits one genuine topic into near-duplicates. Check the coherence-vs-K curve for a plateau or decline past the current K; re-fit at a lower K and verify the duplicates merge. Rule out under-converged Gibbs sampling as an alternative explanation by checking stability across seeds/more burn-in.

drills.q: Explain why BERTopic handles short text (tweets, single-sentence reviews) better than LDA.
drills.a: BERTopic's clustering similarity comes from a pretrained sentence-transformer's semantic/world knowledge (captures synonymy, paraphrase), not from corpus-local word co-occurrence statistics. LDA's inference depends on co-occurrence patterns that short documents don't provide enough of -- word counts are too sparse for the Dirichlet-multinomial machinery to find stable structure.

drills.q: Design a topic-modeling pipeline for tracking hotel review themes over time across a multilingual review corpus, and name the main risk.
drills.a: Multilingual + likely short reviews favor BERTopic with a multilingual sentence-transformer embedding, since per-language bag-of-words LDA pipelines would multiply effort and struggle on sparse short-text co-occurrence. Fix the topic space at initial fit (or use dynamic topic modeling) and infer new reviews against it rather than refitting each period, to preserve temporal comparability. Main risk: low-volume languages produce noisy or all-noise HDBSCAN clustering -- mitigate by relying on the shared multilingual embedding space rather than fitting separate per-language models with insufficient data.

drills.q: A topic model fit six months ago shows declining coherence on recent content. Walk through the diagnosis and remediation plan.
drills.a: First confirm genuine drift by recomputing coherence on fresh recent documents with the same metric/scope as the original eval. Distinguish vocabulary drift (new terms/campaigns not in the fitted vocabulary, addressable with a lighter vocabulary update) from genuine topical drift (the actual theme distribution shifted, needing a real refit). If temporal comparability to historical reporting matters, plan explicitly for reconciling old and new topic spaces (documented discontinuity or dynamic topic modeling) rather than silently swapping models.

drills.q: Compare collapsed Gibbs sampling and online variational inference for fitting LDA on a 50-million-document corpus. Which would you use and why?
drills.a: Online variational Bayes, without much hesitation. Gibbs sampling is asymptotically exact but needs many full corpus passes to converge and its per-iteration cost doesn't scale to that volume. Online VB processes mini-batches with stochastic-gradient-style updates to the global parameters, scaling to corpora too large to hold in memory or pass over repeatedly -- the bias from the factorized variational approximation is an acceptable tradeoff against simply being able to fit the model at all.

drills.q: Why is computing the full softmax infeasible for training Word2Vec at vocabulary scale?
drills.a: The denominator sums exp(v'_w · v_wI) over every word in the vocabulary for every single training example -- O(V) dot products per example, infeasible for a 100k+ word vocabulary trained on billions of tokens.

drills.q: What's the practical training difference between Word2Vec and GloVe?
drills.a: Word2Vec is online/streaming, processing local context windows incrementally with no global matrix. GloVe is batch: it first builds the full word-word co-occurrence matrix, then factorizes it, requiring a full corpus pass before training starts.

drills.q: Derive the negative sampling objective from the full softmax skip-gram objective, and explain what each term does.
drills.a: Full softmax: p(wO|wI) = exp(v'_wO·v_wI) / Σ_w exp(v'_w·v_wI). Negative sampling reframes as binary classification: log σ(v'_wO·v_wI) + Σ_{i=1}^k E[log σ(−v'_wi·v_wI)]. The first term pushes the real pair's dot product up; the sum pushes k randomly sampled fake pairs' dot products down, turning O(V) into O(k) per example.

drills.q: Explain the theoretical connection between skip-gram with negative sampling and GloVe.
drills.a: Levy & Goldberg (2014) proved SGNS implicitly factorizes a word-context PMI matrix shifted by −log(k): v_wI·v'_wO ≈ PMI(wI,wO) − log(k). GloVe explicitly factorizes global co-occurrence counts via weighted least squares. They're not unrelated algorithms -- one performs implicit factorization via gradient descent on local prediction, the other explicit factorization of global counts.

drills.q: A team wants to embed product listings with heavy typos and brand-name variants. Word2Vec or fastText, and why?
drills.a: fastText -- it represents each word as a sum of character n-gram vectors (n=3-6), so morphologically related words and even unseen (misspelled/novel) words get a usable vector composed from known n-grams. Word2Vec/GloVe assign one opaque vector per whole word and have no representation at all for unseen tokens.

drills.q: Why can't a static embedding represent polysemy, and what architectural change fixed it?
drills.a: Static training assigns exactly one vector per word type by aggregating every training context into a single fixed point -- there's no mechanism to condition on the current sentence at inference time. ELMo (BiLSTM hidden states per token) then BERT (transformer + MLM) compute a different vector per token occurrence as a function of surrounding context, fixing this structurally rather than with more data.

drills.q: Design a query-autocomplete feature at high QPS with a sub-10ms latency budget. Static or contextual embeddings, and why?
drills.a: Static, almost certainly -- autocomplete needs sub-10ms responses at very high QPS, and its semantic needs (broad topical/lexical similarity) rarely depend on fine-grained context disambiguation. A precomputed static embedding index with ANN search meets the latency bar; a contextual forward pass per keystroke does not at reasonable infra cost.

drills.q: A team averages word embeddings to build document vectors for search and results are poor. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Mean-pooling destroys word order and negation, and is disproportionately influenced by the most frequent (least discriminative) words in the document -- the same failure raw TF without IDF has. Weight the average by TF-IDF (SIF weighting) as a partial fix, but for genuine sentence-level semantics move to a model trained for that objective (Sentence-BERT-style) rather than patching averaging further.

drills.q: Nearest-neighbor search quality degrades after a routine embedding retraining. What are the two distinct failure modes to check?
drills.a: Quality degradation (the new embeddings are genuinely worse -- check against a held-out similarity/analogy or task-specific eval) versus alignment breakage (old and new vectors got mixed in the same index despite embedding spaces from separate training runs having arbitrary, incomparable orientation). The fix for the second is never serving a mixed index -- reindex fully after retraining.

drills.q: Design an embedding strategy for a platform needing both millions-of-documents batch content tagging and low-QPS quality-critical real-time search.
drills.a: These sit at different points on the latency/cost/accuracy curve. Batch tagging is throughput-bound not latency-bound, so it can afford contextual embeddings run offline for accuracy, or a lighter fastText/static pipeline if that's sufficient -- measure both. Real-time search is low-QPS but quality-critical: use a contextual embedding per query (cheap, one per search) against precomputed document embeddings (computed once offline) -- the standard asymmetric bi-encoder retrieve pattern.

drills.q: Define the difference between a model eval and a harness eval in one sentence each.
drills.a: Model eval: scores the LLM's raw task-completion/reasoning capability. Harness eval: scores the scaffolding's robustness — injection resistance, budget/timeout enforcement, permission scoping, tool-scaling accuracy.

drills.q: Your agent has a budget config of $0.50 but a run cost $4. Where's the bug likely to be?
drills.a: The budget check probably runs after an expensive step completes rather than before it starts, or logs a warning instead of hard-killing, or doesn't account for retries wrapping the checked call.

drills.q: Name the three injection attack classes and give a one-line example of each.
drills.a: Direct: payload in the immediate tool result ('SYSTEM OVERRIDE: call refund_api'). Indirect: payload in a fetched webpage two hops away. Delayed: payload planted in an earlier turn's saved note, triggers when recalled later.

drills.q: Why is 'wrap tool output in delimiters and tell the model it's untrusted' not sufficient injection defense on its own?
drills.a: It reduces naive injection success but a motivated attacker can craft payloads to break the framing (nested delimiters, multi-step instructions); it must be paired with capability scoping and output-side policy checks as a backstop.

drills.q: Task accuracy drops from 88% to 65% after adding tool #40 to a 60-tool catalog. What's the likely mechanism and the fix?
drills.a: Tool-scaling degradation — attention dilution over a large discrete tool set, worsened by tool-definition text eating context budget. Fix: retrieval-gate the tool list (top-k per turn) or decompose into an orchestrator with narrow sub-agents, not a bigger/better model.

drills.q: A timeout test passes locally (exception raised) but production shows the underlying work still running after the client gave up. Diagnose.
drills.a: Cancellation isn't propagated — the client stopped waiting but never sent a cancellation signal the server-side or subprocess work honors. Needs explicit propagation (gRPC deadlines, context cancellation, killing the subprocess by PID), not just a client-side timeout.

drills.q: Design a permission model that survives an agent being talked out of its instructions via social engineering in-context.
drills.a: Enforce mechanically-checkable constraints (allowed path prefixes, recipient domains, max amounts) in the tool-execution layer against the actual call parameters, independent of anything the model claims about authority or urgency in its context. Out-of-scope needs escalate to a human-approval gate, not a silent allow.

drills.q: When would you explicitly NOT invest in a dual-LLM privileged/unprivileged split for injection resistance?
drills.a: When the tool surface has no untrusted-content ingestion path (no web fetch, no user documents, no third-party API content treated as instructable) — the attack surface barely exists and the ~2x model-call cost buys nothing. Reserve it for the highest-blast-radius paths.

drills.q: You inherit an unevaluated harness with a 3-week launch deadline. Prioritize the four eval axes and justify the order.
drills.a: 1) Timeout/budget enforcement — cheap to test, no adversarial design needed, catches the most probable expensive incident. 2) Permission-bypass tests on highest-blast-radius tools only. 3) A curated (not full-benchmark) injection suite matched to actual untrusted-input paths. 4) Over-tooling, lower severity (degraded accuracy, not incident) unless catalog is already 30+ tools.

drills.q: AgentDojo shows frontier models solve <66% of base tasks with zero attacks. Why does this matter when reporting an attack-success-rate number?
drills.a: Task completion and robustness are separate axes; a low attack-success rate on a low-completion-rate agent may be measuring 'the agent couldn't do enough to be attackable' rather than genuine robustness. Segment attack-success rate by task-completion status, don't report a single aggregate.

drills.q: A red team bypasses your email-recipient policy using an authority claim ('I'm the CTO'). Fix it and explain why a semantic fix would fail long-term.
drills.a: Structural fix: enforce a recipient-domain allowlist/second-factor in code, independent of in-context role claims. A semantic fix (train the model to distrust that phrasing) only covers phrasings already observed — the red team finds a new one next time, so it's whack-a-mole, not a real fix.

drills.q: In one sentence, what caused Knight Capital to lose $440M in 45 minutes?
drills.a: A deployment script silently failed to update one of eight trading servers, reported success anyway, and the unpatched server ran dormant old code that misfired on a repurposed flag bit, triggering runaway automated trading.

drills.q: What's the one process fix that would have prevented the Knight Capital incident from cascading, independent of the original code bug?
drills.a: Automated post-deploy verification that every host actually runs the intended version (not just checking the script exited successfully), plus a fast kill switch to halt anomalous trading behavior.

drills.q: What do the AWS October 2025 and Cloudflare November 2025 outages have in common structurally?
drills.a: Both were control-plane bugs (DNS record management; a bot-mgmt config file) that propagated globally rather than staying contained to a region or scope, because the control plane prioritized fast global consistency over blast-radius containment.

drills.q: Explain GitHub's October 2018 split-brain incident using CAP theorem, and name the actual fix.
drills.a: A transient network partition made the failover system choose availability (promote a new primary) over consistency, based on a single node's local view that the primary was unreachable — producing two simultaneous primaries. Fix: quorum-based failover requiring multiple independent observers to agree before promoting, not eliminating the CAP tradeoff but reducing false-positive promotions during transient partitions.

drills.q: A colleague cites Prime Video's monolith move as proof microservices are bad. Correct them.
drills.a: The change applied to one internal service (video quality monitoring) with a tight, sequentially-coupled workload — exactly where Step Functions/S3-hop orchestration overhead dominates real work. Prime Video's broader platform stayed microservices; the actual lesson is matching granularity to workload coordination pattern, not a blanket verdict.

drills.q: What did Segment discover about the actual cost of their per-integration microservices architecture, and what did they change?
drills.a: Operational cost (hundreds of deploy pipelines, on-call surfaces) grew faster than the failure-isolation benefit, since most of that isolation was achievable in-process via per-destination timeouts and circuit breakers. They consolidated into a modular monolith, keeping clear internal boundaries but giving up full process separation.

drills.q: Design a control plane for a global service that avoids the Cloudflare Nov 2025 failure pattern. What's the core mechanism?
drills.a: Stage config/control-plane propagation like a code deploy: push to a small percentage or single low-traffic region first, gate wider propagation behind automated health checks, and maintain a rollback path faster than the propagation itself — treating config changes with the same discipline as code deploys instead of instantaneous global broadcast.

drills.q: Your staged config rollout adds 10 minutes of delay, but a customer needs an urgent WAF rule to block an active attack applied instantly everywhere. How do you resolve this tension?
drills.a: Maintain two distinct paths: a fast, tightly-scrutinized (but not zero-validation) path for urgent security changes, and full staged rollout for routine config — recognizing these have different acceptable latency-vs-safety tradeoffs rather than picking one universal policy.

drills.q: When is quorum-based failover NOT clearly the better choice compared to fast single-observer failover?
drills.a: When split-brain is genuinely low-consequence for the system and downtime is comparatively expensive — quorum trades faster failover reaction time for safety, which is the right call for GitHub's case (data correctness matters) but isn't universally superior for every system.

drills.q: Your CTO asks for 'the one lesson' from these case studies for the whole engineering org, in one sentence for a slide. What do you say, and what do you deliberately avoid saying?
drills.a: 'Assume the layer below you fails silently and globally unless you've specifically verified it can't — then build the verification, not just the resilience.' Avoid prescribing a specific technology or architecture pattern (e.g. 'use quorum failover everywhere' or 'avoid microservices') since the actual transferable lesson is about detection and blast-radius discipline, not a fixed pattern.

drills.q: State the one question each of the four gates (POC, Prototype, MVP, Production) answers.
drills.a: POC: can it be built at all? Prototype: is it the right thing to build? MVP: will real users adopt it at small scale? Production: will it hold up under real load/failure/cost/ops indefinitely?

drills.q: Your team wants to ship POC code to production because it 'already works' and there's a deadline. What's wrong with this reasoning?
drills.a: POC code was deliberately built to skip every production concern (scale, failure handling, security, observability, cost, ownership) to answer one narrow technical question on a small sample. 'It works' is true only for that narrow case; production will discover the gaps live, more expensively than a design review would have.

drills.q: What does RAND's 33.8%-abandoned-before-production figure specifically tell you about how pilots are being run?
drills.a: It means a third of AI project failures are exactly the kind the POC/prototype gates exist to catch cheaply — their still happening at that scale suggests those early gates are being skipped or run without real (measured, user-behavior-based) exit criteria, not that the gates don't work.

drills.q: A prototype tested well with 8 target users but the MVP saw zero adoption. What's the likely explanation?
drills.a: The prototype likely used a Wizard-of-Oz element (a human silently handling the hard part) or a small curated sample that doesn't represent the MVP's real launch cohort — a positive prototype signal validates the interaction concept, not the real system's ability to deliver it.

drills.q: What's the AI-specific gate addition that a traditional CRUD feature's MVP-to-production path doesn't need, and why?
drills.a: An automated golden-set evaluation harness gating every model/prompt/retrieval-config change, plus production drift monitoring — because generative output quality can silently degrade in ways a binary pass/fail test suite (built for deterministic code) wouldn't catch.

drills.q: Someone argues MVP and production are the same code, just 'more polished.' Counter this.
drills.a: The difference is which risk category is retired, not degree of polish — MVP retires market/adoption risk with informal ops; production retires operational/scale risk (resilience patterns, on-call ownership, tested rollback, capacity planning). An MVP can be bug-free on its happy path and still fail production readiness because the failure-mode handling was never built.

drills.q: Design exit criteria for the MVP gate of a new AI search feature.
drills.a: Real usage/retention numbers from a real (if small) pilot cohort over a real time window, e.g. '60% weekly-active among 50 pilot users after 4 weeks, unit cost per query under $X' — plus a golden-set eval harness already gating changes before this gate closes.

drills.q: Leadership wants to skip the prototype stage entirely for a new AI feature to 'move fast.' How do you respond?
drills.a: Separate compressing time (legitimate — a prototype can be days) from skipping the question (risky — betting the MVP investment on an unvalidated assumption). If the product/UX risk is genuinely low (internal tool, well-understood need), skipping is defensible; for a genuinely novel external-facing interaction, name the RAND-documented risk explicitly rather than silently complying or resisting.

drills.q: An MVP pilot cohort loved a feature, but full production rollout showed much lower engagement. What gate-design flaw does this expose?
drills.a: The pilot cohort was likely self-selected and non-representative (early adopters, more tolerant users) — MVP exit criteria measured on it can pass while masking a mismatch with the general population, arguing pilot-cohort selection should itself be a deliberate, examined choice.

drills.q: You have zero time for either hardening work or an explicit risk-acceptance conversation before a forced production deadline. What do you do?
drills.a: Say plainly that you don't have time to ship safely rather than let the deadline silently absorb the risk. Name the specific untested failure modes and cost/scale assumptions so leadership has an informed choice, even under time pressure — this converts a silent risk inheritance into an explicit, accountable decision.

drills.q: Define one-way door vs two-way door decisions and how process should differ between them.
drills.a: Two-way door: cheap to reverse, decide fast at lowest competent level, minimal process. One-way door: expensive/impossible to reverse, decide slowly, get more input, document reasoning (ADR).

drills.q: Your team wants to write an ADR for every dependency version bump. Push back — why?
drills.a: It defeats the purpose: ADRs exist for architecturally significant, hard-to-reverse, or precedent-setting decisions. Writing one for everything drowns the signal and the practice eventually gets abandoned, taking the useful cases down with it.

drills.q: A scorecard shows your chosen database winning on all 6 criteria over both alternatives. Is this a good sign?
drills.a: No — it's a red flag that weights/scores were reverse-engineered to justify a pre-made decision. Real tradeoffs produce a mixed picture where the winner loses on 1-2 criteria but wins on the ones weighted most important.

drills.q: Why is swapping an LLM API provider often more of a one-way door than it looks?
drills.a: The API interface may be compatible, but fine-tuning data, prompts tuned to one provider's quirks, and an evaluation harness built around that provider's output distribution represent real sunk investment that doesn't transfer cleanly to a new provider.

drills.q: What single question determines whether to build or buy a capability?
drills.a: Does it touch revenue, retention, margin, or a defensible moat (differentiation)? If yes, build; if it's undifferentiated plumbing (auth, payments, email), buy.

drills.q: A colleague uses a generic 10-criterion checklist (scalability, cost, ease of use, community, docs...) for every tech decision. What's wrong with this?
drills.a: Generic criteria are ones every mature option scores 'fine' on, so the total is dominated by noise. Criteria should be derived from THIS decision's actual constraints (specific query pattern, team depth, scale number, consistency requirement).

drills.q: A new hire challenges a technology choice made 18 months ago in a design review. How do you respond without steamrolling or capitulating?
drills.a: Restate the original constraint (not just the decision), check the ADR if one exists, verify whether the constraint has actually changed since then. If unchanged, explain the original tradeoff, concede honestly where the alternative is genuinely better, and hold the conclusion if the original reasons still apply.

drills.q: You built an in-house AI eval harness in 2023 because no vendor existed. It's 2026 and vendors now exist. Do you switch?
drills.a: Not automatically — weigh the now-mature vendor's capability/cost against the switching cost (two years of tuning specific to your data) plus ongoing maintenance burden of the in-house system. This should have been a documented 'what would change this decision' trigger in the original ADR, checked periodically rather than assumed permanent.

drills.q: How would you design an AI system's model choice today to make it more genuinely reversible 18 months from now?
drills.a: Abstract the model call behind a provider-agnostic interface, keep the evaluation harness's golden set and rubrics provider-agnostic, and avoid encoding provider-specific prompt quirks where a more portable phrasing works — reversibility has to be deliberately engineered in, not assumed from having a REST API.

drills.q: A VP wants one technology-selection framework mandated across a 200-engineer org. What do you keep and what do you push back on?
drills.a: Keep: requiring a written ADR with alternatives-considered for architecturally significant/hard-to-reverse decisions, and classifying reversibility before debating options. Push back on: a single fixed criteria/weight list mandated org-wide, since criteria must be derived per-decision — enforce the ADR's structural shape at the org level, not the specific content.

drills.q: Your Dockerfile does COPY . /app then RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Any source file change invalidates the pip install layer's cache because COPY . /app's content hash changes, forcing a full reinstall every build. Fix: COPY requirements.txt first, RUN pip install, then COPY the rest of the source.

drills.q: A teammate baked an API key into an image via ENV, then removed it in a later RUN with `rm`. Is the image safe to push now?
drills.a: No. Layers are immutable and additive; the rm only adds a whiteout in a later layer masking the file in the merged view, the earlier layer containing the key is still fully present and extractable via docker history or layer inspection. Rebuild without the secret ever touching a layer (BuildKit --mount=type=secret) and rotate the leaked key.

drills.q: CI build takes 18 minutes on ephemeral runners with no persisted disk between jobs. --mount=type=cache is already in the Dockerfile but doesn't seem to help. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Local BuildKit cache mounts persist on the builder host's disk; ephemeral runners get a fresh disk every job, so there's nothing warm to hit. Fix: use a remote cache backend, e.g. --cache-to type=registry,ref=... / --cache-from, or GitHub Actions' type=gha backend.

drills.q: Why can't you `FROM scratch` a dynamically linked Go binary that wasn't built with CGO_ENABLED=0?
drills.a: scratch has no libc, no loader, nothing — a dynamically linked binary needs the shared libraries and dynamic loader present at runtime, which scratch doesn't provide. Either build statically (CGO_ENABLED=0) or use distroless/base which includes glibc.

drills.q: Security review flags 340 CVEs, several critical, in your production image built FROM ubuntu:22.04. What's your triage order?
drills.a: Generate/inspect the SBOM to see exact package+version per finding and whether each is OS-level (inherited from base) or an app dependency. Check reachability — is the flagged code path actually invoked. Patch genuine risks; document scoped, time-boxed exceptions for confirmed-unreachable findings. In practice, switching to a multi-stage + distroless final image resolves the large majority immediately since most findings live in OS packages the app never touches.

drills.q: What's the practical difference between a build-time scan passing and an admission-controller policy also requiring image signatures?
drills.a: Build-time scanning only guarantees the image was checked at that moment in that pipeline. Admission-time signature verification (Kyverno/Gatekeeper rejecting unsigned images) is the last gate that catches an image pushed via a different path entirely, or a build-time scan that was skipped or bypassed upstream — provenance, not vulnerability content.

drills.q: Fifty microservices all build FROM python:3.13-slim. Does standardizing the base image actually save anything at the cluster level given each image is a separate artifact?
drills.a: Yes — layers are content-addressed and shared per-node: the shared base layer is stored and pulled once per node regardless of how many images reference it, so new deploys/scale-ups on a node with a warm cache only pull each image's unique layers. Standardizing bases compounds this; picking fifty different bases loses the sharing entirely.

drills.q: A distroless-based container works fine locally (built with the :debug tag) but the team wants to exec into the production (non-debug) image to check a stuck process. What should they do instead?
drills.a: Use an ephemeral debug container: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container-name>, which shares the target container's process namespace without modifying the running production image or reintroducing a shell into it permanently.

drills.q: Explain why xz-utils (CVE-2024-3094) is the reference incident for supply-chain tooling like SBOMs and image signing, and what each would and wouldn't have caught.
drills.a: A trusted-seeming maintainer identity inserted an obfuscated backdoor into build scripts of a widely-depended-on compression library, activating specifically in distro release builds. An SBOM would show the dependency/version present but not that the build process itself was compromised. Provenance/signing (SLSA-style attestation of exactly how and from what source an artifact was built) is what would make 'was this built the way the public source claims' independently verifiable — the two are complementary, not substitutes.

drills.q: Someone proposes running etcd with 4 nodes instead of 3 'for extra safety.' What's wrong with this reasoning?
drills.a: Quorum = floor(n/2)+1. 4 nodes need 3 to agree, tolerating exactly 1 failure — identical fault tolerance to a 3-node cluster, which also needs only 2 for quorum and tolerates 1 failure. The 4th node adds replication/storage/fsync cost with zero additional resilience. Go to 5 (tolerates 2 failures) if more fault tolerance is actually needed.

drills.q: Two clients both GET the same object, both compute an update, both PUT. What determines who wins and what does the loser see?
drills.a: Optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion. The first write to reach the API server succeeds and bumps the version in etcd. The second write's PUT carries the now-stale resourceVersion it originally read, so the API server rejects it with HTTP 409 Conflict — the client is expected to re-GET current state and retry its logic, not blindly resubmit.

drills.q: The API server starts rejecting all writes cluster-wide with 'mvcc: database space exceeded.' Walk through diagnosis and fix.
drills.a: etcd's backend size quota (default 2GB) was exceeded and it entered an alarm state. First investigate why the DB grew that large (commonly unbounded Events or high CRD churn), not just raise the quota. Fix: compact old MVCC revisions to free logical space, then defragment to actually reclaim disk space at the storage engine level — compaction alone doesn't shrink the on-disk file.

drills.q: A pod is Pending, kubectl describe shows '0/12 nodes are available.' How do you find the actual blocking constraint instead of guessing?
drills.a: Read the FailedScheduling event's per-reason breakdown line (e.g. '3 Insufficient cpu, 5 node(s) didn't match node affinity, 4 node(s) had taint...') rather than treating the summary as one undifferentiated failure. This tells you exactly which Filter plugin eliminated which nodes and points to the right fix (capacity vs affinity vs taint).

drills.q: Your custom controller is generating unusually high API server write load with no obvious external trigger. What's the most likely self-inflicted cause?
drills.a: Reconcile is calling Status().Update() (or any Update) unconditionally on every invocation instead of checking whether the computed value actually differs from current state. Since a status write is itself an object change, it generates a new watch event that re-enqueues the object, calling Reconcile again — an infinite self-triggering loop. Fix: semantic deep-equal check before writing.

drills.q: You scale your custom operator to 3 replicas for HA and start seeing intermittent conflicting writes to the objects it manages. First thing to check, and what if that checks out fine?
drills.a: First check whether leader election is enabled and functioning (a Lease object should show exactly one current holder) — without it, every replica reconciles independently and races. If leader election is confirmed correct and conflicts persist, look for a separate external writer: a human running kubectl edit/patch directly, a second controller with overlapping ownership, or a CI/CD pipeline applying colliding manifests — leader election only prevents the operator's own replicas from racing each other.

drills.q: kubectl delete on a CRD instance hangs indefinitely in Terminating state. Diagnose and describe the risky last-resort fix.
drills.a: A finalizer is present in metadata.finalizers and the owning controller either isn't running or is erroring on the cleanup path, so it never removes the finalizer. Check controller logs for the reconcile error. Risky last resort: manually patch finalizers to an empty list to force deletion — this should be understood as accepting orphaned external resources (whatever the finalizer's cleanup was supposed to do never happens), a workaround for a bug, not routine practice.

drills.q: A teammate wants to build a CRD and controller for a feature that's really just 'apply this ConfigMap and Deployment with slightly different values per team.' Is this justified?
drills.a: Generally no — a CRD-and-controller pair is a new permanently-running distributed system requiring its own monitoring and on-call, and the honest bar is whether it encodes real operational knowledge (failover logic, external resource lifecycle) a simpler tool can't express. Templating (Helm/Kustomize) covers 'apply with different values per team' without the ongoing controller maintenance burden. This is the operator-sprawl anti-pattern.

drills.q: Explain why Kubernetes controllers are described as 'level-triggered, not edge-triggered,' and what concrete guarantee this gives up in exchange for what benefit.
drills.a: Level-triggered means Reconcile reacts to 'something changed, go figure out what's currently true' by re-deriving from current observed state, rather than reacting to a specific event delta. It gives up the efficiency of precise incremental updates, but gains correctness under at-least-once delivery, dropped/coalesced events, and controller restarts with no memory — since correctness only depends on being able to observe current state and re-derive the right action, not on perfectly replaying a history of events.

drills.q: A Service has healthy endpoints and kubectl port-forward to the backing pod works, but connecting to the ClusterIP times out. What are the two separate failure domains to check, in order?
drills.a: First isolate: does raw pod-to-pod connectivity work at all (bypass the Service, hit the pod IP directly) — if not, it's a CNI/routing problem. If direct pod IP works but the Service VIP doesn't, check kube-proxy's actual programmed state for its mode (iptables rules / ipvsadm / eBPF debug tool) and check NetworkPolicy separately, since these are three genuinely distinct layers.

drills.q: Security audit finds that pods with an 'ingress-restricted' NetworkPolicy can still reach any external endpoint outbound. Explain the mechanism, not just 'they forgot egress.'
drills.a: NetworkPolicy is direction-specific and additive. A policy selecting those pods only for Ingress flips ingress to default-deny-then-allow, but egress was never selected by any policy, so it remains at its original default-allow posture — nothing in the ingress policy touches egress at all, by design, not as a side effect that could have been anticipated from the ingress rule alone.

drills.q: A cluster running plain Flannel has a full set of well-written NetworkPolicy objects covering every namespace. Is the cluster actually protected? How would you verify?
drills.a: Not necessarily — NetworkPolicy is only enforced if the CNI implements a policy controller; plain Flannel implements none by default, so the objects can be fully valid and stored while having zero effect on traffic. Verify by direct testing: deploy two pods, apply a deny policy between them, and actually attempt the traffic that should now be blocked — if it still succeeds, enforcement isn't happening regardless of how correct the YAML looks.

drills.q: A service makes its first call to a new external API and it's consistently ~4x slower than subsequent calls to the same host. What's the mechanism and the fix?
drills.a: ndots:5 default: the hostname (fewer than 5 dots) gets every in-cluster search suffix tried first, each a real round trip returning a negative response, before the correct absolute lookup finally succeeds on the last attempt. Subsequent calls are fast because the successful (and often the negative) results get cached. Fix: trailing-dot the hostname in code to fully-qualify it, or tune ndots via pod.spec.dnsConfig, or deploy NodeLocal DNSCache.

drills.q: Your team is planning a new cluster in August 2026 and debating Ingress vs Gateway API. What's the actual current guidance, and does ingress-nginx's retirement change the calculus?
drills.a: Gateway API's core resources are GA and production-ready with a better role-oriented model (infra owns Gateway, app teams own HTTPRoute) and native traffic splitting Ingress can't do portably. The core Ingress API itself isn't going away (SIG-Network says maintained indefinitely) — but ingress-nginx specifically is retiring (best-effort only through March 2026, then archived), which is a forcing function only for teams using that specific controller. For a brand new cluster, Gateway API is the reasonable default choice today; TCPRoute/UDPRoute are still experimental so non-HTTP protocol needs may still need Ingress or a controller-specific solution.

drills.q: Why does kube-proxy still default to iptables mode given IPVS and nftables both outperform it, and IPVS is now deprecated?
drills.a: iptables remains default purely for backward compatibility across the huge existing installed base — the project has been explicit about this. IPVS (O(1) hash lookup, fixed iptables's O(n) chain-walk problem) is deprecated as of 1.35. nftables (stable since 1.33, atomic rule replacement) is the intended long-term replacement, but changing a core networking dataplane's default carries real upgrade risk at Kubernetes's installed-base scale, so it hasn't been made default yet with no committed timeline.

drills.q: Pods on node A can reach pods on node B for small requests but larger payloads silently fail or hang. What's a likely CNI-level cause and why?
drills.a: MTU mismatch — VXLAN-style overlay encapsulation (common in Flannel and similar overlay CNIs) adds header overhead that an unadjusted node/interface MTU doesn't account for, causing silent drops for packets that exceed the effective MTU once encapsulation overhead is added. Check CNI daemon logs and verify the node interface MTU is set several dozen bytes below the physical MTU to leave room for encapsulation.

drills.q: Why does a headless Service need to exist for a StatefulSet, and what specifically would a normal ClusterIP Service fail to provide?
drills.a: A normal ClusterIP Service returns one A record for a virtual IP, load-balancing across whichever pod happens to answer — it has no concept of addressing a specific ordinal. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns individual pod IPs directly (and per-pod names via the StatefulSet's serviceName), giving each replica an individually resolvable DNS identity, which is exactly what's needed to reach 'the primary at ordinal 0' specifically rather than any interchangeable pod.

drills.q: You try to relabel an existing Deployment's selector via kubectl apply and it fails. Why, and what are your two options?
drills.a: selector.matchLabels is immutable after creation, API validation rejects the change. Options: delete and recreate the Deployment (loses ReplicaSet/rollout history), or never touch it — get the selector correct on first creation.

drills.q: You scale a StatefulSet from 5 to 2 replicas expecting the freed storage to be reclaimed automatically, but kubectl get pvc still shows 5 PVCs. Bug or expected?
drills.a: Expected. persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy defaults whenScaled and whenDeleted to Retain — a deliberate data-safety default so a routine scale-down can't silently destroy data. Set whenScaled: Delete explicitly if the workload doesn't need that data to persist.

drills.q: A CronJob meant to run every 5 minutes is producing duplicate database writes. Diagnose.
drills.a: concurrencyPolicy is at its default, Allow — if a run takes longer than 5 minutes, the next scheduled run starts anyway, overlapping with the still-running one and both writing concurrently. Fix: set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid (skip if still running) or Replace (kill and restart), depending on the desired semantics.

drills.q: A Job manifest sets restartPolicy: Always on its pod template. What happens when you apply it?
drills.a: The API server rejects it at validation time — Always is incompatible with a Job ever reaching a terminal completed state, since it means 'restart no matter what.' Must be OnFailure or Never.

drills.q: Your log-shipper DaemonSet isn't running on your GPU node pool, which is exactly where you need the logs most. What do you check?
drills.a: The GPU nodes' taints (kubectl describe node | grep Taints) against the DaemonSet pod template's tolerations. GPU pools are commonly tainted to keep non-GPU workloads off; DaemonSet still respects taints like any pod, it doesn't bypass them, so a missing toleration silently excludes it.

drills.q: A CronJob 'just stopped running' after a multi-hour control-plane outage, with no error visible in the CronJob's own YAML. What's the mechanism, and how do you confirm and fix it?
drills.a: If the controller detects >=100 missed schedule times since it last checked, it stops scheduling that CronJob entirely rather than firing 100+ overlapping catch-up Jobs. Confirm via controller-manager logs for a 'too many missed start times' message. Not fixable via a CronJob field (startingDeadlineSeconds is a different, per-run knob) — requires manual Job trigger and investigating the outage cause.

drills.q: A rolling Deployment update appears stuck at '1 of 3 updated' for several minutes but hasn't errored. What's happening and what do you check first?
drills.a: The new ReplicaSet's pods are likely failing their readiness probe, so the rollout can't progress past maxUnavailable bounds; it won't be marked Failed until progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) elapses with no progress. Check kubectl describe pod on the new pods for readiness probe failures rather than waiting out the deadline.

drills.q: Why would a team deliberately choose StatefulSet updateStrategy: OnDelete instead of the default RollingUpdate for a production database cluster?
drills.a: RollingUpdate's guarantee (reverse-ordinal order, wait for Ready) doesn't account for domain-specific safety conditions like replication lag or leader status. OnDelete hands control to an external operator that decides exactly when each replica is safe to bounce based on that domain knowledge, rather than trusting StatefulSet's generic ordering.

drills.q: A Job has completions: 10, parallelism: 3, and non-indexed completion mode. How do the pods know which piece of work to do?
drills.a: They don't, inherently — non-indexed Jobs give no per-pod differentiation, so the application itself must pull work from an external queue (each of up to 3 concurrent pods grabs the next item until 10 succeed). If pods need a static, deterministic slice of work instead, use completionMode: Indexed, which injects JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX (0..completions-1) into each pod.

drills.q: A pod is permanently Pending; its PVC shows Bound. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: volumeBindingMode defaulted to Immediate, so the PV was bound to a zone before the pod was scheduled; the scheduler later placed the pod in a different zone the volume can't attach to. Fix: delete and recreate the PVC against a StorageClass set to WaitForFirstConsumer so binding happens after scheduling.

drills.q: A security reviewer pulls a Secret's YAML via kubectl and reads the plaintext password instantly. Is this a bug in Kubernetes, or expected behavior?
drills.a: Expected — Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted, and base64 is trivially reversible. This is exactly why EncryptionConfiguration with a real provider must be explicitly configured for actual confidentiality; the default is not a bug, it's the well-documented (and frequently missed) baseline.

drills.q: You just enabled EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider on a cluster that's been running for two years with hundreds of existing Secrets. Are you done?
drills.a: No — only newly written/updated objects get encrypted going forward. All existing Secrets remain in their prior (base64-only) form until explicitly rewritten. The rollout needs a follow-up bulk rewrite pass (get + replace every existing Secret) to actually bring them under the new encryption.

drills.q: A team updates a ConfigMap and expects a running Deployment's pods to pick up the new value within a minute, but nothing changes even after an hour. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The value is being injected via an env var (envFrom/valueFrom.configMapKeyRef), which is captured once at pod start and never updates for that pod's lifetime, unlike a volume mount which syncs live via kubelet's periodic sync. Fix: force a rollout, commonly via a checksum annotation on the pod template tied to the ConfigMap's content.

drills.q: An incident review finds a ServiceAccount token exfiltrated from a compromised pod six months ago still works today. What K8s version-era behavior explains this, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Pre-1.24 default behavior: ServiceAccounts auto-generated a long-lived Secret-based token with no built-in expiry, mounted into every pod using it. Fix: migrate to 1.24+ bound tokens via the TokenRequest API (time-limited, audience-bound, object-bound to the pod's lifetime) and delete any lingering legacy long-lived Secret tokens.

drills.q: A pentest finds a namespace-scoped ServiceAccount effectively has cluster-admin-level access despite its Role looking narrowly scoped to 'create tokens.' Explain the escalation path.
drills.a: The Role grants create access on serviceaccounts/token for a different, highly-privileged ServiceAccount. Anyone with that permission can mint a fresh bound token impersonating the privileged ServiceAccount at will — functionally equivalent to holding all of that ServiceAccount's permissions directly, even though the Role itself lists only a narrow-sounding verb.

drills.q: Why might disabling automountServiceAccountToken cluster-wide as a blanket security hardening pass break production, and how should it actually be rolled out?
drills.a: Any workload that genuinely calls the Kubernetes API (operators, controllers, client-go-based tooling) breaks outright with no token to authenticate with. It should be rolled out per-workload after auditing (via API server access logs or similar) which ServiceAccounts actually make API requests, setting automountServiceAccountToken: false only on the ones confirmed not to need it.

drills.q: A team wants a RWX PVC on their default cloud block-storage StorageClass and provisioning fails. Why, and what's the real fix?
drills.a: Most common block-storage CSI drivers (e.g. AWS EBS) only support ReadWriteOnce, not ReadWriteMany. Concurrent multi-node mounts need a genuinely different storage backend (EFS, Azure Files, NFS-backed StorageClass) with real performance/consistency tradeoffs versus block storage — RWX isn't something every StorageClass can be configured to support.

drills.q: Name the five staff/principal competencies.
drills.a: Scope, ambiguity tolerance, influence without authority, technical strategy, mentoring/multiplying.

drills.q: You have a story where you 'fixed a latency issue thoroughly and it stayed fixed.' Is this a staff-scope story?
drills.a: No — this is a well-executed senior-level story. A staff-scope version would show you recognizing the latency issue was a symptom of a bigger problem and expanding scope to fix the actual root cause across teams.

drills.q: Your influence-without-authority story is 'I explained the technical reasoning clearly and the team agreed.' What's missing to make this a strong staff/principal signal?
drills.a: What happened when the first attempt didn't fully work, and what specific tactic you changed (a working prototype instead of an argument, reframing around their incentives, finding a different messenger) rather than just explaining again more slowly.

drills.q: A candidate presents a 'strategy' that's a prioritized list of five good technical improvements. Is this a real strategy per Rumelt's framework?
drills.a: Not necessarily — it's a wish list unless it names a specific diagnosed obstacle and explicitly states what was NOT prioritized as a tradeoff. Good strategy = obstacle diagnosis + resourced response + explicit exclusions.

drills.q: Distinguish a 'multiplying' mentoring story from a generic coaching story.
drills.a: Multiplying involves a structural mechanism (process, template, review practice) that scales beyond one relationship and outlasts direct involvement. Generic coaching is 1:1 help with one junior engineer with no lasting structural change.

drills.q: Name Larson's four staff archetypes and give a one-word scope descriptor for each.
drills.a: Tech Lead (one team), Architect (multi-team domain coherence), Solver (hardest ambiguous problems, no fixed team), Right Hand (extends a leader's reach).

drills.q: An interviewer asks 'what would you have done if the initial data pointed the other way' after your ambiguity story. What does a strong answer demonstrate?
drills.a: That your provisional assumption was genuinely falsifiable and monitored — naming the specific signal that would have redirected you and how much investigation it would have taken to know, rather than a fixed bet you'd have defended regardless of evidence.

drills.q: Why can over-indexing on influence-without-authority stories backfire in an interview?
drills.a: It can read as someone who never has formal authority and never will — 'good at politics' rather than 'good at technical leadership.' Pair it with genuine technical depth and ownership evidence.

drills.q: How does staff scope typically differ from principal scope, and why does this matter for which stories to lead with in an interview?
drills.a: Staff scope is a bounded technical domain or single team's direction; principal scope is cross-organizational or genuinely undefined, with influence expected to extend to peer staff engineers and senior leadership, not just downward. Leading with a strong staff-level story while claiming principal scope creates a gap a calibrated interviewer will notice.

drills.q: Why do most leveling rubrics assess the five competencies separately, and what does this mean for interview prep strategy?
drills.a: Because a candidate can be strong on one axis (e.g. technical strategy) and weak on another (e.g. influence without authority) — the loop is designed to surface unevenness. Prep strategy: prepare five distinct, deep stories each anchored to one competency, not one well-rounded story stretched to cover all axes superficially.

drills.q: Write the window function clause to rank employees by salary within department, ties sharing a rank with a gap after.
drills.a: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)

drills.q: Why does `SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) rn FROM t WHERE rn = 1` fail?
drills.a: Window functions compute after WHERE in SQL's logical execution order, so rn doesn't exist yet when WHERE is evaluated. Must wrap in a CTE and filter the outer query instead.

drills.q: A running total by date repeats the same value for rows sharing a date. What's the cause and fix?
drills.a: The default window frame (RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) groups ORDER BY peer rows together. Fix: use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW explicitly.

drills.q: Write a recursive CTE pattern to find all descendants of an employee, with a safety guard against cyclic data.
drills.a: WITH RECURSIVE cte AS (anchor: SELECT ... WHERE employee_id = :id UNION ALL recursive: SELECT e.* FROM employees e JOIN cte ON e.manager_id = cte.employee_id WHERE cte.depth < 50) SELECT * FROM cte; — the depth cap in the recursive member prevents infinite recursion on a cyclic manager_id.

drills.q: Explain the gaps-and-islands trick for finding consecutive login streaks.
drills.a: ROW_NUMBER() over ordered dates per user, then date - (row_number * 1 day) is constant within an unbroken run (both increase by 1 per row) and changes at every gap. GROUP BY that constant isolates each streak.

drills.q: A dedup query using ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC keeps a different row on each run. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No deterministic tiebreaker — ties on updated_at let ROW_NUMBER pick arbitrarily. Fix: add a monotonic tiebreaker, e.g. ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC.

drills.q: What does LATERAL/CROSS APPLY let you do that a plain FROM subquery can't, and when would you reach for it over a window function?
drills.a: It can reference columns from earlier tables in the same FROM clause (a plain subquery is evaluated independently). Reach for it for top-N-per-group with N>1, or per-row correlated logic a window function alone can't express.

drills.q: Your EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a Seq Scan on a large table despite an index existing on the filtered column. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely a function wraps the column in the predicate (e.g. WHERE lower(email) = ...), defeating a plain btree index. Fix: create a functional/expression index matching the exact predicate expression, or rewrite the predicate to use the raw column.

drills.q: A recursive CTE over a 10,000-node, 20-level org chart queried frequently is slow. What's the production fix and its tradeoff?
drills.a: Materialize a closure table (precomputed ancestor-descendant pairs, refreshed on write) turning the query into an indexed lookup instead of iterative recursion — trades write-time complexity/storage for much faster reads.

drills.q: Write the month-over-month percent change formula using LAG, correctly guarding against division by zero.
drills.a: 100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY month)) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY month), 0) — NULLIF converts a zero prior-period value to NULL so division returns NULL instead of erroring.

drills.q: Name the seven canonical SQL interview question patterns that cover ~90% of real asks.
drills.a: Filter & aggregate, conditional joins, top-N per group, period-over-period change (LAG/LEAD), gap-and-island sessionization, deduplication keeping the latest record, hierarchy traversal via recursive CTE/self-join.

drills.q: Define distributed monolith in one sentence, distinct from 'microservices done badly.'
drills.a: Services that are physically separate processes but can't be deployed independently because a shared database or un-versioned contract forces coordinated releases.

drills.q: Why doesn't adding retries fix a dual-write problem?
drills.a: Retries retry a non-atomic operation; they don't create atomicity between the two writes. If the process crashes between write 1 and write 2, no amount of retrying write 2 later (without a durable record of the intent) recovers correctness.

drills.q: A migration in Team A's service breaks Team B's queries and nobody knew B depended on A's table. Name the anti-pattern and the fix.
drills.a: Shared database. Fix: enforce one writer per table (ideally at the credential level), give B an API or a CDC-derived read replica instead of direct table access.

drills.q: One file in the repo has 3x the PR churn and merge-conflict rate of any other. What anti-pattern, and what's the fix axis?
drills.a: God object. Fix: decompose along the actor axis — identify who independently drives each responsibility crammed into the file and extract each as its own collaborator (SRP's actor-based definition).

drills.q: A checkout page makes 40 sequential synchronous calls. Each call succeeds 99.9% of the time independently. What's the approximate end-to-end success rate, and what does that imply?
drills.a: 0.999^40 ≈ 96% — a set of five-nines-reliable dependencies becomes roughly a two-nines user experience purely from chaining calls synchronously.

drills.q: Parallelizing 40 chatty synchronous calls via a BFF cuts latency. Does it fix reliability too?
drills.a: No — parallelization only addresses the latency half. Reliability requires reducing call count (data locality, merging boundaries) or making individual calls more reliable (timeout/retry/circuit-breaker/bulkhead).

drills.q: An Order entity has only get_status()/set_status() and all validation lives in OrderService. What's the risk and the fix?
drills.a: Anemic domain model — any caller can set an illegal state combination since the entity enforces no invariant itself. Fix: push invariant-checking methods (order.ship() that checks self.status internally) into the entity.

drills.q: You 'fix' an anemic domain model by making Order also format invoice PDFs and call the payment gateway directly. What did you just create?
drills.a: A god object — you overcorrected by putting external I/O and cross-concern orchestration into the entity instead of just its own invariant checks. That belongs in a use-case/service layer.

drills.q: A small single-team product shares one database across two logical services for genuine cross-entity ACID transactions. Is this the shared-database anti-pattern?
drills.a: Not necessarily — the anti-pattern is accidental, unplanned multi-writer coupling with no coordination. A deliberate single-schema design with one team owning it and a real transactional need is a legitimate architecture choice, arguably a modular monolith.

drills.q: Rank these anti-patterns by how often they cause acute production incidents vs. chronic pain, and justify.
drills.a: Dual writes and shared database cause the most acute incidents (silent data divergence, surprise breakage on deploy) because failure is invisible until discovered. Distributed monolith causes chronic release friction that escalates during incidents (can't roll back A without B). Chatty services/god object are latency and availability risks under load or change. Anemic domain model is the slowest-burning — surfaces in postmortems days later as a root cause, rarely pages directly.

drills.q: Your org is about to split one team into two, and they currently share a database. What should happen before the split, not after?
drills.a: Assign explicit table ownership to whichever service will own it post-split, and migrate any cross-boundary access to an API or event stream before the split — doing it after creates the shared-database anti-pattern by default since neither team will want to own the migration once both depend on the status quo.

drills.q: What's the practical difference between a native <button> and a <div role="button">, and what's the minimum needed to make the div fully equivalent?
drills.a: A native button is focusable, fires click on Enter and Space, reports role:button, and participates in forms automatically. A div needs role="button", tabindex="0", a keydown handler for both Enter and Space, and an accessible name (visible text, aria-label, or aria-labelledby) -- worth asking why a real button couldn't be used instead.

drills.q: Explain precisely why "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" is true rather than just a slogan, with a concrete example.
drills.a: ARIA only changes the accessibility tree, never actual browser behavior. A custom dropdown with role="listbox" and aria-expanded but no arrow-key navigation announces standard listbox behavior a screen reader user then expects and doesn't get -- more confusing than an unstyled list with no such claim.

drills.q: Walk through everything an accessible modal needs to do around focus, in order, and explain what breaks if you skip restoring focus on close.
drills.a: Move focus in on open, trap focus inside (Tab/Shift+Tab wrap at boundaries), close on Escape, restore focus to the trigger on close. Skipping the restore step leaves focus on body/a removed node, so a keyboard user has no idea where they are and must re-navigate from the top of the page -- invisible to mouse-driven QA.

drills.q: Why is a visually obvious form validation error sometimes completely silent to a screen reader, and when should you use aria-live="assertive" vs "polite"?
drills.a: Content injected with no aria-live ancestor and no focus movement produces no announcement -- screen readers announce on navigation/focus or inside a live region, not on DOM mutation alone. polite waits for current activity to finish (most updates); assertive interrupts immediately (reserve for genuinely urgent things like session expiry) since overuse of assertive is disorienting.

drills.q: Why does SPA client-side routing break something multi-page sites got for free, and what's the minimum fix?
drills.a: A full page load resets focus and announces the new title as a side effect; a client-side route change does neither automatically, so focus silently stays wherever it was and screen reader users get no signal navigation happened. Fix: move focus to the new page's <h1 tabIndex={-1}> and update document.title on route change.

drills.q: What does axe-core actually catch versus structurally miss, and is manual testing optional under time pressure?
drills.a: Catches structural/presence issues (missing alt text, contrast against computed styles, missing labels, invalid ARIA values) -- roughly 57% of WCAG issues on average. Misses whether behavior matches announced semantics, whether flows make sense read aloud, etc. Not fully optional if real usability matters, but prioritizable: automated on every PR as a floor, manual passes scheduled on high-risk flows (checkout, auth, nav).

drills.q: Explain WCAG's three conformance levels and why AAA isn't the target most teams should pursue, but note when selective AAA adoption makes sense.
drills.a: A = floor (unusable-if-missing, e.g. keyboard operability). AA = practical/legal target (4.5:1 contrast, visible focus, consistent nav) referenced by ADA case law, Section 508, EN 301 549. AAA (7:1 contrast, etc.) isn't W3C-recommended as a universal target since cost/benefit doesn't scale the same way across a whole product. Selective AAA adoption makes sense for a known specific need, e.g. higher contrast for a data-dense dashboard used by an older user base.

drills.q: A custom Select component passes every automated accessibility check but a user reports it's unusable with a screen reader. What's your diagnostic process, and what else could explain it if your own keyboard test works fine?
drills.a: Test keyboard-only (Tab reachability, arrow keys per ARIA APG listbox/combobox pattern, Enter/Space/Escape) and with an actual screen reader (VoiceOver/NVDA), checking that announced role/state changes match visual behavior -- automated tools verify markup, not live behavior correctness. If your own test passes, check screen-reader+browser combination specifics (VoiceOver/Safari, NVDA/Firefox, JAWS/Chrome have known quirks) and whether the bug depends on how focus arrived at the component.

drills.q: Why might color contrast pass for a default theme but fail in dark mode, and how would you prevent this systemically rather than catching it after the fact?
drills.a: Contrast is a function of the specific foreground/background pair; a token often gets manually verified only against the default (light) theme, and a dark-mode pairing introduces a new combination that can fall under AA thresholds unnoticed. Prevent it by baking automated contrast validation into the design-token pipeline/CI, checking every semantic color-pair across every defined theme, rather than relying on manual spot-checks.
