drills.q: Give a real example where adding ARIA actively made a component worse than having none, and explain the general lesson.
drills.a: A dropdown given role="listbox" and aria-expanded purely to satisfy an automated scanner, but with no arrow-key navigation or Enter-to-select implemented -- a screen reader announces standard listbox affordances that then fail to work when the user tries them, which is more confusing than an unstyled list creating no such expectation. General lesson: ARIA is a claim about behavior, and an unfulfilled claim is worse than no claim, since it actively misleads rather than leaving an honest gap.

drills.q: Walk through the five stages of the browser rendering pipeline from raw HTML/CSS to pixels on screen.
drills.a: Parse HTML into DOM and CSS into CSSOM (both incremental; CSS is render-blocking). Combine into a render tree of visible nodes with computed style. Layout computes geometry (x/y/width/height) for every box. Paint rasterizes pixel content per layer. Composite (on a separate compositor thread) assembles layers into the final frame, applying transform/opacity as cheap GPU operations.

drills.q: Explain the mechanism (not just the rule) for why transform is cheaper to animate than top/left.
drills.a: top/left are geometry properties -- changing them invalidates layout, which must run on the main thread, followed by paint, followed by composite, contending with all other main-thread work for the frame budget. transform on an already-promoted GPU layer skips layout and paint entirely; the compositor thread reapplies a matrix transform to the already-rasterized texture, running independent of the main thread.

drills.q: Contrast display:none and visibility:hidden in terms of render tree membership and layout cost.
drills.a: display:none removes the element from the render tree entirely: no layout, no paint, zero cost, no occupied space. visibility:hidden keeps it in the render tree, fully laid out (occupies space, affects sibling positions) but skips painting it -- cheaper to toggle when layout stability of surrounding content matters.

drills.q: What is forced synchronous layout / layout thrashing, give a code example of the bug, and the fix.
drills.a: Reading a geometry property (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, getComputedStyle) immediately after a style write forces the browser to synchronously flush layout to answer correctly. Looping write-then-read per element (el.style.width = el.offsetWidth + 10 + 'px') turns one lazy layout pass into N synchronous ones. Fix: batch all reads first, then apply all writes.

drills.q: A DevTools Performance trace shows large purple bars on every frame during a scroll interaction. Diagnose and confirm.
drills.a: Purple = Layout/Recalculate Style; hypothesis is a scroll handler or scroll-triggered effect is changing a geometry property (e.g. animating top for a parallax effect) every frame. Confirm by clicking into a purple bar to see the triggering call stack, and cross-check with paint flashing / Layout Shift Regions in the Rendering tab.

drills.q: What does will-change actually do, what does it cost, and why is applying it broadly a mistake?
drills.a: It promotes the element to its own GPU-backed compositing layer in advance, avoiding a layer-creation cost on the animation's first frame. Cost: each layer consumes GPU memory (~width*height*4 bytes texture) plus compositing overhead. Applying it to many elements or leaving it on permanently causes 'layer explosion,' which measurably degrades performance on GPU/memory-constrained devices -- it should be toggled on right before an animation and off (will-change:auto) after.

drills.q: Why does a render-blocking stylesheet in <head> delay First Contentful Paint even when the HTML itself arrives instantly?
drills.a: The browser can't safely paint until the CSSOM is complete, because any rule anywhere in an unparsed stylesheet could apply to already-parsed DOM nodes -- painting early risks showing incorrectly styled content that must then be redone. Fix: inline critical above-the-fold CSS, defer the rest, mark scripts defer/async so they don't also block parsing.

drills.q: Explain the difference between defer and async on a <script> tag and why an unmarked script blocks parsing at all.
drills.a: An unmarked synchronous script can call document.write() and mutate the DOM being parsed, so the parser halts until it downloads and executes. defer downloads in parallel with parsing but executes after parsing completes, in document order relative to other deferred scripts. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as ready, with no ordering guarantee relative to parsing or other scripts.

drills.q: What is the frame budget at 60Hz vs 120Hz, and why is requestAnimationFrame correct where setTimeout is not?
drills.a: 16.7ms at 60Hz, 8.3ms at 120Hz (1000/refresh rate). requestAnimationFrame schedules its callback synced to the actual next paint at whatever the display's real refresh rate is, adapting automatically. setTimeout has no relationship to the paint cycle at all and will drift or misfire relative to the true frame cadence, especially on non-60Hz displays.

drills.q: A drag-to-reorder list needs siblings to visibly make room as an item is dragged. Can this be done compositor-only, and what's the real technique?
drills.a: Not purely -- siblings' actual flow position is genuinely changing, which is a layout-affecting change. The realistic approach is FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play): commit the real layout change once/synchronously, then animate only the visual delta between old and new position via transform on each affected element -- the dragged item itself can move via pure transform following the pointer the whole time.

drills.q: Why can a large box-shadow be a measurable performance problem, and what CSS tool isolates it without the memory cost of will-change?
drills.a: Rasterizing a shadow's blur/spread is more expensive than a flat fill, and if the element shares a paint-invalidation region with something that repaints often, the expensive shadow gets re-rasterized far more than its own visual state changes. contain:paint (or contain:content) scopes paint invalidation to the element's own subtree without necessarily promoting a full GPU layer the way will-change does -- a lighter-weight fix for this specific problem.

drills.q: Is layout cost a fixed O(1) operation per DOM change? Explain what actually determines its cost, and how contain:layout changes that.
drills.a: No fixed constant -- cost depends on how far the geometry change propagates: a leaf absolutely-positioned node can be nearly free, while an early flow-participating element's height change can force re-layout of every subsequent sibling and a content-sized parent, proportional to the affected subtree. contain:layout gives the engine a real guarantee that an element's internal layout can't affect anything outside its box (and vice versa), letting it scope invalidation to just that subtree rather than relying on heuristics -- valuable for large lists/grids of independently-changing items.

drills.q: Given width:200px, padding:20px, border:5px, compute the final rendered width under content-box and under border-box.
drills.a: content-box: 250px total (200 content + 40px padding both sides + 10px border both sides, all added on top of the declared width). border-box: exactly 200px total -- the content area shrinks to 150px to make room for padding and border within the declared width.

drills.q: State the decision rule for choosing Flexbox vs Grid for a given layout, beyond '1D vs 2D.'
drills.a: Ask whether items need to align across both rows and columns simultaneously as a structural requirement (page shells, card grids that must line up row-to-row, aligned form fields) -- use Grid. If distributing/aligning along a single row or column with wrapping as a secondary concern -- use Flexbox. They compose: Grid for outer structure, Flexbox for alignment within individual grid items is a normal, common pattern.

drills.q: Why doesn't z-index:9999 bring an element above a sibling with z-index:1, and what's the actual debugging method?
drills.a: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context -- if the high z-index element is nested inside an ancestor that itself created a new stacking context (opacity<1, transform, filter, position:fixed/sticky, will-change, isolation:isolate, or position:relative/absolute with non-auto z-index), its z-index has no meaning relative to anything outside that context. Debug by tracing ancestors for stacking-context-creating properties (DevTools Layers panel or computed styles), not by raising the number.

drills.q: List every property/condition that creates a new stacking context.
drills.a: position:fixed or sticky (unconditionally); position:relative/absolute combined with a non-auto z-index; opacity less than 1; transform other than none; filter/backdrop-filter other than none; will-change naming a stacking-context-triggering property; isolation:isolate; being a flex/grid item with a non-auto z-index.

drills.q: A position:fixed modal overlay scrolls away with the page instead of staying pinned to the viewport. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check ancestors for transform, filter, will-change:transform, perspective, or contain:layout -- any of these establishes a new containing block for fixed descendants, overriding the expected viewport-relative behavior, so the 'fixed' element becomes positioned relative to that ancestor and scrolls when it scrolls. Fix: remove the property from the ancestor, or portal the modal to document.body.

drills.q: Explain margin collapsing with concrete numbers, and why Flexbox/Grid children avoid it.
drills.a: Adjacent vertical margins between block-level siblings in normal flow collapse to the larger value, not the sum -- margin-bottom:20px followed by margin-top:30px produces a 30px gap total, not 50px. This is vertical-only, normal-flow-only behavior; Flexbox and Grid items don't participate in margin collapsing at all, which is why gap on a flex/grid container is more predictable than margin-based spacing.

drills.q: A card component must switch to a side-by-side internal layout once it has at least 400px of available width, and it's used in both a wide dashboard and a narrow sidebar. Design the CSS, and explain why media queries can't solve this.
drills.a: container-type:inline-size on the card's wrapper, then @container (min-width:400px) { .card { grid-template-columns: ...; } } on its internal layout -- responds to the actual container width regardless of viewport. Media queries only see viewport width, so they can't distinguish 'this component happens to be in a narrow sidebar' from 'the viewport itself is narrow' -- structurally the wrong signal for a reusable component.

drills.q: What are logical properties, why do they matter beyond RTL support, and what's the tradeoff of adopting them?
drills.a: Logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-block-end, inset-inline-start) express spacing/positioning in flow-relative terms rather than fixed physical directions -- inline-start maps to left in LTR horizontal writing but auto-flips for RTL and reorients for vertical writing modes, eliminating the need for a parallel RTL override stylesheet. Tradeoff: no real performance cost, but genuine unfamiliarity/readability friction for teams used to physical properties.

drills.q: What does isolation:isolate do, when is it a deliberate fix rather than a workaround, and what's its risk if overused?
drills.a: It forces a new stacking context without any other side-effecting property (no forced opacity/transform), used deliberately to sandbox a self-contained component's internal z-index values so they can't leak out and conflict with the rest of the page. Risk: it can trap content that legitimately needs to stack above something outside its own subtree (e.g., a tooltip that must render above a sibling modal), recreating the exact stacking-boundary problem it was meant to solve, just self-inflicted.

drills.q: Before container queries, how did teams solve the 'component must adapt to its actual container width, not the viewport' problem, and what did that cost?
drills.a: ResizeObserver in JavaScript, watching the container element and toggling a class or inline style based on measured width. It worked but added JS runtime cost, a layout-thrashing risk if reads/writes weren't batched carefully, and an extra render-cycle lag -- all of which pure CSS container queries (full browser support as of 2026) eliminate entirely.

drills.q: Explain composition over configuration with a concrete example of where a prop-driven API breaks down, and whether composition is strictly better.
drills.a: A prop-driven Card (imageUrl, title, footerButtons, showDivider...) accumulates a prop per new requirement and eventually can't express an unanticipated layout. A composed API (<Card><Card.Image/></Card>) lets consumers arrange primitives directly. Not strictly better -- composition costs more consumer code for genuinely uniform, simple components where a well-configured prop API with defaults is faster and harder to misuse.

drills.q: How does a compound component share state between its parts without prop drilling, and what does the consumer still control?
drills.a: A parent component holds shared state and provides it via React Context scoped to the compound component; children consume it internally instead of the consumer manually wiring props between them. The consumer still fully controls DOM arrangement and structure, which a monolithic prop API couldn't offer.

drills.q: What problem does the W3C DTCG token standard solve, and what mechanism lets a semantic token reference a primitive one?
drills.a: Before a shared standard (first stable spec Oct 2025), every design tool/pipeline used its own token format, causing manual, error-prone, drift-prone translation between Figma, build pipelines, and code. Token aliasing (e.g. {color.blue.500} inside a semantic token's $value) lets a semantic token point at a primitive, which is the mechanism theming depends on -- components reference only the semantic layer.

drills.q: A component looks fine in light mode but has unreadable low-contrast text in dark mode. Diagnose the architectural cause and a systemic prevention.
drills.a: The component almost certainly references a primitive token directly (hardcoded gray-900) instead of a semantic token (color-text-primary) meant to resolve differently per theme, bypassing the indirection layer. Prevent systemically with a lint rule/token-usage linter in CI that flags direct primitive-token references in component code.

drills.q: Why is versioning a design system genuinely harder than a typical utility library, using a concrete example?
drills.a: Semver assumes the public surface equals the code API, but a token change (e.g. a 2px spacing adjustment) can silently break visual layout across dozens of surfaces with zero function-signature change -- looking like a safe patch while behaving like a breaking change. A mature team runs visual regression across the whole system and treats token renames with API-breaking-change rigor, not routine patch releases.

drills.q: When is building a formal design system premature, and what should happen instead if a second product is planned for 'sometime next year'?
drills.a: Premature for a single product/team with no concrete near-term second consumer -- coordination overhead (versioned package, cross-team review, deprecation policy) only pays off with genuine reuse. For a vaguely planned future second product, avoid building the formal system now (risks guessed requirements); document existing shared patterns lightly and do the formal extraction once the second product's real needs are known.

drills.q: Compare headless/behavior-only component libraries vs fully styled opinionated ones, and state which fits a product needing strong brand differentiation.
drills.a: Headless (Radix, React Aria): correct ARIA/keyboard logic solved once, zero visual opinion, more setup per team. Fully styled (Material UI, Chakra): fastest to consistent UI, but fights distinctive differentiation since consistency IS its value proposition. A product needing strong brand differentiation should choose headless, since fully opinionated systems impose a default look that works against differentiation.

drills.q: A design system's Button has an open style prop most teams use regularly to override appearance. What does this indicate and how do you address it, and is adding more variants always the fix?
drills.a: It indicates the variant system hasn't captured the real design space -- the system provides an illusion of consistency silently bypassed in practice, arguably worse than visible inconsistency since it's often not caught in review. Address by auditing actual override usage and formalizing recurring patterns as first-class variants. Not always the fix: if usage is highly varied/product-specific rather than converging on recurring patterns, the better fix may be a genuine composition point (slot, render prop) rather than an ever-growing incomplete variant list.

drills.q: What happens if a consumer renders a compound subcomponent (e.g. Tabs.Tab) outside its provider, and how should a well-designed API handle it?
drills.a: The context value is null/undefined. A well-designed compound component should explicitly guard this and throw a clear developer-facing error (e.g. "Tabs.Tab must be used within a Tabs component") rather than silently failing or throwing an obscure runtime error from destructuring null.

drills.q: A designer changes a spacing token by 2px and engineering ships it as a routine patch release. What's the actual risk, and how should a mature team handle it differently?
drills.a: The risk is silent layout breakage across every surface referencing that token, shipped with no one specifically reviewing the blast radius since it looks trivial. A mature team runs visual regression across the whole system before releasing any token change and treats token value changes/renames with deliberate versioning rigor comparable to an API change, not a routine patch.

drills.q: Name the frontend XSS sinks that matter in a modern codebase, and explain why React's default rendering avoids the most common class.
drills.a: innerHTML/outerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, eval/new Function, document.write, javascript: URLs, string-arg setTimeout/setInterval. React JSX {value} interpolation auto-escapes by default, so the vulnerability requires deliberately opting into dangerouslySetInnerHTML rather than being the default behavior.

drills.q: If a feature genuinely needs to render user-supplied HTML (rich text), what's the correct approach, and why not a hand-rolled regex sanitizer?
drills.a: Sanitize with a library like DOMPurify using an explicit allowlist of tags/attributes before passing to dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Regex can't reliably parse HTML and is a well-documented source of sanitizer bypasses -- avoidance isn't an option since the feature requirement is real.

drills.q: Why is nonce-based CSP with strict-dynamic preferred over host-allowlist CSP, and what single mistake completely defeats a nonce-based policy?
drills.a: Host allowlists break constantly since third-party scripts load further scripts from unanticipated origins, and any allowlisted domain with an open redirect becomes a bypass. strict-dynamic propagates trust cryptographically instead. A static or reused nonce (not freshly random per HTTP response) completely defeats the mechanism.

drills.q: Explain precisely what CORS protects against, and correct the misconception that a CORS error means the request never reached the server.
drills.a: CORS is a browser-enforced restriction on JS reading a cross-origin response, not a server-side authorization mechanism -- it doesn't stop the request from being sent or processed. A CORS error in the console typically means the request DID reach the server and already had its side effects (e.g. a DB write on POST); the browser just blocked the script from reading the response.

drills.q: Why is dynamically reflecting the Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin dangerous, and how do you correctly support multiple legitimate credentialed origins?
drills.a: It reintroduces the same vulnerability the spec's block on '*' + credentials:true prevents -- any origin can make a credentialed request and read the response -- while looking compliant since it's not the literal wildcard. Correct approach: validate the incoming Origin against an explicit server-side allowlist and only echo it back when it matches.

drills.q: Compare localStorage, HttpOnly cookie, and in-memory token storage, and state the 2026 practitioner consensus.
drills.a: localStorage: readable by any XSS, full silent account takeover risk. HttpOnly cookie: invisible to JS (immune to XSS read) but auto-sent by browser, introducing CSRF surface. In-memory: minimizes exposure window (nothing persisted) but needs a working silent-refresh flow. Consensus: short-lived access token in memory + refresh token in HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie + CSRF token on state-changing endpoints.

drills.q: Explain clickjacking mechanically and the current correct defense, including a common implementation mistake.
drills.a: An attacker embeds the target in an invisible/positioned iframe, overlays decoy UI, tricking clicks on a hidden real button underneath. Defense: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' (or explicit allowlist), which wins over legacy X-Frame-Options in CSP2+ browsers. Common mistake: setting X-Frame-Options via a <meta> tag, which has no effect -- it only works as a real HTTP response header.

drills.q: Describe the September 2025 npm supply-chain incident (chalk/debug/Shai-Hulud) and what it structurally demonstrates about dependency risk.
drills.a: A phishing attack against one npm maintainer compromised 18 packages (chalk, debug, ansi-styles, strip-ansi -- 2.6B combined weekly downloads) with a crypto-wallet-targeting payload, followed by the self-propagating Shai-Hulud worm (500+ packages wave 1, tens of thousands of repos by a November 2025 '2.0' campaign). It demonstrates the vulnerability lived in a transitive dependency several layers removed from any affected team's own code -- direct usage isn't required for exposure.

drills.q: Design CSRF protection for a system that just moved auth tokens from localStorage to HttpOnly cookies, and explain why SameSite alone isn't sufficient.
drills.a: Set SameSite=Lax/Strict as a first layer, then add an explicit CSRF token on state-changing endpoints -- either the synchronizer token pattern (server-issued token embedded in page, validated on submit) or double-submit cookie (a second non-HttpOnly cookie the client must echo as a header, unreadable cross-origin). SameSite=Lax still allows top-level GET navigations to carry the cookie, and browser enforcement nuances mean it's a strong mitigation, not a complete guarantee.

drills.q: A team's own application code never directly imports a package later found compromised in a supply-chain attack. Were they still at risk, and what are the practical mitigations regardless of direct usage?
drills.a: Yes -- if the compromised package was anywhere in the transitive dependency tree, it still executes in the same process/build environment with the same permissions; direct usage isn't required for exposure. Mitigations: commit and enforce lockfiles to prevent silent version drift on install, run supply-chain-specific scanning in CI (behavioral analysis like Socket/Snyk, not just CVE matching), minimize dependency surface, and apply extra scrutiny to auto-merge bots on auth/crypto/build-tooling dependencies.

drills.q: State RTL's core philosophy and what happens to a well-written RTL suite when a component is refactored from class-based to hooks with no behavior change.
drills.a: "The more your tests resemble how software is used, the more confidence they give." A well-written suite queries/interacts like a real user and asserts on visible outcomes, so nothing should break from a pure implementation refactor -- if tests do break, they were coupled to implementation details, not following the philosophy.

drills.q: Why does RTL rank getByRole above getByTestId, and when is getByTestId actually appropriate?
drills.a: getByRole queries by accessible role/name, so failure to find an element this way also signals a potential real accessibility gap. getByTestId bypasses that signal and couples the test to an implementation detail. Appropriate only as a genuine last resort when no accessible query can identify the element and improving semantic markup isn't feasible.

drills.q: Why does MSW intercept at the network layer instead of mocking fetch/an API client module, and what gap does this NOT close on its own?
drills.a: Network-layer interception means application code makes a genuinely real request that's intercepted, so the same handlers work across unit, integration, E2E, and local dev -- avoiding duplicated per-test-file fakes. It doesn't close the mock-accuracy gap on its own; handlers can still drift from what the real API returns without a shared contract source or periodic contract tests.

drills.q: What specifically makes Playwright locators auto-waiting, what flakiness class does it eliminate, and what does it NOT eliminate?
drills.a: Locators/assertions retry against live DOM state until the condition is met or timeout, eliminating the historically biggest E2E flake source: asserting before an async update resolves. It does not eliminate shared test state interference or genuine environment/network timing variance.

drills.q: Explain the testing trophy vs the classic testing pyramid, what specific failure mode the trophy reacts to, and whether it means minimizing unit tests.
drills.a: The pyramid puts unit tests as the widest layer; the trophy (Kent C. Dodds) puts integration tests widest, since most real bugs live in connections between units, not isolated functions -- pyramid-shaped suites can have high unit coverage while missing whole bug classes. It doesn't mean eliminating unit tests -- they remain right for algorithmically complex, isolable logic; the trophy argues for proportion, not elimination of any layer.

drills.q: Name the well-documented causes of visual regression test flakiness and their fixes, plus one additional cause beyond OS/GPU rendering and dynamic content.
drills.a: Font rendering/anti-aliasing/sub-pixel positioning differ by OS/GPU -- fix by generating/comparing baselines only in a consistent Docker environment. Dynamic content (timestamps, IDs) -- fix by masking/excluding before comparison. Additional cause: in-progress animations/transitions or content that hasn't fully settled at capture time -- fix with reduced-motion handling or waiting for a stable state before screenshotting.

drills.q: A team's E2E suite is 40 minutes with a 15% flake rate. Diagnose the likely causes in order of typical prevalence and propose a remediation plan.
drills.a: Likely causes: shared/mutable test state causing cross-test interference, too much coverage pushed to the E2E layer instead of integration, and genuine environment/timing variance. Remediation: move non-browser-dependent tests down to RTL+MSW integration, isolate test data per run, parallelize across CI workers, and quarantine/investigate flaky tests rather than letting them be ignored.

drills.q: Why can a test suite be 100% green while a feature is visibly broken in the browser, and can this still happen even with correctly-used RTL?
drills.a: It happens when assertions target implementation details (internal state, DOM structure) that remain true despite broken user-facing behavior. RTL structurally prevents that specific class since it can only assert on visible/operable output -- but a team can still write insufficiently narrow RTL assertions (checking existence without content, or not exercising the actual interaction that triggers a bug), so behavioral coverage still requires deliberate judgment RTL doesn't enforce.

drills.q: A team pushes back that reducing E2E coverage feels like reducing safety. How do you address this directly?
drills.a: Reframe the tradeoff: a suite nobody trusts (routinely re-run on failure or ignored) provides less real safety than a smaller, fast, reliable suite that's actually respected and actionable. Coverage that exists on paper but is dismissed isn't providing the safety it appears to -- the goal is maximizing trusted signal, not test count.

drills.q: MSW mocks pass in CI but the real integration breaks in staging. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: The mock handler's response shape has silently drifted from what the real API actually returns, since nothing automatically keeps them in sync. Fix: generate MSW handlers from a shared API contract (OpenAPI spec, tRPC types) where possible, or add lightweight contract tests validating the real API against the same shape the mock assumes.

drills.q: Trace the exact output order: console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
drills.a: 1, 4, 3, 2. Synchronous code runs to completion first (1, 4). The microtask queue then drains fully before any macrotask runs (3). Only then does the setTimeout macrotask run (2).

drills.q: Define microtask vs macrotask and give two examples of each, plus the ordering rule between them.
drills.a: Macrotasks (setTimeout/setInterval, UI events, I/O callbacks) -- only one runs per event loop iteration. Microtasks (Promise .then/.catch/.finally, queueMicrotask) -- the ENTIRE queue drains, including newly-added ones, before the next macrotask or paint.

drills.q: Why does a for(var i...) loop with setTimeout inside log the same final value 3 times, but for(let j...) logs 0,1,2?
drills.a: var is function-scoped -- one shared binding across all iterations, so by the time any callback fires (after the sync loop completes), the variable holds its final value. let creates a fresh binding per iteration by specification, so each closure captures its own distinct value.

drills.q: State the four this-binding rules in precedence order and explain why arrow functions are the exception.
drills.a: new binding > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.method(), determined by call site) > default (undefined in strict mode / global otherwise). Arrow functions have no own this slot at all -- they lexically capture this from their enclosing scope at definition time and cannot be rebound by any of the four rules.

drills.q: Explain the prototype chain and how class/extends relates to it mechanically.
drills.a: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link; property lookup checks own properties then walks the chain until it finds a match or hits null. class/extends is syntax sugar that sets up exactly this chain automatically (Dog.prototype.__proto__ = Animal.prototype) -- not a separate inheritance mechanism. instanceof walks this same chain looking for the constructor's .prototype, it isn't a stored type tag.

drills.q: Contrast ES modules and CommonJS on resolution, binding semantics, and loading -- not just syntax.
drills.a: ESM: static resolution (analyzable before execution), LIVE read-only bindings (an import reflects later updates in the source module), async by spec, supports top-level await. CommonJS: dynamic require() (a real function call, can be conditional), VALUE COPY at require-time (later reassignment in the source isn't seen), synchronous loading.

drills.q: What is a dual-package hazard and why is it still a real problem in 2026?
drills.a: When a package is instantiated twice in the same dependency tree -- once via require() and once via import -- producing two separate module instances whose instanceof checks and any shared module-level state diverge. It remains real because the npm ecosystem has decades of CJS-only packages and ESM/CJS interop is not a fully solved problem at the tooling level.

drills.q: What does `await` actually desugar to, and trace: async function f(){ console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b'); } console.log('start'); f(); console.log('end');
drills.a: await expr is equivalent to Promise.resolve(expr).then(continuation) -- everything after await runs as a microtask. f() runs synchronously to the first await ('a'), then returns control to the caller. Output: start, a, end, b.

drills.q: Two independent async operations are called with `await a(); await b();`. What's wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: Sequential await forces b() to not even start until a() fully resolves, serializing independent work (total latency ~= a+b instead of max(a,b)). Fix: start both first (const pa = a(), pb = b();) then await Promise.all([pa, pb]).

drills.q: A recursive .then() chain with no terminating condition freezes a page that is still visibly using CPU. Explain the mechanism and how to fix it.
drills.a: The microtask queue must fully drain -- including new microtasks enqueued during the drain -- before the loop can proceed to the next macrotask or repaint. A chain that keeps scheduling a new microtask from within its own .then() never lets the drain finish, starving rendering and pending macrotasks indefinitely. Fix: insert an actual macrotask boundary periodically, e.g. setTimeout(next, 0) instead of Promise.resolve().then(next).

drills.q: Explain why a generator's local variables persist across .next() calls, and how this differs from a closure-based counter object.
drills.a: A generator's execution context (including local variables and its position in the function body) is suspended, not discarded, between .next() calls -- each resumes exactly where the last yield paused. Unlike a closure-based counter (which only exposes whatever methods you explicitly write), a generator natively implements the iterator protocol and can be consumed directly by for...of, spread, and destructuring, and can pause mid-expression or mid-loop anywhere a yield appears.

drills.q: Why does `this` log undefined when a regular (non-arrow) object method is passed directly as `element.addEventListener('click', obj.method)`?
drills.a: this is determined by the call site, not the definition site. Passing obj.method by reference detaches it from obj -- when the browser invokes the bare function reference (or binds this to the DOM element itself, per addEventListener's own behavior), the original obj context is lost. Fix: pass an arrow function wrapper or .bind(obj) the method before passing it.

drills.q: Distinguish Promise.all and Promise.allSettled behavior on partial failure, and when you'd choose each.
drills.a: Promise.all rejects immediately with the first rejection reason without waiting for the others to settle (though they continue running in the background, their outcomes are lost to the caller). Promise.allSettled waits for every promise to settle regardless of individual failures and returns a status/value or status/reason for each. Choose allSettled when you need to know the outcome of all operations even if some fail; Promise.all when any single failure should short-circuit the whole operation.

drills.q: Explain the fundamental difference between a React Server Component and a component rendered via traditional pre-RSC SSR.
drills.a: Traditional SSR renders HTML on the server but still ships the same component's JavaScript to the client to hydrate and potentially re-render. A Server Component's code never reaches the client at all -- it renders to a serialized RSC payload describing the tree, and if it has no interactive behavior, none of its JS is sent to the browser, directly reducing bundle size rather than just moving the initial render server-side.

drills.q: Can a Client Component import and render a Server Component directly? Explain why or why not, and the correct pattern.
drills.a: No -- a Client Component's code runs in the browser where there's no server execution context to run a Server Component's async data-fetching logic. The correct pattern: a Server Component parent renders a Client Component and passes Server Components to it as children/props; the Client Component treats them as an already-resolved opaque slot rather than importing/rendering them itself.

drills.q: Explain how Suspense-driven streaming SSR fixes the pre-RSC problem where one slow data dependency blocked the entire SSR response.
drills.a: The server sends the shell HTML including Suspense fallbacks immediately, without waiting on slow data. As each Suspense boundary's data resolves, the server streams an additional chunk with the real content plus an inline script that swaps it into the already-delivered DOM. Boundaries resolve independently, so a slow section doesn't block a faster section elsewhere on the page from appearing as soon as it's ready.

drills.q: What is a Server Action, and mechanically why does <form action={serverActionFn}> work before JavaScript has loaded?
drills.a: A function marked 'use server' that's callable from the client like a local async function but actually executes as a request on the server. Passed directly as a form's action, it becomes a genuine HTML form submission -- a real POST carrying a serialized reference to the server function to invoke -- which is native browser behavior requiring no client JS to have loaded or hydrated.

drills.q: Give three concrete, distinct causes of a React hydration mismatch, and explain what React does when it detects one.
drills.a: 1) Reading browser-only APIs (window, localStorage) unconditionally during server render, producing different output server vs client. 2) Non-deterministic values (Date.now(), Math.random(), an incrementing counter) used in initial render output instead of useId(). 3) Invalid HTML nesting that the browser silently restructures during parsing, producing a DOM shape different from what React expected. React discards the mismatched server-rendered subtree and re-renders it client-side, causing visible flicker and potential loss of focus/form state.

drills.q: Mechanically, why does useId() solve the generated-id hydration mismatch where Math.random() or a module counter doesn't?
drills.a: useId() derives a stable identifier from the component's position within the render tree rather than from a random or incrementing runtime source, so the server's render and the client's initial render pass compute the same id for the same component position deterministically -- unlike Math.random() or a counter, which produce different values across separate executions (server process vs browser).

drills.q: What changed about params/searchParams/cookies()/headers() in Next.js 16, and why does the framework want this async?
drills.a: They became strictly asynchronous -- every page, layout, and route handler reading them must await now, versus the pre-16 synchronous object shape. It's the highest-file-count breaking change in the 16 migration (codemod handles most cases). Architecturally it enables more flexible request handling, e.g. Partial Prerendering, where the framework needs to defer resolving request-specific data independently of static shell generation -- making the API async is what allows that flexibility without a separate parallel API.

drills.q: What does Cache Components' 'use cache' directive do in Next.js 16, and when do you use revalidateTag() vs updateTag()?
drills.a: 'use cache' at the top of an async function/component caches its rendered OUTPUT (not just raw fetched data), with a cache key auto-derived from its inputs, composing with Partial Prerendering for a static shell plus separately streamed dynamic content. revalidateTag() is for content where eventual consistency is fine (a blog list that can lag by seconds). updateTag() is used inside Server Actions specifically when the acting user needs to see their own change immediately (a profile update) -- conflating the two produces stale UI after a user's own action or unnecessarily aggressive invalidation.

drills.q: A page renders correctly in local testing but shows a hydration mismatch only under real production streaming. What class of bug is this, and how do you investigate it?
drills.a: The component's output likely depends on timing relative to when its Suspense boundary resolves and gets injected -- behaving identically in a full, non-streamed static render (typical local testing) but differing when boundaries genuinely stagger in production. Investigate by looking for anything the component reads that could differ depending on whether it hydrates early (right after the shell) or late (after a slow boundary resolves) -- wall-clock time, a value another already-hydrated part of the page has mutated, or an unstable measurement/DOM assumption across that timing gap.

drills.q: What's a legitimate reason a team might choose NOT to adopt the RSC/App Router model despite it being the current recommended default?
drills.a: The added mental model cost -- server/client component boundaries, a new explicit caching model (Cache Components), and debugging across a non-HTTP RSC serialization format -- can genuinely outweigh the benefit for a small app or team, especially one that's mostly interactive with modest SEO/first-paint requirements. This is a legitimate, currently-live disagreement in the ecosystem, not a settled 'RSC is always better' conclusion.

drills.q: List the three triggers for a React component re-render, and explain why 'props changed' isn't a fourth independent one.
drills.a: Own state change (useState/useReducer), parent re-renders and the component isn't memoized, or a subscribed context value changes. A prop can only change because the parent re-rendered and passed a new value -- it's a description of what happens during trigger #2, not an independent cause.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why array index as key breaks state when a list is reordered.
drills.a: React matches list children across renders by key to decide whether to reuse a DOM node/component instance. With index as key, the key for 'whatever is now at position 0' is always 0 regardless of which logical item that is after reordering -- React reuses the existing DOM node (including uncontrolled state it holds) and silently reattaches it to the wrong logical item.

drills.q: Why must hooks be called unconditionally and in the same order on every render? What's the actual data structure behind this rule?
drills.a: React tracks each hook's state via its position in a linked list attached to the component's fiber, not by name -- there's no call-site identifier to match against. A conditionally skipped hook shifts every subsequent hook's position on that render, so React reads/writes the wrong stored state for all of them. Enforced primarily by the eslint-plugin-react-hooks rules-of-hooks lint rule.

drills.q: Trace this bug: setInterval inside useEffect(fn, []) calling setCount(count + 1) appears stuck alternating between two values instead of incrementing. Explain why, and give the fix.
drills.a: The effect runs once (empty deps), so the setInterval callback closes over count as it was during that one render (0). Every tick calls setCount(0 + 1), using the same stale captured 0 -- so it goes 0 to 1 then resets to 1 again forever, never incrementing further. Fix: use the functional updater form setCount(c => c + 1), which doesn't depend on the captured count at all.

drills.q: React.memo is applied to a child component but it still re-renders on every parent render. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: memo does a shallow comparison of props; a new object/array/function reference every render (an inline literal, or an unmemoized inline callback) makes the comparison always see a difference even with identical contents. Fix: stabilize the reference with useMemo/useCallback at the source, or rely on the React Compiler if the component is eligible for auto-memoization.

drills.q: Describe a systematic method (not guessing) for diagnosing why a component re-renders unexpectedly.
drills.a: Open React DevTools Profiler, record the interaction, and use the 'why did this render' indicator to identify the specific trigger (props/state/hooks changed or parent re-rendered). If it's an unmemoized parent re-render with genuinely stable props, that's a real memo candidate. If props aren't stable, trace the reference instability to its source (usually an inline object/callback) rather than reaching for memo on the child first.

drills.q: Why is React's reconciliation algorithm O(n) rather than solving the general tree-diff problem (O(n^3))?
drills.a: React makes two heuristic simplifying assumptions: elements of different types at the same tree position are assumed to produce entirely different subtrees (so it just unmounts/remounts rather than diffing across a type change), and key is trusted as the developer-provided identity signal for list children instead of computing a true minimal-edit-distance match.

drills.q: What does the React Compiler do, since when has it been stable, and does it remove the need to follow the Rules of Hooks?
drills.a: It statically analyzes component code and automatically inserts memoization equivalent to hand-written useMemo/useCallback/React.memo. Stable 1.0 since October 2025, works back to React 17. It does NOT remove the need for the Rules of Hooks -- it depends on code following them (and other React rules) to safely analyze and transform it; violations can cause silent bailout to unoptimized behavior rather than an automatic fix.

drills.q: Why does putting all application state in one large top-level context tend to cause a re-render cascade as an app scales, and what are two architectural fixes?
drills.a: Any field update changes the context object's reference, and every consumer re-renders regardless of which specific field they actually read. Fixes: split the context into multiple narrower contexts by concern, or move high-frequency-changing shared state to a selector-based external store (Zustand/Jotai) that lets consumers subscribe to just the slice they read.

drills.q: Is index-as-key always wrong? Under what condition is it actually safe?
drills.a: No -- for a list that's genuinely static or only ever appended-to/replaced wholesale (never reordered, no mid-list insertion or deletion), index and identity coincide and there's no actual bug. The rule against index-as-key specifically applies to lists that can reorder, insert, or delete items.

drills.q: Name the four kinds of state and give a one-line example plus the correct tool for each.
drills.a: Local: a dropdown's open/closed state -- useState. Server: a user's order history fetched from an API -- TanStack Query. URL: current filter/sort/tab selection -- search params. Global client: a shopping cart before checkout, shared across unrelated UI -- Zustand/Jotai.

drills.q: Explain the argument that most global state is actually misplaced server state, and why it matters practically.
drills.a: Data fetched from an API and stuffed into a general-purpose global store (Redux/Zustand/Context) is server state wearing a global-state costume -- it needs caching, deduplication, background refetching, and invalidation-on-mutation that a generic state container doesn't provide, so teams hand-roll loading/error/stale logic per-feature, inconsistently, producing real staleness bugs. Practically, the fix isn't picking a different global-state library, it's recognizing the data doesn't belong in general client-state management at all.

drills.q: List what TanStack Query provides beyond useState+useEffect for data fetching, with the mechanism for each.
drills.a: Deduplication -- identical concurrent queries for the same key share one network request and cached result. Background refetching -- refreshes stale data on window refocus/reconnect/interval automatically. Stale-while-revalidate via staleTime -- cached data renders immediately while an optional background refresh happens. Cache invalidation on mutation -- invalidateQueries in onSuccess ties writes back to cached reads.

drills.q: Why does Zustand avoid the unnecessary re-renders that plain React Context causes for shared state?
drills.a: useContext subscribes to the entire context value -- any field change triggers a re-render in every consuming component regardless of which field it reads. Zustand's hook takes a selector function and subscribes only to that selector's output via reference-equality checking on the selected slice, so a component reading only one field doesn't re-render when an unrelated field changes.

drills.q: A filter/sort selection implemented with useState resets on every page refresh. Diagnose and fix, and name what the fix additionally provides.
drills.a: This state should be URL state -- anything expected to survive a refresh or be shareable via a copied link belongs in the URL. Fix: read the initial value from search params and update the URL when it changes. Bonus: correct browser back/forward navigation through filter changes, and shareable/bookmarkable links -- both real product behaviors a client-only useState implementation can't provide.

drills.q: When is Redux (with Redux Toolkit) still the right choice in 2026, given the dominance of TanStack Query + Zustand/Jotai?
drills.a: When a large team needs strict, enforced unidirectional data flow with every state change as an explicit, named, serializable action for auditability across many engineers, and/or genuinely benefits from Redux DevTools' time-travel debugging for complex, multi-step state transitions that are hard to reproduce. RTK Query additionally lets teams already invested in Redux get a server-state layer sharing the same store/DevTools. Not a default starting point for a new project without that specific profile.

drills.q: A mutation succeeds but a list displayed elsewhere still shows pre-mutation data until manual refresh. Diagnose and fix, then explain the tradeoff of the alternative fix.
drills.a: Missing cache invalidation connecting the mutation to the affected cached query. Fix: call queryClient.invalidateQueries({queryKey:[...]}) in the mutation's onSuccess, triggering an automatic refetch. Alternative: setQueryData writes the new value into the cache instantly (better perceived performance) but is only as correct as the manual update logic -- misuse can introduce drift from actual server truth, exactly what server-state libraries exist to prevent.

drills.q: Design the state architecture for a product listing page with search/filter/sort controls, the product list, and a cross-device 'recently viewed' widget. Categorize each piece.
drills.a: Search/filter/sort: URL state (shareable, survives refresh, back/forward steps through changes). Product list: server state via TanStack Query, keyed by the filter/sort/page values so changing them produces a distinct cache entry. 'Recently viewed,' since it needs to sync across the user's devices, is server state too (associated with the user's account) -- a mutation to record views and a query to read them, not client-only tracking, since cross-device consistency requires server authority.

drills.q: What's the risk of setting staleTime too high globally across all TanStack Query usage?
drills.a: Data can visibly lag behind real server state for longer than acceptable for that specific use case -- e.g. a live order status shouldn't have a long staleTime, while a rarely-changing settings list can. staleTime should be tuned per-query based on how frequently that specific data actually changes, not set as one blanket global default.

drills.q: Is a logged-in user's profile data local, server, or global state, and why is this a common miscategorization?
drills.a: Server state -- it lives on a server, can go stale, and needs the caching/revalidation behavior a server-state library provides. It's commonly miscategorized as 'global state' in codebases because it's broadly accessible across the app, but broad accessibility is not the defining property of server state -- data origin and staleness behavior are.

drills.q: Why is SSE the dominant transport for LLM token streaming instead of WebSockets, and when would you actually pick WebSockets instead?
drills.a: Token streaming is one-directional; SSE over HTTP is stateless per-request, scales horizontally without sticky sessions, and works through standard proxies/load balancers/CDNs. WebSockets earn their keep only when the client must send data mid-stream: voice-agent barge-in, a mid-generation approval gate, or true multi-user collaboration.

drills.q: Why can't you use the browser's native EventSource API for an authenticated LLM chat endpoint, and what do you use instead?
drills.a: EventSource only supports GET with no custom headers and no body, so it can't send the message history (POST body) or an Authorization header. Use fetch() with a ReadableStream reader, decoding chunks with TextDecoder and manually parsing SSE frame boundaries (split on \n\n).

drills.q: Your chat UI stutters badly with a fast model but is smooth with a slow one. Diagnose and fix it.
drills.a: Per-token setState triggers a re-render; if the render tree does expensive work (markdown parse, syntax highlight) and the model emits tokens faster than that completes within a 16.7ms frame budget, the main thread falls behind. Fix: buffer incoming deltas and flush on requestAnimationFrame, and move expensive rendering off the synchronous per-chunk path.

drills.q: SSE has no backpressure mechanism. What does that mean precisely, and does it actually matter for plain text token streaming?
drills.a: The server has no signal the client is falling behind and the client has no way to say "slow down" -- unlike WebSockets (bufferedAmount, TCP receive window). Rarely matters for small text payloads, but matters if something heavier rides the stream (large tool results, base64 chunks); mitigate at the application layer (chunk payloads, defer expensive rendering), not by switching transports.

drills.q: Walk through what actually happens end-to-end when a user clicks Stop mid-generation, and how you'd verify it's wired correctly.
drills.a: controller.abort() rejects the fetch promise (AbortError, expected) and closes the TCP connection, firing a close event on the server's request object. Generation only actually stops if the server explicitly listens for that close event and cancels the upstream LLM call there. Verify by aborting a test stream partway through and checking the provider's usage/billing metrics reflect a truncated, not full, generation.

drills.q: Design the state shape for a chat message with interleaved text and tool calls, and explain how to avoid the tool-call card remounting when its result arrives.
drills.a: A message is { id, role, parts: [...] } with typed entries (text, tool-call, tool-result) in order, not a single string. Avoid remount/flash by keying state by toolCallId and updating the existing part in place when the result arrives, rather than appending a second separate entry.

drills.q: A streamed response arrives all at once instead of incrementally, though the server writes incrementally. Diagnose and fix, and describe how you'd catch this in CI.
drills.a: Likely cause: a reverse proxy (commonly nginx) buffering the response by default. Fix: disable buffering for the route (X-Accel-Buffering: no / proxy_buffering off), verify with curl -N directly against the endpoint. Catch in CI with an integration test against the actual deployed proxy config asserting chunks arrive with measurable gaps, not just testing the app server directly.

drills.q: Why send periodic heartbeat comment lines during a long tool call with no token output, and does this affect billing?
drills.a: Load balancers/proxies with idle-connection timeouts (commonly 30-60s) can't distinguish silent-but-working from dead and will kill the connection. A ": ping\n\n" comment line every ~15s (ignored by the client's event parser since it has no data: field) keeps it alive. No billing impact -- it's a transport-level liveness signal, not part of model output.

drills.q: Why is TextDecoder's { stream: true } option necessary for consuming a chunked stream, and why wouldn't typical English test fixtures catch its absence?
drills.a: Multi-byte UTF-8 characters (emoji, CJK) can split across chunk boundaries; without stream:true each decode() call treats input as complete and corrupts an incomplete trailing sequence into a replacement character. Plain ASCII test fixtures never exercise this since every character is one byte -- catching it requires fixtures with multi-byte characters positioned near expected chunk boundaries.

drills.q: Design resumable streaming for a user whose connection drops mid-generation on a flaky mobile network.
drills.a: Server persists generated content against a stream/request id as it's produced. Client tracks the last received position (cursor/offset or SSE id). On reconnect, client sends that cursor; server replays already-generated content instantly from its persisted buffer, then continues new generation. If the model itself can't resume mid-generation, the honest fallback is a clear "regenerate from here" UI affordance rather than a silent, confusing partial state.

drills.q: What determines token arrival rate at the systems level, and how would you find the real number for a given deployment rather than assuming a constant?
drills.a: Model size, batch size/concurrency on the serving side, hardware, and decoding strategy (e.g. speculative decoding) determine it -- it's not frontend-controlled and varies by provider/tier/load. Instrument the client to log timestamped delta arrivals, compute inter-arrival intervals under realistic concurrent load, and design buffering against the observed p95, not an unloaded local test.

drills.q: What structurally changed in Vercel AI SDK v6 (May 2026) versus v5, and why is it called a "silent" breaking change?
drills.a: useChat's message shape moved to an interleaved parts model (text-delta/tool-call/tool-result/reasoning as an ordered array), the tool-call streaming lifecycle gained explicit step hooks, and the wire format changed. It's silent because old v5 code keeps compiling against the new v6 message shape -- it's a structural shape change, not a renamed export that would fail to build -- so v5 and v6 cannot be mixed in one render tree.

drills.q: Explain structural vs nominal typing and why an object literal can satisfy an interface it never declared implementing.
drills.a: TypeScript checks whether a value's shape is compatible with a target type -- same or superset of required properties with compatible types -- regardless of any declared name or inheritance relationship. An object literal satisfies an interface purely by having the right shape, with no `implements` requirement.

drills.q: Why does distance({x:3,y:4,z:5}) error as an excess property but distance(someVarWithExtraProps) does not?
drills.a: Excess property checks fire specifically on object literals passed directly, to catch likely typos in property names. They don't apply to variables holding an object with genuinely extra properties -- a deliberately narrower check than full structural strictness would imply.

drills.q: What does 'types are erased' mean, and what's the practical consequence for runtime safety?
drills.a: Every type annotation, interface, and generic parameter is deleted during compilation to JS -- zero runtime trace. TypeScript can never enforce anything at runtime; a value crossing an unchecked boundary (an as assertion, untyped import, stale third-party .d.ts) can be structurally wrong at runtime while the type checker reports everything fine.

drills.q: Distinguish unknown from any mechanically, and state where TypeScript itself defaults to unknown as of 4.4+.
drills.a: Both accept any assigned value. any disables type checking entirely for anything it touches -- propagates silently downstream. unknown requires explicit narrowing (typeof/instanceof/custom guard) before any operation. TS 4.4+ types caught errors in catch clauses as unknown by default (useUnknownInCatchVariables), since a thrown value's type is never knowable ahead of time.

drills.q: Write a discriminated union for a fetch state (idle/loading/success/error) and explain why it beats one flat interface with optional fields.
drills.a: type FetchState<T> = {status:'idle'} | {status:'loading'} | {status:'success',data:T} | {status:'error',error:string}. A flat interface with optional data/error/loading fields allows illegal combinations to compile (e.g. loading:true with stale data present) -- a real, common stale-UI bug. The discriminated union makes that structurally impossible since fields only exist in the branch's type where they're valid.

drills.q: How do you force the compiler to catch a missed case when a new discriminated union variant is added later?
drills.a: Add a const _exhaustive: never = value; statement in the default/fallback branch of the switch. If a new variant isn't handled, value in that branch is no longer assignable to never, producing a compile error instead of a silent runtime fallthrough.

drills.q: Why is an `as` type assertion dangerous, and when is it legitimately acceptable to use?
drills.a: It performs zero runtime verification -- if the value isn't actually shaped as claimed, it compiles fine and the mismatch surfaces later, often far from the assertion site. Legitimate use: narrowing a type the compiler can't infer but you can prove safe from context it doesn't see (e.g. a querySelector result's more specific element type when you control the DOM), not silencing an error whose underlying concern is real.

drills.q: Explain function parameter bivariance in TypeScript: what's unsafe by default, what fixes it, and what carve-out remains even under strict mode.
drills.a: Without strictFunctionTypes, (x:Dog)=>void is assignable to (x:Animal)=>void and vice versa, even though only contravariance (accepting a wider parameter) is actually safe. strictFunctionTypes (part of strict mode) fixes this for standalone function types. Method syntax (interface Foo { method(x:Dog):void }) remains bivariant even under strict mode -- a deliberate, documented compatibility carve-out.

drills.q: What is declaration merging, give a legitimate production use, and explain its risk.
drills.a: Multiple interface declarations with the same name across files automatically merge into one combined interface. Legitimate use: augmenting a global or third-party type (e.g. adding a property Express's Request gets from auth middleware) without forking the library's types. Risk: it declares a runtime shape exists with zero verification anything actually sets it -- if the middleware doesn't run on some route, the type still claims the field exists, and access crashes at runtime with no compile-time warning.

drills.q: Derive Pick<T,K> and Partial<T> as mapped types from first principles, without reciting their documented behavior.
drills.a: Pick<T,K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] } -- iterates the keys in K, pulling each corresponding property type from T. Partial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] } -- same iteration over all of T's keys with the ? modifier applied.

drills.q: A third-party library's .d.ts claims a field is always present, but production shows it's sometimes undefined. How did this happen, and what's the fix without waiting on upstream?
drills.a: The .d.ts (bundled or from @types/*) was written by hand or generated against a different version/behavior than what's shipping, and TypeScript has no mechanism to verify a .d.ts file's accuracy against actual runtime behavior -- it's trusted completely. Fix: locally patch via declare module augmentation to reflect actual observed behavior (mark the field optional), and defensively handle the value (optional chaining, runtime checks) regardless of the stale type's claim.

drills.q: What is TypeScript 6.0's significance as 'the last JS-based release,' and what does TypeScript 7.0 change (and not change)?
drills.a: 6.0 (March 2026) flipped defaults toward stricter behavior (broader strict defaults, ESM default module, es2025 target) and was explicitly a bridge release. TypeScript 7.0 is a from-scratch rewrite of the compiler in Go, reported ~10x faster, reaching RC June 18 2026 -- it's a reimplementation targeting build/editor speed, not a new language; the type system's semantics stay the same.

drills.q: Name the three Core Web Vitals with their good thresholds and what each measures, and state which lab tool score is NOT the same thing as passing them.
drills.a: LCP<2.5s (loading), INP<200ms (responsiveness, replaced FID March 2024), CLS<0.1 (visual stability), graded at p75 over CrUX's rolling 28-day window of real users. A high Lighthouse score is a synthetic lab number on a fixed simulated profile and is not equivalent to passing CWV in the field.

drills.q: A page's LCP is 4.2 seconds. Walk through how you'd diagnose which of the four LCP phases is the bottleneck.
drills.a: Use web-vitals attribution data (or DevTools Performance panel) to separately measure TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time, and element render delay. The fix depends on which dominates: slow TTFB -> server/CDN; large load delay -> resource not discoverable early (client-rendered); large load time -> resource size/compression; large render delay -> render-blocking CSS/JS ahead of the element.

drills.q: Why is blanket-applying loading="lazy" to every image on a page a mistake, with real numbers?
drills.a: Applying it to the actual LCP image delays its discovery/download. Measured field data: p75 LCP moves from 364ms to 720ms and the share of good pages drops from 79% to 52%. Lazy-load should apply only below-the-fold images; the LCP candidate should get fetchpriority="high" instead.

drills.q: What is a long task, and why can a click handler that itself runs in only 10ms still produce bad INP?
drills.a: A long task is main-thread JS execution over 50ms without yielding, blocking input processing and paint. INP includes processing time AND presentation delay, not just handler execution -- a fast handler that triggers an expensive synchronous downstream re-render, or one queued behind an already-running unrelated long task, still produces bad INP.

drills.q: Give the prioritized remediation order for a slow, INP-hurting click handler, and explain why a Web Worker isn't always the first move.
drills.a: Order: (1) chunk work and yield between chunks (scheduler.yield/setTimeout fallback) (2) move heavy CPU-bound compute to a Web Worker (3) defer non-critical work via requestIdleCallback (4) reduce DOM work via virtualization. A Web Worker adds serialization overhead and no DOM access -- worth it for genuinely CPU-heavy self-contained work, but if the cost is mostly triggering a large synchronous render, yielding or reducing render scope is cheaper and more targeted.

drills.q: Name the three most common real causes of CLS and the fix for each, then explain why CLS can look fine in local dev but spike for slow-connection users.
drills.a: 1) Unreserved image/embed dimensions -> width/height or aspect-ratio. 2) Font swap metric mismatch -> font-display:optional or size-adjust matching. 3) Content injected above existing content -> reserve space or overlay. On fast connections the font/resource often arrives before first paint, masking the shift; on slow connections there's more time between paint and arrival, making the swap/shift visible -- test CLS under throttled network conditions.

drills.q: A React SPA ships a 2.3MB initial bundle. Give a prioritized reduction plan with realistic expected impact, and state when more code splitting stops helping.
drills.a: First, route-based code splitting (React.lazy/dynamic import) -- commonly gets initial critical-path bundle to ~100-150KB with rest loaded per route. Second, tree shaking plus swapping heavy deps (moment.js -> date-fns). Combined, 60-80% total reduction is realistic. Third, add a CI bundle-size budget to prevent regression. More splitting stops helping when it increases network round trips on high-latency connections or forces multiple sequential fetch-then-execute chunks synchronously on interaction, hurting INP.

drills.q: Your team ships a performance fix; Lighthouse CI shows clear improvement but CrUX field data shows no change three weeks later. What's going on, and how would you get faster feedback?
drills.a: CrUX uses a rolling 28-day window, so a fix needs real traffic to accumulate before the number moves -- three weeks may not be enough data yet. Separately, Lighthouse's fixed simulated profile may not represent your real traffic mix. Get faster feedback by instrumenting your own RUM (web-vitals library reporting to your own analytics backend) rather than waiting on Google's delayed, aggregated CrUX report.

drills.q: Explain font-display: swap vs font-display: optional, when to choose each, and what size-adjust does mechanically.
drills.a: swap shows fallback text immediately and swaps in the custom font whenever it loads (good for LCP, risks CLS on swap). optional gives ~100ms grace; if missed, the fallback is used for the entire page view with zero swap and zero CLS risk, at the cost of sometimes never showing the custom font. Choose optional when zero CLS matters more than brand-font guarantee; choose swap + size-adjust when the font must eventually appear. size-adjust is a font-face descriptor that scales the font's metrics to match a fallback, computed from the numeric difference between the two, minimizing the reflow when swap does occur.

drills.q: Two pages have identical Lighthouse scores but very different real-world INP. Explain why, how you'd find the actual difference, and why the fix for a 'growing list' culprit is virtualization rather than per-item render optimization.
drills.a: Lighthouse runs a short interaction script on a simulated profile and doesn't capture real session length or accumulated state (memory growth, a list grown large through use) that degrades field INP. Find the difference via RUM attribution data (which interaction, which element) rather than blind lab reproduction. Virtualization is the durable fix because at sufficient list length even a well-optimized per-item render still means O(n) DOM nodes and reconciliation work scaling with data size -- virtualization changes the complexity class rather than shaving a constant factor.

drills.q: A security audit flags that the CI pipeline holds a long-lived, cluster-admin-scoped kubeconfig secret. What's the structural fix, and why is it better than just rotating the secret more often?
drills.a: Migrate to pull-based GitOps: run ArgoCD/Flux inside the cluster to reconcile from Git, so CI never holds a cluster-write credential at all. Rotating a static secret more often reduces exposure window but doesn't eliminate the blast radius of CI compromise; removing the credential from CI's scope entirely does.

drills.q: An engineer runs kubectl edit against a GitOps-managed Deployment to quickly test a config change during an incident. Within minutes it reverts to the old value. What happened, and was it a bug?
drills.a: Not a bug — selfHeal/continuous reconciliation detected drift from Git and corrected it automatically, exactly as designed. The fix should have been made in Git (or auto-sync temporarily disabled for a genuine emergency, then codified in Git immediately after).

drills.q: ArgoCD shows a resource as persistently OutOfSync even immediately after a successful sync. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Something else in-cluster is mutating a field after ArgoCD applies it — commonly an admission webhook injecting a default, or an HPA changing replica count that Git doesn't track. Fix with ignoreDifferences for those specific fields rather than treating it as broken reconciliation.

drills.q: A canary rollout for a checkout API proceeds all the way to 100% traffic despite a real, visible error-rate spike in the dashboards afterward. What are two distinct possible root causes in the AnalysisTemplate setup?
drills.a: The Prometheus query or success threshold is misconfigured (wrong metric name/label, threshold too loose), or the metrics provider was unreachable during the analysis window and the check silently no-op'd instead of aborting conservatively. Alert on AnalysisRun failures/errors distinctly from rollout progression to catch the second case.

drills.q: A team is deciding between ArgoCD and Flux and their charts are heavy, complex Helm charts using multiple lifecycle hooks. Which way should this specific factor push them, and why?
drills.a: Toward Flux — its HelmRelease keeps full fidelity with standard Helm lifecycle hooks and tooling, while ArgoCD treats Helm more as a template-rendering engine and doesn't fully preserve that lifecycle fidelity. This is a concrete technical factor, not just popularity.

drills.q: A new microservice was added to the cluster but nobody remembered to onboard it to ArgoCD, and it silently ran unmanaged for weeks. What GitOps pattern prevents this recurring, and how?
drills.a: App of Apps (or ApplicationSet) — a root Application (or generator) watching a directory in Git, so adding a new service's Application manifest is a Git commit under that directory, automatically picked up, rather than a separate imperative argocd app create step that's easy to forget.

drills.q: Why might keeping syncPolicy manual (not automated) for a production ArgoCD Application still be compatible with calling the pipeline 'fully GitOps'?
drills.a: The reconciliation loop still runs continuously and automatically even with manual sync — drift detection and OutOfSync reporting happen in real time regardless. Only the application of a detected diff requires human approval, so drift is still caught and visible immediately, just not auto-corrected without confirmation.

drills.q: A low-traffic internal admin service's canary rollout keeps flapping between proceeding and rolling back on different deploys with no actual code regression. What's the fix, concretely?
drills.a: Use a fixed absolute request count for canary exposure instead of a percentage weight (guaranteeing a meaningful sample regardless of overall traffic volume), or widen the analysis interval/sample window so more requests accumulate per evaluation before a pass/fail decision is made.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks 'should we use ECS or Fargate for our new service?' How do you respond, and what's the actual question you should be answering instead?
drills.a: Point out this conflates two orthogonal axes — orchestrator (ECS vs EKS) and compute (EC2 vs Fargate). The real question is likely 'ECS or EKS' for orchestration, combined separately with 'EC2 or Fargate' for compute — answer both axes, not a false single choice.

drills.q: A platform team runs one EKS cluster per small internal tool (12 clusters, each with 1-3 services). Their AWS bill shows control-plane costs are a disproportionately large line item. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The flat ~$73/month EKS control-plane fee is being multiplied across 12 small clusters, even though the aggregate workload could plausibly fit on far fewer larger clusters where the fee would be negligible. Fix: consolidate onto fewer clusters using namespace-level isolation instead of one cluster per small service.

drills.q: A team runs a large, steady-state, highly predictable fleet entirely on Fargate and wants to cut costs without changing orchestrators. What's the first lever to pull, and why?
drills.a: Evaluate migrating the steady-state, predictable portion of the fleet to EC2-backed capacity (managed node groups, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler) — Fargate's real ~40-60% premium over equivalent EC2 compounds significantly at scale for predictable workloads, while its zero-node-management value is most justified for genuinely bursty/unpredictable portions, which should stay on Fargate.

drills.q: A pod on EKS fails to reach S3 with an access-denied error, even though `aws iam get-role-policy` confirms the referenced role has s3:GetObject. Where do you look next?
drills.a: The ServiceAccount-to-IAM-role association — check whether the IRSA annotation (or EKS Pod Identity association) actually links that ServiceAccount to that IAM role, and whether the pod spec references the correct ServiceAccount at all. A correct IAM policy is irrelevant if the federation linking pod identity to the role is missing or misconfigured.

drills.q: A team adds an EKS Fargate profile to an existing EC2-managed-node-group cluster to handle bursty batch jobs cheaply. A few weeks later they notice their node-level logging DaemonSet isn't capturing logs from the new batch job pods. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: DaemonSets cannot run on Fargate at all — there's no shared-node concept for the one-per-node pattern to attach to, so Fargate-profile pods are structurally invisible to any DaemonSet. Fix: add a sidecar container to the Fargate-profile pods for logging coverage instead, since the cluster now needs both patterns (DaemonSet for EC2 nodes, sidecars for Fargate pods).

drills.q: A new 5-person startup on AWS with no existing Kubernetes investment and no concrete multi-cloud plans is deciding between ECS and EKS. They mention they 'might need multi-cloud eventually.' What's the recommendation, and why?
drills.a: Recommend ECS + Fargate as the default — simpler operational model, no control-plane fee, smaller IAM learning curve. 'Might need it eventually' with no concrete funded plan is a weak signal; taking on EKS's real current operational complexity for a hypothetical future requirement is the same over-engineering mistake as premature module abstraction — migrate when the hypothetical becomes concrete.

drills.q: Nodes across a cluster start intermittently hitting ImagePullBackOff with rate-limit-flavored errors from Docker Hub, especially during scale-up events. What's the AWS-native production fix, and what changes in the manifests to use it?
drills.a: Configure an ECR pull-through cache rule for Docker Hub so pulls hit ECR (in-region, not subject to Docker Hub's rate limits) instead of the public registry directly. Image references in manifests must change to the ECR-proxied path (e.g. <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/docker-hub/library/redis:7) — it's not a transparent, zero-touch fix.

drills.q: An ECR repository has been accumulating images for two years with no storage management, and costs have crept up steadily. What's the standard fix, and what's the default behavior it's correcting?
drills.a: Attach a lifecycle policy (e.g. keep the last N tagged images per repository, expire untagged images after N days) — ECR retains every pushed image indefinitely by default with no automatic expiration, a slow, easy-to-overlook storage cost leak that compounds as CI continuously pushes new tagged and untagged images.

drills.q: A build running directly on the Jenkins controller (as a shortcut, no dedicated agent configured) gets compromised via a malicious dependency. Why is the blast radius worse than if it had happened on a dynamic Kubernetes agent?
drills.a: The controller typically holds credentials (via the Credentials plugin) for every pipeline's deploy targets, so compromising a build there can compromise everything every pipeline has access to. A dynamic agent only holds whatever credentials were explicitly injected for that specific build/stage and is torn down afterward, giving a much smaller blast radius.

drills.q: A pipeline step throws a NotSerializableException-flavored error, but the exact same Groovy code runs fine as a standalone script outside Jenkins. Diagnose and give two possible fixes.
