drills.a: Jenkins pipelines run inside a Groovy CPS sandbox so execution state can be serialized to disk and survive controller restarts; some Groovy constructs (certain closures, non-CPS-transformable library calls) don't survive that transformation. Fix: mark the offending method @NonCPS (loses pause/resume durability for that method), or move the logic into a shared library's src/ classes structured around the constraint.

drills.q: A team notices their Jenkinsfile hasn't changed but a build starts failing differently than before. What's a likely shared-library-related cause?
drills.a: An unpinned @Library reference (e.g. @Library('lib@master')) picked up a new commit merged to the shared library's default branch, silently changing pipeline behavior. Fix: pin @Library references to specific, immutable tags.

drills.q: Builds are stuck Pending in the Jenkins queue, but every agent's Grafana dashboard shows plenty of free CPU and memory. What should you check next, and why wouldn't just raising a number blindly be the right fix?
drills.a: Check the executor count configured per agent in the build queue view — it's a distinct concurrency constraint from raw resource capacity. Raising executor count too high without matching real resource headroom just moves the bottleneck from 'queued and waiting' to 'running but starved,' which is often harder to diagnose since builds appear to be progressing.

drills.q: A build passes reliably on one static Jenkins agent and fails intermittently on another agent with an identical configuration. What's the likely cause and the structural fix?
drills.a: State bleed from a previous build on the long-lived static agent — cached dependencies, leftover processes, or disk artifacts from an earlier build. The structural fix is migrating to dynamic Kubernetes agents that spin up a fresh pod per build with no persisted state, rather than adding ad hoc cleanup steps to static agents.

drills.q: A script authenticating correctly against the Jenkins REST API still gets a 403 on a POST request. The same credentials work fine for GET requests. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: A missing CSRF crumb token — Jenkins requires it by default on state-changing (POST/PUT/DELETE-style) requests but not on read-only GET requests, which explains why GETs succeed and the state-changing call fails with what looks like a permissions error. Fetch a crumb from the crumb issuer endpoint and include it on the request.

drills.q: A new startup building entirely on GitHub with no special compliance requirements asks whether they should set up Jenkins or use GitHub Actions. What's the honest recommendation, and what would change your answer?
drills.a: GitHub Actions — zero infrastructure to patch and secure, no plugin-CVE surface to manage, and tight native integration for a team with normal compliance needs. The answer would change toward Jenkins if they had genuine air-gapped/on-prem requirements, needed deep customization via specific plugins with no hosted equivalent, or already had complex multi-repo orchestration built up that would be costly to re-architect.

drills.q: A security review finds a Jenkins controller with 60 installed plugins, several flagged with known CVEs, and nobody sure why half of them are installed. What's the correct remediation approach, and why isn't 'just remove all unused plugins once' sufficient long-term?
drills.a: Audit installed plugins against actual usage, remove unused ones, and track CVEs against the versions of what remains, restricting who can install new plugins going forward. A one-time cleanup isn't sufficient because a plugin safe at install time can develop a vulnerability or go unmaintained later — this requires ongoing inventory and CVE-tracking discipline, not a single pass.

drills.q: Every deploy causes a brief burst of 502/connection-reset errors even though readiness probes look fine. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No preStop hook (or one shorter than real Endpoints propagation time) means the container dies before endpoint removal has propagated to every kube-proxy, so some requests hit a pod that's already gone. Fix: add a preStop sleep tuned to worst-case propagation, ensure the app drains gracefully on SIGTERM, and make sure terminationGracePeriodSeconds exceeds preStop sleep plus drain time.

drills.q: A team says 'we have a PDB configured, so we're covered for availability during maintenance.' What's the gap in that claim?
drills.a: A PDB only paces voluntary disruptions (drains, upgrades, autoscaler consolidation) via the Eviction API — it provides zero protection against involuntary disruptions like node crashes, OOMKilled pods, CrashLoopBackOff, or an HPA/Deployment scaling down replicas directly. It also doesn't guarantee the surviving replicas are actually healthy.

drills.q: A routine node upgrade hangs indefinitely on one namespace's pods. The PDB looks correctly configured. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: The PDB's minAvailable is set equal to (or too close to) the Deployment's actual current replica count, so no eviction can ever succeed without violating the budget. Check whether replica count shrank over time (deliberate scale-down or HPA) while the PDB stayed static, creating this deadlock.

drills.q: A slow-starting JVM service keeps getting killed and restarted during its first two minutes of startup, even though it eventually becomes healthy. What's missing?
drills.a: A startupProbe. Without it, liveness has to either use a short initialDelaySeconds (kills the app before it finishes starting) or a long one (which then also delays catching genuinely hung processes during steady state). startupProbe decouples the two, gating liveness/readiness until startup succeeds once.

drills.q: A pod creation is rejected with a quota-exceeded error even though the namespace's ResourceQuota shows plenty of CPU/memory headroom. Why might that be?
drills.a: ResourceQuota can also cap object counts (count/pods, count/persistentvolumeclaims), not just compute resources — the namespace may have hit its pod-count or PVC-count ceiling, a separate dimension from the compute numbers usually checked first.

drills.q: A cluster's cloud bill has tripled year over year with no corresponding traffic growth. A colleague proposes buying more reserved instances. What should you check first, and why?
drills.a: The gap between requested and actually-used capacity per namespace/workload via Kubecost/OpenCost attribution. Unoptimized clusters commonly run at only 10-30% actual CPU utilization against requested capacity — buying reserved capacity locks in a discount on that same waste instead of fixing it; rightsize requests first, then commit capacity against the corrected baseline.

drills.q: A team claims they 'do canary deployments with Kubernetes' using a plain Deployment. How do you probe whether this is a genuine traffic-weighted canary or just a rolling update with a different name?
drills.a: Ask specifically what decides to proceed or roll back, and on what signal. A genuine canary system references specific metrics/analysis templates and traffic percentages (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). If the answer is really 'we deploy a few pods first and watch dashboards manually,' that's an informal rolling update, not automated progressive delivery — Deployment's RollingUpdate has no native traffic-percentage or metric-gated logic.

drills.q: A multi-tenant cluster has ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and NetworkPolicy applied per namespace, yet one tenant's batch job is still degrading another tenant's latency-critical service. What isolation gap does this expose?
drills.a: Namespace-level controls (quota, limit range, network policy) don't provide physical isolation — tenants still share a kernel, node network stack, and scheduler. Noisy-neighbor CPU/node contention can cross tenant boundaries even with all three controls correctly applied. The fix is dedicated node pools (taints/tolerations) or separate clusters for tenants needing stronger isolation.

drills.q: p99 latency on a service is terrible but its CPU utilization dashboard shows comfortable headroom the entire time. What's your first hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: CFS quota throttling within individual 100ms periods, invisible to a smoothed average. Confirm via container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total in Prometheus/cAdvisor; if the ratio is high, raise or remove the CPU limit for that workload.

drills.q: A Deployment has both HPA and VPA configured, both watching CPU. Replica count and per-pod sizing are both drifting unpredictably under steady load. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Classic HPA/VPA same-metric oscillation: VPA changes CPU requests, which changes HPA's utilization denominator, which changes replica count, which changes VPA's observed usage. Fix by splitting responsibility — VPA in updateMode: Off (recommend-only) or sizing memory instead, HPA driving off an independent metric like requests-per-second.

drills.q: Pods are stuck Pending, and neither Cluster Autoscaler nor Karpenter is provisioning new nodes even though the cluster is clearly out of capacity. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the pending pods have resources.requests set. Both tools decide to scale up based on determining a pod is unschedulable due to insufficient resources — pods with zero requests give no such signal and are invisible to the scale-up decision, so they sit Pending indefinitely.

drills.q: A traffic spike causes a multi-minute outage before new capacity comes online, even though autoscaling is configured correctly. What's the likely root cause and the fix?
drills.a: Cluster Autoscaler against node groups typically takes 4-8 minutes to bring a new node Ready, too slow for a spike-shaped traffic pattern. Migrate to Karpenter (~45-60s) for faster response, or maintain deliberate warm/buffer capacity for paths that can't tolerate multi-minute cold starts.

drills.q: A team wants to scale a Kafka consumer worker to zero replicas when the topic is empty, to save cost. Plain HPA can't do this. Why not, and what's the fix?
drills.a: HPA's algorithm computes desiredReplicas as a ratio against currentReplicas, requiring at least one running replica to have a metric to compute against — it structurally cannot decide to go from 0 to 1. KEDA adds a separate polling mechanism that watches the external event source (Kafka consumer lag) directly while the Deployment sits at zero, then hands off to a standard HPA it manages once replicas are above zero.

drills.q: Two GPU-inference pods land on the same GPU node, and one fails with an out-of-GPU-memory error even though the node's total GPU count looked sufficient. What happened?
drills.a: GPUs aren't fractionally shared by default — a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 gets a whole physical GPU via the device plugin framework, and simply co-scheduling two pods doesn't make them safely share one device's memory. Real sharing needs an explicit mechanism: MIG (hardware-isolated partitions) or time-slicing (software, no isolation, real contention risk).

drills.q: A GPU workload's pod is stuck Pending and kubectl describe node shows the target GPU node has free GPU capacity. What's the most likely single cause?
drills.a: The pod is missing the toleration for the GPU node pool's taint (commonly nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule). GPU nodes are near-universally tainted to keep ordinary CPU-only workloads off them, and a pod without the matching toleration is excluded from scheduling there regardless of free capacity.

drills.q: A latency-sensitive service is set to Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for both CPU and memory) to protect it from eviction. What tradeoff did this choice quietly introduce?
drills.a: Guaranteed QoS requires a CPU limit equal to the request, which reintroduces CFS-quota throttling risk for exactly the workload where tail latency matters most — there's a real tension between eviction protection (favors Guaranteed) and avoiding throttling (favors no CPU limit, at best Burstable), and the right choice depends on which failure mode is worse for that specific service.

drills.q: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff with an empty kubectl logs output. What's your next command and why?
drills.a: kubectl logs <pod> --previous — the currently running instance may be mid-crash-loop with nothing logged yet, but --previous retrieves the last terminated instance's output, which almost always has the real error.

drills.q: describe pod shows Last State Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Your teammate wants to immediately double the memory limit. What do you check first?
drills.a: container_memory_working_set_bytes history over hours/days — a steadily climbing line indicates a genuine leak that a bigger limit only delays, while a bounded spike justifies a limit increase. Raising the limit without checking first can mask a leak.

drills.q: An entire node's pods start hitting ImagePullBackOff right after a large scale-up event, while other nodes are fine. Diagnose.
drills.a: Registry rate limiting hit during a burst of simultaneous pulls on that node — Events will show a 429-flavored error. Fix by authenticating pulls or running an in-cluster pull-through cache/mirror to absorb burst pulls.

drills.q: A fleet-wide CrashLoopBackOff starts immediately after a deploy. What's your first action, before reading any logs?
drills.a: Roll back (kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>) first, diagnose after — restoring service takes priority mid-incident, and the previous working ReplicaSet is a fast, low-risk revert compared to live debugging while users are impacted.

drills.q: After the rollback in the previous scenario, replicas keep crash-looping even on the old, previously-stable image. What does this tell you?
drills.a: It's probably not the deploy itself — something else changed at the same timestamp (a database migration that already ran and can't be un-run, a rotated secret/config, an independently changed downstream dependency). Investigate what else changed concurrently, not the image.

drills.q: A pod keeps failing its liveness probe and getting killed with exit code 0, but the app has no obvious bug. What's a resourcing-related explanation, and how would you confirm it?
drills.a: Severe CPU throttling (CFS quota exhaustion) can starve the app of CPU time badly enough that it can't respond to the probe within its timeout, producing what looks like a probe-tuning issue. Confirm by correlating container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total spikes against the probe failure timestamps.

drills.q: External API calls from in-cluster services show a steady, not intermittent, latency overhead compared to calls made from outside the cluster. DNS 'works fine.' Diagnose.
drills.a: ndots:5 default causing search-domain expansion — every external name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against cluster search domains first, generating several wasted NXDOMAIN queries before the absolute name succeeds. Fix with a trailing-dot FQDN or a lower ndots value via dnsConfig.options.

drills.q: Some external DNS lookups from pods intermittently hang for exactly ~5 seconds before succeeding. Restarting CoreDNS doesn't help. What's actually happening?
drills.a: A kernel-level conntrack race: two near-simultaneous UDP DNS queries (typically A and AAAA) from the same source port can collide during conntrack table insertion, dropping one packet; the resolver waits out its full timeout. It's not a CoreDNS issue — mitigate by forcing TCP DNS or disabling unnecessary AAAA lookups.

drills.q: A distroless production image with no shell needs live debugging. What's the modern approach, and what does it share with the target container?
drills.a: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> — injects a temporary ephemeral container sharing the target's network namespace and, via --target, its process namespace, without modifying the pod spec or restarting it. GA since Kubernetes 1.25.

drills.q: A node shows a burst of Evicted pods across several unrelated Deployments, none of which individually show high memory usage. What should you check on the node itself, and why might this happen?
drills.a: Node-level disk usage (nodefs/imagefs) via kubectl debug node/<name> -it --image=busybox -- chroot /host sh — a high-volume logger from one unrelated pod can fill node disk and trigger disk-pressure eviction that removes pods in QoS order regardless of whether they caused the pressure ('innocent bystander' pattern).

drills.q: A terraform plan shows changes to a security group's ingress rules that nobody made in the .tf files. What's your first hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: Drift — someone modified the real resource outside Terraform (console, another pipeline, an incident action), and the refresh step in plan caught the mismatch and proposed reverting it. Confirm via cloud audit logs (e.g. CloudTrail) filtered to that resource around the relevant timeframe.

drills.q: The drift in the previous scenario turns out to be a legitimate emergency change made during an incident. What's the correct way to reconcile it, rather than just applying the plan?
drills.a: Update the .tf configuration to match the new, correct desired state, codifying the emergency change properly — applying the plan as shown would silently revert and re-break whatever the emergency change fixed.

drills.q: apply fails with a lock error. The CI job that appeared to hold the lock is confirmed dead. What do you do, and what's the risk if your confirmation is wrong?
drills.a: terraform force-unlock <lock-id> — but only after real confirmation (checking the CI system logs, not just elapsed time) that the holding process is genuinely dead. If it's actually still running, you now have two concurrent writers with no lock protection, exactly the corruption scenario locking exists to prevent.

drills.q: A 'harmless rename' refactor of a production database resource shows a plan with destroy then create for that resource. What's missing, and what do you do before ever applying?
drills.a: No moved block declaring the old and new addresses as the same resource. Add a moved block, re-run plan, and confirm it now shows no destroy/create for that resource before applying — plan output is the actual safety check, no refactor should be applied without verifying it first.

drills.q: A team wants to isolate dev, staging, and prod, which have meaningfully different instance sizes and resource counts. They propose using built-in terraform workspaces. What breaks, and what's the better pattern?
drills.a: Workspaces only isolate state, not configuration — genuine environment differences would have to be threaded through as terraform.workspace-conditional logic inside shared .tf files, unreadable past a couple of real differences. Better pattern: separate backend configs per environment (directory-per-environment or Terragrunt), each with its own variables.

drills.q: A shared module used by 6 teams has grown to 35+ variables and deep nested conditionals, and using it correctly now requires reading its source. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Over-abstraction — the module was designed to cover every team's hypothetical use case upfront instead of being extracted from proven, real duplication. Consider splitting it into smaller, purpose-specific modules per common use-case cluster rather than one maximally generic module.

drills.q: terraform plan now takes several minutes for even a one-line change on a large root module managing 400+ resources. Diagnose and fix, and name the tradeoff of the fix.
drills.a: Every plan refreshes all tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing, regardless of change size. Fix: split state along logical/lifecycle boundaries (networking, data, app tier) into separate root modules/backends. Tradeoff: cross-boundary references now need terraform_remote_state or explicit output/variable passing, and changes spanning boundaries become multi-step instead of one atomic apply.

drills.q: A CI pipeline posts a plan for PR review, then on merge re-runs plan and apply fresh instead of applying the saved plan artifact. What's the risk?
drills.a: A TOCTOU gap — the freshly recomputed plan on merge can differ from what was actually reviewed if anything changed in the interim (another merge, real-world drift caught by a fresh refresh), meaning what gets applied may not be what a human actually approved. Apply the exact saved .tfplan artifact instead.

drills.q: Name the first six integer argument registers in System V x86-64, the first eight in AAPCS64, and where each convention's return value goes.
drills.a: System V x86-64: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 (7th+ spills to stack); return in rax (rdx:rax for 128-bit). AAPCS64: x0-x7 (9th+ spills to stack); return in x0 (x1 for a second word).

drills.q: Distinguish caller-saved from callee-saved registers and explain why the split exists.
drills.a: Caller-saved registers may be freely clobbered by a call, so the caller must save what it needs across it; callee-saved registers must be restored to their original value by the callee before returning. The split avoids every function saving every register on every call, dividing the bookkeeping efficiently between both sides.

drills.q: Why can a leaf function on ARM64 skip stack frame setup entirely while x86-64 always needs at least a ret?
drills.a: ARM64's bl instruction stores the return address in a dedicated register (x30/lr) rather than the stack, so a leaf function can do all its work in registers and return directly via lr. x86-64's call always pushes the return address onto the stack, so even the leanest function must execute ret to pop it back off -- there's no register-only equivalent since the call mechanism itself is stack-based.

drills.q: A release-build backtrace stops after two frames. Diagnose and give two fixes.
drills.a: Frame pointer omission (-fomit-frame-pointer, default at -O2+) repurposed rbp as a general register, breaking naive rbp-chain-walking unwinders past the last frame that still has one. Fixes: rebuild with -fno-omit-frame-pointer, or use a DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinder instead of frame-pointer walking.

drills.q: A function misbehaves only at -O2, not -O0. What's the first hypothesis and how do you confirm it rather than blaming the compiler?
drills.a: Undefined behavior in the source (signed integer overflow, uninitialized read, strict-aliasing violation) that -O0's minimal transformation happened not to expose but -O2's aggressive analysis/transformation does. Confirm with -fsanitize=undefined,address (UBSan/ASan), which instruments these UB classes at runtime independent of optimization level -- compiler bugs are comparatively rare next to application UB.

drills.q: Mechanically explain why a naive CPython arithmetic loop is roughly 50-100x slower than the equivalent compiled C loop.
drills.a: Four stacked per-iteration costs absent in compiled C: bytecode dispatch overhead through the eval loop, boxed PyObject allocation for each arithmetic result (Python ints are heap-allocated, immutable structs with a refcount), reference-counting reads/writes on every object touch, and dynamic __add__ method dispatch instead of a single machine add. A compiled C loop is typically just a register increment/compare, possibly vectorized.

drills.q: Does 'Python is 100x slower than C' apply to all Python code? Explain the boundary.
drills.a: No -- it applies specifically to the interpreter loop's per-element overhead in tight pure-Python numeric loops. Code whose hot path executes inside a C extension (NumPy vectorized ops, most standard-library internals, database drivers) pays essentially none of that overhead, which is why vectorizing with NumPy or compiling with Cython/Numba fixes the problem rather than micro-tuning pure-Python arithmetic.

drills.q: Explain concretely what Windows x64's calling convention does differently from System V x86-64, and why this makes object code non-portable across the two even on identical hardware.
drills.a: Windows x64 uses only 4 register arguments (rcx, rdx, r8, r9 vs System V's 6), requires the caller to reserve a 32-byte shadow space on the stack even when all arguments fit in registers, and has a different caller/callee-saved register split. Object files compiled under each convention disagree about where arguments and saved registers live, so they cannot be linked together without an explicit calling-convention-aware shim, regardless of the underlying x86-64 hardware being identical.

drills.q: In objdump output, how do you tell whether a function call was fully inlined versus the target being dead-code-eliminated for an unrelated reason?
drills.a: Check whether the target function's effects (its actual arithmetic/behavior) are still present inline at the call site with no corresponding call instruction (inlined) versus genuinely absent along with the surrounding logic that would have used its result (dead-code-eliminated because the result was provably unused). Compiler Explorer's source-to-assembly highlighting makes this distinction visible directly; raw objdump requires manually correlating instructions back to source.

drills.q: Your team wants to enable -fno-omit-frame-pointer fleet-wide for continuous production profiling. Make the cost-benefit case, and note the alternative that avoids the runtime cost.
drills.a: Cost: a measurable but typically small (low-single-digit percent, workload-dependent) throughput regression from dedicating rbp to frame-pointer bookkeeping instead of general use. Benefit: perf-based (or equivalent) production profiling relies on stack unwinding to attribute CPU time to call stacks, and frame-pointer-based unwinding is far more reliable and cheaper per sample than the alternative. Alternative: DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinding avoids the runtime register cost but is more expensive to compute per profiling sample and can be unreliable for hand-written or JIT-generated code lacking CFI metadata -- it's a different point on the same tradeoff, not a free escape from it.

drills.q: Walk through the compiler pipeline stage by stage and name each stage's concrete output artifact.
drills.a: Lexer: source text -> token stream. Parser: tokens -> AST. Lowering/semantic analysis: AST -> IR (normalized, often SSA-form, explicit basic-block control-flow graph). Optimization: IR -> optimized IR (same semantics, better properties). Codegen: optimized IR -> machine code via instruction selection and register allocation.

drills.q: Define SSA and explain why it turns most classical optimizations into a local rather than whole-program problem.
drills.a: Static Single Assignment requires every variable to be assigned exactly once textually, with phi nodes reconciling values arriving from different control-flow predecessors at merge points. Because each name has exactly one definition site, 'what value does this hold here' is answered by looking at one place instead of tracing backward through all possible reassignments -- which is what makes constant propagation, DCE, and CSE tractable as local passes.

drills.q: Explain why inlining is considered the most impactful compiler optimization beyond simply removing call/ret overhead.
drills.a: Inlining exposes the callee's instructions directly within the caller's optimization context, unlocking every other pass (constant propagation, dead-code elimination, register allocation) to operate across what used to be an opaque function boundary -- a caller's known argument value can now flow into and simplify the callee's body. The call/ret savings are real but secondary to this cascading unlock effect.

drills.q: A loop that looks obviously vectorizable isn't being vectorized. What's the diagnostic process, and give one genuinely non-vectorizable and one vectorizable-but-order-changing example.
drills.a: Check the compiler's missed-optimization report first (-fopt-info-vec-missed on GCC, -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize on Clang) for the specific blocking reason -- unproven aliasing, a loop-carried dependency, an unanalyzable call -- rather than guessing or reaching for intrinsics. Non-vectorizable: a[i] = a[i-1] * 2 (true loop-carried dependency on the prior result). Vectorizable-but-order-changing: sum += a[i], a reduction usable via multiple partial-sum lanes, but this changes floating-point rounding order since addition isn't associative.

drills.q: Why does restrict matter for vectorization correctness, and what happens if you falsely mark aliasing pointers as restrict?
drills.a: restrict promises the compiler that a pointer doesn't alias certain others in scope; without it, the compiler must conservatively assume aliasing is possible and can't safely reorder memory accesses across loop iterations. If the promise is true, the compiler can prove reordering safe and vectorize. If you lie -- mark genuinely aliasing pointers as restrict -- it's undefined behavior: the compiler generates code assuming no aliasing, and if the arrays actually overlap in a way that matters, results become unspecified and can vary by optimization level or compiler.

drills.q: Explain register allocation's core problem and what a 'spill' is, including how it's visible in disassembly.
drills.a: IR uses an effectively unlimited number of virtual registers/SSA values; the target ISA has a small fixed physical register set (16 GPRs x86-64, 31 ARM64). Register allocation maps virtual to physical registers, and when more values are simultaneously live than available physical registers, some are spilled -- stored to a stack slot and reloaded on demand, trading a register access for a memory access. Visible in disassembly as [rbp-N]-style stack loads/stores in code that would otherwise be register-to-register.

drills.q: Compare what PGO and JIT compilation are both trying to achieve and explain where their tradeoffs diverge.
drills.a: Both use real observed program behavior rather than static heuristics to guide optimization decisions (hot branches, monomorphic call sites, actual loop trip counts). PGO does this ahead-of-time: an instrumented/sampled training run feeds a profile into a subsequent static compile, shipping a statically-optimized binary with zero runtime warmup cost but requiring representative training traffic. A JIT does this continuously at runtime, adapting live to actual behavior but paying warmup cost and able to deoptimize if runtime behavior later diverges from earlier assumptions.

drills.q: Why can a vectorized floating-point reduction produce a numerically different result than the scalar version, and under what compiler conditions is this transformation actually permitted?
drills.a: Floating-point addition is not associative -- rounding at each step depends on operand order -- so summing via multiple SIMD-lane partial accumulators computes a genuinely different order than strict sequential left-to-right accumulation, producing a different (typically very close) rounded result. This is not a bug (both orderings are valid under IEEE-754), but compilers are only permitted to make this transformation under relaxed floating-point flags (e.g. -ffast-math or specific looser contract flags), not under strict default IEEE compliance, precisely because they're aware it changes results.

drills.q: What architectural decision makes LLVM easier to retarget to new hardware backends than a more monolithic compiler design, and what's the practical maintenance gotcha this creates?
drills.a: LLVM is architected around a stable, well-specified SSA-form IR that frontends and backends target independently -- a new backend implements instruction selection and register allocation against that one IR (via TableGen machine descriptions) without touching the frontend or shared optimizer. Gotcha: LLVM IR is not guaranteed stable across LLVM versions the way a wire protocol would be, so projects depending on it as core infrastructure (e.g. Rust) must carefully track compatible LLVM versions -- a real, ongoing maintenance burden.

drills.q: Staff-level: make the cost-benefit case for enabling both LTO and PGO on a latency-sensitive service's release pipeline, and describe how you'd detect a stale PGO profile actively hurting performance.
drills.a: Benefit: LTO lets the optimizer see across translation-unit boundaries (inlining across .c files), and PGO focuses aggressive optimization on genuinely hot paths from real traffic rather than static heuristics -- together commonly cited for single-digit to low-double-digit percent gains on performance-critical services. Cost: LTO can substantially increase link time and peak memory usage on large codebases; PGO requires maintaining and periodically refreshing a training/profiling step. Detecting staleness: compare current production behavior via live profiling/observability against what the PGO-guided binary assumed was hot -- a mismatch (optimized-for call patterns or branches that no longer reflect current traffic) is the concrete signal, fixed by re-running training against current representative traffic rather than abandoning PGO.

drills.q: Distinguish pipelining from out-of-order execution, and state whether you can have one without the other.
drills.a: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages but keeps program order; OoO lets independent instructions execute in a different order, retiring via a ROB in original order. Pipelining without OoO is the classic in-order 5-stage RISC pipeline (common in simple/embedded cores); OoO without pipelining is essentially never built since OoO's benefit compounds with pipelining's overlap.

drills.q: Name the three classic pipeline hazard types and a concrete fix for each.
drills.a: Structural (two instructions want the same resource -- duplicate resources, e.g. separate I/D caches, multiple ALU ports), data (an instruction needs a value not yet produced -- forwarding for close ALU deps, OoO scheduling/stall for load-use), control (branch target unknown -- predict + speculative execution, squash-and-refetch on misprediction).

drills.q: Why can't forwarding fully eliminate a load-use hazard the way it eliminates an ALU-to-ALU dependency?
drills.a: Forwarding routes an already-computed value from one stage's output to another's input; an ALU result exists at end of EX and can forward immediately. A load's result doesn't exist until MEM completes (L1 hit latency ~4-5 cycles), so an instruction consuming it right away has nothing yet to forward -- it stalls, or OoO execution hides the wait with unrelated independent work.

drills.q: Estimate the rough throughput cost of a 2% branch misprediction rate on a 19-stage pipeline with one branch per ~5-6 instructions, given a ~15-20 cycle misprediction penalty.
drills.a: Roughly 1 misprediction per 250-300 instructions, each costing ~15-20 cycles versus ~1 cycle those instructions would otherwise take -- a back-of-envelope estimate puts the overhead in the single-digit percent range of total cycles, directly visible as reduced IPC in perf stat.

drills.q: What is a reorder buffer, why does its size matter, and give rough entry counts for two current designs.
drills.a: The ROB tracks in-flight instructions in original program order so results retire in order despite OoO execution; its size bounds the instruction window the core can search past a stall (e.g. a cache-missing load) for independent work. Golden Cove ~512 entries, Zen4 ~320 entries -- both grown substantially as memory latency became the dominant bottleneck for many workloads.

drills.q: Explain register renaming and the specific hazard class it eliminates that forwarding does not address.
drills.a: Renaming maps the small architectural register set onto a much larger physical register file, giving every write a fresh physical register. This eliminates WAW/WAR false dependencies -- collisions that exist only because two unrelated instructions reuse the same register name, not because data actually flows between them. Forwarding instead addresses true read-after-write dependencies.

drills.q: Explain Spectre mechanically: how does speculative execution leak data despite architectural squash discarding the mispredicted instructions?
drills.a: An attacker mistrains a branch predictor so the core speculatively executes past a check it should have failed, performing a memory read using attacker-influenced data as an index, followed by an access dependent on that read's value. Architectural squash discards registers/memory writes but not microarchitectural state like cache lines pulled in during the speculative read -- the attacker measures cache-access timing afterward to infer which line was touched, reconstructing the leaked value without ever architecturally reading it.

drills.q: A hot reduction loop (sum += arr[i]) shows IPC ~1.0 on a 4+ wide core with all data L1-resident. Diagnose and fix, and note the numerical caveat.
drills.a: A single running accumulator creates a strict serial dependency chain -- each add waits on the previous add's result, so only one addition is ever in flight regardless of core width. Fix: use multiple independent partial-sum accumulators (or let SIMD lanes act as independent accumulators), summing at the end. Caveat: floating-point addition isn't associative, so this changes rounding behavior versus strict left-to-right summation -- not purely free, especially with widely differing magnitudes.

drills.q: When is it acceptable to disable Spectre/Meltdown mitigations for performance, and when is it a red flag?
drills.a: Only defensible when the threat model genuinely excludes the attack surface closed by mitigations -- e.g. a single-tenant, physically isolated batch node running fully trusted code with no untrusted co-tenants or code execution -- and even then as a deliberate, documented decision. It is a red flag on any multi-tenant or shared infrastructure (e.g. Kubernetes nodes with multiple tenants' pods), since that is exactly the scenario the mitigations exist to protect, structurally identical to recommending tcp_tw_recycle for TIME_WAIT.

drills.q: A numeric loop over a large float array shows low IPC and high cache-miss rate under perf stat. Does adding wider SIMD (AVX2 to AVX-512) help, and why or why not?
drills.a: No, or only marginally -- if the loop is memory-bandwidth-bound (confirmed via high cache-miss rate and low IPC despite simple arithmetic), the ALUs are already waiting on data; widening SIMD moves the same total bytes in wider chunks per instruction but doesn't relieve a bandwidth bottleneck. Wider SIMD pays off on compute-bound kernels with more arithmetic per byte loaded (e.g. FMA-heavy inner loops), not bandwidth-bound ones -- profile before concluding an ISA feature doesn't help.

drills.q: What does the GIL actually protect, precisely, and does it protect against application-level race conditions like x += 1 on shared state?
drills.a: It protects CPython's internal data structures, above all the refcount field on every PyObject, from concurrent unsynchronized modification during bytecode execution -- without it, two threads racing to increment the same object's refcount could lose an update, causing premature deallocation and use-after-free. It does NOT protect application logic: individual bytecode instructions are atomic relative to other threads, but a multi-instruction sequence like load-modify-store can still be interrupted between instructions, so higher-level races on shared mutable state remain possible under the GIL.

drills.q: Why can't reference counting alone reclaim reference cycles, and what does CPython do about it?
drills.a: Two (or more) objects referencing each other directly or transitively never reach refcount zero through ordinary dereferencing, even when nothing outside the cycle references any of them -- pure refcounting leaks these permanently. CPython supplements refcounting with a generational cyclic garbage collector (the gc module) that periodically scans candidate container objects for unreachable cycles and collects them.

drills.q: Explain the specializing adaptive interpreter (3.11+) with a concrete example, and what happens when its assumption is violated.
drills.a: A generic instruction like BINARY_OP initially dispatches through a slow, type-generic path. After observing stable operand types (e.g. repeated int+int) at a specific bytecode site, the interpreter rewrites that site in-place to a specialized variant (BINARY_OP_ADD_INT) with an inline type guard that skips general dispatch. If a later execution at that site sees a different type, the guard fails and the interpreter de-specializes back to the generic path rather than running incorrect specialized logic.

drills.q: Is CPython's specializing adaptive interpreter the same thing as a JIT compiler like the JVM's? Explain the distinction.
drills.a: Architecturally similar in spirit (observe real runtime behavior, specialize the hot path, guard and deoptimize on violation) but mechanically different: the adaptive interpreter specializes bytecode instructions executed by the interpreter loop itself with no native machine code generation. A true JIT compiles to native machine code. CPython only began shipping an experimental JIT (copy-and-patch based, built on this same specialization data) starting in 3.13, layered on top of and distinct from the adaptive interpreter.

drills.q: Why does I/O-bound multi-threaded Python get real concurrency benefit under the GIL while CPU-bound multi-threaded Python doesn't, and how does NumPy get around this for CPU-bound work?
drills.a: The GIL is explicitly released around blocking I/O operations, so while one thread blocks on a socket/file read, another can acquire the GIL and run bytecode -- genuine concurrency. CPU-bound Python code never blocks, so the GIL stays continuously held by whichever thread runs, serializing execution with zero parallelism regardless of thread count. NumPy's C-level hot loops explicitly release the GIL during long-running native computation since they're not touching Python objects during that time, letting other Python threads run concurrently -- the CPU-bound work happens entirely outside the GIL's scope.

drills.q: State the concrete performance and memory overhead of Python's free-threaded build as of 3.14, and explain the mechanism that causes it.
drills.a: Roughly 5-10% single-threaded slowdown (down from ~40% during 3.13's initial experimental phase) and roughly 15-20% higher memory usage. Cause: biased reference counting replaces the GIL-protected non-atomic refcount increment with a fast path for the common single-owning-thread case and a slower atomic/shared path for genuine cross-thread references -- even the fast path costs more than the original GIL-protected increment, and per-object lock/metadata adds memory overhead.

drills.q: Why does CPython's free-threading rollout (PEP 703/779) span multiple releases and years instead of switching immediately, and what's the phased plan?
drills.a: The C-extension ecosystem (NumPy and everything on the CPython C API) has relied implicitly on the GIL for thread safety for over three decades without extension authors needing explicit synchronization; an abrupt default switch would silently introduce data races and crashes fleet-wide. Plan: 3.14 officially supported but optional (build tag 't'); ~2026-27 GIL becomes runtime-flag-controllable; ~2028-30 free-threading becomes the default with GIL still available as an opt-in fallback -- giving extension maintainers years of overlap to audit and update.

drills.q: A long-running Python service's memory grows steadily despite objects apparently going out of scope. Give a full diagnostic approach, including how to rule out free-threaded build overhead as the cause.
drills.a: Don't assume Python's GC rules out leaks -- check for reference cycles the generational cyclic collector's thresholds haven't yet swept (force gc.collect(), inspect gc.get_objects()) and separately check for genuine leaks refcounting correctly reports as alive (unbounded module-level caches, closures capturing large objects, unregistered event listeners) via objgraph.show_growth() or tracemalloc snapshots over time. Rule out free-threaded (3.14t) build overhead by checking whether the increase is a flat ~15-20% one-time bump (build overhead) versus continuous unbounded growth over the service's lifetime (a genuine leak) -- the two have distinctly different memory-over-time signatures.

drills.q: How would you decide, as a staff engineer, whether to adopt the free-threaded build for a specific production service today?
drills.a: Audit every C-extension dependency's explicit free-threading support status (increasingly published by major packages), benchmark the actual workload under both builds since the 5-10%/15-20% figures are averages not guarantees for any specific workload, and weigh that against the real multi-core CPU-bound speedup the workload would realize. For a mostly I/O-bound service or one already using multiprocessing/NumPy effectively, the case is weak; for a genuinely CPU-bound, pure-Python-heavy, multi-core-starved workload with fully audited dependencies, it's a real evaluable option now.

drills.q: Trace what happens, mechanically, when two objects with a cyclic reference to each other lose their last external reference -- does either get freed by refcounting alone?
drills.a: No. Object A's refcount drops by one (the external reference) but remains at 1 because B still references A; object B's refcount similarly drops but remains at 1 because A still references B. Neither reaches zero through ordinary dereferencing despite nothing external referencing either -- both leak under pure refcounting. Only the generational cyclic garbage collector, which periodically scans for and identifies unreachable cycles independent of refcount values, can detect and collect this pattern.

drills.q: Define G, M, and P precisely, and state what actually bounds truly parallel Go-code execution at any instant.
drills.a: G=goroutine (lightweight user-space unit of work), M=OS thread (kernel-scheduled), P=logical processor context, exactly GOMAXPROCS of them, each with a local run queue up to 256 entries. An M must hold a P to execute Go code, so the P count bounds parallel execution -- not the M count, since M count can temporarily exceed GOMAXPROCS when a P detaches from a blocked M and reattaches to another.

drills.q: Explain Go's goroutine stack growth mechanism and why the same technique isn't safely available to a naive C runtime.
drills.a: A goroutine's stack starts at 2KB; a cheap check at function entry detects insufficient room and triggers allocating a larger stack, copying the old contents over, and rewriting every pointer in the copied data that referenced the old stack's address range to point into the new stack. This is safe only because the Go compiler emits precise stack maps telling the runtime exactly which stack words are pointers versus plain data -- a C runtime generally can't distinguish a genuine pointer from an integer that merely looks like one, so blind pointer rewriting isn't safely possible there.

drills.q: What changed in Go 1.14's scheduler, what specific bug class did it fix, and what should you suspect if apparent goroutine starvation appears on a modern Go version?
drills.a: Go 1.14 introduced asynchronous preemption via OS signals, interrupting a running goroutine at arbitrary points instead of only at function-call safe points, fixing the pre-1.14 bug where a tight loop with no calls could starve peer goroutines on the same P indefinitely. On 1.14+, that specific cause is ruled out by version -- suspect instead a goroutine holding a lock/resource for a pathologically long time, or a GOMAXPROCS misconfiguration relative to actual available CPU.

drills.q: A Go service in a Kubernetes pod with a 2-core CPU limit shows scheduling throttling despite low reported CPU usage. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Pre-Go-1.25, GOMAXPROCS defaults to the host's total core count, not the container's cgroup CPU limit, so the scheduler oversubscribes Ps relative to the actual CPU quota, triggering cgroup CFS throttling. Fix: upgrade to Go 1.25+ (container-aware GOMAXPROCS by default) or explicitly set GOMAXPROCS to the container's limit (or use uber-go/automaxprocs on older versions).

drills.q: Explain V8 hidden classes and why two objects with identical final property sets can still have different hidden classes.
drills.a: A hidden class (V8's Map) encodes an object's property set and storage offsets, determined by the TRANSITION HISTORY of property additions, not just the final set. Two objects with the same final properties but added in different orders (e.g. x-then-y vs y-then-x) end up with two distinct hidden classes despite looking identical from JS code, defeating the fast fixed-offset access path -- consistent construction order (ideally via one shared constructor/factory) is what actually matters for performance.

drills.q: Distinguish monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic inline caches, and explain what happens to TurboFan's optimization once a site goes megamorphic.
drills.a: Monomorphic: one hidden class ever observed at the site, fastest case (single cached fixed-offset access, no branching). Polymorphic: a small bounded number of distinct shapes (commonly up to ~4), still reasonably fast via a small dispatch table. Megamorphic: more shapes than the polymorphic cache holds, fast path abandoned entirely, falling back to generic slow property lookup -- and TurboFan, seeing megamorphic feedback, declines to generate type-specialized code for that site since there's no stable shape to speculate on.

drills.q: A Node.js function that was previously fast slows down sharply under production load with no code change. Walk through the diagnostic process.
drills.a: Suspect a deoptimization or a shift from monomorphic/polymorphic to megamorphic inline caches at a hot property-access site, likely triggered by a change in the DATA flowing through the function (a new upstream source producing objects with different property-addition order, or values shifting from consistently-integer to sometimes-float) rather than a code change. Diagnose with --trace-deopt (specific deopt events/reasons/locations) and --trace-ic (IC state transitions), and rule out GC pressure changes in parallel via --trace-gc rather than guessing which cause applies.

drills.q: Explain deoptimization in V8 and how it's architecturally similar to mechanisms in other runtimes.
drills.a: When TurboFan-compiled machine code's speculative assumption (a stable hidden class, or a value always being an integer) is violated at runtime, V8 discards the optimized code, reconstructs an equivalent interpreter-level stack frame, and resumes execution in Ignition. This is the same 'speculate aggressively, keep a safe correct fallback' pattern as the JVM's C2 deoptimization back to the interpreter and CPython's 3.11+ specializing adaptive interpreter de-specializing a bytecode site when its type guard fails.

drills.q: Staff-level: your team is deciding between unbounded per-request goroutines and a fixed worker pool for a high-throughput ingestion service. Make the case for each and give a recommendation.
drills.a: Unbounded per-request goroutines are simplest and fine as long as incoming rate times average goroutine lifetime stays within what downstream resources (DB connections, memory, file descriptors) and process memory can sustain -- goroutines being cheap doesn't make downstream dependencies infinitely scalable. A bounded worker pool or semaphore trades minor code complexity for a hard, predictable concurrency ceiling and natural backpressure, protecting downstream resources under traffic spikes. Recommendation: for a high-throughput ingestion service specifically, a bounded pool/limiter is the safer default, sized generously relative to measured downstream capacity rather than arbitrarily small -- unbounded goroutines under a spike (memory exhaustion, downstream connection exhaustion) is a real, common production incident pattern.

drills.q: Why is spawning 100,000 goroutines routine in Go while spawning 100,000 OS threads is impractical? Give the concrete memory math.
drills.a: Goroutine stacks start at 2KB and grow on demand, versus an OS thread's typical fixed default of 1-8MB reserved upfront. 100,000 goroutines at 2KB each is roughly 200MB total; 100,000 OS threads at even a conservative 2MB each is roughly 200GB -- an infeasible memory footprint, plus each OS thread carries real kernel-level context-switch and scheduling cost that goroutines' user-space scheduling avoids.

drills.q: Explain the classloader parent-delegation model and the concrete problem it prevents.
drills.a: Classloaders form a hierarchy (bootstrap -> platform -> application); each delegates a load request to its parent first before attempting to load the class itself. This guarantees core JDK classes (e.g. java.lang.String) always resolve to the trusted bootstrap-loaded version regardless of what an application or library defines with the same fully-qualified name, preventing malicious or accidental shadowing of core classes.

drills.q: Walk through interpreter -> C1 -> C2 tiered compilation and explain why the JVM doesn't just always compile with C2.
drills.a: Interpreter runs bytecode immediately with zero compile latency but slow dispatch. C1 compiles quickly with light optimization once a method crosses a low invocation threshold, giving fast throughput gains while gathering profiling data (branch outcomes, concrete types at call sites). C2 recompiles genuinely hot methods with aggressive, slower-to-produce optimizations informed by that profiling data. Always using C2 would maximize eventual throughput but pay expensive, slow compilation cost even for methods invoked only a handful of times -- terrible warmup latency.

drills.q: What is escape analysis, what two specific optimizations does it enable, and why is it restricted to the C2 tier?
drills.a: Escape analysis proves whether an allocated object can ever be referenced outside its allocating method or thread. Non-escape past the method enables scalar replacement (fields become local variables/registers, eliminating the heap allocation and its GC cost entirely). Non-escape past the thread enables lock elision (synchronized blocks are removed since no other thread could ever contend). It's C2-only because proving non-escape requires expensive whole-method, often cross-call data-flow analysis -- exactly the class of slow analysis reserved for methods that have proven themselves hot enough to be worth C2's compile-time budget.

drills.q: Compare G1 and generational ZGC on pause time, throughput, and memory, and state when you'd choose each.
drills.a: G1 (region-based, collects highest-garbage regions first) targets a configurable pause goal (commonly tens of ms) but still has real stop-the-world phases and can fall back to full GC. Generational ZGC achieves consistent sub-millisecond pauses (~0.1-0.5ms) independent of heap size via concurrent marking/relocation/remapping (colored pointers, load barriers), at the cost of no compressed object pointers (~15-30% more memory) and typically 5-15% lower throughput than G1. Choose G1 as the default for most services; choose generational ZGC specifically for large-heap, latency-SLO-bound workloads where pause consistency matters more than memory/throughput.

drills.q: What is a G1 humongous object, why does it hurt specifically, and how can you tune around it without switching collectors?
drills.a: An object larger than 50% of a region size is allocated specially across contiguous regions rather than fitting into a normal region. Workloads with frequent large allocations (big arrays/collections) suffer extra GC pressure and fragmentation from this special handling, since finding contiguous free regions is a harder bin-packing problem. Tuning lever: raising -XX:G1HeapRegionSize increases the humongous threshold (defined relative to region size), potentially converting previously-humongous allocations into normal regional ones -- though not a universal fix if object sizes vary too widely.

drills.q: A microbenchmark shows a method getting faster over its first several thousand calls before stabilizing. Explain the cause and the correct way to measure it.
drills.a: JIT warmup -- early calls run interpreted or C1-compiled, and once the method crosses C2's invocation threshold and gets recompiled with aggressive optimization (possibly including escape analysis and speculative inlining), performance stabilizes at steady-state C2-optimized levels. Measure with JMH, which explicitly separates warmup iterations (discarded) from measurement iterations and guards against dead-code elimination/constant-folding via blackholes -- a hand-rolled System.nanoTime() loop conflates warmup cost with steady-state performance and doesn't guard against those pitfalls.

drills.q: A hot method's latency regresses sharply and permanently mid-run in production. What's your hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: C2 likely deoptimized the method -- a speculative assumption broke (a previously-monomorphic call site became polymorphic, a class was redefined, an array-bounds-check-elimination assumption was violated), discarding the compiled code and falling back to the interpreter. Confirm via JFR (Java Flight Recorder) or -XX:+PrintCompilation/-XX:+TraceDeoptimization correlated with the regression timestamp. If the pattern causing deopt persists, the method may thrash between compilation and deopt ('deopt storm') -- the fix is usually addressing the polymorphism at the call site, not JVM flags.

drills.q: Your service on G1 shows acceptable average latency but a p99.9 tail with 200-400ms spikes correlated with GC logs. Walk through the diagnosis and options in order of invasiveness.
drills.a: First correlate spikes precisely against GC log timestamps to confirm whether they're young, mixed, or full GCs (full GC is the likeliest culprit for 200-400ms+ pauses), and check for humongous-object allocation or fragmentation contributing to full-GC fallback. Then: tune G1 first (realistic MaxGCPauseMillis, heap/region sizing, address humongous allocation patterns); if that can't close the gap and the SLO is genuinely violated, evaluate generational ZGC for its sub-ms pause guarantee, accepting the throughput/memory cost; in parallel, reduce allocation rate at the source (pooling, escape-analysis-friendly code shapes) since lower allocation pressure helps under either collector.

drills.q: Escape analysis 'should' eliminate an allocation given the source code shape, but profiling shows it's still heap-allocating. Diagnose.
drills.a: First confirm the method actually reached C2 compilation (-XX:+PrintCompilation) since escape analysis is C2-only and unavailable to the interpreter or C1. If it did compile with C2, look for an escape path not obvious from a quick read -- the object passed to a logging call, stored conditionally in a collection, or captured by a lambda/closure that itself escapes. Even one rarely-executed escaping code path defeats scalar replacement for the entire allocation site.

drills.q: Is ZGC's claim of pause time independent of heap size the same as saying GC work itself is free at large heap sizes? Explain.
drills.a: No. Pause time being independent of heap size is a genuine, correctly-cited design property (unlike traditional stop-the-world collectors where pause time scales with live-set size) -- but the concurrent marking/relocation work ZGC does still consumes CPU proportional to live data and allocation rate. That ongoing concurrent cost is exactly where ZGC's throughput deficit versus G1 (typically 5-15% lower) comes from, even though it never shows up as a long stop-the-world pause.

drills.q: Walk through the full memory hierarchy with real latency numbers from register to DRAM, and state the one ratio worth memorizing.
drills.a: Register ~0.3ns -> L1 ~4-5cyc/~1ns (32-48KB) -> L2 ~12-14cyc/~3-4ns (256KB-2MB) -> L3 ~40-75cyc/~10-20ns (tens of MB shared) -> local DRAM ~200-300cyc/~70-100ns -> remote NUMA DRAM (50-100% higher). The ratio worth memorizing: L1 hit vs DRAM access is roughly 100x in cycles.

drills.q: Define false sharing and name the perf tool and specific counter used to detect it in production.
drills.a: Two threads write to logically independent variables sharing one 64-byte cache line, so each write invalidates the whole line for the other core, forcing cross-core cache-to-cache transfers despite no real data contention. Detect with perf c2c record/report, looking for high HITM (hit-modified) counts.

drills.q: Why is padding the correct fix for false sharing, and why is reaching for a mutex or atomic the wrong fix?
drills.a: Padding (alignas(64), @Contended, manual struct padding) puts each variable on its own cache line, eliminating the coherence traffic at its source. A mutex/atomic is wrong because there is no actual data race -- the variables are logically independent; synchronizing them adds real overhead to solve a problem that doesn't require synchronization.

drills.q: Explain what a TLB miss costs and how huge pages address it, including the operational risk of the transparent variant.
drills.a: A TLB miss requires a page-table walk (4 levels on x86-64 for 4KB pages), costing ~100+ cycles on top of the actual data access -- comparable to or worse than an L2 miss. A 2MB huge page covers what would be 512 separate 4KB TLB entries, cutting miss rate for large working sets. Risk: Linux transparent huge pages use background compaction (khugepaged) that has caused documented latency spikes (notably Redis); explicit hugetlbfs avoids this for known large allocations.

drills.q: A dual-socket production host shows bimodal p99 latency not reproducible on single-socket test hardware. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Likely NUMA: threads and their memory ended up on different sockets (scheduler migration or allocation before pinning), so some accesses pay the remote-socket latency penalty (roughly 1.3-2x local) while others don't, producing bimodal latency. Confirm with numastat (cross-node access counts) and numactl --hardware; fix by pinning CPU and memory locality together (numactl --cpunodebind/--membind or runtime equivalent).

drills.q: State the four MESI states and trace what happens when one of three cores holding a Shared line writes to it.
drills.a: Modified (sole dirty owner), Exclusive (sole clean owner, silent upgrade to Modified on local write), Shared (multiple clean readers), Invalid (stale). On a write by one of three Shared holders: it broadcasts invalidation, its own copy goes Shared->Modified, the other two go Shared->Invalid; either of those cores touching the address again triggers a cache-to-cache transfer of the Modified copy.

drills.q: Explain associativity and describe a concrete access pattern that triggers pathological conflict misses.
drills.a: Associativity is how many distinct lines can occupy one cache set simultaneously; low associativity (e.g. direct-mapped) forces addresses hashing to the same set to repeatedly evict each other even with an otherwise-empty cache. A concrete trigger: striding through a large array with a stride that's a power-of-two multiple of the cache's set-mapping period (e.g. iterating columns of a power-of-two-sized matrix) causes nearly every access to land in the same set -- fixed by padding array dimensions or iterating in memory (row-major) order.

drills.q: Design a per-CPU counter/metrics array for a highly concurrent service. What layout eliminates coherence traffic, and what's the tradeoff if you instead need exact real-time consistency?
drills.a: One counter per logical CPU/thread, each padded to its own 64-byte cache line (hardware_destructive_interference_size), so every CPU writes its own line with zero cross-core invalidation; periodic reads sum across per-CPU slots, accepting eventual rather than immediate consistency. If exact, immediately-consistent totals are required, that conflicts with the lock-free design -- you'd need a single contended atomic (accepting real coherence cost) or a coarser synchronized snapshot; you cannot have zero contention and exact real-time consistency simultaneously.

drills.q: Compare the stacked cost of a TLB miss plus a NUMA-remote DRAM access against a fully-cached (TLB hit, L3 hit) access, and explain the practical tuning implication.
drills.a: A TLB miss (~100+ cycles for the page-table walk) happens before the data fetch; combined with a NUMA-remote DRAM miss (200-300+ cycles locally, 50-100% higher remote), a single logical access can exceed 500 cycles. A fully-cached access (TLB hit, L3 hit) costs on the order of tens of cycles. Implication: huge pages and NUMA pinning are paired tuning levers for large random-access workloads (databases, JVMs) -- adding more RAM fixes a capacity problem, not a cache/TLB miss latency problem.

drills.q: Why is a sequential array scan dramatically faster than pointer-chasing a linked list holding the same total data, independent of any cache-capacity difference?
drills.a: Sequential access amortizes each 64-byte cache line fetch across many useful bytes and lets the hardware prefetcher predict the stride and fetch ahead of demand. Pointer-chasing wastes most of each fetched line (nodes are scattered and often smaller than 64 bytes), defeats stride-based prefetching since the next address is data-dependent, and each hop can be a full latency-bound miss if the working set exceeds cache capacity -- a pure locality effect, not an algorithmic-complexity one.

drills.q: Derive why a target network is necessary, not just helpful, for DQN to converge.
drills.a: Without it, y=r+gamma*max_a' Q_theta(s',a') is computed from the same theta being updated by (y-Q_theta(s,a))^2 -- every gradient step changes y for the next computation, a regression problem whose target moves at the rate you're trying to converge. Freezing theta- for C steps makes y stationary for that window, an ordinary SGD-solvable regression problem, with the target only jumping in controlled increments.

drills.q: Derive the overestimation bias in vanilla DQN and explain precisely how Double DQN fixes it.
drills.a: E[max_a' Q(s',a')] >= max_a' E[Q(s',a')] by Jensen's inequality on the convex max operator -- max over noisy estimates preferentially picks whichever overestimated by chance, and this compounds through bootstrapping. Double DQN selects the action with the online network (argmax_a' Q_theta) but evaluates it with the target network (Q_theta-), so an action theta overestimates isn't guaranteed to also be overestimated by the independently-noisy theta-, substantially reducing the bias at zero extra parameter cost.

drills.q: A team's DQN has low, stable training loss but flat evaluated episode return. Walk through your diagnostic process.
drills.a: Low stable loss only means Q_theta fits its own bootstrapped target well, not that the target is correct. Check: (1) is the target network actually syncing, (2) is the terminal-state bootstrap zeroed (the 1-done term), (3) is reward scale sane, (4) plot actual episode return not loss. If all correct, check the exploration schedule -- epsilon may have decayed too fast, leaving the buffer too narrow/unrepresentative to learn a good policy from.

drills.q: Why is mean-subtraction required in Dueling DQN's recombination formula, and what's the tradeoff with subtracting the max instead?
drills.a: Q(s,a)=V(s)+A(s,a) alone is under-determined (add k to V, subtract k from every A, same Q), making V and A gradients ill-posed. Mean-subtraction pins down a unique decomposition using all actions' information. Max-subtraction also resolves identifiability but is noisier since it depends only on the single current-best action, which can change abruptly during training.

drills.q: Explain why the replay buffer's decorrelation benefit and its sample-reuse benefit are genuinely separate justifications, and give a scenario wanting one without the other.
drills.a: Decorrelation fixes a training-stability problem (correlated on-policy samples violate the i.i.d. minibatch assumption) that would matter even with free, unlimited environment interaction. Reuse fixes a cost/efficiency problem that would matter even with uncorrelated data. Scenario: a cheap, fast simulator with unlimited interaction but still-correlated sequential samples -- you'd want shuffling/buffering for decorrelation even without ever reusing a transition.

drills.q: Design a value-based deep RL stack for a 500-item recommendation slate problem, stating what you build and what you deliberately skip from Rainbow.
drills.a: Build: Double DQN (essentially free bias fix), Dueling architecture (many states likely have action-insensitive value), Prioritized Replay (sparse/delayed feedback per item). Skip multi-step returns unless genuine multi-step user-journey structure exists (else it's really a contextual bandit per T31-rl-framing's triage); skip distributional RL and Noisy Nets initially per Rainbow's own ablation showing them as lower-priority, revisited only if the simpler stack plateaus.

drills.q: Prove that greedy policy improvement never makes any state's value worse.
drills.a: By construction Q^pi(s,pi'(s)) >= Q^pi(s,pi(s)) = V^pi(s). Chain this forward: substitute the same inequality at each future timestep (V^pi(s_t+k) <= Q^pi(s_t+k, pi'(s_t+k)) again and again), producing V^pi(s) <= ... <= V^pi'(s). The inequality direction is preserved at every substitution so it holds in the limit.

drills.q: A policy iteration loop never terminates in your implementation. Name the top three things to check, tied to the actual convergence proof.
drills.a: 1) Policy-equality check uses exact per-state action match, not float comparison, with deterministic tie-breaking in argmax. 2) gamma < 1, required for the evaluation contraction. 3) P(s'|s,a) sums to 1 for every (s,a), required for the improvement monotonicity proof.

drills.q: Why is policy iteration's termination argument fundamentally different from value iteration's convergence argument?
drills.a: Policy iteration's argument is combinatorial: finitely many deterministic policies, each iteration strictly improves or stops, so it must terminate -- it gives no rate guarantee. Value iteration's argument is analytic: the Bellman optimality operator is a contraction on a continuous space of value functions (Banach fixed point), which gives a geometric rate gamma^n.

drills.q: A team has a fully-known MDP with 3000 states and wants to train a DQN on it instead of running value iteration. Evaluate this decision.
drills.a: Usually wrong: with a known model and enumerable states, tabular value/policy iteration gives the exact optimum in milliseconds with zero sampling noise or function-approximation error, while DQN adds all of those risks to solve a problem that doesn't need them. Only justified if the model changes frequently or this is deliberately a stepping stone to a much larger version of the problem.

drills.q: Your state space is a 10^9-cell grid with local transitions (each cell reaches ~4 neighbors). Can tabular DP still work, and what modification would you reach for first?
drills.a: Per-sweep cost becomes roughly linear in |S| with sparse transitions, so a sweep is plausible, but storing V over 10^9 states and the sweep count to converge remain issues. Reach for asynchronous DP / prioritized sweeping to focus computation on states with large pending Bellman error rather than uniformly sweeping everything.

drills.q: You extract a policy from V before value iteration has converged. What's wrong with this, precisely?
drills.a: The policy is greedy w.r.t. an intermediate, still-wrong value estimate, with no principled optimality guarantee. The value-error-to-policy-suboptimality bound is 2*gamma*eps/(1-gamma), so an unconverged V (large eps) can produce a policy far from optimal, especially as gamma approaches 1.

drills.q: Explain why fixed-epsilon greedy has linear regret while UCB1 has logarithmic regret.
drills.a: Fixed epsilon spends a constant fraction of all steps on uniform random actions forever, regardless of accumulated evidence, so regret accrues at a constant rate -> O(epsilon*T). UCB1's bonus term shrinks as N(a) grows, so exploration of confidently-bad arms fades over time while still occasionally revisiting any arm (bonus grows slowly with t) -> O(log T).

drills.q: A production ad-serving Thompson sampling bandit suddenly shows dropping revenue with no code change. Diagnose and propose a fix.
drills.a: Likely a non-stationary shift in the reward distribution (seasonality, new user cohort). Thompson sampling assumes stationarity; large accumulated alpha/beta counts make the posterior slow to move even against new contradicting evidence. Fix: discount/window the posterior updates (decay alpha,beta before each update) or add change-point detection triggering a reset.

drills.q: Someone says 'just increase epsilon, we're not exploring enough.' When is this the wrong fix, and what should you check instead?
drills.a: Wrong if the problem is unfocused exploration (uniform, ignoring what's already known) rather than insufficient volume -- raising epsilon wastes more budget re-testing known-bad arms. Check whether it's reward sparsity (needs intrinsic motivation, not more randomness) or whether exploration should be uncertainty-weighted (switch to UCB/Thompson instead of a bigger epsilon).

drills.q: Design an exploration strategy for a sparse-reward robotics task where reward only appears at final task success, hundreds of steps away.
drills.a: Value-uncertainty methods (epsilon-greedy/UCB/Thompson) need some nonzero reward to be uncertain about, which sparse reward may never provide via random exploration. Add intrinsic motivation (RND preferred over forward-model curiosity, since real robot sensors are noisy and would trigger the noisy-TV problem) with total reward r_ext + beta*r_int, tuning or annealing beta so novelty doesn't override the actual task objective.

drills.q: Why is exploration in RLHF/LLM RL considered fundamentally different from classic bandit exploration despite the same action-reward-update framing?
drills.a: The action space (all possible token sequences) is astronomically large, nowhere close to the small enumerable arm sets UCB/Thompson are built for -- no tractable confidence bound or posterior per possible response exists. Practice substitutes cruder mechanisms (sampling temperature, multi-rollout diversity, entropy bonuses) with none of the regret guarantees classic bandit methods provide.

drills.q: An agent's intrinsic reward stays high and behavior looks obsessive around one part of the environment, while task success stays at zero. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely the noisy-TV problem: a forward-dynamics curiosity signal is stuck on a stochastic, unpredictable environment element (e.g. sensor noise) that can never be predicted, so prediction error (and thus intrinsic reward) never decreases there. Fix by switching to RND, whose target is a fixed deterministic random network rather than a stochastic environment outcome.

drills.q: Derive the Bellman expectation equation for V^pi starting only from G_t = r_{t+1} + gamma*G_{t+1}.
drills.a: V^pi(s)=E_pi[G_t|s_t=s]=E_pi[r_{t+1}|s_t=s]+gamma*E_pi[G_{t+1}|s_t=s]. Expand first term over pi(a|s) and P(s'|s,a). For the second term, use the Markov property to replace E_pi[G_{t+1}|s_{t+1}=s'] with V^pi(s') exactly, then average over a and s'. Combine into V^pi(s)=sum_a pi(a|s) sum_s' P(s'|s,a)[R(s,a,s')+gamma V^pi(s')].

drills.q: One state, self-loop, reward +2 every step, gamma=0.5. Compute V(s) two different ways.
drills.a: Geometric series: V=2*sum gamma^k=2/(1-0.5)=4. Self-consistency: V=R+gamma*V => V(1-gamma)=R => V=2/0.5=4. Both give V(s)=4.

drills.q: Explain why value iteration is guaranteed to converge, using the contraction argument, not just 'it's a known result.'
drills.a: The Bellman optimality operator T satisfies ||TV1-TV2||_inf <= gamma||V1-V2||_inf (max is non-expansive, P is a probability distribution so weighted differences are bounded by the max difference). Since gamma<1, T is a strict contraction on a complete metric space, so by the Banach fixed-point theorem it has a unique fixed point V*, reached from any starting V0 at rate gamma^n.

drills.q: A colleague's value iteration implementation converges to a stable but wrong answer (not divergence). What do you check, given that the contraction guarantees a unique fixed point?
drills.a: Since convergence to the wrong fixed point contradicts uniqueness under a correctly implemented T, the bug is in the operator itself: check reward function signature (R(s,a) vs R(s,a,s') mismatch), check the action set used in the max matches actually available actions per state, and check P(s'|s,a) truly sums to 1.

drills.q: A robotics task has meaningful 500-step dependencies but gamma was set to 0.9. What happens mechanically, not just 'it won't learn well'?
drills.a: Effective horizon is 1/(1-0.9)=10 steps. Consequences 500 steps out are discounted by 0.9^500, astronomically close to zero, so they contribute essentially nothing to the value function's gradient — the agent is structurally incapable of representing that dependency at this gamma, independent of how much it's trained.

drills.q: Why does an RLHF reward model still fit inside the standard MDP framework despite looking nothing like a robotics control problem?
drills.a: State = prompt + tokens generated so far, action = next token, transition is deterministic (append the token), reward often arrives only at the end (a single scalar from the reward model). It's a valid but extremely short-horizon, deterministic-transition, sparse-terminal-reward MDP, which is why long-horizon stochastic-transition techniques don't map over unchanged.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why Monte Carlo is unbiased but TD(0) is biased.
drills.a: MC's target G_t is by construction a direct sample of the exact random variable whose expectation defines V^pi(s), so averaging is unbiased. TD(0)'s target r_{t+1}+gamma*V(s_{t+1}) substitutes the current, possibly-wrong V(s_{t+1}) for the true unobserved continuation, so the target inherits whatever error V(s_{t+1}) currently has.

drills.q: Derive the n-step return and show it recovers TD(0) at n=1 and Monte Carlo at n=T-t.
drills.a: G_t^(n) = r_{t+1}+gamma*r_{t+2}+...+gamma^(n-1)r_{t+n}+gamma^n*V(s_{t+n}). At n=1: G_t^(1)=r_{t+1}+gamma*V(s_{t+1}), exactly TD(0). At n=T-t running to termination, the bootstrap term vanishes/isn't needed and the sum becomes the full observed return, exactly MC's G_t.

drills.q: A value function's estimates are stable but consistently wrong in one direction. What's your first hypothesis and how do you test it?
drills.a: First hypothesis: unwashed TD bootstrapping bias from a poor initialization or ongoing non-stationarity. Test by comparing against a Monte Carlo estimate on the same states over many episodes -- if TD is consistently offset from MC's average in one direction, that confirms bootstrapping bias; if MC agrees with TD's error, the cause is upstream (bad reward function, non-Markov state) not TD-specific.

drills.q: Why do Rainbow and Ape-X use precomputed n-step returns instead of literal eligibility traces, and what bias does this introduce?
drills.a: Eligibility traces require sequential online updates along one trajectory; replay buffers sample transitions out of order, breaking that assumption, so n-step returns are precomputed when transitions are stored.
