This introduces an off-policy staleness bias since the n intermediate actions came from an older policy version -- which is why n is kept small (typically 3-5) rather than pushed toward full-episode returns.

drills.q: Under linear function approximation, do TD and MC converge to the same solution? Why does this matter operationally?
drills.a: No -- MC directly minimizes squared error to observed returns (least-squares fit); TD converges to the fixed point of the projected Bellman equation, a different self-referential solution in general. This matters because 'TD converged' and 'TD converged to the best approximation of V^pi' aren't the same claim once you leave the tabular setting -- a stable-but-wrong value function may be expected TD behavior, not a bug.

drills.q: Explain how GAE in PPO is 'the same idea' as TD(lambda), including what's structurally different about it.
drills.a: GAE applies the identical exponentially-weighted lambda blend over n-step estimates, but to the advantage A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s) built from TD errors, not directly to value-function returns. lambda=0 gives the single-step TD-error-based advantage (low variance, biased); lambda->1 approaches a Monte-Carlo-style full-trajectory advantage (unbiased, high variance) -- same bias-variance knob, different target quantity used to scale a policy gradient.

drills.q: State the exact single-term difference between the SARSA and Q-learning update rules.
drills.a: SARSA's target uses Q(s',a') for the action a' actually sampled from the behavior policy; Q-learning's target uses max_a' Q(s',a'), the best possible next action, regardless of what the behavior policy will actually do next.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why Q-learning learns the cliff-edge path but SARSA learns a safer path on cliff walking.
drills.a: Q-learning's target always uses max_a' Q(s',a'), so cliff-adjacent states are valued as if the agent always acts optimally afterward, ignoring its own exploration risk -- making the risky edge look good. SARSA's target uses the actually-sampled a' from the epsilon-greedy policy, so the epsilon-probability of an accidental fall (and its -100 cost) is baked into the value of cliff-adjacent states, pulling them down and pushing the learned policy away from the edge.

drills.q: A colleague claims Q-learning is strictly better than SARSA because it learns the optimal policy. Push back on this.
drills.a: Q-learning's converged Q-table does represent the optimal deterministic policy's values, but that conflates the eventual answer with the training-time process -- Q-learning's training-time behavior is riskier because it doesn't account for its own exploration. Whether it's 'better' depends on whether the training process itself has real consequences; if so, SARSA is the correct choice.

drills.q: Why does Q-learning's off-policy property enable experience replay while vanilla SARSA's on-policy property makes naive replay invalid?
drills.a: Q-learning's target depends only on (s,a,r,s'), independent of which policy generated the data or would act next -- old transitions remain valid. SARSA's target explicitly needs a', the action the CURRENT behavior policy would take; a replayed transition's recorded a' is stale, from a possibly very different old policy, violating the on-policy assumption the update relies on.

drills.q: Your Q-table has stopped changing (converged) for all observed states, but performance is still poor on rare edge cases. Does this contradict Watkins & Dayan's convergence proof?
drills.a: No -- the proof requires every (s,a) pair to be visited infinitely often. If rare edge-case states are under-visited by the exploration policy, the proof simply doesn't apply to them; a converged-looking table can have arbitrarily wrong values there. This is a coverage problem, not a violation of the theorem.

drills.q: Design the algorithm choice and training setup for a real warehouse robot learning to navigate near a physically hazardous zone.
drills.a: Use SARSA (or Expected SARSA for lower variance) since training-time behavior has real physical consequences and Q-learning would keep executing risky near-hazard trajectories throughout exploration. Also: hand-constrain the action set near the hazard, decay epsilon over training (GLIE schedule), and train substantially in simulation first -- while noting that sim-to-real gap remains a separate risk regardless of the tabular algorithm chosen.

drills.q: An RL agent's reward goes up steadily during training but the real-world task success metric stays flat. Name the phenomenon and the first thing you check.
drills.a: Reward hacking / a mis-specified proxy reward. First check: does the reward function actually correlate with the true objective on a few hand-picked known-good vs known-bad trajectories, and log the true metric alongside raw reward from run 1.

drills.q: Your manager wants to use full RL to optimize a news feed's click-through rate. What's your first diagnostic question, and what do you expect the answer to imply?
drills.a: Does the action taken now (which items shown) change the distribution of contexts/users seen next in a way the objective cares about? For most feed ranking it doesn't, implying this is a contextual bandit, not full RL — simpler, more stable, no real credit-assignment problem.

drills.q: Explain why RL training data violates the i.i.d. assumption that most ML theory relies on.
drills.a: The agent's own policy determines which states/actions are visited, and the policy itself is being updated during training, so the data-generating distribution changes as a direct consequence of learning — it is neither independent (states are causally linked along a trajectory) nor identically distributed over time.

drills.q: A single-frame Atari observation is fed to a policy network and performance is inexplicably noisy specifically on tasks requiring motion judgment. Diagnose.
drills.a: The state isn't Markov — one frame can't recover velocity/direction, so perceptually identical frames with different histories require different correct actions and the network can't distinguish them. Fix: frame-stacking or recurrence to approximate the belief state.

drills.q: Explain the deadly triad and why tabular Q-learning is safe from it despite being off-policy and bootstrapped.
drills.a: Function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy learning together can cause divergence with no convergence guarantee. Tabular Q-learning has no function approximation — updates touch only the single (s,a) entry with no generalization bleeding error into unrelated states — so only two of the three legs are present, which is provably safe.

drills.q: Design the reward for a warehouse robot task-assignment system in one sentence, then name one exploitable gap in it.
drills.a: E.g. -1 per timestep, +100 per completed task, penalty for collisions. Exploitable gap: the robot can repeatedly complete trivial nearby tasks to farm completion bonuses while ignoring a hard, high-value task sitting in the queue, since the reward doesn't distinguish task difficulty or priority.

drills.q: What is a container, mechanically? No product names.
drills.a: An ordinary Linux process created with clone()/unshare() using namespace flags (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time) that limit what it can see, combined with cgroup control-file writes that limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O, process count). No container-specific kernel object exists.

drills.q: Namespaces vs cgroups: what's the actual division of responsibility?
drills.a: Namespaces give visibility isolation (what a process can see: its own PID tree, network stack, mount table). Cgroups give resource isolation (hard limits on CPU, memory, process count, I/O). They are independent kernel subsystems -- a namespaced-only process with no cgroup limits has zero resource ceiling.

drills.q: A container keeps exiting with code 137. Diagnose it.
drills.a: 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL), the OOM killer's signature from exceeding memory.max -- memory is incompressible so there's no throttle equivalent. Check actual memory usage trend against the configured limit rather than assuming an application bug; don't just raise the limit without investigating.

drills.q: Explain why CPU limits throttle but memory limits kill.
drills.a: CPU is compressible -- the kernel just stops scheduling a cgroup's threads for the rest of the cfs_quota_us/cfs_period_us period (default 100ms) and resumes next period. Memory is incompressible -- there's no way to pause already-allocated memory, so crossing memory.max triggers immediate OOM-kill (SIGKILL).

drills.q: Walk through the process chain from docker run to a running container.
drills.a: docker CLI -> dockerd -> containerd (image pull, lifecycle) -> containerd-shim (1 per container, survives containerd restarts, holds stdio) -> runc (OCI runtime: clone()/unshare() + cgroup writes, execs into the container process, then exits) -> kernel. The shim, not runc, remains the container's real parent.

drills.q: What is the security significance of the user namespace specifically?
drills.a: It maps UID 0 inside the container to an unprivileged UID on the host, so even a namespace escape doesn't automatically grant host root. Per runc's own guidance, not mapping host root into the container blocks the most severe class of container escape.

drills.q: Explain OverlayFS's layer model and a real performance surprise it causes.
drills.a: Lowerdir (read-only image layers) + upperdir (per-container writable layer) + workdir. Reads search top-down; writes go to upperdir. Modifying a file that only exists in a lower layer triggers a full copy-up of the entire file into upperdir first, making the first write to a large file measurably slower.

drills.q: Why is a container escape considered more severe than a typical VM escape?
drills.a: Containers share the host kernel with no hypervisor boundary, so an escape lands directly in host kernel context. CVE-2024-21626 (runc fd leak giving host filesystem access) is a concrete example. A VM escape must additionally defeat hardware-enforced hypervisor isolation, a structurally harder bug class.

drills.q: What does pids.max protect against and why is it easy to forget?
drills.a: It caps process/thread count per cgroup, defending against a fork bomb in one container exhausting the host's entire PID table (a host-wide outage, not just that container). It's easy to forget because CPU and memory limits dominate attention while process-count exhaustion is a less common but equally severe host-wide failure mode.

drills.q: cgroups v1 vs v2 -- what changed, and is this settled?
drills.a: v1 used separate per-controller hierarchies with unreliable buffered-I/O accounting. v2 (kernel 4.5, 2016) unifies everything into one hierarchy with more consistent accounting. Most distros default to v2 now, but meaningful production infra (older k8s clusters, some monitoring assuming v1) still runs v1 -- this is a live operational question, not settled history.

drills.q: Design question: a CI system runs arbitrary untrusted pipeline code from external contributors. Would you use plain Docker containers?
drills.a: No, not alone -- shared-kernel isolation means a container-escape CVE compromises the CI host directly, exposing every other tenant. Add a stronger boundary (gVisor's syscall interception, or Kata's per-job lightweight VM) accepting extra overhead as the cost of real isolation for untrusted code; if cost/latency rules that out, at minimum harden with seccomp, no host-root mapping via user namespaces, read-only rootfs, dropped capabilities, and fast patching.

drills.q: What is a warp, and why does divergent branching within one cost real cycles?
drills.a: A fixed group of 32 threads executing the same instruction in lockstep on an SM. Divergent threads cause the hardware to serialize both branch paths, masking off inactive threads for each pass -- a 2-way divergence costs roughly double the cycles of no divergence.

drills.q: What is occupancy, and why does it matter more on a GPU than a similarly-named CPU metric?
drills.a: The ratio of resident warps to an SM's max (64/SM on H100). A stalled warp lets the scheduler switch to another resident warp at ~0 cost since full register state lives permanently in the register file, unlike a CPU thread switch requiring save/restore. Low occupancy leaves the SM idle waiting on memory instead of hiding that latency.

drills.q: Why does nvidia-smi showing 100% GPU utilization not mean the GPU is being used efficiently?
drills.a: It reports whether any kernel is running, not how efficiently it uses compute. A memory-bandwidth-bound kernel (e.g. batch=1 LLM inference) can show 100% utilization while compute units sit substantially idle waiting on HBM -- check achieved occupancy/bandwidth utilization via a real profiler instead.

drills.q: Why is LLM inference at batch size 1 memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound?
drills.a: Generating one token requires loading the entire model's weights from HBM but performs relatively few FLOPs per token relative to that data volume -- low arithmetic intensity. Compute units are capable of far higher throughput than bandwidth can feed them at this ratio, leaving them mostly idle.

drills.q: Explain continuous batching and why it beats static/request-level batching.
drills.a: Static batching waits for every request in a fixed group to finish, wasting slots on requests that finish early. Continuous batching removes finished requests and adds new ones at every decode step, keeping the batch continuously full. vLLM reports up to ~23x throughput with reduced p50 latency; Orca reported up to ~36.9x vs static batching.

drills.q: What does PagedAttention add on top of continuous batching, and what problem does it solve?
drills.a: Continuous batching solves scheduling; PagedAttention solves memory layout -- it manages the KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous pages instead of one large contiguous block, reducing fragmentation so more requests' KV caches fit simultaneously, enabling larger effective batch sizes.

drills.q: Why does kernel launch overhead matter for real workloads if it's only a few microseconds?
drills.a: A workload issuing thousands of small sequential kernel launches pays the ~3-10us fixed overhead per launch repeatedly; if per-kernel compute time is comparable to or smaller than that overhead, the overhead dominates total cost. Fix: kernel fusion to amortize launch cost and avoid redundant HBM round-trips.

drills.q: What is arithmetic intensity, and how do you use it to decide whether a kernel needs compute or memory-bandwidth optimization?
drills.a: FLOPs per byte moved from memory. Compared against the GPU's compute-to-bandwidth ridge point (roofline model): below it, the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound and compute optimization won't help until memory traffic drops; above it, the kernel is compute-bound and reducing memory traffic won't help further.

drills.q: What do Tensor Cores add over general-purpose CUDA cores, and why does that matter for mixed-precision inference?
drills.a: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate hardware (Volta, 2017+) optimized for fp16/bf16/fp8, far more efficient per cycle than composing matmul from scalar ALU instructions -- using them is what actually delivers reduced-precision throughput gains; it isn't automatic and requires the code path (e.g. autocast/AMP) to route through Tensor-Core-eligible kernels.

drills.q: Design: you're serving an LLM with a strict p99 latency SLA (200ms/token) while trying to minimize GPU cost per token. How do you reason about batch size?
drills.a: Larger batches amortize weight-loading cost, lowering cost-per-token, but every request waits for the full batch decode step, raising per-step latency. Measure actual per-step latency at increasing batch sizes on real hardware, pick the largest batch size that still clears the p99 budget with margin, and use continuous (not static) batching to adjust concurrency dynamically within that ceiling.

drills.q: Why is epoll faster than select/poll at high fd counts? Give the actual complexity.
drills.a: select/poll re-scan the whole watched list every call (O(n)/call) regardless of what changed. epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel (rbtree via epoll_ctl) and pushes ready fds onto a separate ready-list via driver callbacks; epoll_wait just drains that list, so cost is O(1) per ready event, not per watched fd. epoll_ctl itself is O(log n).

drills.q: Explain edge-triggered vs level-triggered epoll and the bug that shows up from getting it wrong.
drills.a: LT re-fires while the fd stays ready. ET fires only on the transition to ready, so a handler that doesn't read-loop to EAGAIN never gets told about remaining buffered data again — connections silently stop receiving data with no error or crash.

drills.q: Walk through what happens, syscall by syscall, when io_uring reads a file versus epoll+read().
drills.a: epoll+read needs at least 2 syscalls (epoll_wait to learn readiness, read() for bytes) plus one-time epoll_ctl setup. io_uring separates submission (SQE written to a shared-memory ring, no syscall) from notification (io_uring_enter, one syscall that can submit/reap a whole batch), so N reads can complete in roughly 1 syscall instead of up to 2N.

drills.q: What is SQPOLL and what does it cost?
drills.a: IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL spins up a kernel thread that continuously polls the submission queue so the app never calls io_uring_enter() in steady state -- zero submission syscalls. Cost: that thread pins a full CPU core continuously polling whether or not there's work.

drills.q: Why has Google disabled io_uring by default in ChromeOS, Android, and production servers?
drills.a: io_uring's kernel-side complexity made it disproportionately exploitable -- roughly 60% of Google's kCTF bug bounty submissions target it, ~$1M paid out, including CVE-2024-0582 (use-after-free giving read/write on freed kernel pages). Google chose to disable it by default rather than accept that risk.

drills.q: What does sendfile() actually save, concretely?
drills.a: It moves data file-to-socket entirely inside the kernel (page cache to NIC), avoiding the userspace round trip that read()+write() requires. A measured 2.5GiB transfer took 2,972 syscalls with sendfile vs 131,093 with read+write, about a 44x reduction.

drills.q: When would mmap be the wrong choice for reading a large file?
drills.a: For a single sequential pass -- mmap faults pages in lazily on first touch and loses the kernel's sequential readahead that read() benefits from, so it can generate more minor page faults (~1-10us each) than a straight buffered read() loop. mmap wins for repeated random-access workloads (e.g. LMDB).

drills.q: Design the I/O model for serving 1 million idle-most-of-the-time WebSocket connections from one box.
drills.a: Thread-per-connection is disqualified by stack memory and scheduler thrash at that scale. select/poll are disqualified by O(n)-per-call cost against a million mostly-idle fds. epoll (LT is fine since traffic is bursty/idle) scales with actual activity, not watched count. io_uring is an option only if the workload becomes genuinely I/O-saturated and batching applies.

drills.q: What's the difference between splice() and sendfile()?
drills.a: sendfile() is specifically file-descriptor-to-socket (the narrower, older interface). splice() is the general primitive moving data between a pipe and any other fd (including pipe-to-pipe), which is how socket-to-socket proxying (nginx, HAProxy) stays zero-copy when neither side is a plain file.

drills.q: A colleague proposes replacing your epoll-based service with io_uring purely for the performance win. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the workload is actually syscall-bound (profile with strace -c/perf before assuming batching helps); the deployment's trust boundary (multi-tenant/shared-kernel exposure to io_uring's CVE history vs a trusted single-tenant service); and whether seccomp/container runtime policy already restricts io_uring (containerd's default profile does).

drills.q: Why does select() cap out at FD_SETSIZE (typically 1024), and does poll() fix the underlying scaling problem?
drills.a: FD_SETSIZE is a compile-time bitmap size baked into the ABI; raising it isn't portable and doesn't address the real cost. poll() removes the hard cap with a dynamically sized array but keeps the O(n)-per-call scan, so it still hits the same throughput wall at high fd counts with high churn, just at a higher ceiling.

drills.q: Walk a packet from the wire to your application's recv() call.
drills.a: NIC DMAs the frame into an RX ring buffer and raises a hardIRQ; the handler does minimal work and schedules a softIRQ; NAPI's poll routine drains the ring in batches (default budget 64) instead of interrupting per-packet; the driver builds an skb, passed up via netif_receive_skb() -> ip_rcv() -> tcp_v4_rcv() into the socket receive queue, waking a blocked recv()/epoll_wait().

drills.q: What does interrupt coalescing trade off, and when would you tune it differently?
drills.a: ethtool -c settings (rx-usecs/rx-frames) batch more packets per interrupt, cutting CPU overhead under sustained load at the cost of added per-packet latency/jitter. Throughput-oriented bulk transfer benefits from aggressive coalescing; latency-sensitive workloads want it tuned down.

drills.q: What actually changed between TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3's handshake, in round trips?
drills.a: TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTT before app data. TLS 1.3 sends the client's key share speculatively in the first flight, cutting the full handshake to 1 RTT, plus an optional 0-RTT resumption mode with a replay-protection gap on that first flight.

drills.q: Explain TCP head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 precisely -- what guarantee causes it?
drills.a: TCP guarantees strictly ordered delivery for the entire connection as one byte stream with no concept of independent streams. A lost packet for stream A blocks delivery of all later-arrived bytes, including unrelated stream B's, until retransmission restores connection-wide order.

drills.q: How does QUIC solve TCP head-of-line blocking, mechanically?
drills.a: QUIC implements its own reliability/loss-recovery in userspace over UDP with independent per-stream sequencing. A lost packet on stream A is retransmitted independently; stream B's already-arrived data is delivered immediately, with no connection-wide ordering guarantee to violate.

drills.q: Why do browsers open 6-8 parallel connections per origin under HTTP/1.1, and what did that cost?
drills.a: HTTP/1.1 allows one request in flight per connection in practice; browsers parallelize connections to get real concurrency. Cost: each connection pays its own TCP+TLS handshake, multiplying fixed cost 6-8x, and distorts TCP's per-connection congestion-control fairness.

drills.q: A service's p99 has a consistent extra 150ms not showing in application tracing. What do you check, in order?
drills.a: Use curl -w per-phase timing (DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake, TTFB) to attribute the 150ms to a layer. DNS -> check resolver cache/TTL. TCP/TLS connect -> check connection reuse/pooling. Fast connect but slow TTFB -> the problem is in the application/backend, not this stack.

drills.q: What is GRO and why does it matter for CPU efficiency?
drills.a: Generic Receive Offload coalesces multiple physically-received TCP segments of the same stream into one larger skb before upper-layer processing, reducing how often the more expensive IP/TCP processing runs per byte -- an amortization technique similar in spirit to NAPI's batched interrupt handling.

drills.q: Design: a mobile backend has clients frequently switching WiFi to cellular mid-session. What protocol choice addresses this, and why can't TCP do it?
drills.a: HTTP/3/QUIC. TCP identifies a connection by the 4-tuple (src/dst IP:port), which breaks entirely on an IP change, forcing full reconnect. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID independent of IP, surviving the handoff with live connection state intact -- a property TCP can't retrofit without redefining what a connection is.

drills.q: What's the mechanical difference between HPACK header compression and just gzipping headers?
drills.a: HPACK keeps a stateful shared dynamic table across the connection's lifetime so repeated headers are referenced by a short index rather than resent, exploiting cross-request redundancy. Stateless per-message gzip can't do that, and compressing headers with attacker-influenceable and secret data together enabled CRIME/BREACH-style side-channel attacks, which HPACK's design deliberately avoids.

drills.q: Your team is deciding whether to migrate an internal, same-datacenter microservice mesh from HTTP/2 to HTTP/3. Make the case for and against.
drills.a: For: eliminates TCP-level HOL blocking, and connection migration helps if traffic crosses IP-changing boundaries (rare internally). Against: low-loss, low-latency internal traffic barely triggers the HOL-blocking problem QUIC solves, while QUIC's userspace implementation costs more CPU per byte than TCP's kernel-optimized path -- for a low-loss internal mesh this often favors staying on HTTP/2; reserve HTTP/3 for the internet-facing edge with real loss and mobile variability.

drills.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in every mainstream language?
drills.a: 0.1 and 0.2 are repeating binary fractions (like 1/3 in decimal), so neither is exactly representable in IEEE-754 -- both are rounded before addition, and the sum rounds again, landing on 0.30000000000000004. Not fixable with a wider float type, since the base (2 vs 10) is the issue, not the bit width.

drills.q: What is catastrophic cancellation, and how is it different from ordinary rounding error?
drills.a: Subtracting two nearly-equal floats cancels the leading significant digits, so the result is dominated by whatever rounding error the inputs already carried -- amplifying existing error rather than adding new error, and the amplification depends only on how close the operands are, not their magnitude.

drills.q: What's the tell that a numerical result is suffering from catastrophic cancellation?
drills.a: A suspiciously small, clean-looking (often near-integer) result from a computation that involved much larger input magnitudes -- the signature of most meaningful digits having cancelled away.

drills.q: Explain what Kahan summation fixes and give a concrete case where naive summation visibly fails.
drills.a: Naive summation drops small values added to an already-large running total because those low-order bits fall below representable precision at that magnitude. Example: sum([1e16]+[1.0]*10000+[-1e16]) naively gives ~0.0 instead of the correct 10000.0; Kahan's compensation term recovers the lost bits.

drills.q: Compare bf16 and fp16's bit layouts and explain why bf16 became the ML training default despite fewer mantissa bits.
drills.a: bf16: 1+8+7 bits, same exponent range as fp32 so it rarely overflows at training magnitudes. fp16: 1+5+10 bits, more precision but caps around 65,504, which large-model gradients routinely exceed causing inf/NaN. bf16 trades fp16's frequent catastrophic overflow for milder, tolerable precision loss.

drills.q: What is loss scaling in fp16 training, and why does bf16 usually not need it?
drills.a: Multiply the loss by a large constant before backprop so small gradients land in fp16's representable range, then divide gradients back before the optimizer step; dynamic loss scaling auto-adjusts on detected overflow. bf16 doesn't need this because its wider exponent range already matches fp32's, so typical gradient magnitudes don't overflow it.

drills.q: Why does fp8 training need per-tensor or per-block scaling factors rather than one global loss scale?
drills.a: fp8 (E4M3 or E5M2) has only 2-3 mantissa bits, leaving almost no margin for error -- one global scale tuned for one tensor's distribution is very likely wrong for another tensor at a different magnitude, so each tensor (or block) needs its own scale to stay centered in fp8's narrow useful range.

drills.q: When would you use Decimal/BigDecimal instead of float/double, and what's the real cost?
drills.a: For currency and any exact-decimal-arithmetic-under-addition requirement, since accumulated float rounding error is a real correctness bug there. Cost: decimal arithmetic is meaningfully slower (no native FPU support), so it's reserved for correctness-critical paths, not a blanket default.

drills.q: Your fp16 training run's loss goes to NaN at step 40,000 of a multi-week run. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: First suspect gradient overflow (values exceeding ~65,504 becoming inf, then NaN propagating) -- check if loss scaling is enabled and whether the scale factor/dynamic overflow-detection is working. If loss scaling looks correct and NaN persists, suspect a genuine exploding-gradient training instability requiring gradient clipping/learning-rate fixes, not just a numerics-format change.

drills.q: Explain why comparing floats with == is unreliable, and how to fix a test asserting a floating-point result.
drills.a: Two values reached via different computation paths can carry different accumulated rounding error, so exact bitwise equality isn't reliable. Fix: compare with a tolerance, abs(a-b) < epsilon, ideally scaled relative to the magnitude of the values -- the appropriate epsilon depends on how many operations contributed and the value's magnitude.

drills.q: Design: deploying an LLM for inference, you need to pick numeric formats for weights, activations, and KV cache separately. How do you decide?
drills.a: Weights: least sensitive at inference (fixed post-training), best candidate for aggressive quantization (fp8 or lower). Activations: more variable dynamic range, need per-tensor/per-channel scaling, some layers (softmax, layer norm) may need to stay higher precision. KV cache: major memory cost at long context, strong quantization target for throughput, but errors compound across the whole remaining generation so needs empirical validation, especially at long context lengths.

drills.q: What Richardson Maturity level does correct HTTP verb and status code usage correspond to?
drills.a: Level 2.

drills.q: Which RFC currently defines the Problem Details error contract, and which RFC did it supersede?
drills.a: RFC 9457, superseding RFC 7807.

drills.q: What HTTP header enables SSE's built-in reconnection to resume a stream rather than replay it from scratch?
drills.a: Last-Event-ID.

drills.q: A 'load more' feature gets measurably slower every week as a customer's order history grows. Diagnose and name the fix.
drills.a: Offset-based pagination -- the database scans and discards a growing number of rows on every deep page as the dataset grows. Fix: migrate to cursor-based pagination on an indexed sort column, which stays roughly constant-time regardless of depth into the dataset.

drills.q: A public API introduces v2 via a header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) at the same URL as v1, and some clients intermittently receive v1 responses when requesting v2. Diagnose.
drills.a: The CDN or intermediate cache is keying purely on URL, not on the version header, because Vary: Accept (or equivalent) isn't correctly configured at every layer in the caching chain -- a cached v1 response gets served to a v2 request hitting the identical URL. URL-path versioning avoids this bug class entirely by construction.

drills.q: A team wants to build a live order-tracking feature and defaults to WebSocket 'to be safe for real-time.' Is this justified? What should they check first?
drills.a: Not necessarily justified -- check whether the feature is genuinely bidirectional. Order status push (server to client only) is squarely SSE's use case: built-in reconnection, CDN-transparent, less complexity. WebSocket is justified only if the client genuinely needs to push data back through the same low-latency channel, which most 'real-time' features don't actually require.

drills.q: Why do most production REST APIs deliberately stop at Richardson Maturity Level 2 rather than pursuing Level 3 (HATEOAS)?
drills.a: Level 3's benefit -- clients dynamically discovering available actions via response links instead of hardcoding URLs -- rarely pays off for the typical client population of a documented API, since engineers writing integration code are going to hardcode URL patterns regardless of whether a link is offered. The real, ongoing cost of correctly computing state-and-permission-aware links for every response usually isn't justified.

drills.q: Design the pagination and error-handling approach for a GraphQL layer aggregating three internal gRPC services for both a mobile and web client, and explain what happens if one of the three services degrades.
drills.a: Pagination: Relay-style cursor connections (edges/node/cursor/pageInfo), translating to cursor-based pagination in the underlying gRPC services for the same DB-performance reasons. Errors: map gRPC status/messages into GraphQL's errors array with structured extensions, giving both clients one consistent shape regardless of which internal service failed. On a degraded service: GraphQL returns a PARTIAL response -- successfully-resolved fields from healthy services plus a structured error entry for the degraded service's specific fields, rather than failing the whole query, unlike a typical REST aggregation endpoint which more commonly fails atomically.

drills.q: A partner integration reports both slow 'load more' performance and intermittent stale-data issues on a public API using offset pagination and header-based versioning. Diagnose both, and explain which fix requires partner-side changes and which doesn't.
drills.a: Slow load-more: offset-pagination performance cliff, worsening as the partner's dataset grows -- migrate to cursor pagination, which can be introduced as an ADDITIVE, backward-compatible change alongside the existing offset parameters, not requiring immediate partner-side changes. Stale data: likely a Vary-header misconfiguration in the caching chain for header-based versioning, serving a cached response from the wrong version -- fixable entirely server-side by correcting the Vary configuration, again with no client-side change required.

drills.q: Why is tRPC the wrong choice for a public API with external partner consumers, even though it eliminates contract-drift bugs for internal use?
drills.a: tRPC's value proposition depends on both ends sharing TypeScript types directly (same monorepo or a shared type-generation pipeline) -- an external partner's codebase, likely in a different language or an entirely separate repo, can't consume that shared-type mechanism at all. REST (or GraphQL for diverse-shape needs) remains correct for any API surface with consumers outside your own TypeScript codebase.

drills.q: Where do idempotency keys belong architecturally -- API design or the resilience/retry layer -- and why does that classification matter for how you design an endpoint?
drills.a: Both, in different roles: the endpoint's documented contract (accepting an Idempotency-Key header, defining behavior on a repeated key) is an API DESIGN concern, since it's client-visible and must be documented; the actual mechanism preventing double-processing (a dedup store, an atomic INSERT ON CONFLICT) is resilience-layer implementation (T21-resilience-catalogue). Designing an endpoint without documenting idempotency-key behavior leaves clients unable to safely retry costly mutations like payments -- a genuine API design gap, not just a missing retry policy.

drills.q: What is the cited RPS figure for Go (Fiber/Gin-class) vs FastAPI on a JSON CRUD benchmark?
drills.a: Go ~142,000 RPS vs FastAPI ~38,000 RPS.

drills.q: Does making a CPU-bound Python handler async fix its throughput ceiling? Why or why not.
drills.a: No. Async improves I/O concurrency (cooperative waiting), not CPU parallelism -- the GIL still serializes actual bytecode execution regardless of async structure.

drills.q: What migration pattern should a justified Go rewrite follow: big-bang full rewrite, or something else?
drills.a: Strangler-fig: one proven-bottlenecked endpoint or service at a time, shadowed then gradually cut over, never a full-backend big-bang rewrite.

drills.q: A team proposes a Go rewrite citing 'Python is slow' with no profiling data. What's the correct first response, and why?
drills.a: Ask what profiling evidence shows the framework itself, not the database, a blocking call, or missing caching, is the bottleneck. Most 'FastAPI is slow' complaints trace back to those non-framework causes, which are fixable in Python for a fraction of a rewrite's cost -- proposing a rewrite without that evidence risks spending weeks on a guess.

drills.q: A Go rewrite of a 'slow' endpoint shows disappointing improvement over the Python version. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The original bottleneck was never the framework -- likely a slow database query, N+1 queries, or a missing index -- so the same problem exists identically in the Go version against the same schema. The rewrite didn't address the actual cause.

drills.q: Why does a synthetic load-test benchmark showing Go 3.7x faster than FastAPI potentially overstate the real-world production improvement?
drills.a: A synthetic CRUD benchmark isolates pure framework overhead with no real database or downstream calls -- exactly the condition where language choice is the entire cost. Most real production requests are dominated by I/O (database round trips, downstream API latency) that's identical in both languages, so the framework-overhead gap contributes a much smaller fraction of real end-to-end latency.

drills.q: What specific thing breaks for existing API clients if a Go rewrite changes FastAPI's validation error response shape, even if the underlying validation logic is functionally equivalent?
drills.a: Any client parsing the structured error body (FastAPI's {"detail":[{"loc","msg","type"}]} shape) to map errors back to specific form fields breaks silently, since it depends on the exact wire format, not just the logical behavior of rejecting invalid input.

drills.q: Design the decision process for a CPU-bound Python endpoint that's confirmed (via profiling) to be genuinely compute-limited, not I/O-bound. What are the escalating options before a full service rewrite?
drills.a: 1) Algorithmic/implementation optimization of the hot path itself, often overlooked. 2) Horizontal scaling via more uvicorn worker processes, if the per-process memory duplication cost is acceptable, possibly combined with externalizing shared state to Redis to reduce duplication. 3) Offloading just the CPU-bound component to Go/Rust, called from the rest of the Python service. 4) Only if the whole service's profile justifies it, a full service rewrite.

drills.q: A team completes one successful, measured Go migration and leadership wants to rewrite the entire backend on that basis. What's the correct response and why?
drills.a: One measured success validates that specific migration's bottleneck diagnosis, not a blanket 'Go is better, rewrite everything' conclusion. Apply the same profile-first discipline independently to each additional candidate service -- most services proposed next may turn out to be database-bound or cache-missing rather than framework-bound, exactly the pattern cited in real postmortems of rewrites that didn't pay back.

drills.q: Design the shadow-traffic phase of a strangler-fig migration to catch a subtle behavioral divergence before full cutover. What happens when a divergence is found?
drills.a: Route a copy of real production traffic to the new Go service in parallel with the Python service actually serving the response; programmatically diff status codes, response bodies (including error shapes), and latency, logging divergences without ever exposing the shadow response to real users, across enough volume and time to surface rare edge cases. On finding a divergence: a cosmetic difference can be fixed and migration continued; a semantic difference (wrong data, an unfaithfully-ported validation rule) should pause cutover for that path until fixed and re-verified.

drills.q: How large is a goroutine's starting stack, roughly, and does it grow?
drills.a: ~2KB, dynamically grown (and shrunk) by the runtime as needed, versus an OS thread's fixed 1-8MB reserved stack.

drills.q: True or false: sending on a closed channel returns the zero value silently.
drills.a: False -- sending on a closed channel panics. Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately with ok==false.

drills.q: Which Go release made GOMAXPROCS container-aware (cgroup-limit-based) by default?
A service's goroutine count and memory climb steadily under load with no crash or error log. What's the diagnosis process?
drills.a: Suspect a goroutine leak -- pull pprof's goroutine profile (/debug/pprof/goroutine) and look for a large number of goroutines sharing an identical blocked stack trace (same channel receive or lock), which is the diagnostic signature distinguishing a leak from a genuinely busy server doing varied work.

drills.q: Explain why `time.After(d)` called inside a `select` inside a `for` loop is a known anti-pattern.
drills.a: time.After allocates a new *time.Timer internally on every call, and that timer isn't eligible for GC until it actually fires. Calling it every loop iteration accumulates live-but-never-fired timers, producing steady memory and GC pressure in a hot loop. Fix: create one time.NewTimer outside the loop and Reset() it.

drills.q: Why is `defer cancel()` still required immediately after `context.WithTimeout()` even when you fully expect the deadline to fire on its own?
drills.a: Without calling cancel(), the context package's internal timer and cancellation-watching goroutine stay alive until the PARENT context itself ends, not until the current function returns -- a real, cumulative resource leak on the common path. cancel() is cheap and idempotent, so deferring it unconditionally is correct regardless of which path actually ends the context.

drills.q: State the Go memory model's happens-before guarantee for a mutex, and explain what it lets you safely assume.
drills.a: A sync.Mutex/RWMutex unlock happens-before a subsequent lock acquisition of the same mutex -- so any memory writes made while holding the lock are guaranteed visible to the next goroutine that successfully acquires it, without additional synchronization needed.

drills.q: Design a worker pool with N workers reading from a shared input channel and writing to a results channel, correctly handling context cancellation. What's the correct channel-closing sequence, and what breaks if it's wrong?
drills.a: The single producer goroutine feeding input closes the input channel (never a worker, to avoid a double-close panic); each worker selects on a channel receive alongside ctx.Done() to exit cleanly on cancellation; a separate goroutine calls wg.Wait() on all workers before closing the results channel. Closing results before all workers finish sending causes a 'send on closed channel' panic that manifests intermittently under real concurrent timing -- often passing in quick manual tests and failing under load.

drills.q: A `go test -race` suite passes cleanly in CI, but a data race ships to production anyway. Is this a contradiction? Explain.
drills.a: No contradiction -- the race detector only reports races that actually occur during the instrumented test run; it proves nothing about code paths the test suite never exercised or rare goroutine interleavings the run didn't hit. A clean -race run is necessary evidence, not sufficient proof of the absence of races across the whole codebase.

drills.q: A hot path shows unexpectedly high time in runtime.mallocgc in a pprof CPU profile. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: Suspect escape analysis forcing a heap allocation the developer expected to be stack-local -- run `go build -gcflags="-m"` to see the compiler's actual per-variable escape decisions on that function. Common causes: a value returned by pointer, stored in a longer-lived structure, or passed through an interface method boundary the compiler can't statically resolve. Fix by restructuring to keep the value's lifetime provably local, if the allocation is genuinely avoidable.

drills.q: Write a generic constraint that accepts int, int32, int64, float32, float64, AND any named type built on one of those underlying types. What's the key syntax detail?
drills.a: type Number interface { ~int | ~int32 | ~int64 | ~float32 | ~float64 } -- the tilde (~) before each type is essential; without it, the constraint would only match the exact predeclared types and reject a named type like `type Meters int` even though its underlying type is int.

drills.q: Which HTTP header carries a gRPC client's deadline to the server?
drills.a: grpc-timeout, part of the HTTP/2 metadata for the call.

drills.q: Name the four gRPC RPC shapes.
drills.a: Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.

drills.q: Which HNSW parameter is the only one that can be tuned live, per query, without rebuilding the index?
drills.a: efSearch (query-time search breadth).

drills.q: A team deploys a gRPC service behind a Kubernetes Service with 5 replicas but observes one pod handling 90% of traffic. Diagnose.
drills.a: gRPC multiplexes many RPCs over a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection; if the Service uses plain L4 (connection-level) load balancing, it routes once at connection establishment and pins ALL subsequent RPCs on that connection to the same pod. Fix: client-side round_robin load balancing resolving multiple addresses, or an L7-aware proxy like Envoy balancing individual streams.

drills.q: A worker pool is implemented as `for _, item := range items { go process(item) }` with no cap. Under a traffic spike, what breaks, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Goroutine count and any downstream connections/resources those goroutines hold grow without limit, exhausting this service's memory and potentially the downstream's capacity simultaneously -- there's no backpressure. Fix: a fixed-size pool of workers reading from a bounded channel, which blocks the producer (real backpressure) once the pool is saturated.

drills.q: Explain why raising efSearch after a vector index re-index sometimes fails to restore recall to its prior level.
drills.a: efSearch only widens the query-time candidate search -- it cannot compensate for a structurally lower-quality graph if efConstruction was reduced at build time, since the graph's actual connections (chosen once, during build, based on efConstruction's candidate breadth) are already fixed. Check and fix efConstruction, not just efSearch.

drills.q: Design the choice: efSearch value for a live, p99-latency-sensitive user search endpoint vs a background batch re-ranking job with no hard latency constraint.
drills.a: Live endpoint: lower efSearch tuned to hit the latency SLA, accepting somewhat lower recall as the tradeoff. Batch job: much higher efSearch to maximize recall, since total throughput/wall-clock time matters more than any single query's latency -- or better, expose efSearch as a client-controllable request parameter so callers set their own tradeoff instead of the service hardcoding two fixed profiles.

drills.q: A client reports frequent DeadlineExceeded errors against a gRPC server whose own p99 latency looks fine in isolation. Walk through the diagnosis in order.
drills.a: First check whether the client's own configured deadline is realistic given the server's actual p99 (a 200ms client timeout against a 300ms server p99 fails correctly, nothing wrong server-side). Second, check whether the deadline budget is being correctly reduced at each hop in a multi-service chain rather than reused unshrunk. Third, only after ruling those out, investigate genuine server-side tail latency causes: a slow dependency, GC pauses, or connection-pinning load-balancing (uneven pod traffic) concentrating load on one instance.

drills.q: When would you justify building a custom Go microservice wrapping a native HNSW library instead of using a managed vector database, and what do you give up by doing so?
drills.a: Justified when profiling proves the managed DB's network hop and query-abstraction overhead is the actual bottleneck against a genuinely tight latency budget, or per-traffic-class efSearch control is needed that the managed API doesn't expose. You give up persistence/durability, replication, native filtered-search support, and operational tooling (backups, monitoring, scaling) the managed option provides out of the box -- all of which the custom service must now build and operate itself.

drills.q: Why does errgroup's fail-fast, first-error-wins cancellation model sometimes NOT fit a coordination need, and what would you reach for instead?
drills.a: errgroup cancels all sibling goroutines the moment any one returns an error, which is wrong when you need to collect ALL errors from a batch (e.g. reporting every failed item in a bulk operation) or want remaining independent work to continue despite one failure. In that case, hand-roll coordination with a WaitGroup and a channel/slice collecting every error instead of relying on errgroup's shared-cancellation-on-first-error behavior.

drills.q: Name the two operations that cause a virtual thread to pin its carrier, and which JDK version fixed one of them.
drills.a: synchronized blocks/methods (fixed in JDK 24, JEP 491) and native/JNI calls (still pins in JDK 25).

drills.q: True or false: adding a fourth implementor to a sealed interface silently compiles as long as existing switches have a default branch.
drills.a: True in effect, but that defeats the point -- an exhaustive switch with no default would instead fail to compile, forcing every dispatch site to be updated. A default branch reopens the hole sealing was meant to close.

drills.q: Can a record have a mutable field? Why or why not.
drills.a: No. Every component of a record is implicitly private final by design -- records are value types, not general-purpose classes.

drills.q: A service migrates to virtual threads and throughput plateaus below expectation with carrier threads reported idle elsewhere. What's the first thing to check, and what JDK-version-specific detail matters?
drills.a: Check for synchronized blocks pinning virtual threads to carriers -- if pre-JDK 24, this is the known synchronized-block pinning issue (fixed by JEP 491 in JDK 24); if JDK 24+, check for native/JNI calls instead, which still pin.

drills.q: Explain why ThreadLocal is a worse fit than ScopedValue at virtual-thread scale, specifically.
drills.a: Millions of short-lived virtual threads each touching ThreadLocal.set() means millions of per-thread allocations, plus leak risk if remove() in finally is forgotten (state bleeds into a reused pooled thread). ScopedValue is bound only for a scope's duration and auto-unbinds on exit -- no leak by construction, and avoids the per-thread-instance allocation pattern.

drills.q: Why does moving a CPU-bound image-processing workload from a fixed platform-thread pool to virtual-thread-per-task NOT improve throughput?
drills.a: Virtual threads fix I/O-bound thread scalability by unmounting from the carrier while blocked. A CPU-bound task never blocks -- it occupies its carrier for its full duration exactly like a platform thread would, so more virtual threads just means more contention for the same core count, with added scheduling overhead.

drills.q: Is Structured Concurrency (JEP 505) safe to treat as a stable, finalized API in a Java 25 interview answer?
drills.a: No -- it is still in preview (sixth preview round in JDK 25). Claiming it's finalized is a specific, checkable mistake; the correct answer names the preview status.

drills.q: Design question: an I/O-heavy service needs to pick between virtual threads with blocking clients and full Reactor/Netty. What's the default, and when do you deviate?
drills.a: Default to virtual threads with blocking-style clients for most I/O-bound services -- plain sequential code, normal stack traces, easy onboarding. Deviate to full reactive only when measured requirements sit at the genuine top throughput tier, where cited 2025-2026 benchmarks still show reactive Netty ahead by roughly 25-30% over virtual-thread stacks on some workloads.

drills.q: A team ships a fixed platform-thread pool of 200 threads for downstream calls taking 100ms each. What's the theoretical max throughput, and why is that a hard ceiling regardless of downstream speed?
drills.a: 200 concurrent / 0.1s = 2,000 req/s. It's a hard ceiling because each in-flight call permanently occupies one pooled thread until it returns; no thread means no new call can start, independent of how fast the downstream could actually respond if given more concurrency.

drills.q: Explain the bug class Structured Concurrency fixes that manual ExecutorService + Future.get() does not prevent.
drills.a: With manual Futures, there's no enforced relationship between a parent task and the children it spawned -- if the parent times out or stops caring, nothing automatically cancels still-running children, so they keep consuming resources for a result that will never be used. StructuredTaskScope ties subtask lifetime to the enclosing scope, so exiting it (normally, by exception, or by joiner fail-fast) cancels any subtasks still running.

drills.q: A record-based DTO deserializes via Jackson but every field silently comes back as a default value. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: The Jackson version lacks native record support for the canonical constructor (needs jackson-module-parameter-names or an explicit @JsonCreator on older versions, better handled natively in 2.15+). Confirm the Jackson version, or annotate the canonical constructor explicitly.

drills.q: What is the default value of -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, and is it a guarantee?
drills.a: 200ms, and it's a soft target G1 tries to hit by sizing young-gen and mixed-GC work -- not a hard guarantee.

drills.q: What size threshold makes an object 'humongous' in G1?
drills.a: Larger than 50% of the region size.

drills.q: Since which JDK version has G1 been the default collector?
drills.a: Java 9.

drills.q: A team doubles -Xmx to 'fix' GC pauses and pauses get worse, not better. Explain why.
drills.a: A bigger heap means more live data to scan and compact during a collection, which can lengthen individual pause duration even while reducing how often collections happen. Whether more heap helps depends on whether the problem is frequency-driven or scan-cost-driven -- check the GC log before resizing.

drills.q: Explain the mechanism that lets ZGC relocate objects concurrently without stopping the application to fix up references.
drills.a: Colored pointers encode object state (marked, remapped) in unused high bits of the 64-bit pointer. Every reference read goes through a load barrier that checks those bits and transparently redirects/fixes a stale reference on the spot if the object moved -- references self-heal lazily on next access instead of requiring a stop-the-world fixup pass.

drills.q: A service switches from G1 to ZGC for a nightly batch ETL job with no latency SLO, and total job time gets worse. Diagnose.
drills.a: ZGC's structural 15-30% memory / 5-10% CPU overhead (the cost of concurrent relocation) was paid for a throughput-bound workload with no pause-time requirement to benefit from -- the switch should be reverted to G1, since ZGC's value proposition (low pause time) was never relevant here.

drills.q: What specific failure mode ended CMS's use in production, and name its G1 analog.
drills.a: CMS never compacted concurrently, so old-gen fragmentation eventually left no contiguous space for a large allocation, forcing a full single-threaded stop-the-world compaction ('concurrent mode failure'). G1's analog is falling back to a Full GC when allocation outpaces concurrent marking -- same underlying class of failure: a concurrent collector that falls behind degrades to a stop-the-world pause.

drills.q: A hot method is repeatedly compiled, discarded, and recompiled according to JFR's jdk.Deoptimization events. What's the likely root cause and the code-level fix?
drills.a: C2 compiled the method assuming a call site was monomorphic (based on C1's profiling data); a second concrete implementation later showed up, invalidating the specialized inlined code, forcing deoptimization back to the interpreter and eventual recompilation with corrected polymorphic data -- if this repeats, the call site is thrashing. Fix: reduce polymorphism at that call site if possible (bound an unbounded strategy/plugin pattern, avoid heavy reflection-based dispatch there).

drills.q: Design the diagnostic sequence for 'the service is slow' before touching any JVM flag.
drills.a: Capture a GC log (-Xlog:gc*) and a JFR recording (or attach one live) first. Read the GC log triage: frequent short young GCs are usually fine; climbing frequency and pause length together signals working-set growth; Pause Full (Allocation Failure) signals the G1 fallback failure mode; a shrinking before->after reclaim gap over time signals a leak. Only after the log/JFR evidence points to a specific mechanism (heap sizing, humongous objects, JIT deopt, an actual leak) do you touch a flag -- guessing at flags without log evidence risks subtle regressions.

drills.q: Explain why Generational ZGC displaced non-generational ZGC entirely (JEP 490) rather than the two modes coexisting.
drills.a: Non-generational ZGC treated every object uniformly with no cheap young-gen fast path, costing real throughput on allocation-heavy workloads since short-lived objects paid the same barrier/relocation overhead as long-lived ones. Generational ZGC (default since JDK 23, JEP 474) cut CPU overhead roughly 30-40% for allocation-heavy workloads and won essentially every benchmark, so non-generational mode was removed to reduce long-term maintenance burden for a mode nobody had a reason to prefer.

drills.q: A JMH-less benchmark shows a code change is 3x faster locally, but production load tests show no measurable difference. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The local benchmark measured JIT warm-up cost (interpreter and C1 tiers) rather than steady-state C2-optimized throughput, since it had no explicit warm-up phase discarded before measurement. Rerun with JMH's @Warmup iterations, or discard the first several seconds/minutes of a load test before computing throughput/latency.

drills.q: What percentage of organizations are actively consolidating microservices back into larger units, per the CNCF 2025 report?
True or false: a modular monolith is defined mainly by having a clean folder structure separating concerns.
drills.a: False -- the defining property is ENFORCED, checkable boundaries where a violation is a build/CI failure, not a folder-structure convention that can be silently violated.

drills.q: Name Segment's real-world outcome from over-splitting into 140+ microservices.
drills.a: A shared library change required deploying all 140+ services together, defeating independent deployability -- they consolidated back into a single application.

drills.q: A team wants to split a module into a microservice because 'it feels more scalable.' Is this one of the four defensible justifications? What's missing from the argument?
drills.a: No. It's missing a concrete, evidence-based reason: independent deployment cadence (a real team-blocking conflict), independent scaling profile (a measured, different resource need), fault isolation (a genuinely different, isolatable failure mode), or forced polyglot (a proven language/runtime need). A vague sense that something 'should scale better' is premature optimization without one of these backing it.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why debugging a single user request takes longer in microservices than in a monolith.
drills.a: A monolith's request execution is one call stack in one process, debuggable via a stack trace or log grep. Microservices scatter the same request's execution across multiple processes connected by network calls, requiring distributed tracing with correctly-propagated trace context at every hop -- any hop that fails to propagate context leaves a gap in the trace exactly where the bug likely is.

drills.q: Correctly summarize Amazon Prime Video's 2023 case study, and name the common overstatement of it.
drills.a: One specific monitoring tool was moved from a serverless/microservices design to a monolith, cutting infrastructure cost 90%. Common overstatement: treating this as 'Amazon abandoned microservices for the entire Prime Video platform' -- it was scoped to one tool, starting from a serverless architecture, not a general microservices claim across the platform.

drills.q: Is 'monorepo' synonymous with 'monolith,' and 'polyrepo' synonymous with 'microservices'? Give real counter-examples.
drills.a: No, they're orthogonal decisions. Shopify runs a monorepo housing a modular monolith. Amazon runs polyrepo with real microservices. Google runs a monorepo housing many independently-deployed services -- all valid, real combinations depending on whether cross-cutting refactor ease or per-team deployment autonomy matters more.

drills.q: A team's monolith deploy pipeline takes 45 minutes and Team A is repeatedly blocked by Team B's unrelated changes going through the same release. Is a full microservices decomposition the right response? What's the more targeted alternative?
drills.a: This is a real instance of justification #1 (independent deployment cadence), so SOME split is directionally justified -- but the right move is extracting the specific component(s) causing the actual blocking, not a wholesale fine-grained decomposition. A narrower fix (better feature flagging, decoupling the deploy pipeline for unrelated modules within the same codebase) might resolve the pain without paying the full distributed-systems cost.

drills.q: Design the extraction path for pulling a genuinely justified microservice out of a modular monolith. What's the most common mistake to avoid?
drills.a: 1) Confirm the module already has enforced in-process boundaries -- extracting an unenforced boundary just moves it across a network, making it worse. 2) Resolve data ownership BEFORE extraction, converting any cross-module data access to an API call first. 3) Extract behind a stable interface matching how it was called in-process. 4) Shadow-then-gradual-cutover, monitoring for new latency/partial-failure modes. Most common mistake: extracting the code before resolving data ownership, leaving the new 'service' still reading/writing the monolith's shared database directly -- recreating coupling through the schema while paying full network/deployment overhead.

drills.q: A 30-service microservices fleet is genuinely painful to operate. Should the team consolidate everything back to one monolith? How would you decide which services to consolidate?
drills.a: Not a blanket full consolidation -- diagnose empirically which services are actually causing pain. Check deployment logs for services frequently deployed together (tight coupling, Segment-style consolidation candidates) and check whether each service has ever actually exercised independent scaling or had an isolated failure that mattered (weak justification if never) versus services with a documented instance of either (stronger case to keep separate). Consolidate the evidence-backed coupled/painful subset, not the whole fleet reflexively.

drills.q: What is libuv's default thread pool size?
Which queue has strictly higher priority: process.nextTick's queue, or the V8 Promise microtask queue?
drills.a: process.nextTick's queue -- it drains completely before the V8 microtask queue is touched.

drills.q: Name the stream helper that handles backpressure and error propagation automatically, preferred over hand-wiring 'data'/'drain' events.
drills.a: stream.pipeline() (from node:stream/promises), or .pipe().

drills.q: A Node service's throughput collapses under concurrent load with CPU pegged near 100% on a single core. Diagnose it, and name the fix.
drills.a: A synchronous, CPU-heavy operation is blocking the single event-loop thread, stalling every other concurrent request on the process. Fix: offload the work to a worker_thread (a real OS thread with message-passing), not the libuv thread pool, which is meant for I/O-adjacent blocking calls, not arbitrary CPU-bound compute.

drills.q: A login endpoint hashing passwords via bcrypt/scrypt bottlenecks at exactly 4 concurrent operations regardless of CPU core count. Explain why.
drills.a: crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt-style hashing runs on libuv's thread pool, which defaults to size 4 -- the 5th and later concurrent hash operation queues behind the first 4 completing, a fixed constraint unrelated to CPU cores or I/O bandwidth. Fix: raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (set before any pool-using module loads) or move to appropriately-sized worker_threads.

drills.q: Explain precisely why Node's backpressure protocol is called 'cooperative' rather than enforced, with the mechanism.
drills.a: writable.write(chunk) returns false once the internal buffer exceeds highWaterMark, which is a SIGNAL requesting the producer pause -- but nothing in the runtime stops the producer from ignoring it and calling write() again anyway. Node still accepts and buffers the data, succeeding right up until memory pressure becomes an incident -- the exact class of bug behind the cited Walmart production memory leak, which traced to a missing backpressure check in Node core's own C++.

drills.q: Why does a backpressure bug in a hand-rolled stream pipeline often pass testing but fail only under sustained production load?
drills.a: At low traffic volume, the producer's write rate never actually exceeds what the consumer can drain, so the missing backpressure check is never exercised -- the bug is latent until sustained high-throughput traffic exposes the gap between producer and consumer speed, making it a notoriously hard class of bug to catch in normal testing.

drills.q: Design the decision between NestJS-with-Fastify-adapter and plain Fastify for a new service. What's the actual tradeoff axis?
drills.a: Team size and structural need, not raw performance alone (though performance differs too). NestJS-with-Fastify-adapter: larger teams benefiting from enforced DI/decorator/module structure while recovering most of Express's overhead. Plain Fastify: smaller teams, performance-critical services where NestJS's structural ceremony isn't worth even its reduced overhead, or teams wanting schema-first, compiled-ahead JSON Schema validation as a first-class feature.

drills.q: A candidate claims 'Node can't handle concurrent requests well because it's single-threaded.' Correct this claim precisely.
drills.a: Node's single JavaScript thread is precisely what makes it GOOD at I/O-bound concurrency -- libuv's event loop lets one thread juggle thousands of concurrent I/O-waiting connections cheaply, avoiding OS thread-per-connection memory/context-switch cost. The single thread is a real constraint specifically for CPU-bound PARALLELISM (genuinely simultaneous computation) within one process, a different axis entirely from I/O concurrency -- addressed by worker_threads, not evidence Node handles concurrent requests poorly in general.

drills.q: A team building a backend-for-frontend service is deciding between Node/TypeScript and Go. What decision process should they follow, and what's the underrated argument for Node specifically?
drills.a: Apply profiling-first discipline analogous to T11-fastapi-to-go: if the service is predominantly I/O-bound (aggregating downstream API calls, typical BFF work), Node is a strong default, especially with a frontend team that benefits from shared TypeScript types across the frontend/backend boundary -- a real, underrated tooling-continuity argument. Reach for Go only once a specific, profiled CPU-bound bottleneck or true multi-core parallelism need justifies it, not by assuming Node's single-thread model is automatically insufficient.

drills.q: What is Quarkus's build-time CDI-Lite DI container called?
drills.a: ArC.

drills.q: What annotation routes a Quarkus REST method to a worker thread instead of the default Vert.x event loop?
drills.a: @Blocking.

drills.q: Name the Mutiny type for a reactive stream of zero-to-many items, and its Reactor equivalent.
drills.a: Multi<T>, equivalent to Reactor's Flux.

drills.q: A native-image build fails at build time with a reflection-related ClassNotFoundException-style error. What's the mechanism, and what are the two fix options in order of preference?
drills.a: GraalVM's closed-world static reachability analysis couldn't prove a dynamically-loaded class/method reachable from the app's entry points, so it wasn't included in the compiled binary. Fix: prefer a Quarkus extension that already ships native-image metadata for that library; failing that, add explicit reflect-config.json entries.

drills.q: A team's Quarkus service passes all tests in `quarkus:dev` but throws a reflection error only when deployed as a native image on a rarely-hit code path. Explain why dev mode didn't catch it.
drills.a: quarkus:dev runs on the full JVM, where any reflective call works normally. Native image applies closed-world static reachability analysis at build time, which can fail to prove a reflective call site reachable -- a failure mode that literally does not exist in JVM/dev mode, so testing only there gives false confidence for native deployment.

drills.q: Why might a long-running, high-steady-throughput Quarkus service perform worse in native mode than in JVM mode, despite native's dramatically faster startup?
drills.a: Native image is AOT-compiled with every optimization decision fixed at build time -- no adaptation to actual live traffic. The JVM's JIT (C2) profiles real production traffic and progressively specializes hot paths over the process's lifetime, which can out-optimize AOT's build-time-only guesses at true steady state. Native's win is startup latency and idle memory, not necessarily peak sustained throughput.

drills.q: Design the framework choice for two new services: (a) an AWS Lambda function, (b) a long-running Kubernetes Deployment with steady, predictable traffic and no scale-to-zero requirement. Justify each.
drills.a: (a) Quarkus compiled to native image -- cold-start latency is directly billed and user-visible, and native's tens-of-milliseconds startup is decisive over a JVM cold start in the low seconds. (b) Spring Boot on the JVM is more defensible -- the process runs for hours/days between restarts so startup time amortizes to irrelevance, the JIT has time to pay off at steady state, and Spring's ecosystem depth reduces integration risk.

drills.q: A dependency has no documented GraalVM native-image support. List the options in order of preference before concluding the service can't go native.
drills.a: 1) Check for a Quarkus extension wrapping the library with native-image metadata already included. 2) Check the community graalvm-reachability-metadata project for an entry. 3) Hand-write reflect-config.json/resource-config entries by iteratively testing the native build. 4) Run that specific service in JVM mode instead -- native image is one feature of Quarkus, not mandatory for using the framework.

drills.q: What's the real design cost of choosing Panache's active-record style (PanacheEntity) over its repository style (PanacheRepository<T>)?
drills.a: Active-record couples the domain entity directly to persistence concerns (methods live on the @Entity class itself), making it harder to test business logic in true isolation from Hibernate and blurring separation of concerns -- more concise, but a real tradeoff, not a free win, versus the repository style's cleaner separation (closer to Spring Data's convention).

drills.q: Beyond faster startup, what's the deeper argument for ArC's build-time DI resolution over Spring's runtime resolution?
drills.a: Build-time resolution surfaces wiring errors (missing bean, ambiguous injection point) at build time / in CI rather than only at application startup in a deployed environment, or worse, only when a specific code path is first exercised in production -- shifting a class of bugs earlier in the pipeline. Spring's ApplicationContext also fails fast, but at runtime startup of that specific deployment, not at build time.

drills.q: A Quarkus bean's configuration value needs to come from a runtime environment variable unknown at build time. Does ArC's build-time DI model prevent this? Explain what's actually fixed at build time versus what can still vary at runtime.
drills.a: No, it doesn't prevent it. ArC fixes the EXISTENCE and wiring shape of beans at build time (which implementations get injected where), but individual configuration VALUES flowing into that fixed structure still resolve at runtime via Quarkus's config system (@ConfigProperty, MicroProfile Config) -- reading environment variables, config maps, or secrets normally. What ArC can't easily do is make a bean's very EXISTENCE conditional on a runtime-only value, unlike Spring's @ConditionalOnProperty, since the graph shape must be known before the runtime environment is.

drills.q: What Next.js function marks a server-side function as callable directly from a Client Component?
drills.a: "use server" (the Server Action directive).

drills.q: Which of Next.js's four caching layers survives server restarts and is shared across different users' requests?
drills.a: The Data Cache.

drills.q: What Next.js function invalidates a tagged cache entry after a mutation?
drills.a: revalidateTag() (or revalidatePath()).

drills.q: A code reviewer approves a Server Action PR with no visible auth check, reasoning 'the UI already hides this button from unauthorized users.' What's wrong with this reasoning, in one sentence?
drills.a: UI-level hiding controls what renders, not what's callable -- a Server Action is a separately-callable public HTTP endpoint, discoverable in the client bundle, that anyone can invoke directly regardless of whether the associated button ever appears for them.

drills.q: A team updates a product's price via a Server Action, and the database write succeeds, but users keep seeing the old price for an extended period afterward. Diagnose.
drills.a: The mutation almost certainly forgot to call revalidateTag/revalidatePath after the write, leaving the persistent Data Cache serving the pre-mutation value to every subsequent reader -- mechanically the same bug class as forgetting to invalidate a Redis key after a database write in a traditional backend.

drills.q: Why does deploying database-querying code on the Edge runtime risk connection exhaustion under load, when the same code on the Node runtime typically doesn't?
drills.a: Edge executes in many short-lived, geographically distributed V8 isolates rather than a small number of long-running processes -- each ephemeral invocation opening its own raw connection (or contending for a small shared limit) is a structural mismatch with a traditional database's connection-count ceiling, unlike Node's ability to hold a real, properly-sized, long-lived connection pool.

drills.q: What was the key lesson from Next.js's July 2026 security release regarding where authorization checks should live?
drills.a: Real authorization checks must live inside Server Actions and Route Handlers themselves, not rely solely on middleware.ts/proxy.ts -- one of the nine disclosed vulnerabilities was specifically a middleware authorization bypass, showing middleware-only enforcement is insufficient as the sole defense layer.

drills.q: Design the caching strategy for a product page with three data elements of different freshness needs: static product description, occasionally-changing sale price, and frequently-changing live inventory count.
drills.a: Product description: Full Route Cache or long-TTL Data Cache, invalidated via revalidateTag only on admin edit. Sale price: Data Cache with a shorter TTL or explicit tag-based invalidation tied to the pricing-update mutation, since stale pricing has real business consequences. Live inventory: too high-frequency for cost-effective tag-based invalidation -- better served by making that specific fetch genuinely dynamic (excluded from persistent caching) or streamed/polled client-side.

drills.q: A Next.js Server Action deployed on the Edge runtime starts failing with database connection errors under moderate production load. Propose two fixes at two different levels of architectural change, and explain the decision criterion for choosing between them.
drills.a: Smaller fix: add a serverless/edge-aware connection-pooling proxy between edge invocations and the database, keeping the architecture otherwise unchanged -- appropriate under time pressure or for a genuinely small app with no other data consumers. Larger fix: extract a real backend service (on a traditional runtime with its own managed connection pool) that Next.js calls instead of touching the database directly, converting Next.js to a BFF role -- appropriate once multiple consumers need the same data, review discipline for inline DB access is a concern, or this incident is one of a recurring pattern rather than a one-off.

drills.q: When would you choose a Route Handler over a Server Action for a new Next.js endpoint, and give a concrete example where a Server Action would NOT work.
drills.a: Choose a Route Handler when the caller isn't your own React component tree -- a webhook receiver, mobile app, or third-party integration needs a stable, documented URL to call. Example: a payment provider's webhook notifying your app of a completed charge needs a Route Handler at a fixed endpoint; a Server Action relies on Next.js's internal client-to-server calling convention that an external system has no way to invoke.

drills.q: State Resilience4j's fixed AOP decorator order from outermost to innermost.
drills.a: Retry -> CircuitBreaker -> RateLimiter -> TimeLimiter -> Bulkhead (Bulkhead innermost, closest to the actual method call).

drills.q: True or false: reordering @Retry and @CircuitBreaker annotations on a Spring method changes which one executes first.
drills.a: False. The aspect order is hardcoded by the library regardless of annotation declaration order; override only via explicit *AspectOrder configuration properties.

drills.q: Name Resilience4j's two Bulkhead implementations.
drills.a: SemaphoreBulkhead (default, counting semaphore on caller's thread) and ThreadPoolBulkhead (dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor + bounded queue).

drills.q: A team configures limitForPeriod=20, limitRefreshPeriod=1s expecting a smooth ~20 req/s cap, but downstream still sees short traffic spikes near 40 requests in 20ms. Explain why.
drills.a: Resilience4j's RateLimiter is a fixed-window algorithm, not a token bucket -- permissions reset in a step function at the start of each cycle. A full 20-permit burst at the very end of cycle N followed immediately by a full 20-permit burst at the start of cycle N+1 is fully compliant with the configuration, producing up to ~2x the nominal rate in the boundary window.

drills.q: A @CircuitBreaker(fallbackMethod="fallbackPrice") never invokes its fallback -- the original exception always propagates. What are the two most likely causes to check, in order?
