drills.a: Example-based tests only check inputs an engineer thought to write, systematically under-sampling the true input space (unusual unicode, boundary lengths, nesting). Fix: add a Hypothesis round-trip property test (decode(encode(x))==x) over the actual input domain, letting generated and auto-shrunk examples surface the missed case class.

drills.q: If a mutant is killed by your test suite, does that guarantee the corresponding code is bug-free?
drills.a: No -- it only proves sensitivity to that one specific mechanical mutation (e.g. one operator swap). It says nothing about a different kind of bug in the same line that doesn't correspond to any mutation in the catalog, or a bug from interaction with other code.

drills.q: Design a test-quality improvement plan for a payments module with 90% coverage and two recent production incidents.
drills.a: First, run mutation testing scoped to the module to get a ranked list of surviving mutants -- targeted, evidence-based gap identification. Second, for revealed weak spots, decide Hypothesis property tests (numerical invariants like transaction reconciliation) vs added parametrize cases (specific boundary/rounding edge cases) as appropriate. Third, add tests, then re-run mutation testing to verify previously-surviving mutants are now killed.

drills.q: A full mutation-testing pass on your payments module takes 6 hours. How do you make this a sustainable ongoing practice?
drills.a: Don't run the full pass on every commit -- schedule it periodically (monthly, or before major releases of that module) as a diagnostic/validation tool. Add the newly-identified test cases to the fast, always-on test suite so their value is captured continuously, even though the mutation-testing verification itself stays periodic.

drills.q: After shipping a performance-optimized function validated with a differential Hypothesis property against the old reference implementation, should you delete the reference implementation and its test?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- keep the reference implementation as a clearly-marked test-only artifact so the differential test continues providing value on every future change to the optimized version. Deleting it removes the ability to keep verifying 'still behaves the same as the known-correct-but-slow version' going forward.

drills.q: How would you decide whether a specific module in your codebase actually warrants investing in mutation testing, versus relying on example-based tests and monitoring/rollback?
drills.a: Weigh the module's blast radius if a subtle bug slips through, the cost/reversibility of an incident there (quickly rolled back with minimal harm, or lasting damage before detection), and its historical incident rate. High blast radius + low reversibility + a track record of incidents is a strong candidate; scoring low on all three is a weak candidate not worth the computational and triage cost.

drills.q: A team enables mypy --strict on their entire existing codebase in one commit and gets hundreds of errors. What went wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: Strict mode was enabled globally at once on a codebase without existing comprehensive type coverage -- the bundled checks (no untyped defs, no implicit Any) cascade into an avalanche of errors. Fix: scope --strict to already-well-typed modules first via per-module overrides in pyproject.toml, expanding incrementally.

drills.q: A pre-commit config includes the full test suite and commits now take 30+ seconds, so developers use --no-verify routinely. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: A slow, comprehensive check was placed in the fast local per-commit feedback loop where only cheap checks belong -- once commits are slow enough, developers bypass ALL hooks, not just the slow one. Fix: move the full test suite to CI, keep pre-commit scoped to fast checks (ruff lint/format, maybe a narrowly-scoped type check on changed files).

drills.q: Two developers' machines produce different resolved dependency versions from 'the same' requirements.txt. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No lockfile -- pip re-resolves transitive dependencies at install time, which can differ across time/machine even for an identical top-level list. Fix: migrate to a lockfile-based tool (uv) and commit uv.lock so every install resolves to identical pinned versions.

drills.q: A build fails with 'no build backend' errors despite uv managing dependencies fine. What's the cause?
drills.a: [build-system] is missing or misconfigured in pyproject.toml -- uv manages dependencies but delegates actual package building to whatever backend is configured there (hatchling, setuptools, flit-core). These are separate, independently-configured concerns.

drills.q: After migrating from requirements.txt to uv, the resolver produces different transitive dependency versions than the old hand-curated file. Is this a bug, and how should the team handle it?
drills.a: Not necessarily a bug -- a fresh resolver run can legitimately differ from a previously hand-adjusted or older-resolved file, especially with loose constraints. Review the new uv.lock deliberately, run the full test suite against it, and only then commit it as the new source of truth -- or, for a lower-risk migration, pin uv's initial resolution to match the old file's exact versions first, decoupling the tooling change from any dependency-version change.

drills.q: A team's mypy --strict pre-commit hook scans the entire repo on every commit and has become slow. What do you try, in order?
drills.a: First, scope the hook to only changed files (least disruptive). Second, verify mypy's incremental cache is actually being used/persisted between runs. Third, and only as a last resort, move the full-repo strict pass to CI entirely, keeping pre-commit to a fast scoped check or none -- this loses valuable fast local feedback, so it should not be the first response.

drills.q: A team wants to add a large, less-strictly-typed vendored third-party codebase to a project that enforces mypy --strict everywhere. What's the right approach?
drills.a: Add an explicit per-module override excluding or relaxing strictness for that specific vendored path, rather than failing CI on code the team doesn't control or weakening the whole project's strictness bar to accommodate it -- this is exactly the scoping problem per-module overrides exist to solve.

drills.q: pyright and ty both check a codebase and disagree on whether a piece of code is correctly typed. How do you resolve which is 'right'?
drills.a: Check both interpretations against the actual PEP-defined typing specification (PEP 484 and extensions) for the construct in question, since checker behavior is supposed to conform to that shared spec, not either tool's independent judgment. In genuinely ambiguous or under-specified areas, pick one checker as the team's source of truth and stay consistent, rather than trying to satisfy every checker simultaneously.

drills.q: A function passes mypy --strict cleanly but throws a TypeError at runtime on data from an external API. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Type hints are erased at runtime -- mypy only guarantees internal consistency under the assumption that declared types match actual values, which it can't verify for external data. Fix: add explicit runtime validation (a Pydantic model, isinstance checks) at the trust boundary where external data enters.

drills.q: mypy rejects a call passing an actual list[Dog] variable to a parameter typed list[Animal], even though the function body never mutates the list. What's the fix and why does it work?
drills.a: Change the parameter type to Sequence[Animal] (covariant, read-only) instead of list[Animal] (invariant). Since Sequence excludes mutation, list[Dog] safely satisfies Sequence[Animal] -- the fix correctly reflects that the function only reads, never writes, through this parameter.

drills.q: A code reviewer questions why list[T] must be invariant while Iterator[T] can be covariant. Give the concrete unsafe scenario that justifies the difference.
drills.a: If list[Dog] were covariant with list[Animal], code holding the Animal-typed alias could legally .append(Cat()) into what is, underneath, an actual list[Dog], silently inserting a wrong subtype. Iterator[T] only ever produces values (no input/write position), so Iterator[Dog] safely substitutes for Iterator[Animal] with no way to smuggle a wrong type in.

drills.q: Your team just bumped a Pydantic v1 dependency pin to v2 expecting it to be a drop-in upgrade. What breaks, and what's the actual migration effort?
drills.a: Real API surface changed: @validator -> @field_validator/@model_validator, class Config -> model_config=ConfigDict(...), .dict()/.json() -> .model_dump()/.model_dump_json(). v2 also has stricter default coercion than v1 in several cases. bump-pydantic automates the mechanical renames, but custom validators and config usage need manual review since automated tooling can't safely infer intent behind v1-specific coercion reliance.

drills.q: You're designing a library function that should accept 'anything file-like' (has .read() and .close()), used by callers you don't control. Protocol or ABC, and why?
drills.a: Protocol -- callers can pass any object with the right shape (a real file, BytesIO, a test double, a third-party file-like object) without needing to retrofit inheritance from your library's base class, which matters since some callers are outside your control. This mirrors how Python's actual duck typing already permits calling .read()/.close() regardless of class hierarchy.

drills.q: You later need to add a shared default implementation (e.g. a mixin providing .close() that calls .read() for cleanup) to the file-like interface from the previous question. Does Protocol still work?
drills.a: No -- Protocol only describes a shape, providing no mechanism for shared implementation code to be inherited. Genuine shared behavior requires an actual base class (possibly an ABC) that callers explicitly inherit from. Conflating 'I want type compatibility' with 'I want shared implementation' is the mistake to avoid here.

drills.q: Explain why Callable[[Arg],Ret] is contravariant in Arg but covariant in Ret simultaneously, and why this isn't a contradiction.
drills.a: For parameters (input position), accepting a broader type is safe (a function handling any Animal can substitute for one handling only Dog) -- contravariant. For return values (output position), producing a narrower type is safe (a function returning only Dog can substitute for one expected to return any Animal) -- covariant. These are different positions within the same generic type, each independently governed by the substitution-safety argument for that position, which is a correctly-modeled case of mixed variance, not a contradiction.

drills.q: Why is Pydantic v2's Rust core meaningfully faster on large nested JSON specifically, and does that mean validation is now effectively free?
drills.a: v2 compiles annotations once into composable Rust validators executed largely outside Python's per-field interpreter overhead, which v1 paid per field -- this overhead compounds most on large, deeply-nested payloads, which is exactly where the 5-50x speedup is largest. It is not free: validation cost still scales with data size/complexity, just at a much lower constant factor than v1.

drills.q: A teammate proposes a decaying epsilon schedule (eps_t=c/t) to fix epsilon-greedy's linear regret. Does this work, and what's the remaining downside?
drills.a: Yes, a properly decaying epsilon can achieve logarithmic regret matching UCB/Thompson asymptotically, but it reintroduces a hand-tuning problem (decay rate and schedule shape) that UCB/Thompson largely avoid -- too fast decays to a possibly-wrong arm prematurely, too slow keeps regret closer to the fixed-epsilon case for a long transient period.

drills.q: Why does UCB1's bonus term include ln(t) in the numerator rather than depending on n_i alone?
drills.a: The ln(t) term tightens the confidence bound as the total number of rounds grows, accounting for making more simultaneous confidence-interval claims across all arms over time -- without it, the exploration guarantee wouldn't hold uniformly as the horizon grows, a detail that matters for the formal regret proof even though n_i is the dominant term.

drills.q: A contextual bandit performs well on average but poorly for one specific, identifiable user segment. Diagnose.
drills.a: That segment's context region has likely been under-explored -- either the confidence bonus is poorly calibrated (lambda or alpha_bonus mistuned) or the segment is simply rare in traffic. Check per-segment cumulative regret specifically, not just aggregate regret, and consider a segment-specific or hierarchical prior for genuinely rare segments.

drills.q: Your bandit-driven pricing system occasionally serves a clearly bad price to a real customer. Is this a bug? What's the standard production fix?
drills.a: Not a bug -- it's inherent to any exploring bandit, which must occasionally choose a non-best-known option to gather information. Fix: an explicit safety floor (exclude options below an offline-vetted minimum quality/price threshold from the live exploration set) or a hard cap on the fraction of traffic exploration can consume.

drills.q: You're asked to add a contextual bandit to a currently-static recommendation ranker. What would you check before concluding this is the right addition?
drills.a: Confirm there's a genuine ongoing decision with real uncertainty (not a one-time variant choice better suited to a fixed A/B test); confirm sufficient informative context features exist to make LinUCB's added complexity worth it over plain UCB/Thompson; and confirm the org has operational maturity (safety floors, per-segment regret monitoring, off-policy eval) to safely run something that will occasionally serve suboptimal recommendations.

drills.q: LinUCB systematically underperforms in a setting with a strongly nonlinear context-reward relationship. How do you detect this, and is switching to a neural bandit the right fix?
drills.a: Detect by comparing, on logged data, how well a flexible nonlinear model (tree ensemble, neural net) predicts observed rewards versus the linear ridge model -- a large persistent gap that doesn't close with more data indicates the linear assumption (high bias) is the bottleneck. Before switching to a nonlinear bandit, check whether hand-engineered interaction/nonlinear features fed into the same LinUCB framework close most of the gap -- often sufficient and much simpler to maintain.

drills.q: What does inverse propensity scoring correct for in off-policy bandit evaluation, and what does it require to be valid?
drills.a: It reweights each logged reward by 1/P(old policy chose this action in this context), correcting for the old policy's own action-selection frequencies so the reweighted average unbiasedly estimates the new policy's expected reward. Requires knowing or reliably estimating the old policy's exact per-context action probabilities -- not always available for undocumented systems -- and the estimator's variance grows large when old and new policies disagree substantially.

drills.q: Is minimizing cumulative regret always the right objective for a production bandit?
drills.a: No -- if the actual business goal is 'identify the single best arm as fast as possible, accepting reward loss during a dedicated exploration phase' (the pure/best-arm-identification bandit variant), that's a different objective than cumulative regret minimization, and UCB/Thompson sampling (tuned for regret minimization while running) aren't the right algorithm family for it. Conflating the two objectives is a real, consequential mismatch.

drills.q: Explain why the kernel trick works for SVM's dual formulation but wouldn't apply the same way to the primal.
drills.a: The dual objective and decision function depend on data only through pairwise dot products x_i.x_j, so any valid kernel function can substitute directly. The primal involves w living explicitly in the (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature space, so there's no clean scalar-substitution point the way there is in the dual -- this is why kernelized SVMs are always solved via the dual.

drills.q: A production kNN recommendation system's latency degrades badly as the catalog grows from 100k to 5M items. Diagnose and propose a fix with its tradeoff.
drills.a: Naive kNN is O(n) per query -- brute-force distance to every stored point becomes the bottleneck at 5M items. Fix: switch to an approximate nearest-neighbor index (HNSW or IVF-PQ), trading a small tunable amount of recall for sub-linear query time.

drills.q: Why does Naive Bayes still classify well even though its independence assumption is almost always false?
drills.a: The bias from assuming independence buys large variance reduction -- estimating d one-dimensional per-class distributions needs far less data than modeling the full joint. Getting the argmax class right is a weaker requirement than getting calibrated probabilities right, so decisions can be correct even when probabilities are distorted.

drills.q: k-means produces clusters that look visually wrong -- splitting an apparent single group or merging two distinct ones. What's the likely cause and what would you try instead?
drills.a: Non-spherical, unequal-variance, or unequal-size true cluster structure violates k-means's isotropic-blob assumption baked into minimizing squared Euclidean distance to a centroid. Try DBSCAN (arbitrary shape, handles noise) or a Gaussian mixture model (elliptical, differently-sized clusters) and compare against domain knowledge.

drills.q: A stakeholder points at a UMAP plot and claims two customer segments are 'very different' because they're far apart on the plot. How do you respond?
drills.a: UMAP's objective preserves local neighborhood structure, not global pairwise distances -- nothing constrains between-cluster distance in the embedding to reflect true separation in the original feature space. Validate the claim with an actual statistical test or distance metric computed on the original features, not the 2D plot's visual gap.

drills.q: You're asked to find natural customer segments in unlabeled transaction data. Walk through choosing among k-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering, and what you'd validate before trusting the result.
drills.a: Visualize first (PCA for linear structure, UMAP for local structure, with its interpretation caveats in mind) to see if groups look spherical/similar-sized (k-means), irregular/noisy (DBSCAN), or nested (hierarchical). Run more than one method -- agreement is corroborating, disagreement is itself informative. Before trusting the result for a business decision, validate against an external held-out signal (e.g. do segments differ on retention/spend not used to form them), not just an internal metric like silhouette score.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants exactly 5 customer segments for a planned campaign, but your clustering analysis suggests 3 or 7 fits better. How do you handle this?
drills.a: Report both: what the data-driven analysis actually shows (with evidence, e.g. an elbow/silhouette peak at 3 or 7) and a clearly-labeled forced-5-cluster result if the business constraint requires it -- don't silently pick whichever k matches the stakeholder's preference and present it as data-driven, since that's a credibility risk if it surfaces later that 5 was decided before the analysis.

drills.q: Two models have identical classification accuracy -- one is Naive Bayes, one is logistic regression. Does that mean their predicted probabilities are equally trustworthy for a downstream threshold-based decision?
drills.a: No. Accuracy only depends on whether the argmax class is correct, a much weaker condition than calibration. Naive Bayes's independence assumption tends to push probabilities toward 0/1 more than warranted (multiplying correlated evidence as if independent), while logistic regression directly optimizes cross-entropy on its own outputs -- equal accuracy does not imply equal calibration, and this matters a great deal if probabilities feed a downstream threshold rather than just a top-class label.

drills.q: A churn model reports 98% AUC in cross-validation, far above any comparable benchmark. What's your first hypothesis and how do you check it?
drills.a: Suspect leakage before a breakthrough -- genuine improvements on well-studied problems come in modest increments, so an implausible jump is more likely an information shortcut. Check feature importances for one implausibly dominant feature, trace its real-world data-generation timing against the prediction point, and try removing it to see if performance collapses toward the expected range.

drills.q: A colleague computes a rolling 30-day feature with df.groupby('user_id').rolling(30).mean() directly on sorted data. What's the bug?
drills.a: Pandas' rolling window includes the current row by default -- if the intent is 'average of the prior 30 days, not including today,' this leaks the row's own value into its own feature. Fix by shifting the window by 1 row (or by the actual reporting lag) before rolling.

drills.q: A time-series forecasting model backtests excellently but performs poorly the week after deployment. Diagnose.
drills.a: Random k-fold CV was likely used instead of time-respecting CV, giving the model an implicit look-ahead advantage (training on 'future' relative to some validation rows) that production never has. Switch to TimeSeriesSplit or rolling-window backtesting and expect the honest validation number to be meaningfully lower.

drills.q: A churn model trained on multiple snapshots per user performs far worse on brand-new users than validation predicted. What CV mistake caused this and what's the fix?
drills.a: Plain k-fold let some of a user's rows land in training and others in validation, letting the model memorize per-user idiosyncrasies rather than genuinely generalize. Fix: GroupKFold keyed on user ID, so each user's entire row set goes to exactly one fold -- expect validation metrics to drop toward a more honest new-user estimate.

drills.q: Your production system continuously retrains to predict the NEXT snapshot for already-known users, not genuinely new users. Is GroupKFold still the right CV choice?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- if the true production task is within-group prediction (same known users, next snapshot) rather than cross-group generalization, GroupKFold's stricter unseen-entity estimate could understate real achievable performance. CV strategy must match the actual deployment scenario, not be applied as an unconditional rule.

drills.q: You're predicting hospital readmission from multi-year patient visit records. Design the CV strategy and name the single most important leakage check.
drills.a: Combine group and time: assign whole patients to folds (no patient split across train/val) while also respecting temporal order if the production system predicts forward for new visits. Most important check: audit every feature for whether it could only be known AFTER the readmission outcome is determined (e.g., a discharge summary finalized only once the outcome is known) -- medical records are a well-documented high-risk domain for this kind of leakage.

drills.q: After fixing a group-leakage bug, validation AUC drops 15 points from what the previous team reported. How do you communicate this to an excited stakeholder?
drills.a: Present both numbers with a clear explanation of what each measures: the old ungrouped number reflects a mix of genuine pattern learning and per-patient/user memorization that won't generalize to new entities; the new grouped number is the honest estimate of new-entity generalization, which is what production will actually face. The lower number should drive the go/no-go decision, and explaining the mechanism (not just asserting correctness) is what earns trust.

drills.q: A rolling aggregate feature is correctly computed using only strictly-prior data in the training pipeline. Is the feature now guaranteed leakage-free in production?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- if training used a batch process with more complete/less-noisy historical data than what's actually available in the live serving path (e.g. a nightly job without the production data-completeness lag), there's a training/serving skew that behaves like leakage: validation performance won't replicate in production even though temporal leakage in the strict sense was avoided.

drills.q: Derive dL/dz for binary cross-entropy on top of sigmoid, starting from L = -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)].
drills.a: dL/dp = -y/p + (1-y)/(1-p); dp/dz = p(1-p). Multiply: -y(1-p)+(1-y)p = -y+yp+p-yp = p-y. Every p-dependent term cancels, leaving exactly p-y.

drills.q: Your loss oscillates and diverges to nan within a few dozen steps of training a logistic regression with Adam. What do you check first, second, third?
drills.a: First, halve the learning rate as a fast diagnostic. Second, check for an upstream data issue producing inf/nan (log of zero, division by zero feature, extreme unnormalized targets). Third, check eps isn't effectively zero relative to gradient scale in the Adam denominator, which can blow up updates on a near-zero second-moment estimate.

drills.q: A colleague says 'we should always use Adam, it's just better.' How do you push back with a specific citation and mechanism?
drills.a: Wilson et al. 2017 ('The Marginal Value of Adaptive Gradient Methods') showed SGD+momentum can generalize better than Adam on some vision tasks despite slower convergence. Adam's per-parameter adaptive scaling can converge to sharper minima that generalize less well -- training-loss speed is not evidence of better held-out performance; validate both before locking in a choice for production.

drills.q: Two features in your linear regression are highly collinear. What happens to their individual coefficients, and does this make the model's predictions unreliable?
drills.a: Coefficients become highly unstable -- many different (w1,w2) combinations fit almost equally well, so small data perturbations can swing them by large amounts or flip signs. Predictions, however, can remain stable and accurate, because it's the decomposition of effect between the two collinear features that's poorly identified, not the combined fit.

drills.q: Why does RMSprop's per-parameter scaling specifically help sparse features?
drills.a: A sparse feature's weight has a gradient of zero most steps, so its running average of squared gradients s stays small. When a nonzero gradient does occur, dividing by sqrt(s)+eps produces a comparatively large effective step -- the parameter catches up fast on its rare updates instead of being swamped by a global rate tuned for dense features.

drills.q: You inherit a converged logistic regression pipeline where one customer segment has systematically worse accuracy than the rest. Is this an optimizer bug? How do you find out?
drills.a: Almost certainly not -- logistic regression's loss is convex, so a converged fit found the global optimum for that feature representation. Check training loss actually plateaued and gradient norm is near zero to rule out an optimization bug, then investigate segment-specific feature coverage, class balance, and whether a linear boundary can separate that segment at all.

drills.q: What would make you suspect a converged-looking logistic regression fit actually has an optimization problem, not a data/capacity problem?
drills.a: If training loss hasn't actually converged (still decreasing when stopped, or a ConvergenceWarning was ignored), or if different solvers/seeds (L-BFGS vs SGD) produce meaningfully different coefficients and segment-level accuracy -- a convex problem shouldn't be solver-sensitive at true convergence, so solver-sensitivity is itself diagnostic evidence of an optimization issue.

drills.q: Explain, mechanically, why Adagrad stalls on long training runs and what RMSprop changed to fix it.
drills.a: Adagrad accumulates the SUM of squared gradients over all of training history, so its denominator only ever grows, monotonically shrinking the effective learning rate toward zero regardless of recent gradient behavior. RMSprop replaces the sum with an exponential moving average, which 'forgets' old squared gradients at a controlled rate, letting the effective learning rate recover if recent gradients shrink.

drills.q: A teammate says 'our new model has higher AUC-ROC, so it's strictly better.' What's the specific scenario where this is wrong?
drills.a: AUC-ROC aggregates across all thresholds, but production operates at one specific threshold. A model can win on average AUC-ROC while performing worse at the actual operating region that matters (e.g. low-FPR region relevant to a fraud alert budget) -- compare precision-recall curves at the real deployment operating point, not the aggregate area.

drills.q: On a dataset with 1,000 positives and 99,000 negatives, a model catches 800 true positives with 2,000 false positives. Compute FPR and precision and explain why they tell different stories.
drills.a: FPR = 2000/99000 ~ 2.0% (looks great, keeps AUC-ROC high). Precision = 800/(800+2000) ~ 28.6% (more than 70% of flagged items are false alarms). FPR is normalized against the huge negative class, hiding the false-alarm burden that precision reveals.

drills.q: You have 200 calibration examples with a 5% positive rate. Would you use Platt scaling or isotonic regression, and why?
drills.a: Platt scaling -- with only ~10 positive examples, isotonic regression's flexible many-parameter step function would almost certainly overfit badly in the sparse positive region, while Platt's two-parameter sigmoid fit is far more robust to limited data, even though it assumes a specific shape.

drills.q: A fraud model has false-negative cost $500 and false-positive cost $15. Derive the cost-minimizing probability threshold, and state what must be true of the model for this derivation to be valid.
drills.a: Flag as fraud when p*500 > (1-p)*15, giving threshold p* = 15/515 ~ 2.9%. This derivation requires the model's probabilities to be genuinely calibrated -- if p is miscalibrated (e.g. systematically overconfident), the derived cutoff is applied to the wrong underlying probabilities and won't actually minimize expected cost.

drills.q: A model's accuracy and AUC-ROC dashboards look stable in production, but a teammate suspects calibration has quietly degraded. What monitoring would catch this, and why wouldn't accuracy/AUC show it?
drills.a: Track a reliability diagram or ECE on a rolling window of production data with ground truth, watching for drift away from the diagonal. If the underlying base rate shifts while relative ranking of risk stays intact, AUC-ROC (rank-based) and accuracy (if the threshold still roughly separates classes) can look stable even though every predicted probability is now systematically wrong relative to the new true rate.

drills.q: Why is it wrong to calibrate a model on the same data it was trained on, and does this same concern extend to your final evaluation set?
drills.a: A model's scores on its own training data are systematically overconfident (partial memorization), so a calibration mapping fit there matches that overconfidence, not true out-of-sample behavior. Yes, the same leakage risk applies if the calibration set is also your final evaluation set -- reported calibration quality (ECE, reliability diagram) would be optimistically biased toward that data. Use three splits when sample size allows: train base model, calibrate, final-evaluate.

drills.q: Explain why isotonic regression's calibrated output is a step function rather than a smooth curve, and when that's actually a problem.
drills.a: Pool-adjacent-violators merges adjacent blocks violating monotonicity and assigns each merged block's average as the calibrated value for every point in it -- producing a non-decreasing step function with jumps at block boundaries, not a smooth curve. This is a problem when a smooth estimate is needed downstream (e.g. feeding a gradient-based optimization) or when a boundary falls in an operationally important, sparsely-populated region, producing an abrupt, poorly-estimated jump exactly where precision matters most.

drills.q: A stakeholder is impressed by an AUC-PR of 0.3 on one project and unimpressed by the same 0.3 on another. Could both reactions be correct?
drills.a: Yes -- a random classifier's AUC-PR equals the positive class prevalence, not a fixed baseline like AUC-ROC's 0.5. An AUC-PR of 0.3 on a 1%-prevalence dataset is a large lift over the 0.01 random baseline; the same 0.3 on a 30%-prevalence dataset is barely above random baseline. AUC-PR values are not comparable across datasets without accounting for base rate.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks why you don't just use one large model end-to-end instead of the retrieval-ranking-reranking pipeline. What's the technical answer?
drills.a: No single model can simultaneously be cheap enough to score millions-to-billions of items within a real-time latency budget AND rich enough for genuine cross-features -- these requirements are in direct tension. The funnel resolves this by applying a cheap high-recall model to the full catalog, reserving the expensive high-precision model for only the small candidate set retrieval narrowed down to.

drills.q: A two-tower retrieval model's top candidates look topically relevant but miss a known user-item-specific signal (e.g. 'user always buys this brand during this promotion'). Diagnose.
drills.a: This is the expected structural limitation of two-tower architecture -- towers never see each other's features, interacting only via a final dot product, so genuine cross-features can't be captured at retrieval. Verify the downstream ranking stage (which CAN see cross-features) is correctly re-scoring and promoting these cases; don't expect retrieval-stage recall to reflect this signal.

drills.q: A LambdaMART ranking model shows strong offline NDCG but the online A/B test is flat or negative. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: Selection bias in logged data -- historical logs only show outcomes for items the previous policy already chose to show, so offline metrics implicitly evaluate re-ranking of already-selected items, not the full candidate distribution. Use counterfactual/off-policy evaluation (e.g. inverse propensity weighting) where possible, and always confirm with an online A/B test before a significant launch.

drills.q: Why would naively binarizing implicit feedback and running explicit-rating MF on it produce a biased model?
drills.a: It treats every non-interaction as a confident negative rating, conflating 'saw it and disliked it' with 'never saw it at all' -- for most catalogs the vast majority of zero cells are the latter, so this systematically biases the model against low-exposure items and users regardless of true preference.

drills.q: You're launching a new product category with zero historical interaction data inside an existing mature recommendation system. Walk through the end-to-end cold-start handling.
drills.a: Retrieval: fall back to content-based similarity (metadata/pretrained embeddings, no collaborative signal yet) for likely-interested users based on other-category behavior. Ranking: blend a popularity/content-relevance prior with early weak collaborative signal, increasing CF weight as interaction count grows. Layer explicit exploration via a contextual bandit to accelerate data accumulation, and monitor the rate of items crossing a 'sufficient interaction' threshold as a leading indicator for phasing down cold-start treatment.

drills.q: How would you decide whether a deep cross-feature neural ranker is worth its added complexity over a well-tuned LambdaMART model for a specific ranking problem?
drills.a: Run both on the same feature set and data, and check whether the deep model's gain is concentrated in patterns genuinely hard to hand-engineer (e.g. long user-behavior sequences) versus patterns a few additional cross-features would let LambdaMART capture just as well at much lower serving cost. If cheap feature engineering closes most of the gap, that's usually the better investment than switching architectures.

drills.q: Your cold-start exploration budget (contextual bandit traffic to new items) -- how do you know if it's too large or too small?
drills.a: Track the overall business metric (revenue, engagement) with and without the exploration allocation via a held-out control group, and separately track the rate at which new items accumulate sufficient interaction data to exit cold-start status. A sustained hit to the business metric signals reducing/targeting the budget; a too-slow graduation rate despite reasonable budget suggests an exposure/impression problem rather than a ranking-model problem.

drills.q: ALS training scales well with more users/items in Spark but convergence quality degrades on a very sparse, heavy long-tail catalog. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Extremely sparse rows leave many items/users with too few observed interactions for a stable per-row least-squares solve, even with L2 regularization -- V_obs^T V_obs can be poorly conditioned with very few observations. Fix: increase lambda for sparse rows specifically, use a hybrid content+CF model for the long tail, or apply a minimum-interaction-count filter before including an entity in pure CF training.

drills.q: A learning curve shows train and val error both plateau at 15% error from 10k to 200k examples with a small gap. What's the diagnosis and what should you NOT do?
drills.a: High-bias signature -- more data and more regularization will not help. Fix: more expressive features or model class. Do not add regularization (it would only make the underfitting worse) and do not spend a week collecting more of the same-distribution data.

drills.q: Derive why ridge's (X^T X + lambda*I) is always invertible even when X^T X is singular.
drills.a: Adding lambda*I shifts every eigenvalue of X^T X up by exactly lambda (shared eigenvectors). If X^T X has a zero eigenvalue (singular, e.g. perfect collinearity), the shifted matrix has all-positive eigenvalues for any lambda>0, hence is invertible.

drills.q: A teammate builds a hyperparameter grid for sklearn LogisticRegression assuming larger C means more regularization. What's wrong and how would you notice?
drills.a: C is the inverse of regularization strength (C=1/lambda) -- larger C means LESS regularization, so the grid's intended direction is inverted. Notice by sanity-checking that the smallest C in the grid visibly underfits; if the 'most regularized' end doesn't behave as expected, the direction is backwards.

drills.q: Why is lasso feature selection unstable when features are highly correlated, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Lasso's corner-touching mechanism arbitrarily selects one member of a correlated group and zeros the rest -- which one gets picked can flip across resamples/noise. Elastic net (combining L1 and L2) retains L2's grouping effect so correlated features get similar nonzero coefficients together, while still allowing some exact zeros.

drills.q: A teammate says 'L1 regularization in XGBoost gives feature selection just like lasso.' Correct this.
drills.a: XGBoost's reg_alpha penalizes leaf weights within trees whose splits were already chosen by a gain criterion -- it doesn't zero out feature coefficients the way lasso does, and a feature can still be used across many splits. True feature-level selection in tree ensembles needs a separate step like SHAP-based pruning, not just tuning reg_alpha.

drills.q: You're asked to add regularization to a production XGBoost model that's slightly overfitting on 500 tabular features. What do you check before reaching for reg_alpha/reg_lambda?
drills.a: max_depth, min_child_weight, and subsampling (subsample, colsample_bytree) usually have larger, more predictable effects on tree-ensemble overfitting than the L1/L2 leaf-weight penalties -- check and tune those first.

drills.q: How would you convince a skeptical teammate that more regularization won't fix a model's poor validation performance, without spending a week trying it first?
drills.a: Show a learning curve with training error itself already high and converged, with validation error at a similar level and a small gap. If the model isn't even fitting the training data well, regularization -- a tool for reducing overfitting (the gap) -- cannot address a problem that isn't a gap problem; it would only increase training error further.

drills.q: What does double descent complicate about the classical bias-variance picture, and how should you state it in an interview to avoid overclaiming?
drills.a: Past the interpolation threshold, test error can decrease again as capacity keeps growing (Belkin et al. 2019), which the classical U-shape doesn't predict. State it as a real, empirically documented phenomenon mainly in high-capacity models (deep nets, some kernel settings) -- not as a general rule that bigger models are always eventually better, since compute cost and inconsistent occurrence across settings argue against that generalization.

drills.q: Derive the ~36.8% out-of-bag fraction for bootstrap sampling and explain what it's used for.
drills.a: P(row never drawn in n draws with replacement from n rows) = (1-1/n)^n, which converges to 1/e ~ 0.368 as n grows. The excluded ~36.8% of rows per tree are usable as a free out-of-bag validation estimate without a separate holdout set.

drills.q: A LightGBM model overfits badly even though max_depth looks conservative. What's the likely cause and fix?
drills.a: Leaf-wise growth with an uncapped/high num_leaves grows one branch very deep regardless of max_depth's nominal limit -- max_depth alone doesn't bound leaf count for leaf-wise trees the way it does for level-wise growth. Fix: cap num_leaves explicitly, roughly below 2^max_depth, and tune the two jointly.

drills.q: A target-encoded categorical feature performs great in CV but degrades sharply in production. Diagnose and connect to CatBoost's fix.
drills.a: Naive target encoding computes each category's value using the full training set including the current row's own label -- CV run after this global encoding inherits the leakage, inflating CV performance. CatBoost's ordered target statistics fix this by encoding each row using only rows preceding it in a random permutation, so no row ever sees its own label in its encoding.

drills.q: A colleague claims 'gradient boosting always beats random forests.' Give a concrete counterexample and how you'd verify it on your own data.
drills.a: On data with heavy label noise, boosting's sequential residual-fitting can end up fitting the noise in later rounds, while random forest averaging is more robust since noisy per-tree errors partially cancel. Verify by fitting both with reasonable defaults and comparing validation performance directly -- an unstable-across-seeds or widening train/val gap for boosting is a concrete signal this dataset is in the exception case.

drills.q: Explain GOSS's reweighting factor (1-a)/b and why dropping low-gradient rows without reweighting would be wrong.
drills.a: GOSS keeps all top-a% high-gradient rows and samples a fraction b of the rest, multiplying the sampled low-gradient rows by (1-a)/b when computing gain. This keeps the expected gradient sum close to the full-data value; dropping without reweighting would systematically underestimate the aggregate contribution of low-gradient rows, biasing split selection.

drills.q: You have 50M rows, 200 mostly-numeric features, and a same-day training budget. Which library first, why, and what single experiment validates the choice?
drills.a: LightGBM first -- leaf-wise growth plus GOSS row subsampling target exactly this shape (large rows, numeric-heavy so EFB's categorical benefit matters less). Validate with a small-scale (2-5M row) timed comparison against XGBoost hist with matched effective capacity (num_leaves vs max_depth), since XGBoost's histogram adoption has narrowed the historical LightGBM speed gap and old benchmarks shouldn't be assumed to hold on this specific data/hardware.

drills.q: Derive XGBoost's closed-form leaf weight from the second-order Taylor approximation and explain what happens when a leaf has very few examples and lambda is small.
drills.a: w* = -sum(g_i)/(sum(h_i)+lambda), minimizing the 2nd-order Taylor-approximated loss for a fixed tree structure. With few examples, sum(h_i) is small, and a small lambda barely dampens the denominator, producing a large, unstable weight -- min_child_weight (minimum sum of Hessians per leaf) exists specifically to disallow splits creating such thinly-supported leaves.

drills.q: Explain CatBoost's 'prediction shift' and why it's distinct from ordinary train/test leakage from preprocessing.
drills.a: Prediction shift is internal to standard boosting: the residual for row i at round m comes from a model that already used row i's own label in earlier rounds, producing systematic optimism that compounds -- most pronounced on small datasets. This is distinct from a data-pipeline leak (e.g. global encoding computed on the full dataset including test rows), which is avoidable by strict train/test separation; prediction shift persists even with zero cross-set leakage unless the boosting algorithm itself guards against it, as ordered boosting does.

drills.q: True or false: in Rust, assignment always copies the value being assigned.
drills.a: False -- assignment moves by default for non-Copy types (like String or Vec<T>); only types implementing the Copy marker trait (pure stack data with no Drop impl) are bit-copied on assignment.

drills.q: Can a type that implements Drop also implement Copy?
drills.a: No -- Copy requires a bit-for-bit duplicate to be safe, but a custom Drop implementation means there's a resource/cleanup action that would run twice on two 'copies', which is unsound. The compiler rejects this combination.

drills.q: What Rust edition introduced Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL)?
drills.a: Rust 2018.

drills.q: A function holds a &Vec<T> shared reference and then tries to push() to the same Vec through a separate &mut Vec<T> in the same scope, with the shared reference still used afterward. Does this compile, and why or why not?
drills.a: No -- the borrow checker rejects it because the shared reference is still live (used later) when the mutable borrow is attempted, and push() could reallocate the Vec's backing buffer, which would invalidate the shared reference. This is exactly the aliasing-plus-mutation bug class the borrow rule prevents.

drills.q: Explain why a String parameter taken by value (fn f(s: String)) forces the caller to either move or clone their String, and when that's the right API choice.
drills.a: Taking String by value means f takes ownership -- the caller's binding becomes invalid after the call unless they clone first. It's the right choice when f genuinely needs to own, store, or consume the data (e.g. building a struct that holds it); for read-only access, &str is the correct, more flexible parameter type.

drills.q: Why does thread::spawn require captured data to be 'static, and what's the usually-correct fix when this error appears?
drills.a: A spawned thread may outlive the stack frame that created it, so any borrowed data it captures could become dangling. The usually-correct fix is to move an owned value into the closure (so no borrow, and thus no lifetime constraint, exists) rather than reaching for Box::leak to manufacture a 'static reference.

drills.q: What are the three standard escape hatches for implementing a doubly-linked list (or any back-pointer/graph shape) in Rust, and what's the real cost of each?
drills.a: Rc<RefCell<Node>> (shared ownership + interior mutability; refcounting overhead, reference cycles can leak memory since Rc alone doesn't collect cycles); arena + usize indices instead of pointers (sidesteps the borrow checker entirely, usually the fastest and used by libraries like petgraph); unsafe raw pointers with manually-upheld invariants (what the standard library's own LinkedList does internally).

drills.q: Explain the connection between the borrow checker's single-thread aliasing rule and Rust's compile-time data-race freedom across threads.
drills.a: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent memory access where at least one access writes -- exactly what the borrow rule (no &mut T alongside any other live reference) already forbids within one thread. Extending this guarantee across threads requires the Send and Sync marker traits, which certify a type is actually safe to transfer or share between threads; combined, the type system statically rejects data races for all safe Rust code, a guarantee no mainstream garbage-collected language provides.

drills.q: A codebase has .clone() calls scattered across nearly every function that touches a shared data structure, and profiling shows meaningful time in allocation. Diagnose and propose a fix.
drills.a: This is the classic 'fought the borrow checker with clone() instead of restructuring ownership' anti-pattern -- each clone is a real O(n) heap allocation and byte copy, not free. Fix by identifying which call sites genuinely need an owned, independent copy (keep those) versus which only need read-only or temporarily-exclusive access (convert to & or &mut references), and consider Rc/Arc deliberately for the cases that do need genuine shared ownership rather than repeated cloning.

drills.q: What does Box<dyn Trait> default to in terms of lifetime, and when does this surprise people?
drills.a: It defaults to Box<dyn Trait + 'static>, meaning the boxed value must not internally borrow anything with a lifetime shorter than 'static. This surprises people trying to box a trait object that holds a borrowed reference internally -- it requires an explicit Box<dyn Trait + 'a> annotation instead of the default.

drills.q: How many patches does a 224x224 image split into 16x16 patches produce (before adding the CLS token)?
True or false: vision tokens fed into an LLM are discrete ids looked up in the same vocabulary table as text tokens.
drills.a: False -- vision tokens are continuous vectors produced by a vision encoder plus a projection layer, with no vocabulary entry and no decode() step.

drills.q: What was the batch size used in the original CLIP paper's pretraining, and why does batch size matter for contrastive pretraining?
drills.a: 32,768. A larger batch provides more and harder in-batch negatives per gradient step, since every non-matching pair in the batch is a free negative for the contrastive loss.

drills.q: A candidate says 'GPT-4o just converts the image to some tokens, it's basically free compared to text.' Correct this.
drills.a: A single 1024x1024 image in GPT-4o high-detail mode costs roughly 765 tokens (85 base + 170 per 512x512 tile) -- comparable to 500-800 words of text. It is not free; three or four such images can consume as much context budget as several pages of text, and vision tokens incur the same O(n^2) attention cost as text tokens.

drills.q: Explain why LLaVA-1.5 always produces exactly 576 vision tokens per image regardless of image content, and name one production consequence.
drills.a: LLaVA-1.5 always resizes input to 336x336 and uses a fixed 14x14 patch grid (24x24=576 patches), with a simple 2-layer MLP projecting each patch embedding independently -- no dynamic sizing. Consequence: a visually simple icon costs the same 576 tokens as a visually dense photo, and fine detail below one patch's spatial resolution is lost regardless of the source image's actual resolution.

drills.q: Why does a Vision Transformer need learned positional embeddings when a CNN's architecture doesn't require an equivalent mechanism?
drills.a: Self-attention is permutation-invariant by construction -- it has no inherent notion of which patch came from where. A CNN's convolution is inherently local and translation-equivariant, baking spatial structure into the architecture itself. ViT must explicitly add positional embeddings to each patch to recover spatial order information.

drills.q: Is Whisper a fused multimodal architecture in the same sense as LLaVA or GPT-4o's vision handling? Justify.
drills.a: No -- Whisper's audio encoder output doesn't share an embedding space with a downstream LLM by default. It's a standalone encoder-decoder producing discrete text tokens directly, typically integrated as a cascaded ASR-then-text pipeline, unlike a VLM which projects continuous vision embeddings directly into the LLM's own sequence for joint attention.

drills.q: A production RAG pipeline adding full-page document images alongside existing OCR'd text saw cost and latency roughly triple. Diagnose the cause and propose two fixes.
drills.a: Each full page image adds several hundred to 1000+ vision tokens on top of existing OCR text tokens, and vision tokens incur the same O(n^2) attention cost as text, so prefill latency scales worse than linearly. Fixes: (1) drop the raw image for pages where OCR text alone suffices, reserving image input for pages with important non-text visual content (tables, diagrams); (2) use low-detail/downscaled modes, or crop to only the specific regions OCR struggled with, instead of sending full-resolution full pages by default.

drills.q: Design the vision-token budget policy for an agentic browsing tool that screenshots every step of a multi-step task. What breaks without a policy, and what should the policy be?
drills.a: Without a policy, appending every step's full-resolution screenshot to growing conversation history burns roughly linear context purely on images (a 20-step task could hit 15,000-20,000 tokens on screenshots alone), risking hitting the context ceiling or unexpected cost. Policy: keep only the most recent 1-2 screenshots in context, drop older ones once acted on unless explicitly needed for comparison, use low-detail mode where fine text-reading isn't required, and summarize stale screenshot content into text once no longer the active focus.

drills.q: What is a CLIP typographic attack and why does it succeed? Does the vulnerability carry forward into VLMs built on top of CLIP?
drills.a: Pasting text onto an image (e.g. writing 'iPod' on a photo of an apple) shifts the CLIP embedding toward that word's semantic neighborhood strongly enough to flip zero-shot classification, because contrastive training never explicitly taught the model to distinguish depicted content from depicted text -- both correlate with caption text in training data. Yes, it carries forward into any VLM whose vision encoder is a frozen or lightly fine-tuned CLIP, unless the downstream LLM's own training independently learned to discount text-in-image, which isn't guaranteed -- a real prompt-injection-via-image attack vector.

drills.q: Explain the mechanical role of the projection layer in a VLM like LLaVA, and contrast its form with Qwen-VL's approach.
drills.a: The projection layer bridges the vision encoder's output dimension to the LLM's embedding dimension so the resulting vectors can be concatenated into the LLM's input sequence. LLaVA uses a simple 2-layer MLP with GELU, applied per-patch independently, always producing as many output tokens as input patches. Qwen-VL uses a merger module with 2D-RoPE-aware attention that can compress/merge adjacent patches, producing a variable token count rather than a fixed one-to-one mapping.

drills.q: Name the two structurally distinct root causes of training-serving skew.
drills.a: Definition drift (two independently-maintained implementations of the 'same' feature) and point-in-time leakage (naive join uses current value instead of the value as-of the label's timestamp).

drills.q: True or false: a feature store fully eliminates training-serving skew once adopted.
drills.a: False -- it fixes definition-level drift by materializing one shared definition into offline and online stores, but doesn't guarantee execution-context equivalence between the batch job and the real-time read path.

drills.q: Which two internal systems first productized the offline/online feature-store pattern?
drills.a: Uber's Michelangelo Palette and Airbnb's Zipline, both mid-2010s.

drills.q: Explain mechanically what pd.merge_asof(..., direction='backward') does differently from a standard merge on entity ID, in a training data pipeline.
drills.a: It performs a time-aware (as-of) join: for each label row it finds the feature row with the latest feature_timestamp that is still <= the label's own timestamp, rather than joining to whatever the feature's current/latest value happens to be regardless of the label's actual event time -- preventing future information from leaking into training.

drills.q: A model's offline AUC is unusually high for the problem domain. What's the first thing to investigate, and how?
drills.a: Suspect point-in-time leakage first. Manually reconstruct a few training examples' true as-of feature values from raw historical data and compare against what the training set's join actually produced -- a mismatch confirms leakage.

drills.q: A team wants to adopt Tecton for a workload that only ever scores in nightly batch jobs. What's wrong with that choice?
drills.a: Tecton's differentiated strength -- real-time/streaming feature computation via a push-based architecture -- is entirely wasted on a batch-only workload; you'd pay its consumption-based pricing for capability the use case never exercises. A simpler batch-oriented store (Feast, or even a warehouse table with point-in-time-correct retrieval) fits better.

drills.q: Design online/offline consistency monitoring for a feature store in production. What specifically gets alerted on, and how do you avoid false positives from normal materialization lag?
drills.a: Continuously sample matched entity/timestamp pairs, comparing the online store's currently served value against the offline store's materialized value, alerting on systematic divergence. Avoid false positives by setting an expected lag tolerance based on the materialization pipeline's actual cadence (e.g. hourly refresh implies some expected short-window mismatch is normal); alert on divergence that persists beyond that window or appears in features with no legitimate lag source.

drills.q: Explain the 'unified execution layer' critique of feature stores and why it argues feature stores don't fully solve skew.
drills.a: Feature stores manage data artifacts (materialized values) but don't control execution -- when training and serving run through different execution contexts (different query planners, timing/retry semantics), even identical feature definitions can produce subtly different results, e.g. differing handling of late-arriving or out-of-order events. The critique argues the deeper fix is collapsing training and serving onto one shared execution engine computing features inline at query time, rather than syncing artifacts between two separate systems.

drills.q: A team needs sub-minute-fresh features for a real-time fraud model but runs an hourly-batch Feast deployment. What's the fix, and what new correctness problem does it introduce?
drills.a: Move the freshness-critical features to a streaming-first computation path (e.g. Tecton's push-based architecture or an equivalent stream processor), possibly keeping batch for features that don't need the freshness -- a mixed architecture. This makes point-in-time correctness harder, not easier: a streaming pipeline needs correct handling of out-of-order/late-arriving events at much tighter timing tolerances than an hourly batch job.

drills.q: Leadership mandates platform-wide feature store adoption citing 'training-serving skew,' including for workloads that are batch-only scoring with no live serving path. What's the pushback?
drills.a: Training-serving skew only exists where there are two separate execution paths (training and real-time serving) computing features independently -- a batch-only workload has exactly one computation path, so there's no skew risk the online/offline split fixes. Recommend scoping the online-store mandate to workloads with an actual real-time serving path, and applying point-in-time-correctness discipline within existing batch pipelines for the rest, rather than paying for unused online-store infrastructure everywhere.

drills.q: Distinguish target leakage from point-in-time leakage with a concrete example of each.
drills.a: Point-in-time leakage: a feature's CURRENT value is joined to a historical label instead of its as-of value (e.g. today's lifetime purchase total joined to a 3-month-old label). Target leakage: a feature is a near-direct proxy for the label itself, e.g. a 'will_cancel' feature computed from data that only exists because the customer already canceled -- this is non-temporal and a point-in-time join won't catch it.

drills.q: What percentage of traffic does a canary deployment typically start at, and does its output reach real users?
drills.a: Typically 1-5% to start, ramping to 20%/50%/100%. Yes -- unlike shadow, canary output DOES reach real users at whatever percentage is currently routed to it.

drills.q: True or false: reverting the serving container to the previous model version is a complete rollback.
drills.a: False -- a complete rollback also needs to address the response/feature cache, the feature pipeline's schema compatibility, and any batch/offline scoring jobs still running the bad version.

drills.q: What does CML (Continuous Machine Learning) add to a generic CI runner?
drills.a: It posts model metric comparisons and plots directly as pull-request comments and can provision cloud GPU runners for training -- making a model-quality regression visible in code review like a failing test.

drills.q: Explain why shadow deployment gives a statistical advantage over an unpaired A/B comparison, in terms of variance.
drills.a: Shadow sends the identical request to both models, producing paired observations -- shared request-level noise cancels out in the paired difference, reducing the variance of the estimated effect compared to an unpaired comparison across two separate traffic groups that don't share the same requests.

drills.q: A CI gate passes a new model because it clears an absolute AUC threshold of 0.85. What's the flaw in this gate design?
drills.a: It doesn't compare against the CURRENT CHAMPION's metric on the same fixed eval set -- if the champion is at 0.90 AUC, a 0.85 model is a real regression that an absolute-threshold-only gate would let through.

drills.q: Design a rollback for a real-time recommendation model with a response cache and a nightly batch re-scoring job. What does a naive rollback miss?
drills.a: A naive rollback only reverts the serving container. The full rollback needs: cache entries invalidated or version-tagged so stale bad-version outputs stop serving, the feature pipeline confirmed compatible with the reverted version's expected schema, and the nightly batch job's model version explicitly updated since it runs on a separate schedule and won't pick up a serving-only rollback.

drills.q: Explain how a rollback can itself introduce training-serving skew.
drills.a: If the feature pipeline was updated to support the newer model version (e.g. added a feature) and isn't reverted alongside the model, the rolled-back-to older model now receives feature vectors in a shape/distribution it was never trained on -- a mismatch the rollback created, not one that pre-existed.

drills.q: Why can shadow deployment never validate whether a new model improves a real business outcome, no matter the traffic volume?
drills.a: The shadow model's predictions are logged but never returned to a user or acted upon -- the causal path from 'model outputs X' to 'a real decision or action changes as a result' is never exercised, so you can measure that predictions differ but never that the difference is good.

drills.q: Design a canary ramp gate that decides 'hold / ramp / rollback' automatically rather than relying on a human glancing at a dashboard. What does it need before it can make any decision?
drills.a: It needs a pre-registered minimum sample size (based on a chosen minimum detectable effect) and a significance threshold (e.g. alpha=0.05) defined BEFORE the canary starts. The gate holds until sample size is reached, runs a significance test (e.g. t-test) on the outcome metric, ramps if canary is significantly better, rolls back if significantly worse, and holds if not yet significant.

drills.q: Why is shadow deployment fundamentally unable to validate a contextual bandit system, unlike a standard classifier?
drills.a: A bandit's future inputs depend on its own past served actions (the exploration/exploitation history) -- a shadow-mode bandit's logged predictions reflect what it WOULD have shown, but never generates the real served-action history that drives what the bandit would actually see and learn from next, so the comparison is measuring a structurally different process than real deployment.

drills.q: A fraud-detection canary shows improved fraud catch-rate at 20% traffic. Is that sufficient to ramp to 50%? What else must be checked?
drills.a: No -- false-positive rate must also be checked and gated, not just catch-rate/recall. A model that catches more fraud while also blocking significantly more legitimate transactions is a real regression on user experience and revenue even though the primary metric improved; both metrics need significance checks before ramping.

drills.q: Which orchestrator's DAG structure is discovered implicitly at runtime rather than declared upfront?
drills.a: Prefect -- flows are plain Python functions where the actual execution graph emerges as the function runs, supporting genuine runtime branching and dynamic loops.

drills.q: True or false: pre-Airflow-3, backfill was a first-class scheduler operation.
drills.a: False -- pre-3.0, backfill was CLI-only and disconnected from normal scheduler operation, or required a hand-rolled separate backfill DAG. Airflow 3 moved it into the scheduler.

drills.q: What is Dagster's primary orchestration abstraction, in one phrase?
drills.a: Software-defined assets -- the artifact produced (table, file, model) is primary, with native lineage tracking between assets.

drills.q: Explain what DAG versioning in Airflow 3 fixes and why it matters for correctness.
drills.a: Before it, a code deploy mid-flight while a DAG run was executing could cause the running instance to pick up new task definitions partway through, mixing old and new code inconsistently within one run. Airflow 3 pins a run to the exact version it started with through completion, and the UI associates every run with its specific version for auditing.

drills.q: A team notices their Dagster pipeline re-materializes a downstream asset every run even when upstream data hasn't changed. What's likely missing?
drills.a: A freshness/staleness policy wasn't explicitly configured -- skip-if-unchanged behavior isn't automatic just from declaring assets with the @asset decorator; it requires configuring the policy or partition-based logic that lets Dagster determine nothing relevant changed.

drills.q: An Airflow scheduler is falling behind as DAG count grows. What's the first thing to check before concluding you need to migrate orchestrators?
drills.a: Whether expensive computation sits at DAG-file module level (re-executed on every scheduler parse cycle) rather than inside task callables (executed only at actual run time) -- a common, fixable, non-architectural cause of scheduler slowdown.

drills.q: Compare how Airflow 3, Dagster, and Prefect each handle backfilling 90 days of data after a transformation bug fix.
drills.a: Airflow 3: scheduler-managed backfill across the date range via idempotent partition-parameterized tasks. Dagster: select the partition range in the UI and materialize, native one-click, with lineage flagging downstream assets needing re-materialization too. Prefect: re-trigger the deployment with date-range parameters, relying on flow logic rather than a first-class backfill UI primitive.

drills.q: Why does Dagster make it easiest to confirm which downstream artifacts need reprocessing after a data bug, compared to Airflow or Prefect?
drills.a: Its native asset lineage graph makes dependencies between assets explicit and automatically traceable -- downstream assets that consumed the buggy data are identifiable via the graph itself. Airflow and Prefect require manually reasoning about or separately tracking which downstream DAGs/flows consumed the affected data, since neither has an equivalent built-in lineage graph.

drills.q: A team is heavily invested in dbt for transformation logic. How does that change the orchestrator recommendation, and what's the counter-consideration?
drills.a: Dagster treats dbt models as first-class assets in one shared lineage graph with Python assets -- deeper than Airflow's typical 'dbt run as one opaque task' integration, arguing for Dagster. Counter-consideration: if the org has significant existing Airflow infrastructure and expertise elsewhere, introducing a second orchestrator has real operational overhead, and the right call depends on how large/central the dbt workload is relative to everything else.

drills.q: A platform team wants to mandate a single orchestrator company-wide for consistency. What's the staff-level position, and how do you evaluate a team's exception request?
drills.a: Consistency has real value but Airflow/Dagster/Prefect suit genuinely different workload shapes -- recommend a default/primary orchestrator with a documented, narrow exception process rather than a rigid mandate or ungoverned free-for-all. Evaluate exception requests by requiring a specific structural mismatch argument (e.g. dbt-asset-centricity, runtime-determined branching), not just developer preference.

drills.q: Explain the retry/failure semantics difference between Airflow's task-level retry and Dagster's asset-level retry, and whether one is strictly better.
drills.a: Airflow retries a task instance and blocks downstream tasks until resolved -- simple, task-scoped, and directly legible ('this task is blocking'). Dagster's asset-level retry leverages the lineage graph to reason about exactly which downstream assets become stale as a consequence. Not strictly better either way -- it's a tradeoff between explicit lineage-awareness (Dagster) and simpler, more directly legible task-blocking behavior (Airflow).

drills.q: Name the three distinct reproducibility gaps that experiment tracking, model registry, and data versioning each close.
drills.a: Tracking = reproduce a run (code/params/metrics). Model registry = govern which artifact is live where. Data versioning = reproduce the exact input data used.

drills.q: True or false: MLflow model registry stages let a single version hold both 'staging' and a canary role simultaneously.
drills.a: False -- stages are exclusive, one per version. That limitation is exactly why MLflow deprecated stages in favor of multi-assignable aliases.

drills.q: Which company acquired the DVC open-source project, and when?
drills.a: lakeFS acquired DVC from Iterative.ai on November 18, 2025.

drills.q: A 10-person team is deciding between W&B Teams and self-hosted MLflow. What's the rough monthly cost comparison, and what does the MLflow number leave out?
drills.a: W&B Teams ~$500/mo for 10 seats (~$50/user/mo). Self-hosted MLflow: ~$150-500/mo infra, but that excludes engineer time for setup/maintenance/on-call, which often exceeds the infra cost itself.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why DVC's checkout model doesn't scale well to a multi-TB data lake, and what LakeFS does differently.
drills.a: DVC checkout materializes real local file copies resolved from .dvc pointers -- copy-on-checkout, fine at GB scale, slow/expensive at TB+ scale. LakeFS implements branch/commit/merge as metadata operations directly over the object store with zero-copy branching, so creating an isolated branch is instant with no storage duplication.

drills.q: Why is a prompt change treated as having the same 'blast radius' as a model weight change?
drills.a: A wording change (added example, reordered instructions) can shift output quality, safety behavior, and token cost as significantly as swapping model weights -- but a prompt is far easier to edit with zero review gate since it's often just an inline string with no version history.

drills.q: A model's registry entry shows the artifact but no data-version tag on its originating run. Six months later, someone needs to explain why the model behaves a certain way. What's broken?
drills.a: The lineage chain is broken at the data-version link -- you have the weights but no reproducible path back to the exact training data snapshot, which blocks retraining, auditing, or explaining behavior tied to specific data characteristics.

drills.q: Design the promotion flow for a new model version using aliases instead of stages, including an eval gate. What's the atomic operation that makes rollback cheap?
drills.a: Register the version from a run's artifact, tag it 'candidate', run eval and check against a threshold, then reassign the 'champion' alias to it if it passes. Serving code resolves models:/name@champion at load time. Rollback = reassigning 'champion' back to the prior version, a single atomic registry operation, no redeploy.

drills.q: A prompt registry shows 'production' pointing at v14, but deployed behavior doesn't match v14's content. Walk through the debugging order.
drills.a: First check whether serving code actually resolves the alias at request/load time vs. caching or hardcoding an older version at deploy time. Second, check for a second code path pointed at a different alias or pinned version. Third, confirm the alias reassignment itself succeeded and targeted the right registered prompt name. If all check out, suspect the underlying model (a pinned model alias moved, or non-determinism at temperature>0) rather than the prompt registry.

drills.q: A team wants to skip a prompt registry because they deploy often and it 'feels like overhead.' Make the counter-argument, and state what would legitimately change your mind.
drills.a: Frequent deploys are exactly when prompt regressions are hardest to catch -- no diff between the working prompt and what shipped an hour ago, and rollback means finding the right prior code commit instead of reassigning an alias. Overhead (a registration call + alias reassignment) is small relative to the cost of an unreviewed regression reaching users. Would change the recommendation given a track record showing this system's prompt changes never caused a measurable regression across a meaningful sample -- and even then, keep at minimum a lightweight versioned history rather than fully unversioned strings.

drills.q: Explain the distinction between 'the pipeline didn't change' and 'the data didn't change,' with a concrete failure example.
drills.a: A training pipeline reading a live source table can run identical code against silently mutated underlying data (a backfill, a schema migration, new rows landing) between two runs -- the pipeline is unchanged but the data isn't, and without an explicit immutable data version tagged per run, this produces an unreproducible model even though 'nothing changed' from the code's perspective.

drills.q: True or false: it's safe to rebuild an image for prod from the same Dockerfile that was already tested in staging, as long as the source code hasn't changed.
drills.a: False -- an unpinned base image tag or transitive dependency can resolve differently at rebuild time even with identical source. Promote the same tested digest instead.

drills.q: What's ECR's per-GB storage price, and what's the typical storage reduction from a good untagged-image lifecycle rule?
drills.a: $0.10/GB-month; pruning untagged images older than ~14 days typically cuts storage 50-80%.

drills.q: Name the three components in cosign's keyless signing flow and what each does.
drills.a: OIDC provider (authenticates signer identity), Fulcio (issues short-lived certificate binding identity to an ephemeral keypair), Rekor (transparency log durably recording the signature event).

drills.q: A Kyverno image-verification policy exists in the cluster, but a pen tester successfully deploys an unsigned image. What's the first config field you check, and what value would explain it?
drills.a: validationFailureAction -- if set to Audit instead of Enforce, violations are logged but not blocked, letting unsigned images through despite the policy 'existing.'

drills.q: A Grype scan against a generated SBOM reports zero vulnerabilities for a Java service, but a manual audit finds a known-CVE'd library bundled inside an uber-jar. Explain the gap.
drills.a: SBOM generators struggle to resolve transitive dependencies in compiled/shaded artifacts -- a Java uber-jar that relocates/renames packages during shading breaks the generator's ability to statically recover the original dependency graph, so the vulnerable component never appears in the SBOM at all.

drills.q: Why should an SBOM be attached to an image via `cosign attest` rather than stored as a plain JSON file in an artifact bucket?
drills.a: A cosign attestation is a signed, digest-bound in-toto statement -- verifiable proof the SBOM belongs to and hasn't been altered relative to that specific image. A plain file has no cryptographic binding and could be swapped without detection.

drills.q: Compare ECR's and Nexus Pro's billing models for a team with high CI pull volume but modest storage footprint. Which one's bill grows faster with pull volume, and why?
drills.a: Nexus Pro bills storage AND data transfer combined under one consumption meter (~$0.90-1.10/GB beyond an included tier), so high pull volume directly drives the bill up regardless of stored data size. ECR bills storage separately from data transfer, so a high-pull, low-storage workload's ECR storage line stays small even though transfer costs still apply separately.

drills.q: Design the correct gate order for a CI pipeline stage that builds, SBOM-scans, signs, and pushes an image, and explain why the order matters.
drills.a: Build -> generate SBOM -> scan SBOM and fail on policy violation -> sign -> push -> (separately) promote by digest. Scanning before signing/pushing ensures a known-vulnerable image is never signed or shipped; signing after a passed scan gives the signature meaning as an implicit 'this passed policy' signal, not just 'this is authentic.'

drills.q: An org's ECR bill has grown steadily for a year despite no growth in deployed workload count, and a lifecycle policy targeting untagged images is already in place. What's the likely remaining cause, and how do you find it?
drills.a: The rule likely doesn't match the actual accumulation pattern -- e.g. it targets untagged images only, while the real growth is many TAGGED CI-preview images (pr-1042, pr-1043...) that are never cleaned up. Pull per-repository tagged image counts over time to confirm, then add a tagged-image-count-based expiration rule.

drills.q: A regulated client demands 'verifiable provenance,' and the team responds that their images are already signed with cosign and carry an SBOM attestation. Is that sufficient, and why or why not?
drills.a: Not by itself. Signing proves the artifact wasn't tampered with after signing by a known identity; the SBOM attests contents.
