Neither proves HOW the artifact was built -- SLSA provenance is a separate signed claim about source commit, builder identity, and build parameters, addressing build-process integrity that signature+SBOM don't cover.

drills.q: What changed about ECR's layer storage behavior in January 2026, and why does it matter for an org running many services off a shared base image?
drills.a: ECR began deduplicating each unique layer once across all repositories in the same private registry, instead of storing shared base-image layers once per repository. For an org with many services sharing a common base image, this meaningfully reduces total storage versus pre-2026 per-repository storage.

drills.q: True or false: a test suite passing against LocalStack is sufficient proof the same code will work against real AWS IAM policies.
drills.a: False -- AWS documentation states IAM policy evaluation and quotas are not fully modeled by emulators; a real staging AWS account is still needed for IAM/quota-sensitive validation.

drills.q: What sidecar container does Testcontainers use for automatic resource cleanup, and what triggers it?
drills.a: Ryuk -- it watches for the test-runner process's exit and removes every Testcontainers-labeled container/volume/network once the parent process dies.

drills.q: At single-user scale, are Ollama and vLLM's tokens/second roughly comparable or is there already a large gap?
drills.a: Roughly comparable -- both land in about the 130-180 tok/s band on the same hardware/model. The large gap (vLLM ~793 vs Ollama ~41 tok/s in one benchmark) appears specifically under concurrent load.

drills.q: A CI runner using Docker-in-Docker slowly runs out of disk space over several weeks with no single failing job pointing at the cause. What's the likely mechanism, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Ryuk's automatic cleanup is documented to fail on Docker-in-Docker/rootless-Docker CI, leaking Testcontainers-created containers silently. Fix: set TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true for that runner and add an explicit `docker container prune --filter "label=org.testcontainers=true"` step.

drills.q: Two engineers report different bugs from the same codebase despite both claiming to use 'the same devcontainer.' What's the likely misconfiguration?
drills.a: The devcontainer's base image is referenced by a mutable tag rather than a pinned digest -- the upstream image was rebuilt with different system package versions between when each engineer last built their container, so their actual environments silently diverged.

drills.q: Explain the architectural (not tuning-related) reason vLLM outperforms Ollama under concurrent load.
drills.a: vLLM implements continuous batching and PagedAttention-based KV-cache management specifically to serve many concurrent requests efficiently against shared GPU memory. Ollama, built on llama.cpp, is architected for single-user local convenience and doesn't implement the same concurrent-request-batching sophistication -- it's a structural design difference.

drills.q: Design a test suite for a service with a Postgres database and an S3 dependency. Assign each to LocalStack or Testcontainers and justify.
drills.a: Postgres -> Testcontainers: SQL dialect and constraint-enforcement fidelity matter for catching real bugs, worth the container startup cost. S3 (if the test is just 'did we call put_object correctly') -> LocalStack is sufficient and faster, since no IAM/quota-sensitive behavior is being exercised.

drills.q: A team's free-tier LocalStack dev environment resets all fixture data on every container restart, slowing onboarding. What are the two realistic options, and what does each cost?
drills.a: Script fast automatic fixture re-seeding at container startup (one-time engineering cost, also makes starting state version-controlled and explicit), or adopt LocalStack Cloud Pods (Base plan+, ~$45/month) for persistent state snapshot/restore across restarts -- an ongoing subscription cost.

drills.q: A team validated a RAG prototype entirely against Ollama locally, reports it's 'fast, ready to ship,' and wants to skip a load test before launch. What's the risk, and under what condition would skipping be reasonable?
drills.a: Risk: Ollama's single-user throughput says nothing about concurrent-load behavior, and the gap versus a production serving stack (e.g. vLLM) is architectural, not a missing tuning flag -- one benchmark shows a ~19x throughput gap under peak concurrent load. Skipping a dedicated load test is more reasonable only if genuine expected production concurrency stays in the single-digit range Ollama's benchmarks reasonably cover, and even then a lightweight concurrent smoke test is safer than none.

drills.q: Why is filtering `docker container prune` by the Testcontainers label important rather than pruning all stopped containers on a CI runner?
drills.a: A blanket prune could remove containers belonging to another concurrent job or process on the same shared runner that still needs them; filtering by the org.testcontainers=true label scopes cleanup to exactly the resources Ryuk would have been responsible for.

drills.q: What structural change happened to LocalStack's community and pro Docker image distribution in the 2026.3.0 release, and what does it NOT mean for free-tier users?
drills.a: The two images were unified into one; service access is now gated by auth-token entitlement instead of image choice. It does NOT mean the free tier gained access to everything pro has -- the free/Hobby tier still has a limited service subset and resets state on container restart; persistent state and broader coverage remain paid features.

drills.q: True or false: the safest way to rotate a secret is to revoke the old credential immediately after generating the new one, minimizing the exposure window.
drills.a: False -- revoking immediately, before every reader has picked up the new credential, causes an outage for any reader still using the old one. The grace period must exceed the slowest reader's refresh cadence.

drills.q: What's the 2026 consensus TTL range for a JWT access token, and why not just use 1 hour?
drills.a: 5-15 minutes. A 1-hour TTL means a compromised or should-be-revoked token stays dangerous for up to an hour with no additional infrastructure needed to bound that -- the TTL is a direct blast-radius cap.

drills.q: Why can't a legacy application with a hardcoded database connection string use Vault dynamic secrets as-is?
drills.a: Dynamic secrets require the application to be lease-aware -- able to request/renew a fresh credential before the lease's TTL expires. A hardcoded connection string read once at startup has no such renewal mechanism.

drills.q: A rotation script generates a new DB credential, immediately drops the old DB user, then updates the config store. Half the fleet starts throwing auth errors. Diagnose.
drills.a: The old credential was revoked before the grace period allowed slower readers (cached config, infrequent restarts) to pick up the new one -- classic dual-secret pattern violation. Fix: create new, wait for a grace period exceeding the slowest reader's refresh cadence, THEN revoke old.

drills.q: Explain why refresh token rotation with reuse detection makes a 30-day refresh token acceptably safe despite being long-lived.
drills.a: Every refresh token is single-use; using it invalidates itself and issues a new one. A stolen refresh token, once the legitimate client has rotated past it, becomes detectable the moment it's replayed -- the replay of an already-invalidated token is the theft signal, triggering revocation of the entire token family.

drills.q: A team adds a Redis-backed JWT deny list and reports request latency increased noticeably across the whole API. What's the likely mistake, and the fix?
drills.a: The deny-list lookup is being hit on every single request with no local caching. Fix: cache the 'not revoked' result locally with a short TTL (seconds), chosen against the actual revocation-propagation SLA needed, instead of hitting Redis on every request.

drills.q: An admin clicks 'revoke user session' in a pure short-TTL JWT system with no deny list. How long can the user realistically keep acting, and why?
drills.a: Up to the full remaining lifetime of their most recently issued access token (5-15 min TTL) -- the refresh token is invalidated immediately so no new access tokens can be minted, but an already-issued access token has no revocation mechanism and remains valid until its own exp.

drills.q: Design the rotation for a shared database credential used by 50 service instances with varying config-cache TTLs (some 1 minute, some 30 minutes) and a weekly deploy cadence for the slowest consumer. What determines the grace period?
drills.a: The grace period must exceed the SLOWEST reader's actual refresh mechanism -- here, that's whichever is longer between the 30-minute cache TTL and the weekly deploy cadence for any consumer that only re-reads config on restart/deploy. If any consumer only refreshes on deploy, the grace period effectively needs to span up to that deploy cadence, not just the longest cache TTL.

drills.q: Why does a Secrets Manager rotation Lambda demote the old credential to AWSPREVIOUS instead of deleting it in the finishSecret step, and what's the tradeoff of retaining it indefinitely?
drills.a: Retaining it as AWSPREVIOUS provides an immediate rollback path if the newly-promoted credential has a problem discovered shortly after rotation. The tradeoff: retaining it indefinitely leaves a valid-but-unused credential as its own lingering exposure -- teams should set an explicit retention/cleanup policy rather than leaving AWSPREVIOUS unmanaged forever.

drills.q: A fleet of 50 microservices shares a handful of databases; 40 are legacy with hardcoded connection strings, 10 are newer and cloud-native. Design the secrets strategy.
drills.a: Mixed approach: adopt Vault dynamic secrets for the 10 lease-aware-capable services (centralizes issuance/expiry/revocation, better amortized operational cost at scale), and keep disciplined static-secret dual-secret rotation for the 40 legacy services rather than forcing a refactor or forcing dynamic secrets onto apps that can't handle mid-operation lease expiry gracefully.

drills.q: A team claims caching JWT signature-verification results is equivalent in value to caching a Redis deny-list lookup. Evaluate and correct this claim.
drills.a: Not equivalent -- signature verification is a local cryptographic operation with no network call and negligible cost; caching it saves little and risks incorrectly treating a token as valid past a boundary if done wrong. Deny-list lookup caching avoids a real network round-trip to Redis on every request, a genuinely meaningful cost -- the two are different classes of optimization.

drills.q: True or false: SSM Parameter Store SecureString values are stored unencrypted and rely on IAM alone for protection.
drills.a: False -- SecureString values are encrypted at rest via KMS, free at standard tier, same as Secrets Manager's encryption.

drills.q: What's Secrets Manager's flat monthly fee per stored secret?
drills.a: $0.40/secret/month, prorated hourly, plus $0.05 per 10,000 API calls.

drills.q: Is AppConfig a replacement for Parameter Store and Secrets Manager, or a layer on top of them?
drills.a: A layer on top -- it sources data from Parameter Store, Secrets Manager, S3, or its own profiles, and adds canary rollout strategies with automatic rollback.

drills.q: A service fleet of 500 instances polling Parameter Store every 5 seconds starts seeing throttling errors. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: 500 instances / 5 sec = 100 req/sec, exceeding the 40 ops/sec standard-throughput ceiling. Fix: enable higher throughput mode (up to 3,000 ops/sec), understanding this then bills every account-wide API call at $0.05/10k, or reduce poll frequency / add local caching instead.

drills.q: A team wants automatic credential rotation for a self-hosted PostgreSQL instance not covered by Secrets Manager's native RDS/Aurora templates. What do they need to build?
drills.a: A custom rotation Lambda implementing the four-step contract: createSecret (stage new candidate), setSecret (apply to the actual Postgres instance), testSecret (verify it works), finishSecret (promote to AWSCURRENT, demote old to AWSPREVIOUS) -- Secrets Manager provides the framework/orchestration, not the Postgres-specific logic.

drills.q: Why is granting an IAM role read access to /myapp/* instead of /myapp/prod/api/* a real security risk, even within a single AWS account?
drills.a: It grants cross-environment and cross-component access -- a compromised or buggy prod api service could read staging secrets (often with weaker rotation/access hygiene) or other components' credentials it has no legitimate need for. Scope to the narrowest environment- and component-specific prefix.

drills.q: An engineer pushes a feature-flag change via `aws ssm put-parameter --overwrite` directly to production. Name the two capabilities they lose that AppConfig would have provided.
drills.a: No canary/percentage-based gradual rollout with bake time, and no automatic rollback triggered by a CloudWatch alarm breach -- the change is instantly and globally live to every reader on next poll, with no controlled blast radius and no automated recovery path.

drills.q: Calculate the monthly cost of storing 300 static config values in Secrets Manager versus migrating them to Parameter Store SecureString, ignoring API call costs.
drills.a: Secrets Manager: 300 x $0.40 = $120/month ($1,440/year). Parameter Store SecureString at standard tier: $0, assuming each value is under 4KB and total stays under 10,000 parameters and standard throughput isn't exceeded.

drills.q: Design an AppConfig deployment strategy for a high-risk feature flag rollout that needs both controlled blast radius and per-user consistency during the rollout. What two mechanisms do you combine, and why aren't they redundant?
drills.a: A percentage-based canary deployment strategy with defined bake time and a CloudWatch-alarm-triggered auto-rollback (controls blast radius / limits how much traffic sees a bad change before it's caught), combined with entity-based sticky targeting (2026+) keyed on a stable user/session identifier (ensures a given user consistently sees the same flag state throughout the rollout rather than flipping per-request). They solve different problems -- blast radius control vs. rollout consistency -- so both are needed together.

drills.q: A rotation Lambda for a production RDS credential has been silently failing its testSecret step for two months. What's the observable state of the secret during that time, and why didn't it cause an outage sooner?
drills.a: The secret remains on its last successfully-rotated AWSCURRENT credential -- rotation halts before finishSecret runs if testSecret fails, so the currently-working credential is never invalidated. The lack of an outage masked the failure; the real gap is no alerting on the rotation failure itself, only on downstream symptoms that would eventually appear once the credential's max age/expiration policy (if any) forces the issue.

drills.q: Two teams both create a parameter at /shared/db-host with different intended meanings, and a deploy in one service accidentally reads the other team's value. What's the actual root cause and the structural fix?
drills.a: Root cause: ambiguous, non-namespaced path naming with no per-team/per-component scoping under the shared prefix. Fix: enforce strict /{app}/{env}/{component}/{key} namespacing everywhere, including genuinely shared values (e.g. /platform/common/db-host with an explicit owning namespace), rather than an unscoped /shared/ prefix multiple teams write into independently.

drills.q: True or false: a PR that passes every test and has no correctness bugs cannot fail a principal-level review.
drills.a: False -- it can still have large architectural blast radius, hidden coupling, or be the wrong problem to solve right now, none of which a test suite catches.

drills.q: What's the one-sentence question that turns a blast-radius review from guesswork into something concrete?
drills.a: 'If the owning team changes this in the most likely next way, does this PR's assumption still hold?'

drills.q: Is 'I'd have structured this differently' with no stated cost a blocking comment or a suggestion?
drills.a: A suggestion -- it should be phrased as 'consider,' not used to block a correct, tested PR.

drills.q: A PR adds a direct database read from service A into service B's internal schema, bypassing B's API. It passes all tests. What's the review concern, and how do you surface it without omniscience about B's future plans?
drills.a: Blast radius: B's team can no longer freely change that table's schema or add a write path without knowing A silently depends on its current shape. Surface it by asking B's team directly whether their likely next change would break this assumption -- that question is the review comment.

drills.q: Explain why hidden coupling is harder to catch in review than an interface violation, and what mechanical check helps.
drills.a: An interface violation is checkable by a linter/type checker. Hidden coupling is an implicit runtime assumption (ordering, timing, always-populated field) with nothing declaring it anywhere. The mechanical check: grep every caller of anything the PR changes the behavior of, and read their assumptions, not just whether they still compile.

drills.q: A reviewer blocks your PR with 'I wouldn't have built it this way.' Apply the triage test: how do you respond?
drills.a: Ask them to name the specific cost and when it manifests. If they can name a concrete, compounding cost, treat it as a real objection and address it. If no cost is named, it's a preference -- push back on the merits rather than complying reflexively.

drills.q: Why does teaching-oriented feedback (naming the transferable pattern) matter more at senior/principal level than simply fixing the line?
drills.a: It's a multiplier: the same category of mistake shouldn't recur in the author's next 50 PRs. Corrective-only feedback ('fix this line') produces compliance on one PR; naming the pattern behind it produces judgment the author can apply without this reviewer present next time.

drills.q: A staff engineer from another team blocks your PR on an architectural concern you believe misunderstands your system's actual constraints. What's the correct sequence of moves?
drills.a: Ask them to state the specific cost and scenario concretely. Supply the missing local context directly. If the concern dissolves once context is exchanged, that's a legitimate resolution. If they still insist, escalate to a shared forum or third senior engineer rather than unilaterally overriding or silently standing off.

drills.q: A principal engineer's review comments are always technically correct, but the team increasingly avoids sending them risky PRs. Diagnose the failure and name the observable evidence.
drills.a: Being correct isn't sufficient -- feedback delivery is training data for team behavior, and purely corrective (non-developmental) feedback teaches people to route around the reviewer. Observable evidence: PRs to this reviewer shrink and get more conservative relative to the same authors' PRs to others, and risky architectural decisions ship without going through this reviewer at all -- the opposite of what review authority is for.

drills.q: Distinguish a compounding cost from a one-time cost in a design disagreement, and explain why the distinction changes the right call under deadline pressure.
drills.a: One-time cost: paid once, doesn't recur (an awkward one-off migration). Compounding cost: recurs and grows (every future feature in this area works around a wrong abstraction). Under deadline pressure, a one-time cost is often legitimate to accept and ship; a compounding cost is usually cheaper to pay immediately than repeatedly at growing scale -- name a plausible next occurrence to validate the claim that a cost actually compounds.

drills.q: As AI-assisted review absorbs mechanical checks (import verification, style, null-safety patterns), what happens to the principal-level human review job, and why can't AI review tooling absorb it too?
drills.a: The human review budget concentrates on architectural blast radius and 'is this the right problem to solve,' because both require organizational context (roadmap, dependency graph's likely future changes, prior incident history) that repo-local AI tooling structurally cannot access -- the job doesn't shrink, it gets more concentrated and more valuable.

drills.q: True or false: trunk-based development means committing directly to main with no branches at all.
drills.a: False -- it means short-lived branches (under ~24h) merged into main at least daily, with incomplete work hidden behind feature flags, not zero branching.

drills.q: Name the three prerequisites for trunk-based development to work in practice, not just in name.
drills.a: Fast/reliable CI, a merge queue, and feature-flag discipline.

drills.q: Which IDE shipped native git worktree UI in its 2026.1 release?
drills.a: JetBrains.

drills.q: Two PRs each pass CI independently, merge back-to-back, and main breaks even though neither PR's own CI run showed a problem. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No merge queue -- each PR was tested against main-at-branch-time, not the actual resulting state after the other PR landed. Fix: adopt a merge queue that serially re-tests each PR against the real current main before it merges.

drills.q: Explain why squash-merge is bisect-friendly and what it costs.
drills.a: Every commit on main becomes atomic and independently testable, so bisect's binary search converges on a coherent state every time. It costs the true intra-feature development history -- false starts and fine-grained fix commits collapse into one commit.

drills.q: Why does a single shared git checkout break down when running several AI coding agents against one repo concurrently?
drills.a: All agents share one working directory and index -- one agent's file write can be read mid-edit by another, git status becomes meaningless with concurrent changes, and there's real lock contention on the index. A worktree per agent isolates the working directory and index while sharing one object database.

drills.q: What does a git worktree NOT automatically duplicate when you create one, and why does this matter for agent setups?
drills.a: Untracked local state, like .env files -- worktree only clones git-tracked content. Each new agent worktree needs untracked config copied in explicitly, or its dev environment silently uses stale/missing config.

drills.q: Why is rebasing an already-shared, pushed branch categorically different from rebasing your own unpushed local branch?
drills.a: Rebase produces new commit SHAs (same tree, different parent). On a pushed branch others have pulled, this creates a genuinely diverged history with no shared ancestor at those points for them -- their next pull duplicates commits or fails. On your own unpushed branch, there's no shared state to diverge, so it's safe to rebase freely.

drills.q: A team's git bisect results have been unreliable for months and nobody trusts them. What do you check first, and what's the actual root-cause fix versus the per-instance rescue?
drills.a: Check whether branching topology has drifted from trunk-based into long-lived branches with merge commits, which breaks bisect's linearity assumption -- this is the most common root cause. Per-instance rescue: rebase a suspect range onto a synthetic linear line before bisecting it. Root-cause fix: restore genuinely short-lived branches and consistent squash-merging so every FUTURE bisect is reliable without rescue.

drills.q: Design the branching workflow for 40 engineers plus a dozen AI agents working against one repo, avoiding both merge chaos and agent-collision chaos.
drills.a: Trunk-based with all three prerequisites (fast CI, merge queue, feature flags) for the shared branching strategy. Each AI agent gets its own git worktree on its own short-lived branch, sharing the team's single object database, integrating through the SAME merge-queue-and-flag pipeline as human work. Branch-age limits in CI catch both humans and agents drifting long. Squash-merge given the volume of agent commits that would otherwise clutter main's history.

drills.q: A team resists shortening feature branches, arguing 'our features are just bigger than a day of work.' What's the actual gap this argument is masking?
drills.a: Usually a feature-flag gap wearing a branch-lifetime costume -- a large feature can still merge incrementally, dark behind a flag, in small daily pieces, flipped on only when complete. 'The feature is big' argues for flagging, not for a long branch; conflating the two produces trunk-based-in-name-only.

drills.q: What refactor from Fowler's catalogue targets a Long Method smell?
drills.a: Extract Method.

drills.q: True or false: a refactor is allowed to change observable behavior as long as the code looks cleaner afterward.
drills.a: False -- behavior preservation is the defining property of a refactor. A behavior-changing change is a rewrite, not a refactor, and needs the corresponding review scrutiny.

drills.q: What percentage of enterprise strangler migrations (2022-2025 analysis) stalled before 90 days without replacing their first monolith component?
Explain Replace Conditional with Polymorphism using a concrete example, and state the payoff for adding a new case later.
drills.a: A switch/if-chain branching on type (e.g. shipping cost by carrier) is replaced with a class hierarchy where each branch becomes a subclass overriding a shared method. Payoff: adding a new carrier becomes adding one new subclass instead of hunting down and editing every scattered switch statement across the codebase.

drills.q: Why does the Strangler Fig pattern require a routing layer specifically, and what does that layer let you do that a big-bang cutover can't?
drills.a: The router (proxy/gateway/flag) decides per-request whether legacy or new code serves it, allowing per-capability cutover and per-capability rollback. A big-bang cutover has no such component -- it's all-or-nothing, so a problem in any part means rolling back the entire system at once.

drills.q: A strangler migration project picks its 'logical' but slow-to-build first capability for architectural cleanliness. Using the 90-day velocity data, explain why this is a mistake.
drills.a: Projects extracting under 5% of monolith functionality in the first 90 days fail 92% of the time -- the mechanism is organizational: an invisible-progress infrastructure phase erodes executive patience before anything ships. The first capability should be chosen for shipping speed and visibility, not architectural elegance.

drills.q: What is a shadow-traffic (dark-launch) verification phase, and what happens if it's skipped?
drills.a: Running the legacy and new implementations in parallel against real traffic and diffing their outputs before cutting the router over. Skipping it means silent divergence is discovered only after cutover, in production, potentially as a customer-facing incident instead of a caught log discrepancy.

drills.q: A migration cuts every capability's router over successfully, but 18 months later the legacy system is still running in production alongside the new one. Diagnose the failure and name the fix.
drills.a: Cutting the router over per capability was mistaken for finishing the migration -- decommissioning the legacy code is a distinct milestone that got skipped once organizational attention moved on. Fix: track decommissioning as its own explicit, separately tracked milestone per capability, not an assumed automatic follow-on to cutover.

drills.q: A refactoring pitch framed as 'the code quality here is bad' keeps getting deprioritized every planning cycle. Reframe it using the principles in this module.
drills.a: Tie the specific, catalogue-named refactor to a specific, already-observed production cost (e.g. three incidents in two months traced to this exact conditional-on-type logic, costing N hours of on-call time each) using the same currency (incident cost, deploy risk) the stakeholder already prioritizes features in -- not an abstract code-quality appeal they can't weigh against a concrete feature request.

drills.q: An org successfully strangler-migrated the highest-visibility 30% of a legacy monolith over 18 months, but the remaining 70% (harder, more tangled, less visible) has stalled for 6 months. Diagnose and propose a path forward.
drills.a: The easy, high-visibility capabilities were deliberately migrated first (per the early-velocity playbook), which means the remaining 70% is disproportionately harder to extract AND harder to fund, since it produces no comparable visible win. The path forward requires reframing the pitch around the concrete, growing cost of running two systems indefinitely (doubled maintenance burden, unmonitored legacy risk) rather than an abstract 'finish the migration' appeal -- and honestly testing whether continuing is even still worth it against that cost.

drills.q: Why doesn't dependency-mapping tooling fully eliminate the risk of a strangler migration's timeline blowing out (a 6-month estimate becoming 18 months)?
drills.a: Static call-graph analysis can surface code-level dependencies more completely than manual reverse-engineering, reducing the volume of surprises -- but legacy systems often have runtime-only coupling (shared database tables with no code reference, timing assumptions, config-driven branching) that static analysis doesn't capture, so real production-like testing still surfaces genuine surprises the tooling couldn't predict.

drills.q: What defect-density reduction range do cited industrial TDD case studies (IBM, Microsoft) report?
drills.a: Roughly 40-90%.

drills.q: True or false: a CI gate that requires a new test for new logic guarantees the test is high quality.
drills.a: False -- it only enforces that a test exists (the mechanical form of the practice), not that its assertions actually verify behavior. A mutation-testing audit is needed to check quality.

drills.q: What's the one genuine PREREQUISITE (not refinement) chaos engineering needs before it's safe to run at all?
drills.a: Mature observability and a fast, tested rollback/abort mechanism.

drills.q: Explain the 2026-specific argument for writing a test before delegating implementation to an AI coding agent.
drills.a: A failing test is a falsifiable oracle the agent can build against; a vague natural-language prompt gives the agent no such oracle, and its documented failure mode is confidently building on a wrong assumption rather than asking for clarification.

drills.q: A team announces 'we do TDD now' but a code-shape audit shows tests written after implementation, matching it line for line. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No enforcement mechanism -- the practice depended on individual discipline, which eroded under deadline pressure. Fix: a CI check blocking a PR with new business logic and no new test that fails on main, converting the practice from a request into a policy.

drills.q: Why does contract testing specifically require starting with the highest-incident-cost service boundary rather than rolling out broadly?
drills.a: The provider team has to do the verification work but the consumer team feels most of the pain when it's skipped -- an incentive mismatch. Starting where the provider has recently felt real production pain from a break gives them their own motivation to invest, rather than mandating uncompensated work everywhere at once.

drills.q: A Testcontainers rollout reverts to mocks within a quarter. What's the most likely root cause, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No one owns the shared container-startup infrastructure, so flaky starts (port collisions, image pull timeouts) get blamed on 'the tests' rather than fixed as infrastructure. Fix: assign explicit ownership of the harness with the same seriousness as any shared CI tooling, plus a documented startup-failure runbook.

drills.q: A green, 100%-line-coverage AI-generated test suite let a regression ship anyway. Explain the mechanism and the systematic fix.
drills.a: Tests assert mock-call structure or implementation details rather than observable behavior, so no assertion fails even when the real behavior is wrong -- coverage measures execution, not verification. Systematic fix: run mutation testing (mutmut/Stryker/PIT) periodically against critical modules to measure whether tests actually catch deliberately introduced bugs.

drills.q: An org wants to adopt TDD, contract testing, Testcontainers, and chaos engineering simultaneously as one quality initiative. What's wrong, and how would you sequence it instead?
drills.a: Each practice has a distinct adoption obstacle requiring dedicated organizational attention; doing all four at once dilutes the focus any one needs to stick, producing a 'we tried everything, nothing stuck' outcome. Sequence instead by tracing the org's actual recent incidents to root cause: recurring integration-boundary bugs -> Testcontainers/pyramid work first; cross-service breaking changes -> contract testing first; a fallback path that failed once it mattered -> chaos first; defects in poorly-understood complex logic -> TDD first.

drills.q: Six months after enforcing test-presence gates (new-logic-needs-a-test, contract verification as a deploy gate, Testcontainers as default), a mutation-testing audit shows most tests would still pass against deliberately broken implementations. What does this reveal, and what's the fix?
drills.a: It reveals the expected limit of presence-based gates: they enforce that something got written, not that it's good. This isn't evidence the practices failed -- it's evidence presence and quality need separate enforcement layers. Fix: add a quality-measuring layer on top (mutation-score thresholds in CI, pact matcher-strictness audits, chaos-finding follow-through tracking).

drills.q: Why is chaos engineering's adoption curve steeper than TDD's, contract testing's, or Testcontainers', specifically?
drills.a: The other three can be adopted incrementally with limited downside if done imperfectly. Chaos engineering's prerequisite (observability + fast rollback) must exist BEFORE the practice is safe to run at all -- skipping it and attempting an ambitious first experiment risks turning it into an actual production incident, which reliably kills organizational appetite for the practice afterward.

drills.q: True or false: a test with no assertions can still achieve 100% line coverage on the code it executes.
drills.a: True -- coverage only tracks execution, not whether the test checked anything about the result. This is Martin Fowler's 'Assertion-Free Testing' anti-pattern.

drills.q: What does it mean for a mutant to 'survive' mutation testing?
drills.a: Every test in the suite still passed despite the mutation changing the code's actual behavior -- meaning a real, deliberate behavior change went completely undetected, the exact shape of an unnoticed regression.

drills.q: Name the three mutation testing tools for Python, JVM, and JS/TS respectively.
drills.a: mutmut (Python), PIT/pitest (JVM: Java, Kotlin), Stryker/StrykerJS (JavaScript/TypeScript; Stryker.NET for C#).

drills.q: A team wants to gate merges at a 100% mutation score. What's wrong with this target, mechanically?
drills.a: Equivalent mutants -- mutations that are syntactically different but behaviorally identical to the original code under every input -- can never be killed by any test, so 100% is an unreachable target in any non-trivial codebase; chasing it wastes engineering effort or pressures people into contorting code just to eliminate equivalent mutants.

drills.q: Why is full mutation testing expensive, mechanically, and what's the rough cost multiplier?
drills.a: Each mutant requires a full rerun of the relevant test suite to classify kill/survive, and a modest codebase can generate hundreds to thousands of mutants -- naive full runs commonly cost 10-100x the underlying test suite's own runtime.

drills.q: A team mandates an 80% mutation-score CI gate on day one against a legacy codebase with historically weak tests. Predict the failure mode.
drills.a: Recreates the same Goodhart's-Law dynamic that broke coverage-as-a-target: intense pressure to satisfy the gate quickly produces either blocked PRs on unrelated pre-existing debt or superficial tests written specifically to kill mutants rather than genuinely verify behavior. PIT's guidance is to start around 70% and ratchet up as the suite genuinely improves.

drills.q: How does PIT use existing coverage data as a cost optimization before running mutants?
drills.a: It skips placing mutants on lines with zero test coverage, since a mutant there would trivially survive (no test reaches it) -- that outcome is already known from a plain coverage report, so PIT avoids wasting a full test-suite rerun confirming a certain result.

drills.q: Explain how StrykerJS's --incremental mode changes mutation testing's practical cost profile, with the reported numbers.
drills.a: It caches the previous run's mutant results in reports/stryker-incremental.json and only re-mutates/re-tests code changed since the last run, rather than the whole codebase. Reported real-world improvement: roughly 30 minutes down to under 2 minutes on typical PR-sized diffs -- the difference between mutation testing being a nightly-only batch job and living inside PR-gated CI.

drills.q: A mutant flips `age >= 18` to `age > 18` and survives. Diagnose the specific test gap, and explain why adding more non-boundary tests would not fix it.
drills.a: No existing test case exercises the exact boundary value age == 18 -- every test is either strictly above 18 (both operators agree) or strictly below (both agree). Only a test asserting the expected classification at exactly 18 can kill this mutant, because that's the only input where >= and > diverge; coverage of the line was already 100%, so more non-boundary tests add nothing to killing this specific mutant.

drills.q: Design a mutation testing rollout for a team that has 85% line coverage they're proud of and has never run mutation testing before. What do you tell them first, and what do you NOT do?
drills.a: Reset expectations: 85% line coverage says nothing about assertion quality, and surviving mutants in 'covered' code should be treated as new information, not a failure of the existing number. Scope the first run to one business-critical module, treat survivors as a small actionable backlog, and run it as a visibility tool for several cycles BEFORE gating any PR on a threshold -- don't run full-codebase mutation on day one and don't gate merges immediately.

drills.q: How would you decide which modules in a large codebase are worth the cost of mutation testing at all?
drills.a: Scope by regression cost and change frequency, not codebase size: modules where a silent behavior regression is expensive (billing, auth, anything touching money or access control) and modules with high churn are highest value. Stable, rarely-changed utility/glue code with minimal business logic is a poor use of the expensive per-mutant test-rerun cost. If the highest-risk module also has the slowest test suite, invest in speeding up that suite first, since mutation cost is a direct multiple of test runtime.

drills.q: What tool would you reach for if a JVM process is alive (health check passes) but making no progress?
drills.a: A thread dump -- jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print -- to see every thread's state and stack, and check for an auto-detected deadlock.

drills.q: True or false: ulimit -c is unlimited by default on most Linux distributions.
drills.a: False -- it defaults to 0, meaning no core dump is written at all unless explicitly raised via `ulimit -c unlimited` or a systemd unit's LimitCORE=infinity.

drills.q: What command gives you a live Python process's current call stack for every thread, with zero instrumentation and no restart?
drills.a: py-spy dump --pid <pid>

drills.q: Explain the difference between shallow size and retained size in a heap dump, with a concrete example of why the distinction matters.
drills.a: Shallow size is what the object itself occupies; retained size is the total memory freed if the object became unreachable (the object plus everything it exclusively keeps alive). A small HashMap instance has a tiny shallow size but can have a massive retained size if it holds millions of cached entries -- only retained size (via MAT's Dominator Tree) reveals this.

drills.q: A JVM service's memory grows steadily toward OOM. What's a cheaper first diagnostic step than a full heap dump, and what does it show?
drills.a: jmap -histo:live <pid> -- prints a live object histogram (class name, instance count, aggregate bytes) without writing a full .hprof file, often enough to spot an obviously runaway allocation (millions of instances of a class that should have a few thousand) at a fraction of the cost of a full dump.

drills.q: Why is it safe to run py-spy dump against a live production process, mechanically?
drills.a: py-spy reads the target Python interpreter's process memory from outside via OS-level inspection (ptrace-equivalent), rather than injecting code or requiring pre-installed hooks -- it doesn't pause or measurably slow the target process for a dump operation.

drills.q: A Python worker hangs with no crash or error log. What should you do before restarting it, and why?
drills.a: Run py-spy dump --pid <pid> first -- it takes milliseconds to seconds and shows every thread's exact current stack. Restarting first destroys the only evidence of what the process was actually stuck on, meaning the bug may recur with no additional diagnostic information ever gained.

drills.q: Contrast Parca's and Pyroscope's approaches to continuous profiling, including overhead numbers, and explain when you'd pick one over the other.
drills.a: Parca uses eBPF at the kernel level, needs no per-language SDK, reported under 1% overhead -- operationally simpler across a polyglot fleet. Pyroscope uses language-runtime sampling (~100Hz), needs a per-language agent, reported 1-3% overhead but gives richer language-aware stack detail eBPF can struggle to resolve in JIT-compiled code. Pick eBPF/Parca for a polyglot fleet wanting one collector; pick Pyroscope if deep in one language ecosystem wanting richer frame detail and already invested in Grafana/Prometheus tooling.

drills.q: Why does jstack auto-detect deadlocks but py-spy does not, for the equivalent Python scenario?
drills.a: The JVM has first-class, centralized bookkeeping of synchronized monitor locks, letting jstack walk the held-by/waiting-for graph across all threads to detect a genuine cycle programmatically. Python's threading.Lock has no equivalent interpreter-level centralized tracking a stack-dumping tool can query -- py-spy shows each thread's stack (including that it's blocked in acquire()), but reconstructing the lock-cycle graph requires manual cross-referencing of which locks each thread waits on versus holds.

drills.q: Design a debugging plan for a production issue that recurs roughly once a week at unpredictable times and is gone by the time anyone investigates. What category of tool is required, and what's a real gap in that tool for a suspected deadlock specifically?
drills.a: Point-in-time tools (dumps, one-off py-spy runs) require being present at the right moment, which is unreliable for unpredictable weekly timing -- continuous profiling (Pyroscope or Parca) running always-on means the profile data for the exact incident window already exists and can be queried retroactively. Gap: continuous profilers are typically CPU/memory samplers, not thread-state/lock-cycle detectors, so for a suspected deadlock specifically, pair continuous profiling with an alerting-triggered automated thread dump capture (a script running jstack/jcmd when a latency alert fires) to close that gap.

drills.q: A candidate says they always take a heap dump first for any JVM production issue since it 'gives the most information.' Critique this as a default strategy.
drills.a: A full heap dump is the most expensive standard capture (potentially minutes of impact on a large heap, historically a full application pause on older tooling) and only answers 'what's retaining memory' -- irrelevant if the actual symptom is a hang, deadlock, or CPU-bound slowness with no memory growth. The correct approach is diagnosing the symptom category first (crash/hang/memory growth/slow) and picking the cheapest tool that answers that specific question, not defaulting to the most expensive tool regardless of symptom.

drills.q: What is TD3's standard default for the delayed policy update ratio d?
drills.a: d=2 -- the actor and target networks update once for every 2 critic updates.

drills.q: True or false: a deterministic policy like DDPG's actor explores on its own without any added mechanism.
drills.a: False -- a deterministic policy outputs one exact action per state with no inherent randomness. Exploration noise (e.g. Gaussian noise on the actor's output) must be added externally at data-collection time.

drills.q: What target value does TD3 use given twin critics Q1 and Q2?
drills.a: y = r + gamma * min(Q1_target(s', a~), Q2_target(s', a~)) -- the MIN of both target critics, not an average or either one alone.

drills.q: Explain the specific mechanism by which DDPG's actor and critic can compound each other's errors, leading to sudden training collapse.
drills.a: The actor's gradient ascent walks toward whatever action the critic currently rates highest. If that rating is inflated (overestimation), the actor exploits it, and because the critic's own bootstrap target is computed using the actor's chosen next action, the inflated estimate feeds back into the critic's own training target -- compounding across updates rather than self-correcting.

drills.q: Why can't Double DQN's selection/evaluation decoupling be applied directly to fix TD3's overestimation problem?
drills.a: Double DQN's fix requires a discrete argmax operation to decouple between an online and target network. TD3's actor outputs a single continuous action directly with no discrete argmax step to decouple -- so TD3 instead trains two independent critics and takes their min, which works without needing any discrete selection step.

drills.q: What specific failure geometry does target policy smoothing fix, and why is it a distinct fix from twin critics?
drills.a: It fixes sharp, narrow Q-value peaks at one specific action that a deterministic actor could converge onto and exploit -- a local, likely-spurious function-approximation artifact. Twin critics instead fix systemic overestimation bias spread across the value surface broadly -- two independently motivated fixes for two different failure geometries.

drills.q: Write SAC's soft value function and explain why folding entropy into it produces a genuinely different optimal policy than an entropy bonus added only to the actor's loss.
drills.a: V(s) = E_a[Q(s,a) - alpha*log pi(a|s)]. Because entropy is part of the value function used in Q's own bootstrap target (Q(s,a)=E[r+gamma*V(s')]), it propagates through every future backup, not just the current gradient step -- making the actual fixed point of training a policy that trades reward against staying spread out at every future state, not merely a reward-only optimum trained with extra exploration noise.

drills.q: Derive SAC's automatic temperature update and explain the direction alpha moves when the policy's current entropy falls below the target entropy.
drills.a: J(alpha) = E[-alpha*(log pi(a|s) + H_bar)]. When entropy is below target (log pi(a|s) too large in magnitude / policy too concentrated), the gradient pushes alpha UP, increasing the entropy term's weight and encouraging more exploration -- self-adjusting rather than a fixed, hand-tuned constant.

drills.q: A team trains TD3 in simulation for a robot arm, gets excellent simulated performance, but the policy fails badly on real hardware. Is this a TD3 bug? What's the actual issue and fix?
drills.a: Not a TD3 bug -- this is the sim-to-real gap. Neither TD3's twin critics, delayed updates, nor target smoothing address discrepancies between simulated and real dynamics (friction, latency, sensor noise). The fix is domain randomization during simulated training (varying physical parameters so the policy generalizes) or real-world fine-tuning, not a change to the RL algorithm itself.

drills.q: Design a safety-constrained continuous controller using SAC for a datacenter cooling system (never exceed a rack temperature threshold). Does SAC's entropy maximization provide any safety guarantee here?
drills.a: No -- entropy maximization encourages the policy to stay diverse/unconcentrated for exploration and robustness, but says nothing about whether that diversity is SAFE; a max-entropy policy can place probability mass on constraint-violating actions just as easily as a low-entropy one. Safety requires an explicit addition: a constrained MDP formulation (a cost signal plus Lagrangian-adapted penalty) or a hard shielding mechanism that overrides the learned action at execution time.

drills.q: Why would you prefer TD3 over SAC for a deployment scenario requiring a highly reproducible, auditable exact control policy?
drills.a: SAC's policy remains genuinely stochastic even after convergence -- some residual entropy is provably part of its optimal solution unless alpha is pushed to near zero. TD3's near-deterministic actor is easier to audit and reproduce exactly for regulatory or safety-review purposes, at the cost of needing manually tuned exploration noise during training instead of automatic entropy-based exploration.

drills.q: What are MCTS's four phases, in order?
drills.a: Selection, Expansion, Simulation (rollout), Backpropagation.

drills.q: Roughly how many legal moves does Go have per position on average, versus chess?
drills.a: Go: roughly 250. Chess: roughly 35.

drills.q: True or false: MCTS, once search completes, executes its entire most-visited simulated line of moves before replanning.
drills.a: False -- MCTS commits to only the single immediate real action with the highest visit count at the root, then discards the tree and replans fresh from the new real state.

drills.q: Write the UCT formula and identify which part of it comes from the UCB1 bandit algorithm.
drills.a: UCT(s,a) = Q(s,a) + c*sqrt(ln N(s)/N(s,a)). The entire exploration term (the sqrt confidence-bound expression) is a direct instantiation of UCB1's bandit exploration bonus, applied at every node by treating each node's children as an independent multi-armed bandit.

drills.q: What replaces the random rollout in AlphaZero, and why is that a variance improvement, not just a speed improvement?
drills.a: A learned value/policy network f_theta(s) -> (p(.|s), v(s)) replaces the rollout. A random playout to a game's end is an extremely high-variance, weakly-informative signal, while a trained value network gives a much lower-variance point estimate in one forward pass, having learned correlations with actual outcomes across many training games.

drills.q: A Dyna-Q implementation trains slower than plain model-free Q-learning on the same task. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: The learned model is a poor approximation of the true dynamics (common early in training or in rarely-visited states), so simulated updates are training the Q-function toward a systematically wrong target -- the same failure signature as DQN's 'stable loss, wrong bootstrap target' problem, just introduced via the model instead of a stale target network.

drills.q: Explain why PUCT's prior term p(s,a) is especially important for a game like Go rather than a lower-branching-factor game.
drills.a: With ~250 legal moves per position, uniformly exploring every child a few times before any accumulates meaningful statistics (pure UCT's early behavior) wastes an enormous fraction of a realistic simulation budget. PUCT's prior immediately concentrates search on the subset of moves the policy network already considers promising, which matters far more when the branching factor is large.

drills.q: Derive, informally, why compounding model error is a fundamentally different problem from one-step model prediction error, and state the practical mitigation.
drills.a: A model with per-step error epsilon produces rollout divergence that grows roughly with horizon times epsilon in a favorable case, and worse when small errors push the trajectory out-of-distribution for the model (a further, self-reinforcing error source). One-step accuracy says nothing about whether multi-step errors compound benignly or catastrophically. Mitigation: short planning horizons with frequent replanning against real observations, rather than long open-loop plans.

drills.q: Compare the role of a learned value function in AlphaZero's MCTS versus PPO's critic. Are they serving the same purpose?
drills.a: Related but structurally different. PPO's critic shapes a bootstrapped advantage estimate used to compute a gradient for training the actor's parameters -- it doesn't directly select actions at decision time. AlphaZero's value network is used INSIDE the search itself, at decision time, to estimate leaf-node values that directly influence which branches get explored and which real action is ultimately chosen.

drills.q: Design a model-based path-planning system for a warehouse robot sharing space with unpredictable human workers. What planning horizon and replanning frequency should you use, and why?
drills.a: Short planning horizon with frequent (ideally every real step) replanning, MPC-style. The map's deterministic portions can be modeled and planned through accurately, but the unpredictable elements (human/robot movement) are exactly where model predictions are least reliable, and errors there compound fastest in the parts of the plan furthest from the current observed real state -- frequent replanning lets real observations correct the plan before that error compounds.

drills.q: A colleague claims model-based RL is strictly more sample-efficient than model-free RL with no real downside. Push back with the specific mechanism.
drills.a: Model-based sample efficiency is conditional on model accuracy, not unconditional. A learned model's compounding error over multi-step rollouts or planning can train a value function or select actions against a systematically wrong picture of the world -- a risk pure model-free methods never carry, since they never extrapolate through a learned dynamics model. The efficiency gain is real but must be weighed against this qualitatively different failure mode plus the added engineering cost of maintaining and validating a second learned system (the model).

drills.q: What is the standard default value for PPO's clip epsilon, and what's the typical explored range?
drills.a: Default 0.2, typical range 0.1-0.3.

drills.q: What is r(theta) in PPO's clipped objective, and what value does it take at the very start of an update?
drills.a: r(theta) = pi_theta(a|s) / pi_theta_old(a|s), the probability ratio. It equals exactly 1 at the start of the update, before any gradient step is taken.

drills.q: True or false: TRPO enforces its trust region via a soft penalty term added to the objective.
drills.a: False -- TRPO enforces a hard constraint (KL(theta_old,theta) <= delta) solved via constrained optimization (natural gradient + conjugate gradient + line search), not a penalty term.

drills.q: What does GAE's lambda parameter equal to 0 reduce to, and what does lambda=1 reduce to?
drills.a: lambda=0 reduces to the single-step delta_t (low variance, high bias, critic-dependent). lambda=1 reduces to the full Monte Carlo advantage (unbiased, high variance) since the infinite sum telescopes fully.

drills.q: Derive why the gradient of PPO's clipped objective vanishes once the ratio r exceeds 1+epsilon for a positive-advantage action.
drills.a: Once r > 1+eps, clip(r,1-eps,1+eps) equals the constant 1+eps, whose gradient w.r.t. theta is zero. Since A>0, the unclipped term r*A keeps growing past the clipped term (1+eps)*A, so the min operator selects the clipped (now zero-gradient) branch -- the optimizer gets no signal to push r any higher.

drills.q: A production RLHF pipeline uses only PPO's clip with no separate KL penalty against the reference model. What failure mode is this exposed to?
drills.a: Cumulative policy drift from the reference/SFT model across many training updates -- the clip only bounds a single update's ratio excursion relative to the immediately preceding policy, not the total drift accumulated over the whole run, even if every individual step looks well within bounds.

drills.q: Why is conjugate gradient used in TRPO instead of directly computing F^-1 g via matrix inversion?
drills.a: Explicitly forming and inverting the Fisher information matrix F costs O(|theta|^2) to O(|theta|^3), infeasible for a deep network's parameter count. Conjugate gradient computes F^-1 g using only Fisher-vector products, which are cheap to compute via automatic differentiation without ever materializing F.

drills.q: Explain why PPO takes the min of the clipped and unclipped surrogate terms rather than just using the clipped term by itself.
drills.a: Taking the min guarantees L^CLIP is a pessimistic lower bound on the true unclipped surrogate in every case. Using the clip alone without the min comparison can, in certain edge cases (e.g. the ratio moving opposite to what the advantage's sign would suggest is helpful), report a MORE optimistic value than the true surrogate, defeating the purpose of bounding over-optimization.

drills.q: Derive the n-step advantage estimator's telescoping form and show how GAE's compact geometric-sum form falls out of exponentially weighting every n-step estimator.
drills.a: A_t^(n) = sum_{l=0}^{n-1} gamma^l delta_{t+l}, which telescopes to -V(s_t) + sum of discounted rewards + gamma^n V(s_{t+n}). Weighting every n-step estimator by (1-lambda)*lambda^(n-1) and summing, then re-collecting terms by power of (gamma*lambda), gives the compact form A_t^GAE = sum_l (gamma*lambda)^l * delta_{t+l}.

drills.q: A colleague argues TRPO is strictly obsolete now that PPO exists. Give a concrete scenario where you'd still reach for TRPO.
drills.a: A safety-critical or regulated control application where a verifiable, per-update monotonic-improvement guarantee (backed by an explicit, checkable KL constraint and a line search that verifies it) is a genuine risk-management requirement -- PPO only approximately bounds step size via a first-order proxy with no formal per-step guarantee, so where that formal guarantee has real value, TRPO's extra implementation cost is justified.

drills.q: Why does running PPO for many more epochs than the typical 3-10 per batch become unsafe, even though the clip bounds each sample's ratio excursion?
drills.a: Even with per-sample clip bounds, running enough epochs lets theta drift far enough in aggregate from theta_old that the importance-sampling correction underlying data reuse becomes unreliable overall -- many individually-small-looking updates compound. There's no formal guarantee covering arbitrarily many epochs; 3-10 is the empirically found range balancing reuse against this drift.

drills.q: Write the KV cache formula from memory, then apply it: Llama 3.1 8B has num_hidden_layers=32, num_attention_heads=32, num_key_value_heads=8, head_dim=128, bfloat16. Bytes per token?
drills.a: kv_bytes_per_token = 2 (K and V) x n_layers x n_key_value_heads x head_dim x dtype_bytes = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. Use num_key_value_heads (8), not num_attention_heads (32); GQA is a 4x saving on this model and using 32 would give a wrong 512 KiB.

drills.q: Compute this: how much VRAM does a single 128k-context request cost against Llama 3.1 8B in BF16, and how does that compare to the weights?
drills.a: 131,072 tokens x 131,072 bytes/token = 1.718e10 bytes = 16.0 GiB of KV for one request. Weights are 8.03e9 x 2 = 1.606e10 bytes = 14.96 GiB. One max-context request costs MORE than the entire model. Past a certain context you are not serving a model, you are serving a cache.

drills.q: Compute this: on an H100 80GB (nvidia-smi reports 79.6 GiB) running Llama 3.1 8B BF16 with vLLM defaults, how many concurrent sequences fit at 8k average context?
drills.a: usable = 79.6 x 0.92 (gpu_memory_utilization default) = 73.2 GiB. Minus 14.96 GiB weights minus ~3 GiB profiled activations/CUDA graphs = 55.2 GiB KV pool. 55.2 x 1024 MiB / 0.125 MiB-per-token = ~452,800 tokens. At 8,192 tokens per sequence: 55 concurrent sequences. (221 at 2k, 13 at 32k, 3 at 128k.) Note max_num_seqs defaults to 1024 on this device, so the sequence limit is not what binds you; the KV pool is.

drills.q: Compute this: derive Llama 3.1 8B decode throughput on an H100 SXM (3.35 TB/s) at batch 256 with 1,800 tokens average live context. Show both terms.
drills.a: Per decode step you read all weights plus the entire live KV cache. Weights: 1.606e10 bytes. KV: 256 x 1800 x 131,072 = 6.04e10 bytes. Total 7.65e10 bytes. Step time = 7.65e10 / 3.35e12 = 22.8 ms. Throughput = 256 tokens / 0.0228 s = ~11,200 output tok/s. Note the KV term is 79% of the bandwidth work at this batch; the weight-only floor would be 4.79 ms and 209 steps/s.

drills.q: Compute this: p5.48xlarge is $98.32/hr on-demand for 8x H100. What is the cost per 1M output tokens at full batch, and at 35% utilisation?
drills.a: $98.32 / 8 = $12.29 per H100-hour. At 11,200 tok/s a GPU produces 11,200 x 3600 = 40.32M tokens/hour. $12.29 / 40.32 = $0.305 per 1M output tokens at 100% utilisation. At 35% utilisation, divide by 0.35: $0.87 per 1M. Utilisation is a pure division and it dominates any instance-class choice.

drills.q: Compute this: compare $/1M output tokens for g5.2xlarge (1x A10G 24GB, $1.212/hr, 600 GB/s) and p5.48xlarge per-GPU (H100, $12.29/GPU-hr, 3.35 TB/s) serving Llama 3.1 8B. Which is cheaper and why is that counter-intuitive?
drills.a: A10G: KV pool is only 20.7 - 15.0 - 1.5 = 4.2 GiB = ~34,700 tokens, so batch caps at 8 at 4k context. Weight-read step = 1.606e10 / 6.0e11 = 26.8 ms, 37 steps/s, so ~300 tok/s. 300 x 3600 = 1.08M tokens/hr, $1.212 / 1.08 = $1.12 per 1M. H100: $0.305 per 1M. The $12.29/hr GPU is 3.7x cheaper per token than the $1.21/hr one, because the small card loses on both factors simultaneously: less bandwidth (slower steps) AND less VRAM (smaller batch), and throughput is their product.

drills.q: Compute this: what is the 1-year and 3-year reserved breakeven utilisation for g5.2xlarge (on-demand $1.212, 1yr std RI $0.7636, 3yr std RI $0.5236)? What does that mean in hours?
drills.a: breakeven = reserved_rate / on_demand_rate. 1yr: 0.7636 / 1.212 = 63.0%, i.e. you must run the instance more than ~5,520 of the year's 8,760 hours. 3yr: 0.5236 / 1.212 = 43.2%. Same ratio applies across the g5 family (g5.12xlarge is also 63.0% / 43.2%). p5.48xlarge 3yr: 43.157 / 98.32 = 43.9%.

drills.q: Given us-east-1 rates on 2026-08-05 (p5.48xlarge: on-demand $98.32, spot $57.762, 3yr RI $43.157), price three strategies for ten node-equivalents of steady demand and pick one.
drills.a: All on-demand: 10 x 98.32 = $983.20/hr. All spot: 10 x 57.762 = $577.62/hr (-41.2%). 60% reserved + 40% spot: 6 x 43.157 + 4 x 57.762 = 258.94 + 231.05 = $489.99/hr (-50.1%). The blend beats all-spot on price AND carries less risk, because the reserved floor is non-interruptible. Note the underlying surprise: 3yr RI ($43.157) is cheaper than spot ($57.762) on this SKU, so spot is only worth using above your confident baseline.

drills.q: Compute this: your cold GPU replica takes 300 seconds end to end and traffic can double over 5 minutes. What steady-state utilisation ceiling does that force, and what does cutting the cold start to 90 seconds buy?
drills.a: required_headroom >= growth_rate x scale_out_latency = (100% / 300 s) x 300 s = 100%. So you must hold as much idle capacity as you are using: utilisation ceiling = 1/(1+1.00) = 50%. At L = 90 s: headroom >= (100%/300) x 90 = 30%, ceiling = 1/1.30 = 76.9%. That is a 1.54x cost reduction with no hardware change, which is why cold-start reduction beats autoscaler tuning as a cost lever.

drills.q: Size the fleet: 500,000 requests/day, 1,200 input tokens, 400 output tokens, 3:1 peak-to-average, Llama 3.1 8B on H100. Show the arithmetic and the honest recommendation.
drills.a: Average 500,000/86,400 = 5.8 rps; peak 17.4 rps. Peak decode load = 17.4 x 400 = 6,960 output tok/s, against ~11,200 tok/s per H100 = 0.62 GPU. Peak prefill = 17.4 x 1,200 = 20,880 prompt tok/s against a derived ~24,900 tok/s at 40% MFU, so prefill alone nearly saturates one card and the phases contend: call it 2 H100s of real work. Add 100% headroom for a 4-minute cold start: 4 H100s, half a p5.48xlarge. Cost check: 500,000 x 400 = 200M output tokens/day, at $0.305/1M = $61/day of useful work against a $2,360/day on-demand p5 bill. Recommendation: this workload belongs on 2-3 L40S (g6e.2xlarge) or a hosted API, not a p5.

drills.q: You are handed a dashboard: vllm:num_requests_waiting is 180, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc is 0.24, nvidia-smi shows 20% GPU utilisation, and one CPU core is pinned at 100%. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The GPU is starved by the front end, not saturated. HTTP parsing, tokenization, or detokenization is bottlenecked on a single process. vLLM V1 already splits the API server from the engine core, but one API server process still caps request rate: use --api-server-count=N. Also verify the fast Rust tokenizer is loaded rather than the Python fallback, that nothing constructs a tokenizer per request, and that request logging is not doing per-token string work. Adding GPUs would make the ratio worse and double the bill for zero throughput. General rule: num_requests_waiting > 0 is necessary but not sufficient for scaling out; always pair it with a saturation signal.

drills.q: Rank these autoscaling signals for a vLLM endpoint and justify the ranking: CPU utilisation, GPU utilisation, requests per second, vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds p95.
drills.a: Best: vllm:num_requests_waiting (directly measures unserved demand) with vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds p95 as the SLO-facing co-trigger. Then vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc as early warning only. Unusable: GPU utilisation, because nvidia-smi measures kernel residency and reads near 100% at batch 1 and batch 256 alike during memory-stalled decode. Worse: requests per second, because decode length varies 100x so request count is a terrible load proxy. Worst: CPU utilisation, which tells you about your tokenizer and nothing about the engine.

drills.q: State the interruption notice window for AWS EC2 Spot, GCP Spot VM, GCP Preemptible VM, and Azure Spot, then say what each implies for draining an inference replica.
drills.a: AWS: 2 minutes (plus a rebalance recommendation typically 10-20 min earlier, not guaranteed to precede it). GCP Spot VM and Preemptible VM: 30 seconds, best effort; Preemptible additionally has a hard 24-hour lifetime. Azure: minimum 30 seconds via Scheduled Events Preempt, and immediate eviction with no notice is documented as possible. Implication: AWS's 120 s is enough to fail readiness, wait ~15-30 s for load-balancer deregistration, and drain in-flight generations. GCP/Azure's 30 s is less than readiness propagation alone, so you must proactively deregister and cap max_tokens so p99 generation fits, or accept that in-flight requests die and the client retries.

drills.q: A vLLM fleet moved to spot shows unchanged per-replica throughput but 40% lower aggregate throughput. Name the failure mode and give the quantitative test for whether spot is defensible.
drills.a: Preemption thrash: replicas are drained and replaced faster than they warm, so a growing fraction of the fleet is in cold start rather than serving. With a 4-minute warm-up and a 20-minute mean replica lifetime, 20% of the fleet is permanently useless. The test: require mean_replica_lifetime > 10 x warmup_time before spot is defensible. Fixes: diversify instance types and AZs, keep a reserved/on-demand floor at minimum viable capacity, and cut warm-up with pre-pulled images and node-local weight staging. Also check whether 3-year RI is simply cheaper than spot on your SKU, which it currently is on g5.2xlarge, p4d.24xlarge and p5.48xlarge.

drills.q: Leadership wants 40% off a $180k/month, 40-GPU bill in one quarter. Order your actions by (savings x confidence) / effort and name the rollback trigger for the two that can backfire.
drills.a: 1) Measure $/1M tokens per workload and endpoint first (one week; the only way to tell a utilisation problem from a workload problem). 2) Kill or consolidate the low-utilisation tail, typically 15-30% of spend at near-zero risk. 3) Separate batch from interactive and move batch to spot with its own policy, 10-15%. 4) FP8 weights plus FP8 KV cache, typically 1.5-2x throughput. 5) Reserve the p50 baseline once you have a utilisation history, 43-57% off that portion. 6) Cold-start reduction, which raises the utilisation ceiling. Instance-class changes last. Backfire risks: quantisation degrades quality silently, so gate on a task-level eval canary comparing refusal rate, structured-output validity and task success against BF16; raising utilisation eats SLO headroom, so gate on p95 TTFT and shed rate, not the cost graph. State both rollback triggers before starting.

drills.q: Name the three layers of a serving stack and say which one your latency numbers come from.
drills.a: Packaging (BentoML, Dockerfile), control plane (SageMaker endpoint, KServe InferenceService, Ray Serve deployment), engine (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM). The engine owns the numbers. Migrating control planes typically moves p50 by single-digit percent because it is the same vLLM underneath.

drills.q: What is KServe's default minReplicas, and what does that mean for scale-to-zero?
drills.a: 1. You do not get scale-to-zero unless you explicitly set minReplicas: 0. This is the opposite of what most people assume from the 'serverless inference' framing on the KServe homepage.

drills.q: Can SageMaker Serverless Inference serve a GPU model?
drills.a: No. GPUs are an explicit documented feature exclusion, along with multi-model endpoints, VPC configuration, network isolation, data capture, Model Monitor, multiple production variants, and inference pipelines. Max RAM is 6144 MB. It is for small CPU models with bursty traffic.

drills.q: Quote the SageMaker Real-Time markup over EC2 with a concrete instance pair.
drills.a: About 1.25x: ml.g5.24xlarge at $10.18/hr versus g5.24xlarge at $8.144/hr in us-east-1 (the small pair, ml.g5.2xlarge $1.52 vs g5.2xlarge $1.212, reproduces the same ratio). Against spot at $3.955 it is roughly 2.6x, and SageMaker Real-Time does not offer spot for inference.

drills.q: A request hits a SageMaker endpoint scaled to zero. Trace exactly what happens.
drills.a: It fails. The failure increments NoCapacityInvocationFailures in AWS/SageMaker. A CloudWatch alarm on that metric (period 60, threshold 1, 1 evaluation period) fires a step scaling policy against the inference component's DesiredCopyCount. SageMaker then provisions instances, documented as taking several minutes, and every request in that window errors. There is no activator buffering the request the way Knative has.

drills.q: Derive the utilization at which SageMaker Serverless Provisioned Concurrency beats on-demand.
drills.a: PC costs 0.000010 + 0.000023u per second; on-demand costs 0.000040u. Setting them equal: 0.000010 = 0.000017u, so u = 0.588. PC pays for itself above roughly 59% utilization of the provisioned concurrency and is a pure loss below it.

drills.q: p99 doubled when you scaled from one replica to two; p50 is flat. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Prefix cache fragmentation from round-robin. With one replica the shared system prompt is prefilled once; with two, roughly half of requests land on the replica that lacks the prefix and pay full prefill. p50 is flat because the median request was cheap. Fix with prefix-cache-aware routing: KServe InferencePool plus the Gateway API Inference Extension endpoint picker, or Ray Serve's ConsistentHashRouter. Verify with vllm:prefix_cache_hit_rate. Reported gain: 3x output tokens/s, 2x lower TTFT.

drills.q: Which KServe autoscaler works in which deployment mode, and what do you give up either way?
drills.a: KPA only in Knative mode: scales on concurrency or QPS, and you keep the activator that buffers cold-start requests. KEDA only in Raw/Standard mode: scales on any Prometheus or OTel metric including vllm:num_requests_waiting, but you lose the activator so a cold start is a hard failure. HPA also works in Raw. They are mutually exclusive, and people pick Raw to avoid the Knative dependency without realising they forfeited the buffering.

drills.q: State the Knative Pod Autoscaler constants and explain the panic mechanism.
drills.a: 60-second stable window for average concurrency, 6-second panic window, panic entered when the panic window reaches 2x target concurrency, and exited after 60 seconds of the condition not holding. Panic mode exists so a burst does not have to wait a full minute of averaging before scaling, at the cost of oscillation risk against slow-starting pods.

drills.q: A Ray Serve service starts returning 503s after an upgrade. Traffic unchanged, GPUs at 30%. What is it?
drills.a: max_ongoing_requests default dropped from 100 to 5 in Ray 2.32.0, a 20x cut in per-replica admission. Each replica now admits 5, the router queue backs up, and callers get BackPressureError on handles or HTTP 503 on the proxy. GPUs sit low because the bottleneck is admission control, not compute. target_ongoing_requests also moved from 1.0 to 2.0 in the same release. Fix: set both explicitly, max about 20-50% above target for heavyweight deployments.

drills.q: Why is GPU utilization the wrong scaling signal for LLM serving? Give the two states it cannot distinguish.
drills.a: 95% GPU with an empty waiting queue (healthy, do not scale) and 40% GPU with 200 requests waiting because the KV pool is full (saturated, must scale). Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so SM occupancy does not reflect headroom. Request count is also bad because output lengths vary by two orders of magnitude. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting or vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc.

drills.q: Design serving for 400 per-tenant fine-tuned LLMs sharing one base model.
drills.a: One resident base model per GPU plus per-tenant LoRA adapters swapped per request, not 400 endpoints and not a multi-model endpoint. Adapters are tens to hundreds of MB against a 16 GB base, so the tail is tractable. vLLM serves multi-LoRA natively; KServe auto-enables a lora-affinity-scorer in its router when adapters are present. MME fails here because density packing competes with the KV cache for VRAM and two 8B fp16 models are 32 GB of weights before any cache.

drills.q: Budget the cold start for a 70B on a scaled-to-zero Kubernetes endpoint and say what you optimize first.
drills.a: Detect (ms on Knative, tens of seconds polling), schedule a GPU node 90-180s if the autoscaler must launch one, pull an 8-15 GB CUDA image 60-200s cold, fetch 140 GB of fp16 weights at ~1 GB/s for ~140s, then CUDA graph capture and KV pool allocation 20-90s. Roughly 8-15 minutes cold. Optimize weight pre-staging (LocalModelCache / LocalModelNamespaceCache on node-local NVMe) and image pre-pull via DaemonSet first; autoscaler tuning is noise against a 140-second weight fetch.

drills.q: Size and place a RAG chat product: 5,000 req/hr peak, 300/hr overnight, heavy shared system prompt, p95 TTFT 800ms, one 8B open-weight model.
drills.a: Peak-to-average is ~16:1, which drives everything. 8B fp16 is 16 GB so a g5.2xlarge (24 GB A10G, $1.212/hr) holds it with a modest KV pool; g5.12xlarge at $5.672 covers peak. The 800ms TTFT target rules out scale-to-zero on the user path, so minReplicas=1 sized to overnight. Enable vLLM prefix caching and prefix-aware routing because the shared prompt makes round-robin the p99 killer. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting via KEDA. Burst on spot at $0.595 with on-demand baseline and a managed endpoint as overflow. Platform: KServe LLMInferenceService if the org already runs Kubernetes, otherwise a SageMaker endpoint with an LMI/vLLM container and app-layer session-sticky routing, since the 25% markup here is a few hundred dollars a month.

drills.q: Two teams want KServe, one wants to stay on SageMaker, across 30 models. Make the call and justify it with numbers.
drills.a: Do not force uniformity for its own sake. Decide on GPU footprint: above roughly ten GPU nodes the SageMaker markup is $25,000+/month against EC2 on-demand and more against spot, which pays for the platform work; at three nodes it does not and the KServe request is résumé-driven. The likely right answer splits by workload rather than team: LLMs on KServe where prefix-aware routing and node-local weight caching produce measurable wins, classical models on SageMaker where operational simplicity is worth 25%. Insist on a common contract regardless: OpenAI-compatible HTTP surface, one Prometheus, one model registry, so the platform under a model can change without callers noticing.

drills.q: Someone recommends ModelMesh for high-density multi-model serving. Respond, and say what replaced it.
drills.a: It is dead: both kserve/modelmesh and kserve/modelmesh-serving were archived 2026-04-14, last release v0.12.0 in July 2024, docs 404 on KServe 0.18 and 0.19 (the landing page still advertises it, which is stale copy). Nothing replaced it as a general density layer, and that is the honest answer: the problem bifurcated into MME-style managed density for small classical models and multi-LoRA for LLMs, while KServe's investment went entirely into LLMInferenceService, InferencePool routing, and llm-d.

drills.q: In one sentence each, what question do RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC answer?
drills.a: RBAC: what may this job function do. ABAC: under what conditions. ReBAC: what relationship does this user have to this specific object.

drills.q: Write the Zanzibar tuple format and give one example with a userset subject.
drills.a: object#relation@subject. Example: doc:roadmap#viewer@group:eng#member -- the subject is itself a userset, so every member of group:eng is a viewer of doc:roadmap.

drills.q: Name the three logical components in NIST SP 800-207 and which two form the PDP.
drills.a: Policy Engine (decides), Policy Administrator (establishes or tears down the session credential), and Policy Enforcement Point (sits in the data path in front of every resource). PE + PA together form the PDP.

drills.q: Name the five pillars of the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 and its four maturity stages.
drills.a: Pillars: Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, Data. Plus three cross-cutting capabilities (Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, Governance). Stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal. Published April 2023.

drills.q: A team has 3 job functions, 4 regions, 3 environments, and 2 data classifications, all encoded as roles. How many roles, and what do you actually do about it?
