drills.a: 3 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 72 roles for one conceptual job function. The fix is not consolidating roles, it is moving the exploding dimensions out: region and environment become attribute conditions (or relationships if they are really resource scoping), and RBAC keeps only the genuinely static coarse function. Adding one more dimension multiplies again, which is why 'just add a role' is a trap.

drills.q: Your RLS policy is written, the table has ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and every tenant still sees every row. Give three candidate causes in likelihood order.
drills.a: 1) The app connects as the table OWNER, and owners bypass RLS by default -- needs ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY plus separating the migration role from the runtime role. 2) The app role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS; the built-in postgres role has BYPASSRLS and it cannot be removed. 3) The policy reads a setting that was never set, so current_setting(..., true) returns NULL and the comparison is NULL rather than false.

drills.q: Explain why SET LOCAL matters for tenant context, and what exactly goes wrong with plain SET.
drills.a: SET is session-scoped and persists on the backend connection after the transaction ends. Under a pooler in transaction pooling mode (PgBouncer), the next request that borrows that connection inherits the previous tenant's context, so tenant A reads tenant B's rows. SET LOCAL (or set_config(name, value, true)) is transaction-scoped and is discarded at commit or rollback, so it cannot leak. It must be inside an EXPLICIT transaction to have any effect. Symptom signature: cross-tenant reads that appear only under load, because that is when connection reuse actually occurs.

drills.q: Reads are correctly tenant-scoped but rows are appearing under the wrong tenant_id. What is missing from the policy?
drills.a: WITH CHECK. USING filters reads and the pre-image of a write; WITH CHECK validates the post-image of INSERT and UPDATE. With only USING, an UPDATE ... SET tenant_id = <other tenant> passes because the row was visible before the change and nothing validates it after. Add WITH CHECK with the same predicate.

drills.q: Why can ABAC not power a sharing UI or a quarterly access review?
drills.a: Because access is computed, not stored. Answering 'who can access this document' requires evaluating the policy against every principal in the system, which is O(subjects). ReBAC answers the same question with an Expand over the userset tree, bounded by the actual relationship graph and typically tens of tuples. If a product manager will ever ask to display who has access, you need stored grants for at least that surface.

drills.q: Give both flavors of the new enemy problem and say what the zookie actually guarantees.
drills.a: Flavor 1, ACL updates out of order: remove Bob from the folder at t1, add a secret doc at t2; a replica applying t2 first lets Bob read it. Flavor 2, old ACL applied to new content: remove Bob from the doc at t1, add sensitive content at t2; if the content read is authorized against a pre-t1 ACL snapshot, Bob reads the new content under the old permission. The zookie is an opaque token carrying a Spanner timestamp recorded when content is written; a Check passing that zookie is guaranteed to evaluate at a snapshot no earlier than that timestamp. It preserves causal ordering between content and ACL updates while leaving Zanzibar free to choose any LATER timestamp, which is what keeps the cache hot enough for p95 under 10 ms at 4.2M Check QPS.

drills.q: Design tenant isolation for a SaaS going from 20 to 2,000 tenants. State the model, the enforcement, and the escape hatch.
drills.a: Silo does not survive: 2,000 databases means 2,000 migrations per release and a per-tenant cost floor that kills the low tier. Target pool with rungs 3 and 4: shared database with RLS plus FORCE, SET LOCAL inside an explicit transaction, tenant_id as the leading column of every composite index, and dynamically-scoped STS credentials at the compute layer so enforcement sits outside the process that has the bug. Build a bridge escape hatch NOW: a routing layer reading tenant metadata so contractually-isolated tenants get their own database or KMS key with an identical code path and only a different connection target. Budget separately for the surfaces RLS does not cover: cache keys, background jobs, search index, object storage. The sequencing point is that adding routing indirection at 20 tenants is a week and retrofitting it at 2,000 is a multi-quarter project.

drills.q: Argue why RLS is not a complete tenant-isolation boundary, with named CVEs.
drills.a: It is bypassed by superusers and BYPASSRLS roles (the built-in postgres role has BYPASSRLS and cannot have it removed), and it silently no-ops for table owners without FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. It has had boundary CVEs: CVE-2024-10976, where incomplete tracking of RLS tables let a reused plan under a subquery, WITH query, security-invoker view, or SQL-language function return rows for the wrong user; and CVE-2025-8713 (14-Aug-2025, fixed in 17.6/16.10/15.14/14.19/13.22), where optimizer statistics -- histograms and most-common-values lists -- leaked sampled data RLS intended to hide via a crafted leaky operator. And it only covers Postgres: the cache, search index, object storage, and message queue are all outside it.

drills.q: Your centralized PDP is down. Fail open or fail closed? Defend the answer.
drills.a: Per action class, decided in advance and written down. Money movement, permission changes, and data export fail closed, always. Reads of non-sensitive data may serve from a decision cache with a bounded TTL. The two wrong answers are 'fail closed everywhere' without acknowledging you have made the PDP a single point of total outage, and 'fail open' without naming which specific actions you are willing to let through unauthorized. Not deciding is deciding, and it defaults to whatever the HTTP client's error handling does.

drills.q: Someone presents a completed zero trust rollout as remediation for your Broken Access Control findings. Respond.
drills.a: They are orthogonal. Zero trust is about the network and the session: mTLS, device posture, identity-aware proxies, per-session credentials. Object-level authorization is about the row. A fully zero-trust network still returns tenant B's document to tenant A when the handler fetches by id and never checks ownership, because the PEP authorized access to the SERVICE and A01/BOLA live entirely behind it. A01:2025 is #1 in the web Top 10 with 40 CWEs at 3.73% average incidence and API1:2023 BOLA is #1 in the API Top 10 precisely because these bugs survive every network control you can buy.

drills.q: You inherit a pool-model SaaS where tenant filtering is hand-written in every repository. Sequence the remediation and name the operational cost of step two.
drills.a: 1) Audit: query-log check in staging asserting every statement touching a tenant table carries a tenant predicate, so you have a count rather than a feeling. 2) Ship the enforcement rung that catches everything at once: RLS with FORCE, a tenant_scope context manager using SET LOCAL in an explicit transaction, and a fail-closed assertion when no tenant context is set. This converts every existing missing-predicate bug from a confidentiality failure into an empty result set. 3) Fix what RLS does not cover, in incident-frequency order: background jobs, cache keys, search index, object storage. 4) Two-tenant integration suite in CI asserting zero cross-tenant rows on every endpoint. 5) Only then remove the now-redundant hand-written predicates, and only where tests cover them. The operational cost of step two is a wave of tickets in week one as previously-silent bugs become loud empty responses -- staff for it, and treat each one as a found bug, not a regression. Failing toward availability instead of confidentiality is the correct direction.

drills.q: Name the OWASP Top 10:2025 categories A01 through A05 in order.
drills.a: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures (new), A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection.

drills.q: Which 2021 category no longer exists as its own entry in 2025, and where did it go?
drills.a: SSRF, which was A10:2021, folded into A01:2025 Broken Access Control.

drills.q: Give the time-based blind SQLi sleep function for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQL Server.
drills.a: PostgreSQL: pg_sleep(5). MySQL: SLEEP(5). SQL Server: WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'. Oracle typically uses dbms_pipe.receive_message.

drills.q: List the four Django/SQLAlchemy escape hatches you would grep for in a SQLi audit.
drills.a: Django: .raw(), .extra(), RawSQL(). SQLAlchemy: session.execute(text(f'...')) without bindparams. Add Hibernate HQL concatenation for the Java side (CWE-564).

drills.q: A code review shows cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY %s', (col,)). Is it injectable? Is it correct?
drills.a: Not injectable, and not correct. It binds a string constant, producing ORDER BY 'created_at', which sorts by a constant and silently returns unsorted rows with no error. Bind parameters can only occupy value positions because the plan is built at Parse time before Bind. Fix with a server-controlled allowlist mapping the user key to a column, plus a two-value direction map, composed with sql.Identifier().

drills.q: An endpoint returns 200 for every request, but its p50 latency is clustered at 5.02s, 10.04s, and 15.03s. Diagnose and give the same-day mitigations.
drills.a: Time-based blind SQL injection using pg_sleep / SLEEP / WAITFOR. Same-day mitigations, none of which are the fix: set a server-side statement_timeout of ~2s so the sleeps fail fast, rate-limit the unauthenticated route, and block the pattern at the edge. The remediation is finding the concatenated query and parameterizing it. Do not let the mitigation close the remediation ticket.

drills.q: Explain second-order SQL injection with a two-step example, and say which tool class misses it.
drills.a: Step 1: INSERT INTO users (username) VALUES (%s) with the value admin'-- , parameterized and safe; it is stored as literal text. Step 2, months later, a report job runs f"SELECT * FROM audit WHERE username = '{row['username']}'", producing ... WHERE username = 'admin'--'. SAST usually misses it because it taints the HTTP request object and stops at the INSERT. IAST catches some of it at runtime on exercised paths. The durable control is a CI rule banning string-formatted SQL everywhere, not just near request handlers.

drills.q: Someone proposes validating the ORDER BY column with the regex ^[a-z_]+$ instead of an allowlist. What does that fail to stop?
drills.a: Authorization bypass. ORDER BY password_hash passes that regex. Combined with a paging endpoint the sort becomes a boolean oracle you can binary-search to extract the column. An allowlist is not about character classes, it is about which columns the SERVER has decided are sortable.

drills.q: Your team wants to build the IN clause as 'WHERE id IN (' + ','.join(map(str, ids)) + ')'. What is the safe form and what else does it fix?
drills.a: Use 'WHERE id = ANY(%s)' with a real Python list on Postgres, or one placeholder per element. Beyond removing the injection, it also gives the planner a single stable statement to cache instead of a new query text for every list length, which stops prepared-statement cache churn on high-cardinality lists.

drills.q: Why is prompt injection categorically different from SQL injection, and what follows from that for defense?
drills.a: Every working injection defense uses two transport channels so the interpreter never re-parses data as grammar: Parse/Bind for SQL, argv for shells, DOM APIs for HTML. A transformer has one token stream, so system prompt, user turn, retrieved chunk, and tool output are attended to identically. There is no bind parameter for attention. It follows that the defense is containment rather than prevention: least-privilege tools enforced at the gateway, no high-risk tool in the same turn as an untrusted read, per-agent identity, budgets, and human gates on irreversible actions.

drills.q: A vendor's pentest report says 'no OWASP Top 10 findings.' What do you conclude, and what do you ask for instead?
drills.a: Almost nothing about security, and something about scope. The Top 10 covers 248 CWEs out of 968 in MITRE's dictionary; A01 alone is 40 CWEs at a measured 3.73% incidence, which is a floor set by what scanners can find. Business logic, tenant isolation, and multi-step authenticated state are usually out of scope and are where the expensive incidents live. Ask for the test scope, whether authenticated multi-role testing was performed, and coverage against ASVS L2. The Top 10 is an awareness document; ASVS is the requirements standard.

drills.q: You inherit a monolith with 60 open injection findings and one engineer-month. Sequence the work and defend the sequence.
drills.a: Triage by reachability and privilege, not scanner severity: unauthenticated routes and high-privilege DB roles first. Week one, ship the two systemic controls that cap the entire population at once: drop the app DB role to least privilege (converts every finding from 'read everything' to 'read what this service owns') and suppress DB error propagation (kills error-based extraction across all 60). Add the CI rule as ERROR with a shrinking grandfather allowlist so the count cannot grow. Then fix by clusters, because 60 findings usually come from 5 or 6 helper functions. Then add tests asserting sort order and tenant scoping so the fixes cannot silently regress.

drills.q: Design the security posture for a production agent with tool access, then say which two controls you would ship first with one week.
drills.a: Gateway-enforced tool allowlist rather than a prompt instruction, per-agent identity with short-lived scoped credentials (ASI03), no high-risk tool available in the same turn as a read of untrusted external content, human confirmation on irreversible actions (send, delete, pay, deploy), hard step count plus wall-clock timeout plus token and cost budget (LLM10 / ASI08), full prompt-to-action traces, and treating every model output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it (LLM05). With one week: the gateway-enforced tool allowlist and the step-plus-cost budget. Both are days of work, both are enforced outside the model so injection cannot argue with them, and they bound the two failure modes that end careers: irreversible actions and runaway cost. Per-agent identity is highest value and slowest, so it is a quarter item.

drills.q: CVE-2026-42208 hit your LiteLLM deployment. You have patched to 1.83.7-stable. Are you done? Justify.
drills.a: No. It was a PRE-AUTHENTICATION SQL injection on the key-verification path, reachable from every LLM route with no credentials, and observed exploitation used UNION payloads against LiteLLM_VerificationToken, litellm_credentials, and litellm_config. You must assume every upstream provider key the proxy held was read: rotate all of them, audit provider-side usage logs across the full exposure window (exploitation began within 36 hours of advisory indexing, so the window may predate your detection), and then change the architecture so the gateway does not hold every provider credential in the same database it queries before authenticating anyone.

drills.q: Argue the counter-position: ORMs and modern frameworks have made SQLi a solved problem not worth senior interview time. Where is that right and where is it wrong?
drills.a: Right about greenfield application code written entirely through the ORM's typed query API, where the framework parameterizes by construction. Wrong about the seams, which is where every real finding lives: identifier positions the ORM must emit from user input (Django CVE-2024-42005 used a JSONField key as a column alias), raw-SQL escape hatches, second-order paths where DB reads are treated as trusted, stored procedures using EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, analytics query builders, and every gateway and admin tool in the dependency tree. CVE-2026-42208 was written in 2026 by people who knew what SQL injection was. The senior framing is that prevention is achievable for new code and containment (least-privilege DB role, error suppression, egress deny) is what actually bounds the damage everywhere else.

drills.q: Name the four ICS-derived incident roles.
drills.a: Incident Commander, Operations Lead, Communications Lead, Scribe.

drills.q: 99.9% availability over a 30-day window. How many minutes of full unavailability is the error budget?
drills.a: About 43.2 minutes. 30 days = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2.

drills.q: Which of these belongs on a pager and which on a dashboard: (a) 'CPU on host-7 at 92%', (b) 'fraction of /v1/search requests under 400ms below SLO burn threshold'?
drills.a: (b) pages. It is a symptom alert and fires only when users are affected, by any cause including ones you never instrumented. (a) is a cause alert: dashboard or ticket. It fires when nobody is harmed and misses breakage whose cause you did not anticipate.

drills.q: What is the maximum sustainable pager load per 8-to-12-hour on-call shift, and what is the stated reason for that number?
drills.a: About 2 paging events. The reason given in the Google SRE Book is operational, not humane: below that the on-call has time to handle the event accurately, restore service, clean up and write the postmortem. Above it, incidents stop being investigated thoroughly and the team stops learning from them.

drills.q: Write the first external status update at minute 6 of an incident where you have no idea what is wrong. Name the four required parts.
drills.a: Parts: what users see, when it started, what we are doing, when the next update comes. 'Since 14:12 UTC, a portion of requests to /v1/search are returning HTTP 500. Other endpoints are unaffected. We are investigating and have engineers engaged. Next update by 14:45 UTC.' No cause, no resolution ETA, no speculation. The next-update-by promise is the load-bearing part.

drills.q: Rewrite these two postmortem findings so they are not blame: (a) 'the on-call missed the page', (b) 'reviewer approved a bad config'.
drills.a: (a) 'The page was one of 41 fired in that 8-hour shift, of which 4 were actionable. Fix: delete the 17 alerts with zero actions in 90 days, convert 12 cause-alerts to tickets.' (b) 'The config had no schema validation and no canary stage; review was the only gate. Fix: schema-validate at build time, canary to 1% of the fleet for 10 minutes before global propagation.' Test: if the finding cannot be falsified by a code, config or alert change, it is not a finding.

drills.q: You are IC. A mitigation reduces the error rate from 40% to 12% but does not resolve. The team wants another 30 minutes tuning the same lever. What do you do and why?
drills.a: Force a hypothesis reset. A mitigation that reduces but does not eliminate impact is evidence the current hypothesis is downstream of the cause, not evidence you are close. Run an explicit 'what else could produce this?' round before allowing more tuning. Cloudflare on 18 November 2025 spent 11:32 to 13:05, about 93 minutes, chasing elevated Workers KV errors that were downstream of a core-proxy panic; the 13:05 bypass reduced impact and did not resolve it.

drills.q: Your service oscillates between fully healthy and fully broken roughly every 5 minutes. Two engineers are convinced it is a DDoS. What is your first hypothesis?
drills.a: A periodic job producing bad state, not an adversary. A five-minute oscillation is a five-minute cron. Match the oscillation period against scheduler intervals before reaching for the attack hypothesis. This is exactly the Cloudflare November 2025 saw-tooth: a feature file regenerated every 5 minutes while a ClickHouse cluster was updated node by node, so it was sometimes good and sometimes bad.

drills.q: Give the three cases where mitigate-before-diagnose is the wrong default, with one concrete example each.
drills.a: (1) The mitigation is irreversible or data-destructive: failing over a primary with unknown replication lag permanently loses unreplicated writes (GitHub, 21 Oct 2018, where a 43-second partition produced a split write set and 24h 11m of reconciliation). (2) You cannot state the mitigation's own blast radius: 'restart the fleet' when you do not know whether it comes back. (3) The suspect is a stateful in-flight operation: rolling back a half-applied schema migration is usually worse than letting it finish.

drills.q: State the Google SRE Workbook's three burn-rate alert tiers, including short windows and budget consumed.
drills.a: Tier 1: 14.4x burn, 1-hour long window, 5-minute short window, 2% of budget consumed, PAGE. Tier 2: 6x, 6-hour long window, 30-minute short window, 5% consumed, PAGE. Tier 3: 1x, 3-day long window, 6-hour short window, 10% consumed, TICKET. Both windows must breach; the short window exists so the alert clears within minutes once burning stops.

drills.q: List at least four contributing factors for the Cloudflare 18 November 2025 outage, then say which single fix you would prioritise and why.
drills.a: (1) A query against system.columns written without a database-name filter, relying on implicit behaviour. (2) A permissions change making r0 access explicit, which altered that behaviour. (3) A gradual node-by-node rollout that made the fault intermittent and delayed diagnosis. (4) A hard 200-feature preallocation limit (normal usage ~60) with no graceful degradation. (5) Rust error handling that turned a failed Result into a panic instead of falling back to last-known-good. Prioritise (5): it converts an entire class of bad-config events from a global outage into a stale-config degradation. Rank by how many future incidents a fix prevents, not by proximity to the trigger.

drills.q: Your org writes excellent postmortems and keeps having the same outages. Diagnose it with a metric and name the mechanical fixes.
drills.a: Metric: fraction of incidents in the last 12 months whose contributing factors recur from an earlier incident. Above about 20% the writing is not the problem, action-item completion is. Causes: items owned by a team not a person; items living only in the postmortem doc and never entering the backlog where they compete with feature work; items phrased so they cannot be completed; too many, since 14 items completes about 3. Fix: cap Sev1 at 5 ranked items, each with a named individual, a real ticket and a date, plus an explicit 'considered and not doing' list with one-line reasons.

drills.q: You are the only person on the incident call who understands the failing system. You are also the IC. What do you do?
drills.a: Hand off IC, do not try to do both. Give the IC role to someone who can run a call (a manager, a TPM, another on-call engineer) and become the Ops Lead yourself, announcing the handoff explicitly in the channel. The IC role requires coordination skill, not domain expertise, which is the entire reason the split works. Doing both means the coordination machine halts silently and nobody notices for ~20 minutes.

drills.q: Your error budget is exhausted and a VP wants the feature shipped anyway. What do you actually do?
drills.a: Do not say 'I enforce the freeze', which signals you have never had this conversation. The budget is decision support, not a veto: present the cost concretely ('this consumes budget we do not have, so the next incident this quarter breaches the customer SLA and costs $N in credits'), let the accountable person decide, and write down what was decided. Then escalate the policy rather than each ship decision, because an error budget nobody will ever honour is worse than none, since it looks like a control while being a dashboard.

drills.q: An interviewer asks what you would have done differently in your worst outage. Give the answer shape that scores at staff level, and the trap.
drills.a: The trap is a counterfactual about yourself ('I should have noticed sooner'), which sounds humble and signals you still think in terms of individual carefulness. Answer with a system change: 'Nothing about my actions given what I knew at 03:12. The system change is that there was no symptom-based alert on query memory pressure, so detection depended on a human watching an error-rate graph. A burn-rate alert would have cut time-to-detect from N minutes to about 2.' Same discipline as a postmortem: findings must be properties of systems, falsifiable by a code, config or alert change.

drills.q: Name Nygard's five ADR sections in order, and the one rule about numbering.
drills.a: Title, Context, Decision, Status, Consequences. Numbers are assigned sequentially and monotonically and are never reused; a reversed decision gets a new ADR and the old one's Status becomes "superseded by ADR-NNN".

drills.q: Classify each as goal or non-goal: (a) "the service should not crash", (b) "ACID compliance", (c) "median model-update lead time under 2 days", (d) "migrating the other 7 services off the JVM".
drills.a: (a) neither, it is a negated goal and belongs in Goals or nowhere. (b) valid non-goal, the canonical example: could reasonably have been a goal, deliberately excluded, and you might still pick a solution that provides it. (c) goal, and a good one because it is measurable and falsifiable. (d) valid non-goal, because it is the scope question reviewers will otherwise raise four separate times.

drills.q: Rewrite as value-neutral ADR Context: "Weaviate is bloated, expensive, and a pain to operate."
drills.a: "Weaviate is the eighth independently operated stateful service in a platform with a 4-engineer on-call rotation. It accounted for 3 of 11 retrieval-path pages last quarter, none caused by a retrieval defect. Its managed tier prices per stored vector; at 41M vectors that is $X/month against a $Y/month budget." Same argumentative work, zero advocacy, so a reader who disagrees with the decision still trusts the section.

drills.q: In one sentence each: what artifact do you write for (a) a genuinely ambiguous storage choice with three defensible options, (b) a decision already made that you want a durable record of, (c) a change where there is no real tradeoff?
drills.a: (a) Design doc / RFC, because you need reviewers who can still change your mind. (b) ADR, which is honest about being a record rather than pretending to seek input. (c) Nothing; write the code. Google's own guidance is that a doc with no trade-offs is an implementation manual and you should have written the program instead.

drills.q: Write the deciding-criterion sentence for choosing pgvector over Weaviate, in the form the module recommends.
drills.a: "We weighted operational surface above p99 retrieval latency because we have 4 on-call engineers and 8 services and no dedicated platform group; a team with a platform group would reasonably weight the other way." It names the criterion, admits it is a weighting rather than a law, and tells a disagreeing reviewer exactly where to push, which is a faster conversation than attacking the conclusion.

drills.q: Your ADR's Consequences section lists three benefits and no costs. What are the two things wrong with it?
drills.a: First, it is factually incomplete: Nygard specifies all consequences, positive, negative and neutral, because the negative ones become the Context for the next ADR. Second, it is strategically self-defeating: an all-upside section reads as marketing and triggers adversarial review, whereas leading with the regression ("p99 rises from 45ms to 70ms") buys the benefit of the doubt on everything else in the document.

drills.q: Three separate reviewers ask "why not option X?" about an option you already rejected in the doc. What does that tell you and what do you do?
drills.a: It is evidence your rejection was not argued, not that they did not read. Either X was omitted or it was strawmanned, so readers reconstruct the real version themselves. Fix: rewrite X at its strongest in its advocate's words, ideally asking the advocate to review that paragraph, then name the deciding criterion and what would flip it. Answering three threads individually is 3x the latency and produces an adversarial tone.

drills.q: Turn "Phase 2: roll out to more traffic once we're confident" into a real gate.
drills.a: "Phase 2 (week 3-4): 5% then 25% live traffic. Gate to phase 3: p99 < 50ms at 900 RPS, error rate within 0.01% of the incumbent path, |score delta| < 1e-6 on 99.9% of shadow-sampled requests over 72h, no scoring-attributable CTR regression on any of the 8 surfaces. Rollback: split to 0% via config push, ~90 seconds, no data migration." "Once we're confident" is where a schedule goes to die.

drills.q: All the comments on your 12-page doc are about naming, the diagram, and formatting. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Bikeshedding, Parkinson's law of triviality: reviewers comment on the part they can evaluate in 90 seconds, which is the trivial part everyone understands. Fixes: put the decision and its one deciding number in the first three sentences so skimmers still receive it; state explicitly which sections are open for feedback this round and which are not; pre-review with the two most likely blockers before going wide, so the substantive objections are already in the doc when it lands.

drills.q: Why is "what does this foreclose?" a sharper question than "what are the downsides?" Give an example from a vector-store decision.
drills.a: Downsides are costs you pay now: visible, bounded, usually already priced in. Foreclosure is optionality you destroy, which is invisible at decision time and unbounded. Example: standardising on 1024-dim embeddings and building the HNSW index around them forecloses cheap experimentation with other models, because a dimension change means a ~50-minute rebuild on 41M rows plus re-tuning the hybrid fusion weights, turning "try a new embedding model" from an afternoon into a scheduled operation. Nobody would list that under "downsides" because it is not a cost today.

drills.q: A VP mandates a design doc for every project over two weeks. You think most of them are waste. What do you actually do?
drills.a: Comply and write the 1-page version, because the mandate is almost always a reaction to a real failure such as a project that shipped without cross-cutting security or privacy review. Then attack the real problem with evidence: measure what fraction of those docs contain an alternatives section with a genuinely considered rejected option. If it is under half, the mandate is manufacturing implementation manuals, and you have a data-backed case for gating one-way doors (data model, public API, anything with a migration) and merely advising on two-way doors.

drills.q: Name the live disagreement about ADR mutability and take a position with a reason.
drills.a: Nygard's position is immutability: supersede, never edit, because the record's value is what the team believed at the time with the information it had. Many MADR-in-practice shops edit in place. Position: immutability wins, because an edited corpus reads as though the team was always right, teaches nothing about how decisions are made, and destroys the one thing that cannot be reconstructed, the constraint set that no longer exists. The cost of immutability is a reader who must follow a supersession chain, which is cheap and mechanical.

drills.q: An interviewer says "design docs matter less now that code is cheap to generate." Respond.
drills.a: Push back on the premise. Cheap implementation raises the cost of building the wrong thing quickly and at volume, so the decision matters more, not less. What got cheaper is producing an implementation; what did not is knowing which one to produce, which is precisely the doc's job. Concede the real change: in-repo ADRs now have a second consumer in coding agents, which raises the value of hygiene (stable numbers, accurate Status, superseded-not-deleted) because an agent infers staleness worse than a human does.

drills.q: Your team ships an approved design and two teams build to different readings of it. What section failed, and why is that the likely culprit rather than the design section?
drills.a: Non-goals. Goals were written but the boundaries were not, so each team filled the gap with its own assumption. The divergence is almost always a scope question the doc never answered rather than a technical ambiguity, because a technically ambiguous design section usually generates review comments, whereas an unstated scope boundary generates silent, confident, incompatible assumptions.

drills.q: Give the 90-second verbal form of a design decision, the structure you would use in an interview when asked to walk through a doc you wrote.
drills.a: Six beats: the decision in one sentence; the goal that drove it, with a number; the single most important non-goal; the strongest rival option stated fairly; the deciding criterion, admitted as a weighting; and what would flip it. Then one beat on what review changed, which is the part that proves the doc was real rather than a paper trail. If you have to reach for context that is not in the document to give this answer, the document is missing it.

drills.q: Name the four places a piece of agent-facing knowledge can live, and the one-line test for each.
drills.a: CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md: the agent must know this in EVERY session (facts). .claude/rules/*.md with paths: frontmatter: needed whenever touching these files. SKILL.md: needed for SOME tasks (a procedure with steps). Hook: must happen regardless of what the agent decides. Only the hook is enforcement; the other three are context.

drills.q: Someone adds 'always write comprehensive tests' to CLAUDE.md. What is wrong with that line?
drills.a: Three things. It is unverifiable, so nothing checks compliance. It is context rather than configuration, so there is no guarantee it is followed. And it consumes attention budget in every session while displacing rules that are concrete. The enforcement version is a CI gate or hook that fails when coverage on changed lines drops.

drills.q: Your CLAUDE.md rule is being ignored. Give the first two diagnostic steps, in order.
drills.a: 1) Run /context and check the Memory files list. If the file is not there it was never loaded, which is a path/scope problem, not an adherence problem. 2) If it did load, audit the whole hierarchy for a contradicting instruction, since ancestor files concatenate rather than override and the model picks arbitrarily between conflicts. Only then consider dilution from file length.

drills.q: A teammate splits a 700-line CLAUDE.md into six files pulled in with @ imports and reports the context problem is fixed. Is it?
drills.a: No. Imports expand and load at launch, up to 4 hops deep, so the token cost is unchanged; only readability improved. Real reductions come from paths:-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ (load on matching file read), skills (body loads on invoke), or deletion.

drills.q: You maintain a repo with an existing AGENTS.md and want Claude Code to honor it without duplicating content. What do you do?
drills.a: Create a CLAUDE.md whose first line is `@AGENTS.md`, then append any Claude-specific instructions below it. A symlink (ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md) works if there is nothing Claude-specific to add, though on Windows that needs Administrator or Developer Mode so the import is preferable. Verify with /context that CLAUDE.md appears under Memory files. Never maintain two hand-edited copies.

drills.q: A path-scoped rule stopped applying halfway through a long session. Explain the mechanism and give two fixes with their costs.
drills.a: Path-scoped rules load into message history when a matching file is read, so compaction summarizes them away like everything else; they reload only on the next matching read. Fix 1: drop the paths: frontmatter or move the content to the project-root CLAUDE.md, which survives compaction by re-injection, at the cost of always-loaded tokens. Fix 2: if it must never be skipped, make it a hook, which is not context at all.

drills.q: Design the delegation for 'find every caller of this deprecated function across a 400k-line monorepo and tell me which ones pass a null.' What goes to a subagent and what stays?
drills.a: The search and the reading go to a subagent: it is high-volume-in / low-volume-out and you will never reference the raw grep output again. Constrain the return format explicitly ('return file:line plus the argument expression, nothing else'), because unconstrained detailed returns are how parallelism ends up costing more context than inline work. The decision about what to do with the callers stays in the main conversation.

drills.q: Three subagents implement one cross-cutting change across three services and produce three incompatible contract shapes. Name the mechanism and the fix.
drills.a: Context fragmentation: each subagent has an isolated window and only summaries return to the parent, and summaries drop exactly the kind of detail ('I named the field userId') that a shared contract depends on. Fix: decide the contract in the main conversation first, write the interface, and pass it verbatim in each delegation prompt. Better: do not split writes that share an invariant. Delegate reads, keep writes.

drills.q: CI is green, the feature is broken, the agent ran for two hours. Give the fastest discriminating check and the number that explains why you check that first.
drills.a: `git diff <pre-implementation-commit> -- tests/`. If assertions were weakened, a test deleted, a skip added, or a sleep/retry inserted around a flaky assertion, that is the answer in ten seconds. You check it first because oversight collapses onto the test suite, and SpecBench measured the visible-versus-held-out pass-rate gap growing about 28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size, so a two-hour run is exactly the regime where this dominates.

drills.q: Write the shape of the enforcement (not the advice) that prevents an agent from editing tests during implementation.
drills.a: A PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json matching Edit|Write that runs a script; the script reads the tool call as JSON on stdin, extracts tool_input.file_path, and exits non-zero for anything under tests/ or matching *_test.py / *.test.ts. Non-zero blocks the call. Pair it with a `git diff --quiet HEAD -- tests/` assertion inside the single verify script so the check also holds when the hook is not configured.

drills.q: Justify running the type checker before the test suite in the agent's verify gate, when the unit tests are faster in wall-clock terms.
drills.a: Order by signal quality per token, not wall-clock. A type error is deterministic, localized, and names the exact defect in one line, and it kills whole classes of failure (fabricated APIs, signature drift) before an expensive run. A failing test is a symptom that needs interpretation and can dump tens of thousands of tokens into the window. If the type checker genuinely takes minutes, that is a build problem to fix, not a reason to reorder.

drills.q: Your team wants to expose the internal deployment CLI to the coding agent as an MCP server. Argue both sides and land on a recommendation.
drills.a: Against: the agent already has shell access, so a bash invocation costs zero startup context while the server costs a process, a schema, and an auth surface. For: MCP gives a per-capability permission boundary and an audit trail rather than blanket shell access, and reaches clients with no shell. Recommendation: skip it unless you specifically want the permission boundary or audit trail; wrapping an existing CLI for its own sake is a step backwards.

drills.q: An agent produced a confident summary of a staging-database query through an MCP server, and the conclusion was wrong. Name the failure mode and the three fixes.
drills.a: MCP output truncation: a warning fires above 10,000 tokens of tool output and the default hard cap is 25,000, so an unpaginated result silently became partial and then became a premise. Fixes: paginate at the server, add the anthropic/maxResultSizeChars annotation for that tool, or raise MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS. The general lesson is never to let a truncated result be treated as complete.

drills.q: You are asked to write a spec for 'add rate limiting' so an agent can verify against it. Show what makes a clause checkable.
drills.a: Each clause must map to at least one test. 'Requests over 100/min per API key return 429', 'the 429 carries an integer Retry-After in seconds', 'the counter keys on API key not client IP', 'windows are fixed 60s not sliding', 'a rejected request does not consume normal quota', 'keys with no configured limit are unlimited, not defaulted to 100'. Add explicit non-goals (no distributed coordination in v1) and invariants (no new dependency without asking) to bound scope creep.

drills.q: Leadership asks for a metric proving the agentic-coding rollout is working. What do you refuse to report and what do you report instead?
drills.a: Refuse PRs merged, lines generated, and velocity: generating more unreviewed code moves work into a queue nobody can see, and human review capacity is the binding constraint. Report change failure rate and time-to-restore on AI-assisted changes versus the baseline, plus review latency. The honest question is whether verification kept pace with generation, not whether generation went up.

drills.q: Defend a boundary: an engineer wants the agent to fix an intermittent deadlock in a connection pool. Talk them out of it, and say what you would delegate instead.
drills.a: The agent's feedback signal is 'the tests passed', and a race that manifests once per 10,000 interleavings passes every run, so the loop reports success on a broken fix and stops. The failure shape is also the characteristic weakness: correct-looking locking around the wrong critical section. Delegate the surrounding work instead: build the stress harness, add instrumentation, summarize thread dumps, generate the reproduction script. Decide the lock placement yourself.

drills.q: Cite the METR result correctly, including the part most people get wrong.
drills.a: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks, mature repos they averaged 5 years on: allowing early-2025 AI tooling increased completion time by 19%. The part people get wrong is the scope and the direction of the interesting finding. It does not show AI makes everyone slower; it shows that in that setting the developers forecast 24% faster, self-reported 20% faster afterwards, and were measurably slower. The perception gap is the durable, transferable result.

drills.q: What happens when you call `let f = fetch_user(42);` and never await it?
drills.a: Nothing. Zero lines of the body run. `f` is an inert state machine value on the stack. `Future` is `#[must_use]`, so `unused_must_use` fires, and that warning is almost always a real bug. Contrast asyncio's create_task and Go's `go f()`, both of which start immediately.

drills.q: How many worker threads does `#[tokio::main]` start by default, and how do you change it without touching code?
drills.a: One per CPU core (the multi_thread flavour is the default). Change it with the `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS` environment variable, or `#[tokio::main(worker_threads = 4)]`, or `Builder::new_multi_thread().worker_threads(4)`.

drills.q: You drop a `JoinHandle` returned by `tokio::spawn`. Is the task cancelled?
drills.a: No. Dropping a JoinHandle detaches the task; it keeps running to completion. To cancel you call `handle.abort()`, which drops the task at its next .await point, or you put the task in a `JoinSet`, whose drop aborts every member.

drills.q: What is the default cap on Tokio's blocking thread pool, and how long does an idle blocking thread live?
drills.a: max_blocking_threads defaults to 512, and thread_keep_alive defaults to 10 seconds of idleness. The 512 is a cap, not a preallocation, and it excludes the async worker threads. Calls beyond the cap queue.

drills.q: `broadcast::channel(3)`: how many messages must a receiver fall behind before it lags?
drills.a: More than 4. The capacity is rounded UP to the next power of two, so channel(3) allocates a 4-slot ring and lag detection is based on that rounded size. RecvError::Lagged(n) does not close the receiver; the cursor advances to the oldest retained value and the next recv() succeeds.

drills.q: A hand-written `poll` returns `Poll::Pending` and forgets to store the waker. What is the production symptom?
drills.a: The task is silently lost forever: no panic, no log, no timeout from the runtime. It surfaces as a request that hangs until the client's own timeout fires. The subtler variant is storing the waker only once: work-stealing may migrate the task to another worker between polls, so the stale waker targets the wrong scheduler slot and the hang appears only under load.

drills.q: Why does an `async fn` that holds a 64 KiB buffer across an `.await` matter at 100,000 concurrent tasks?
drills.a: Every local live across an .await becomes a field of the generated state machine, so the future is at least 64 KiB, and tokio::spawn heap-allocates it per task: 6.4 GiB before a single byte is processed. Locals NOT live across an await are ordinary stack locals inside poll and cost nothing, so shrinking the buffer's live range (or moving the allocation after the last await) is a real, measurable fix. Box::pin at the spawn site helps the move cost but not the size.

drills.q: This compiles: `let g = mutex.lock().unwrap(); do_io().await; g.push(x);` using std::sync::Mutex. What can go wrong?
drills.a: A full-runtime deadlock. std::sync::MutexGuard is Send when T: Send, so the future is Send and spawn accepts it. But worker A holds the lock and suspends at the await; workers B through H block on the lock; now no thread is left to poll the task that would release it. Symptom is zero CPU and zero forward progress under load. Fix: drop the guard before the await, or use tokio::sync::Mutex whose lock() is async.

drills.q: Rewrite this so it does not lose bytes: `loop { select! { r = sock.read_exact(&mut hdr) => f(r?), _ = shutdown.recv() => break } }`
drills.a: read_exact is not cancellation-safe: if shutdown fires after 3 of 8 header bytes, those bytes are consumed from the socket and absent from hdr, and the stream desynchronizes. Either hoist it out of the loop so it survives iterations (`let mut read = pin!(sock.read_exact(&mut hdr));` then `r = &mut read`), or use cancel-safe `sock.read(&mut buf)` and reassemble frames yourself, or move the connection into its own task and cancel the whole task.

drills.q: p99 goes 5ms, 250ms, 500ms, 750ms as load rises, in clean steps. What does the shape tell you?
drills.a: Quantized steps mean a fixed-cost blocking call times queue position, not contention (which gives a smooth curve). Some synchronous ~250ms operation, bcrypt at cost 12 being the classic, is pinning a worker thread. Confirm with two checks: your own timers firing late (sleep(10ms) returning in 260ms proves the executor is starved, not the downstream), and tokio-console showing high worker_mean_poll_time.

drills.q: You move the 250ms bcrypt call into `spawn_blocking` on a 16-core box. What is the remaining problem?
drills.a: max_blocking_threads is 512, sized for I/O blocking where threads park in syscalls, not for CPU work. 512 threads hashing on 16 cores is 32x oversubscription: context-switch storms visible in `pidstat -w`, and p99 degrading roughly linearly with the oversubscription factor. Gate it with a Semaphore sized to core count, or use rayon bridged by a oneshot. Also note spawn_blocking tasks cannot be aborted once started, so shutdown now hangs without Runtime::shutdown_timeout.

drills.q: Explain the LIFO slot and why it is bounded to 3 consecutive uses.
drills.a: When a running task wakes another, the woken task goes into a single-slot LIFO register and is polled immediately next, which is a cache-locality win for request/response ping-pong. It is bounded so it cannot starve the worker's local queue; after 3 consecutive uses it is temporarily disabled until the worker schedules a task from elsewhere. The task in the slot is also not stealable by other workers, and the coop budget is deliberately NOT reset through it, so a ping-pong pair cannot mutually re-arm each other's 128-op budget forever.

drills.q: Why is `Mutex::lock` listed as not cancellation-safe, and how is that different from `read_exact`?
drills.a: Different failure mode. read_exact holds partial progress in the future's own state, so dropping it loses data. Mutex::lock (and RwLock::read/write, Semaphore::acquire, Notify::notified) uses a fair FIFO wait queue, so cancelling loses your place in line. That is not data loss but it is a starvation hazard: a select! loop that repeatedly re-acquires can send a task to the back of the queue indefinitely.

drills.q: You fan out to 50 providers with a 5-second budget and return after the first 5 answers. What actually happens to the other 45 requests?
drills.a: Their futures are dropped, which closes the connections. Two consequences. You lose the pooled keep-alive connection and pay a TLS handshake (roughly 1-3 RTTs) next time, so size the client pool accordingly. And the providers may already have executed and will still bill you: cancellation is not rollback. If the calls have side effects or cost money, let them run to completion into a oneshot you ignore, or use a CancellationToken so the adapter can finish its accounting first.

drills.q: A trait has an `async fn`. Your generic function tries to `tokio::spawn(t.get(k))` and fails to compile. Why, and what are the options?
drills.a: AFIT desugars to `-> impl Future + '_`, which is anonymous, so the trait cannot declare it Send and a generic caller cannot write a bound for it. Options: the `trait-variant` crate (`trait_variant::make(Store: Send)`) generates a parallel Send-bounded trait; `#[async_trait]` bakes `+ Send` into a `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>` at the cost of one heap allocation per call; or make the concrete type generic so the compiler sees the real future. Return-type notation (`T::get(..): Send`) is the accepted long-term fix and is still unstable as of Rust 1.97.1.

drills.q: worker_mean_poll_time is low, injection_queue_depth is high, and there is no blocking call anywhere. What else could it be?
drills.a: Genuine saturation (need more workers), or a task that participates in nothing: one wrapped in task::coop::unconstrained, or a hand-written future that never decrements the 128-operation coop budget, monopolizing a worker without any single poll being long. The other candidate is a lock convoy on a tokio::sync::Mutex with its FIFO wait queue, where mean poll time is small but every task spends its life queued.

drills.q: In one sentence, state the pattern that predicts whether a component in an AI stack gets rewritten in Rust.
drills.a: A hot loop that is not a matmul, called millions of times, with small per-item work, that cannot be batched onto a GPU or handed to BLAS. Equivalently: Rust owns the band where the unit of work is a byte or token, Python keeps the band where it is a tensor.

drills.q: You are about to write your first PyO3 binding. What is the very first number you should measure, and why?
drills.a: The cost of an empty call. Measured: 54.56 ns for an empty #[pyfunction] vs 50.71 ns for an empty Python def, with a 34.31 ns floor for the attribute lookup alone. That is your floor: every function you expose must do meaningfully more work than it, or the binding makes things worse. Practical break-even is ~1 microsecond of Rust work per call.

drills.q: A colleague benchmarks a Rust tokenizer against a pure-Python one and reports 14x. What is the first thing you check before believing it?
drills.a: That both produce identical output. Assert py.encode(text) == hf.encode(text).ids before timing anything; without it you are benchmarking two different algorithms and the number is meaningless. Second, ask which cache state and which API: the same comparison ranges from 2.4x to 17.5x, and in one condition (warm memo cache vs HF encode()) the pure-Python version actually wins, 33.8 ms vs 43.2 ms.

drills.q: Your data pipeline wraps tokenizers.encode_batch in ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) and sees no speedup. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: encode_batch already releases the GIL and saturates the cores via its internal rayon pool, so the Python threads have nothing to take. Measured 147.0 / 147.3 / 152.3 ms for 1 / 2 / 4 threads, flat then slightly worse from oversubscription. Fix: remove the pool and set RAYON_NUM_THREADS. Verify the internal parallelism is on with TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=true, which measured 142.7 ms vs 324.6 ms for false, a 2.27x on 2 vCPUs.

drills.q: Tokenization throughput halved after a deploy with no code change. Trace it.
drills.a: Something set TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false, almost always copy-pasted from a HuggingFace issue to silence the fork-safety warning. Measured cost: 324.6 ms vs 142.7 ms, 2.27x. The warning exists because rayon's thread pool does not survive os.fork(): the child inherits a pool whose threads do not exist and hangs. The correct fix is the fork ordering, not disabling parallelism: construct the tokenizer after forking, or use the spawn start method.

drills.q: A teammate binds a per-item Python helper to Rust and it comes out slower. Explain the mechanism and give the fix.
drills.a: The ~55 ns boundary plus argument conversion exceeded the work done. Concretely, a Rust add(a: i64, b: i64) measured 79.16 ns against 70.85 ns for the Python equivalent, 12% slower, because two PyLong_AsLongLong conversions plus boxing the result cost more than an add instruction saves. Fix: move the LOOP into Rust, not the loop body. One call per batch, never one per item.

drills.q: Someone proposes a Rust binding whose signature is `fn process(items: Vec<String>) -> Vec<String>`. What do you predict and why?
drills.a: No speedup, probably a regression. A Python container argument makes the boundary O(n) at roughly the per-element cost the builtin was already paying: my sum_list(Vec<i64>) measured 0.40x-0.68x of builtin sum() at every N from 1 to 1,048,576 with no crossover, at 7.6-12.3 ns/element extraction. The return side is worse: Vec<String> allocates a Python object per element. Redesign so the input is bytes/str and the output is a numpy array or bytes.

drills.q: Your zero-copy Rust f64 reduction is 2x SLOWER than np.sum on a 1M-element array. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: iter().sum() on f64 does not autovectorise, because IEEE-754 addition is non-associative and LLVM will not reorder your numerics; it compiles to a serial chain of scalar addsd. numpy uses pairwise summation with hand-written SIMD. Measured 1,206,878 ns vs 609,451 ns at N=1,048,576. Fix: split into 8 independent accumulators via chunks_exact(8) with a horizontal reduce, accepting that last-bit results change. Same failure documented in T20-rust-perf.

drills.q: Explain why py.detach() is not free, and give the threshold for using it.
drills.a: A detach/attach round trip costs ~30-40 ns. Measured overhead: 48.5% at zero work (92.9 vs 62.5 ns), 45.5% at 10 iterations, 5.1% at 100, 0.9% at 10,000. So detach when the closure does more than roughly 1 microsecond of work. This is why tokenizers detaches in encode_batch (milliseconds) and not in encode() on a 7-token prompt. Note also that Python<'py> is not Send, so the compiler prevents you touching Python objects inside.

drills.q: Your Rust extension is deployed and the whole Python process dies with SIGABRT under load, no traceback, all in-flight requests lost. Root cause?
drills.a: panic = "abort" in the extension's [profile.release]. PyO3 normally catches panics at the #[pyfunction] boundary (unwinding across FFI is UB) and converts them to a Python PanicException that kills only that request; abort disables the catch. Remove it from extension builds. Then audit what panics: slice indexing on user-controlled lengths, unwrap on parses, and PyRefMut borrow violations from two threads mutably borrowing the same #[pyclass].

drills.q: An interviewer asks: 'our LLM serving p99 is 4 seconds, why not rewrite it in Rust?' Give the full answer, including where you WOULD use Rust.
drills.a: Ask for the CPU-bound-Python fraction of p99; on a generation request it is under 2% because the GPU owns prefill and decode. Tokenizing a real 30-char prompt measured 11.02 microseconds = 0.00028% of a 4-second request, so the whole rewrite's ceiling is single-digit ms out of 4,000. The real levers are batching config, KV-cache hit rate and eviction, prefill/decode interference, queueing, and cold model loads. Where I WOULD use Rust: the router doing cache-aware prefix-match tokenization at high QPS (exactly what sgl-router and vLLM's router do), and the offline data pipeline where encode_batch's GIL release is worth ~one core per core owned.

drills.q: Give a five-step decision procedure for whether to write a Rust binding.
drills.a: 1) Profile: get the CPU-bound-Python fraction of p99. Under 10%, stop. 2) Exhaust the free wins first, they are usually bigger: encode_batch over encode measured 2.87x, encode_batch_fast a further 1.19x, TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=true 2.27x, all zero new code. 3) Estimate per-call work; under ~1 microsecond, move the loop not the loop body. 4) Check what crosses: list/dict is O(n) and expect no win, bytes or buffer-protocol array is O(1) and expect one. 5) Price the team cost: build time, who maintains it, whether the weekly changers can write Rust. Then prototype and measure the empty call before committing.

drills.q: Two Rust tokenizers, same algorithm, byte-identical output, 7.8x apart. Explain, and say what this generalises to.
drills.a: hf.encode() 400.1 ms vs tiktoken.encode_ordinary() 51.5 ms on 738,046 bytes producing an identical 191,673 ids. The difference is the return type: HF's Encoding carries eight parallel vectors including a heap String per token plus char-to-byte offset bookkeeping; tiktoken returns Vec<u32>. encode_batch_fast, which skips offsets, recovers 1.19x, confirming offsets were ~16% and the per-token String is the rest. Generalises to: the shape of what you hand back across the boundary is often a larger term than the language of the hot loop.

drills.q: Free-threaded Python is officially supported in 3.14. Argue both sides of what that does to Rust bindings.
drills.a: Against Rust: PEP 779 moved free-threading to phase two (supported, opt-in as 3.14t), single-threaded overhead down to ~5-10% from ~40% in 3.13, so the 'Rust to escape the GIL' argument has a multi-year expiry date and a new binding written purely for parallelism is harder to justify. For Rust: the constant factor is untouched (104.00 ns per interpreted iteration vs 1.81 ns, 57.5x), and compile-time Send/Sync checking becomes MORE valuable because a large amount of Python and C-extension code has latent races the GIL was accidentally serialising. Practical trap: an extension that has not declared gil_used = false makes CPython re-enable the GIL at import, silently.

drills.q: You are asked to evaluate candle for a production embedding service. Design the evaluation and state what would make you say no.
drills.a: Benchmark YOUR model, not a blog's. Reported candle-vs-PyTorch results are bimodal because the variance is entirely which ops have tuned kernels: 35-47% faster on some BERT/ResNet paths, but candle issue #2877 documents all-MiniLM-L6-v2 at 122.30 ms/batch vs ~14.34 ms in PyTorch, 8.5x slower, and issue #942 the same for YOLOv8 vs ONNX Runtime. Say yes if the constraint is the deployment artifact: static binary vs a 4+ GB container, serverless cold start, edge/WASM, or removing a 1-3 ms sidecar hop. Say no if the constraint is GPU throughput at scale, if you need day-one support for new architectures, or if the people who change this code weekly write Python.

drills.q: Fill in the 2x2: which type do you reach for at (one owner, single thread), (many owners, single thread), (one owner, many threads), (many owners, many threads)? Then the interior-mutability version of each.
drills.a: One owner / single thread: Box<T>; interior mut Cell<T> or RefCell<T>. Many owners / single thread: Rc<T>; interior mut Rc<RefCell<T>>. One owner / many threads: Box<T> moved into the thread; interior mut Mutex<T>, RwLock<T>, or Atomic*. Many owners / many threads: Arc<T>; interior mut Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<AtomicUsize>. The compiler picks the row for you: Rc is !Send and RefCell is !Sync, so the top row cannot cross a thread boundary.

drills.q: State the definitions of Send and Sync in one sentence each, without using the phrase 'thread safe'.
drills.a: Send: the value can be moved to another thread. Sync: &T can be shared with another thread, which the standard library defines formally as T: Sync if and only if &T: Send. Both are auto traits, derived structurally by the compiler from a type's fields rather than implemented by hand.

drills.q: List the five things unsafe enables, and name three things it does NOT turn off.
drills.a: Enables: dereference a raw pointer; call an unsafe fn or method; access or modify a mutable static; implement an unsafe trait; access union fields. Does NOT turn off: the borrow checker (it still runs inside unsafe blocks), lifetime checking, type checking, move semantics, or Drop. The only real change is that rustc stops demanding a proof and starts assuming one, then optimizes on it.

drills.q: Quote the two RefCell panic messages on current stable Rust and say which operation produces each.
drills.a: On rustc 1.97.1: borrow_mut() while a Ref is live gives `RefCell already borrowed` (error type BorrowMutError). borrow() while a RefMut is live gives `RefCell already mutably borrowed` (error type BorrowError). Older releases and most blog posts phrase these as `already borrowed: BorrowMutError` and `already mutably borrowed: BorrowError`; the type names are the stable part and are what try_borrow_mut()/try_borrow() return in the Err arm.

drills.q: Give the measured ns/op for Rc::clone+drop, Arc::clone+drop, AtomicUsize::fetch_add, Mutex lock+unlock, and RefCell::borrow_mut, and explain how the Arc number is consistent with the atomic number.
drills.a: On rustc 1.97.1 -O, x86_64, i5-12450H: Rc clone+drop 1.53 ns; Arc clone+drop 14.44 ns (9.4x Rc); AtomicUsize::fetch_add(Relaxed) 6.04 ns; Mutex lock+unlock 13.19 ns; RefCell borrow_mut+drop ~0.25 ns. Arc clone+drop is two atomic RMWs (a lock xadd on clone and a lock xsub on drop) plus a branch, so 2 x 6.04 = 12.08 ns plus overhead reconciles with the measured 14.44 ns. Mutex at 13.19 ns is likewise about two atomic RMWs.

drills.q: Explain why Arc::clone can use Relaxed ordering but Arc's Drop cannot, and what the last dropper does.
drills.a: Clone publishes nothing: you already held a valid Arc, so the value already exists and no other memory needs to become visible to anyone, which makes Relaxed sufficient. Drop uses fetch_sub(1, Release) because any writes made through this Arc must be visible to the thread that eventually runs the destructor. The last dropper, seeing the previous count was 1, executes atomic::fence(Acquire) before touching the data; that fence pairs with every other thread's Release decrement, establishing the happens-before that makes running T's destructor with exclusive access sound. Overflow is checked against MAX_REFCOUNT = isize::MAX as usize and calls abort() rather than panic!, since a caught panic would leave the count corrupt.

drills.q: Here is a bug: `for l in self.listeners.borrow().iter() { l.on_event(&ev); }`. Name the failure, the exact panic, why it is rare, and the fix.
drills.a: Failure: re-entrant borrow. The Ref from borrow() is alive for the whole loop, so if any handler calls back in and does listeners.borrow_mut() (to unsubscribe itself, typically) you get a runtime panic reading `RefCell already borrowed`. It is rare because it requires a specific re-entrant path, often an error branch, so it may fire once in ten million requests. It is hard to debug because the panic's line number is the SECOND borrow, not the still-live first one. Fix: end the borrow before dispatch, e.g. `let snapshot: Vec<_> = self.listeners.borrow().iter().cloned().collect();` then iterate the snapshot with no guard held. Where you cannot restructure, use try_borrow_mut() and log with your own context.

drills.q: Explain to a Java engineer, in under a minute, the one structural thing Rust's Mutex<T> does that synchronized cannot, and two ways Rust's is worse.
drills.a: Rust's Mutex owns the data. The only route to the T is lock(), which returns a guard that derefs to &mut T, so `forgot to take the lock` is not expressible; Java's synchronized guards a block and the lock-to-fields mapping lives in a @GuardedBy comment checked only by optional tooling. Worse in two ways: (1) Rust's std Mutex is NOT reentrant, and std documents a second lock on the same thread as unspecified behaviour that will not return, so a recursive helper that works in Java hangs, the symptom being a thread in futex_wait at 0% CPU with no logs; (2) it poisons, so a panic while holding the guard makes every later lock() return Err(PoisonError) forever. parking_lot::Mutex drops poisoning and is 1 byte instead of 8.

drills.q: RSS grows monotonically under steady load, no crash, no errors. Give your diagnostic sequence and the structural fix.
drills.a: Rule out unbounded queues and caches first, then suspect an Rc/Arc cycle, because Rust's guarantee explicitly excludes leak-freedom (mem::forget and Box::leak are safe, and there is no cycle collector since that needs a tracing runtime). Sequence: assert Rc::strong_count/weak_count in unit tests around the suspect structure; run `cargo +nightly miri test`, whose leak checker reports any allocation live at exit that is not reachable from a static; use a heap profiler to find allocations with no live root. Fix: owning edges are Rc/Arc, back-edges are Weak, upgraded with .upgrade() which returns Option and yields None once the target is gone. Weak does not contribute to the strong count, so it cannot keep the value alive.

drills.q: Why is MutexGuard Sync but not Send? Derive it, and name the async consequence.
drills.a: !Send because unlocking must happen on the locking thread: POSIX makes pthread_mutex_unlock from a non-owning thread undefined behaviour, and the guard's Drop is what unlocks, so allowing the guard to move to another thread would allow the unlock to happen there. Sync (when T: Sync) because &MutexGuard<T> only yields &T, and sharing a &T is exactly what T: Sync licenses; sharing a reference to the guard never moves the guard, so the unlock stays put. Async consequence: holding a std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await makes the whole future !Send, so tokio::spawn rejects it with an error naming the guard type. Fix by scoping the guard to drop before the await, or use tokio::sync::Mutex whose guard is Send and whose lock() is awaitable.

drills.q: p99 doubled after a deploy that added a shared counter behind Arc<Mutex<u64>>. The single-threaded benchmark is unchanged. Diagnose and give three fixes in order of preference.
drills.a: The counter is one cache line and every core writes to it, so it ping-pongs across the interconnect; perf shows time in lock cmpxchg/lock xadd and in futex once threads actually block. The single-threaded benchmark showed nothing because uncontended the numbers are benign: Mutex lock+unlock 13.19 ns, AtomicUsize::fetch_add 6.04 ns measured. Fixes: (1) drop the mutex, use Arc<AtomicU64> with fetch_add(1, Relaxed), which halves the cost and cannot deadlock; (2) shard it, one padded counter per shard summed on read, which removes contention entirely at the cost of a non-atomic total; (3) batch it, increment a thread-local and flush every N events, which is what metrics libraries do. Also check for Arc::clone inside the loop; passing &Arc<T> or &T saves ~14 ns per iteration. RwLock is usually not the answer: I measured RwLock::read at 15.12 ns, slower than Mutex::lock, because a read lock still does an atomic RMW.

drills.q: Define soundness for an unsafe abstraction, then explain why 'our crate passes Miri' does not establish it.
drills.a: Sound iff no safe caller, using any combination of the public API in any order, can cause undefined behaviour. Three teeth: any combination and order (two individually safe methods can be jointly unsound, which is why Vec::set_len is an unsafe fn), composition with any other sound crate (which is what makes unsafe impl Send so consequential), and panics (unwinding runs Drop on a temporarily invalid object; Miri has found exactly this in std, including Vec and BTreeMap leaking under panicky conditions). Miri does not establish soundness because it tests executions, not callers: it runs one interleaving by default (seed 0), -Zmiri-many-seeds explores a bounded range defaulting to 0..64, preemption is 1% per basic block, and it cannot execute networking or most FFI. Miri's own README says this. Passing Miri means these tests, on these interleavings, had no UB.

drills.q: Miri reports a Stacked Borrows error on code you believe is correct. Walk through your decision procedure, and say what you would NOT do.
drills.a: Re-run with MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-tree-borrows". If Tree Borrows also rejects it, it is a real bug: you almost certainly cached a raw pointer derived from a reference and used it after a later reborrow invalidated it, so rederive from the live reference at each use or restructure with UnsafeCell/NonNull so the provenance chain is unbroken. If only Stacked Borrows rejects it, you have hit a known over-restriction — Tree Borrows (PLDI 2025, Distinguished Paper) rejects 54% fewer test cases across the 30,000 most-downloaded crates — so document it and track the model discussion. What I would NOT do is switch CI to Tree Borrows to make the error go away: Miri's README warns that Tree Borrows is more experimental and that the eventual official model is likely STRICTER than Tree Borrows, so code TB accepts today may be declared UB later. Gate on Stacked Borrows; use Tree Borrows as a diagnostic.

drills.q: Tests pass in debug and the release build dies with SIGILL. Explain the mechanism, give the verified minimal example, and say what you must not do about it.
drills.a: That is the signature of undefined behaviour. At -O0 the optimizer does almost nothing so a broken assumption often has no consequence; at -O the optimizer USES the assumption and, finding it false, can emit ud2, delete a branch it proved unreachable, or produce a value that is neither true nor false. Verified minimal case on rustc 1.97.1: reading an uninitialized bool via MaybeUninit::<bool>::uninit().assume_init() prints `saw-false` and exits 0 in debug, and dies with `Illegal instruction (core dumped)`, exit status 132, at -O, from identical source on the same machine. Diagnose with `cargo +nightly miri test`, plus -Zsanitizer=address / -Zsanitizer=thread for anything Miri cannot run. What you must NOT do is make the symptom disappear by reordering statements or inserting black_box; that hides UB and it returns on the next compiler upgrade. Note that integer overflow is not UB: it is specified to panic with debug_assertions and wrap without.

drills.q: Someone proposes Rc<RefCell<Node>> for a large in-memory graph. Argue the alternative, and state the honest counter-argument against your own recommendation.
drills.a: Rc<RefCell<Node>> stacks four costs simultaneously: a refcount on every clone (1.53 ns, or 14.44 ns if it becomes Arc), an 8-byte borrow flag per node, pointer chasing with poor cache locality, plus the runtime panic risk and the cycle-leak risk. An arena (Vec<Node> plus usize or slotmap keys) removes all four: no refcount, no borrow flag, cycles are not expressible, and storage is contiguous. This is what petgraph and rustc's own data structures do. Honest counter-argument: arena indices can go logically stale when a slot is reused, producing a silently wrong-node bug rather than a crash, which is exactly why slotmap adds generation counters; and Rc<RefCell<_>> is genuinely the right call when ownership is dynamic and shared across subsystems that cannot share an arena.

drills.q: How big is a cache line on x86-64, and name three separate Rust performance phenomena that follow directly from that one number.
drills.a: 64 bytes (128 on aarch64/Apple silicon at some levels). It explains: (1) AoS vs SoA, because you pull a whole line and use 4 bytes of every 32; (2) false sharing, because 4 AtomicU64 = 32 B all land on one line and 4 cores fight over it; (3) why `#[repr(align(64))]` / `CachePadded` is the fix; (4) why linked lists lose to `Vec` at equal asymptotic complexity. Measured stride curve over 64 MB: 0.36 ns/touch at stride 1 B, 3.22 ns at stride 64 B, 6.63 ns at 256 B. The knee is exactly at 64.

drills.q: Your colleague benchmarks a `--debug` build and reports iterators are 4x slower than index loops. What do you say?
drills.a: The measurement is meaningless: `cargo build` defaults to `opt-level=0`, where nothing is inlined, no loop is vectorised, and every bounds check is live. It is a different program. Re-run with `--release`. Measured on rustc 1.97.1 release: `sum_iter` 35 instructions vs `sum_loop` 34, with an identical SSE2 `paddq` core; the only difference was label names and the order of two `xor` register-zeroing instructions. In the zip case the iterator was strictly better: 37 instructions and 0 panic edges vs 63 instructions and 2 panic call sites.

drills.q: Name the three tools for inspecting generated Rust assembly and when you'd pick each.
drills.a: (1) Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) for a self-contained snippet with a pinned rustc version and `-C opt-level=3`; mark the fn `pub` in a `--crate-type=lib` or `#[no_mangle]` so it survives DCE. (2) `cargo-show-asm`: `cargo asm --lib 'crate::f' --rust` for code inside a real crate with real dependencies; `--rust` interleaves source with assembly, and it also emits `--llvm` and `--mir` (MIR is the right view for what rustc did before LLVM). (3) `objdump -d target/release/libfoo.rlib` for ground truth. Always `--release`.

drills.q: A Criterion benchmark reports 900 picoseconds for a function that loops over 10 million elements. Diagnose it in one sentence, then give the 30-second proof.
drills.a: The optimiser deleted the work: 900 ps is under three clock cycles at 3 GHz. Proof: run at N and 2N and check the time roughly doubles for an O(n) function; if it doesn't, the loop is gone. Criterion's own output gives it away too, e.g. 'Collecting 100 samples in estimated 5.0000 s (5.2B iterations)'. Measured case: `(0..10_000_000).fold(0u64, wrapping_add)` benchmarked at 975.34 ps and STILL 958.84 ps with `black_box` on the input, because LLVM found the triangular-sum closed form. `black_box` on the argument is not sufficient when the body itself is analytically foldable.

drills.q: Explain why `v.iter().sum::<f32>()` stays scalar on an AVX2 machine while `sum::<i32>()` vectorises, and give the fix plus its cost.
drills.a: IEEE-754 addition is not associative, so splitting a serial reduction into 4 or 8 lanes is a reassociation that changes the result; LLVM refuses. Integer wrapping addition IS associative, so `sum_i32` used 8 `ymm` registers under `-C target-cpu=native` while `sum_f32` was 39 instructions of 8x-unrolled scalar `addss` all into `%xmm0` (so the unroll bought nothing, every add depending on the previous at ~4 cycles latency). Fix: manually split into 8 independent accumulators, measured 6.67x on 4096 f32s (1.9323 us -> 289.69 ns). Cost: it's a correctness change, last-bit results differ, so it's unacceptable where output must be bit-reproducible.

drills.q: Quantify the monomorphisation tax and name the tool plus the refactor that fixes it.
drills.a: One small generic fn over 200 concrete types vs the `&dyn` version instantiated once: rebuild 536 ms vs 169 ms (3.17x), .rlib 494,904 vs 387,256 B (+107,648 B, 1.28x), LLVM IR 10,847 vs 5,690 lines (1.91x). That is ONE small function; a real service instantiates thousands, which is why builds are slow (the borrow checker is typically single-digit percent, verify with `cargo build --timings`). Tool: `cargo llvm-lines --release | head -30`, which ranks by IR lines and correlates with both compile time and binary size. Refactor: thin generic wrapper over a non-generic inner fn, `fn load<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) { load_inner(p.as_ref()) }`.

drills.q: Throughput went DOWN when you added threads and the threads share no data. Give the hypothesis, the measured cost, and the diagnostic command.
drills.a: False sharing. Cache coherence works on 64-byte lines, not variables, so logically independent counters that are physically adjacent live on one line and each core's write invalidates it in the other cores' L1, turning an L1 hit into a coherence transaction. Measured: 4 threads x 50,000,000 relaxed `fetch_add`, packed `AtomicU64` 1768.298 ms vs `#[repr(align(64))]` 481.023 ms = 3.68x. Diagnose with `perf c2c record` then `perf c2c report`, which reports HITM events and names the cache line and the contending instructions. Fix with `crossbeam_utils::CachePadded` (pads to 128 B on aarch64, where hand-rolled `align(64)` is subtly wrong).

drills.q: Is `Vec::with_capacity` always worth it? Give three measurements that determine the answer.
drills.a: No. 1M `u64` pushes: 0.677 ms vs 0.674 ms with capacity, no win, because amortised doubling is only ~20 reallocs and glibc `realloc` extends large mappings in place. 200k `String` pushes: 10.491 vs 6.619 ms = 1.58x, a real win, because each realloc memcpys 24-byte String headers and the heap is fragmented by 200k separate allocations. Best of all: `(0..1M).collect::<Vec<u64>>()` at 0.203 ms = 3.33x over the push loop, using `size_hint` to allocate once and write through a raw pointer with no per-push capacity check. The rule: pre-allocation matters in proportion to element-move cost and existing heap fragmentation.

drills.q: Given a hot loop over `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>` where the implementation set is closed, what do you change and what does it cost?
drills.a: Enum dispatch: `enum Op { A(A), B(B), C(C) }` with a `match` in the method (the `enum_dispatch` crate generates it from a trait). That gives a jump table or a few compares instead of `call *0x18(%rcx)`, stores payloads inline so the `Vec` is contiguous with no per-element allocation, and lets LLVM inline into each arm. Costs: every element is as large as the largest variant plus a discriminant, so one 200-byte variant among five 8-byte variants wastes 192 B per element (fix: box just the fat variant); and the enum is closed, so downstream crates cannot add implementations. The often-bigger structural win is batching work by concrete type so each inner loop is monomorphic.

drills.q: State the current cross-crate inlining rule correctly, and say what LTO actually buys with numbers.
drills.a: The folklore ('a non-generic cross-crate fn without `#[inline]` cannot be inlined without LTO') is now only partly true: rustc's MIR inliner does cross-crate inlining of small-to-medium functions on stable regardless. Tested with a two-crate workspace, no `#[inline]`, `lto = false`: zero `call` instructions to the dependency's function, and it still inlined after being made bulky. `lto = "fat"` + `codegen-units = 1` bought binary size: 4,426,416 -> 2,221,304 B (49.8%) at 0.14 s -> 2.48 s build (17.7x), for a 3.6% runtime delta that was noise.
