So LTO is a size and devirtualisation tool first; `lto = "thin"` is the sane default, and it doesn't belong on a crate the team iterates on daily.

drills.q: Design a performance CI gate for a Rust service. What actually works and what fails?
drills.a: Wall-clock Criterion on a shared CI runner fails: noisy neighbours, frequency scaling and thermal throttling give 5-10% run-to-run variance, larger than the effect sizes you care about, so the false-positive rate exceeds the true-positive rate and the team learns to ignore the alert, which is worse than no alert. What works: either a dedicated pinned runner with boost disabled and the `performance` governor (still ~5% resolution), or instrumented counting for the CI signal, i.e. cachegrind instruction counts, which are deterministic with zero run-to-run variance at 50-100x slowdown (the technique CodSpeed productised). Use wall-clock for the release check, instruction counts for the gate. Store `target/criterion/` as an artifact either way.

drills.q: Write the release profile you'd ship for a compute-bound service and justify every line, including one you'd argue against.
drills.a: `opt-level = 3` (default; never `"z"`/`"s"`, which disable unrolling and vectorisation). `lto = "thin"` (most of fat LTO's size benefit at ~1/3 the build cost). `codegen-units = 1` (better optimisation, but serialises the backend). `debug = 1` (line tables so prod flamegraphs are readable, near-free at runtime). `strip = "debuginfo"` (never `"symbols"`, which destroys the flamegraph). `incremental = false` (incremental + release is a known deoptimisation). The one to argue against: `panic = "abort"` saves 5-10% of binary size by removing unwind tables, but makes `catch_unwind` a no-op, so on a service where a panicking request handler must not kill the process, Tokio's task-panic isolation breaks and `unwind` is correct.

drills.q: Someone claims rewriting a Python service in Rust will be 100x faster. Give the decision framework and the five reasons it might come out at only 3x.
drills.a: Framework: first ask what fraction of latency is actually CPU. If 90% is waiting on a vector store, LLM endpoint or S3, the language constant factor is rounding error and the work is batching/caching/pooling. If CPU-bound, ask whether the CPU is in Python bytecode or already in C extensions, because NumPy/PyArrow paths win maybe 1-2x, not 100x; the real 10-100x is Python-level loops over Python objects, refcounting, and GIL-serialised threading. Pragmatic middle: a PyO3 extension for the hot kernel, not a full rewrite. If it lands at 3x: the workload was I/O-bound; the Rust version allocates as much (57x measured between `String` clone and `&str` borrow); the hot loop is behind `dyn Trait` and never inlined; shipped with default opt settings and no LTO; or it is memory-bandwidth-bound. Diagnose with `perf stat` for IPC first: at 0.4 the answer was never the language.

drills.q: You need AVX2 in production on a mixed fleet. Give the full deployment shape and the two traps.
drills.a: Never `-C target-cpu=native` in a shipped build; it SIGILLs on any host missing an instruction it used, silently until it doesn't. Set a floor in `.cargo/config.toml`: `x86-64-v2` (SSE4.2/POPCNT) or `x86-64-v3` (AVX2/FMA/BMI2, Haswell 2013+ / Zen 1+), verified against your actual instance families (Graviton needs `neoverse-n1`/`v1` instead). Above the floor: `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] unsafe fn` guarded by `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")`, resolved once into a fn pointer in a `OnceLock`. Trap 1: calling a `#[target_feature]` fn from a non-AVX2 context blocks inlining across that boundary, so use one big `#[inline(always)] #[target_feature]` region, not per-operation calls. Trap 2: the win is often small because you're memory-bandwidth-bound, so check arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte loaded) before investing a week.

drills.q: Bounds checks: give the three distinct outcomes with evidence, and rank the fixes.
drills.a: Outcome 1, eliminated: `v[i]` with `i` from `0..v.len()`, no check emitted. Outcome 2, hoisted: `v[i]` with an unrelated `n` got a single `cmp; jbe` before the loop plus a fully vectorised body, which is why adding `assert!(n <= v.len())` frequently measures as zero change. Outcome 3, survives: `out[i] = src[idx[i]]` kept two checks per iteration and blocked vectorisation entirely. Measured over 1M elements: random indirect 1.896 ms, sequential indirect 0.714 ms, iterator zip 0.179 ms (10.6x and 4.0x). Fixes ranked: iterators (`zip`/`chunks_exact`/`windows`), slice once up front to unify lengths, `chunks_exact(8)` for a compile-time trip count, `assert!` (often a no-op), and only last `get_unchecked` with a `// SAFETY:` proof after the profile shows `panic_bounds_check` executing.

drills.q: State the trait bound difference between arguments 1..15 and argument 16 of an axum handler, and name the hard arity cap.
drills.a: Arguments 1..15 are bound by `FromRequestParts<S>` (takes `&mut http::request::Parts`, head only). The last argument is bound by `FromRequest<S>` (takes `Request` by value, consuming the body). The cap is 16, generated by `all_the_tuples!` in axum-core; a 17th argument fails the `Handler` bound with an opaque error.

drills.q: Recite the sqlx `PoolOptions::new()` defaults for max_connections, acquire_timeout, idle_timeout, max_lifetime, and test_before_acquire.
drills.a: max_connections = 10, acquire_timeout = 30 s, idle_timeout = 600 s (10 min), max_lifetime = 1800 s (30 min), test_before_acquire = true. Also min_connections = 0, acquire_slow_threshold = 2 s, fair = true, statement cache capacity 100.

drills.q: What is axum's `DefaultBodyLimit`, and which extractors does it apply to?
drills.a: 2 MB. It applies to `Bytes` and everything built on it: `String`, `Json`, `Form`. It does NOT apply to an extractor that consumes the body directly via `Body::poll_frame`. Override per-route with `DefaultBodyLimit::max(n)` or globally with `tower_http::limit::RequestBodyLimitLayer`.

drills.q: Given `ServiceBuilder::new().layer(A).layer(B).service(router)` and `router.layer(A).layer(B)`, which layer sees the request first in each?
drills.a: ServiceBuilder: A first (it builds A(B(router)); tower's docs say layers added first are called with the request first). Chained Router::layer: B first (it builds B(A(router)), because each `layer` call wraps whatever the router currently is). The two read identically and mean the opposite, which is why the convention is one ServiceBuilder passed to one `.layer()` call.

drills.q: A service serves 2,000 rps, each request holds a connection for 3 ms, and runs 10 replicas with maxSurge 2 against a default Postgres. Size the pool and show the arithmetic.
drills.a: Little's Law: L = 2000 x 0.003 = 6 mean connections. Target utilisation 0.7 (queueing delay grows as 1/(1-rho)), so ~9. But the constraint is the database: (10 + 2) x pool <= 100 - 3 reserved, so pool <= 8. Take 8 per replica. If you need more, add PgBouncer in transaction mode rather than raising Postgres max_connections, and set acquire_timeout to ~3 s so exhaustion is a fast 503.

drills.q: An endpoint returns 200 with no auth token. `.layer(RequireAuth)` is present in the code. Name the two most likely causes.
drills.a: (1) `.layer()` was called before the `.route()` that declares the endpoint; `Router::layer` only wraps routes that already exist, so it wrapped nothing. (2) The route lives in a sub-`Router` that was `merge`d in after the layer was applied. Fix: all routes first, layer last; use `route_layer` for auth so 404s do not become 401s; add an integration test that hits every route unauthenticated over HTTP.

drills.q: Your `count(*)` came back typed `Option<i64>` from `sqlx::query!`. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Postgres reports nullability conservatively for aggregates, expressions, and columns on the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN, so sqlx types them as `Option<T>`. Fix with the column annotation: `count(o.id) as "order_count!: i64"`, where `!` forces non-null, `?` forces nullable, and `: Type` overrides the Rust type. Note sqlx 0.9.0 changed Postgres nullability inference (breaking), so this can shift on upgrade.

drills.q: Traces show unrelated requests nested under each other, only in production under load. Diagnose in one sentence and give the fix.
drills.a: Someone held a `span.enter()` guard across an `.await`; `Span::enter()` sets a thread-local current span, so when the task yields the worker polls a different task whose events are attributed to the entered span. Fix: `#[tracing::instrument]` or `.instrument(span)`, which enter and exit around each individual poll.

drills.q: Write the four-stage cargo-chef Dockerfile skeleton and say which layer is the cached one.
drills.a: chef base (`lukemathwalker/cargo-chef:latest-rust-<ver>`); planner (`COPY . .` then `cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json`); builder (`COPY --from=planner recipe.json`, then `cargo chef cook --release --recipe-path recipe.json`, then `COPY . .` and `cargo build --release`); runtime (`FROM gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot`, COPY the binary). The cached layer is `cargo chef cook`, invalidated only by Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock. Measured: cold 117 s, warm 24 s, 4.9x.

drills.q: Throughput scales fine to 2 threads and flattens at 8; only in the Alpine image; `perf` shows time in `malloc`. Root cause and two fixes.
drills.a: musl's allocator serialises multithreaded allocation far harder than glibc's ptmalloc, and Rust allocates on every String/Vec/boxed future; reported slowdowns reach 7x and worsen with thread count. Fix 1 (preferred): build for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and run on distroless/cc-debian12. Fix 2 (if a static binary is mandatory): `#[global_allocator]` set to mimalloc or tikv-jemallocator.

drills.q: Every pod restarts within 30 seconds of a brief database slowdown, and the database then falls over. Walk the causal chain and the fix.
drills.a: The liveness probe queries the database. Kubernetes defaults are periodSeconds 10 / timeoutSeconds 1 / failureThreshold 3, so 30 s after the first failed probe every pod is SIGKILLed simultaneously; they all restart and reconnect at once, so the database gets a connection storm from every replica and stays down. Fix: liveness checks the process only; move the DB check to readiness (which removes traffic without killing the pod); add a startupProbe; cap acquire_timeout so pool waits do not stall the probe.

drills.q: Design the shutdown path so a rolling deploy produces zero 502s and no lost work.
drills.a: preStop `sleep 5` so Endpoints propagate before you stop accepting (SIGTERM and Endpoints removal are concurrent; kube-proxy converges in 1-5 s). `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(signal)` to drain in-flight requests, wrapped in a `tokio::time::timeout(25s)` so a long-poll cannot outlast terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s). Then `pool.close().await` and shut down the tracer provider so the last span batch flushes. Detached `tokio::spawn`ed work is NOT drained by graceful shutdown: use a CancellationToken plus TaskTracker or an mpsc you drain.

drills.q: Pods die with exit code 137 and no logs. Rust has no GC, so where did the memory go, and what do you check?
drills.a: There is no `OutOfMemoryError`; the kernel SIGKILLs on the cgroup limit, so you get no stack, no log, no flushed spans. Check: unbounded request bodies (DefaultBodyLimit is 2 MB but streaming extractors bypass it, so add RequestBodyLimitLayer), unbounded channels, and glibc arena growth (ptmalloc creates up to 8 x ncores arenas retaining freed memory, which looks like a leak; set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or switch to jemalloc/mimalloc). Alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes vs the limit rather than waiting for the restart.

drills.q: Argue against building a new internal CRUD service in Rust. Give four concrete conditions.
drills.a: (1) The bottleneck is not the service: at 200 rps with 95% of time waiting on Postgres, axum/FastAPI/Spring Boot have the same p99 within noise. (2) The shape changes weekly: in discovery, every schema change means `cargo sqlx prepare` plus a wave of type errors, which is a feature in year three and a tax in month two. (3) Staffing: the hiring pool is an order of magnitude smaller and ramp is 2-3 months for async Rust. (4) Ecosystem gaps that matter to you: Kafka client, AWS SDK, and OpenTelemetry traces (still Beta at the 0.32 line while Logs and Metrics are Stable). The honest case for Rust is operational, not benchmark: 8 replicas instead of 40, no GC saw-tooth in p99, a 26 MB image with a dozen packages of CVE surface.

drills.q: You set `panic = "abort"` and added `CatchPanicLayer`. What actually happens when a handler panics, and why?
drills.a: The whole process dies, taking every in-flight request with it. `CatchPanicLayer` is built on `std::panic::catch_unwind`, which is a no-op under `panic = "abort"` because there are no unwind tables; Tokio's per-task panic isolation (`JoinError::is_panic`) is gone for the same reason. On a service, keep the default `panic = "unwind"`, add `CatchPanicLayer` inside the trace layer so the span still closes, and set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`.

drills.q: How many bytes is `&dyn Draw` on a 64-bit target, and what are the two halves?
drills.a: 16 bytes: a data pointer to the value plus a pointer to the vtable for that (concrete type, trait) pair. A plain `&u32` is 8. Slices are also fat (`&[u32]` is 16: pointer plus length).

drills.q: Write the `?` desugaring from memory.
drills.a: `let n = f()?;` becomes `let n = match f() { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(From::from(e)) };`. The `From::from` is the point: one `impl From<E> for MyError` serves every `?` in the crate.

drills.q: Fill in the sizes on 64-bit: `size_of::<Option<&u8>>()`, `size_of::<Option<u32>>()`, `size_of::<Option<NonZeroU32>>()`, `size_of::<Option<bool>>()`.
drills.a: 8, 8, 4, 1. `Option<&u8>` uses null as the niche so it costs nothing over `&u8`; `u32` has no spare bit pattern so `Option<u32>` needs a real tag plus padding, doubling it; `NonZeroU32` donates 0 as the niche; `bool` has 254 spare patterns.

drills.q: Name three traits from std that are NOT dyn compatible, and give the one-line reason for each.
drills.a: `Clone` (`fn clone(&self) -> Self` returns a type of unknown size to the caller), `PartialEq` (`fn eq(&self, other: &Self)` puts `Self` in argument position, so a shared vtable would let you compare a Circle to a String), and `From`/`Into` (`Self` in return position). `Sized` and `Copy` fail as marker/supertrait constraints.

drills.q: You want `impl Display for Vec<u8>`. It won't compile. What error, and what do you do?
drills.a: error[E0117]: the orphan rule, because both `Display` and `Vec` are foreign. Wrap in a newtype: `struct Hex(Vec<u8>); impl Display for Hex { ... }`. A single-field tuple struct has identical layout to its field, so it is zero-cost.

drills.q: Why does `Iterator` use `type Item` rather than `Iterator<Item>` as a generic parameter?
drills.a: So each type implements `Iterator` exactly once and `Item` is determined by that impl. If it were generic, a type could implement `Iterator<u32>` and `Iterator<String>`, making every `.next()` call ambiguous and requiring a turbofish, and every combinator signature in std would have to thread the item type through. Associated types exist to keep inference tractable.

drills.q: Your crate exports `pub enum ApiError` with 12 variants. You add a 13th in a patch release and downstream builds break. What went wrong and what is the fix?
drills.a: Adding an enum variant is a semver-major break because every downstream exhaustive `match` now fails with error[E0004]. Fix is `#[non_exhaustive]` on the enum, which forces downstream crates to include a wildcard arm and lets you add variants in minor releases forever. Your own crate keeps full exhaustiveness checking. It is major-breaking exactly once, when you add it.

drills.q: A dependency in your service calls `.unwrap()` on a parsed header. Trace what your users see under `panic = "unwind"` versus `panic = "abort"`.
drills.a: Under unwind, the panic unwinds to the nearest catch boundary. In Tokio that is the spawned task, surfacing as `JoinError::is_panic`, so one task dies and if nobody awaits the handle it vanishes silently; an Axum/Actix middleware converts it to a bare 500 with no structured body. Under abort, there is no unwinding at all and the entire process dies, taking every in-flight request with it. Across an `extern "C"` boundary it is a guaranteed abort regardless of profile.

drills.q: `match &opt` where `opt: Option<String>`, arm `Some(s) =>`. What is the type of `s`, and what rule produced it?
drills.a: `s: &String`. Matching a reference against a non-reference pattern auto-dereferences and flips the default binding mode from `move` to `ref`, so bindings come out as references. Before match ergonomics (Rust 1.26) you wrote `&Some(ref s)`. Rust 2024 added the RFC 3627 reservations: once the DBM is not `move`, an explicit `mut`/`ref`/`ref mut` on a binding is an error.

drills.q: Your alert says 'database error' and nothing else. The thiserror enum has a `#[from] sqlx::Error` variant. What is the bug in the logging?
drills.a: Someone logged `e.to_string()` or `error = ?e`, which renders only the top layer's `#[error("...")]` string. The cause lives in `Error::source()`, which `#[from]` wired up. Fix: walk the chain when logging (`error = %chain(&e)` with a five-line loop on `source()`), or use anyhow's `{:?}`, or `tracing-error`'s SpanTrace. Corollary: do NOT duplicate the inner message into the outer `Display`, or the walked chain repeats it.

drills.q: Compile time went 40s to 9 minutes after adding one generic parameter. Give the diagnostic sequence and the fix, by tool name.
drills.a: `cargo build --timings` to confirm codegen dominates one crate, then `cargo llvm-lines --release | head -30` for IR lines and copy count per generic function, then `cargo bloat --release --crates` for binary attribution. Fix with the inner-function trick std uses on itself: `fn read<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) { fn inner(p: &Path) { /* 60 lines */ } inner(p.as_ref()) }` so the wrapper monomorphises and the body compiles once. If that's not enough, move the boundary to `&dyn`.

drills.q: You are designing a public API: `fn process(r: impl Read)` or `fn process(r: &mut dyn Read)`. Argue both sides and pick.
drills.a: `impl Read` monomorphises into the caller's crate: inlinable, no indirection, but one copy per caller type, cannot be stored in a struct field without threading the parameter through the whole type, and cannot appear in a dyn-compatible trait. `&mut dyn Read` is one copy, one indirect call per operation, and keeps trait objects possible. Switching between them post-publication is semver-major, so it is a one-way door. For a per-request I/O function, take `&mut dyn Read`: the indirect call is invisible next to a syscall. Take `impl Read` only when the body is small and hot enough that inlining matters, and have criterion numbers.

drills.q: A colleague argues generics are always faster than `dyn` because they are zero-cost. Rebut it precisely.
drills.a: The indirect call itself is a few cycles when the target is stable in the indirect branch target buffer, and ~15-25 cycles only on a megamorphic mispredict. The real cost of dyn is lost inlining, which stops constant propagation, loop unrolling, and auto-vectorisation. But monomorphisation has its own cost: 60 copies of a 4 KB body compete for a ~32 KB L1 instruction cache, so a single resident dyn copy can win. Plus compile time and binary size grow as roughly n_types x body_size. The correct position is that it is measurable: criterion plus `perf stat -e instructions,branch-misses,L1-icache-load-misses` on both builds.

drills.q: A teammate wants to add `impl<T: Serialize> Persist for T` to your published trait so users get it for free. What do you say?
drills.a: It is a semver-major break despite adding no method to any signature. Any downstream crate that already wrote `impl Persist for TheirType` where `TheirType: Serialize` now gets error[E0119], and there is no opt-out and no `specialization` on stable (RFC 1210, unstable since 2015, with known soundness holes around lifetime-dependent specialisation). Options: ship it as a new trait, seal the original with a private supertrait so nobody could have written a conflicting impl, or accept a major version bump.

drills.q: A hot function returns `Result<u64, MyError>` where MyError is a thiserror enum with a `String` variant, and profiles show stack spills. What is happening and what do you do?
drills.a: `size_of::<Result<T, E>>()` is roughly `max(size_of::<T>(), size_of::<E>())` plus a tag, so an enum whose largest variant holds a `String` (24 bytes) plus other fields is easily 32-64 bytes, and that size propagates into every `Result` up the call chain, exceeding what fits in return registers. Fix: `Result<u64, Box<MyError>>`, making the Err arm 8 bytes. This is exactly what `std::io::Error` does internally, which is why it is 8 bytes on 64-bit despite carrying errno, static messages, or boxed custom errors.

drills.q: Fill in: Go's default GOGC is ___, which means collect when the heap reaches ___ x live. GOMEMLIMIT was added in Go ___ and is a ___ limit.
drills.a: 100; 2x; Go 1.19; SOFT. Soft means exceeding it causes a GC death spiral (100% GC CPU, no forward progress) rather than a clean OOM, so keep a real container memory limit as well.

drills.q: A goroutine starts with how much stack? A Rust future costs how much? An asyncio task costs how much (measured)?
drills.a: Goroutine: 2 KB initial stack, grown by copying and updating pointers (it was 8 KB before Go 1.4). Rust future: no stack at all; its size is the largest live state across await points, computed at compile time. Asyncio task: 2,185 bytes measured, from 100,000 tasks costing 213,372 KB of RSS.

drills.q: True or false: Go's race detector and Rust's Send/Sync solve the same problem the same way.
drills.a: False. Rust's Send and Sync make data races a COMPILE error, checked on all code. Go's -race is a RUNTIME detector: it instruments memory accesses, costs roughly 5-10x CPU and 5-10x memory, and only finds races on code paths your tests actually execute. This is a correctness argument for Rust, and for most services it is stronger than the latency argument.

drills.q: Compute: if 99% of your GC cycles complete in under 10 ms, what fraction of 100-request user sessions is consistently under 10 ms? What percentile do you actually need?
drills.a: 0.99^100 = 0.366, so only about 37% of sessions. To get 99% of USERS under the bar you need the 99.99th percentile, not the 99th. This is Go's own 'tyranny of the nines' framing from the ISMM 2018 keynote, and it is why any tail-latency argument that stops at p99 is incomplete.

drills.q: Your Go service's p99.9 regressed after you added an in-memory cache. gctrace shows STW pauses of 180 microseconds. Explain the contradiction and give the first three fixes in cost order.
drills.a: No contradiction: the STW pause is not where the cost lives. The collector must trace the entire LIVE heap to prove reachability, and the pacer charges that work to allocating goroutines as mark assist, so it appears as your handlers running slower rather than as a pause. Go also forces a GC at least every 2 minutes regardless of allocation rate. Fixes in cost order: (1) raise GOGC to 200-400 or set GOMEMLIMIT to ~90% of the container limit with GOGC=off; (2) reduce pointer density in the cache ([]T not []*T, indices not pointers) so there is less to trace; (3) move the cache off the Go heap entirely (off-heap arena, freecache, or an external Redis/memcached). Only after all three is the language the problem.

drills.q: A colleague proposes moving a CPU-bound Python service to threads because 'the GIL is basically gone in 3.14'. Give the two-part rebuttal with numbers.
drills.a: Part one, the default build: I measured two CPU-bound threads on two cores at 1,062 ms against 898 ms serial, which is 0.85x, an 18% regression, from GIL handoff and eval-breaker overhead alone. Part two, the free-threaded build: 3.14t is officially supported under PEP 779 but is a SEPARATE binary, not the default; it costs ~1% (macOS aarch64) to ~8% (x86-64 Linux) single-threaded, uses more memory (None is 32 B vs 16 B, interned strings immortal, mimalloc, QSBR-deferred frees), and any C extension not marked free-threading-compatible silently re-enables the GIL at import. PEP 779's roadmap has GIL-off-by-default no earlier than the 2028-2030 window.

drills.q: You are asked to justify a Rust rewrite. What three numbers must you have before you walk into the room?
drills.a: 1) The fraction of p99 (and p50) spent in your own code versus the database, TLS and the network, because Amdahl bounds the win. 2) The instance-count or cost reduction, sized against a real reference: PostHog went from ~300 pods at ~$8.8k/month to ~90 pods at ~$2.8k/month for identical ~500k req/min traffic. 3) The fraction of the team that could review the result; below ~40% you are proposing a bus factor of two. Also bring a falsification condition and propose extracting the hot component rather than rewriting the service.

drills.q: Rank these five workloads by first-choice language and give one reason each: (a) k8s operator, (b) CLI tool shipped to users, (c) LLM inference router, (d) batch feature pipeline, (e) firmware on a microcontroller.
drills.a: (a) Go: the entire ecosystem is Go, and in Rust you will reimplement client-go badly. (b) Rust: single static binary, clap, and every fastest-in-category tool (ripgrep, fd, uv, ruff) is Rust; Go is a close second on the same distribution argument. (c) Rust for the router/batcher/tokenizer tier (CPU-bound, latency-sensitive, memory-per-pod sensitive, stable spec) with Python for the model tier. (d) Python: PySpark, pandas and Arrow are the whole reason, with a Rust hot transform via PyO3 if one step dominates. (e) Rust or C: no GC, no runtime, no_std; nothing else qualifies.

drills.q: An interviewer cites the Discord Go-to-Rust post as proof you should use Rust. Give the four caveats that the post itself contains.
drills.a: 1) The Go version was 1.9.2, a 2017-2018 collector; they tried 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10, all before GOMEMLIMIT (1.19) and eight-plus releases before Green Tea (1.26). 2) The port was completed in May 2019 and required committing to NIGHTLY Rust for async, framed as an acceptable-risk bet by a team with a documented history of early adoption (Elixir, React Native, Scylla). 3) The service was chosen because it was 'small and self-contained', i.e. a deliberately low-risk first bet, not a wholesale migration. 4) Footnote 2 says verbatim: 'To be clear, we don't think you should rewrite everything in rust just because.'

drills.q: PostHog reported a 21x synthetic benchmark and a 10.6x p99 improvement but only 1.8x at p50. Explain the shape of that result and what it implies for how you should promise a rewrite.
drills.a: The synthetic measured the framework in isolation; production measures the database, TLS and the network, so Amdahl caps the achievable win. The p50 barely moved because the median request was already dominated by work the language does not touch. The tail collapsed because they fixed tail-specific problems: they moved flag evaluation out of SQL into parallel in-memory evaluation, added application-level cohort caching, deleted PgBouncer, and gained proper code-level timeout primitives. Implication: promise improvement only on the measured fraction of latency that is your own code, and be explicit about which part of the win is architectural rather than linguistic. Test the architecture change first, in the current language, before attributing it to the rewrite.

drills.q: You picked Rust two quarters ago. PR cycle time has doubled, review is concentrated in two engineers, and the production win came in at half the promise. Do you revert?
drills.a: Usually no, and saying so is the senior answer. Reverting costs another quarter and burns the team's confidence. Contain instead: stop expanding the Rust footprint, freeze the component at its current scope, ship all new work in the language the team is fluent in, and staff a second and third reviewer onto the existing component (pairing, training, relaxing lint strictness). Separately, attack the mechanical costs, because they are often self-inflicted: ~36% of Rust teams who call CI build time a blocker use no cache at all. Fix CI caching, switch to LLD or mold, set debug = 'line-tables-only', run cargo llvm-lines and apply the thin-generic-wrapper refactor, and give Rust Analyzer its own target directory so it stops fighting Cargo for the build lock.

drills.q: Design the FFI boundary for a Python RAG service whose reranking loop is the bottleneck. What are the rules and the failure modes?
drills.a: Rules: use PyO3 with maturin, expose ONE coarse-grained entry point (rerank(query, candidates) -> scores) rather than a per-document call, and wrap the compute in py.allow_threads() so the GIL is released for the duration, which is what buys you real parallelism inside a GIL-bound process. Failure modes: (1) a fine-grained boundary, where a ~100-200 ns per-call overhead plus argument conversion makes 10,000 crossings per request worse than pure Python; (2) build-matrix cost, since you now ship manylinux, macOS x86-64 and aarch64, and Windows wheels, plus a second language in CI; (3) if you later move to 3.14t, this extension must be explicitly marked free-threading-compatible or it silently re-enables the GIL, so assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False at startup. Prefer an existing Rust-backed library (tokenizers, orjson, pydantic-core, polars) before writing your own.

drills.q: State the strongest argument against choosing Go for a new backend service, and then the strongest argument against your own rebuttal.
drills.a: Against Go: expressiveness at scale. Generics arrived only in 1.18 (2022) and generic METHODS only in 1.27 (2026); there are no sum types, so 'this is either A or B' is an interface plus a type switch with no exhaustiveness checking; error handling is if err != nil at every call site; and the compiler does far less inlining and essentially no autovectorisation, so hot scalar loops run commonly 2-5x slower than Rust with no way to rescue them (simd/archsimd landed in 1.26 behind GOEXPERIMENT=simd, amd64-only and explicitly unstable). Against that rebuttal: the minimalism is the point. It is why a new hire ships in a week, why every Go codebase looks the same, why the build is ~8 seconds where a comparable Rust service is ~4 minutes, and why the operational tooling (built-in pprof, native OTel, the 1.26 goroutine-leak profile) is the best of the three. Reasonable senior engineers land on opposite sides and you should present it that way rather than picking silently.

drills.q: Name the silent failure mode unique to each concurrency model and the tool that finds it.
drills.a: Go: goroutine leak. A goroutine blocked forever on a channel consumes 2 KB plus everything it retains, never logs, and keeps its retained heap alive against the collector. Tool: /debug/pprof/goroutine, or Go 1.26's experimental goroutineleak profile (GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile, contributed by Uber, targeting default-on in 1.27). Rust: lost wakeup. If poll returns Pending without arranging waker.wake(), or fails to re-store the waker on every poll after work-stealing migrates the task, the task is never polled again with no panic and no log. Tool: tokio-console with RUSTFLAGS=--cfg tokio_unstable. Python: a synchronous call inside a coroutine stalling the single event loop for every concurrent request. Tool: asyncio debug mode with loop.slow_callback_duration set to about 0.1.

drills.q: An interviewer asks 'Rust, Go or Python?' with no other context. What is the highest-signal answer, and what is the trap in the follow-up?
drills.a: Answer: refuse to pick without a constraint, but say exactly what constraint would move you. 'Default Python unless something disqualifies it, because it ships fastest and hires easiest. To move off that I need a number: a p99.9 budget, a memory ceiling per instance, a throughput floor, or a target with no runtime. If it is Kubernetes-adjacent, Go without hesitating.' The trap in the follow-up ('assume no constraints, now pick') is that saying 'it depends' twice reads as evasion. Commit: 'Then it is whatever the team already runs, because the switching cost is real and the benefit is zero by construction.' Refusing to have a favourite is the signal; refusing to ever commit is the failure.

drills.q: Name ImageBind's six modalities and the dimensionality of its joint space.
drills.a: Image/video, text, audio, depth, thermal, and IMU. Joint space d = 1024. The image and text encoders come from a frozen pretrained OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 (roughly 630M vision parameters, roughly 302M text).

drills.q: What is the value of a symmetric InfoNCE loss at random initialisation with batch size B, and what is it for B = 32,768 and B = 128?
drills.a: log(B), because all similarities are roughly equal so the softmax is uniform. log(32768) = 10.40 nats; log(128) = 4.85 nats. This is the single cheapest assertion to add to a contrastive training run: if step-0 loss equals log(per_device_batch) rather than log(global_batch), your all-gather is not propagating gradients.

drills.q: CLIP initialises tau to 0.07 and clamps it. What is the clamp, in both parameterisations, and why does it exist?
drills.a: The clamp is 1/tau <= 100, i.e. tau >= 0.01 (logit_scale = log(1/tau) clamped so exp(logit_scale) <= 100). It exists because gradient magnitude scales as 1/tau, so the model can reduce loss faster by shrinking tau than by improving alignment, and it will, until fp16 logits overflow and training diverges. In practice the learned logit_scale saturates at the clamp: the model wants the sharpest temperature it is allowed.

drills.q: How many pair-specific models would a naive 6-modality system need, and how many of those pairs have abundant naturally-paired data?
drills.a: N(N-1)/2 = 15 models. Only about 2 of the 15 (image-text, image-audio via video) have abundant natural pairing; audio-thermal, IMU-depth, thermal-text and the rest have essentially none at any price. That asymmetry is the entire argument for hub-and-spoke: 5 spoke models instead of 15 pair models, each trained on data that a sensor stack already produces for free.

drills.q: A colleague proposes reaching a contrastive batch of 32,768 via gradient accumulation over 256 microbatches of 128 on one node. What do you say?
drills.a: It does not work. Accumulation gives you 256 separate 128-way softmaxes whose gradients are summed; the negatives never appear in the same denominator, so the task stays a 128-way problem with a mutual-information ceiling of log(128) = 4.85 nats. Real options: a gradient-propagating all-gather across devices, a MoCo-style memory bank, or SigLIP's pairwise sigmoid loss, which removes the global softmax entirely and is already strong at batch 4,096-8,192.

drills.q: Derive emergent cross-modal alignment, then state the strongest number that shows its limit.
drills.a: If f_A(a) ~ f_I(i) for paired (i,a) and f_T(t) ~ f_I(i) for paired (i,t), then f_A(a) ~ f_T(t) for anything both describe: the hub is a shared basis and both spokes were fitted to express themselves in it. The limit: ImageBind's emergent ESC-50 audio classification is roughly 66.9% top-1, against roughly 68.6% for text-audio-supervised AudioCLIP and 95%+ for a fully supervised audio specialist. Quote both halves.

drills.q: Two text embeddings from a CLIP space score 0.68 cosine and are unrelated. A correctly matching text-image pair scores 0.31. What is happening and what does it mean for thresholds?
drills.a: The modality gap. All text embeddings live in one narrow cone (within-modality mean cosine around 0.68) and all image embeddings in a different one, separated by roughly 0.87 in centroid distance, so 0.31 is a typical cross-modal magnitude rather than a weak match. Consequence: never use a global similarity threshold. Calibrate one per (query_modality, corpus_modality) pair on a labelled set, or drop thresholds and use top-k plus a reranker score, which is scale-free. A 0.75 threshold tuned on text returns zero image results and the latency graph looks perfectly healthy.

drills.q: Cross-modal recall in a single HNSW index is under 5% while within-modality recall@10 is 0.95. You raised ef from 64 to 512 and nothing changed. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Modality gap plus greedy graph traversal. With within-modality cosine around 0.68 and cross around 0.31, every node's M nearest neighbours are same-modality, so the graph is two components with a few bad bridge edges and greedy descent from a text entry point never crosses. ef does not help because it is a topology problem, not a search-effort problem. Confirm by running brute-force search: if exact finds the matches, the diagnosis holds. Fix: one index per modality with RRF fusion at k = 60, or a metadata-filtered search that confines each traversal to one cone.

drills.q: Someone claims per-modality mean-centring fixes the modality gap. Design the experiment that settles it, and state the expected result.
drills.a: Compute, before and after centring: cross-modal mean cosine, matched-pair cosine, and the median rank of the true match among N candidates. Measured on untrained encoders (N = 512): before, cross 0.3091 / matched 0.3095 / median rank 257; after, cross 0.0000 / matched 0.0015 / median rank 260. Centring collapses the score range and leaves ranks identical. It is threshold hygiene, not a quality fix. Any claim about gap-fixing that does not report ranks before and after is unfalsifiable.

drills.q: Design multimodal RAG over 10M mixed documents, images and audio for a team already running Weaviate, ClickHouse HNSW, pgvector and BGE rerankers. Give the ordered plan and the cost model.
drills.a: (1) Caption/OCR/ASR everything into ONE text index with BM25 hybrid and the existing BGE reranker; handles most queries, one calibrated score space, roughly 0.5-3 s and a fraction of a cent per asset to build, so 10M is a multi-day five-figure batch job. (2) Add per-modality native indices with concurrent fan-out and RRF at k = 60 only for genuinely cross-modal queries or where captioning is provably lossy; roughly 2-5 ms per index at ef = 128, roughly 6-10 ms p50 for four in parallel. (3) Add ColPali-style late interaction for layout-sensitive documents under a few million pages. (4) Always rerank the top 50. Storage: 1024-d fp32 = 4 KB/asset (40 GB), int8 = 1 KB (10 GB), binary = 128 B (1.28 GB); late interaction roughly 264 KB/page (2.6 TB, a 130x multiplier). Never one joint index over mixed modalities.

drills.q: Which of the multimodal-RAG design decisions is the one-way door, and why does that ordering matter?
drills.a: The 264 KB per page of late-interaction storage. A 130x storage multiplier changes the class of system (columnar store and a two-stage retrieve-then-MaxSim design rather than an in-memory ANN index), so it must be decided first. By contrast the captioning batch job is a re-runnable one-off, and the fp32-versus-int8-versus-binary quantisation choice is reversible in an afternoon. Rank decisions by reversibility, not by magnitude.

drills.q: You want to add tactile sensor data as a seventh modality to an ImageBind space. Walk the plan, and say what you do when the emergent tactile-to-text results come back poor.
drills.a: Freeze the hub. Collect naturally-paired (camera frame, tactile reading) from the robot rig, which is free: 10 hours at 30 Hz is roughly 1.08M pairs with no human labelling. Build a small spoke encoder (1D conv stem plus a 4-6 layer transformer, following ImageBind's IMU treatment of 6 channels over 5 s with a kernel-8 conv) plus a linear projection to d = 1024. Train symmetric InfoNCE against the frozen image embeddings, ideally with sigmoid loss so batch 4,096-8,192 suffices. When emergent results are poor: check whether 'separation' is genuinely below 0.02 rather than the score range merely looking low; then collect 10k-100k direct (tactile, text) pairs, or swap to a language hub. Do NOT full-fine-tune the hub; LoRA r = 8-16 with an original-pair regression gate if you must.

drills.q: Argue both sides of 'the modality gap is a bug that should be fixed', then give your position.
drills.a: For fixing: the original NeurIPS 2022 paper showed that deliberately shifting embeddings along the gap direction moves zero-shot accuracy and fairness metrics, so gap magnitude is not causally inert, and 2025-2026 work on Gramian alignment and pairwise-alignment regularisers takes that line. Against: the gap does not change within-pair ranking (centring moves cross cosine 0.3091 to 0.0000 with median true rank 257 to 260, unchanged), so its real costs are threshold calibration and shared-index topology, both cheap engineering fixes. My position: it is primarily a measurement problem, fix it with per-pair thresholds and per-modality indices, but do not claim it is causally inert, because a mixed ANN index genuinely loses recall to it.

drills.q: What does LanguageBind's result imply for how you choose a hub, and what did it cost?
drills.a: Implies the hub is a design variable, not a property of the universe: binding to language beat ImageBind by roughly 5.8 R@1 on MSR-VTT zero-shot video-text with roughly 15% of the parameters. Choose the hub with the densest semantics AND adequate natural pairing; for anything ending in a text query that is language, because the downstream consumer is an LLM. The cost: images were chosen originally because the pairing was free (video carries audio, RGB-D emits depth), whereas LanguageBind had to construct VIDAL-10M with substantial automated annotation to get language pairing for infrared and depth. Data-acquisition cost against alignment quality.

drills.q: Write the one diagnostic function you would ship with any multimodal retrieval system, and say which line predicts quality.
drills.a: Given L2-normalised A and B holding the same N items in two modalities, report: within-A and within-B mean cosine, cross-modal mean and sd, matched-pair mean, separation = matched - cross mean, gap = mean(within) - mean(cross), centroid distance ||mu_A - mu_B||, and the median rank of the true match. 'separation' is the only line that predicts retrieval quality (healthy 0.05-0.15, below 0.02 means not aligned on your data). 'gap' and 'centroid distance' predict whether thresholds and a shared ANN index will misbehave, which is an operational problem rather than a quality one.

drills.q: Name the four components of a JEPA and state which ones receive gradients from the loss.
drills.a: Context encoder (ViT, receives gradients, this is the artefact you keep), target encoder (identical architecture, EMA-updated only, stop-gradient, NO gradients ever, runs on the FULL unmasked input), narrow predictor (ViT at dim 384 vs the encoder's 1280, receives gradients), and an L2 or smooth-L1 loss on embeddings. Only the context encoder and the predictor are trained by SGD.

drills.q: Recite the I-JEPA multi-block masking parameters from memory: how many target blocks, at what scale and aspect ratio, and what happens to the context block.
drills.a: 4 target blocks at area scale U(0.15, 0.20) and aspect ratio U(0.75, 1.5), allowed to overlap each other. 1 context block at area scale U(0.85, 1.0) and aspect ratio 1.0, from which every patch overlapping any target block is removed. Targets are sliced out of the target encoder's output over the full unmasked image.

drills.q: What is the I-JEPA EMA momentum schedule, and what averaging window does the starting value imply?
drills.a: Linear from 0.996 to 1.0 over the full run. At m = 0.996 the effective window is 1/(1-m) = 250 steps. The ramp to 1.0 freezes the target encoder at the end of training as a stability measure.

drills.q: Give the compute figure for pretraining I-JEPA's ViT-H/14 on ImageNet and its two published efficiency comparisons.
drills.a: Under 1,200 GPU-hours (16 A100s in under 72 hours wall-clock). Over 10x more compute-efficient than a ViT-H/14 pretrained with MAE, and over 2.5x faster than a far smaller ViT-S/16 pretrained with iBOT, while producing better frozen-probe representations than MAE.

drills.q: Derive, in two lines, why an embedding-space prediction objective can ignore unpredictable detail while a pixel objective cannot.
drills.a: H(y|x) = H(y_predictable|x) + H(y_noise|x). A pixel objective has an externally fixed target, so minimising it requires modelling both terms (squared error gives you the conditional mean, i.e. blur; a likelihood objective gives you an accurate model of noise, which is worse because you paid parameters for it). An embedding objective has a LEARNED target, so the system can reduce loss by simply not encoding the noise term. Measured consequence: roughly 10x less compute than MAE at the same ViT-H/14 architecture.

drills.q: Your JEPA training loss falls from 1.2 to 1e-4 within 300 steps and flatlines. List the checks in order, cheapest discriminating first.
drills.a: Treat as collapse until disproven. (1) Assert the target encoder's params have grad None after backward(), catching a missing torch.no_grad() or requires_grad=False. (2) Run collapse metrics on a held-out batch: per-dim std of L2-normalised embeddings against 1/sqrt(D) = 0.028 at D=1280, alert below 0.3/sqrt(D) ~ 0.008; RankMe against D, single digits out of 1280 means full collapse. (3) Assert set(ctx_idx) & set(tgt_idx) is empty, since overlap leakage produces exactly this too-good loss curve. (4) Verify the EMA momentum actually applied, not just configured. (5) Check LR warmup length; too-high early LR is a common trigger.

drills.q: Define RankMe, give its healthy range, and say what value indicates partial rather than full collapse.
drills.a: Centre a batch of at least 4xD embeddings, take singular values sigma_i, normalise p_i = sigma_i / sum(sigma), then RankMe = exp(-sum p_i log p_i), the exponentiated entropy of the normalised spectrum. Healthy vision backbones land in roughly 0.2-0.8 x D (about 250-1000 at D=1280). Full collapse reads 1. Partial or dimensional collapse reads roughly 20-60, and this is the dangerous case because the loss and the ImageNet linear probe both still look fine.

drills.q: Explain why an ImageNet linear probe within 1-2 points of the reference is not sufficient evidence that a JEPA run is healthy, and say what you would add.
drills.a: Coarse classification survives enormous information loss; a representation collapsed onto a few dozen well-separated semantic clusters still probes well. Add a detail-sensitive probe: monocular depth, object counting, keypoint localisation or segmentation mIoU. Add RankMe as a first-class tracked metric. Probe multiple layers, since partial collapse often shows as the final block being much worse than the second-to-last.

drills.q: State the V-JEPA 2 two-stage recipe with data scale and the exact robot deployment claim.
drills.a: Stage 1: 1.2B-parameter ViT-g, masked latent prediction on VideoMix22M (over 1 million hours of internet video plus images), no actions or rewards. Benchmarks: SSv2 77.3% top-1, EK100 anticipation 39.7 recall-at-5, and with an 8B LLM alignment, PerceptionTest 84.0 and TempCompass 76.9. Stage 2: freeze the encoder, train V-JEPA 2-AC to map [repr(o_t), a_t] to repr(o_{t+1}) on under 62 hours of unlabelled Droid video. Deployment: zero-shot on Franka arms in two unseen labs, image goals, latent-space rollouts scored against the goal representation, replanning every step, roughly 65-80% pick-and-place success on novel objects, with no deployment-environment data, no task-specific training and no reward.

drills.q: A colleague says V-JEPA 2 'learned to control robots from 62 hours of raw video.' Correct them precisely.
drills.a: Droid trajectories include robot proprioception and action logs, so actions are present and the predictor is action-conditioned. What is absent is task labels, rewards, curated demonstrations of the target task, and any data from the deployment environments. So 'unlabelled' means no task supervision, not no actions. Overstating it loses credibility; understating it to 'so it's just imitation learning' misses that there were no demonstrations of the deployment tasks at all.

drills.q: Argue both sides of 'is JEPA a fundamentally better path or an elegant SSL method?', then state what evidence would change your mind.
drills.a: For the narrow claim: latent prediction is roughly 10x cheaper than MAE at equal architecture, needs no augmentation design, gives the best low-level spatial and motion probes, and produced the only published zero-shot cross-lab robot planning result off under 62 hours of robot data, which is a closed-loop task-success class of evidence. Against the broad claim: H-JEPA, the hierarchical stack that is the actual load-bearing proposal of the 2022 paper, has no scaled demonstration as of August 2026; I-JEPA sits roughly 7 points below DINOv2 on ImageNet linear probe (about 79% vs 86.5%); DINO-family and CLIP-family models remain the production default; no JEPA system has displaced a scaled generative model on a general benchmark. Mind-changers: an H-JEPA at V-JEPA-2 scale showing planning horizons a flat model cannot reach, or a JEPA system beating a comparably-resourced generative model on a general suite.

drills.q: Explain, without overclaiming, why the EMA target encoder helps prevent collapse. Then name the paper that undercuts the standard story.
drills.a: Collapse is a GLOBAL MINIMUM of the naive objective, so the defence cannot be that the objective disfavours it; it must be that gradient descent from a reasonable init does not reach it. Three mechanisms: stop-gradient removes the gradient path that would move the target toward the prediction; the EMA lag (250-step window at m=0.996) means a shrinking context encoder is scored against a not-yet-shrunk target, producing an opposing loss; the narrow predictor (384 vs 1280) is too weak to absorb a degenerate encoder cheaply. SimSiam (CVPR 2021) showed stop-gradient alone suffices with no momentum encoder, so EMA is not the sole mechanism. LeJEPA (Balestriero and LeCun, arXiv 2511.08544, November 2025) calls the whole stack heuristics, proves the isotropic Gaussian uniquely minimises worst-case downstream risk, and replaces it with SIGReg (random 1D projections plus characteristic-function matching, linear cost, ~1 hyperparameter).

drills.q: Design the evaluation gate you would require before a JEPA-based world model touches a robot control loop. Give five levels with numbers.
drills.a: (1) Representation health: RankMe above 0.2xD, per-dim normalised std within 30% of 1/sqrt(D), plus a depth or keypoint probe above a stated floor, to rule out partial collapse. (2) One-step latent prediction error on held-out real transitions, reported per action type, since aggregates hide contact cases. (3) Multi-step rollout error vs horizon: encode a real state, roll H steps under recorded actions, plot error for h = 1..4H, set the planning horizon BELOW the knee. (4) Closed-loop task success on real hardware in an environment absent from training, with a stated baseline (the V-JEPA 2-AC format: 65-80% zero-shot on Franka in two unseen labs). (5) Rank correlation between in-model score and real outcome across 10-20 candidate policies, because if the model chooses actions, monotonicity is what you depend on and low prediction error does not imply it. Plus a runtime guard on the prediction residual before production hardware, because an optimising controller actively seeks regions where the model is optimistically wrong.

drills.q: Resolve: JEPA deliberately discards unpredictable detail, yet I-JEPA beats DINO on depth and object-counting probes. Why is that not a contradiction, and why can't you just add augmentations to get both?
drills.a: They discard along orthogonal axes. JEPA discards what is not predictable from context (grain, micro-texture, aleatoric noise) and is incentivised to KEEP spatial layout, object extent, depth ordering and motion, since those make the target predictable. Invariance methods discard what their augmentations declare irrelevant, and random resized crop plus colour jitter explicitly say position, scale and colour do not matter, which is exactly what depth and counting probes need. You cannot simply combine them: adding augmentations reintroduces the invariance pressure that destroys spatial information, and it also makes target embeddings of different views more similar, which moves the system toward the degenerate region and weakens an anti-collapse condition. If you need both, use two backbones or a multi-task head.

drills.q: You are porting the JEPA recipe to industrial sensor time series with no augmentation intuition. What is the argument for it, and what is the one design parameter you must derive from the data rather than copy from I-JEPA?
drills.a: Argument: the transferable property is augmentation-freedom. Contrastive SSL requires you to specify what should be invariant, and for vibration spectra, radar, seismic or plant telemetry that is a multi-month research project where a wrong choice silently destroys the information the downstream task needs. A JEPA needs only a masking scheme, a weaker and more auditable commitment. The parameter you must derive: MASK SPAN LENGTH, set relative to the signal's autocorrelation length, not by analogy to a 15-20% image area. In a smooth series a short masked span is trivially interpolable from its neighbours, which is exactly the identity-function failure (low loss, useless representation). Measure the autocorrelation, mask well beyond it, then run the context-ablation test (feed zeros for the context) and confirm the loss rises substantially.

drills.q: Name the three Cosmos WFM roles (Predict, Transfer, Reason) and what each one is for, in one line each.
drills.a: Predict: video world generation from text, image or video (7B/14B diffusion and 4B/12B autoregressive in 1.0; unified 2B/14B in Predict 2.5). Transfer: spatially-controlled world-to-world translation conditioned on edge, blur, depth or segmentation, i.e. change appearance while preserving real geometry (2B in 2.5). Reason: a physical-commonsense vision-language model (7B in Reason 1; 2B/8B/32B in Reason 2), which also serves as the text encoder inside Predict 2.5.

drills.q: What does Cosmos-1.0-Diffusion-7B-Text2World emit by default, and how long does one clip take?
drills.a: 121 frames = 5 seconds at 24 fps at 1280x704. About 380 seconds end to end on a single H100 (14B is about 590 seconds). Aspect ratios are configurable to 960x960, 960x704, 704x960, 1280x704 or 704x1280; fps 12-40; prompt under 300 words. BF16 and Linux only.

drills.q: Decode 'DV8x16x16' and 'CV8x8x8'.
drills.a: DV8x16x16: Discrete Video tokenizer, 8x temporal and 16x16 spatial compression, feeds the autoregressive WFMs. CV8x8x8: Continuous Video tokenizer, 8x temporal and 8x8 spatial, feeds the latent diffusion WFMs. Cosmos offers spatial 8x8 or 16x16 and temporal 4x or 8x, for a maximum total compression of 2048x.

drills.q: A colleague says 'we'll run PPO inside Cosmos to train the policy'. Give the one-sentence rebuttal and the number that closes it.
drills.a: An RL loop needs reset(seed) to an exact state and step(dt) with deterministic replay, and a diffusion video model has neither, plus no queryable forces. The closing number: ~380 s on an H100 for 5 seconds of 7B output is about 76x slower than real time for ONE environment, against Isaac Lab running 2,048-4,096 environments each faster than real time. Use the physics engine for the loop and the WFM offline to build a dataset.

drills.q: Show your working on why '9,000 trillion tokens' is a corpus figure rather than a training figure.
drills.a: 20M hours = 7.2e10 s, x24 fps = ~1.73e12 frames. 9e15 / 1.73e12 = ~5,200 tokens/frame, plausible for 1280x704 at 8x8 spatial with 8x temporal pooling, so the figure is reachable only by tokenising the whole uncurated corpus. But the curated training set is ~100M clips; at ~211,200 latent tokens per 121-frame clip that is ~2.1e13, about 21 trillion. The headline is ~430x above the defensible training-token number. Add the honest caveat: video latents are far more redundant than text tokens, so cross-modality token comparisons are meaningless anyway.

drills.q: A policy is 95% in Isaac Lab and 20% on hardware. Give your first three diagnostic moves, in order, before changing any code.
drills.a: 1) Classify failures by episode phase: approach-phase points at perception, contact-phase at dynamics, post-contact at control. 2) Run the two-number decomposition: hold dynamics simulated and feed real imagery for the appearance drop; take vision out of the loop with a state-based policy on hardware for the dynamics drop. 3) Check the boring things: control-frequency mismatch, action-space mismatch (position targets vs torques), unit and frame errors, observation latency, and seed variance in sim, because a 95% single-seed number is often 80% +/- 12% across seeds.

drills.q: You have confirmed a dynamics-dominated gap. Rank the fixes by expected value per unit effort, and say what is NOT on the list.
drills.a: 1) System identification on the real actuators: days of work, often the single largest win. 2) An actuator network trained on real torque/position traces, the standard fix for the servo-model gap. 3) Randomise link mass +/- 20-30% and friction 0.5x-2.0x and retrain: costs GPU time, buys robustness at the price of asymptotic performance. 4) Add 1-3 steps of action latency: nearly free, frequently matters more than expected. Also vary solver substeps, since PhysX's effective compliance is a function of substep count rather than of any physical property. NOT on the list: generating photorealistic video. Photorealism does not fix a friction coefficient.

drills.q: Your team wants to disable the RetinaFace face blur because the task is human-robot interaction and pixelated faces destroy the label. What do you say?
drills.a: You cannot. The NVIDIA Open Model License auto-terminates if you 'bypass, disable, reduce the efficacy of, or circumvent any technical limitation, safety guardrail or associated safety guardrail hyperparameter'. That is a licence termination, not a config change, and it retroactively taints every artefact derived from the weights. The legitimate routes are a custom licence via cosmos-license@nvidia.com or a different model. Note the threshold that caused the problem: RetinaFace pixelates any detection larger than 20x20 pixels, so anything with people at reasonable distance is affected by default.

drills.q: Sort these into benchmarked / internally evaluated / asserted: Transfer 2.5's detection gains; 'physics-aware' generation; GR00T N1.5 success rates; 9,000 trillion tokens; tokenizer speed versus prior art.
drills.a: Benchmarked with an external-style metric: Transfer 2.5's up-to-60% improvement in 3D lane and cuboid detection versus Transfer1-7B-Sample-AV using LATR and BEVFormer; GR00T N1.5 at 38.3% versus N1 at 13.1% on the 12-task DreamGen suite. Internally evaluated: 'physics-aware' generation, which rests on NVIDIA-defined metrics over NVIDIA-chosen prompts, and the tokenizer's claimed 2x-12x speedup, which is a vendor table rather than an independent benchmark. Asserted: 9,000 trillion tokens, and the general claim that WFM-generated data improves robot policies. The distinction is comparability, not honesty.

drills.q: Write the contamination assertions you would put in the training harness for a neural-trajectory pipeline.
drills.a: Three. (1) No scene_id appears in both train and eval. (2) No eval sample has origin != 'real'. (3) The subtle one: for every training sample with origin == 'neural', its seed_episode_id must not resolve to a scene present in eval, because a neural trajectory generated from a real episode inherits that episode's scene and is therefore a paraphrase of the test set. All three should raise, not warn. Also fix the interleave seed so two arms see the same real samples in the same order, otherwise you are measuring data-order noise, which is worth several success-rate points on small robot datasets.

drills.q: Design the budget-matched experiment that would justify a seven-figure synthetic-data programme, and say why the existing DreamGen ablations do not.
drills.a: Fix real-data budget N and total compute C. Arm A: N real + M synthetic. Arm B: N real + the same compute C on longer training and stronger classical augmentation. Arm C: the dollar cost of generating M synthetic trajectories spent instead on collecting more real demonstrations. Evaluate on a suite chosen by a disinterested party, >=20 trials per task, confidence intervals, >=3 seeds, with the contamination assertions in place. DreamGen holds the real budget fixed and adds synthetic data for free, which answers 'does it help?' (yes, up to +8.8% even with real demos present) but not 'is it the best use of this budget?', because there is no Arm C. Conflating those two is exactly the marketing move.

drills.q: Adding synthetic clips has stopped helping and is now hurting, while validation loss keeps dropping. Diagnose and fix without generating more data.
drills.a: Diversity collapse: the generator samples a narrow mode, so extra clips are near-duplicates in embedding space and model-generated data reinforces the generator's own priors. Validation loss drops because the validation set shares the collapsed distribution. Measure effective_rank(synth)/effective_rank(real) on a FROZEN third-party encoder (DINOv2 or SigLIP, not the generator's own); below ~0.6 is collapse. Measure coverage: the fraction of real samples with a synthetic neighbour inside their own k-NN radius. Fixes: prompt from a stratified scenario taxonomy rather than free text, raise sampler diversity, deduplicate at the embedding level, and cap the synthetic:real ratio at 1:1 as in the published co-training setting. Generating more is the one thing that cannot help.

drills.q: Make the total-cost-of-ownership argument against this stack to a CFO, in numbers.
drills.a: Four line items. Generation: ~380 s per 5-second clip on an H100 means ~7,600 H100-hours for 100 hours of video, roughly $23k-30k at $3-4/hr, before discarding bad generations and guardrail rejections. Workstations: Isaac Sim 5.1's floor is a 16 GB RTX 4080 with 32 GB RAM, per engineer, with no AMD, Apple or CPU path, and CI requires GPU runners. Vendor lock: NIM microservices move inference spend onto NVIDIA-licensed infrastructure. Licence risk: the NVIDIA Open Model License is revocable, auto-terminates on guardrail circumvention, and propagates a 'Built on NVIDIA Cosmos' attribution obligation into every model trained on its outputs, which is a provenance-tracking requirement on the data pipeline. Counterweight: the same $30k buys ~24,000-45,000 real teleoperated demonstrations, so the synthetic path must be justified by scenarios you cannot safely stage, not by cost.

drills.q: A scene is authored in OpenUSD so it is portable across engines. Is the policy trained against it portable? Explain the gap.
drills.a: No. USD with the UsdPhysics schema guarantees geometry and declared physical properties (mass, friction, joints, materials) transfer. It does not guarantee solver behaviour transfers. A policy trained against PhysX has absorbed PhysX's specific iterative contact resolution, positional penetration bias, and effective compliance at your substep count, none of which is a physical property of the scene. Swapping to Newton or OVPhysX under Isaac Lab 3.0's multi-backend abstraction is a distribution shift for the policy even when the USD file is byte-identical. Consequence: solver settings belong inside your domain-randomisation ranges, not in a config nobody varies.

drills.q: State what would change your mind about the strong 'WFM as learned simulator' claim, and pre-empt the accusation that the bar is unfair.
drills.a: A published result with all four properties: a policy trained predominantly or entirely inside a generative WFM; deployed on real hardware; in an environment with no data in the model's training set; beating a matched-budget baseline trained in a physics simulator, on a benchmark the authors did not design. V-JEPA 2's zero-shot Franka pick-and-place is the nearest structural analogue and it is a joint-embedding model, not a video generator. On the fairness objection: it is a high bar and it is precisely the bar the marketing claims to have cleared. Lower the bar and the claim weakens with it, at which point 'generated video is useful training data' is well supported and worth building on. Accept the weaker claim rather than arguing the bar down.

drills.q: Define a VLA in one sentence and name the three questions that determine every design decision in one.
drills.a: A VLA is a vision-language model whose output space is robot actions instead of text. The three questions: how is the action represented (discrete bins / continuous regression / diffusion-flow expert), how fast must it come out (control frequency in Hz), and where did the data come from (teleoperation hours times dollars per hour).

drills.q: How many bins per action dimension did RT-1 and RT-2 use, and how did RT-2 fit them into the vocabulary?
drills.a: 256 uniform bins per dimension. RT-1 over 11 action dimensions (7 arm, 3 base, 1 mode switch); RT-2's mobile manipulator over 8 (terminate, 6-DoF delta pose, gripper). In PaLI-X, integers up to 1000 already have dedicated tokens so bin k is just the token for the string k; in PaLM-E they overwrite the 256 least-frequently-used tokens in the existing vocabulary.

drills.q: State the action-chunking effective-rate formula, and apply it to π0.
drills.a: Effective control rate = H / inference latency. π0 emits H=50 actions in ~73 ms, so it has ~685 actions per second of capacity, which supports 50 Hz control with roughly 13x headroom. That headroom is what makes real-time chunking (computing chunk i+1 while executing chunk i) viable and lets you hide latency entirely.

drills.q: Quote ACT's chunking ablation and the temporal-ensembling delta. Then state the caveat about ACT's real-hardware numbers.
drills.a: 1% success at k=1 rising to 44% at k=100, averaged across settings, tapering slightly for larger k. Temporal ensembling adds about 3.3 percentage points. Caveat: ACT's real ALOHA numbers of 80-95% are on a different task suite from the 44% simulated ablation, so the two must not be compared or plotted together. This is a small instance of the general non-comparability problem across VLA papers.

drills.q: Work out the inference budget at 50 Hz and explain why a 7B model cannot meet it.
drills.a: 50 Hz is a 20 ms period. Subtract camera exposure/readout and transport plus controller overhead, realistically ~15 ms, leaving ~5 ms of inference budget. A 7B model in FP16 is 14 GB of weights; at ~2 TB/s HBM bandwidth one full weight read is ~7 ms, and 7 sequential action tokens needs 7 of them, so ~49 ms is the hardware floor. Measured OpenVLA-7B is 292 ms on an A6000 and 405 ms on an L4, which is 5-8x above that floor. Quantisation and compilation give 2-3x, not the 15x required.

drills.q: Explain why 10 flow-matching integration steps in π0 is cheaper than 7 autoregressive decode steps in OpenVLA.
drills.a: The 10 steps run on the 300M (0.315B) action expert only; the 3B PaliGemma backbone processes images and language once and its KV cache is reused across all 10 steps. Ten passes over 300M is roughly one pass over 3B, so the total is about 2 backbone-equivalents rather than 10. OpenVLA's 7 decode steps each traverse the full 7B model. The architectural separation, not the loss function, is what buys the speed.

drills.q: Why is per-dimension independence in a discrete action head a correctness bug rather than a precision issue?
drills.a: A softmax over 256 bins can represent a bimodal marginal within one dimension. The problem is across dimensions. If mode A is (Δy=+0.05, Δz=+0.02) and mode B is (Δy=-0.05, Δz=-0.02), a head that picks each dimension's argmax independently can emit (+0.05, -0.02), which is in neither mode and is typically a collision. Autoregressive decoding over dimensions fixes it in principle if the model learned the conditional, but costs you the latency. That tension is why diffusion and flow-matching heads, which sample jointly in a fixed small number of steps, won.

drills.q: A colleague says Open X-Embodiment proves cross-embodiment transfer works. Correct them with numbers.
drills.a: Partially true. 60 datasets, 34 labs, 1M+ trajectories, 22 embodiments, 527 skills, 160,266 tasks. RT-1-X beat the original per-dataset SOTA by ~50% on average across 5 evaluated datasets and RT-2-X showed ~3x on emergent-skill evals. But on the most data-rich datasets, RT-1-X was worse than the original single-embodiment model: negative transfer. It is the multilingual-model pattern, helping low-resource and costing high-resource. And no published result shows transfer to a morphology absent from training; every cross-embodiment number is on an embodiment in the pooled set or one that received fine-tuning data.

drills.q: Your policy stalls halfway to the object every time. Give the diagnostic sequence.
drills.a: First confirm the signature in the logs: commanded deltas near zero for hundreds of consecutive steps with a static observation. That means an absorbing state, not hardware. Primary hypothesis: operator pauses in the demonstrations, so the same observation maps to both 'move' and 'don't move' and an L2 head predicts the average, which self-reinforces. Fixes by leverage: raise H (ACT's 1%→44%), filter near-zero-motion segments, swap L2 for flow matching. If chunking does not fix it and the stall is at a fixed point in the trajectory, the hypothesis is wrong and it is a visual OOD problem, most likely gripper occlusion of the target on approach; check whether the wrist view at the stall resembles anything in training.

drills.q: Design the async two-rate control loop. Name the four rules that make it safe.
drills.a: Thread A (slow, 1-10 Hz, GPU): grab frames plus instruction, run the VLM, sample the action chunk, publish it with a monotonic timestamp into a double buffer. Thread B (fast, 50-200 Hz, hard real-time): read proprioception at full rate, read the latest chunk without ever blocking, index it by wall-clock (idx = (now - t0) * hz, not by loop counter, so a skipped cycle does not accumulate drift), crossfade 4-10 steps at a new chunk's seam, send the command, and increment a late-command counter when the deadline slips. Rules: (1) B never blocks on A; (2) B is pinned, SCHED_FIFO, isolated core, no GC or malloc in the hot path; (3) A emits a latent intent, not a target pose, because a stale pose is a wrong command while a stale intent is roughly right; (4) on chunk exhaustion, hold position, never extrapolate.

drills.q: Design a defensible evaluation protocol for a VLA, and justify each element with the arithmetic.
drills.a: Pre-register task list, scene randomisation procedure, and n before running anything, otherwise the suite is selected post-hoc. Report Wilson 95% intervals always: at n=10 a 90% observation spans roughly [60%, 98%], so it is compatible with a 65% policy; separating 80% from 70% at p<0.05 needs ~n=300 per arm, which at 60 s per trial-plus-reset is ~5 robot-hours per number. Randomise object and initial robot pose from a script, not by a human's idea of 'roughly here'. Stratify into in-distribution / novel-object / novel-scene and report all three, because the held-out number is routinely 30-60 points below the headline. Report interventions per hour and MTBF, not just binary success. Version camera intrinsics and extrinsics, gripper serial, firmware, and ambient lux so you can explain a 15-point move next month. Treat sim numbers (SIMPLER, LIBERO) as regression gates only, since every VLA scores materially higher on SIMPLER than on comparable suites due to few environments, one viewpoint, and biased scenarios.

drills.q: Design the serving architecture for a fleet of 50 robots running a 3B VLA, including the network-failure path.
drills.a: Split by rate, not by machine boundary convenience. On-robot: a hard-real-time process in C++ or Rust running the action expert at 50-100 Hz against a locally cached latent, reading proprioception at full rate, enforcing joint/velocity/force limits and workspace geometry outside the model so it can veto any command, and holding on chunk exhaustion. Off-robot: a shared GPU pool serving the VLM backbone at 1-10 Hz per robot, which is 50-500 aggregate RPS of independent requests, so continuous batching is a straight win here in a way it is not for a single robot at batch size 1. Autoscale on queue depth, target p99 not mean. Network failure: the current chunk buys H·dt seconds of buffer (1.0 s at H=50, 50 Hz); beyond that transition to a safe hold, never extrapolate and never replay the last chunk. Put a watchdog on latent staleness in the fast loop that trips independently of what the network stack reports. The design rule is that every layer degrades to a safe state, not to a plausible one.

drills.q: Make the case for not using a VLA, then steelman the other side with the crossover argument.
drills.a: Against: if objects are known, poses estimable, and the task set fixed, a classical perception-plus-planning pipeline gives 99%+ reliability with a debuggable failure mode against a VLA's 60-90% and an opaque one; bin picking of known SKUs is solved classically. Also against when control needs >20 Hz genuine mid-loop reactivity (force-controlled insertion, in-hand manipulation, locomotion), because a chunk is open loop exactly when the interesting information arrives; also when the safety case needs verifiable behaviour, in which case the VLA sits inside a classically-enforced envelope; also when you have one task, because the whole economic argument is amortisation. Steelman: the classical argument collapses as task count grows and specifiability falls. At 500 loosely-specified household tasks no amount of classical engineering scales, and a 70% policy that improves with data beats a 99% pipeline covering 12 of the 500. Correct framing is the marginal cost of task N+1 in each approach, with the crossover somewhere in the tens of tasks.

drills.q: Cost out a data-collection plan for a new bimanual task and state what you would optimise.
drills.a: Post-training a pretrained VLA on a new task genuinely works at 50-200 demonstrations, which is 2-6 operator-hours at a yield of 30-60 short demos per hour. At roughly $50-200 per usable hour once hardware amortisation and a supervising engineer are included (order-of-magnitude estimate, not a published number), a 200-demo task is low hundreds to low thousands of dollars, and a 500-hour corpus is roughly 3 person-months and $25k-100k. What to optimise: variation over volume. Fifty demos across ten object instances and five lighting conditions beats 200 of the identical setup, and randomising camera extrinsics during collection is the single highest-value habit because it pre-empts the most common deployment failure. Also compute and version per-dimension normalisation statistics with the checkpoint using 1st/99th percentiles rather than min/max, so one bad demo does not squash the range.

drills.q: Trace the RT-1 → RT-2 → RT-X → OpenVLA → π0 → GR00T lineage, one contribution each.
drills.a: RT-1 (Dec 2022, 35M, EfficientNet-B3 + FiLM + TokenLearner 81→8 tokens, 6-image history, 11 dims × 256 bins, 130k episodes over 700+ tasks collected across 13 robots over 17 months, 3 Hz): control as sequence modelling works, but a 35M robot-only model has no world knowledge. RT-2 (2023, PaLI-X 55B and PaLM-E 12B): encode actions in the VLM's own vocabulary and co-fine-tune with web data, roughly doubling unseen-split generalisation (about 62% vs 32%) and ~3x on emergent skills; ran at 1-3 Hz over cloud TPUs. RT-X (Oct 2023): pool 60 datasets from 34 labs into 1M+ trajectories over 22 embodiments, +50% average over per-dataset SOTA but negative transfer on the data-rich sets. OpenVLA (2024, 7B, Llama-2 + DINOv2/SigLIP, 970k episodes): open weights and single-24GB LoRA fine-tuning, beating 55B RT-2-X by 16.5 points on 29 tasks. π0 (2024, 3.3B): flow-matching 300M action expert, H=50, 73 ms, giving genuine 50 Hz; π0.5 adds knowledge insulation and open-world home generalisation from ~400 h of mobile-manipulator data (97.6% of training from other sources). GR00T N1 (2025, 2.2B, 1.34B Eagle-2 VLM): explicit two-system architecture with a DiT System 1 at 120 Hz, open checkpoint, per-embodiment adapters; N1.5 is the 3B successor.

drills.q: In one sentence, what is a world model, and what single property disqualifies Sora from being one?
drills.a: A learned p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) you can roll forward without touching the real environment. Sora is not action-conditioned, so it is a prior over plausible futures rather than a conditional next-state distribution you can act inside. Genie's contribution over Sora was exactly this: an unsupervised latent action model recovering a controllable action space (a VQ-VAE codebook of 8 latent actions) from video with no action labels.

drills.q: Name the three components of Ha & Schmidhuber's 2018 architecture and the parameter count of the controller.
drills.a: V, a convolutional VAE (~4.35M params, z in R^32 for CarRacing). M, an MDN-RNN with a 256-unit LSTM emitting a 5-component Gaussian mixture over z_{t+1} (~422K params). C, a LINEAR controller a = W[z;h]+b at 867 parameters, trained by CMA-ES with population 64. V and M are trained on 10,000 random rollouts and never see the reward signal at all.

drills.q: State the two arguments for building a world model. Bonus for the trade being made.
drills.a: Sample efficiency (one real trajectory amortises into many imagined ones; PlaNet solved DMC image tasks in ~2,000 episodes where D4PG needed ~50x more, and ~500x on Cheetah Run) and off-system policy evaluation (score a policy inside the model before it touches reality). The trade: you are converting sample cost into model-error risk, always.

drills.q: At a 5% per-step model error, roughly how many steps can you roll before half your rollouts have diverged? Show the formula.
drills.a: H_1/2 = ln(2) / -ln(1-eps) ~= 0.693/eps for small eps, so about 14 steps at eps=5%. At 1% it is ~69 steps, at 2% ~34, at 10% ~7. This formula explains why Dreamer imagines 15 steps and MBPO branches k=1..15 off real states: those horizons sit right at the half-life of a well-trained latent dynamics model.

drills.q: Why does giving Ha & Schmidhuber's controller the RNN hidden state h_t matter, and by how much?
drills.a: 632 +/- 251 with z_t alone, 788 +/- 141 with an added hidden layer, 906 +/- 21 with h_t included, against a 900 solve threshold. h_t is the model's compressed belief about the future, so the controller consumes predictive information without planning at decision time. 274 points from representation alone, with zero rollout risk. This is the version of world models that most often survives production.

drills.q: Why predict in latent space instead of pixel space, and what is the price?
drills.a: Capacity: a 1080p frame is 6.2M numbers versus a latent 10^3-10^4 times smaller, and reconstruction loss spends capacity on texture no controller reads.
