Noise: minimising squared error on aleatoric content converges to the conditional mean, which is blur, and is why pixel predictors go to mush in 10-20 frames. Price: no external ground truth, so encoder and predictor can collude on a constant mapping. That is representation collapse; defences are a reconstruction anchor (Dreamer), an EMA target encoder with stop-gradient (JEPA), or a variance-covariance regulariser (VICReg).

drills.q: Trace PlaNet to DreamerV3 in four sentences, naming what each fixed.
drills.a: PlaNet (2019) introduced RSSM (deterministic GRU path plus stochastic variable, because pure stochastic washes out long-range info and pure deterministic collapses branch points) and latent overshooting, planning with CEM every step. Dreamer (2020) replaced CEM with an actor-critic backpropagating imagined return through the differentiable dynamics at H=15 with a critic bootstrapping the tail. DreamerV2 (2021) swapped Gaussian latents for 32x32 categoricals with straight-through gradients plus KL balancing, hitting human-level on the 55-game Atari 200M benchmark inside a world model. DreamerV3 (2023, Nature 2025) added symlog, twohot over 255 buckets and percentile return normalisation, delivering one fixed configuration across 150+ tasks and the first Minecraft diamonds from scratch.

drills.q: Your agent scores 950 in imagination and 190 in the real environment against a random baseline of 210. Name the failure mode and the counter-intuitive fix.
drills.a: Model exploitation. The optimiser searches for the argmax of predicted return, so it is drawn toward regions where the model is optimistically wrong; the error is adversarially sought rather than averaged out, and it worsens with stronger optimisers. Nearly the exact numbers from Ha & Schmidhuber's tau=0.1 row (2086 dreamed, 193 real, below random's 210), caused by mode collapse so severe monsters never fired. The counter-intuitive fix: raise the model's sampling temperature so the dream is HARDER than reality. tau=1.15 gave 918 dreamed and 1092 real, the best transfer. Modern equivalents: uncertainty penalties (MOPO/MOReL), ensemble disagreement, domain randomisation.

drills.q: What is the representation-versus-dynamics split, and how do you test each?
drills.a: Representation q(z|x) does compression with sufficiency; it fails by dropping information, and the symptom is confidently wrong predictions no dynamics training can fix. Test it by linear-probing z for known ground-truth state variables. Dynamics p(z'|z,a) does accuracy over a horizon; it fails by compounding error, and the symptom is great one-step and terrible 20-step accuracy. Test it with an open-loop H-step error curve. Reconstruction loss alone measures neither. The decoder is a third object that exists only as an anti-collapse anchor and is never called during imagination.

drills.q: Someone shows you a Genie 3 clip as proof that world models can train agents. Respond.
drills.a: Sort the claim. Genie 3 (5 Aug 2025) is a real engineering achievement: navigable 720p worlds at 24fps, consistent for a few minutes, real-time. But there is no technical report, no benchmark table and no published closed-loop agent-training or transfer result, and its own stated limits are the load-bearing ones: navigation-only action space, roughly one minute of effective memory, non-robust multi-agent interaction. Compare with V-JEPA 2, which reports 65-80% zero-shot pick-and-place on Franka arms in two unseen labs after post-training on under 62 hours of unlabelled robot video. That is a closed-loop result on real hardware; a clip is not.

drills.q: Derive why compounding error is worse than linear, then say what that implies for horizon selection.
drills.a: The union bound gives H*eps, linear. The multiplicative view gives (1-eps)^H, exponential: at eps=2%, 74% at H=15, 36% at H=50, 13% at H=100, 0.6% at H=250. But eps is not constant: drift pushes the rollout off-distribution where error is larger, so with eps_h = eps_0(1+beta*h) the accumulated error picks up eps_0*beta*H^2/2, quadratic. At eps_0=1%, beta=0.05, the quadratic term dominates past H~40. Implication: never pick a horizon from theory. Plot open-loop error against h out to 4H on held-out real trajectories, find the knee, and set the planning horizon at roughly half of it.

drills.q: Give the strongest published evidence that scaling video generation does not induce physical law, and then steelman the other side.
drills.a: PhyWorld (ICML 2025, ByteDance Seed): textureless 2D physics simulator, DiT-S through DiT-XL, 30K to 3M samples, measuring velocity error parsed from generated video against ground truth. In-distribution error fell to 0.012 against a 0.010 ground-truth floor; out-of-distribution on the same model was 0.427, ~35x worse, and scaling did nothing (DiT-B OOD across 30K/300K/3M: 0.433, 0.328, 0.358). Mechanism: case-based retrieval with attribute priority colour > size > velocity > shape. Steelman: it tested 2D synthetic scenes at DiT-XL scale, orders of magnitude below frontier models on data with none of real video's diversity, so it constrains rather than settles the claim. And exact physics may be the wrong bar if the product is diverse synthetic training data for a policy that gets fine-tuned on real data anyway, which is exactly how Cosmos is positioned.

drills.q: Design the evaluation protocol you would gate a world-model-based production launch on. Be specific about which metrics you refuse.
drills.a: Refuse FVD, SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS and human preference as gates; PhyWorld's PHYRE table shows SSIM 0.943-0.951 across videos whose abnormal rate spanned 67% to 10%, so they are blind to the property that matters. Gate on: extracted-quantity prediction error rather than pixel error; conservation-law and object-permanence checks under scripted occlusion; OOD extrapolation with a contiguous held-out parameter region; counterfactual consistency (same state, different action); closed-loop task success against a no-model baseline for anything that acts; and Spearman rank correlation between dreamed and real return across 10-20 candidate policies for anything used as an evaluation harness. Plus a live shadow or A/B deployment as the actual decision gate.

drills.q: Why is DreamerV3's real contribution a systems result rather than an algorithms result?
drills.a: Every prior model-based paper reported strong numbers after per-domain hyperparameter tuning, which silently excluded hundreds of tuning runs from the reported sample cost. A method needing 200 tuning runs at 10^6 steps each to demonstrate a 10^5-step result is not sample-efficient in any practical sense. DreamerV3's robustness layer (symlog for scale-invariance across rewards spanning 0.01 to 100,000, twohot regression over 255 buckets for scale-invariant multimodal value prediction, percentile return normalisation for sparse-reward gradient stability) removes that hidden cost, which is what makes one fixed configuration work across 150+ tasks out of the box. Bonus finding: across 8M to 200M parameters, larger models were MORE data-efficient per environment step, not less.

drills.q: A team proposes training a warehouse-robot policy inside a learned world model. What is your recommendation and what do you demand before approving the rollout?
drills.a: Start representation-only: use the model's predictive features to feed a conventionally trained policy, which buys the 632 to 906 effect with zero compounding-error and zero model-exploitation exposure because nothing is imagined. Split the problem so the classical planner handles routing over the known map (write the dynamics down where you can) and the learned model covers only the short-horizon hard part: contact, other robots, humans. Before approving any imagination-trained policy I want a multi-step error curve with a knee well past the intended horizon, dreamed-versus-real rank correlation over at least 10-20 candidate policies, an OOD detector that refuses to plan outside the envelope, continuous monitoring of one-step and H-step error that automatically shortens the horizon as error rises, a validated safety layer with override authority, and a shadow deployment as the real gate. If those cannot be produced, degrade to representation-only and keep the rollout out of the decision path.

drills.q: Write the traceparent header format, naming the length of each field.
drills.a: 00-<32 hex chars trace id>-<16 hex chars span id>-<2 hex chars flags>. Example: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01. The low bit of the flags byte is the sampled flag, which is how a head-based sampling decision made at the root propagates to every downstream service so they all agree.

drills.q: Given a root span of 4200ms whose children are 1000ms, 960ms and 2100ms and which are strictly serial, compute the root's self time. Then say what you do with the number.
drills.a: self_time = 4200 - union(children) = 4200 - 4060 = 140ms, or 3.3%. Below 10% self time means this service is a pure router: it is not the culprit, and the next move is to descend into whichever child finishes last (the critical-path child), not to profile this service. Note the union, not the sum: if those three children had overlapped, summing would have produced a negative self time.

drills.q: You see three sibling spans to the same peer with durations 2001ms, 1998ms and 2000ms. Name the failure and the single feature of that data that identifies it.
drills.a: Retry storm. The identifying feature is the UNIFORMITY of the durations, not their magnitude: real work has variable duration, so three calls landing within 0.2% of each other means they were all terminated by the same client timeout at 2000ms. Confirm with the error status on all but the last, and the growing jittered gaps between them. Parent duration is about 3 x timeout + backoff.

drills.q: Write the LogQL query that finds every log line for trace id 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 in the prod checkout service, and explain why the trace id is not in the stream selector.
drills.a: {service="checkout", env="prod"} | json | trace_id = "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736". Three low-cardinality labels select the streams; the high-cardinality join key is filtered from the parsed body. {trace_id="..."} would create one stream per request, one tiny chunk flushed per request, and an unbounded index. Loki enforces this with defaults of 15 index labels, 10,000 streams per tenant and 50,000 global.

drills.q: A dashboard reads fleet p99 as avg(p99) over 20 pods and shows 480ms while users report multi-second latency. Explain the error and write the correct query.
drills.a: Percentiles do not average; there is no operation on twenty p99 values that yields the fleet p99. One pod at 8s among nineteen at 100ms averages to 495ms and the incident disappears. Correct: sum the bucket counters across pods first, then compute the quantile from the summed histogram. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

drills.q: You enable exemplars in the OTel SDK, redeploy, and Grafana still shows no metric-to-trace jump link. List the checks in order.
drills.a: Three independent requirements, all of which must hold. (1) SDK: exemplar filter is TraceBased AND the measurement is recorded inside an active span; measurements taken outside a span get no exemplar. (2) Scrape format: the Prometheus exporter must emit OpenMetrics; the classic Prometheus text format cannot carry exemplars and drops them silently. (3) Server: prometheus must run with --enable-feature=exemplar-storage, which is off by default. Most deployments fail on (2) or (3).

drills.q: A trace shows a 900ms gap before the first database span; the query itself takes 4ms. Give the diagnosis, the confirming metric, and the instrumentation change that makes this a one-trace answer next time.
drills.a: Connection-pool exhaustion, not a slow database. The asymmetry is the diagnosis: pool exhaustion leaves query duration FLAT while checkout wait climbs, whereas a slow database grows the query span itself. Confirming metric: pool used at max, idle at zero, pending requests non-zero. Instrumentation fix: stamp pool state (used/idle/pending) as attributes on every DB span, so one trace answers it without a second query. Terminal case: gap followed by no DB span at all means the checkout timed out and the query never ran.

drills.q: p99 doubled, p50 is flat. Give three ranked hypotheses and the cheapest discriminating check for each.
drills.a: (1) One bad host: group p99 by pod. If one pod diverges and all its routes are equally affected, it is host-local (GC, noisy neighbour, degraded disk). (2) A minority code path got slower: group by route, tenant and shard; a cache hit-rate drop is the classic instance, since the 2% missing now pay a degraded downstream. (3) A queued resource: check saturation and queue depth, since a pool or scheduler produces exactly this shape (most requests find capacity, a minority wait). In all three the confirming artifact is an exemplar trace from the TOP histogram bucket, not a randomly opened trace.

drills.q: A customer supplies a trace id and your backend returns nothing. Enumerate the drop points in likelihood order before you suspect a bug.
drills.a: (1) Never sampled: the head-based decision at the root said no. (2) Ingested but not retained: in Datadog, ingestion controls and retention filters are separate knobs, and spans are indexed and searchable for 15 days only if a retention filter matched. 100% sampling with a restrictive retention filter still leaves you nothing. (3) Outside the retention window entirely. (4) The id is a home-grown correlation id, not a W3C trace id. Only then suspect a pipeline failure.

drills.q: Half of your log lines carry a null trace_id. Explain the cause, why the missing half is the worse half, and the fix.
drills.a: Context loss at a concurrency boundary: thread-pool handoff, an asyncio task created without copying context, a callback, Spring @Async, a background queue consumer. It is not a logging-config bug. The missing half is the async half, which is where retries, background writes, and cleanup live, so the correlation gap is concentrated in exactly the code with the hard bugs. It also biases your mental model: the well-correlated parts look good because they are the simple parts. Fix: propagate context explicitly across the handoff (copy contextvars, capture Context.current() before submit, use an instrumented executor).

drills.q: Your team turned on tail sampling and trace quality got WORSE. Diagnose without seeing the config, and say why this is worse than head sampling.
drills.a: The Collector is almost certainly running as multiple replicas behind a plain round-robin service, so each replica sees only a fraction of each trace and evaluates its policies against a partial trace. Fix: a two-tier deployment with loadbalancingexporter and routing_key: traceID in front of the sampling tier. This is worse than head sampling because head sampling yields COMPLETE traces of a subset, whereas broken tail sampling yields INCOMPLETE traces of the subset you care about, and the incompleteness is silent: nothing errors, spans just quietly are not there.

drills.q: Design a tail-sampling policy set for a payments platform and justify each clause, including the one people omit.
drills.a: Head-based probabilistic pre-filter to cut raw volume; then tail policies: status_code=ERROR at 100%, latency above the SLO threshold at 100%, always_sample on the named critical payment routes, plus a small probabilistic slice (1-5%) of everything else. That last clause is the one people omit and it is not optional: if you keep only errors and slow traces you have no healthy trace to diff against, and 'what does a normal one look like' becomes unanswerable at the exact moment you need it. Size decision_wait against your longest normal trace (default 30s truncates batch jobs and long agent runs), budget memory as in-flight traces x spans x window, and generate span metrics with the spanmetrics connector UPSTREAM of the sampler so aggregate rates are not off by 1/p.

drills.q: A downstream dependency has degraded but a 98% cache hit rate hides it. Explain why 1% head sampling misses it, what you change, and what that change breaks.
drills.a: The culprit span only exists in the 2% of requests that miss cache, so at 1% head sampling it appears in 0.02% of stored traces and browsing for one is hopeless. The fix is not more sampling but outcome-aware selection: a tail latency policy keeping 100% above a duration threshold, or an exemplar pulled from the top histogram bucket, which by construction points at a slow request. What it breaks: if you now keep only errors and slow traces you have destroyed your baseline, so you must retain a small probabilistic slice of healthy traffic to diff against.

drills.q: The incident is over, the pod is gone, and you have no repro. Name the minimum set of things that had to be instrumented six months ago for this to be debuggable, then name the two you would keep under a budget cut.
drills.a: Six, in cost order: (1) W3C context propagation across every hop INCLUDING async handoffs; (2) structured logs with trace_id/span_id injected from active context, high-cardinality ids in the body not in index labels; (3) latency histograms with buckets straddling the SLO plus exemplars enabled end to end; (4) tail sampling keeping 100% of errors and 100% over a latency threshold plus a probabilistic baseline, with trace-id-aware Collector routing; (5) spans at boundaries carrying the business attributes that partition your traffic (tenant_id, shard, model_version, cache_hit); (6) always-on continuous profiling. Under a cut, keep (1) and (2): they are the substrate everything else assumes, since exemplars point at traces that must exist and profiles need a window you get from a trace. Sampling policy changes in an afternoon; retrofitting context propagation through an async codebase does not.

drills.q: A service's latency is 3s at p99 and its always-on CPU flame graph for that window is completely flat and unremarkable. Explain what that combination proves, and how you narrow the profile to the slow requests.
drills.a: It is positive evidence that the service was WAITING, not computing. A CPU profile samples on-CPU stacks only, so a thread blocked on a socket read, a lock, a pool acquire, or disk consumes zero samples and is structurally invisible. 'The flame graph looks fine' is the EXPECTED result for a wait-bound problem, not a clean bill of health. Switch to wall-clock or off-CPU profiling (py-spy --idle, async-profiler wall mode, off-CPU eBPF), or return to the trace where a wait appears as a gap. To narrow the window, use span profiles: Grafana's traces-to-profiles integration scopes the flame graph to one span's time range and service and embeds it in the span detail pane, so you profile that request rather than 30 seconds of all requests. It requires a per-language span-profiling bridge package; without it, traces and profiles stay unlinked.

drills.q: In one sentence: why can't you run stock DQN on a logged dataset even though DQN is off-policy?
drills.a: Because DQN's off-policy-ness is mild and self-correcting -- the buffer is refilled by nearby policies and reality contradicts overestimated actions when they get executed -- whereas offline the behaviour policy is frozen, the mismatch grows unboundedly over 1e6 steps, and nothing ever contradicts an overestimate.

drills.q: Your offline SAC run has mean(Q) = 4.7e6 at step 200k with gamma=0.99 and |r| <= 1. Is the run salvageable, and what single assertion would have caught it at step 20k?
drills.a: No. True values are bounded by 1/(1-gamma) = 100, so the estimate is ~5e4 times the entire legal value range -- the extrapolation-error recursion has run away. The assertion: abs(mean(Q)) * (1 - gamma) < 5 * R_max, checked every 1000 steps. Note the TD loss was probably fine the whole time, since prediction and target inflate together.

drills.q: Name the two distribution shifts in offline RL and say which one destroys training.
drills.a: (1) State shift at deployment -- the learned policy visits states pi_beta never visited; this hurts after you ship. (2) Action shift inside the Bellman target during training -- max_a' Qhat(s',a') evaluates actions with zero support under pi_beta. Number 2 destroys training, on data you already have, without ever touching the environment. Conflating the two is the most common interview error on this topic.

drills.q: Give the one-line summary of what BCQ, CQL, TD3+BC and IQL each constrain.
drills.a: BCQ: the action set fed to the max (VAE generates 10 candidates, perturbed by <= Phi=0.05). CQL: the Q-values themselves (alpha * logsumexp penalty pushing OOD Q down, giving a lower bound on Q^pi). TD3+BC: the policy (squared-error BC term with lambda = alpha/mean|Q|, alpha=2.5). IQL: nothing -- it never queries an OOD action, fitting an in-sample expectile instead.

drills.q: Compute the per-backup overestimation bias for an Atari-scale action set with per-action error scale sigma = 1, and propagate it to the fixed point at gamma = 0.99.
drills.a: E[max of |A| mean-zero errors] ~ sigma*sqrt(2 ln|A|). With |A| = 18: sqrt(2 * ln 18) = sqrt(2 * 2.89) = 2.40, so b = 2.4 per backup. The recursion e_{k+1} <= gamma*e_k + b has fixed point b/(1-gamma) = 2.4 * 100 = 240 -- on a value function whose entire legal range with |r| <= 1 is +/-100. The error is 2.4x the whole range.

drills.q: A stakeholder says 'we have 4 billion rows of ranker logs, surely that's enough for offline RL.' Rebut it with the specific quantity and the specific experiment.
drills.a: The binding quantity is the concentrability coefficient C = max d^pi(s,a)/d^pi_beta(s,a), which depends on the SUPPORT of the logging policy, not on row count. A near-deterministic ranker has essentially no action diversity per context, so C is effectively infinite and 4 billion rows have roughly the coverage of 4 million. The experiment: Fujimoto et al. 2018 trained DDPG online, saved its ENTIRE replay buffer, and trained a fresh DDPG on exactly that data -- coverage as good as a successful agent's own experience -- and it still failed.

drills.q: Write the expectile loss and explain in one line why tau = 0.9 approximates an in-sample max.
drills.a: L2^tau(u) = |tau - 1(u < 0)| * u^2. At tau = 0.9 negative residuals are penalised 9:1 versus positive ones, so the minimiser is dragged toward the top of the residual distribution; applied to Q(s,a) over actions actually present in the dataset at s, the minimiser approximates max over the support of pi_beta -- the maximisation policy improvement needs, with no unseen action ever evaluated.

drills.q: You have 50,000 logged trajectories. WIS says the candidate policy is 30% better than the incumbent. What three numbers do you compute before believing it, and what are your thresholds?
drills.a: ESS = (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 (gate: >= 100); ESS/n (gate: >= 0.01); max single-trajectory weight share (gate: < 10%). If ESS = 3 out of 50,000, the estimate averages three episodes and the bootstrap interval is fiction because the bootstrap resamples the same three. Also require WIS, DR and FQE to agree -- disagreement between estimators with different failure modes is a hard block.

drills.q: A colleague prefers ordinary IS over WIS because it is unbiased. Rebut in two sentences.
drills.a: Unbiasedness is a property of an estimator averaged over datasets you will never collect, and ordinary IS's variance can be 2^H -- 1.27e30 at H=100 -- so any finite sample is confidently wrong in an unpredictable direction. WIS self-normalises, making the estimate a convex combination of observed returns and therefore bounded by [min G_i, max G_i], with bias vanishing at O(1/n); on one dataset that is strictly the better trade.

drills.q: You get D4RL AntMaze total: BC ~0, IQL 378.0. On halfcheetah-medium: BC 42.6, IQL 47.4. What single property of the data explains the difference in gap size?
drills.a: Whether the solution requires stitching. In AntMaze no single logged trajectory solves the maze, so the answer must be composed from sub-trajectories across episodes -- which only multi-step bootstrapping can do, and BC structurally cannot, hence ~0. On locomotion, decent whole trajectories already exist, so imitating them gets most of the value and the 5-point gap is within the range of seed and reproduction variance (CORL moved published numbers several normalised points in both directions).

drills.q: Explain why FQE is not a trustworthy referee for a policy trained by CQL, in mechanistic terms.
drills.a: FQE's target is r + gamma*Q_k(s', pi(s')), which evaluates the network at the TARGET policy's actions at s' -- exactly the out-of-distribution actions that caused the problem in the first place. So FQE inherits the extrapolation error it is meant to measure, and because evaluator and learner share the data distribution and usually the architecture, the errors are correlated in the same direction: the referee is optimistic about the same phantom actions the policy learned to prefer.

drills.q: Design the decision architecture for shipping an offline-trained policy when a limited online test is available. Where exactly does OPE sit?
drills.a: Offline RL produces a shortlist of 3-5 candidates. OPE (WIS + DR + FQE, each reported with ESS) acts purely as a FILTER that eliminates obviously broken candidates -- never as the decision. A guarded online test on 1-5% of traffic with hard safety constraints and automatic rollback on a guardrail metric makes the actual choice. Runtime, an out-of-support detector (VAE reconstruction error or ensemble disagreement on s) falls back to the incumbent policy. Gottesman et al. 2019 reach the same conclusion clinically: OPE is for rejecting policies, not certifying them.

drills.q: Your CQL policy's actions are statistically indistinguishable from the logging policy's, and returns match the logger exactly. Diagnose and give the next two actions.
drills.a: Alpha is too large: the pessimism penalty has flattened Qhat so much that argmax_a Qhat(s,a) is just the dataset action -- you paid CQL's 2-4x compute and received behaviour cloning. Next: (1) reduce alpha into the 0.5-5 range or switch to the Lagrange variant with a target action gap; (2) run plain 10%BC and compare, because if it matches, CQL is not earning its complexity and you should ship the BC policy and redirect the effort to acquiring exploration coverage.

drills.q: Argue that RLHF reward hacking and offline RL Q-divergence are the same failure, and name the shared fix.
drills.a: Both are a policy exploiting a region where a learned function was never constrained by data: max_a' Qhat(s',a') at an action pi_beta never took, versus a generation where the reward model saw no preference comparisons. Neither the critic nor the reward model has any pin there, and in both cases the optimiser is an argmax that actively HUNTS that region. The shared fix is a policy constraint keeping the optimiser inside the trained region -- RLHF's KL penalty to the reference policy is structurally the same object as TD3+BC's squared-error BC term.

drills.q: Give five situations where you would decline to use offline RL, each with the substitute you would build instead.
drills.a: 1) Horizon is 1 -> contextual bandits; the weight is 1/pi_beta not a product of 100 of them, so evaluation actually works. 2) Data is near-expert -> BC or 10%BC; nothing beats BC on expert data. 3) Logger is narrow and near-deterministic -> nothing works; buy a 1-5% randomised traffic slice, since C is a support property. 4) No online test possible and the decision is consequential -> a constrained policy with a worst case bounded by construction; the OPE evidence standard cannot be met. 5) Gain over 10%BC is within seed variance -> ship 10%BC; the offline RL stack (critic, OPE, propensity logging, support detector, untunable hyperparameters) needs a large win to justify its surface area.

drills.q: What value of gamma do you use for RL fine-tuning an LLM, and why is 0.99 wrong?
drills.a: gamma = 1.0. Discounting asserts that a distant reward matters less, which is false inside a single response: the token at position 3000 is not worth 0.99^3000 (about 8e-14) of the token at position 0. The horizon is exactly one generation, 256 to 32,768 tokens, so there is nothing to discount. Some implementations use 0.999 out of numerical habit. A candidate quoting '0.99, the standard value' has not thought about the horizon.

drills.q: How many models does PPO-RLHF hold in memory, and which are trainable?
drills.a: Four: policy, critic/value network, reward model, frozen reference (usually the SFT model). Exactly two are trainable, the policy and the critic, at 16 bytes/param for mixed-precision Adam. The reward model and reference are inference-only at 2 bytes/param. At 7B that is 112 + 112 + 14 + 14 = 252 GB of parameter state.

drills.q: Write the Bradley-Terry reward model loss from memory.
drills.a: L_RM = -E_{(x,y_w,y_l)~D}[log sigma(r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l))]. It is the negative log-likelihood of the Bradley-Terry model P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)). r_phi is the SFT model with the LM head replaced by a scalar head reading the final token's hidden state.

drills.q: In one sentence each, what do PPO's clip and the reference-KL penalty each protect against in an RLHF run?
drills.a: The clip bounds how far the probability ratio moves in a SINGLE update relative to the immediately preceding policy, protecting against one destructive step. The reference KL penalty bounds CUMULATIVE drift from a fixed anchor (the SFT model) across the whole run, which the clip structurally cannot see. Neither protects against reward hacking, because both constrain how the policy MOVES, not whether the signal it chases is correct.

drills.q: Prove that subtracting the group mean reward in GRPO leaves the policy gradient unbiased.
drills.a: For any b(s) not depending on the action: E_{a~pi}[grad log pi(a|s) * b(s)] = b(s) * sum_a pi(a|s) * (grad pi(a|s) / pi(a|s)) = b(s) * grad(sum_a pi(a|s)) = b(s) * grad(1) = 0. The group mean is a function of the prompt only, so it qualifies. Caveat: the sample sits inside its own baseline, giving a small (G-1)/G-type correlation; RLOO's leave-one-out mean (1/(G-1)) sum_{j != i} R_j removes it exactly. Dividing by std(R) is a separate, genuinely biased operation.

drills.q: Derive the closed-form optimum of max_pi E_{y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta*KL(pi || pi_ref).
drills.a: Flip to a minimisation and fold the reward into the log: min_pi E_{y~pi}[log(pi(y|x) / (pi_ref(y|x) e^{r(x,y)/beta}))]. Normalise the denominator with Z(x) = sum_y pi_ref(y|x) e^{r(x,y)/beta}, defining pi*(y|x) = pi_ref e^{r/beta} / Z(x), a valid distribution. Substituting gives min_pi [KL(pi || pi*) - log Z(x)]. Z is independent of pi and KL >= 0 with equality iff the arguments match, so the unique optimum is pi*(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) e^{r(x,y)/beta}.

drills.q: In the DPO derivation, exactly why does the partition function Z(x) cancel, and what does that cancellation cost you?
drills.a: Inverting the optimum gives r(x,y) = beta log(pi*/pi_ref) + beta log Z(x). Z depends only on x, and Bradley-Terry only ever uses the DIFFERENCE of two rewards at the same x, so the beta log Z(x) terms subtract away. The cost: Z(x) is a sum over ALL completions, so cancelling it means the loss constrains only the relative log-ratio of the two completions in your dataset and says nothing about how probability mass is allocated over completions you never sampled. That is the mechanism behind likelihood displacement and behind DPO exploiting out-of-distribution responses.

drills.q: A run's proxy reward is up 40% at step 600; human win-rate peaked at step 180 and is now 6 points below. Your colleague proposes raising the KL coefficient and rerunning. Respond.
drills.a: It is reward-model overoptimisation, and raising beta will not fix it. Gao et al. measured this directly: in the RL setting the KL penalty does NOT change the KL-versus-gold-reward frontier, it only changes how fast you travel along it. Every point reachable by tuning beta is reachable with beta=0 plus early stopping at the same measured KL. Roll back to step 180 (the post-peak run is not recoverable by more training), then attack the frontier itself: hold out a gold signal you never optimise and stop on it, retrain the RM on fresh on-policy comparisons, ensemble 3-5 RMs pessimistically, and scale the RM, since larger RMs push the peak later and higher.

drills.q: Your GRPO run's clip_frac is exactly 0.0 for the first several hundred steps. Bug or expected?
drills.a: Expected, if num_iterations == 1 (one gradient step per generation batch, TRL's default). The ratio pi_theta/pi_old is then identically 1.0 at the moment the gradient is taken, so nothing is ever clipped. The clip only starts doing work with multiple inner epochs over the same rollout, or with asynchronous/stale rollouts where the generating policy has drifted from the training policy. If you set num_iterations > 1 and clip_frac is still 0, then look for a bug in how old_logps are stored.

drills.q: Mean response length in a GRPO run is climbing, but only for incorrect answers. Derive the mechanism from the loss.
drills.a: GRPO divides each completion's loss by its own length: (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t (...). An incorrect answer has negative advantage after group centring, so its per-token penalty is A_i/|o_i|: the LONGER the wrong answer, the smaller the penalty on each token. Gradient descent therefore has a direct incentive to lengthen wrong completions to dilute the punishment. Correct completions have positive advantage, so the same 1/|o_i| SHRINKS their per-token reward with length, giving no matching pressure. Fix: normalise by total tokens in the batch, not per sequence (Dr. GRPO; TRL's loss_type='dapo').

drills.q: Size a cluster for PPO-RLHF on a 70B policy, then say what GRPO changes and by how much.
drills.a: 16 bytes/param trainable (2 bf16 weights + 2 grads + 4 fp32 master + 4 m + 4 v), 2 bytes/param frozen. Policy 1120 GB + critic 1120 + RM 140 + reference 140 = 2520 GB of parameter state = 32 H100-80GB holding nothing but state, before activations, KV cache for rollouts, or sharding overhead; realistically 48-64 GPUs. GRPO removes the critic: 1400 GB, 18 GPUs of state, a 44.4% cut. With a verifiable reward and beta=0 you also drop the RM and reference: 1120 GB, 14 GPUs, 2.25x total. That is an engineering argument, not a statistical one.

drills.q: Argue both sides of 'does RL add capability to an LLM or only elicit it', then say how you would hold both.
drills.a: Elicitation: Yue et al. (2504.13837) show RLVR models win at pass@1 and pass@4 but base models catch up and overtake as k reaches the tens and hundreds, without exception; the RL model's reasoning paths already lie in the base's sampling distribution, and mechanistic work finds under ~3% of positions materially changed with promoted tokens already in the base's top-5. Addition: ProRL (2505.24864) trains past 2000 steps with KL control and reference resetting and beats base across the whole pass@k range including tasks base fails at any k (+14.7% math, +13.9% code pass@1 from 2000 to 3000 steps). Holding both: pass@k at large k is a COVERAGE metric and concentration lowers coverage by construction; the runs differ by an order of magnitude in length; and 'capability' is undefined. Under 'unbounded sampling with a perfect verifier' the base has most of it; under 'first sample is right', RL adds a lot, and that is the only definition a product cares about.

drills.q: Design the post-training stack for a code-generation model and name what you monitor.
drills.a: (1) SFT for instruction-following and parseable output format. (2) RLVR with GRPO on problems with complete test suites: G=8-16, gamma=1.0, eps_low 0.2 / eps_high 0.28, beta=0 or 0.001, loss_type='dapo', dynamic sampling to drop unanimous groups, num_iterations=1, execution in a no-network sandbox with hard per-test timeouts. (3) A preference/RM stage for what tests cannot see: readability, idiom, library choice, length. (4) Safety RLHF deliberately diversified beyond chat-shaped prompts, because Anthropic (2511.18397) showed chat-only safety training leaves agentic misalignment intact. Monitor: mean length split by correct vs incorrect, entropy and within-group reward std, KL to reference against a hard budget, pass rate on held-out tests never used in training, and a human read of 50 high-reward completions every few hundred steps.

drills.q: Cut RLHF cost 10x with minimal quality loss. Give the ordered plan and justify the ordering.
drills.a: (1) PPO -> GRPO or RLOO: removes the critic, 44% of parameter state, plus the whole critic-tuning failure surface. (2) Move any reward you can to a verifier: removes the RM AND the overoptimisation ceiling, so beta can go to 0 and the reference drops too, reaching 2.25x on state. (3) Attack generation, which is 60-80% of wall-clock in a synchronous critic-free run: vLLM rollouts, continuous batching, async/partially off-policy collection. (4) LoRA with a frozen base as the implicit reference in DPO, so the reference is free (disable adapters) and optimiser state shrinks. (5) Cut G and max_completion_length before cutting steps. (6) Only last, move online RL -> offline DPO. Ordering rationale: items 1-5 are pure engineering and do not change the objective; item 6 changes WHAT you optimise, since offline DPO's KL binds only on data support, and cutting cost usually shrinks that support further.

drills.q: Your GRPO reward has flatlined at step 220 and entropy is near zero. Walk through diagnosis and the fix ladder.
drills.a: Diagnosis: entropy collapse. Check within-group reward std, it will be near 0 because all G samples per prompt are identical, which zeroes every advantage and kills the gradient; the run will not self-recover. Mechanism: clip-high fires on low-probability 'exploration' tokens being pushed up, so they are suppressed faster than promoted, and the entropy change is dominated by a small set of tokens with high covariance between log-prob and logit change. Fix ladder: (1) clip-higher, eps_high 0.28 vs eps_low 0.2, a one-line change; (2) dynamic sampling, oversample prompts and keep only groups with non-zero reward variance; (3) small entropy bonus ~1e-3, larger degenerates into noise; (4) KL-Cov or Clip-Cov to constrain only the offending tokens; (5) ProRL-style reference resetting with optimiser restart. Distinguish premature collapse from healthy convergence: if reward was still climbing as entropy fell, that is convergence; if reward plateaued below the base model's pass@64, you collapsed early.

drills.q: In one sentence: what question decides bandit versus full RL?
drills.a: Does the action change the distribution of states you will be asked to act on later? If P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) does not depend on a_t, it is a contextual bandit.

drills.q: gamma = 0.99. What is the effective horizon, and what does that imply if your business metric resolves in 2 decisions?
drills.a: 1/(1-gamma) = 100 steps. If the metric resolves in 2 decisions you are massively over-discounting the wrong problem: widen the bandit's reward attribution window instead of paying for 100-step credit assignment.

drills.q: Write the potential-based shaping term and state what it guarantees.
drills.a: F(s,a,s') = gamma*Phi(s') - Phi(s) for any Phi: S -> R. Guarantees the shaped MDP has the same set of optimal policies as the original, for every transition model P (Ng, Harada & Russell, ICML 1999).

drills.q: You see episode return climbing steadily while your task-success metric sits flat at zero. Name the failure and the general rule it teaches.
drills.a: Reward hacking / specification gaming, the CoastRunners pattern (the boat circled a lagoon hitting three respawning targets, never finished a lap, and scored 20% above a human). Rule: always instrument at least one metric the agent is not optimising, and put it in the guardrail set with automated rollback.

drills.q: Prove that potential-based shaping does not change the optimal policy.
drills.a: sum_{t=0}^{T-1} gamma^t (gamma*Phi(s_{t+1}) - Phi(s_t)) = sum_t (gamma^{t+1}Phi(s_{t+1}) - gamma^t Phi(s_t)), which telescopes to gamma^T*Phi(s_T) - Phi(s_0). The total shaping reward over any trajectory depends only on start and end states, not the path, so two policies from the same s_0 have shaped returns differing by the same constant and the policy ranking is preserved exactly. Set Phi(terminal)=0 and the terminal term vanishes. Equivalent to initialising V_0(s)=Phi(s).

drills.q: Your agent gets +1 whenever it moves closer to the goal, 0 otherwise. What policy is optimal for that reward, and what is the one-line fix?
drills.a: Looping forever near the start: the loop integral of the shaping term around a cycle is strictly positive (you earn on the approach and pay nothing on the retreat), so infinite looping has infinite shaped return. This is the Randlov & Alstrom 1998 bicycle agent. Fix: Phi(s) = -distance_to_goal(s) and F = gamma*Phi(s') - Phi(s), which makes the retreat cost exactly what the approach earned and zeroes the loop integral.

drills.q: Compute ESS for importance weights [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 98.0] and say what you conclude.
drills.a: sum w = 100.0, sum w^2 = 4*(0.25) + 9604 = 9605. ESS = 100^2/9605 = 10000/9605 ~ 1.04. With n=5 that is ~21% of n, and in absolute terms the estimate is driven by a single record. Conclusion: this is not an evaluation. Gate on ESS < ~10% of n, and inspect max_weight and the weight histogram whenever a lift looks surprisingly large.

drills.q: Offline OPE says +7%, the online A/B says -2%. List your ranked hypotheses with the cheapest discriminating check for each.
drills.a: (1) Low ESS: compute ESS, max_weight, weight histogram. (2) Wrong propensities: check mean importance weight is ~1.0 across the log; if not, a downstream filter, dedupe, business rule, or retry changed the action after the propensity was recorded (a serving bug, not a statistics bug). (3) Support violation: fraction of decisions where the target policy puts mass on actions the logging policy never took. (4) Training/serving feature skew: diff feature vectors from both paths for the same request. (5) Interference: randomised by request instead of by user when actions affect future state. (6) Non-stationarity: log predates a product or seasonal change.

drills.q: A colleague says 'shadow mode ran clean for two weeks, so the policy is good.' Correct them precisely.
drills.a: Shadow mode executed none of the actions, so it produced no reward signal at all. It tells you the policy runs, is fast enough, does not crash on real context distributions, has no training/serving feature skew, and how its action distribution compares to the incumbent. Policy quality is measured by offline OPE (with ESS and support diagnostics) and then by a guarded ramp, not by shadow mode.

drills.q: Real robot chatters and limit-cycles while the simulated policy is smooth. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Control-loop latency present in reality (typically 20-80 ms sensing-to-actuation) and absent in the simulator. A policy trained with zero delay learns a bang-bang control law that oscillates the moment delay is introduced. Fix: model actuation delay explicitly in the sim and randomise it over the plausible range, and add an action-jerk or action-difference penalty to the reward.

drills.q: Your cost curve sawtooths around the constraint threshold with a period of tens of policy iterations. Name the mechanism and the standard fix.
drills.a: Lagrangian multiplier oscillation from plain integral-only dual ascent: lambda overshoots, the policy over-corrects into extreme conservatism, lambda collapses, the constraint is violated again. Standard fix is a PID controller on the multiplier update (PID-Lagrangian) rather than pure integral, or a lower multiplier learning rate with a warm start.

drills.q: Design the six-week plan for 'use RL to improve our ranking system' with one engineer, and justify why weeks 1-3 are not wasted if the project is cancelled.
drills.a: Week 1: add propensity logging to the existing ranker plus a 1-5% epsilon-greedy floor over the top-k, so the log has action diversity. Weeks 2-3: build the OPE harness (IPS, SNIPS, DR, ESS, support overlap) and validate it by reproducing the incumbent's known online value from its own logs. Weeks 3-5: train a contextual bandit with the widest reward attribution window the join supports, evaluate offline, run shadow mode. Week 6: ramp to 1% and 5% behind guardrails. Weeks 1-3 are a strict prerequisite for ANY RL system on this surface, so nothing is wasted; without propensity logging no future policy of any kind is evaluable.

drills.q: A PM asks for an RL agent that optimises 'user satisfaction'. Run the reward-design conversation out loud.
drills.a: Satisfaction is a construct, not a reward; RL needs a scalar computable per decision from telemetry. Ask which logged events we believe correlate with it and over what attribution window, then adversarially test each candidate: session length -> agent makes things hard to find; clicks -> clickbait; thumbs-up rate -> agent solicits thumbs-up; 30-day retention -> too delayed and confounded to attribute to actions. Land on a short-horizon logged proxy as the reward, a constraint set for everything the proxy can destroy (complaint rate, unsubscribe rate, diversity floor, repeat-exposure cap), and at least one unoptimised metric on the guardrail dashboard. If the proxy and constraints cannot be agreed in one afternoon, the project is not ready.

drills.q: Why is a permanent 1-2% counterfactual holdout worth its cost, and what question can you not answer without it?
drills.a: After six policy iterations each measured only against its immediate predecessor, you have six local comparisons and no measurement of the system's total value versus baseline. Without a holdout you cannot detect slow cumulative drift, cannot detect that iterations three through five were collectively negative, and cannot answer 'what happens if we turn this off', which is the question a cost review eventually asks. The holdout costs a known fraction of a percent; not having it costs an unbounded, unmeasurable amount.

drills.q: Explain why retraining an RL or bandit policy on its own production logs is a feedback loop, name the observable symptom, and give three defences.
drills.a: The policy chose which actions to log, that log trains the next policy, and the two co-adapt into a narrow region of action space that looks excellent on-policy and is badly suboptimal globally. Symptom: action entropy falling and top-1 action share climbing week over week, with metrics that look fine and then plateau. Defences: a propensity floor guaranteeing every action retains minimum probability (which both bounds importance weights and keeps the log informative), a permanent counterfactual holdout arm, and an explicit exploration budget monitored as a first-class metric. Retraining cadence is not a substitute for any of them.

drills.q: EU-regulated bursty chatbot: which Azure OpenAI deployment type?
drills.a: Data Zone Standard (EU): processing confined to EU data zone with pay-per-token economics; Global would process anywhere (compliance fail); Regional pins one region and throttles painfully on bursts.

drills.q: PTU deployment creation fails despite available quota. Explain.
drills.a: Quota is a policy ceiling; capacity is physical compute held at deploy time and changes dynamically. Check the capacities API / alternate regions before promising dates - owning quota guarantees nothing.

drills.q: Launch day 429s on a shared deployment used by three features. Restructure.
drills.a: Split deployments per criticality with own TPM ceilings, batch work to Batch API, backoff+jitter everywhere, client concurrency caps, PTU for interactive path if steady economics justify, per-deployment token dashboards.

drills.q: Design permission-safe retrieval for 5M chunks with group-based access.
drills.a: AI Search S2-class, integrated vectorization, hybrid RRF fusion, semantic ranker gated to user-facing paths after measured lift; security-trim filter INSIDE queries (group list resolved server-side), never post-top-k filtering.

drills.q: Why does post-retrieval permission filtering leak?
drills.a: Top-k truncation happens first: forbidden items displace permitted ones users should have seen, and any pre-filter exposure bug is catastrophic. Permissions must enter the query as filter predicates.

drills.q: Agent conversation transcripts are regulated data. Basic or Standard setup?
drills.a: Standard: capability hosts binding your Cosmos DB (threads), AI Search (vectors), Blob (files) makes transcripts auditable/exportable/deletable under your retention policy; Basic keeps them Microsoft-side where erasure SLAs depend on platform APIs.

drills.q: Team fine-tuned a model and hallucinations increased. Why?
drills.a: Fine-tuning optimizes form not facts; baked-in knowledge goes stale and training-data errors get amplified confidently. Knowledge belongs in retrieval; fine-tune only format/style/behavior compression.

drills.q: Semantic ranker bill spiked but quality unchanged. What happened?
drills.a: Ranker applied to internal/low-value query paths without measuring lift; gate it to user-facing surfaces, A/B measure before paying, monitor free-allowance consumption and per-path usage.

drills.q: Shadow deployment on ML managed endpoint doubles costs - explain mechanics.
drills.a: Mirror mode executes candidate deployments fully on their instances for regression comparison without returning responses to users; budget limited soak windows or size candidates for doubled load rather than leaving mirrors on.

drills.q: Legitimate medical queries get content-filtered. Response plan?
drills.a: Tune severity thresholds within policy, provide grounded context helping classifiers, build escalation path for false positives, log filter-hit rates per surface; never disable filters wholesale - document residual-risk decisions instead.

drills.q: Pick compute for: legacy .NET Framework site, bursty queue consumer, 40-service estate with platform team.
drills.a: .NET Framework: App Service Windows plans (Flex is Linux-only). Queue consumer: Container Apps with KEDA scaler min 0. 40 services + platform team: AKS Standard with node autoprovisioning.

drills.q: Why does Terraform-recreated VM lose all access despite identical config?
drills.a: System-assigned MI: new VM = new principalId = zero role assignments. Use user-assigned identity decoupled from compute lifecycle, or re-run assignment against new principalId in same apply.

drills.q: Container Apps app thrashes between 0 and 1 replicas on a latency-sensitive endpoint. Options?
drills.a: Set minReplicas=1 (idle billing at reduced rate) to avoid activation latency; note Dapr actors require it anyway; scale-down stabilization ~300 s and cooldown ~300 s shape the flapping otherwise.

drills.q: AKS cluster is two minors behind current GA. What's the upgrade path constraint?
drills.a: Cannot skip more than one minor per hop - sequential N-2 -> N-1 -> N upgrades, control plane then node pools, surge nodes for disruption control; automate cadence quarterly to stay within N-2.

drills.q: Pods Pending, nodes have free CPU. Systematic diagnosis?
drills.a: Check events: FailedCreatePodSandBox = subnet IP exhaustion (plain CNI); then taints/tolerations, topology/zone constraints, PVC zonal mismatch, regional vCPU quota blocking autoscaler. Read autoscaler logs for provisioning failures.

drills.q: Design zone HA for stateless API + PostgreSQL Flexible Server.
drills.a: API instances spread across zones behind zone-redundant LB/Front Door; PG Flexible zone-redundant HA sync standby other zone (~99.99% SLA, failover ~60-120 s); size headroom to survive losing one full zone.

drills.q: Nightly batch on Spot VMs keeps dying mid-run. Make it survivable.
drills.a: Checkpointed idempotent work units, drain on Scheduled Events (~30 s notice), eviction-rate monitoring, spot baseline plus regular-capacity ceiling, orchestrator-level retry-on-evict.

drills.q: Staging-tested change breaks prod instantly after slot swap. Two likely causes?
drills.a: Slot-sticky settings inversion (config didn't swap) or cold-start masquerade (warm-up passed but first real requests hit unexercised paths). Audit sticky settings, real warm-up paths, verify config parity.

drills.q: VMSS autoscale rules correct but instances stop growing at N. Root cause class?
drills.a: Regional vCPU quota exhausted, not a scale-rule problem; check quota before debugging rules and request increases proactively in IaC pipelines.

drills.q: Argue against AKS for a 4-service team, then counter yourself.
drills.a: Against: CA delivers revisions/KEDA/ingress with fraction of ops (upgrades, RBAC, security). Counter: imminent GPU needs, company standards assume cluster tooling. Resolve: start CA with explicit promotion criteria - reversible beats speculative platform investment.

drills.q: Greenfield analytics on Azure 2026: Fabric, Synapse, or Databricks? Decision tree.
drills.a: Default Fabric for MS-aligned BI+lakehouse (CU billing, OneLake, Power BI native). Databricks for ML lifecycle depth/Spark scale/multi-cloud/Unity Catalog. Synapse only for existing estates - new dedicated pools deprecated-by-guidance.

drills.q: Nightly Spark job slows month-end dashboards in Fabric. Root cause and fix?
drills.a: Shared CU pool: smoothed background usage raised baseline pressure; interactive requests delay first under throttling. Fix = capacity separation per workload severity/environment plus schedule staggering, not job tuning alone.

drills.q: Clickstream 200k events/s at ~500 bytes with strict per-user ordering. Design Event Hubs.
drills.a: ~100 MB/s -> Premium (~10-14 PUs) territory beyond Standard's ~40 MB/s ceiling. 64-128 partitions sized for parallelism headroom; partition key user_id for co-partitioned ordering; consumers <= partition count.

drills.q: Event Hubs consumers idle while lag grows. Why?
drills.a: More consumer instances than partitions - partitions cap consumer-group parallelism and extra instances sit idle. Raise partitions (Premium/Dedicated only) or repartition upstream; size instances to partition count.

drills.q: Serverless SQL exploration queries are blowing the budget. Controls?
drills.a: Partition files by date/predicate paths enabling pruning, enforce predicate pushdown patterns, isolate exploration into separate accounts with alerts, move production consumption to provisioned engines entirely.

drills.q: ADF copy from on-prem SQL Server - which IR and how run reliably?
drills.a: Self-hosted IR mandatory for private/on-prem sources: 2+ nodes sharing one IR for HA, sized VMs near data, patch policy defined, queue depth + heartbeats monitored.

drills.q: Synapse dedicated pool fine weekdays, regresses every Monday. Diagnosis order?
drills.a: Weekend-growth hash skew (uneven space usage/data movement in plans) -> stale statistics post-load -> tempdb contention from concurrent CTAS -> stale materialized views -> resource-class slot starvation via workload classifiers.

drills.q: OLTP changes must appear in dashboards within ~2 minutes. Two architectures?
drills.a: Fabric mirroring (Azure SQL/Cosmos -> OneLake Delta, Direct Lake dashboards, minimal code) or CDC -> Event Hubs -> eventstream/KQL for en-route transforms and sub-minute SLAs; never point BI at OLTP primaries directly.

drills.q: Same Spark logic: 40 min in Fabric notebook vs 8 min in Databricks. Plausible causes?
drills.a: Runtime version pinning, Native Execution Engine availability, pool sizing/node counts, V-order write overhead (~15-33% write-heavy stages), missing acceleration on specific operators, shortcut-vs-local data latency. If ML-lifecycle-heavy: keep on Databricks landing shared Delta.

drills.q: Rank incident frequency: CU throttling, partition starvation, scan-cost blowouts, pool skew regressions.
drills.a: 1 scan-cost blowouts (every per-scan model punishes exploration silently), 2 CU throttling (rises as Fabric concentrates workloads), 3 partition starvation (well-known, bites migrations), 4 pool skew (frozen legacy estates). Frequency tracks platform share x failure silence.

drills.q: New event-driven service on Azure Functions in 2026: which plan and why?
drills.a: Flex Consumption - GA Nov 2024, scale-to-zero, fast per-concurrency scaling, VNet integration, per-function scaling groups, up to 1000 instances; legacy Consumption is deprecated-track.

drills.q: Client HTTP calls time out at exactly ~4 minutes despite 10-minute functionTimeout. Explain.
drills.a: ~230 s Azure Load Balancer idle timeout caps HTTP responses regardless of config; return 202 Accepted with a Durable status URL instead of extending timeouts.

drills.q: Orchestrations produce duplicate charges after scale-out. Diagnose.
drills.a: Non-deterministic code (wall-clock/random/direct I/O) replayed divergently or non-idempotent activities retried. Enforce determinism, context-provided time, idempotency keys on payment activities; version orchestrators when fixing history.

drills.q: Queue messages vanish without errors logged. Where did they go?
drills.a: Poison queue: moved to <queue>-poison after MaxDequeueCount=5 failed attempts. Alert on poison depth, add handler, keep processing idempotent (at-least-once delivery).

drills.q: Bill tripled after moving off Consumption to Premium to kill cold starts. Why?
drills.a: Premium bills continuous core-seconds with >=1 always-billed instance and no execution charges; for spiky low-traffic apps the floor dominates. Use Flex always-ready sized to baseline instead of whole-plan Premium.

drills.q: Design a nightly 50k-row pipeline with per-tenant emails using Functions.
drills.a: Durable fan-out/fan-in: starter fetches count, chunk into ~500-row activity batches with retry options, aggregate incrementally via entity to bound fan-in memory, emails as final activities. Move task hub to Durable Task Scheduler if throughput high.

drills.q: An LLM agent loop (minutes-long multi-step turns) is proposed as a plain HTTP-triggered Function. Critique.
drills.a: Wrong twice: synchronous HTTP hits ~230 s ceiling and cold starts mid-loop; crash at step 7/10 loses paid progress. Use Durable orchestrator per turn (tool calls = activities, poll status URL) or Container Apps with externalized state.

drills.q: After migrating Consumption to Flex, the downstream database starts timing out. What changed?
drills.a: Concurrency multiplication: N instances x C concurrent requests now hit dependencies simultaneously. Cap maximumInstanceCount x concurrency below the DB connection budget; note Python defaults C=1 until set.

drills.q: What do you give up choosing Flex Consumption over Premium?
drills.a: Windows runtimes, deployment slots (replaced by traffic-weighted site update strategies), PowerShell managed dependencies, polling blob triggers (Event Grid only); one app per plan.

drills.q: Rank by incident frequency: cold starts, poison queues, non-deterministic orchestrators, connection exhaustion.
drills.a: 1 connection exhaustion (silent growth), 2 poison queues (constant silent loss), 3 non-deterministic orchestrators (rare but catastrophic), 4 cold starts (annoyance once mitigated) - inverts how often each gets discussed.

drills.q: An Azure Function gets 401 from Key Vault seconds after a role assignment was added. First two things you check?
drills.a: Whether the grant went through a group (claim cache ~24h) and whether the instance needs restart/remint; also confirm RBAC propagation delay of minutes.

drills.q: Name the three systems involved when a user calls an API backed by Azure SQL.
drills.a: Entra ID issues tokens; Conditional Access gates issuance; data-plane authorization checks the resource side (SQL permissions / data-plane roles).

drills.q: Why does Microsoft recommend user-assigned identities over system-assigned now?
drills.a: Lifecycle decoupling: pre-provision role assignments before compute, survive blue/green replacement, one identity shared per workload pattern; avoids Entra object-quota churn from rapid create/delete.

drills.q: A daemon hits IMDS 429s during scale-out burst. Root cause and fix?
drills.a: MI category limit ~20 req/s + 5 concurrent; fix is minting once per process and reusing the token for its full lifetime, not fetching per request.

drills.q: Explain why 'shorten tokens' failed as a revocation strategy and what replaced it.
drills.a: It taxed legitimate users while attackers use stolen tokens immediately; refresh/session policies retired Jan 2021; CAE revokes near-real-time on events and lets tokens live up to 28h.

drills.q: Your Terraform apply recreates a VM and the app loses all access despite identical config. Why?
drills.a: System-assigned MI: new VM = new principalId = zero role assignments. Fix with user-assigned MI or re-run assignment against new principalId in same apply.

drills.q: One admin user fails authz everywhere; they're in 230 groups. Explain and fix.
drills.a: JWT group overage (>~200): _claim_names indirection instead of inline groups. Handle overage via Graph transitive lookup or switch to direct app-role assignments.

drills.q: How would you collapse hundreds of tenant-scoped storage role assignments without widening access?
drills.a: ABAC role assignment conditions on Blob (prefix/tenant attribute matching) so one role covers many tenants within enforced boundaries.

drills.q: CI pipeline still stores an Entra client secret. Migrate it.
drills.a: GitHub Actions OIDC federation: register app/MI federated credential trusting the repo's OIDC issuer+subject, swap azure/login to use OIDC, delete secret; cap note: max 20 FICs per app.

drills.q: Front Door vs App Gateway - decision factors?
drills.a: Scope first: multi-region users/origins -> FD (anycast, edge TLS/cache, cross-region failover); single-region/internal -> AGW. Both do L7+WAF; adopt both only when global steering AND regional path-routing depth are both real requirements.

drills.q: Spoke A can't reach spoke B in hub-spoke. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Peering is non-transitive: hub must forward (NVA/gateway transit) with UDRs on spokes pointing inter-spoke CIDRs at hub plus symmetric return routes; verify Azure Firewall sees traffic only if UDRs force it.

drills.q: Random outbound resets appear after scale-out events. Diagnose.
drills.a: SNAT port exhaustion: per-instance port allocation shrinks as instance count grows (~1024 small instances) while connections multiply. Confirm via SNAT metrics; fix with NAT Gateway or sized LB outbound rules.

drills.q: On-prem clients bypass your private endpoint. Why?
drills.a: DNS split-brain: on-prem resolver lacks privatelink conditional forwarding so names resolve publicly. Add forwarders to Azure DNS or sync records; treat DNS records as IaC; test from failing vantage point.

drills.q: Lock App Gateway to Front Door-only traffic - three layers.
drills.a: NSG allow only AzureFrontDoor.Backend tag on AGW subnet; validate X-Azure-FDID header equals your FD ID via custom rule; optionally FD Premium Private Link origin eliminating AGW public IP entirely.

drills.q: Design ingress for 3-region app with WAF compliance and private backends.
drills.a: FD Premium WAF globally -> Private Link origins to zone-redundant AGW v2 per region locked via tag+FD-ID -> private-endpoint backends; probe-tuned origin groups, priority/weight failover, alias DNS record; rehearse regional kill switch.

drills.q: Post-Basic-LB-migration everything inbound is blocked. What changed?
drills.a: Standard SKU is secure-by-default: inbound flows need explicit NSG allow rules (Basic was open-by-default); also outbound stops until configured; public IPs must be Standard/static.

drills.q: Mystery 502s from Front Door with healthy-looking backends. First check?
drills.a: Health probe configuration: wrong path/port returning 404s marks all origins unhealthy -> 502s. Align probes with a real health endpoint; monitor probe-failure metrics before touching backends.

drills.q: When is ExpressRoute wasteful vs S2S VPN?
drills.a: Sub-Gbps sporadic/dev/test needs: VPN's near-zero idle cost and days-level provisioning beat circuit pricing and weeks-long lead times. ER earns keep at sustained multi-Gbps, compliance isolation, latency-sensitive replication.

drills.q: Argue against private-endpoint-everything, then counter.
drills.a: Against: per-endpoint costs, DNS-as-critical-path complexity, hybrid forwarding sprawl. Counter: eliminates exfiltration classes, audit mandates private paths, DNS pain is one-time IaC investment. Verdict: PE-default for data services, selective elsewhere, DNS-as-code mandatory.

drills.q: Assign table plans: request telemetry, verbose debug traces, 7-year audit events, security logs.
drills.a: Requests -> Analytics (joins, included queries, 31d). Debug traces -> Basic (cheap ingest, single-table scans OK). Audit -> Auxiliary + LTR years (search jobs on demand). Security -> Analytics if Sentinel (90d incl., alerting needs) + LTR beyond.

drills.q: Observability bill 5x after container migration. First suspect?
drills.a: Console logging provider left enabled in production - documented case cut ~87% of observability cost just disabling it; also filter health-check endpoints in DCR transformations.

drills.q: Error logs missing during outage investigation. What happened and fix?
drills.a: Daily cap hit - ingestion silently stopped. Alert on cap-near metrics; caps are emergency brakes only; real control = transformations, plan routing, sampling upstream.

drills.q: Dashboards fine but users report slowness. Sampling connection?
drills.a: Adaptive sampling thinned the slow-tail individual traces while pre-sample metrics stayed accurate; keep metrics for truth, add full-fidelity capture on error paths, surface trace-ids to clients for targeted hunting.

drills.q: One log alert fired 400 times in minutes during a blip. Redesign.
drills.a: Match evaluation frequency to remediation cadence, add suppression via alert-processing rules, migrate volume conditions to metric alerts (possibly custom metrics via summary rules); log alerts reserved for semantic cross-resource conditions.

drills.q: Finance can't reconcile invoice to teams. Two fixes.
drills.a: Use amortized views so reservations/savings plans spread correctly, and enforce tag governance via Policy deny-on-missing + inherit-from-RG with compliance dashboards from Resource Graph queries.

drills.q: KQL over billions of rows takes minutes. Optimization sequence?
drills.a: TimeGenerated filter first, project columns early, summarize before joins, has > contains, summary-rule aggregates for dashboards; structural answer: move that workload's raw data to cheaper plans and query summaries.

drills.q: Budget alerted, nobody acted, bill doubled. What failed?
drills.a: Operating model: budgets notify but never enforce; budget events must route into owner-tagged actionable workflows with escalation runbooks; actual guardrails live in Policy (allowed SKUs, tag requirements, region constraints).

drills.q: Synthetic availability tests pass but users broken. Why layer RUM?
drills.a: Synthetics test happy-path reachability from Azure POPs, not user reality (third-party scripts, ISP issues, client rendering); OTel browser SDK real-user telemetry beneath synthetics; alert on divergence between the two.

drills.q: Rank ops failure frequency: ingestion cost creep, sampling-blind forensics, alert fatigue misses, cap-induced evidence loss.
drills.a: 1 cost creep (every new service adds silently), 2 alert fatigue (accumulates until real page drowns), 3 sampling-blind forensics (bites when debugging outliers), 4 cap evidence loss (rarest, most catastrophic per event).

drills.q: Design blob tiering: heavy access 30 days, occasional a year, audit 7 years.
drills.a: Lifecycle policy Hot->Cool day 30, Cold ~day 180-365, Archive at year+ for audit; WORM immutability on audit container; ZRS baseline; watch early-deletion fees on transitions.

drills.q: Cosmos throttles at peak despite 100k RU/s provisioned. Diagnosis?
drills.a: Hot logical partition concentrating traffic - one physical partition caps ~10k RU/s regardless of total. Check per-partition normalized consumption, re-key with synthetic/hierarchical keys.

drills.q: Why can't Cosmos Strong consistency span multiple write regions?
drills.a: Strong needs RPO=0 via global-majority commits; multi-region writes with low global latency violate physics - Microsoft blocks the combination; strong multi-region write latency ~= 2x RTT furthest regions + overhead p99.

drills.q: Autoscale Tmax=50k RU/s at 15% average utilization vs manual 7.5k. Compare billing shape.
drills.a: Autoscale bills max(observed, 0.1xTmax)=5k floor hourly - valleys pay the floor; deep-valley workloads favor autoscale only if floor < manual need. Compute per hour-class from traces, never intuition.

drills.q: Postgres 'too many connections' after adding Functions consumers. Fix?
drills.a: Instances x concurrency exceeded max_connections (process-per-connection); enable built-in PgBouncer transaction pooling sized to the fleet math.

drills.q: SQL failover succeeded but app still errors. What's happening?
drills.a: DNS flipped but cached connections pin old primary; use short retry windows with connection reset, rely on retry-logic providers; async geo-replication also means possible ~5 s data loss window to design for.

drills.q: Stakeholder wants instant access to Archive-tier logs. Resolve.
drills.a: Instant = Cool/Cold tier pricing (online). Offer 90-day online + older Archive with hours-level rehydration runbook, or export queried subset to searchable store; present invoice deltas per option.

drills.q: pgvector vs AI Search for 2M-chunk RAG - pick and defend.
drills.a: pgvector HNSW comfortably handles it keeping embeddings transactional beside content metadata; switch to AI Search when semantic-ranker lift measured, faceting/security-trim needs, or scale grows beyond index comfort.

drills.q: Multi-tenant Azure SQL isolation options and progression?
drills.a: RLS single DB (cheap density, SESSION_CONTEXT predicates, noisy neighbors) -> elastic pools of per-tenant DBs (isolation + per-tenant restore) -> dedicated servers for whales/compliance. RLS risk: one missed context set reads cross-tenant silently.

drills.q: Storage Queue or Service Bus for order events? Factors.
drills.a: Service Bus for FIFO sessions, dedup windows, DLQ semantics, topics/transactions, premium VNet privacy; Storage Queues for cheap huge-volume simple decoupling with <=7-day TTL. Quantify op counts before defaulting.

drills.q: 50M-doc RAG system on GCP: name every layer and one decision per layer.
drills.a: Chunk+embed (batch mode ~50% off ~) -> Vector Search (billion-scale headroom, filtered namespaces) -> Gemini Flash serving with cached static prefix -> citation-forced prompts + eval CI -> dedicated agent identities. Layer decisions: corpus size justifies managed ANN; Flash for volume, Pro routed for hard queries.

drills.q: 'Why not just paste the whole wiki into the 1M window instead of RAG?' Answer with economics.
drills.a: 400k-token corpus re-sent per query = linear cost unless cached; caches bill TTL storage and expire; latency 30-90s first token at that span (~); citations unreliable. RAG: embed once, ~2-4k tokens/query. Long context wins one-shot analysis of static docs, not repeated queries.

drills.q: Team of two needs a stateful multi-tool agent live in weeks. ADK where, and why?
drills.a: ADK on Agent Engine: sessions/Memory Bank/auth wired by the platform while they build logic. Two devs rebuilding session stores on Cloud Run burn runway. Revisit portability when platform team exists.

drills.q: Filtered Vector Search returns fewer than k neighbors. Bug or feature?
drills.a: Feature: pre-filtering restricts candidates before ANN traversal, so sparse filters legitimately yield short result sets - post-filtering would pad with irrelevant hits. Confirm which behavior your client expects and design k accordingly.

drills.q: Agent bill tripled month-over-month. Diagnose in order.
drills.a: 1) usage_metadata per feature: history growth into prompts? thinking tokens globally on? 2) -latest alias moved traffic to pricier version? 3) cache TTL misaligned (all misses)? 4) retry storms multiplying calls? Fix: compact histories, cap thinking budgets, pin versions, restructure prefixes, per-feature unit dashboards.

drills.q: Design evaluation for an agent before allowing prompt changes to ship.
drills.a: Golden sets (input->expected outcome/tool trajectory) in CI; LLM-as-judge rubrics calibrated against human-labeled subsets; refusal-behavior tests alongside accuracy; shadow new model versions against live traffic before alias switches. Judge disagreement is fine as regression detection, not ground truth.

drills.q: When do you self-host vLLM on GKE instead of calling Gemini API? Give the break-even intuition.
drills.a: Residency bars, custom/open weights, steady high volume amortizing GPU pools, deep serving control. Sustained utilization above roughly half of GPU capacity favors owning; below it API zero-idle wins. Include ops labor - teams underestimate 24/7 GPU fleets.

drills.q: RAG agent cites sources but users report wrong answers. What's broken?
drills.a: Citation presence != fidelity. Add claim-level entailment checks against retrieved chunks, sample-audit judge agreement, log low-confidence paths for human review, gate generation on retrieval-similarity thresholds. Perfect prevention impossible; measured degradation detection is the goal.

drills.q: Prompt injection succeeds against your agent. Why does identity design decide the blast radius?
drills.a: If the agent runs as a broad human/shared credential, injection inherits those permissions. Dedicated agent identity + least-privilege tool roles + app-level authz inside tools confines it to the agent's own narrow scope regardless of injected instructions.

drills.q: 2M-vector internal search over HR docs - Vector Search or AlloyDB AI? Defend.
drills.a: AlloyDB AI (ScaNN indexes, pgvector-compatible): below the ~10M threshold where managed ANN pays; same database serves operational data, less infra, simpler ops. Vector Search earns its cost at billion-scale/high-QPS - headroom nobody uses here is platform tax.

drills.q: 24/7 N2 VM costs $0.10/hr on-demand. Approximate monthly cost with SUD?
drills.a: 730h x $0.10 = $73 full price; full-month SUD nets ~30% off -> ~$51/month. Tiers apply incrementally below 100% usage.

drills.q: Team wants cheapest VMs and picks E2 for a 24/7 baseline. What discount reality check do you run?
drills.a: E2 gets no SUD. Compare E2 list price vs discounted eligible family (N2/N4 at up to ~30% off or CUD-covered). For steady baselines the discounted N-series can close or invert the gap.

drills.q: Design capacity for 40 vCPU steady + 60 vCPU daytime burst + nightly render farm.
drills.a: Steady: resource-based CUD (commit 80-90% of measured baseline) possibly with reservations. Burst: autoscaled on-demand/SUD, or Autopilot pods. Renders: Spot MIGs with checkpointing. Never commit CUDs to burst/spot components.

drills.q: Post-migration Autopilot bill doubled. Give four causes ranked.
drills.a: 1) Inflated pod requests carried from Standard sizing (requests are the bill). 2) Special-hardware pods flipped to per-node billing + premium. 3) DaemonSets/storage requests now billed per pod/node. 4) Regional spread multiplying footprint via zone skew.

drills.q: Render farm on Spot keeps losing work mid-frame. Redesign.
drills.a: Checkpoint partial state to GCS every N minutes; handle the 30-second ACPI notice with a termination handler that drains; size for throughput-after-evictions; prefer smaller tasks so eviction loses less; keep results idempotent.

drills.q: New cluster, team of 5, variable load, one GPU inference service. Mode?
drills.a: Autopilot: variable load favors per-pod billing; GPUs supported via ComputeClass - but note that GPU pod bills per-node+premium, so compare against a small Standard pool with CUD if GPU runs hot 24/7. Default Autopilot unless GPU economics dominate.

drills.q: Standard cluster at 35% utilization. Rank interventions by effort-to-impact.
drills.a: 1) Packing/consolidation + tighter autoscaler scale-down. 2) Move bursty services to Cloud Run/Autopilot keeping steady platform workloads. 3) Migrate remaining variable workloads to Autopilot. 4) Only then right-size families/CUDs. Discounts before discipline just discount waste.

drills.q: Kafka on GKE loses quorum every node upgrade. YAML fixes vs platform answer?
drills.a: YAML: PDB maxUnavailable=1, zonal anti-affinity, regional PDs StatefulSet, maintenance windows. Platform answer: managed messaging or dedicated VMs decouple quorum availability from node churn - shared nodes couple them by construction.

drills.q: When is plain Compute Engine the right choice over both GKE modes?
drills.a: Few long-lived monoliths, node-locked licensed software, workloads whose ops model is one-VM-one-service, or strict requirements (custom kernel, specific OS) Kubernetes adds nothing to. K8s overhead buys nothing there.

drills.q: Why might you NOT buy 3-year CUDs on a service launched 6 months ago?
drills.a: Baseline unproven - resource CUDs bill regardless of usage for 3 years. Commit below measured baseline (~80-90%), consider spend-based flexible commitments, revisit after a year of stable telemetry.

drills.q: Analyst runs SELECT * on an unpartitioned 8TiB table 5 times. On-demand cost?
drills.a: ~40 TiB scanned = ~$250 (minus free tier). Fixes: partition+cluster, explicit columns, maximum_bytes_billed, dry-run discipline. LIMIT would not have helped.

drills.q: Estate scans 400 TiB/month with high scan-per-slot ratio. Which billing mode and why?
drills.a: Capacity: at that volume Enterprise PAYG 100-slot floor ($4,380/mo) buys ~701 TiB equivalent on-demand; if GiB/slot-hour ratio exceeds ~9.8 the slots are cheaper. Verify ratio from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS before committing.

drills.q: Moved to Enterprise Edition, bill rose 40%. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely compute-heavy/scan-light workload (joins/aggregations on small tables) - few GiB per slot-hour means byte metering was cheaper. Fix: mixed assignments (reserve only scan-heavy projects), autoscaler baseline sizing, or revert mode.

drills.q: Duplicates appear in BigQuery from Pub/Sub pipeline. Explain and list fix tiers.
drills.a: At-least-once redelivery (ack deadline expiry, client restarts) is normal. Tiers: idempotent sink via message_id dedup; exactly-once subscriptions (pull-only, regional); BigQuery subscriptions writing once per message. Never trade duplicates for losses by retrying less.

drills.q: One device's telemetry must be processed strictly in order at high volume. Design.
drills.a: Ordering keys per-device for FIFO, accepting per-key throughput caps and availability cost; DLQ configured so a poison event can't block its key forever; consumers handle key-affinity shifts. If using Dataflow instead: rely on Beam windowing, not Pub/Sub keys.

drills.q: Dataflow watermark falls hours behind after a backfill starts. Debug sequence?
