drills.a: Check backlog age metric; identify hot keys concentrating state (re-key/fan-out); check source quotas/backpressure; verify worker CPU and autoscaling bounds; confirm allowed lateness accommodates the burst rather than dropping data.

drills.q: Nightly PySpark job runs 2h/day on a persistent cluster. Redesign options ranked.
drills.a: 1) Dataproc Serverless batch (zero cluster mgmt). 2) Ephemeral cluster per run with Spot secondaries. Persistent only if interactive sessions share it - otherwise delete after each job.

drills.q: Poison messages never reach your DLQ despite config. Root cause?
drills.a: Pub/Sub service agent missing roles/pubsub.publisher on the DLQ topic - forwarding is best-effort and fails silently without IAM. Grant service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com and alert on dead_letter_message_count.

drills.q: Marketing asks why they should pay for Looker when Looker Studio is free.
drills.a: Looker sells governance: one governed definition per metric compiled to SQL, API access, central permissions, drilling/exploration. If metrics live consistently in dbt + modeled tables already, Studio achieves similar outcomes free - decide on definition-drift pain, not features.

drills.q: What breaks first at 10x volume across this stack? Rank with reasons.
drills.a: 1) Ordering keys (per-key serialization caps). 2) Dataflow hot keys (state concentration). 3) Slot contention under concurrent transforms (autoscaler absorbs if bounded). 4) Looker dashboards on raw detail tables (pre-aggregate). Serialization points fail before raw throughput limits.

drills.q: A request fails with PERMISSION_DENIED naming an IAM deny policy. The caller has roles/owner. What happened and what are the options?
drills.a: Deny policies outrank every allow including Owner. Options: use the exceptionPrincipals path (break-glass principal carved out of the rule), or have a deny-admin modify the rule. There is no allow that overrides it.

drills.q: Your CI needs to deploy Cloud Run services as a dedicated SA. Which two grants does the pipeline identity need, and where?
drills.a: roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser on the deploy SA (if federated) so it can impersonate, plus roles/iam.serviceAccountUser (actAs) on the runtime SA so deployments can attach it; deployment roles bound to the deploy or runtime SA in the target project.

drills.q: Design the WIF setup for one GitHub org with 40 repos where only repo 'api' may touch production.
drills.a: Pool + OIDC provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com with attribute condition repository_owner_id == <your-org-id>; bind workloadIdentityUser to principalSet filtered on attribute.repository/my-org/api impersonating the prod-deploy SA. Two gates: condition at provider, selector at binding.

drills.q: Pods get 403s after you annotated the KSA correctly. Give three causes ranked by likelihood.
drills.a: 1) Workload Identity not enabled on cluster or node pool (no metadata config). 2) workloadIdentityUser bound to the wrong principal string (project number vs id, namespace/name typo). 3) Binding granted to namespace-wide principalSet but GSA itself lacks resource roles â€” check both hops.

drills.q: Security wants 'nobody can ever create service account keys' enforced. Name the two complementary controls and their gap.
drills.a: Org policy iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation (blocks configuration path, supports dry-run first) plus IAM deny policy on iam.googleapis.com/serviceAccountKeys.create as request-time backstop with break-glass exception. Gap: deny coverage is permission-subset â€” verify; also enforce key upload ban.

drills.q: A contractor needs viewer on staging only, expiring in 30 days. Implement without human babysitting.
drills.a: Binding with CEL condition: resource-tag match env=staging AND request.time < timestamp('2026-09-22T00:00:00Z'). Note tokens minted before expiry stay valid until their own expiry; pair with short-lived access (impersonation) if revocation matters.

drills.q: Troubleshooter says ALLOW but the API call still fails. List four non-IAM layers to check.
drills.a: VPC Service Controls perimeter denial, org-policy enforcement blocking the write, CMEK key permissions missing for the service agent, quota/limits errors. Read the exact error string â€” each layer phrases denial differently.

drills.q: 500 projects still run workloads as the Editor-granted default compute SA. Sequence the migration.
drills.a: 1) Audit actual API usage per default SA from audit logs. 2) Create per-workload SAs with observed-minimal predefined roles. 3) Roll service-by-service behind explicit SA config. 4) Enforce via org policy/deny that default SAs get no new editor grants. Measure before removing.

drills.q: Why is granting TokenCreator broadly worse than serviceAccountUser?
drills.a: actAs still requires launching/attaching a resource (auditable creation event); TokenCreator mints ~1h tokens via API directly â€” silent full impersonation, no resource trail beyond the mint call itself. Scope TokenCreator to specific signing/minting workloads only.

drills.q: Multi-customer SaaS: which GCP primitive gives the hardest tenant boundary and why?
drills.a: Project-per-tenant(-tier): IAM inheritance, quotas, networking defaults all stop at project edges â€” the oldest hard boundary. Layer conditions/PAB/VPC-SC as refinement; folder+tags+conditions alone leaves softer edges.

drills.q: AWS engineer asks 'where are the NACLs?' Answer and translate the model.
drills.a: No per-subnet NACLs: firewall rules live at VPC level, stateful, priority-ordered, targeting tags/service accounts. Scoping = target tag (destination) + source range/tag. Implied deny-ingress at 65534.

drills.q: Service project deployer gets PERMISSION_DENIED naming a subnet. Fix?
drills.a: Grant roles/compute.networkUser on the host-project subnet to the deploying principal; for GKE also cluster SA + node SAs. Service-project IAM alone cannot fix host-side subnet access.

drills.q: You need CDN + single global IP but someone reserved Standard-tier IPs. What now?
drills.a: Global LBs/CDN require Premium tier; IPs are tier-locked so re-reserve Premium IPs, plan DNS cutover (low TTL), keep old rule during convergence (~7 days) before release.

drills.q: Design WAF rollout for a new public API with zero false-positive tolerance.
drills.a: Attach backend Armor policy; enable preconfigured OWASP sets in PREVIEW mode; analyze logged matches for legit traffic; sensitize overbroad signatures; enforce gradually per path; add rate limiting keys (IP+API key); Adaptive Protection alerts first, enforcement later.

drills.q: Three VPCs need full mesh connectivity as they grow. Peering or what?
drills.a: Peering is non-transitive -> mesh grows O(n^2). Move to Network Connectivity Center hub-and-spoke for transitive routing, or consolidate into Shared VPC when IAM centralization is acceptable.

drills.q: VM without external IP must download from storage.googleapis.com AND reach private Cloud SQL. Which features?
drills.a: Private Google Access for the API call (no external IP needed); Private Service Access range peered for Cloud SQL private IP. Independent - enable both.

drills.q: 800Mbps steady hybrid link today, 5Gbps in 18 months, no colo presence. Plan?
drills.a: Partner Interconnect ~1-2Gbps redundant now; HA VPN as encrypted backup; revisit Dedicated circuits when colo + sustained multi-Gbps justify fixed cost. BGP via Cloud Router throughout.

drills.q: L7 DDoS from residential proxies with valid TLS and headers. What still works?
drills.a: Behavioral layer: Adaptive Protection anomaly detection, rate-based bans on session/token keys, reCAPTCHA Enterprise bot scores, cache-first for anonymous GETs, per-account limits. IP/rate signatures alone insufficient - acknowledge business-layer dimension.

drills.q: Why do GKE secondary ranges need CIDR planning before first node pool?
drills.a: Pods/services draw alias IPs from immutable-range choices made early; undersized /20 pods range caps nodes x max-pods-per-node. VPC-native addressing makes pods firewall-visible - plan /16-ish for pods on big clusters (~).

drills.q: Attack hits a TCP passthrough NLB endpoint. Does Cloud Armor OWASP apply? Explain.
drills.a: No - L7 Armor rides proxy LBs only. Passthrough endpoints get inherent L3/L4 volumetric absorption plus advanced network DDoS protection under Enterprise enrollment. Policy-type-to-endpoint mapping is the tested detail.

drills.q: Logging bill is $30k/month. First three moves?
drills.a: 1) Volume-by-log-name report to find offenders. 2) Exclusion filters on _Default for health checks + system info logs (often 40-60% cut). 3) Tier retention: compliance copies to GCS/BQ instead of extended bucket retention; keep queryable windows only. Then budget alerts at 50/80%.

drills.q: Can you shorten _Default retention? What happens to expired logs?
drills.a: Yes, project-level buckets configure 1-3650 days. Shortening: expired logs become unqueryable but a 7-day grace period lets you restore access by extending again; grace-period logs still bill.

drills.q: Design alerting for a checkout API at 99.9% availability SLO.
drills.a: Availability SLI from request counts (exclude health checks); multi-window burn alerts: page at 1h>=14.4x AND 5m>=14.4x, ticket at 6h>=6x AND 30m>=6x; wire to on-call with runbook links; document budget policy (freeze threshold) before go-live.

drills.q: SLO dashboard green for months but users complain daily. Diagnose.
drills.a: SLI likely measures wrong plane or averages away recurring pain: health-endpoint uptime vs real flows; server-side latency missing client time; weekly window hiding daily storms. Fix: client-perspective synthetics, per-endpoint SLIs, segment slicing by region/tenant/version.

drills.q: Spans vanish between service A and B through an internal LB. Likely causes?
drills.a: LB/proxy stripping traceparent headers; instrumentation version mismatch; sampler dropping parent while keeping children. Verify header propagation hop-by-hop, align OTel versions, embed context into message payloads at async boundaries.

drills.q: Team wants everything queryable for 2 years in Log Explorer. Cost-aware counter-proposal?
drills.a: Hot bucket 30-90d for incident windows; aggregate/compliance copies routed to GCS or BQ-linked Log Analytics for long-term - not extended bucket retention ($0.01/GiB/mo compounding). Query needs beyond that window are rare and served from cold tier.

drills.q: Budget alert fires at 80% mid-month. What automation should already exist?
drills.a: Pub/Sub-triggered actions from budget notifications: cap autoscaling ceilings, disable non-prod schedules, notify owning team with labeled attribution. Alerts without pre-wired responses are just early disappointment.

drills.q: Error budget exhausted; product lead refuses deploy freeze. What failed?
drills.a: Governance, not telemetry: the freeze must be executive-agreed when the SLO is signed, with documented escalation. An error-budget policy without teeth agreed upfront is dashboard decoration.

drills.q: Why do structured logs earn their payload overhead?
drills.a: Same $0.50/GiB ingestion buys filterable fields instead of regex archaeology: log-based metrics, precise sink routing, SQL analysis via Log Analytics, mechanical trace-ID correlation. Signal-per-GiB rises dramatically; enforce schemas via libraries+CI linting.

drills.q: Alerting pricing lands in 2027. Delete half the alert policies now?
drills.a: No - audit and consolidate dead/duplicate policies as hygiene, model post-pricing spend from policy counts, prefer log-based metrics where they collapse references. Deleting working coverage to dodge future pricing optimizes the wrong thing.

drills.q: Service at 500 rps, 100ms avg latency, concurrency 80. Instances needed? Latency doubles - now what?
drills.a: in-flight = 500 x 0.1 = 50 -> 1 instance. At 200ms: 100 in flight -> 2 instances. Latency not rps drives the bill.

drills.q: p99 spikes to ~1.2s exactly once each morning. Diagnosis and two fixes with cost implications.
drills.a: Overnight scale-to-zero cold start on first request. Fix 1: min-instances=1 (continuous small cost). Fix 2: smaller image + lazy init + startup CPU boost (free-ish). Measure container/startup_latency first.

drills.q: Launch day traffic spike returns HTTP 429s. What happened and what do you check before raising max-instances?
drills.a: Hit max-instances (default 100/revision) with saturated queues and router timeouts. Before raising: downstream capacity - DB connection budget / per-instance pool size; NAT throughput; dependency rate limits. Cap is protection, not just cost knob.

drills.q: A metrics-scraper goroutine inside your service reports stale data intermittently. Root cause?
drills.a: Default CPU throttling freezes background threads between requests. Switch to always-allocated CPU (--no-cpu-throttling); accept continuous billing and pair with min-instances deliberately.

drills.q: Wire GCS uploads under gs://incoming/*.csv to a processor service. Which trigger type and why?
drills.a: Audit-log Eventarc trigger: type google.cloud.audit.log.v1.written, serviceName storage.googleapis.com, methodName storage.objects.create, resourceName path pattern /buckets/incoming/objects/*.csv. Direct object.v1.finalized events cannot prefix-filter.

drills.q: Processor runs twice for one upload occasionally. Why and what do you change?
drills.a: Pub/Sub-backed delivery is at-least-once (retries after slow/failed handling). Dedup on CloudEvent id or object name+generation in a fast store; keep handler fast or offload long work to jobs; monitor DLQ.

drills.q: Estimate monthly cost shape: steady 10 rps, 150ms, conc 80, 1 vCPU/512MB vs bursty 0-500 rps 5% of the time. Which pricing mode wins each?
drills.a: Steady: ~2 instances always -> instance-based/committed comparison vs small GKE pool; Cloud Run competitive but check GKE consolidation. Bursty: scale-to-zero request-based billing wins massively - pay only for the burst windows.

drills.q: Deploy must reach an internal 10.x API and present one fixed egress IP to a partner allowlist. Design.
drills.a: Direct VPC egress on a chosen subnet -> private routing; Cloud NAT on that subnet provides the static egress IP. Ingress: internal-and-cloud-load-balancing only.

drills.q: Interviewer says 'Cloud Functions can run 60 minutes.' Correct precisely.
drills.a: Cloud Run functions: HTTP-triggered up to 60 min; event-driven via Eventarc capped at 9 min; gen1 legacy capped at 9 min for everything. Longer than that = jobs/Batch/Workflows.

drills.q: Canary plan for a risky deploy using native features only.
drills.a: Deploy creates new revision; smoke-test revision URL; shift 5% traffic, watch per-revision error/latency metrics; promote 100% or roll back by retagging 100% to prior revision - seconds, no rebuild. Keep N-1 revisions warm if rollback speed matters.

drills.q: Bucket accessed ~once per month, 5TB. Best class and why?
drills.a: Nearline: ~half the storage price of Standard with $0.01/GB retrieval; at monthly access the break-even favors it. Respect 30-day minimum to avoid early-deletion fees.

drills.q: Access pattern unknown across a 50TB mixed bucket. Autoclass or manual lifecycle? Defend.
drills.a: Autoclass: per-object observation beats guessing; waives retrieval/early-deletion fees so misprediction is cheap. Revisit if metrics show uniformly hot data (mgmt fee buys nothing).

drills.q: Explain Spanner commit-wait including why Paxos hides most of it.
drills.a: commit_ts = TT.now().latest; must wait until TT.now().earliest > commit_ts so no later transaction anywhere gets an earlier timestamp. Paxos quorum RTT runs in parallel - residual wait only when quorum finishes inside the eps window (~1-7ms).

drills.q: Fintech audit needs 'trade B definitely executed after trade A' globally. Which DB and which guarantee?
drills.a: Spanner: external consistency/strict serializability backed by hardware-bounded TrueTime. CRDB serializable via HLC does NOT promise cross-node real-time ordering. If staying multi-cloud, state explicitly that wall-clock ordering evidence weakens.

drills.q: Bigtable telemetry table: one node pegged at 100%, cluster idle. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Hot tablet from monotonic keys. Fix schema: hash or salt the leading key component (hash#id#ts), pad IDs; create table with pre-split rows matching key distribution. Scaling nodes adds nothing until keys distribute.

drills.q: Postgres app at 90% CPU on Cloud SQL primary, reads 70% of traffic. Decision path?
drills.a: Read load first: add Cloud SQL replicas (accept lag) or move to AlloyDB read pool for stronger consistency reads. Write/CPU ceilings: AlloyDB disaggregated storage + bigger shapes + columnar engine for any analytical queries. Wire-compatible so no code change.

drills.q: Firestore bill exploded after launch. Three likely causes and fixes.
drills.a: 1) N+1 doc reads -> batch gets/cache. 2) Realtime listeners active on backgrounded screens -> attach/detach lifecycle management. 3) Aggregate queries re-read collections -> scheduled functions writing summary docs. Alert on per-collection read rates.

drills.q: Compliance: objects must survive accidental deletion >=90 days. Layered design?
drills.a: Versioning (prior versions survive overwrite/delete) + soft delete (configurable retention ~) + bucket retention policy 90 days (undeletable before age) + optional retention lock making even admins unable to shorten. Legal holds per object where needed.

drills.q: 200k QPS feature lookups, ms latency, realtime ML serving. Store choice and fallback plan.
drills.a: Bigtable: horizontal node scaling (~10k QPS/node heuristic ~), hashed key prefixes for distribution. Fallback: replication with multi-cluster routing + client cache absorbing gaps; Redis only if dataset fits memory comfortably.

drills.q: 'AlloyDB made our queries 100x faster' - what follow-up questions prove or disprove it?
drills.a: Baseline: tuned PG on fast storage or default config? Which queries - columnar-eligible scans/aggregations or point lookups (row path anyway)? Columnar engine coverage configured for those tables? Data volume warehouse-scale or operational-scale? The claim is benchmark-shaped, not universal.

drills.q: True or false: a Scala Future starts executing only when you call .map or await it.
drills.a: False -- Futures start eagerly on construction using the implicit ExecutionContext. (Laziness is what IO/ZIO provide, or Future { ... } wrapped in a by-name call-by-need structure.)

drills.q: Name two things a case class generates that a Java record does not.
drills.a: copy() for named-field cloning and unapply-based pattern matching wired into match expressions (records gained deconstruction patterns only in Java 21). Also case classes can extend traits/classes; records are implicitly final.

drills.q: A service on the global ExecutionContext slows to a crawl under load with zero errors. Diagnose.
drills.a: Classic blocking-on-global-pool starvation: JDBC/HTTP calls park all ForkJoinPool threads (sized = cores) while tasks queue; logs show latency not failures. Fix: dedicated pools per blocking source or effect-runtime blocking brackets.

drills.q: Why can't Catalyst optimize Python UDFs the way it optimizes Scala Dataset lambdas?
drills.a: Scala lambdas in typed Datasets are JVM closures Catalyst can inspect/inline into the plan; Python UDFs cross a process boundary with serialization per row (narrowed by Arrow columnar batches since Spark 2.3 but never eliminated).

drills.q: Your company's revenue exceeds Akka's BSL threshold. Three legal paths forward?
drills.a: 1) Migrate to Apache Pekko (Apache 2.0 fork, namespace-change tooling exists); 2) purchase Lightbend subscription/license; 3) freeze on last Apache-licensed versions (security risk accrues). Migration is the standard answer.

drills.q: Can a Scala 2.13 application depend on a library published with Scala 3.8?
drills.a: No -- the TASTy reader ceiling is Scala 3.7 for 2.13 consumers; 3.8+ artifacts are unreadable. The reverse direction (Scala 3 consuming 2.13 artifacts) remains supported indefinitely.

drills.q: Greenfield CRUD service, Java-only team, no Spark anywhere. Pick the stack and defend in one sentence each.
drills.a: Java 21: records/sealed interfaces/switch patterns/virtual threads deliver Scala's everyday wins natively with a bigger hiring pool; Kotlin if null-safety and concision matter more than ecosystem orthodoxy; Scala buys compile friction and FP learning curve here for marginal gain.

drills.q: What do virtual threads NOT give you that ZIO/Cats Effect do?
drills.a: Cancellation-as-value, retry policies, timeouts-as-values, fiber supervision/structured joins, and resource brackets (acquire/release guaranteed on failure). Virtual threads fix blocking cost, not correctness tooling for concurrent composition.

drills.q: Either[String, User] vs throwing UserNotFoundException: which for 'user not found' in a domain API and why?
drills.a: Either -- absence of a user is an expected, recoverable outcome that belongs in the signature so callers must handle it (flatMap short-circuit or mapped error response). Exceptions suit bugs/infrastructure failures, not modeled outcomes.

drills.q: True or false: Trino stores table data locally on worker disks like a database.
drills.a: False -- Trino is stateless between queries; all data lives in source systems accessed through connectors, and workers only hold transient query state in memory/disk scratch.

drills.q: Which component assigns splits to workers and enforces query memory limits?
drills.a: The coordinator -- it schedules splits, aggregates per-worker memory reports continuously, and kills queries that breach user-memory limits (EXCEEDED_MEMORY_LIMIT).

drills.q: Your federated Postgres dashboard query ships 40M rows per refresh. Name the first two things you check.
drills.a: 1) EXPLAIN: does the WHERE clause appear inside the Postgres connector's table handle (pushdown) or as a filter above the scan? 2) Does the filtered column have an index on the Postgres side? Pushdown without an index still scans remotely.

drills.q: Query fails with EXCEEDED_MEMORY_LIMIT naming a hash join operator. Give the ordered fix list.
drills.a: 1) Gather/refresh table statistics; 2) force PARTITIONED join or cap join.broadcast-threshold if broadcast picked an underestimated side; 3) reduce input cardinality earlier in the plan; 4) enable spill so pressure becomes revocable; 5) raise limits last -- limits are isolation against cluster-wide OOM, not an inconvenience.

drills.q: Why does 'it worked with LIMIT 10' prove nothing about the un-LIMITed query?
drills.a: LIMIT returns early while stages keep running client-side, but blocking operators (hash join build, full aggregation, ORDER BY) must consume entire inputs before emitting -- the full query's memory profile is invisible to the LIMIT run.

drills.q: BI runs five federated dashboards hourly against Aurora. Federation or copy? Defend briefly.
drills.a: Copy: hourly refreshes re-transfer the same rows ~120x/day and put analytical load on an OLTP primary. A scheduled incremental sync into Iceberg amortizes transfer once and removes OLTP exposure, costing one pipeline to own instead of per-query network tax.

drills.q: What changes about running multi-hour batch SQL on Trino once fault-tolerant execution is enabled?
drills.a: Worker loss no longer restarts the whole query: stage intermediates persist to the exchange manager (S3/HDFS) and only lost splits retry. This moves long batch transforms out of Spark's monopoly -- at the price of exchange IO overhead and enabling the exchange manager.

drills.q: An Athena bill doubles month over month. First three checks?
drills.a: 1) Scanned-bytes by query/user via Athena API (find new full scans); 2) dashboards that switched from partition-pruned patterns to full-table patterns; 3) format regression (raw JSON/CSV replacing Parquet). Cost incidents are scan-discipline incidents at $5/TB.

drills.q: Design rule-of-thumb: which joins belong on Spark instead of Trino?
drills.a: Skew-heavy, multi-TB shuffles with long tails -- Spark's AQE skew-partition splitting is mature where Trino's handling stays coarser; also ML/UDF-heavy pipelines and streaming. Trino keeps interactive/light-ELT and federation workloads.

drills.q: Write the validation checklist a full node runs on each incoming block, in order.
drills.a: Structural: parse, size<=4M WU (BTC), Merkle root matches body, header hash meets target. Contextual: parent known+valid, height/difficulty correct for epoch, timestamps within tolerance, coinbase claims only subsidy+fees. Execution: replay all txs against state - sigs, UTXO unspent or account nonce/balance. Then fork choice.

drills.q: Two valid chains: one 5 blocks at low difficulty, one 3 blocks at high difficulty. Which wins and why?
drills.a: The heavier one wins - Bitcoin's rule is most cumulative WORK, not length. Work per block ~= expected hashes = 16^d for d leading zero hex digits; sum across the chain. A longer-but-lighter chain loses.

drills.q: Why can't an attacker cheaply rewrite blocks from last month?
drills.a: Every edit changes the block hash, invalidating descendants' prev-hash pointers AND requiring PoW redo of the whole edited suffix faster than the honest network extends the real tip. Catch-up probability from z behind is ~ (q/p)^z - exponential decay with depth.

drills.q: Half the global hashpower disappears tonight. Trace BTC's difficulty response over the next weeks.
drills.a: Block interval doubles to ~20 min immediately; retarget only fires every 2016 blocks, so ~4 weeks later actual/expected=2 -> target doubles (difficulty halves), clamped at x4. Cadence restores after the window. This lag was real during the mid-2021 China miner exit.

drills.q: Design reorg-safe deposit crediting for an exchange handling both BTC and ETH.
drills.a: BTC: value-tiered confirmations (1 small / 3 mid / 6 large), RBF-aware mempool monitoring, alarm on conflicting UTXO spends. ETH: UX reads latest slot, money moves on finalized tag (~12.8 min). Both: index by txid + (sender,nonce), idempotent ledger entries so reversals book as journal events, alert when observed reorg depth exceeds historical max.

drills.q: What exactly does assume-valid skip and why is that defensible?
drills.a: Skips ECDSA signature verification for historical blocks below a community-published hash during initial sync; structure, difficulty, and state transitions still verify fully. Defensible because any invalid old block would have been rejected live at publication; sync drops from days to hours; opt-out exists (full replay).

drills.q: Walk through the March 2013 Bitcoin fork: cause, resolution, prevention.
drills.a: Cause: v0.8 LevelDB accepted a block v0.7 BerkeleyDB rejected (lock limits) -> two valid chains ~6h. Resolution: social - major pools downgraded to v0.7 chain, orphaning ~24 blocks incl one double-spend. Prevention: cross-implementation consensus test vectors, staged activation windows, fork-detection alarms shipped in clients.

drills.q: Explain Ethereum's post-merge fork choice and finality to a backend engineer using ACID analogies.
drills.a: attn-GHOST picks head by attestation weight (latest messages); Casper FFG justifies checkpoints at 2/3 stake and finalizes on second justification (~2 epochs). latest=dirty read, safe=read-committed-ish, finalized=committed transaction no one can roll back without >=1/3 stake being slashed.

drills.q: Your CTO wants a private L1 for supplier tracking. Give the honest counter-case.
drills.a: No token means no security budget, so either one party runs everything (database with extra steps) or goodwill secures it (historically collapses: we.trade shut 2022, TradeLens wound down early 2023). Tamper-evidence without replication is trivially rewritten by the operator. Alternatives: append-only log + periodic anchoring to a public chain, or a rollup if multi-party neutrality is genuinely needed.

drills.q: Estimate the cost of a 1-hour 51% attack on Bitcoin vs ETC circa 2020 and explain the asymmetry.
drills.a: BTC: network hashrate ~700-900 EH/s of dedicated SHA-256 ASICs - not rentable on markets; attack requires billions in capex or covert pool corruption = state-level project. ETC 2020: ~250 GH/s class network where $10-50k/day of rented hashrate produced four successful reorgs (3.4k-5.3k blocks). Asymmetry = absolute hashrate + hardware specificity + rental market depth.

drills.q: Why 3f+1 replicas for f Byzantine faults? Show the quorum-intersection argument.
drills.a: Quorums of size 2f+1 among N=3f+1: any two intersect in >=2(2f+1)-3f+1... compute: |A n B| = |A|+|B|-N = (4f+2)-(3f+1) = f+1, so at least one HONEST node sits in both. Two conflicting commits would each need an honest member to sign both - impossible.

drills.q: Name all three Ethereum slashing conditions and the penalty curve.
drills.a: 1) Double proposal: two headers signed for same slot. 2) Double vote: conflicting attestations for same target epoch. 3) Surround vote: attestations with illegally nested source/target ranges. Penalty: initial slash 1/32 of effective balance (<=1 ETH), then correlation penalty ~min(3 * fraction_slashed_within_4096_epochs, 1) * balance - solo ~1 ETH, coordinated mass events -> total loss.

drills.q: What is weak subjectivity and why must PoS accept it?
drills.a: New/returning nodes cannot distinguish canonical chain from an attacker's long-range fabricated history (no cumulative work metric exists). Mitigation: trust a recent state root from the live network. Accepted because fabricating requires majority stake colluding publicly and self-slashing.

drills.q: Compare PBFT vs HotStuff on message complexity and why it mattered for production chains.
drills.a: PBFT: every replica broadcasts to everyone, O(n^2) per phase, quadratic view-change - dead beyond ~100 validators. HotStuff: votes go only to leader who aggregates threshold-signed QCs, O(n) per view, linear view change, pipelined 3-chain commit. This is what let Diem/Aptos/Sui-class chains run hundreds of validators at sub-second finality.

drills.q: Finality stalls but blocks keep being produced on Ethereum. What happened in May 2023 and how do you monitor for it?
drills.a: Client bugs (Prysm, then Teku) split attestation weights so no checkpoint reached 2/3 - finality froze ~25 min and again ~60+ min while blocks continued. Monitor justification-gap alarms (epochs since last finality), not block height; prevent via client diversity targets (no client >1/3 of stake).

drills.q: Explain the inactivity leak and its CAP-style tradeoff.
drills.a: If >1/3 of stake is offline >4 epochs, finality can never resume; leak drains offline balances quadratically until online remainder holds 2/3 and finalizes. Chooses availability over frozen consistency, paid by the absent minority. Rejoining side syncs forward; no reconciliation with its stale history.

drills.q: Design consensus for 12 banks settling tokenized deposits. Pick the family and defend against 'just use a database'.
drills.a: BFT family (HotStuff/QBFT/Tendermint lineage): bounded known membership, N=13 tolerates f=3, second-level deterministic finality fits settlement, no token needed (legal/reputational bonds substitute). Database wins if settlement truth never leaves one operator; blockchain earns its seat when counterparties need shared verifiable settlement without a designated operator.

drills.q: An L2 advertises soft confirmations in 200 ms. Decompose what that guarantee actually is.
drills.a: One operator's local ordering promise - not consensus. Ladder: soft confirm (sequencer) -> batch posted to L1 blobs (data available, reorderable until finality) -> L1 finalization (~12.8 min). Risks: sequencer equivocation, forced-inclusion delays. Use for UX; gate irreversible actions on finalized state or priced preconfirmation markets.

drills.q: Why does BLS aggregation matter more than TPS for Ethereum's architecture?
drills.a: ~10^6 validator units cannot broadcast individual signatures: committees attest per slot and BLS collapses thousands of sigs into one ~96-byte aggregate, making GHOST weighting by millions of votes and FFG checkpoints fit home-node bandwidth. Costs: slower verification than ECDSA, rogue-key defenses needed (deposit proofs-of-possession).

drills.q: Quantify Bitcoin's daily security budget and name its structural fragility.
drills.a: Subsidy 3.125 BTC/block post-April-2024 halving ~450 BTC/day plus fees; miners recoup via hardware+energy so attack means outbidding that flow or buying majority ASIC capacity unavailable on rental markets. Fragility: subsidy halves every 4 years while fee share remains volatile - long-run fee-only security is unresolved.

drills.q: Where do rollups sit in the trilemma? State precisely what they rent.
drills.a: They rent decentralization+security from L1 (data availability via blobs, settlement) and buy scalability through compressed execution off-chain; their own sequencer is currently centralized - the honest weak point until shared/decentralized sequencing ships. Trilemma relocated, not solved: L1 blob bandwidth is the global bottleneck.

drills.q: Here is a withdraw() with an external call before the balance deduction. Fix it two ways and rank them.
drills.a: Reentrancy. Fix A: checks-effects-interactions - zero balance BEFORE call, re-entry fails its own check. Fix B: OpenZeppelin nonReentrant mutex. A is primary (covers cross-function variants a per-fn mutex misses); B layered on critical paths.

drills.q: Give an ERC-721 cross-contract reentrancy scenario.
drills.a: _safeMint calls onERC721Received - attacker code runs mid-flow. If minting logic updates accounting AFTER the transfer, attacker reenters via the hook at the inconsistent moment. Defense: finalize all state before ANY token movement; treat every token transfer as potential code execution.

drills.q: What is read-only reentrancy? Name the incident class.
drills.a: View functions report inconsistent state during callbacks: attacker triggers pool X's update, and inside X's callback calls victim V which reads X's view (get_virtual_price) against stale values. Curve pools 2021-23 patched by locking views themselves. Views consumed by other protocols are attack surface.

drills.q: End-to-end: manipulate an AMM spot oracle, then defend it. Include the TWAP caveat.
drills.a: Attack: flash-borrow token B, swap into target pool (constant product: price moves quadratically), protocol lends against inflated collateral, unwind, repay, keep profit - cost = two swaps' fees. Defend: never settle vs own-pool spot; Chainlink deviation ~0.5% + heartbeat staleness; Uniswap V3 TWAP >=30min; caps + breakers. Caveat: ONE manipulated block shifts 30-min TWAP ~+66% - TWAP raises cost, doesn't eliminate.

drills.q: Reconstruct Mango Markets $110M mechanically.
drills.a: Oct 11 2022: build long on MNGO perps, pump thin MNGO spot books ~10x in minutes, inflated mark price = huge unrealized PnL usable as collateral, borrow $110M USDC, walk away. Perpetrator convicted April 2024. Preventers: multi-venue median marks, price-band breakers, borrow caps, near-zero collateral factors for illiquid assets.

drills.q: Why did Euler lose $197M despite four audits? What does it teach?
drills.a: March 2023: donation/convertible sub-account interaction - economic composition no reviewer modeled; audits verify specified behavior vs known patterns, not novel compositional economics. Nearly all funds returned via whitehat negotiation - audit failure AND response success simultaneously. Lesson: audits are one input among fuzzing/formal/monitoring/response.

drills.q: Beanstalk $182M: mechanics and the design lesson.
drills.a: April 17 2022: flash-loaned ~$1B, acquired 67% governance weight in ONE block, voted treasury transfer to self, executed, repaid loan - netted $182M in seconds. Lesson: temporally-naive voting is attack surface; add snapshots/multi-block voting, decouple thresholds from transferable tokens.

drills.q: Curve/Vyper July 2023: what actually failed and what's the meta-lesson?
drills.a: Vyper compiler versions 0.2.15/0.3.0 silently disabled @nonreentrant guards - battle-tested pools drained (~$70M) despite clean audit history. Meta: 'dead' bug classes resurrect through toolchain regressions; pin compilers, diff bytecode against source expectations, monitor guard presence.

drills.q: Design the monitoring + response stack for a live lending protocol.
drills.a: Detect: Forta/Tenderly alerts (TVL drop %, utilization spikes, oracle deviation), balance-diff watchers, simulate pending governance proposals. Respond: pause authority matrix (responsive multisig, rehearsed), automated circuit breakers on oracle deviation, standing whitehat channels, Immunefi bounty ($10M-class). Measure time-to-pause as SLO - it bounds loss once prevention fails.

drills.q: Chainlink integration checklist: which checks are mandatory, what remains risky?
drills.a: latestRoundData staleness vs heartbeat (e.g., 1h majors), answeredInRound sanity, price>0, L2 sequencer uptime feed, deviation-from-last bounds. Remains: feed-wide compromise/halt, missing feeds forcing synthetics, L2 latency windows. Mitigate: median across INDEPENDENT providers (correlation!), manual emergency feed behind timelock, treat silence as halt.

drills.q: Are flash loans a vulnerability? Argue precisely.
drills.a: No - amplifier. Atomic (repay or revert), adds unbounded temporary capital: capital-gated attacks (manipulation, governance capture) drop to tx fees. Weaponizes existing flaws: manipulable oracles, instant-finality governance, mispriced collateral. Fix underlying designs; assume free temporary capital in threat models.

drills.q: Whiteboard ECDSA sign+verify over secp256k1 from memory, then identify the single step whose failure compromises the key.
drills.a: Sign: z=H(m); R=kG; r=x_R mod n; s=k^-1(z+r d) mod n. Verify: w=s^-1; X=zwG+rwQ; check x_X==r mod n. Failure point: nonce k generation - reuse leaks d via k=(z1-z2)(s1-s2)^-1.

drills.q: Compute the Merkle proof size for a block with 4096 transactions and state how many hashes verification costs.
drills.a: log2(4096)=12 levels; proof = 12 sibling hashes = 384 bytes; verification = 12 SHA-256 compressions. Root stored in the 80-byte header commits to all txs.

drills.q: An attacker shows you two documents with identical MD5. Which hash property failed and roughly how much work was that in 2012 vs today?
drills.a: Collision resistance. Chosen-prefix MD5 collisions were practical from ~2008 (rogue CA 2008-2012 era, minutes-to-hours on clusters). For SHA-256 the same attack is ~2^128 - infeasible.

drills.q: Your API authenticates requests with SHA256(secret_key || body). What breaks and what do you ship instead?
drills.a: Length extension: digest reveals internal state so suffixes can be appended and re-hashed without the key. Ship HMAC-SHA256 (nested keyed construction) or truncate-with-care alternatives like KMAC/SipHash.

drills.q: Implement RFC 6979 in one paragraph: inputs, primitive, loop structure.
drills.a: Inputs: private scalar x (32-byte BE) and digest h1 reduced mod n. V=0x01*32, K=0x00*32; K=HMAC(K,V||0x00||x||h1); V=HMAC(K,V); K=HMAC(K,V||0x01||x||h1); V=HMAC(K,V); loop: V=HMAC(K,V); candidate=int(V); if 1<=candidate<n use it else K=HMAC(K,V||0x00), V=HMAC(K,V). Deterministic k from (key,message): RNG failures stop being catastrophic.

drills.q: A mempool watcher reports your confirmed transaction's hash changing while sender/signature stay constant. Diagnose.
drills.a: Signature malleability: attacker rebroadcast (r, n-s) which verifies identically but has a different txid. Fix at protocol level: low-s enforcement (EIP-2, BIP-62); at app level track by intent (nonce/sender) not raw txid.

drills.q: Design tamper-evidence for a 500 GB audit log where auditors occasionally challenge one record. Full blockchain, or something else?
drills.a: Merkle tree over log chunks + externally anchored root (CT-log style or periodic chain anchoring). Challenge served as a 25-hash branch (~800 bytes). Running a blockchain adds consensus you don't need - one honest party holding roots plus append-only storage suffices.

drills.q: Explain why a naive binary Merkle tree without leaf/node prefixes admits a forged proof, concretely.
drills.a: Internal node value H(A||B) is just bytes; craft a fake 'leaf' whose content equals those bytes. Now present the shorter proof path for the fake leaf - verifier cannot distinguish leaf-level from node-level hashing without domain separation (RFC 6962 prefixes 0x00/0x01).

drills.q: Your team wants BLS aggregation everywhere. Give two reasons to push back.
drills.a: Verification is ~5-10x ECDSA cost per signature, hurting high-throughput single-sig paths; aggregation needs distinct-message discipline or proofs-of-possession to prevent rogue-key attacks; ecosystem/hardware support is ECDSA-centric. Use BLS where aggregation pays (consensus committees), not universally.

drills.q: Quantum adversary timeline: rank primitives here by urgency and justify with numbers.
drills.a: 1) ECDSA/Schnorr/BLS keys: Shor breaks them in poly time - existential. 2) SHA-256: Grover halves exponent, preimage ~2^128 - safe indefinitely for practical purposes. Migration pain: ML-DSA sigs ~2.4-4.6 KB vs 64 B; lost keys (dead wallets) cannot be rotated, so quantum raid of unmovable coins remains unsolved.

drills.q: Run the decision tree on 'blockchain supply-chain traceability' vendor pitch.
drills.a: Who writes? If one company owns the system of record -> database+API. Suppliers verifying without trusting you -> public hash anchoring (read-only verification needs no shared ledger). Multiple distrusting writers with no acceptable operator AND neutral execution needed -> public chain first, permissioned second. Then price integration + key mgmt + year-ten funding.

drills.q: Why did TradeLens fail despite Maersk scale and IBM backing?
drills.a: Competitors wouldn't route critical workflows through rival-influenceable infrastructure; adoption stayed thin beyond Maersk while IBM carried costs. Benefits never beat EDI+email because the trust problem was smaller than assumed - DCSA standards took the messaging role. Wound down late 2022 into early 2023.

drills.q: ASX CHESS DLT cancellation (~A$250M): the transferable lesson?
drills.a: ASX kept itself as SINGLE operator so decentralization was decorative while adding novel failure modes and years of delay. When the operator is trusted by construction (licensed market utility), DLT buys nothing - honest project is boring modernization. Cancelled Nov 2022. Evaluate architecture-category fit BEFORE technology.

drills.q: GDPR vs immutable ledger: design patterns that reconcile them.
drills.a: PII never on-chain - hashed personal data is still personal data (EDPB). Patterns: PII off-chain in erasable storage with commitments/references on-chain; crypto-shredding = client-side encryption + key destruction for erasure. Design erasure pre-launch; retrofitting immutability is impossible by definition.

drills.q: When is permissioned chain genuinely right over public? Preconditions.
drills.a: All must hold: bounded identified membership (regulated institutions); validator funding committed long-term; confidentiality beyond what public+ZK offers today; regulatory constraints on public settlement. Kinexys fits (known banks, funded infra, ~$2B/day interbank deposits). Otherwise public L1/L2 + compliance wrappers wins.

drills.q: Why did stablecoins succeed where trade-finance consortia died?
drills.a: Stablecoins serve strangers globally with 24/7 neutrality: holders needn't trust a consortium, just regulated issuers (GENIUS Act reserves, July 2025). Organic demand (dollar access, settlement speed), self-onboarding wallets, no competitor-cooperation requirement. Consortia inverted incentives: rivals funding shared infra for marginal gains.

drills.q: Design the compliance stack for a tokenized fund on public chains.
drills.a: Transfer restrictions in token contract enforced between allowlisted KYC'd wallets (transfer agent), continuous sanctions re-screening, travel-rule data off-chain, freeze/recover roles for court orders held by regulated parties, chain-analytics surveillance hooks. BUIDL shape: SEC-registered wrapper + permissioned transfers + public settlement. Tradeoff admitted: composability shrinks to approved venues.

drills.q: Auditors want tamper-evident internal trade logs. Blockchain? Design the alternative.
drills.a: No: append-only DB with hash chaining, Merkle roots published daily to EXTERNAL anchors (public-chain tx, notary API) - CT-log generalized. Auditors verify any entry against any day's root without trusting your storage; retroactive edits break all future proofs. Doesn't cover: counterparties WRITING shared state, or you colluding with the anchor at publication time (cross-anchor to two points).

drills.q: Leadership wants 'a blockchain strategy'. What do you deliver instead?
drills.a: Decision memo: use-cases run through the tree (most die Q1/Q2), 1-2 narrow pilots with measured ROI (stablecoin vendor payments FX savings; anchored audit logs for one regulator flow), explicit non-goals, cost envelope including key management, kill-criteria per pilot. Options with prices, not platform choices - reframes blocker as architect.

drills.q: Why do optimistic rollups use a ~7-day challenge window, and what actually enforces it?
drills.a: Window = max time for an honest verifier to detect fraud and litigate the dispute game down to one on-chain-executed instruction. Enforcement: L1 bridge refuses finalization until expiry; any challenger can slash via valid fraud proof; Arbitrum BoLD (Feb 2025) made challenging permissionless.

drills.q: Contrast 1-of-N honest vs 0-of-N trust assumptions across optimistic and ZK rollups.
drills.a: Optimistic: safety holds if at least ONE honest party watches every assertion and challenges in-window - liveness is social/economic. ZK: zero watchers needed - validity proofs verified mechanically by L1 math; invalid transitions cannot finalize even with universal operator collusion. ZK pays prover costs upfront for this.

drills.q: Walk through a bisection-based fraud proof resolution.
drills.a: Challenger disputes post-batch root; both submit intermediate roots at successive halves of execution until they disagree about exactly ONE step; on-chain mini-interpreter re-executes that single step and declares winner; loser's bond pays challenger. Total L1 work O(log steps) - that amortization is what makes optimism cheap.

drills.q: Lay out Vitalik's zkEVM type taxonomy with tradeoffs.
drills.a: Type 1: full Ethereum-equivalence (verifies L1 itself) - slowest proving. Type 2: EVM-equivalence (Scroll/Taiko class). Type 2.5: gas tweaks for proving ease. Type 3: some precompiles removed. Type 4: language-level compile to zk-IR (zkSync Era) - fastest proofs, bytecode-level tooling breaks. Compatibility falls as prover cost falls.

drills.q: What did blobs change for rollup economics, and what does pruning mean?
drills.a: Dencun (3/13/2024): dedicated blob market - ~128 KiB each, own fee curve, pruned after ~4096 epochs (~18 days). L2 fees fell roughly an order of magnitude overnight. Pruning = consensus guarantees availability only through the settlement/challenge window; long-term archival shifts to rollups/indexers by design.

drills.q: Blob supply trajectory: targets/maxes from Dencun through BPO2.
drills.a: Dencun 3/6 (3/2024); Pectra 6/9 (5/7/2025); Fusaka PeerDAS (12/3/2025) then BPO1 10/15 (12/9/2025), BPO2 14/21 (1/7/2026). PeerDAS: erasure-code into 128 columns + sampling gives ~8x headroom toward 48 blobs without per-node load growth.

drills.q: Rank Ronin, Wormhole, Nomad by root cause and name each design lesson.
drills.a: Ronin $624M (3/2022): 5-of-9 validator keys phished by Lazarus - committees are key-management problems. Wormhole $325M (2/2022): deprecated sig-verification path accepted forged guardian signatures - where signatures ARE trust, sig bugs are fatal; Jump recapitalized. Nomad $190M (8/2022): initialization let zero proofs validate - copy-paste free-for-all; lesson: adversarial init vectors. All: 2022 saw $2B+ across 13 bridges.

drills.q: Design a bridge between two EVM chains you don't control.
drills.a: Light-client contracts verifying other chain's consensus (headers or ZK-proven consensus attestations), message passing with Merkle inclusion proofs against posted roots, replay nonces, per-asset rate limits with anomaly throttling, governance timelock for client updates separate from pauser multisig, monitoring on mint events. Never: small attestation committees above insured value.

drills.q: Sequencer goes down for two hours on your L2. What happens to funds and why isn't it catastrophic?
drills.a: UX freezes; funds don't move - sequencing controls ordering, not custody. Users retain forced-inclusion via L1 inbox; withdrawals resume when sequencer returns or via escape hatches. Real risks are fairness: MEV extraction, soft censorship. Real fixes: hardened forced inclusion, shared sequencers (Espresso), based rollups.

drills.q: CTO asks: general rollup vs app-specific rollup vs appchain. Give the decision tree.
drills.a: General-purpose (Base/Arbitrum) if composability with liquidity matters and ops burden must stay low. App-rollup (Orbit/CDK/zkStack) if custom fee tokens, dedicated blockspace, sovereignty over upgrades, and infra staffing exist. Appchain only with consensus-level needs AND token-funded security. Always price: liquidity fragmentation, bridge exposure, stage/decentralization compliance.

drills.q: Validium vs rollup for a high-value exchange product? Justify.
drills.a: Exchange already holds custody keys, so validium's committee adds marginal trust risk while cutting DA costs dramatically - defensible internally. For anything market-facing: default full rollup; committee withholding freezes assets (availability risk), fatal for leveraged positions. Volitions allow per-account choice.

drills.q: Explain how PeerDAS sampling preserves security as blob count scales.
drills.a: Each blob erasure-coded into 128 columns; nodes custody a subset (scaled by validator count) and randomly sample others. k successful samples imply >=50% data exists with overwhelming probability -> full reconstruction possible. Per-node verification stays constant while network capacity grows toward 48 blobs; new failure surface = custodial coverage during correlated churn.

drills.q: Explain CALL vs DELEGATECALL vs STATICCALL: what changes, what persists?
drills.a: CALL: callee context - their storage, msg.sender becomes calling contract. DELEGATECALL: caller's storage + preserved msg.sender/value, foreign code only - the proxy primitive and the most dangerous opcode. STATICCALL (Byzantium): read-only frame, reverts on state writes.

drills.q: Where does uint128 a; uint64 b; uint64 c; uint256 d; land in storage? Gas implication of writing all four?
drills.a: a+b+c pack into slot 0 (16+8+8=32 bytes), d takes slot 1. Writing the packed trio = up to one SSTORE on slot 0 vs three separate 20k/2.9k writes unpacked. But reads pay per slot touched - keep hot fields with hot fields.

drills.q: Why does a naive proxy store its implementation pointer at keccak(...)-1 instead of slot 0 or 1?
drills.a: EIP-1967: pseudo-random slots like keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation')-1 (0x360894...) can never collide with realistically declared Solidity variables which occupy low sequential slots. Early structured-storage proxies collided exactly this way.

drills.q: Cost math: event vs storage for recording a transfer. When must you use storage anyway?
drills.a: Event: ~375 base + 375/topic + 8/byte ~ 1.3k gas typical Transfer; storage fresh write 20000, update 2900. Events are OFF-CHAIN only - no contract can read past receipts - so any value logic branches on must live in storage.

drills.q: Walk through msg.sender across user -> proxy -> implementation -> external token call.
drills.a: EOA->proxy: EOA. Proxy->impl via delegatecall: still EOA (context preserved). Impl->token via CALL: token sees proxy address, not EOA - hence approve/transferFrom dances and ERC-2771 meta-tx sender-forwarding patterns; tx.origin auth breaks here.

drills.q: Reconstruct the Parity multisig disaster precisely and name today's defenses.
drills.a: Shared wallet LIBRARY had public default-initializable functions: July 2017 attacker took ownership via init; Nov 2017 someone triggered its suicide(), freezing 513k ETH (~$150M then) in dependent wallets forever. Today: initializer modifiers, pre-initialized/disabled-initializer deployments, owned bases, no shared mutable libraries.

drills.q: UUPS vs transparent proxy - pick one for a new protocol and defend against UUPS's main failure.
drills.a: UUPS default: cheaper minimal proxy, atomic upgradeToAndCall. Main failure = bricking (bad impl consumes last chance) - mitigate with fork-tested upgrades, authorization guards on upgrade fns, deploying implementations pre-initialized, emergency pause. Transparent costs per-call gas but keeps upgrades in simpler proxy code.

drills.q: Design initialization for an upgradeable system with modules and roles.
drills.a: Single initialize() with initializer guard, reinitializer versions per module; deploy impls pre-initialized; wire admin/upgrader/pauser roles during init then transfer LAST to Safe+timelock to avoid front-run windows; verify post-init storage on a mainnet fork. Atomic init via upgradeToAndCall closes interim-state attacks.

drills.q: Diamond selector clash: how does it manifest and how do you catch it before mainnet?
drills.a: Two facets claim one selector; proxy routes silently to the winner - wrong auth/storage assumptions, fund-loss shapes; crafted collisions were exploited deliberately. Catch: CI asserting global selector uniqueness across facets, diamondCut rejecting duplicates, loupe introspection tests.

drills.q: Should this system be upgradeable at all? Give the decision procedure.
drills.a: Enumerate change classes expected (bugfix/parameter/logic); threat-model the admin path (key compromise = total loss?); check trust constraints (immutable sells neutrality); define exits (migration contracts, pausable bridges). Immutable if setters suffice; upgradeable only if iteration is certain AND governance credible (multisig + 1-7d timelock + monitoring). Immutables die with bugs; upgradables die with keys.

drills.q: Compute Grover's optimal iteration count and success probability for N=64, M=1.
drills.a: theta = arcsin(1/8) ~ 0.1253 rad; k ~ pi*8/4 = 6 iterations (floor/round); success = sin^2(13*theta) ~ 0.9995. Formula: k ~ (pi/4)sqrt(N).

drills.q: Why does DJ need the ancilla in |-> rather than |0>?
drills.a: U_f XORs f(x) into |y>. With y=|->, X|-> = -|->, so the XOR becomes a phase (-1)^f(x) on the control register (kickback) without collapsing anything; with |0> you'd just entangle data with ancilla bits and lose the interference pattern.

drills.q: A colleague claims a 2026 hardware demo 'ran Shor'. What follow-ups separate honest claim from hype?
drills.a: Ask: what N was factored (15? 21?), was the period hard-coded or compiled away, logical or physical qubits, error mitigation used. Full Shor for real keys needs millions of physical qubits in fault-tolerant mode; demos verify compilers/control, not threat.

drills.q: Give the two-line business answer to 'when do we need PQC done by?'.
drills.a: 1) Data confidentiality horizon > ~2033 means encrypt with PQC now because of harvest-now-decrypt-later. 2) Signatures/certificates can migrate later but inventory and vendor pressure should start immediately since enterprise migrations take 2-5 years against CNSA-2.0/NIST timelines of 2027-2035.

drills.q: Why is there no Grover-style win to be had over a B-tree index lookup?
drills.a: Grover needs black-box oracle access and unstructured search; an index exploits structure to answer in O(log n) comparisons already, beating sqrt(N) asymptotically, and quantum memory access costs would erase constants. Quantum search only wins when nothing better than linear scan exists classically.

drills.q: In Shor, why measure register 2 at all before the QFT?
drills.a: Measuring g^x mod N collapses register 1 onto {x : g^x = c}, i.e., an exact arithmetic progression with spacing r - which is what the QFT reads out. Skipping it works too (the QFT acts on both registers), but measuring is simpler and loses nothing: the progression structure is identical.

drills.q: Your Grover demo on hardware returns near-uniform counts. Three diagnosis steps?
drills.a: 1) Check post-transpile depth vs coherence budget (oracle Toffolis inflate depth). 2) Verify iteration count matches M and N (wrong k overshoots back down toward uniform). 3) Inspect qubit ordering/oracle sign conventions between simulator and ISA.

drills.q: Rank speedup quality: DJ (exponential query), Grover (quadratic), Shor (exponential structural). Which transfers to practice and why?
drills.a: Shor transfers: exponential AND applies to real deployed cryptanalysis (RSA/ECC) since inputs are natural numbers, not promised oracles. DJ's exponential is promise-artificial; Grover is real but quadratic and mostly eaten by fault-tolerance constants outside crypto. Structure beats raw exponent when inputs are natural.

drills.q: State the continued-fraction step precisely enough to implement.
drills.a: From measured c/Q with gcd(c,Q)=1, expand c/Q as continued fractions; take convergents k'/r' with r' < N; test each r' via g^{r'} == 1 mod N; first hit gives order r. Success needs gcd(k,r)=1 which happens with probability phi(r)/r.

drills.q: What single sentence kills 'quantum breaks all encryption' panic in a design review?
drills.a: Shor breaks public-key (RSA/ECC) but Grover only halves symmetric strength, so AES-256 + SHA-384 survive while key exchange and signatures migrate to ML-KEM/ML-DSA per FIPS 203/204.

drills.q: Compute success probability of a depth-800 circuit at two-qubit error 1e-3.
drills.a: exp(-800 * 1e-3) = exp(-0.8) ~ 0.45. Rule of thumb: every ~1000 two-qubit gates at p2=1e-3 costs e-fold (~37% survival).

drills.q: 3-qubit repetition code: what does the syndrome (s01=True, s12=False) tell you?
drills.a: Qubits 0 and 1 disagree, qubits 1 and 2 agree -> qubit 0 flipped. Apply X on qubit 0. Syndrome pairs localize a single X error exactly.

drills.q: Why can't the naive 'is state still in code space' check detect triple errors in the repetition code?
drills.a: XXX maps |000> to |111> and |111> to |000>: a permutation of codewords. The state stays in code space while carrying wrong amplitudes; only amplitude overlap against the original detects it.

drills.q: Estimate physical qubits for one logical qubit at target logical error 1e-9 with p=1e-3 (surface code).
drills.a: Need 0.1^((d+1)/2) <= 1e-8 -> (d+1)/2 >= 8 -> d >= 15 (use 17 for margin). Qubits ~ 2d^2: d=17 -> 578 physical/logical.

drills.q: Two vendors claim logical qubits: A says 50 @ 2:1 encoding, B says 200 logical planned on ~10k+ physical. Which question separates them?
drills.a: What logical operations run fault-tolerantly and at what magic-state/routing cost? Memory-level encoding (A) is cheap; algorithm-capable logical machines need gate sets + factories + routing (B). Demand Lambda and decoder latency too.

drills.q: Your decoder p99 latency exceeds the 1us stabiliser round under load. Consequences and mitigations?
drills.a: Backlog stalls rounds or forces drops - both convert directly into logical error since idle/lost cycles accumulate memory errors. Mitigate: bounded-latency decoders (union-find), FPGA offload, admission control that pauses rounds before overflow.

drills.q: Explain why halving physical error p saves roughly 4x qubits at fixed target logical error.
drills.a: eps_L ~ (100p)^((d+1)/2): halving p moves you one full exponent step down per distance unit... concretely log(eps)/log(100p) shrinks by ~1, so required (d+1)/2 drops by ~1, i.e., d by 2, and cost 2d^2 falls by factor ~(d/(d-2))^2 ~ 4x near d~25.

drills.q: Why do trapped-ion platforms favour different codes than superconducting?
drills.a: Ions have all-to-all connectivity and slow gates (~300us) vs superconducting nearest-neighbour fast (~50ns). High-rate small-block codes exploiting connectivity suit ions; planar surface codes suit superconducting layout constraints despite overhead.

drills.q: Connect QEC progress to PQC migration urgency in two sentences.
drills.a: RSA-2048 estimates (20M qubits / 8h) are QEC-overhead arithmetic: below-threshold operation plus ~1000:1 encoding plus magic factories. Each fidelity or code improvement compresses that multiplier, so migration deadlines hedge against QEC engineering accelerating, not just hardware scaling.

drills.q: Willow showed logical lifetime beating best physical qubit ~5x. Why did that matter commercially?
drills.a: It converts threshold theory into demonstrated engineering: memory persists longer encoded than raw, meaning added qubits now buy reliability instead of noise. Every roadmap qubit-count estimate assumes exactly this regime; it was the first direct superconducting proof.

drills.q: Write the 4x4 matrix for CNOT(0->1) and state its action on |01>.
Show S^4 = I but T^8 = -I... wait: compute T^8.
drills.a: T = diag(1, e^{i pi/4}), so T^8 = diag(1, e^{i 2 pi}) = I up to global phase exactly I. The point: T has order 8 as a phase gate; combined with H it generates a dense (infinite) group, unlike S whose Clifford group is finite.

drills.q: A colleague writes circuit 'X then Z' as U = X . Z applied left-to-right. What is wrong and what does the state become from |+>?
drills.a: Matrix application is right-to-left: U = Z first then X if drawn X,Z. From |+>: Z|+> = |-> , X|-> = -|->. Order matters only when both gates act on the same wire and do not commute; X and Z anti-commute so order changes global sign here (unobservable), but in general it changes the result.

drills.q: Why must ancillas holding garbage be uncomputed before the rest of an algorithm?
drills.a: Un-uncomputed ancillas remain entangled with data; acting on data alone then operates on a mixed reduced density matrix, destroying interference. Bennett's trick computes-then-uncomputes so scratch returns to |0> at zero coherence cost.

drills.q: Estimate physical cost of one CNOT between qubits 5 apart on a heavy-hex device with p2 = 1e-3.
drills.a: Routing needs ~2 SWAPs per edge-distance beyond 1: distance 5 => 4 edges => ~3 SWAPs x 3 CNOTs = 9 routing CNOTs + target CNOT ~10 two-qubit gates; success factor exp(-10 * 1e-3) ~ 0.99 for that operation alone; depth compounds across the whole circuit.

drills.q: Give a concrete reason optimization_level=3 could change your results vs level=0 even with identical math.
drills.a: L3 resynthesises blocks and reorders commuting gates; floating-point rotation merges introduce tiny numerical differences, layout remapping changes which physical qubits' calibration errors you hit, and seed-dependent search picks different but equivalent decompositions. Always compare count_ops/depth and set seed_transpiler.

drills.q: Is {H, T, CNOT} still universal if you drop CNOT? Justify.
drills.a: No: single-qubit gates alone cannot entangle; products stay product states across wires. Universality for all n-qubit unitaries needs an entangling gate; any entangling gate plus all single-qubit rotations suffices (Brylinski theorem).

drills.q: Implement controlled-Ry(theta) using one CNOT plus single-qubit gates.
drills.a: Decompose Ry(theta) = Rz(pi/2)... standard construction: CRy(theta) = A . CNOT . A^-1 with A chosen so A^-1 D A = Ry: concretely CRy = Ry(theta/2) on target unconditionally, CNOT(control,target), Ry(-theta/2) on target, CNOT again. Two CNOTs or optimised to fewer via phase tricks.

drills.q: Your stabiliser-heavy QEC syndrome circuit runs slowly on a statevector simulator. Fix?
drills.a: Switch simulation method: Clifford-only circuits are polynomial under Gottesman-Knill. Use Aer method='stabilizer' or Stim; thousands of qubits become tractable versus 30-ish for statevector.

drills.q: Rank by fault-tolerant cost: one extra CNOT, one extra T gate, one extra ancilla prepared in |0>, one extra measurement.
drills.a: Typically: T gate most expensive (magic-state distillation factory throughput), CNOT cheap-transversal in surface code but costs depth, ancilla |0> preparation near-free locally, measurement cheap transversally. Exact ranking depends on architecture; T dominates footprint.

drills.q: Name what Shor breaks and the one-line why.
drills.a: RSA (factoring), DH/ECDH and ECDSA/EdDSA (discrete log in abelian groups): all reduce to abelian hidden-subgroup problems that the QFT solves in poly time. Symmetric crypto untouched by Shor; Grover only halves it.

drills.q: Effective security of AES-256 under Grover, and the policy consequence?
drills.a: ~2^128 quantum operations: still safe. Consequence: standardize on AES-256 (and SHA-384 for long-lived hashes); do not replace symmetric primitives during PQC migration.

drills.q: Your nginx edge enables X25519MLKEM768 and handshake failures spike. Two likely causes?
drills.a: 1) Middleboxes/load balancers rejecting larger ClientHello (~2KB bigger). 2) Clients without hybrid group support hitting bad negotiation ordering. Fix LB firmware, keep X25519 ordered last as fallback, watch rollout telemetry.

drills.q: JWT auth uses RS256. What are your two realistic PQC paths?
drills.a: 1) Move to ML-DSA JOSE when supported end-to-end, accepting ~3.3KB signatures per token. 2) Refactor to opaque short-lived access tokens + introspection, signing only at issuance - shrinks signed surface and makes future rotations config-level.

drills.q: Why does SLH-DSA suit root CAs but not per-request API signing?
drills.a: Hash-based signatures reduce to conservative hash assumptions but cost 7-49KB per signature with slow hash-tree signing (hundreds/sec class). Root-of-trust cadence absorbs this; request-path workloads need ML-DSA's smaller/faster signatures.

drills.q: A PM says 'we'll migrate when quantum computers actually exist'. Rebut in two sentences.
drills.a: Harvest-now-decrypt-later means traffic recorded today is already compromised against a mid-2030s CRQC, so confidentiality has a deadline independent of hardware arrival. Enterprise migration takes 3-7 years; starting at Q-day guarantees being too late.

drills.q: What three artifacts prove PQC readiness to a federal customer?
drills.a: FIPS 140-3 validated crypto modules (140-2 historical since Sep 2026), CNSA 2.0 conformance statement mapped to acquisition dates (Jan 2027+), and a published CBOM/migration roadmap with algorithm inventory and dated milestones.

drills.q: Explain the LWE problem in one sentence and why it resists Shor.
drills.a: Recover a secret from noisy linear equations mod q (b = As + e): no abelian group structure means no reduction to hidden-subgroup/period-finding, so Shor's machinery does not apply; best attacks remain exponential/subexponential classical-and-quantum.

drills.q: Rank migration order: external TLS KEM, internal mTLS KEM, code signing, root CA rotation. Justify.
drills.a: 1) External TLS (HNDL-exposed now), 2) internal mTLS (same threat, more control), 3) code signing (no retro risk but long verification lifetimes), 4) root CA rotation (slowest cascade, plan last but start planning first).

drills.q: What does 'crypto agility' require architecturally, learned from SIKE/Rainbow?
drills.a: Algorithm choice behind configuration not code, dual-stack capability tested regularly, rollback rehearsals - because competition-grade algorithms died overnight to classical math, so the next transition must be a swap, not archaeology.

drills.q: Write current-API Qiskit code to sample a Bell circuit at 1024 shots.
drills.a: qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1); qc.measure_all(); counts = StatevectorSampler(default_shots=1024, seed=42).run([qc]).result()[0].data.meas.get_counts() ~ {'00': 512, '11': 512}.

drills.q: You see counts {'00': 497, '11': 527} for a Bell circuit. Broken?
drills.a: No: sigma = sqrt(0.5*0.5/1024) ~ 1.6%, so +-16 counts is one sigma; deviation of 30 total is normal shot noise. Only systematic imbalance (e.g., '01' appearing) indicates real error.

drills.q: Estimator rejects your circuit. Why?
drills.a: Circuits passed to Estimator must not contain measurements; it appends basis rotations internally per observable term. Strip measure_all()/measure() before submission.

drills.q: A 60-qubit Clifford-only QEC syndrome circuit crawls on the default simulator. Fix and quantify.
drills.a: Switch to stabiliser method: AerSimulator(method='stabilizer') or Stim. Stabiliser runs in polynomial time (O(n^2)-ish per gate), handling thousands of qubits vs ~45 cap for exact statevector.

drills.q: Your variational loop does one sampler.run() per parameter candidate. Restructure.
drills.a: Batch all candidates into ONE run call as multiple PUBs (or one PUB with a parameter sweep list) inside a Session; result[i] maps back to candidate i. Round-trip/queue latency dominates otherwise - batching cuts wall-clock several-fold.

drills.q: Simulator matches theory but FakeSherbrooke noisy sim already diverges. What changed?
drills.a: The fake backend injects calibration-derived noise: per-edge CX errors ~1e-3, readout error, T1/T2 decoherence. Divergence means your depth x error budget is exhausted; reduce 2Q count via optimization_level=3 or restructure layout.

drills.q: Why pin qiskit versions per project even for tutorials?
drills.a: Annual major releases carry breaking changes by design (18-month support). Unpinned code hits removals like 2.0's execute()/V1 primitives and fails with AttributeError instead of DeprecationWarning.

drills.q: Design a fair A/B of two backends for your circuit.
drills.a: Same logical circuit + seeds; transpile per backend at L3; record post-transpile 2Q count/depth and edge fidelities used; equal shots sized for smallest resolved probability; same mitigation level; >=3 sessions across days; compare with confidence intervals, prefer the backend whose worst day wins.

drills.q: When is resilience_level=0 the RIGHT choice despite available mitigation?
drills.a: Benchmarking raw hardware honestly, short-depth circuits where gate error sits below the statistical floor you care about, and cost-constrained screening runs - mitigation adds bias-reduction at 2-10x shot cost and contaminates machine-characterisation experiments.

drills.q: Porting Cirq->Qiskit, GHZ results come out reversed. Root cause and permanent fix?
drills.a: Endianness: Cirq measurement keys big-endian, Qiskit bitstrings little-endian. Fix: convert once at boundaries with explicit index mapping; validate with an asymmetric known-answer state since symmetric states (Bell) hide the bug.

drills.q: Name the three families under the 'quantum ML' label and rank by evidence.
drills.a: 1) Quantum simulation (VQE): credible physics, gated on hardware. 2) QAOA optimisation: unproven, loses empirically to classical heuristics so far. 3) QML on classical data: weakest; no scaled advantage through 2026.

drills.q: Why is VQE's energy always an upper bound on the ground state?
drills.a: Rayleigh-Ritz: <psi|H|psi> >= E_min for any normalised psi, with equality iff psi is the ground state. Any ansatz state yields a valid upper bound; optimisation tightens it from above.

drills.q: Your VQE hardware energies sit consistently ABOVE simulator optimum. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Depolarising noise biases expectation values upward (mixed states raise <H> toward maximally-mixed average). Fixes: error mitigation (ZNE), shorter-depth ansatz, fake-backend pre-checks; cannot fully remove without correction.

drills.q: A vendor cites a quantum kernel paper beating SVMs. Give the three audit questions.
drills.a: Was the classical baseline tuned or defaults? Is data-encoding circuit depth counted end-to-end? Does the gap survive standard benchmarks at scale rather than curated splits? Published scaled advantages do not exist as of 2026.

drills.q: Why might barren plateaus spare chemistry-inspired ansaetze but kill random ones?
drills.a: UCCSD-style circuits stay near low-excitation manifolds with symmetry constraints, keeping gradient signal localised; random hardware-efficient circuits explore uniformly over Hilbert space where almost all directions are indistinguishable - variance collapses as O(1/2^n).

drills.q: QAOA approximation ratio degrades past p=5 on hardware but not in simulation. Diagnose.
drills.a: Hardware noise compounding with depth: each added layer adds two-qubit gates whose ~1e-3 errors outweigh marginal structure discovery. Verify via noiseless sim at same depths; mitigate with error mitigation/layout work or accept depth ceiling.

drills.q: Explain why data loading kills most QML speedup claims in one paragraph.
drills.a: Encoding N-dimensional classical data into amplitudes needs log2(N) qubits but ~N-depth state preparation without QRAM; angle encoding scales linearly with features but caps expressivity. Either way the loading step consumes the claimed advantage unless the data is natively quantum.

drills.q: What would constitute legitimate evidence of QML advantage that does not exist today?
drills.a: Peer-reviewed result beating TUNED classical baselines on a natural dataset, with encoding costs included in runtime, scaling demonstrated beyond toy widths, and access assumptions stated. Nothing published meets all four through mid-2026.

drills.q: Why is SPSA preferred over Adam for variational loops on noisy hardware?
drills.a: SPSA estimates gradients from just 2 total evaluations per step regardless of parameter count (simultaneous random perturbations); per-parameter methods need 2P evaluations whose shot noise dominates at P in the hundreds. SPSA averages noise efficiently across steps.

drills.q: Draft the two-line executive answer: should we fund quantum ML now?
drills.a: Fund quantum simulation research pilots only if we own hard chemistry/materials problems; treat optimisation/QML-on-data as watch-list items because no quantum model beats strong classical baselines today and credible wins are gated on post-2028 error-corrected hardware.

drills.q: Write the state vector of (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2) and give its Bloch coordinates.
drills.a: [1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2)]; theta = pi/2 (equator), phi = pi. This is H|1>, the |- > state; measuring in the Z basis gives 50/50, after H it gives 1 deterministically.

drills.q: Compute X applied to alpha|0>+beta|1>, and Ry(pi/2)|0>.
How much RAM to hold a 40-qubit state vector in complex128?
Apply CNOT(control=0,target=1) to |10>. Then explain why CNOT alone on |+-> cannot create entanglement from every input.
drills.a: |10> -> |11> (control is 1, target flips). CNOT is a permutation and maps product states like |+-> to entangled states (it does create entanglement there); but on computational-basis inputs it only permutes bits and never entangles - entangling power depends on the input basis.

drills.q: Is (|00>+|01>+|10>+|11>)/2 entangled? Justify without full algebra.
drills.a: No: it factors as H|0> (x) H|0>, each qubit independently 50/50. Spread over all four basis strings is not entanglement; failure to factorise is.

drills.q: A teammate says their simulator 'uses the 2^70 amplitudes of its 70 qubits to compute in parallel'. Give the two-line rebuttal.
drills.a: 1) You cannot read those amplitudes: one measurement returns one 70-bit sample via the Born rule. 2) Without an interference schedule (an algorithm) plus error rates low enough to survive it, the amplitude space is unreachable structure, not usable memory.

drills.q: Given counts {'010': 498, '110': 502} from a 3-qubit circuit, which qubits are entangled and how would you verify?
drills.a: Qubit 1 is always 1 (deterministic); qubits 0 and 2 are perfectly anti... actually perfectly correlated with qubit1 fixed: they form a Bell-like pair across positions 0 and 2. Verify by computing reduced density matrices over {q0,q2} and checking purity Tr(rho^2) < 1, or run a SWAP test.

drills.q: Why does applying H twice return |0> while flipping a classical fair coin twice does not return heads?
drills.a: H acts on amplitudes: H(H|0>) = H((|0>+|1>)/sqrt2) = (|0>-|1>)/sqrt2 + ... sums to |0> exactly because amplitudes cancel/interfere. A coin mixer acts on probabilities, which are non-negative and cannot cancel.

drills.q: Your numpy simulator outputs probabilities that sum to 1 but disagree with Qiskit counts. First two things to check?
drills.a: 1) Endianness/qubit ordering: kron order vs Qiskit little-endian bitstrings. 2) Basis-change gates before measurement missing. Both are convention bugs, not linear-algebra bugs.

drills.q: Rank these claims for honesty: (A) '200 qubits explore 2^200 states', (B) 'our device prepares Bell pairs at 99% fidelity', (C) 'entanglement boosts our ML model accuracy'.
drills.a: (B) is falsifiable engineering language (state fidelity is measurable). (A) is dimension-counting marketing unless paired with an interference-based algorithm and readable output. (C) needs a baseline showing classical simulation of the same feature map loses - most such papers fail that control.

drills.q: Fraud prevalence 0.1%. Model flags 5% of transactions, catches 80% of fraud. Compute precision.
drills.a: True positives = 0.8 x 0.001 = 0.0008; flagged = 0.05 -> precision = 0.0008/0.05 = 1.6%. Accuracy ~95%+ yet precision is terrible - exactly why accuracy is a vanity metric here.

drills.q: Selection rates: group A 45%, group B 30%. Adverse impact ratio and verdict under the four-fifths guideline?
drills.a: AIR = 0.30/0.45 = 0.667 < 0.80 -> fails the heuristic flag. Not legal proof by itself but triggers investigation: proxy features, threshold placement, segment-level decomposition before any remediation decision.

drills.q: Why can't you satisfy calibration-within-groups AND equal error rates when base rates differ?
drills.a: Mathematical impossibility (Kleinberg et al 2016; Chouldechova 2017): with differing base rates, equalizing FPR/FNR forces different positive-predictive values across groups, breaking calibration - and vice versa. Estimator quality changes magnitudes, never removes the tradeoff. Choose per context + document.

drills.q: A challenger credit GBM improves AUC +0.02 but drops the protected-group AIR from 0.91 to 0.77. Walk the governance path.
drills.a: Fairness guardrails are blocking metrics: no promotion. Quantify profit delta vs regulatory/litigation exposure, investigate driver (threshold vs feature), test mitigations (reweighting, feature removal) with re-audits, then escalate options memo to model governance + fair-lending compliance for a documented decision. Never ship silently.

drills.q: Your bank's credit-scoring system serves EU customers. Which EU AI Act date changes your roadmap and what must exist by then?
drills.a: Aug 2, 2026: Annex III high-risk obligations bite - risk-management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, robustness, conformity assessment. Retrofit takes quarters, so inventory mapping + gap analysis start now; watch simplification proposals for schedule shifts.

drills.q: Generate adverse-action reasons from a GBM: pipeline steps?
drills.a: Per-applicant SHAP attributions -> map top attributions to legal-approved reason-code vocabulary ('insufficient length of credit history') -> rank by magnitude -> fill Reg B letter templates within 30 days.
